Introduction to Elementary Particle Physics — Contents Appendices / Appendix E

Appendix ESolutions to the Exercises

This appendix gives the solutions to all 147 exercises placed in Chapters 1–16 and Appendices A–D of this book.

The solutions are written in the same spirit as the main text: that is, no intermediate steps are skipped. We never dispose of a step with “simplifying gives”; we write out, line by line, what was simplified and how. Every solution carries four parts: a strategy, the computation of every step, a verification, and the physical meaning. The verification is one of the following: dimensional analysis, a limit (the nonrelativistic limit, the massless limit, the low-temperature limit, and so on), or a comparison with a known measured value. All values in the numerical problems have been recomputed.

There is an order in which to use this appendix. First try to solve the problem yourself. If you get stuck, look at the hint attached to the problem in the main text. Only when you still cannot make progress should you open this appendix. If you read the solution first, all that remains is the feeling that “it is clear when you read it,” and your hands do not learn to move. Calculations in particle physics, whether the trace of $\gamma$ matrices or an integral over phase space, are of the kind that does not become yours until you have worked through them once with your own hands.

How to use this appendix
  • Read only the “Strategy.” of a solution and carry out the rest of the calculation yourself—this is the most effective way to use it.
  • When a number does not match, suspect the units first. This book uses natural units $\hbar=c=1$, so when restoring SI units, use $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$ and $(\hbar c)^2=0.3894\ \mathrm{GeV^2\,mbarn}$ (Appendix B, Section B.3).
  • Do not skip the “Verification.” part. Learning how to verify a result is the most practical skill this book can teach.
  • In the “Meaning.” part we have written the connection to materials science wherever possible. This, more than the answer of the calculation itself, is the subject of this book.
Caution: In this appendix we have not assigned equation numbers (since 20 chapters’ worth of material is put on a single page, the numbers would collide). When we refer to an equation of the main text, we do so in words, as in “the Dirac equation of Chapter 9.”

E.1 Solutions for Chapter 1: Particle Physics for Materials Scientists — Why Study It?

Exercise 1.1: Converting energy scales

Problem (restated)

Using the conversion table in Table 1.11 ($1\ \mathrm{THz}=4.136\ \mathrm{meV}=33.36\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}=47.99\ \mathrm{K}$, $1\ \mathrm{eV}=1.1605\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{K}$), find the following.

(1) The $\Gamma$-point optical phonon of Si is $15.6\ \mathrm{THz}$. Express it in meV, cm$^{-1}$, and K. How does it compare with the room-temperature $k_BT$?

(2) Express the superconducting gap of Nb, $2\Delta=3.05\ \mathrm{meV}$, in THz and K. Also, using $T_c=9.25\ \mathrm{K}$, find $2\Delta/(k_BT_c)$ and compare it with the BCS weak-coupling value 3.53.

(3) What temperature in K corresponds to the neutron of the DT reaction with $14.05\ \mathrm{MeV}$? Also, from the momentum $p_nc=163.0\ \mathrm{MeV}$, find the de Broglie wavelength $\lambda=hc/(p_nc)$ in fm and compare it with the radius of an iron nucleus (about 4.6 fm).

Solution

Strategy. As stated in Section 1.7.3 of this chapter, THz, meV, cm$^{-1}$, and K are all the same single physical quantity (energy) written in different units, and they can be identified only when we set $\hbar=k_B=1$. This problem is therefore not a “unit conversion” but “practice with natural units.” The only tools we need are the conversion factors of Table 1.11 and $hc=2\pi\hbar c=1239.84\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$.

(1) It suffices to multiply the given conversion $1\ \mathrm{THz}=4.136\ \mathrm{meV}=33.36\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}=47.99\ \mathrm{K}$ by $15.6$.

$$ \hbar\omega = 15.6\times4.136\ \mathrm{meV} = 64.52\ \mathrm{meV} $$ $$ \tilde\nu = 15.6\times33.36\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}} = 520.4\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}, \qquad \Theta = 15.6\times47.99\ \mathrm{K} = 748.6\ \mathrm{K} $$

For the comparison with room temperature, we use $k_BT\big|_{300\,\mathrm{K}}=25.85\ \mathrm{meV}$ from Section 1.7.3 of this chapter.

$$ \frac{\hbar\omega}{k_BT} = \frac{64.52}{25.85} = 2.496 \simeq 2.5 $$

That is, the optical phonon of Si is about 2.5 times the thermal energy at room temperature. Putting this ratio into the Bose distribution, the mean occupation number at room temperature is

$$ n_B = \frac{1}{\ee^{\hbar\omega/k_BT}-1} = \frac{1}{\ee^{2.496}-1} = \frac{1}{12.13-1} = 0.0898 $$

In other words, even at room temperature, less than one tenth of the optical phonons are excited. The small intensity ratio of the anti-Stokes line to the Stokes line in Raman scattering, $\ee^{-\hbar\omega/k_BT}=\ee^{-2.496}=0.082$, is a direct reflection of this fact.

(2) We use $1\ \mathrm{THz}=4.136\ \mathrm{meV}$ for division, and $1\ \mathrm{eV}=1.1605\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{K}$, that is, $1\ \mathrm{meV}=11.605\ \mathrm{K}$, for multiplication.

$$ 2\Delta = \frac{3.05}{4.136}\ \mathrm{THz} = 0.7374\ \mathrm{THz}, \qquad 2\Delta = 3.05\times11.605\ \mathrm{K} = 35.40\ \mathrm{K} $$

(Going through THz also gives $0.7374\times47.99=35.39\ \mathrm{K}$, in agreement.) Next we form the dimensionless ratio. Since $k_B=8.617\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{meV/K}$,

$$ \frac{2\Delta}{k_BT_c} = \frac{3.05\ \mathrm{meV}}{8.617\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{meV/K}\times9.25\ \mathrm{K}} = \frac{3.05}{0.7971} = 3.83 $$

This is larger than the BCS weak-coupling value $3.53$ by about 8%. It means that Nb is a strong-coupling superconductor, that is, the electron–phonon coupling constant $\lambda_{\text{ep}}$ is close to 1 and the corrections of Eliashberg theory are significant. Note also that dividing $35.4\ \mathrm{K}$, the temperature equivalent of $2\Delta$, by $T_c=9.25\ \mathrm{K}$ gives the same $3.83$. It is precisely because energy and temperature can be identified that these two calculations agree.

(3) For the conversion to temperature we simply use $1\ \mathrm{eV}=1.1605\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{K}$.

$$ \Theta_n = 14.05\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV}\times1.1605\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{K/eV} = 1.63\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{K} $$

For the wavelength we use $hc=1239.84\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$ (which is $2\pi$ times $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$).

$$ \lambda = \frac{hc}{p_nc} = \frac{1239.84\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{163.0\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 7.61\ \mathrm{fm} $$

The radius of an iron nucleus is $R=1.2\,A^{1/3}\ \mathrm{fm}=1.2\times56^{1/3}=4.59\ \mathrm{fm}$, or $9.2\ \mathrm{fm}$ as a diameter. That is, the wavelength of the neutron is about the same as the diameter of the iron nucleus, and is not short enough to resolve the internal structure of the nucleus. Therefore the 14 MeV neutron sees the nucleus as “a single lump,” and in elastic scattering it kicks the whole nucleus away as one body. This is why, in Section 1.5.2 of this chapter, we may compute the energy of the primary knock-on atom (PKA) as a rigid-sphere two-body collision.

Verification. We check the internal consistency of the conversion factors. Using “$1\ \mathrm{eV}=241.80\ \mathrm{THz}$” of Table 1.11, we get $4.136\ \mathrm{meV}\times241.80\ \mathrm{THz/eV}=4.136\times10^{-3}\times241.80=1.0001\ \mathrm{THz}$, so $1\ \mathrm{THz}=4.136\ \mathrm{meV}$ is indeed the reciprocal relation. Also, the $hc=1239.84\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$ used in (3) is the same number as “$1\ \mathrm{eV}\leftrightarrow1239.84\ \mathrm{nm}$” in Table 1.11. This is because $1\ \mathrm{MeV}=10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $1\ \mathrm{fm}=10^{-6}\ \mathrm{nm}$, so the $10^{6}$ and the $10^{-6}$ cancel; it is exactly the same circumstance as the one we described for $\hbar c$ in Section 1.3.4 of this chapter.

Meaning. These three subproblems span ten orders of magnitude, from $10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}$ (phonons) to $10^{7}\ \mathrm{eV}$ (fusion neutrons), yet the only tools we used were one row of Table 1.11 and $hc$. That materials scientists write phonons in THz, in cm$^{-1}$, or in meV means that they are already using $\hbar=k_B=1$; particle physics merely adds $c=1$ to this. And, as in (1) “$\hbar\omega/k_BT=2.5$” and (2) “$2\Delta/k_BT_c=3.83$,” what carries the content of the physics is only the dimensionless ratio. The freedom to choose units has no effect on the physics.

Exercise 1.2: Dielectric breakdown of the vacuum and of a semiconductor

Problem (restated)

Consider the unified form $F_{\mathrm{c}}=E_{\text{gap}}^{2}/(4e\hbar v)$ (the unified critical-field formula of Chapter 1 of this book).

(1) Compute $F_{\mathrm{c}}$ for the vacuum ($E_{\text{gap}}=2m_ec^2=1.022\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $v=c$) and confirm that it is $1.32\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{V/m}$.

(2) $F_{\mathrm{c}}$ is proportional to $E_{\text{gap}}^2$ and inversely proportional to $v$. Find the ratio of the value for Si ($E_g=1.12$ eV, $v=1.38\times10^{6}$ m/s) to the value for the vacuum.

(3) When a field $F=1\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{V/m}$ is applied to a Si pn junction, find the value of the Zener-tunneling exponential factor $\exp(-\pi F_{\mathrm{c}}/F)$. Also, what is the exponential factor when the same field is applied to the vacuum?

Solution

Strategy. First we reduce $F_{\mathrm{c}}=E_{\text{gap}}^2/(4e\hbar v)$ to a numerical formula that can be evaluated with $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$ alone. Then (1) and (2) are handled by substitution into the same formula, and we no longer need to line up the SI physical constants each time. This is the practical benefit of natural units.

Reduction to a numerical formula. If we measure the gap by the number $E_{\text{gap}}[\mathrm{eV}]$ in units of eV, we can write $E_{\text{gap}}=e\times E_{\text{gap}}[\mathrm{eV}]$ ($e$ is the elementary charge, and the second factor on the right is the number in units of volts). Substituting this,

$$ F_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{\left(e\,E_{\text{gap}}[\mathrm{eV}]\right)^2}{4e\hbar v} = \frac{E_{\text{gap}}[\mathrm{eV}]^2}{4\,(\hbar c/e)}\cdot\frac{c}{v} $$

Here $\hbar c/e = 197.327\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}/e = 1.97327\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{V\,m}$ (we read $\hbar c$ in eV·nm and used $1\ \mathrm{nm}=10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}$). Therefore

$$ F_{\mathrm{c}}\,[\mathrm{V/m}] = \frac{\left(E_{\text{gap}}[\mathrm{eV}]\right)^{2}}{4\times1.97327\times10^{-7}}\times\frac{c}{v} = \frac{\left(E_{\text{gap}}[\mathrm{eV}]\right)^{2}}{7.89308\times10^{-7}}\times\frac{c}{v} $$

(1) For the vacuum, $E_{\text{gap}}=1.022\ \mathrm{MeV}=1.022\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $v=c$, so $c/v=1$.

$$ \left(1.022\times10^{6}\right)^2 = 1.04448\times10^{12} $$ $$ F_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{1.04448\times10^{12}}{7.89308\times10^{-7}} = 1.3233\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{V/m} $$

This agrees with the $1.32\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{V/m}$ of the main text. Lining up the SI constants directly gives the same result. We have $E_{\text{gap}}=1.022\times10^{6}\times1.602\times10^{-19}=1.6374\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{J}$, and the denominator is

$$ 4e\hbar c = 4\times1.602\times10^{-19}\times1.055\times10^{-34}\times2.998\times10^{8} = 2.0268\times10^{-44}\ \mathrm{C\,J\,m} $$ $$ F_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{\left(1.6374\times10^{-13}\right)^2}{2.0268\times10^{-44}} = \frac{2.6811\times10^{-26}}{2.0268\times10^{-44}} = 1.323\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{V/m} $$

which agrees with the value obtained in natural units to three digits. It is also worth confirming that in this case the unified form returns to Schwinger’s critical field of Section 1.2.3 of this chapter. Substituting $E_{\text{gap}}=2m_ec^2$ and $v=c$ gives

$$ F_{\mathrm{c}} = \frac{\left(2m_ec^2\right)^2}{4e\hbar c} = \frac{m_e^2c^3}{e\hbar} $$

which reproduces exactly the $F_{\mathrm{c}}=m_e^2c^3/(e\hbar)$ of this chapter. The “4” in the denominator of the unified form was a coefficient placed there to make up for the fact that the gap is $2m_ec^2$, that is, twice the mass. In a semiconductor $E_{\text{gap}}=E_g$ is the gap itself, so the same “4” appears as a numerical coefficient on the side of the Kane model.

(2) For Si, $E_g=1.12\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $v=1.38\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s}$. First, the velocity ratio is

$$ \frac{c}{v} = \frac{2.998\times10^{8}}{1.38\times10^{6}} = 217.2 $$

(The “$c/218$” written in Table 1.2 of the main text is the rounded value of this.) Hence

$$ F_{\mathrm{c}}^{\mathrm{Si}} = \frac{(1.12)^2}{7.89308\times10^{-7}}\times217.2 = \frac{1.2544}{7.89308\times10^{-7}}\times217.2 = 1.5893\times10^{6}\times217.2 = 3.45\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{V/m} $$

This agrees with the $3.5\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{V/m}$ of Table 1.2. The ratio is

$$ \frac{F_{\mathrm{c}}^{\text{vacuum}}}{F_{\mathrm{c}}^{\mathrm{Si}}} = \frac{1.3233\times10^{18}}{3.45\times10^{8}} = 3.83\times10^{9} $$

that is, about ten orders of magnitude. We check by breaking this down into its parts. The square of the gap ratio is

$$ \left(\frac{1.022\times10^{6}}{1.12}\right)^{2} = \left(9.125\times10^{5}\right)^2 = 8.33\times10^{11} $$

and dividing this by the velocity ratio $217.2$ gives $8.33\times10^{11}/217.2 = 3.83\times10^{9}$, which indeed agrees. Of the ten orders of magnitude of difference, twelve come from the gap, and a little over two orders are the inverse correction from the velocity.

(3) Applying $F=1\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{V/m}$ to Si, we get

$$ \frac{F_{\mathrm{c}}^{\mathrm{Si}}}{F} = \frac{3.45\times10^{8}}{1\times10^{8}} = 3.45, \qquad \pi\frac{F_{\mathrm{c}}}{F} = \pi\times3.45 = 10.84 $$ $$ \exp\!\left(-\pi\frac{F_{\mathrm{c}}}{F}\right) = \ee^{-10.84} = 1.95\times10^{-5} $$

(The $\ee^{-10.9}=1.9\times10^{-5}$ in the hint of the main text is the value with $F_{\mathrm{c}}/F$ rounded to $3.46$, and it is the same number. That a slight difference in the exponent moves the result by several percent is also a manifestation of the high sensitivity of the exponential function.) Although $10^{-5}$ is a small number, the prefactor $(eF)^2/(4\pi^3\hbar^2 c)$ of Section 1.2.3 of this chapter is huge, so in practice the current is large enough to be measured. On the other hand, when the same field is applied to the vacuum,

$$ \frac{F_{\mathrm{c}}^{\text{vacuum}}}{F} = \frac{1.3233\times10^{18}}{1\times10^{8}} = 1.32\times10^{10}, \qquad \pi\frac{F_{\mathrm{c}}}{F} = 4.16\times10^{10} $$ $$ \exp\!\left(-4.16\times10^{10}\right) = 10^{-1.81\times10^{10}} $$

The exponent is $-4\times10^{10}$. This means that not a single pair production would occur even if the experiment were continued for the age of the universe, so it is effectively zero.

Verification. We check the dimensions. The dimension of $E_{\text{gap}}^2/(4e\hbar v)$ is $\mathrm{J^2}/(\mathrm{C\cdot J\,s\cdot m\,s^{-1}}) = \mathrm{J}/(\mathrm{C\,m}) = \mathrm{V/m}$, which is indeed an electric field. We also look at the limits. For $E_{\text{gap}}\to0$ (a semimetal with a closed gap, or a Weyl semimetal), $F_{\mathrm{c}}\to0$, and pair production occurs for however weak an electric field. This is consistent with the known fact that linear response is violated in a gapless system. Also for $v\to\infty$ we have $F_{\mathrm{c}}\to0$, which fits the intuition that the steeper the band (the lighter the effective mass), the easier the tunneling.

Meaning. The result of (2) is the most basic guideline for choosing power-device materials. Since $F_{\mathrm{c}}\propto E_g^2$, GaN ($E_g=3.4\ \mathrm{eV}$) should have a breakdown voltage $(3.4/1.12)^2=9.2$ times that of Si, and the measured breakdown fields, $3.3\times10^{8}$ versus $3\times10^{7}$, differ by a factor of about 11, in good agreement. Since a drift layer of the same thickness can support a higher voltage, the on-resistance drops by orders of magnitude. The reason wide-gap semiconductors are at the center of energy-saving technology comes out of the formula that Schwinger wrote for the vacuum in 1951. Note that in an actual pn junction, avalanche multiplication sets in first, at a field one order of magnitude lower than the $F_{\mathrm{c}}$ of Table 1.2, so pure Zener tunneling plays the leading role only in heavily doped junctions with a thin depletion layer.

Exercise 1.3: The exciton is a rescaled positronium

Problem (restated)

Use the exciton formulas of Chapter 1 of this book, $E_X=-\mathrm{Ry}\,(m_r/m_0)/\varepsilon_r^2$ and $a_X=a_0\varepsilon_r/(m_r/m_0)$. Take $\mathrm{Ry}=13.606\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $a_0=0.0529\ \mathrm{nm}$.

(1) Find the exciton binding energy and Bohr radius of GaAs ($m_r=0.059\,m_0$, $\varepsilon_r=12.9$).

(2) Compare the result of (1) with the room-temperature value $k_BT=25.9\ \mathrm{meV}$, and discuss whether excitons in GaAs can exist stably at room temperature. On the other hand, the experimental exciton binding energy of ZnO is $60\ \mathrm{meV}$. Explain why ZnO and GaN are candidates for room-temperature light-emitting devices.

(3) From the same formula, find the binding energy and radius of positronium ($m_r=m_e/2$, $\varepsilon_r=1$), and compare them with those of the GaAs exciton. By what factors do they differ, and from which physical quantities does the ratio arise?

Solution

Strategy. As we saw in Section 1.2.4 of this chapter, the exciton and positronium are the same two-body Coulomb bound-state problem, and the differences amount to just two points: (i) the mass changes from $m_e/2\to m_r$, and (ii) the Coulomb interaction is screened by $\varepsilon_r$. Therefore the answer follows from a mechanical rescaling of the Rydberg formula.

(1) Substitute $m_r/m_0=0.059$ and $\varepsilon_r=12.9$ for GaAs. First, $\varepsilon_r^2 = 12.9^2 = 166.41$, so

$$ E_X = -13.606\ \mathrm{eV}\times\frac{0.059}{166.41} = -13.606\times3.5455\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV} = -4.824\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV} = -4.82\ \mathrm{meV} $$

The radius is

$$ a_X = 0.0529\ \mathrm{nm}\times\frac{12.9}{0.059} = 0.0529\times218.6\ \mathrm{nm} = 11.57\ \mathrm{nm} $$

The measured values are $4.2\ \mathrm{meV}$ and $11.6\ \mathrm{nm}$, so the radius agrees almost perfectly and the energy agrees to within 15%. The discrepancy in the energy comes from the choice between the static and the high-frequency permittivity for $\varepsilon_r$, and from polaron effects; it does not affect the order-of-magnitude argument. Note also that $a_X=11.6\ \mathrm{nm}$ is about 20 times the lattice constant of GaAs, $0.565\ \mathrm{nm}$, which means that the exciton extends over several tens of lattice sites. This is why the effective-mass approximation (the Wannier exciton picture) is justified.

(2) At room temperature $k_BT=25.9\ \mathrm{meV}$, so

$$ \frac{\abs{E_X}}{k_BT} = \frac{4.82}{25.9} = 0.186 $$

That is, the binding energy is less than 20% of the thermal energy. Whether a bound state is destroyed by thermal excitation is determined by this ratio, and when $\abs{E_X}\ll k_BT$ most of the equilibrium population consists of free electron-hole pairs. Therefore excitons in GaAs are thermally dissociated at room temperature, and the room-temperature luminescence is due to the recombination of free carriers. To observe exciton effects one must cool to liquid-nitrogen temperature or below ($k_BT=6.7\ \mathrm{meV}$ or less).

In contrast, for ZnO with $\abs{E_X}=60\ \mathrm{meV}$,

$$ \frac{\abs{E_X}}{k_BT} = \frac{60}{25.9} = 2.32 > 1 $$

so the excitons survive even at room temperature. Since an exciton is a state in which the electron and hole are already bound, the oscillator strength of its emission is large, and luminescence and laser oscillation with a low threshold can be expected. GaN is a candidate for the same reason. Why $\abs{E_X}$ is large in ZnO and GaN is answered by the formula $E_X\propto m_r/\varepsilon_r^2$ itself. In wide-gap materials, (i) from $\bm{k}\cdot\bm{p}$ perturbation theory $m_r$ becomes heavier, nearly in proportion to $E_g$, and (ii) $\varepsilon_r$ is small because the electronic polarization is small. Both the numerator and the denominator work in our favor, so $\abs{E_X}$ increases rapidly with $E_g$. Being wide-gap is itself a necessary condition for room-temperature exciton luminescence.

(3) For positronium, set $m_r/m_0=0.5$ and $\varepsilon_r=1$ in the same formulas.

$$ E_{\mathrm{Ps}} = -13.606\times\frac{0.5}{1^2}\ \mathrm{eV} = -6.803\ \mathrm{eV}, \qquad a_{\mathrm{Ps}} = 0.0529\times\frac{1}{0.5}\ \mathrm{nm} = 0.1058\ \mathrm{nm} $$

These agree with the values in Section 1.2.4 of the main text. The ratios to the GaAs exciton are

$$ \frac{\abs{E_{\mathrm{Ps}}}}{\abs{E_X}} = \frac{6.803}{4.824\times10^{-3}} = 1.41\times10^{3}, \qquad \frac{a_X}{a_{\mathrm{Ps}}} = \frac{11.57}{0.1058} = 109 $$

That is, the energies differ by a factor of about 1400 and the radii by a factor of about 110. The origin of these ratios can be read directly from the formulas. Writing the mass ratio as $R_m\equiv(m_r/m_0)_{\mathrm{Ps}}/(m_r/m_0)_{\mathrm{GaAs}}=0.5/0.059=8.47$, we have

$$ \frac{\abs{E_{\mathrm{Ps}}}}{\abs{E_X}} = R_m\,\varepsilon_r^2 = 8.47\times166.41 = 1410, \qquad \frac{a_X}{a_{\mathrm{Ps}}} = R_m\,\varepsilon_r = 8.47\times12.9 = 109.3 $$

so the numbers are reproduced exactly. The energy ratio originates in the product of “the effective mass being 8.5 times lighter” and “screening acting as a square, giving a factor of 166”; the radius ratio originates in the product of “the lightness, a factor of 8.5” and “the screening, a factor of 12.9.”

Verification. Taking the quotient of the two ratios gives

$$ \frac{\abs{E_{\mathrm{Ps}}}/\abs{E_X}}{a_X/a_{\mathrm{Ps}}} = \frac{1410}{109.3} = 12.9 = \varepsilon_r $$

This is no accident. For a Coulomb bound state, $\abs{E}\sim e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r a)$ always holds (the virial theorem), so $\abs{E}a$ depends only on $1/\varepsilon_r$, and the mass dependence drops out completely. Indeed $\abs{E_{\mathrm{Ps}}}a_{\mathrm{Ps}}=6.803\times0.1058=0.7198$ and $\abs{E_X}a_X=4.824\times10^{-3}\times11.57=0.05580$, and the ratio is exactly $12.90$. This is strong evidence that the part that depends on the mass and the part that depends on the screening have been correctly separated.

Meaning. The theory of bound states treated in Chapter 7 (positronium, charmonium) can be read directly as a theory of excitons simply by rewriting $m$ and $e^4$ inside $\mathrm{Ry}$. Conversely, the terms “exciton Bohr radius” and “exciton Rydberg,” which materials scientists use every day, are exactly the language of bound states of elementary particles. That quantum confinement begins to take effect at dimensions of about $a_X$ (around 12 nm for GaAs), and that positronium can be used to characterize the pores of low-$k$ materials (Section 1.6.2 of this chapter), are both applications of this identity.

Exercise 1.4: Finding the photon mass from the London penetration depth

Problem (restated)

Use $\lambda_L=\sqrt{m_e/(\mu_0n_se^2)}$, $m_\gamma c^2=\hbar c/\lambda_L$, and $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$.

(1) For a superconducting electron density $n_s=1.0\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, find $\lambda_L$ in nm.

(2) Find the photon mass in eV corresponding to the $\lambda_L$ of (1), and compare it with the band gap of Si, $1.12\ \mathrm{eV}$.

(3) For the $W$ boson ($m_Wc^2=80.377\ \mathrm{GeV}$), find the corresponding “penetration depth” $\lambda_W=\hbar c/(m_Wc^2)$ in fm, and compare it with the proton radius $0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$. Explain why the weak interaction is “weak” in terms of the range, not the coupling constant.

(4) From the Al value $\lambda_L=16\ \mathrm{nm}$, work backward to find the superconducting electron density $n_s$, and compare it with the valence electron density of Al, $1.81\times10^{29}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$.

Solution

Strategy. As derived in Section 1.3.4 of this chapter, $\nabla^2\bm{A}=\bm{A}/\lambda_L^2$, obtained by combining the London equation with Ampère’s law, is literally the same equation as the static form of the Proca equation, and comparing coefficients gives $m_\gamma c^2=\hbar c/\lambda_L$. Therefore “measuring the penetration depth” and “measuring the photon mass” are the same task. All the calculation requires is $m_e,\mu_0,e$ in SI units and the single quantity $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$.

(1) The constants are $m_e=9.109\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$, $\mu_0=1.2566\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{N/A^2}$, and $e=1.6022\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$. We compute the denominator first.

$$ e^2 = \left(1.6022\times10^{-19}\right)^2 = 2.5670\times10^{-38} $$ $$ \mu_0 n_s e^2 = 1.2566\times10^{-6}\times1.0\times10^{28}\times2.5670\times10^{-38} = 3.2259\times10^{-16} $$

Therefore

$$ \lambda_L^2 = \frac{m_e}{\mu_0n_se^2} = \frac{9.109\times10^{-31}}{3.2259\times10^{-16}} = 2.8238\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m^2} $$ $$ \lambda_L = \sqrt{2.8238\times10^{-15}} = 5.314\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m} = 53.1\ \mathrm{nm} $$

Let us check that the order of magnitude is reasonable. Since $\lambda_L\propto n_s^{-1/2}$, a tenfold increase in density reduces the penetration depth only by a factor of $\sqrt{10}=3.16$. Thanks to this insensitivity, $\lambda_L$ falls within the very narrow range of a few tens of nm however one chooses the metallic element. Indeed, in Table 1.3 Al has $16\ \mathrm{nm}$ and Pb and Nb both have $39\ \mathrm{nm}$, and the $53\ \mathrm{nm}$ obtained here lies on the extension of these values. Conversely, to change $\lambda_L$ by one order of magnitude, $n_s$ must change by two orders. That YBCO in Table 1.3 has $\lambda_L=150\ \mathrm{nm}$, nearly an order of magnitude longer than the $16\ \mathrm{nm}$ of Al, means a factor of $(150/16)^2=88$, that is, $n_s/m^*$ smaller by nearly two orders of magnitude; this is the quantitative content of the statement that cuprates are “superconductors with a low carrier density.”

(2) We use “$m_\gamma c^2 = 197.327/\lambda_L[\mathrm{nm}]$ eV” of Section 1.3.4 of this chapter as it stands.

$$ m_\gamma c^2 = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{53.14\ \mathrm{nm}} = 3.71\ \mathrm{eV} $$

This is 3.3 times the band gap of Si, $1.12\ \mathrm{eV}$. In other words, inside this superconductor the photon travels around carrying a “mass” comparable to the band gap of a semiconductor. The photon mass, which is exactly zero in vacuum, takes a finite value of the eV scale inside the condensate. This is the most tabletop manifestation of the Anderson–Higgs mechanism. (The $3.72\ \mathrm{eV}$ in the hint in the main text is the value obtained by dividing after rounding $\lambda_L$ to $53.1\ \mathrm{nm}$; using $53.14\ \mathrm{nm}$ gives $3.71\ \mathrm{eV}$. It is merely a difference in how the third significant figure is rounded.)

(3) Reading $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$ and dividing (the numerical value is the same as for $\mathrm{eV\,nm}$): since $m_Wc^2=80.377\ \mathrm{GeV}=80377\ \mathrm{MeV}$,

$$ \lambda_W = \frac{\hbar c}{m_Wc^2} = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{80377\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 2.455\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm} = 2.46\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{m} $$

The ratio to the proton radius is

$$ \frac{0.84\ \mathrm{fm}}{2.455\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}} = 342 $$

That is, the range of the $W$ is only 1/342 of the size of the proton. This is why the weak interaction is “weak.” A Yukawa-type potential has the form $\ee^{-r/\lambda_W}/r$, so even at $r\simeq1\ \mathrm{fm}$, where nucleons are in contact, the exponential factor is

$$ \ee^{-r/\lambda_W} = \ee^{-1/(2.455\times10^{-3})} = \ee^{-407} $$

and the interaction does not reach at all. In terms of the size of the coupling constant, the $g$ of the weak interaction is in fact larger than the $e$ of electromagnetism (Chapter 12). The reason it nevertheless looks weak at low energies is that the propagator becomes $1/(q^2-m_W^2)\simeq-1/m_W^2$, so that the effective coupling is $g^2/m_W^2$, a quantity divided by the mass squared. This is word for word the same reasoning as the fact that, in the Meissner effect, a magnetic field cannot penetrate beyond $\lambda_L$. A superconductor is a model that shows us “finite range” on a tabletop.

(4) Solving $\lambda_L=\sqrt{m_e/(\mu_0n_se^2)}$ for $n_s$ gives $n_s=m_e/(\mu_0e^2\lambda_L^2)$. Since $\lambda_L=16\ \mathrm{nm}=1.6\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m}$,

$$ \lambda_L^2 = 2.56\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{m^2}, \qquad \mu_0e^2 = 1.2566\times10^{-6}\times2.5670\times10^{-38} = 3.2259\times10^{-44} $$ $$ n_s = \frac{9.109\times10^{-31}}{3.2259\times10^{-44}\times2.56\times10^{-16}} = \frac{9.109\times10^{-31}}{8.258\times10^{-60}} = 1.10\times10^{29}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}} $$

The ratio to the valence electron density is $1.10\times10^{29}/1.81\times10^{29}=0.61$, so this works out to roughly 60% of the valence electrons being in the superfluid component (this refers to the limit $T\to0$). However, this “60%” must not be taken at face value. London’s formula uses the bare $m_e$, which in reality should be replaced by the effective mass $m^*$, and Al is an extreme type-I superconductor whose coherence length $\xi_0\simeq1600\ \mathrm{nm}$ is far longer than $\lambda_L$, so because of Pippard’s nonlocal effect the effective penetration depth is larger than the London value. The correct statement is that “only the combination $n_s/m^*$ is being measured,” which is also the reason that the Uemura plot of Section 1.6.1 of this chapter plots $n_s/m^*$.

Verification. Rewriting $\lambda_L$ in terms of the plasma frequency provides a powerful check. Using $\omega_p^2=n_se^2/(\varepsilon_0m_e)$ and $\varepsilon_0\mu_0=1/c^2$,

$$ \lambda_L^2 = \frac{m_e}{\mu_0n_se^2} = \frac{m_e\varepsilon_0c^2}{n_se^2} = \frac{c^2}{\omega_p^2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \lambda_L = \frac{c}{\omega_p}, \qquad m_\gamma c^2 = \frac{\hbar c}{\lambda_L} = \hbar\omega_p $$

That is, the “photon mass” is exactly the plasmon energy $\hbar\omega_p$. Checking with $n_s=1.0\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ of (1), we get $\omega_p=5.641\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $\hbar\omega_p=6.582\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}\times5.641\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}=3.71\ \mathrm{eV}$, in complete agreement with (2). Furthermore, inserting the valence electron density of Al, $1.81\times10^{29}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, gives $\hbar\omega_p=15.8\ \mathrm{eV}$, which agrees with the “plasmon of Al, 15.8 eV” that Table 1.3 lists as the point of comparison. Table 1.3 lists the $m_\gamma c^2=12.3\ \mathrm{eV}$ of Al side by side with the plasmon $15.8\ \mathrm{eV}$ because the two differ merely by $n_s$ versus $n_{\text{val}}$ in the same formula.

Meaning. The statement in particle-physics language that “the photon has a mass,” the statement in superconductivity language that “a magnetic field penetrates only $\lambda_L$,” and the statement in metal-optics language that “light below the plasma frequency is reflected” are all paraphrases of one and the same formula, $m_\gamma c^2=\hbar c/\lambda_L=\hbar\omega_p$. The $\hbar\omega_p$ that a materials scientist reads off a reflection spectrum is exactly “the mass the photon has acquired inside that material,” and the $W$ boson mass that a particle physicist writes as $80.377\ \mathrm{GeV}$ is exactly “the penetration depth of the electroweak vacuum, $2.46\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}$.” The gap between them is $80.377\ \mathrm{GeV}/3.71\ \mathrm{eV}=2.2\times10^{10}$, and measured in length, $53.1\ \mathrm{nm}/2.46\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{m}=2.2\times10^{10}$ as well, so both span the same ten orders of magnitude (as is natural, since energy and length are reciprocal to each other). Two numbers ten orders of magnitude apart sit at the two ends of the same formula.

Exercise 1.5: The charge of a Bogoliubov quasiparticle

Problem (restated)

Use the BdG Hamiltonian and the Bogoliubov transformation of Chapter 1 of this book.

(1) For $H_{\text{BdG}}=\xi_\kk\tau_3-\Delta\tau_1$, show that $H_{\text{BdG}}^2=(\xi_\kk^2+\Delta^2)\mathbf{1}$, and conclude that the eigenvalues are $E_\kk=\pm\sqrt{\xi_\kk^2+\Delta^2}$.

(2) Verify $u_\kk^2+v_\kk^2=1$ and $2u_\kk v_\kk=\Delta/E_\kk$ from the definition of the Bogoliubov transformation.

(3) The expectation value of the charge carried by the quasiparticle $\gamma_{\kk\uparrow}=u_\kk c_{\kk\uparrow}-v_\kk c^\dagger_{-\kk\downarrow}$ is $q=-e(u_\kk^2-v_\kk^2)$. Express this in terms of $\xi_\kk$ and $E_\kk$, and show that it vanishes at $\xi_\kk=0$.

(4) For a quasiparticle in Nb ($\Delta=1.5\ \mathrm{meV}$) with $\xi_\kk=1.5\ \mathrm{meV}$, find numerically $u_\kk^2$, $v_\kk^2$, and the expectation value of the charge (in units of $-e$).

Solution

Strategy. As we saw in Section 1.4 of this chapter, the BdG Hamiltonian is isomorphic to the Dirac Hamiltonian in one respect alone: it is “a linear combination of two anticommuting matrices.” The properties we need come down to just three facts about the algebra of the Pauli matrices: $\tau_i^2=\mathbf{1}$, $\{\tau_1,\tau_3\}=0$, and $\Tr\tau_i=0$.

(1) We simply expand.

$$ H_{\text{BdG}}^2 = \left(\xi_\kk\tau_3-\Delta\tau_1\right)\left(\xi_\kk\tau_3-\Delta\tau_1\right) = \xi_\kk^2\tau_3^2 - \xi_\kk\Delta\left(\tau_3\tau_1+\tau_1\tau_3\right) + \Delta^2\tau_1^2 $$

Here $\tau_1^2=\tau_3^2=\mathbf{1}$, and since $\tau_1$ and $\tau_3$ anticommute, $\tau_3\tau_1+\tau_1\tau_3=\{\tau_1,\tau_3\}=0$. The cross term cancels cleanly, and we obtain

$$ H_{\text{BdG}}^2 = \left(\xi_\kk^2+\Delta^2\right)\mathbf{1} $$

Next we draw the conclusion about the eigenvalues. Let $\lambda$ be an eigenvalue of $H_{\text{BdG}}$. Acting with $H_{\text{BdG}}^2$ on the eigenvector gives $\lambda^2=\xi_\kk^2+\Delta^2$, and hence $\lambda=\pm\sqrt{\xi_\kk^2+\Delta^2}$. That both signs actually occur follows from the vanishing of the trace. Since $\Tr\tau_1=\Tr\tau_3=0$, we have $\Tr H_{\text{BdG}}=0$; that is, the sum of the two eigenvalues must be zero. Two eigenvalues that are both $+\sqrt{\cdots}$ or both $-\sqrt{\cdots}$ cannot satisfy this, so the eigenvalues are one $+E_\kk$ and one $-E_\kk$. Therefore

$$ E_\kk = \pm\sqrt{\xi_\kk^2+\Delta^2} $$

This has exactly the same form as the Dirac result $E=\pm\sqrt{p^2c^2+m^2c^4}$, with $\Delta$ playing the role of $mc^2$. Writing out the matrix explicitly and solving the eigenvalue equation $\det(H_{\text{BdG}}-\lambda\mathbf{1})=\lambda^2-\xi_\kk^2-\Delta^2=0$ gives the same result, but the argument above has the merit of hardly using the fact that the matrices are $2\times2$. Any pair of anticommuting matrices, of any number of components, leads to the same conclusion, so the argument carries over as it stands to the four-component Dirac equation.

(2) The definitions are

$$ u_\kk^2 = \frac12\left(1+\frac{\xi_\kk}{E_\kk}\right), \qquad v_\kk^2 = \frac12\left(1-\frac{\xi_\kk}{E_\kk}\right) $$

Taking the sum, the terms in $\xi_\kk/E_\kk$ cancel, and

$$ u_\kk^2+v_\kk^2 = \frac12\left(1+\frac{\xi_\kk}{E_\kk}\right)+\frac12\left(1-\frac{\xi_\kk}{E_\kk}\right) = 1 $$

This is also the condition for $\gamma_{\kk\uparrow}$ to satisfy the proper anticommutation relation $\{\gamma,\gamma^\dagger\}=1$. Next we take the product.

$$ u_\kk^2v_\kk^2 = \frac14\left(1+\frac{\xi_\kk}{E_\kk}\right)\left(1-\frac{\xi_\kk}{E_\kk}\right) = \frac14\left(1-\frac{\xi_\kk^2}{E_\kk^2}\right) = \frac14\cdot\frac{E_\kk^2-\xi_\kk^2}{E_\kk^2} $$

Now using the result of (1), $E_\kk^2=\xi_\kk^2+\Delta^2$, that is, $E_\kk^2-\xi_\kk^2=\Delta^2$, we obtain

$$ u_\kk^2v_\kk^2 = \frac{\Delta^2}{4E_\kk^2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad u_\kk v_\kk = \frac{\Delta}{2E_\kk} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 2u_\kk v_\kk = \frac{\Delta}{E_\kk} $$

(We took $\Delta>0$ and chose the signs so that $u_\kk,v_\kk\ge0$.) This quantity $2u_\kk v_\kk$ is called the BCS coherence factor; it governs the Hebel–Slichter peak in the nuclear magnetic relaxation rate of a superconductor and the behavior of ultrasonic absorption.

(3) Taking the difference of the definitions of $u_\kk^2$ and $v_\kk^2$, this time the terms equal to 1 cancel.

$$ u_\kk^2-v_\kk^2 = \frac12\left(1+\frac{\xi_\kk}{E_\kk}\right)-\frac12\left(1-\frac{\xi_\kk}{E_\kk}\right) = \frac{\xi_\kk}{E_\kk} $$

Therefore the expectation value of the charge is

$$ q = -e\left(u_\kk^2-v_\kk^2\right) = -e\,\frac{\xi_\kk}{E_\kk} = -e\,\frac{\xi_\kk}{\sqrt{\xi_\kk^2+\Delta^2}} $$

At $\xi_\kk=0$ (exactly on the Fermi surface) the numerator vanishes, so $q=0$. A Bogoliubov quasiparticle on the Fermi surface is electrically neutral.

Let us read this expression a little further. $q(\xi_\kk)$ is an odd function of $\xi_\kk$: it approaches $q\to-e$ (a pure electron) as $\xi_\kk\to+\infty$ and $q\to+e$ (a pure hole) as $\xi_\kk\to-\infty$, and it connects the two smoothly through the neutral point at $\xi_\kk=0$. The magnitude $\abs{q}$ is at most half of $e$ when

$$ \frac{\abs{\xi_\kk}}{\sqrt{\xi_\kk^2+\Delta^2}} \le \frac12 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \abs{\xi_\kk} \le \frac{\Delta}{\sqrt3} = 0.577\,\Delta $$

and the width of the region where the charge is diluted is determined by the gap $\Delta$ itself. In a normal metal ($\Delta=0$) this region collapses to zero width, and $q$ jumps discontinuously between $-e$ and $+e$ according to the sign of $\xi_\kk$. That is, “being able to carry an intermediate charge” is a direct consequence of the opening of the gap. In terms of the correspondence in (1), where $\Delta$ plays the role of $mc^2$, this is the same phenomenon as the mass mixing positive-energy and negative-energy solutions in the Dirac equation.

(4) For Nb, with $\Delta=\xi_\kk=1.5\ \mathrm{meV}$,

$$ E_\kk = \sqrt{1.5^2+1.5^2} = 1.5\sqrt2 = 2.121\ \mathrm{meV}, \qquad \frac{\xi_\kk}{E_\kk} = \frac{1.5}{2.121} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} = 0.7071 $$

Hence

$$ u_\kk^2 = \frac12\left(1+0.7071\right) = 0.854, \qquad v_\kk^2 = \frac12\left(1-0.7071\right) = 0.146 $$ $$ q = -e\times0.7071 = -0.707\,e $$

That is, even a quasiparticle only $\Delta$ away from the Fermi surface already has its charge diluted to 71% of the elementary charge. It is a superposition of an 85% electron component and a 15% hole component, and the hole component cancels part of the charge. The amount of cancellation is $\abs{q}/e=u^2-v^2$, that is, $0.854-0.146=0.708$; equivalently, since the hole component counts twice, we can write $1-2v^2=1-0.293=0.707$.

The point $\xi_\kk=\Delta$ is where the quasiparticle energy is $E_\kk=\sqrt2\,\Delta=2.12\ \mathrm{meV}$, which for Nb is only $0.6\ \mathrm{meV}$ above the gap edge $\Delta=1.5\ \mathrm{meV}$. When one observes the coherence peak at the gap edge in tunneling spectroscopy, the quasiparticles sitting there are therefore already electron–hole hybridized to this extent. In terms of temperature, $0.6\ \mathrm{meV}=7\ \mathrm{K}$, so in Nb with $T_c=9.25\ \mathrm{K}$ hybridized quasiparticles are routinely created by thermal excitation. “Particles with an intermediate charge” are not a theoretical artifact: they exist commonly inside a superconductor at temperatures below room temperature.

Verification. We check that the two relations of (2) hold for the numerical values of (4). $u_\kk^2+v_\kk^2=0.854+0.146=1.000$. And

$$ u_\kk^2v_\kk^2 = \frac12\left(1+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\cdot\frac12\left(1-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right) = \frac14\left(1-\frac12\right) = \frac18 = 0.1250 $$ $$ 2u_\kk v_\kk = 2\sqrt{0.1250} = 2\times0.35355 = 0.7071 = \frac{\Delta}{E_\kk} = \frac{1.5}{2.121} = 0.7071 $$

which agree. We also check the limits. For $\Delta\to0$ (a normal metal) with $\xi_\kk>0$, $E_\kk\to\xi_\kk$, so $u_\kk^2\to1$, $v_\kk^2\to0$, and $q\to-e$, returning to the bare electron. For $\xi_\kk\ll-\Delta$, $q\to+e$, and we have a hole. Both agree with the description in Section 1.4.2 of this chapter.

Meaning. It seems strange at first that the charge of a quasiparticle takes an intermediate value that is neither $-e$ nor $+e$, but this is a manifestation of the fact that in a superconductor, charge is exchanged with the condensate. As a result of the spontaneous breaking of the U(1) symmetry, particle number (and hence charge) ceases to be a good quantum number, and the quasiparticle becomes a superposition of an electron and a hole. The missing fraction of $\pm e$ is taken up by the Cooper-pair condensate, and for the system as a whole the charge conservation law holds exactly. This “nonconservation of charge” can be measured directly as Andreev reflection (an incoming electron is reflected as a hole, and $2e$ flows into the condensate). And it is precisely the result of (3), that $q=0$ at $\xi_\kk=0$, that is the prerequisite for the Majorana condition $\gamma=\gamma^\dagger$ of Section 1.4.3 of this chapter to be possible. A charged particle cannot be its own antiparticle, so neutrality is a necessary condition for being Majorana. The zero-energy bound state appearing at the edge of a topological superconductor is called a Majorana zero mode because it sits exactly at the point $\xi_\kk=0$, $E=0$.

Exercise 1.6: Kinematics of the DT reaction and damage to the first wall

Problem (restated)

Use the mass values in Table 1.7, the formula for the maximum recoil energy in Chapter 1 of this book, and the NRT formula.

(1) Find the $Q$ value of the reaction $\mathrm{D}+{}^3\mathrm{He}\to p+{}^4\mathrm{He}$ ($m_{^3\mathrm{He}}c^2=2808.391\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_pc^2=938.272\ \mathrm{MeV}$). Also find how the energy is shared between the proton and the $\alpha$ particle. Explain why this reaction is called “neutron-free fusion.”

(2) Find the maximum recoil energy $T_{\max}$ when a 14.05 MeV neutron scatters elastically from tungsten ($A=184$), and compare it with the value $0.969\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for iron ($A=56$). Why is the recoil smaller for heavier elements?

(3) For the tungsten of (2), take the mean recoil $\braket{T}=T_{\max}/2$, the damage efficiency $\xi=0.6$, and $E_d(\mathrm{W})=90\ \mathrm{eV}$, and find the number of displacements $N_d$ from the NRT formula.

(4) For a wall loading of $2\ \mathrm{MW/m^2}$ and $\sigma_{\text{tot}}(\mathrm{W})=5.3\ \mathrm{b}$, find the annual dpa of tungsten and compare it with the 15 dpa/year of iron.

Solution

Strategy. We retrace the path of Section 1.5 of this chapter for tungsten. All we need are five facts: (i) the $Q$ value is simply the difference of rest masses; (ii) in a two-body decay with zero total momentum, the kinetic energy is shared in inverse proportion to the masses; (iii) the maximum recoil in elastic scattering is $T_{\max}=4A E_n/(1+A)^2$; (iv) the NRT formula $N_d=0.8\,T_{\text{dam}}/(2E_d)$; and (v) the damage rate $=\phi\,\sigma_{\text{tot}}\,N_d$.

(1) We add and subtract the mass energies. Before the reaction we have $m_{\mathrm{D}}c^2=1875.613\ \mathrm{MeV}$ from Table 1.7 and the given $m_{^3\mathrm{He}}c^2=2808.391\ \mathrm{MeV}$; after the reaction we have $m_pc^2=938.272\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $m_\alpha c^2=3727.379\ \mathrm{MeV}$ from Table 1.7.

$$ \text{(before the reaction)} = 1875.613+2808.391 = 4684.004\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ $$ \text{(after the reaction)} = 938.272+3727.379 = 4665.651\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ $$ Q = 4684.004-4665.651 = 18.353\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

This is slightly larger than the $17.590\ \mathrm{MeV}$ of DT. For the energy sharing, since the total momentum is zero, $p_p=p_\alpha$, and with the nonrelativistic $T=p^2/2m$ we have $T\propto1/m$. Therefore

$$ T_p = Q\,\frac{m_\alpha}{m_p+m_\alpha} = 18.353\times\frac{3727.379}{4665.651} = 18.353\times0.79890 = 14.66\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ $$ T_\alpha = Q - T_p = 18.353-14.66 = 3.69\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The reaction is called “neutron-free fusion” (also called aneutronic fusion) because the products are only two charged particles, a proton and an $\alpha$ particle. Charged particles can be confined in the plasma by a magnetic field, and their energy is either used to heat the plasma or extracted as electric power by direct energy conversion. They do not strike the wall and displace lattice atoms, nor do they activate the material by nuclear transmutation. The first-wall damage problem treated in Section 1.5.2 of this chapter therefore does not arise, in principle. In reality, however, the $\mathrm{D}+\mathrm{D}$ side reactions between D nuclei contained in the fuel emit neutrons, so the fusion is not completely neutron-free. Moreover, as stated in Section 1.5.1 of this chapter, this reaction has a cross section two orders of magnitude smaller than that of DT and requires a temperature more than five times higher, so its practical use is far more distant than that of DT.

(2) We insert $A=184$ for tungsten into $T_{\max}=4A E_n/(1+A)^2$.

$$ \frac{4A}{(1+A)^2} = \frac{4\times184}{185^2} = \frac{736}{34225} = 0.02150 $$ $$ T_{\max}^{\mathrm{W}} = 0.02150\times14.05\ \mathrm{MeV} = 0.302\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

For iron, $4\times56/57^2=224/3249=0.06894$ and $T_{\max}^{\mathrm{Fe}}=0.969\ \mathrm{MeV}$, so the ratio is $0.302/0.969=0.312$; that is, the recoil in tungsten is about one third of that in iron. The reason heavier elements have smaller recoil is written in the formula for $T_{\max}$ itself. For $A\gg1$,

$$ \frac{4A}{(1+A)^2} \simeq \frac{4}{A} $$

so it decreases as $1/A$. Indeed $56/184=0.304$, which agrees well with the ratio $0.312$ above. Physically, when a light particle collides head-on with a heavy target, the momentum is returned almost doubled ($2p$), but the kinetic energy $\left(2p\right)^2/(2M)$ received by the heavy target is small, being inversely proportional to $M$. It is the same reduced-mass effect as the fact that if you throw a table-tennis ball at a bowling ball, the bowling ball hardly moves. Incidentally, for $A=1$ (hydrogen), $4A/(1+A)^2=1$, and a neutron hands over all its energy in a single head-on collision. The same formula also explains why hydrogen is the best neutron moderator.

(3) We find the mean recoil and the damage energy in turn.

$$ \braket{T} = \frac{T_{\max}}{2} = \frac{0.302}{2} = 0.151\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ $$ T_{\text{dam}} = \xi\braket{T} = 0.6\times0.151\ \mathrm{MeV} = 0.0906\ \mathrm{MeV} = 9.06\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{eV} $$

Inserting $E_d(\mathrm{W})=90\ \mathrm{eV}$ into the NRT formula,

$$ N_d = \frac{0.8\,T_{\text{dam}}}{2E_d} = \frac{0.8\times9.06\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{eV}}{2\times90\ \mathrm{eV}} = \frac{7.25\times10^{4}}{180} = 403 $$

A single elastic scattering of one neutron creates about 400 Frenkel pairs. This is about 1/5.5 of the $2.2\times10^{3}$ for iron (Section 1.5.2 of this chapter). The breakdown is as follows: the product $3.2\times2.25=7.2$ of the reduction of the recoil energy to $1/3.2$ ($T_{\max}$) and the 2.25 times higher displacement threshold ($40\to90\ \mathrm{eV}$), reduced by the factor of 1.33 by which the damage efficiency is larger ($0.6$ versus $\xi=0.45$ for iron), gives $7.2/1.33=5.4$, which agrees.

(4) The neutron flux is determined by the wall loading alone, independent of the material. The wall loading is the neutron energy received by the wall per unit area and per unit time, so dividing it by the energy of one neutron, $T_n=14.05\ \mathrm{MeV}$, gives the particle flux. This is the same value as in Section 1.5.2 of this chapter.

$$ \phi = \frac{P}{T_n} = \frac{2\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{W/m^2}}{14.05\times10^{6}\times1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}} = \frac{2\times10^{6}}{2.251\times10^{-12}} = 8.9\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}s^{-1}} $$

The damage rate is

$$ \frac{\dd(\mathrm{dpa})}{\dd t} = \phi\,\sigma_{\text{tot}}\,N_d = 8.9\times10^{17}\times5.3\times10^{-28}\times403 = 1.90\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

Multiplying by 1 year $=3.156\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}$,

$$ \mathrm{dpa/year} = 1.90\times10^{-7}\times3.156\times10^{7} = 6.0 $$

This is about 1/2.6 of the 15 dpa/year for iron (15.4 without rounding). Let us pin down the meaning of this number. 6 dpa/year means that each atom of the first wall is knocked off its lattice site an average of six times in a year. The crystal is, in effect, rebuilt six times every year, and in iron 15 times. If the design lifetime of a fusion reactor is 5 years, even tungsten receives an irradiation dose of 30 dpa, and iron 77 dpa. Considering that a fission reactor pressure vessel receives $\sim0.1\ \mathrm{dpa}$ over its lifetime, and even the core structural materials receive some tens of dpa, we can see how harsh an environment the fusion first wall is. Moreover, the damage rate $\phi\sigma N_d$ is a simple product of three factors, so raising the wall loading from $2\to4\ \mathrm{MW/m^2}$ doubles $\phi$, and the dpa doubles along with it. The fundamental trade-off in fusion reactor design, that raising the power density and making the material last longer are in direct conflict, appears in this single multiplication.

Verification. We check the ratio to iron by decomposing it into its factors. The damage rate is $\phi\sigma N_d$ and $\phi$ is common, so

$$ \frac{(\mathrm{dpa})_{\mathrm{Fe}}}{(\mathrm{dpa})_{\mathrm{W}}} = \frac{\sigma_{\mathrm{Fe}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{W}}}\times\frac{N_d^{\mathrm{Fe}}}{N_d^{\mathrm{W}}} = \frac{2.5}{5.3}\times\frac{2200}{403} = 0.472\times5.46 = 2.58 $$

This agrees with the direct ratio $15.4/6.0=2.6$. The cross section of tungsten is twice as large, which acts to increase the damage, but the number of displacements is 5.5 times smaller, so on balance tungsten is favored by a factor of 2.6; this is the breakdown we can read off. We also check the dimensions. The dimension of $\phi\sigma N_d$ is $\mathrm{m^{-2}s^{-1}}\times\mathrm{m^2}\times1=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, which matches the dimension of dpa per second, “the number of times one atom is displaced per unit time.”

Meaning. This calculation shows that the engineering decision of choosing the first-wall material of a fusion reactor is largely settled by just three quantities: $T_{\max}$ (kinematics), $E_d$ (bonding in the crystal), and $\sigma_{\text{tot}}$ (nuclear physics). One reason tungsten is the leading candidate is precisely the two points calculated here: “because it is heavy the recoil is small, and because the bonding is strong the threshold is high” (its highest melting point, low sputtering yield, and low tritium retention also play a part). However, dpa is only a crude measure of damage. The high-temperature embrittlement due to He production (9.1 appm/dpa) described in Section 1.5.2 of this chapter, and, in the case of W, the nuclear transmutation to Re and Os by $(n,\gamma)$ with the accompanying embrittlement and reduction of thermal conductivity, are equally serious, and these too are all determined by cross sections, a quantity of particle physics. Note that $\mathrm{D}+{}^3\mathrm{He}$ in (1) looks attractive because it avoids this damage problem altogether.

Exercise 1.7: Deriving the neutron wavelength formula in natural units

Problem (restated)

Derive the formula $\lambda\,[\mathrm{\AA}]=9.045/\sqrt{E\,[\mathrm{meV}]}$ used in neutron scattering. Use $m_nc^2=939.565\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $hc=1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$.

(1) The nonrelativistic momentum is $pc=\sqrt{2(m_nc^2)E}$. For $E=25.3\ \mathrm{meV}$, find $pc$ in eV.

(2) From $\lambda=hc/(pc)$, find the wavelength in nm and confirm that it is $1.80\ \mathrm{\AA}$.

(3) In general, reduce $\lambda\,[\mathrm{nm}] = hc/\sqrt{2(m_nc^2)E}$ to a numerical formula for $E$ measured in meV, and derive $\lambda[\mathrm{\AA}]=9.045/\sqrt{E[\mathrm{meV}]}$.

(4) Find the energies of a photon (X-ray) and an electron having the same wavelength of $1.80\ \mathrm{\AA}$, and compare them with the neutron’s $25.3\ \mathrm{meV}$. Explain why neutrons are used for phonon measurements.

Solution

Strategy. Following the usual practice of natural units, we treat mass, momentum, and energy all in a single unit, the “eV,” and at the end multiply by $hc$ to return to a length. In this way we never need the SI values of $\hbar$ or $m_n$, and the calculation closes with just two numbers, $m_nc^2$ and $hc$.

(1) Substitute $m_nc^2=939.565\ \mathrm{MeV}=9.39565\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $E=25.3\ \mathrm{meV}=2.53\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{eV}$.

$$ (pc)^2 = 2\left(m_nc^2\right)E = 2\times9.39565\times10^{8}\times2.53\times10^{-2} = 4.7542\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{eV^2} $$ $$ pc = \sqrt{4.7542\times10^{7}} = 6.895\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{eV} = 6.895\ \mathrm{keV} $$

What deserves attention here is that the momentum of a particle with a “thermal energy” of $25.3\ \mathrm{meV}$, measured as $pc$, comes out at $6.9\ \mathrm{keV}$, which lies in the X-ray region. Since $pc=\sqrt{2(m_nc^2)E}$ is the geometric mean of $E$ and $m_nc^2$ (times $\sqrt2$), it is a necessary consequence that it falls midway between the two numbers $25\ \mathrm{meV}$ and $940\ \mathrm{MeV}$, which are separated by a little more than ten orders of magnitude, namely at $\sqrt{2.5\times10^{-2}\times9.4\times10^{8}}\sim5\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{eV}$. That a neutron can have “a keV momentum at an energy of meV” is due to nothing other than its large mass.

We can also confirm the validity of the nonrelativistic approximation here. Since $\beta=pc/E_{\text{tot}}\simeq pc/(m_nc^2)=6895/(9.396\times10^{8})=7.3\times10^{-6}$, the relative size of the relativistic correction is of order $\beta^2\sim5\times10^{-11}$, which is completely negligible for an argument at four significant figures.

(2) Divide $hc=1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$ by the momentum.

$$ \lambda = \frac{hc}{pc} = \frac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{6.895\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{eV}} = 0.1798\ \mathrm{nm} = 1.798\ \mathrm{\AA} \simeq 1.80\ \mathrm{\AA} $$

It is indeed $1.80\ \mathrm{\AA}$. Note that the eV cancel and only nm remains. It is an advantage of natural units that the bookkeeping of dimensions requires nothing but multiplication and division.

Let us verify with the numerical formula derived in (3). We get $\lambda[\mathrm{\AA}]=9.045/\sqrt{25.3}=9.045/5.030=1.798$, which agrees. And this value of $1.80\ \mathrm{\AA}$ is precisely the reason thermal neutrons can be used for crystal diffraction. A typical lattice-plane spacing $d$ is about $1\text{–}3\ \mathrm{\AA}$, and for the Bragg condition $\lambda=2d\sin\theta$ to be satisfied within the range $\sin\theta\le1$ we need $\lambda\le2d$, that is, $\lambda$ must be at most a few $\mathrm{\AA}$. With an energy of $25\ \mathrm{meV}$, which is room temperature itself, this condition is met without any acceleration. The starting point of the method of neutron scattering is that neutrons emerging from a nuclear reactor or a spallation source acquire a wavelength usable for diffraction merely by passing through a room-temperature moderator.

(3) We reduce the general formula to a numerical formula. If we measure $E$ by its numerical value $E[\mathrm{meV}]$ in meV, then in eV we have $E=10^{-3}E[\mathrm{meV}]$. Substituting this,

$$ \lambda\,[\mathrm{nm}] = \frac{hc}{\sqrt{2\left(m_nc^2\right)E}} = \frac{1239.84}{\sqrt{2\times9.39565\times10^{8}\times10^{-3}\times E[\mathrm{meV}]}} $$

We first compute the constant part under the square root.

$$ 2\times9.39565\times10^{8}\times10^{-3} = 1.87913\times10^{6}, \qquad \sqrt{1.87913\times10^{6}} = 1370.81 $$

Therefore

$$ \lambda\,[\mathrm{nm}] = \frac{1239.84}{1370.81\,\sqrt{E[\mathrm{meV}]}} = \frac{0.90446}{\sqrt{E[\mathrm{meV}]}} $$

Since $1\ \mathrm{nm}=10\ \mathrm{\AA}$, multiplying both sides by 10 gives

$$ \lambda\,[\mathrm{\AA}] = \frac{9.0446}{\sqrt{E[\mathrm{meV}]}} \simeq \frac{9.045}{\sqrt{E[\mathrm{meV}]}} $$

which is what we wanted to derive. The true identity of the number “9.045” that everyone in the neutron-scattering community has memorized is nothing other than the combination of $hc$ and $m_nc^2$, $hc/\sqrt{2m_nc^2\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}}$.

(4) Consider a photon and an electron with the same wavelength $\lambda=0.1798\ \mathrm{nm}$.

Since the photon is massless, $E=pc$, and

$$ E_\gamma = \frac{hc}{\lambda} = \frac{1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{0.1798\ \mathrm{nm}} = 6.895\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{eV} = 6.90\ \mathrm{keV} $$

For the electron, the same wavelength means the same momentum, $pc=6895\ \mathrm{eV}$. Nonrelativistically,

$$ E_e = \frac{(pc)^2}{2m_ec^2} = \frac{\left(6.895\times10^{3}\right)^2}{2\times5.11\times10^{5}}\ \mathrm{eV} = \frac{4.754\times10^{7}}{1.022\times10^{6}} = 46.5\ \mathrm{eV} $$

Putting the three side by side, for the same $1.80\ \mathrm{\AA}$ we have

$$ E_\gamma = 6.90\ \mathrm{keV}, \qquad E_e = 46.5\ \mathrm{eV}, \qquad E_n = 25.3\ \mathrm{meV} $$

If the phonon energy is $10\ \mathrm{meV}$, the relative resolution needed to resolve it is

$$ \left(\frac{\Delta E}{E}\right)_\gamma = \frac{10^{-2}}{6895} = 1.5\times10^{-6}, \qquad \left(\frac{\Delta E}{E}\right)_e = \frac{10^{-2}}{46.5} = 2.2\times10^{-4}, \qquad \left(\frac{\Delta E}{E}\right)_n = \frac{10^{-2}}{2.53\times10^{-2}} = 0.40 $$

Only the neutron gets by with a comfortable resolution of order $10^{-1}$. This is why the measurement of phonon dispersions was for a long time the exclusive domain of inelastic neutron scattering. With X-rays, too, a resolution of order $10^{-7}$ can be achieved by using synchrotron radiation (inelastic X-ray scattering), but this requires building the crystal spectrometer to the utmost extreme. The electron is intermediate in terms of resolution, but its interaction with atoms is so strong that it is buried in multiple scattering. Since the neutron has no electric charge, its interaction is weak, and it even comes with the advantage that the kinematic approximation (single scattering) can be used.

Verification. Among the energies of the three particles, an exact relation holds because of the condition of equal wavelength. If the wavelength is the same, $pc$ is common, so for the two massive particles $E=(pc)^2/(2mc^2)\propto1/m$, that is,

$$ \frac{E_e}{E_n} = \frac{m_nc^2}{m_ec^2} = \frac{9.39565\times10^{8}}{5.11\times10^{5}} = 1839 $$

and indeed $46.5/2.53\times10^{-2}=1838$ agrees. For the photon and the electron,

$$ \frac{E_\gamma}{E_e} = \frac{pc}{(pc)^2/(2m_ec^2)} = \frac{2m_ec^2}{pc} = \frac{1.022\times10^{6}}{6895} = 148 $$

and indeed $6895/46.5=148$ agrees. We have confirmed that the three independently computed numbers are tied together by the mass ratios alone.

Meaning. Combining $E=(pc)^2/(2mc^2)$ with $\lambda=hc/(pc)$ gives $E\propto1/(m\lambda^2)$. When the wavelength is fixed at the interatomic distance ($\sim2\ \mathrm{\AA}$), whether the energy falls to the scale of lattice vibrations (a few to a few tens of meV) is determined by the mass of the particle alone. The neutron’s mass is “coincidentally” such that this double coincidence holds just right. As Section 1.6.3 of this chapter emphasizes, this is a property possessed by the neutron alone, and it is the very reason giant facilities such as J-PARC MLF, ISIS, SNS, and ILL have been built around the world. The mass of an elementary particle, a number that humans cannot choose, determines the shape of the infrastructure of materials research.

Exercise 1.8: Numbers for elementary-particle probes

Problem (restated)

Use $m_\pi c^2=139.570\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_\mu c^2=105.658\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $\tau_\mu=2.197\ \mu\mathrm{s}$, $\gamma_\mu/2\pi=135.5\ \mathrm{MHz/T}$, and $m_ec^2=511.0\ \mathrm{keV}$.

(1) Without using the surface-muon formula in Chapter 1 of this book, derive the momentum of the surface muon, $pc=(m_\pi^2-m_\mu^2)c^2/(2m_\pi)$, from energy-momentum conservation. Also find its numerical value.

(2) Find the precession frequency and period of a $\mu^+$ in a local magnetic field of $0.05\ \mathrm{T}$, and find how many times it precesses during the lifetime $\tau_\mu$.

(3) For copper ($E_F=7.0\ \mathrm{eV}$), find the angular-correlation broadening of positron annihilation, $\Delta\theta=p_Fc/(m_ec^2)$, in mrad. Also find the Doppler broadening $\Delta E=p_Fc/2$ in eV, and compare it with the resolution of a Ge detector, $1.2\ \mathrm{keV}$.

(4) Find the Bohr radius $a_\mu=a_0\,m_e/\mu_{\text{red}}$ of the muonic atom of deuterium formed with a $\mu^-$, in fm ($\mu_{\text{red}}=195.7\,m_e$, $a_0=0.529\ \mathrm{\AA}$). Compare it with the internuclear distance of an ordinary $\mathrm{D}_2$ molecule, $0.74\ \mathrm{\AA}$, and state by how many orders of magnitude it shrinks.

Solution

Strategy. Part (1) is the most basic problem of relativistic kinematics, which is treated in earnest in Chapter 4: the two-body decay of a particle at rest. Parts (2)–(4) are the task of pinning down in numbers how effective each of the three methods, $\mu$SR, positron annihilation, and muon-catalyzed fusion, is, and each amounts to recomputing the content of Section 1.6 of this chapter.

(1) A $\pi^+$ at rest decays into $\mu^+ + \nu_\mu$. Since the total momentum before the reaction is zero, the $\mu^+$ and $\nu_\mu$ have momenta $p$ of equal magnitude and opposite direction. If the neutrino is taken to be massless, $E_\nu=pc$, and for the muon $E_\mu=\sqrt{p^2c^2+m_\mu^2c^4}$. Energy conservation reads

$$ m_\pi c^2 = \sqrt{p^2c^2+m_\mu^2c^4} + pc $$

To isolate the square root, we move $pc$ to the left-hand side.

$$ m_\pi c^2 - pc = \sqrt{p^2c^2+m_\mu^2c^4} $$

Square both sides.

$$ m_\pi^2c^4 - 2m_\pi c^2\,pc + p^2c^2 = p^2c^2 + m_\mu^2c^4 $$

Here the $p^2c^2$ on both sides cancels. This is the key point of the calculation: it leaves a linear equation in $p$.

$$ m_\pi^2c^4 - m_\mu^2c^4 = 2m_\pi c^2\,pc \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad pc = \frac{\left(m_\pi^2-m_\mu^2\right)c^2}{2m_\pi} $$

Now insert the numbers.

$$ m_\pi^2c^4 = 139.570^2 = 19479.8\ \mathrm{MeV^2}, \qquad m_\mu^2c^4 = 105.658^2 = 11163.6\ \mathrm{MeV^2} $$ $$ pc = \frac{19479.8-11163.6}{2\times139.570} = \frac{8316.2}{279.14} = 29.79\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

This is the true identity of the “29.8 MeV/$c$ surface muon.” The kinetic energy is

$$ T_\mu = \sqrt{(29.79)^2+(105.658)^2}-105.658 = \sqrt{12051}-105.658 = 109.78-105.66 = 4.12\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

which agrees with the value in Section 1.6.1 of the main text.

(2) The Larmor precession frequency is $f=(\gamma_\mu/2\pi)B_{\text{loc}}$.

$$ f = 135.5\ \mathrm{MHz/T}\times0.05\ \mathrm{T} = 6.775\ \mathrm{MHz} $$ $$ T_{\text{prec}} = \frac{1}{f} = \frac{1}{6.775\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}} = 1.476\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{s} = 147.6\ \mathrm{ns} $$

The number of precessions during the lifetime $\tau_\mu=2.197\ \mu\mathrm{s}$ is

$$ N = \frac{\tau_\mu}{T_{\text{prec}}} = \frac{2.197\times10^{-6}}{1.476\times10^{-7}} = 14.9 $$

That is about 15 times. The actual observation window can be taken to be several times the lifetime ($\sim10\ \mu\mathrm{s}$), during which it turns $10\times10^{-6}/1.476\times10^{-7}=68$ times. Since a sufficient number of oscillations can be counted, the frequency can be determined accurately. This is the reason $\mu$SR can be used as an absolute magnetometer. Note that $0.05\ \mathrm{T}$ is a perfectly ordinary size for the internal field of a magnetic material; for a weak field of order $10^{-5}\ \mathrm{T}$, as listed in Section 1.6.1 of this chapter, the muon cannot complete a precession within its lifetime, so it is detected not as an oscillation but as a relaxation (of Kubo–Toyabe type).

(3) First we find the Fermi momentum in natural units. With $E_F=7.0\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $m_ec^2=511.0\ \mathrm{keV}=5.110\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{eV}$,

$$ p_Fc = \sqrt{2\left(m_ec^2\right)E_F} = \sqrt{2\times5.110\times10^{5}\times7.0}\ \mathrm{eV} = \sqrt{7.154\times10^{6}}\ \mathrm{eV} = 2675\ \mathrm{eV} = 2.67\ \mathrm{keV} $$

The spread of the angular correlation is

$$ \Delta\theta = \frac{p_Fc}{m_ec^2} = \frac{2675}{5.110\times10^{5}} = 5.23\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad} = 5.23\ \mathrm{mrad} $$

The Doppler broadening is

$$ \Delta E = \frac{p_Fc}{2} = \frac{2675}{2} = 1337\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.34\ \mathrm{keV} $$

This is roughly the same as the Ge detector resolution of $1.2\ \mathrm{keV}$. Therefore the observed spectrum takes the form in which the physical broadening and the instrument function are convolved with nearly equal widths, and as it stands the valence-electron component and the core-electron component cannot be separated. In practice one either performs deconvolution or uses the coincidence Doppler broadening method (CDB), in which both $\gamma$ rays are detected in coincidence by two detectors; this lowers the background to $10^{-4}$ or below, after which the tail of the core electrons is measured. This is the standard method that determines the chemical environment of a defect (the $S$ parameter and the $W$ parameter).

(4) The Bohr radius is inversely proportional to the reduced mass. Since $a_0=0.529\ \mathrm{\AA}=0.529\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{fm}=52900\ \mathrm{fm}$,

$$ a_\mu = a_0\frac{m_e}{\mu_{\text{red}}} = \frac{52900\ \mathrm{fm}}{195.7} = 270\ \mathrm{fm} $$

The ratio to the internuclear distance of the $\mathrm{D}_2$ molecule, $0.74\ \mathrm{\AA}=7.4\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{fm}$, is

$$ \frac{7.4\times10^{4}}{270} = 274 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \log_{10}274 = 2.44 $$

That is, it shrinks by about 2.4 orders of magnitude (a factor of a little over 270). When the nuclei come this close, the tunneling probability through the Coulomb barrier jumps up exponentially, and as described in Section 1.6.3 of this chapter, fusion occurs within the short time of $10^{-12}\ \mathrm{s}$. However, if we apply the ratio $0.74/0.529=1.40$, that is, $1.4\,a_0$, found for $\mathrm{D_2}$ directly to $\mathrm{dt}\mu$, we get $1.4\times270=378\ \mathrm{fm}$, which differs somewhat from the “about 500 fm” of the main text. This is because in an ordinary molecule the electron mass is far lighter than the nuclear mass, so the Born–Oppenheimer approximation works extremely well, whereas in a muonic molecule $m_\mu/m_d=105.658/1875.613=0.056$, so the muon is not lighter by orders of magnitude, and the simple scaling that ignores the motion of the nuclei does not hold.

Verification. We look at two limits of (1). For $m_\mu\to m_\pi$ (the energy margin of the decay goes to zero), $pc\to0$, which matches the physics that the phase space closes. For $m_\mu\to0$, $pc\to m_\pi c^2/2$, which is the correct answer for two massless particles flying back to back. For (3) we can use the fact that $\Delta E$ and $\Delta\theta$ are not independent. From the definitions, $\Delta E/(m_ec^2)=(p_Fc/2)/(m_ec^2)=\Delta\theta/2$, and indeed $1337/5.110\times10^{5}=2.62\times10^{-3}=5.23/2\ \mathrm{mrad}$ agrees. Also, compared with Al in Section 1.6.2 of the main text ($E_F=11.7\ \mathrm{eV}$, $p_Fc=3.46\ \mathrm{keV}$), since $p_Fc\propto\sqrt{E_F}$ the ratio should be $\sqrt{7.0/11.7}=0.7735$, and $2675/3458=0.7736$ agrees. For (4) we can verify the reduced mass itself: $\mu_{\text{red}}=m_\mu m_d/(m_\mu+m_d)=105.658\times1875.613/1981.271=100.02\ \mathrm{MeV}/c^2$, and dividing this by $m_ec^2=0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$ gives $195.7$, which reproduces the given value.

Meaning. All four subproblems show that numbers fixed on the particle-physics side directly determine the performance of materials measurements. The surface muon’s $29.8\ \mathrm{MeV}/c$ is a value determined solely by the mass difference between the $\pi$ and the $\mu$, and it gives the muon a range of “traveling $0.1$–$1\ \mathrm{mm}$ in a solid before stopping,” which is just right for bulk measurements. $\gamma_\mu$ is the magnetic moment of an elementary particle, and it makes possible an absolute magnetometer requiring no calibration. The positron’s $\Delta\theta$ and $\Delta E$ appear as quantities divided by $m_ec^2$, and they let us read off the Fermi momentum, a quantity of solid-state physics, directly. The $270\ \mathrm{fm}$ of the muonic atom is determined by $m_\mu/m_e$ alone. None of these was designed by the experimenter; they are properties of elementary particles given by nature. To borrow the words of Section 1.6 of this chapter, to make full use of these probes one needs to know the language of particle and nuclear physics (decay rate, cross section, polarization, parity).

E.2 Solutions for Chapter 2: A History of Particle Physics

Exercise 2.1: Rutherford scattering and the size of the nucleus

Problem (restated)

An $\alpha$ particle ($z_1=2$) with kinetic energy $E=5.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is directed at silver ($z_2=47$, $A=108$). Use $e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)=1.44\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$.

(1) Find the distance of closest approach $d$ in a head-on collision ($b=0$).

(2) Take the nuclear radius of silver to be $R=1.2A^{1/3}\ \mathrm{fm}$, find $R$, and compare it with $d$. Can we expect the Rutherford formula to hold?

(3) Find the energy of the $\alpha$ particle at which $d=R$. What happens at energies above this?

(4) Using the $b$–$\theta$ relation $b=\dfrac{\kappa}{2E}\cot\dfrac{\theta}{2}$ of Chapter 2 of this book, find the impact parameter $b$ for scattering through $\theta=90^\circ$.

Solution

Strategy. We need only two tools. One is energy conservation in a head-on collision (all the kinetic energy is converted into Coulomb potential energy); the other is the relation between $b$ and the scattering angle $\theta$ that we derived in this chapter from the hyperbolic orbit. Both are purely classical mechanics. First, let us collect the Coulomb strength in the notation of this chapter:

$$ \kappa \equiv \frac{z_1z_2e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0} = 2\times47\times1.44\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm} = 135.36\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm} $$

(1) In a head-on collision ($b=0$), the $\alpha$ particle climbs the wall of the repulsive potential and comes momentarily to rest, so its kinetic energy is zero at that point. Letting $d$ be the distance of closest approach,

$$ E = \frac{\kappa}{d} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad d = \frac{\kappa}{E} = \frac{135.36\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{5.5\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 24.61\ \mathrm{fm} $$

That is, $d = 24.6\ \mathrm{fm}$.

(2) The nuclear radius is

$$ R = 1.2\times108^{1/3}\ \mathrm{fm} = 1.2\times4.7622\ \mathrm{fm} = 5.715\ \mathrm{fm} $$

(Since $4.76^3 = 107.85$, $108^{1/3}=4.762$ is adequate.) Taking the ratio,

$$ \frac{d}{R} = \frac{24.61}{5.715} = 4.31 $$

Even at its closest approach, the $\alpha$ particle is turned back at $4.3$ times the nuclear radius, so it does not touch the surface of the nucleus. The range of the nuclear force is about $1\ \mathrm{fm}$ (Section 2.3 of this chapter), so at a distance of $24.6\ \mathrm{fm}$ the nuclear force is completely negligible. Therefore the only force acting is the pure $1/r^2$ Coulomb force, and we may expect the Rutherford formula $\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega\propto\sin^{-4}(\theta/2)$ to hold as it stands.

Let us also check that a classical treatment is justified. The mass of the $\alpha$ particle is $m_\alpha c^2=3727\ \mathrm{MeV}$, so nonrelativistically $p=\sqrt{2m_\alpha E}$ gives $pc=\sqrt{2\times3727\times5.5}\ \mathrm{MeV}=202.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and the reduced de Broglie wavelength is $\hbar/p = 197.327/202.5 = 0.97\ \mathrm{fm}$. This is much shorter than $d=24.6\ \mathrm{fm}$, so the classical picture of an orbit is legitimate.

(3) Solving $d=\kappa/E$ for $E$ and imposing $d=R$ gives

$$ E_{\mathrm{crit}} = \frac{\kappa}{R} = \frac{135.36\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{5.715\ \mathrm{fm}} = 23.7\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

If $E>E_{\mathrm{crit}}$, then $d<R$ and the $\alpha$ particle reaches the surface of the nucleus. There the strong interaction (the nuclear force) acts: part of the elastic scattering is “eaten” by nuclear reactions (absorption, nuclear excitation), and in addition the Coulomb amplitude and the nuclear-force amplitude interfere. As a result, the measured cross section begins to deviate systematically from the Rutherford formula. The important point is that, conversely, the energy at which the deviation begins tells us the nuclear radius $R$. This is precisely the central argument of this chapter, “deviations from the formula reveal the internal structure,” and it was later inherited by the measurement of the proton form factor by electron–proton scattering, and then by the discovery of quarks through deep inelastic scattering.

(4) For $\theta=90^\circ$ we have $\theta/2=45^\circ$ and $\cot45^\circ=1$, so

$$ b = \frac{\kappa}{2E}\cot45^\circ = \frac{135.36}{2\times5.5}\ \mathrm{fm} = 12.31\ \mathrm{fm} $$

That is, $b=12.3\ \mathrm{fm}$. This is exactly half the distance of closest approach in (1). In fact, in general $b(\theta=90^\circ)=\kappa/(2E)=d/2$ holds.

Verification. We check both the dimensions and the limits. Since $\kappa$ is in $\mathrm{MeV\,fm}$ and $E$ is in $\mathrm{MeV}$, $\kappa/E$ is in $\mathrm{fm}$, so in (1), (3) and (4) the dimensions of length and energy all match. As for the limits, as $\theta\to180^\circ$, $\cot(\theta/2)\to0$, that is, $b\to0$ (the closer to head-on, the larger the deflection), and as $\theta\to0$, $\cot(\theta/2)\to\infty$, that is, $b\to\infty$ (a particle passing far away is not deflected), in agreement with intuition. Moreover, the relation $b(90^\circ)=d/2$ is an identity that follows analytically from $d=\kappa/E$ and $b=(\kappa/2E)\cot(\theta/2)$, so it also confirms that the numerical values in (1) and (4) are mutually consistent, independently.

Meaning. This calculation fixes numerically the “safe region” in which the analysis of Rutherford scattering is valid. For $\mathrm{MeV}$-class ions the distance of closest approach is several times the nuclear radius, and the nuclear force has no effect at all. That is exactly why Rutherford backscattering spectrometry (RBS) can trust the theoretical value that the cross section is proportional to $z_2^2$ as it stands, and the composition ratio can be quantified without a reference sample. For example, if $\mathrm{He}$ ($z_1=2$) with $E_0=2.0\ \mathrm{MeV}$, the energy commonly used in RBS, is fired at gold ($z_2=79$), then $d=2\times79\times1.44/2.0=113.8\ \mathrm{fm}$, which is $16$ times the nuclear radius of gold, $7.0\ \mathrm{fm}$, away. The reliability of compositional analysis in the depth direction of thin films, an everyday materials characterization, rests on the same inequality $d\gg R$ that underlay the discovery of the atomic nucleus in 1911.

Exercise 2.2: The Compton wavelength and the Compton edge

Problem (restated)

Use $hc=1239.84\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}=1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$.

(1) Find the Compton wavelength of the proton, $h/(m_pc)$, in fm. What can be said in comparison with the size of a nucleon ($\sim1\ \mathrm{fm}$)?

(2) Mo $K\alpha$ radiation ($\lambda=70.9\ \mathrm{pm}$) is Compton-scattered at $\theta=90^\circ$. Find $\lambda'$ and the relative wavelength shift $\Delta\lambda/\lambda$.

(3) For the same incident X-rays, find the scattering angle at which the kinetic energy received by the electron is maximal, and the corresponding $T_e$ (the Compton edge).

(4) What would $\Delta\lambda/\lambda$ be if the same experiment were done with visible light ($\lambda=500\ \mathrm{nm}$)? Why did Compton use X-rays?

Solution

Strategy. We use only the Compton formula that we derived in this chapter from the square of the four-momentum

$$ \lambda'-\lambda = \lambda_C\,(1-\cos\theta), \qquad \lambda_C = \frac{h}{m_ec} = \frac{hc}{m_ec^2} $$

and the relation $E=hc/\lambda$ between photon energy and wavelength. We take $m_ec^2=0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $m_pc^2=938.272\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(1) We simply substitute into the definition:

$$ \frac{h}{m_pc} = \frac{hc}{m_pc^2} = \frac{1239.84\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{938.272\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 1.321\ \mathrm{fm} $$

The charge radius of the proton is $0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$ and the “size” of a nucleon is roughly $1\ \mathrm{fm}$, so the size of the proton and its Compton wavelength are of the same order. This has strong implications. The Compton wavelength is the length such that “if one tries to confine the particle to a region of size $\lambda_C$ or smaller, the uncertainty relation requires an energy exceeding $m c^2$, and a particle–antiparticle pair is created.” When we look inside the proton with a resolution of $1\ \mathrm{fm}$, its contents are necessarily relativistic, and quark pairs and meson fields are welling up. That is, the proton cannot be treated as “a system of pointlike constituents bound nonrelativistically.”

For contrast, consider the atom. The reduced Compton wavelength of the electron is $\hbar/(m_ec)=386.2\ \mathrm{fm}$, and the Bohr radius $a_0=0.0529\ \mathrm{nm}=52900\ \mathrm{fm}$ is $137$ times that (that is, $1/\alpha$ times). Since an atom is far larger than its own Compton wavelength, it is well described by the nonrelativistic Schrödinger equation. For a nucleon, this hierarchy has disappeared.

(2) First we evaluate the electron Compton wavelength numerically:

$$ \lambda_C = \frac{1239.84\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 2426\ \mathrm{fm} = 2.426\ \mathrm{pm} $$

For $\theta=90^\circ$, $\cos\theta=0$, so $1-\cos\theta=1$ and

$$ \lambda' = \lambda + \lambda_C = 70.9 + 2.426 = 73.33\ \mathrm{pm} $$ $$ \frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{2.426}{70.9} = 3.42\times10^{-2} = 3.4\% $$

A shift of $3\%$ is large enough to be resolved with room to spare by Bragg spectroscopy with a calcite crystal.

(3) By energy conservation, the kinetic energy received by the electron is $T_e=E-E'$. In terms of wavelengths,

$$ T_e = hc\left(\frac{1}{\lambda}-\frac{1}{\lambda'}\right) = hc\,\frac{\lambda'-\lambda}{\lambda\lambda'} = hc\,\frac{\lambda_C(1-\cos\theta)}{\lambda\,[\lambda+\lambda_C(1-\cos\theta)]} $$

The right-hand side is a monotonically increasing function of $1-\cos\theta$, so $T_e$ is maximal at $\theta=180^\circ$ (backscattering), where $1-\cos\theta$ is maximal. In this case the electron is knocked forward.

$$ \lambda' = 70.9 + 2\times2.426 = 75.75\ \mathrm{pm} $$

Converting to energies (with $hc=1239.84\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$, $\lambda=0.0709\ \mathrm{nm}$, $\lambda'=0.07575\ \mathrm{nm}$):

$$ E = \frac{1239.84}{0.0709} = 17487\ \mathrm{eV} = 17.49\ \mathrm{keV}, \qquad E' = \frac{1239.84}{0.075753} = 16367\ \mathrm{eV} = 16.37\ \mathrm{keV} $$ $$ T_e^{\max} = 17.487 - 16.367 = 1.120\ \mathrm{keV} $$

This is the Compton edge. Only $6.4\%$ of the incident photon energy is passed to the electron.

(4) For visible light,

$$ \frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda}\bigg|_{\theta=90^\circ} = \frac{2.426\ \mathrm{pm}}{500\ \mathrm{nm}} = \frac{2.426\times10^{-12}}{5.00\times10^{-7}} = 4.85\times10^{-6} $$

A relative shift of $5\times10^{-6}$ cannot in principle be measured with the spectrometers of the 1920s (even in today’s high-resolution spectroscopy it would be buried under the linewidth of the light source and the Doppler broadening due to thermal motion). This is the reason Compton chose the characteristic X-rays of molybdenum. The shift $\lambda_C(1-\cos\theta)$ is an absolute quantity independent of the incident wavelength, so the only way to make it visible in relative terms is to bring the incident wavelength itself close to $\lambda_C=2.4\ \mathrm{pm}$. The $70.9\ \mathrm{pm}$ of $\mathrm{Mo}\,K\alpha$ is about $29$ times $\lambda_C$, and gives an easily measurable shift of just $3\%$.

Verification. We check (3) with an independent formula. From the energy form of the Compton formula, $1/E'-1/E=(1-\cos\theta)/(m_ec^2)$, at $\theta=180^\circ$ we have

$$ T_e^{\max} = E\,\frac{2E/(m_ec^2)}{1+2E/(m_ec^2)} = 17.487\times\frac{0.06844}{1.06844}\ \mathrm{keV} = 1.120\ \mathrm{keV} $$

This agrees with the answer obtained via wavelengths. Furthermore, in the limit $E\ll m_ec^2$ the denominator approaches $1$ and $T_e^{\max}\to 2E^2/(m_ec^2)=2\times17.487^2/511\ \mathrm{keV}=1.197\ \mathrm{keV}$, which exceeds the correct value $1.120\ \mathrm{keV}$ by only $7\%$. The accuracy of the approximation is commensurate with the smallness of $E/m_ec^2=0.034$, which shows that the calculation has not broken down.

Meaning. The Compton edge is today a basic ingredient in reading $\gamma$-ray spectra. For example, for the $511\ \mathrm{keV}$ line from positron annihilation treated in Exercise 2.8, $2E/(m_ec^2)=2$, so $T_e^{\max}=511\times2/3=341\ \mathrm{keV}$: a step (the Compton edge) stands up there, and it always appears on the low-energy side of the photopeak.
