In interpreting detector spectra, the key point is not to mistake this step for “information about the sample.” On the other hand, the property that $\Delta\lambda$ is independent of the incident wavelength is also used in the opposite direction: with hard X-rays (of the $100\ \mathrm{keV}$ class) the shift can be made large, so from the shape of the scattered X-ray spectrum one can extract precisely the projection of the electron momentum density $n(\bm p)$ (the Compton profile). The “shift of the peak” that Compton measured as evidence for the particle nature of light has now taken on a new form in materials science: a means of measuring the “width of the peak.”

Exercise 2.3: Range, mediator mass, and screening length

Problem (restated)

Use $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$.

(1) If the range of a force is $1.0\ \mathrm{fm}$, what is the mass of the mediator?

(2) Find the range when a $K$ meson ($m=494\ \mathrm{MeV}$) is exchanged. Explain why the $K$-exchange contribution to the nuclear force is so small.

(3) The conduction electron density of copper is $n=8.47\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$. Find $k_F$ from $k_F=(3\pi^2n)^{1/3}$, convert it to atomic units ($1\ \mathrm{a.u.}=1.8897\ \text{Å}^{-1}$), and then find the Thomas–Fermi screening length $\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}$ from $k_{\mathrm{TF}}^2=4k_F/(\pi a_0)$.

(4) Convert the $\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}$ of (3) into an “effective photon mass.”

Solution

Strategy. We use Yukawa’s relation of this chapter, $R=\hbar/(mc)$, that is, $mc^2=\hbar c/R$, three times. The Yukawa potential $\ee^{-mr}/r$ and the Thomas–Fermi screening $\ee^{-r/\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}}/r$ are the same expression with only the symbols changed, so if we put $\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}$ directly in the place of $R$, we can read off the “effective mass of the photon.” Only (3) is dominated by unit conversion, so we proceed carefully, in separate stages.

(1) Substitute $R=1.0\ \mathrm{fm}$:

$$ mc^2 = \frac{\hbar c}{R} = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{1.0\ \mathrm{fm}} = 197.3\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

That is, about $200\ \mathrm{MeV}$, or $386$ times the electron mass. The actual $\pi$ meson has $m_\pi c^2=139.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and the corresponding range is $197.327/139.57=1.41\ \mathrm{fm}$. Yukawa’s estimate of the meson mass from the range of the nuclear force was exactly this one-line calculation.

(2) We use the same formula in reverse:

$$ R = \frac{\hbar c}{m_Kc^2} = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{494\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 0.399\ \mathrm{fm} $$

That is $0.40\ \mathrm{fm}$. This is less than half the charge radius of the proton, $0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$; to approach to the distance at which $K$ exchange becomes effective, two nucleons would have to overlap deeply. Since nucleons have a short-distance repulsive core, they cannot approach that closely, and geometrically the contribution is already small.

More decisive, however, is the prohibition by quantum numbers. The $K^+=u\bar s$ has strangeness $S=+1$. The strong interaction conserves $S$, so the vertex $N\to N+K$ at which a nucleon emits a $K$ would have $S:\,0\to0+1$ and does not occur. The only allowed process is $N\to\Lambda+K$ ($S:\,0\to-1+1=0$). Therefore, if a $K$ is exchanged between two nucleons, the nucleons at both ends are both changed into hyperons ($\Lambda$, $\Sigma$), and the final state is no longer $NN$. In other words, the contribution of the exchange of a single $K$ to the elastic $NN$ force is completely forbidden by strangeness conservation. $K$ exchange becomes meaningful in the $\Lambda N$ force, that is, in the physics of hypernuclei. The answer is that both the shortness of the range and the selection rule are at work.

(3) We divide the calculation into three stages.

Stage 1: Find the Fermi wave number in CGS units.

$$ k_F = (3\pi^2 n)^{1/3} = \left(3\pi^2\times8.47\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\right)^{1/3} = \left(2.508\times10^{24}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\right)^{1/3} = 1.359\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}} $$

Since $1\ \mathrm{cm}=10^{8}\ \text{Å}$, $k_F = 1.359\ \text{Å}^{-1}$, which rounds to $1.36\ \text{Å}^{-1}$.

Stage 2: Convert to atomic units. In atomic units the unit of length is $a_0=0.5292\ \text{Å}$, that is, $1\ \mathrm{a.u.}=1.8897\ \text{Å}^{-1}$, so

$$ k_F = \frac{1.359}{1.8897}\ \mathrm{a.u.} = 0.719\ \mathrm{a.u.} $$

Stage 3: The Thomas–Fermi wave number and screening length. In atomic units $a_0=1$, so $k_{\mathrm{TF}}^2=4k_F/\pi$, and

$$ k_{\mathrm{TF}} = \sqrt{\frac{4\times0.719}{\pi}} = \sqrt{0.9155} = 0.9568\ \mathrm{a.u.} = 0.9568\times1.8897\ \text{Å}^{-1} = 1.808\ \text{Å}^{-1} $$ $$ \lambda_{\mathrm{TF}} = \frac{1}{k_{\mathrm{TF}}} = 1.045\ \mathrm{a.u.} = 1.045\times0.5292\ \text{Å} = 0.553\ \text{Å} $$

That is, $\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}\approx0.55\ \text{Å}$.

(4) Converting $\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}$ to fm, $0.553\ \text{Å}=5.53\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{fm}$, so

$$ m_\gamma^{\mathrm{eff}}c^2 = \frac{\hbar c}{\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}} = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{5.53\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{fm}} = 3.57\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{MeV} = 3.6\ \mathrm{keV} $$

Inside copper, we may say that the photon mediating the static Coulomb interaction effectively has a mass of $3.6\ \mathrm{keV}$. This is a restatement in the sense that the pole of the static response function lies at $q^2=-k_{\mathrm{TF}}^2$, and it holds only for the static longitudinal response. The “mass” that a transverse-wave photon acquires in a metal is the plasma energy $\hbar\omega_p$ (about $11\ \mathrm{eV}$ for copper), which is different by orders of magnitude (Exercise 8.6(3)).

Verification. Let us reproduce the input electron density itself from the structure. Copper is face-centered cubic with lattice constant $a=3.615\ \text{Å}$, four atoms per unit cell, and one free electron per atom (the $4s$ electron of $3d^{10}4s^1$), so

$$ n = \frac{4}{(3.615\ \text{Å})^3} = \frac{4}{47.25\ \text{Å}^3} = 0.0847\ \text{Å}^{-3} = 8.47\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} $$

This agrees with the value in the problem statement. Next we compare with the aluminum values in this chapter. For Al, $k_F=0.926\ \mathrm{a.u.}$, $\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}=0.49\ \text{Å}$, and $m_\gamma^{\mathrm{eff}}c^2=4.0\ \mathrm{keV}$. Copper has a smaller $k_F$ ($0.719$), so $k_{\mathrm{TF}}\propto k_F^{1/2}$ is also smaller; the screening length is longer ($0.55>0.49\ \text{Å}$) and the effective photon mass is lighter ($3.6<4.0\ \mathrm{keV}$). The inequalities come out in the right direction, so there is no mix-up in the calculation. The dimensions also match: $\hbar c$ is in $\mathrm{MeV\,fm}$ and $\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}$ is in $\mathrm{fm}$, so the quotient is in $\mathrm{MeV}$.

Meaning. Since copper is fcc, its nearest-neighbor interatomic distance is $a/\sqrt2 = 3.615/1.414 = 2.56\ \text{Å}$. The value $\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}=0.55\ \text{Å}$ is $0.55/2.56=0.22$ times that, that is, only a little less than $1/4$. The screening factor $\ee^{-r/\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}}$ falls to $\ee^{-4.6}=1.0\times10^{-2}$ at the nearest-neighbor distance, so the extra charge of an impurity placed in a metal has already been $99\%$ canceled by the time it reaches the neighboring atom. It is thanks to this short screening length that impurities in a dilute alloy are “invisible” to one another, and that first-principles supercell calculations containing charged defects do not require such enormous cells. And from the particle-physics side, this is a familiar analog of the phenomenon in which a gauge field acquires mass (though, as noted above, the correspondence is limited to the static longitudinal response). In a superconductor the magnetic field decays with the London penetration depth $\lambda_L$, and this too can be translated into a photon mass $\hbar c/\lambda_L$ (for the London value of Al, $\lambda_L=16\ \mathrm{nm}$, it is $12.3\ \mathrm{eV}$; the measured penetration depth, including nonlocal effects, extends to about $50\ \mathrm{nm}$, and using that gives $3.9\ \mathrm{eV}$; Table 1.3 and Exercise 1.4(4) adopt the London value). The range of the weak interaction is only $2.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}$ because the $W$ boson has a mass of $80\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and the mechanism that gives it that mass (the Higgs mechanism) is the same logic that condensed matter physics had found earlier in superconductivity.

Exercise 2.4: Kinematics of beta decay and the neutrino mass

Problem (restated)

Let $m_n=939.565$, $m_p=938.272$, and $m_e=0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(1) Find the $Q$ value $Q=m_n-m_p-m_e$.

(2) Suppose the two-body decay $n\to p+e^-$ were to occur, and find the electron kinetic energy $T_e$. Explain, from the magnitude of the recoil energy of the proton, why it is nearly equal to the $Q$ of (1).

(3) In the actual three-body decay $n\to p+e^-+\bar\nu_e$, $T_e$ is distributed continuously from $0$ to $Q$. What is the kinematic configuration in which $T_e$ is maximal?

(4) To distinguish $m_\nu=0.45\ \mathrm{eV}$ in the beta decay of tritium ($Q=18.6\ \mathrm{keV}$), to how many digits must the endpoint energy be measured?

Solution

Strategy. We use exactly the same technique that we also used for Compton scattering in this chapter: “square the four-momentum to eliminate the particle we do not measure.” We work in natural units $\hbar=c=1$ with metric $\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$. All masses are handled in $\mathrm{MeV}$.

(1) Subtract, following the definition:

$$ Q = m_n - m_p - m_e = 939.565 - 938.272 - 0.511 = 0.782\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

$Q$ is the mass energy left over when all the final-state particles are at rest, that is, the total kinetic energy that the final state can share among its particles.

(2) Let the neutron at rest have $p_n^\mu=(m_n,\bm 0)$, and let $p_n=p_p+p_e$. To eliminate the proton, which we do not want to measure, we move terms across and square:

$$ p_p = p_n - p_e \quad\Longrightarrow\quad m_p^2 = p_p^2 = m_n^2 + m_e^2 - 2\,p_n\cdot p_e $$

Here $p_n\cdot p_e = m_n E_e$ (because the neutron is at rest, the dot product of the spatial components vanishes), so

$$ E_e = \frac{m_n^2+m_e^2-m_p^2}{2m_n} $$

Inserting numbers: $m_n^2=882782.39$, $m_e^2=0.2611$, $m_p^2=880354.35$ (all in $\mathrm{MeV^2}$), so

$$ E_e = \frac{882782.39+0.26-880354.35}{2\times939.565} = \frac{2428.30}{1879.13} = 1.29225\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ $$ T_e = E_e - m_e = 1.29225 - 0.511 = 0.78125\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The difference from $Q=0.78200\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is only $0.75\ \mathrm{keV}$. The origin of the difference is the recoil kinetic energy of the proton. To estimate it, note that the electron momentum is

$$ p_e = \sqrt{E_e^2-m_e^2} = \sqrt{1.29225^2-0.511^2} = 1.1869\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

and the proton has momentum of the same magnitude in the opposite direction, so (since the proton is sufficiently nonrelativistic)

$$ T_p \simeq \frac{p_e^2}{2m_p} = \frac{(1.1869)^2}{2\times938.272}\ \mathrm{MeV} = 7.51\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{MeV} = 0.751\ \mathrm{keV} $$

This agrees precisely with $Q-T_e = 0.75\ \mathrm{keV}$. The momentum is shared equally, but the kinetic energy is distributed in inverse proportion to the mass, so the proton, heavier by a factor $m_p/m_e\approx1836$, receives almost none of the kinetic energy. This is why $T_e\approx Q$.

(3) In a three-body decay the final-state momenta can be shared in many ways, so $T_e$ is continuously distributed. The electron obtains its maximum kinetic energy when the other two particles carry away as little energy as possible, that is, when the antineutrino momentum is zero. In that case $\bar\nu_e$ (if it is massless) carries away no energy either, and momentum conservation closes between the electron and the proton alone, so the kinematics is exactly the same as in the two-body decay of (2). Therefore the electron and the proton fly off in exactly opposite directions, and $T_e^{\max}=0.78125\ \mathrm{MeV}$. This is the endpoint of the $\beta$ spectrum.

Conversely, $T_e$ is minimal (zero) when the electron is almost at rest and $\bar\nu_e$ and the proton share the energy. This produces a continuous distribution $0\le T_e\le T_e^{\max}$. The continuous spectrum that Chadwick saw in 1914 was thus direct evidence for the existence of a third particle.

(4) If the neutrino has a mass, the endpoint moves down from $Q$ to $Q-m_\nu$, and the Kurie plot bends away from a straight line just before the endpoint. Therefore, to distinguish $m_\nu$ at the level of $0.45\ \mathrm{eV}$, the energy near the endpoint must be measured to a relative precision of

$$ \frac{m_\nu}{Q} = \frac{0.45\ \mathrm{eV}}{18.6\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{eV}} = 2.42\times10^{-5} $$

That is, five digits (the $10^{-5}$ level) of precision are required.

That is not the only difficulty. The fraction of decays that fall within $\Delta E$ of the endpoint is only $\sim(\Delta E/Q)^3$, obtained by integrating $\dd N/\dd T\propto(Q-T)^2$. With $\Delta E=0.45\ \mathrm{eV}$,

$$ \left(\frac{0.45}{18600}\right)^{3} = 1.4\times10^{-14} $$

so only one in $10^{14}$ decays yields a usable event. Experiments such as KATRIN need an enormous gaseous tritium source and long measurement times in order to overcome this statistical wall.

Verification. We check the $E_e$ of (2) by another route. From energy conservation, the total energy of the proton is $E_p=m_n-E_e=939.565-1.29225=938.27275\ \mathrm{MeV}$, so its kinetic energy is $E_p-m_p=0.00075\ \mathrm{MeV}=0.75\ \mathrm{keV}$. This agrees with the $0.751\ \mathrm{keV}$ obtained from the nonrelativistic approximation $p_e^2/(2m_p)$ to the two digits that survive this subtraction (if $E_e$ is carried to $1.2922493\ \mathrm{MeV}$, then $T_p=0.7507\ \mathrm{keV}$, and the two agree to four digits). The approximation is good because $T_p/m_p\sim8\times10^{-7}$, so everything is consistent. In fact, this agreement is no coincidence; it is an identity. From energy conservation $E_p=m_n-E_e$,

$$ T_p = E_p - m_p = m_n - m_p - E_e = (Q+m_e) - E_e = Q - T_e $$

so $T_e+T_p=Q$ holds without any approximation. This is just the interpretation in (1) that $Q$ is the total kinetic energy of the final state. Checking the limit as well: if we hold $Q$ fixed and let $m_p\to\infty$, then $T_p\simeq p_e^2/(2m_p)\to0$, so $T_e\to Q$. This agrees with the intuition that an infinitely heavy proton does not recoil and the electron receives all of $Q$. For the actual neutron, $T_p/Q = 0.751/782 = 9.6\times10^{-4}$, which is close to this limit to an accuracy of $0.1\%$.

Meaning. This exercise is the prototype of the reasoning of particle physics: “if energy goes missing, suspect an invisible particle.” And the difficulty in (4) comes down to experimental technique, and hence to a problem of materials. To measure the endpoint to $10^{-5}$, everything must be controlled below the $\mathrm{eV}$ level: the molecular final-state distribution of the tritium source itself, the scatter of the work function of the electrode surfaces (this is the very $W$ that appeared in the photoelectric effect in Section 2.2 of this chapter; even for the same gold it differs by $0.3\ \mathrm{eV}$ between crystal orientations), scattering from the substrate, and so on. The deepest question of particle physics, the absolute value of the neutrino mass, thus appears as a problem of surface science and materials purity.

Exercise 2.5: Putting the Gell-Mann–Nishijima relation to work

Problem (restated)

Answer the following about the Gell-Mann–Nishijima relation $Q=I_3+(B+S)/2$ of Chapter 2 of this book.

(1) Compute the charges of the $\Sigma^0$ ($I=1$, $I_3=0$, $B=1$, $S=-1$) and the $\Xi^0$ ($I=1/2$, $I_3=+1/2$, $B=1$, $S=-2$), and check that they agree with the actual values.

(2) Write down $I_3$, $B$, and $S$ of the antiproton $\bar p$, and show that the formula correctly gives $Q=-1$.

(3) When the charm quark is added, the formula is extended to $Q=I_3+(B+S+C)/2$ ($C$ is the charm number). Find the charge of the $D^+=c\bar d$ ($I_3=+1/2$, $B=0$, $S=0$, $C=+1$).

(4) Check that the formula holds for the $u$, $d$, and $s$ quarks themselves. Explain why the same formula holds for both hadrons and quarks.

Solution

Strategy. The calculation itself is only addition. The point lies in the combination of two properties: $Q$, $I_3$, $B$, $S$ (and $C$) are all additive quantum numbers, and the relation is a linear relation among the quantum numbers. Using the hypercharge $Y\equiv B+S$, we can write $Q=I_3+Y/2$.

(1) The $\Sigma^0$ has $B=1$ and $S=-1$, so $Y=B+S=1+(-1)=0$, and therefore

$$ Q = I_3 + \frac{Y}{2} = 0 + \frac{0}{2} = 0 $$

Indeed the $\Sigma^0$ is neutral. The $\Xi^0$ has $B=1$ and $S=-2$, so $Y=1+(-2)=-1$, and therefore

$$ Q = +\frac12 + \frac{-1}{2} = +\frac12-\frac12 = 0 $$

This is neutral too, in agreement with the actual value. Incidentally, looking at its partner in the same multiplet, the $\Xi^-$ ($I_3=-1/2$), we get $Q=-1/2-1/2=-1$, which is also correct. Within an isospin multiplet only $I_3$ changes while $Y$ is common, so the difference in $Q$ is exactly equal to $\Delta I_3$. This is why the charge steps by one within a multiplet.

(2) For an antiparticle, the signs of all additive quantum numbers are reversed (the mass and the magnitude of the spin are the same). The proton has $I_3=+1/2$, $B=+1$, $S=0$, so for the antiproton

$$ I_3(\bar p) = -\frac12, \qquad B(\bar p) = -1, \qquad S(\bar p) = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad Y(\bar p) = -1 $$

Therefore

$$ Q(\bar p) = -\frac12 + \frac{-1}{2} = -1 $$

Indeed $Q(\bar p)=-Q(p)=-1$. Since the relation is linear (with no constant term) in both $Q$ and $(I_3,Y)$, reversing the signs of all the inputs automatically reverses the output. That the formula holds trivially for antiparticles is a consequence of the fact that the linearity has no constant term.

(3) The $D^+$ has $B=0$, $S=0$, $C=+1$, so the extended hypercharge is $B+S+C=0+0+1=1$, and therefore

$$ Q = I_3 + \frac{B+S+C}{2} = +\frac12 + \frac{1}{2} = +1 $$

Verifying directly from the quark content, the charge of $c$ is $+2/3$ and that of $\bar d$ is $+1/3$, so $Q=2/3+1/3=+1$, which agrees. The $D^+=c\bar d$ has $I_3=+1/2$ because the only light quark carrying isospin is the $\bar d$, and the $I_3$ of $\bar d$ is $-(-1/2)=+1/2$ ($c$ is an isospin singlet with $I_3=0$).

(4) We check the three quarks in turn. All have $B=1/3$.

  • $u$: from $I_3=+1/2$ and $S=0$, $Y=1/3$. $Q=+\dfrac12+\dfrac{1/3}{2}=\dfrac12+\dfrac16=\dfrac23$ ✓
  • $d$: from $I_3=-1/2$ and $S=0$, $Y=1/3$. $Q=-\dfrac12+\dfrac16=-\dfrac13$ ✓
  • $s$: from $I_3=0$ and $S=-1$, $Y=1/3-1=-2/3$. $Q=0-\dfrac13=-\dfrac13$ ✓

The reason the same formula holds for both hadrons and quarks is as follows. $Q$, $I_3$, $B$, and $S$ are all additive quantum numbers, and the value for a composite system is the simple sum of the values of its constituents. Suppose now that $Q_a=I_{3a}+Y_a/2$ holds for each constituent $a$. Summing over the constituents, we obtain

$$ Q = \sum_a Q_a = \sum_a\left(I_{3a}+\frac{Y_a}{2}\right) = \sum_a I_{3a} + \frac12\sum_a Y_a = I_3 + \frac{Y}{2} $$

so the same form is preserved for the composite system. All we used along the way was the distributivity of the sum; the details of the binding (orbital angular momentum, spin coupling, strength of the interaction) do not enter at all. A linear relation is invariant under summing additive quantum numbers; that is all there is to it.

Looking deeper, $Q$, $I_3$, and $Y$ are all commuting generators (diagonal generators) of the flavor symmetry group, and $Q=I_3+Y/2$ is an identity among generators. An equality that holds as an operator equation holds automatically in every irreducible representation, and also in composite systems built from their tensor products. This is the group-theoretic restatement of “if it holds for quarks, it holds for hadrons.”

Verification. Table 2.5 of this chapter checks the relation by giving $I_3,B,S$ of the hadrons as measured values. So we reverse the direction and see whether the quantum numbers of the particles in the same table can be reproduced by assembling them from the quark content. This is a check that actually runs the additivity claim of (4).

$\Omega^-=sss$: $I_3=0+0+0=0$, $B=1/3\times3=1$, $S=(-1)\times3=-3$, so $Y=1-3=-2$. Therefore $Q=0+(-2)/2=-1$, in agreement with the value in the table. $K^+=u\bar s$: $I_3=+1/2+0=+1/2$, $B=1/3-1/3=0$, $S=0+(+1)=+1$ (since $S=-1$ for $s$, $\bar s$ has $S=+1$), so $Y=+1$ and $Q=1/2+1/2=+1$ ✓. For $K^-=\bar us$, all the signs are reversed, giving $I_3=-1/2$, $S=-1$, $Q=-1$ ✓. The reason $B=0$ comes out automatically for mesons is that the $B=\pm1/3$ of the quark and the antiquark cancel. The same operation can be carried out for all 11 entries of Table 2.5, and the values built up from the constituents agree without exception with those measured for the hadrons.

Meaning. This relation pointed ahead in two senses. First, the fact that the charge is determined by two independent numbers, $I_3$ and $Y$, suggests that the symmetry of the strong interaction is a group of rank 2. That group is SU(3), which led directly to the Eightfold Way and the quark model. Second, exactly the same form of formula reappears in the electroweak theory as $Q=T_3+Y_W/2$ (Chapter 13). Both reflect the same structure: “a $\mathrm{U}(1)$ charge appears as a linear combination of the diagonal generators of a larger group.”

For readers in materials science, it should suffice to say that the handling of additive quantum numbers follows the same logic as the bookkeeping of formal oxidation states and valence electron counts. The operation of adding up the electron numbers per formula unit, imposing electrical neutrality, and from it determining the valence of an unknown ion (for example, electron counting by the Zintl rule) makes use of precisely the fact that “a linear relation among additive labels is preserved for composite systems.” Only the objects differ; the logic is the same.

Exercise 2.6: The equal-spacing rule of the decuplet and the $\Omega^-$

Problem (restated)

Let $m(\Delta)=1232$, $m(\Sigma^*)=1385$, and $m(\Xi^*)=1533\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(1) Find the mass differences between adjacent rows, and state how well the equal-spacing rule holds.

(2) Predict the mass of the $\Omega^-$ from the equal-spacing rule, and find the relative error with respect to the measured value $1672.45\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(3) The $\Omega^-$ has $S=-3$. The lightest final state of a strong decay that conserves strangeness is $\Xi K$. Using $m(\Xi^0)=1314.9$ and $m(K^-)=493.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$, compute the threshold and show that the $\Omega^-$ cannot decay by the strong interaction.

(4) From the result of (3), what lifetime would you expect for the $\Omega^-$? Is this consistent with its track being visible in a bubble chamber? (Take $\tau=8.2\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{s}$ and $\beta\gamma\approx2$, and compute the flight distance.)

Solution

Strategy. (1) and (2) are only subtraction and extrapolation. (3) comes down to comparing the selection rule “the strong interaction conserves strangeness” with the energy threshold, and (4) comes down to the kinematics of obtaining the flight distance from the lifetime. The decuplet is arranged in four rows by the value of $Y$ ($\Delta$: $Y=1$, $\Sigma^*$: $Y=0$, $\Xi^*$: $Y=-1$, $\Omega^-$: $Y=-2$), and the equal-spacing rule is the statement that the mass differences between adjacent rows are equal.

(1) Take the differences between adjacent rows:

$$ m(\Sigma^*)-m(\Delta) = 1385-1232 = 153\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ $$ m(\Xi^*)-m(\Sigma^*) = 1533-1385 = 148\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The difference between the two spacings is $5\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and relative to the spacing itself (average $150.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$),

$$ \frac{153-148}{150.5} = 3.3\times10^{-2} = 3.3\% $$

That is, the equal-spacing rule holds to an accuracy of about $3\%$ (strictly, $3.3\%$). Considering that the masses within the decuplet change by as much as $24\%$, from $1232$ to $1533\ \mathrm{MeV}$, that is, that the SU(3) symmetry is clearly broken to a large extent, it is quite good agreement that the first-order perturbation prediction is right to $3\%$. The physical origin of the spacing is the mass increment from one additional $s$ quark for each step down (the difference of constituent masses, $m_s-m_{u,d}\approx150\ \mathrm{MeV}$).

(2) One more step down from the $\Xi^*$ is the $\Omega^-$. Using the average of the two spacings, $(153+148)/2=150.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$, as the spacing,

$$ m(\Omega^-)^{\mathrm{pred}} = 1533 + 150.5 = 1683.5\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ $$ \frac{1683.5-1672.45}{1672.45} = 6.61\times10^{-3} = 0.66\% $$

The prediction is right to $0.66\%$. Since the mass of an undiscovered particle was pinned down to within $1\%$, it is an extremely powerful prediction. Incidentally, if we use only the last spacing $148\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for the extrapolation, we get $1533+148=1681\ \mathrm{MeV}$ with an error of $0.51\%$, so the conclusion is unchanged either way. The value that Gell-Mann read out at the 1962 conference was $1685\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(3) The $\Omega^-$ has $Q=-1$ and $S=-3$. The strong interaction conserves both charge and strangeness, so the final state must satisfy both. The lightest combination of the $\Xi K$ type is

$$ \Omega^- \to \Xi^0 + K^- \qquad \big(Q:\ -1 \to 0+(-1)\ ✓, \quad S:\ -3 \to (-2)+(-1)\ ✓\big) $$

Its threshold (the sum of the rest masses of the final state) is

$$ m(\Xi^0)+m(K^-) = 1314.9+493.7 = 1808.6\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

This exceeds the $\Omega^-$ mass of $1672.45\ \mathrm{MeV}$ by as much as $136.15\ \mathrm{MeV}$. The other combination, $\Xi^-\bar K^0$, is $1321.7+497.6=1819.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$, which is heavier still. Therefore a strong decay that conserves $S$ is closed energetically.

On the other hand, $\Xi^0\pi^-$ has $1314.9+139.6=1454.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$, which is amply open energetically. However, this final state has $S=-2$, so $\Delta S=+1$, and it is forbidden for the strong interaction, which conserves strangeness. In the end, the only decay channel left for the $\Omega^-$ is the weak interaction, which allows $\Delta S=\pm1$.

(4) Since the decay is weak, the lifetime is expected to be of order $10^{-10}\ \mathrm{s}$, the same as for the similar $\Lambda$ ($2.6\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{s}$) and $\Xi$ ($1.6\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{s}$). The measured value is $\tau=8.2\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{s}$. The mean flight distance in the laboratory frame, including time dilation, is $\ell=\beta\gamma\,c\tau$, so

$$ \ell = 2\times(2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s})\times(8.2\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{s}) = 4.92\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{m} = 4.9\ \mathrm{cm} $$

This is about $5\ \mathrm{cm}$. In the $80$-inch ($203\ \mathrm{cm}$) liquid-hydrogen bubble chamber at BNL, this is a length clearly visible to the naked eye, and moreover the decay point can be identified on the photograph. This is fully consistent with the fact that the $\Omega^-$ could be identified as a “track” in 1964.

Verification. To contrast, we estimate what would happen if a strong decay were open. The $\Delta$ of the same decuplet has the strong decay $\Delta\to N\pi$ open, with width $\Gamma=117\ \mathrm{MeV}$. From the uncertainty relation the lifetime is

$$ \tau_\Delta = \frac{\hbar}{\Gamma} = \frac{6.582\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{MeV\,s}}{117\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 5.6\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{s}, \qquad c\tau_\Delta = 1.7\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m} = 1.7\ \mathrm{fm} $$

The flight distance is only about the size of one atomic nucleus, and it can never be seen in a bubble chamber (it can be observed only as a resonance peak in the mass distribution). The lifetime of the $\Omega^-$ is $1.5\times10^{13}$ times that of the $\Delta$, and this difference of $13$ orders of magnitude translates directly into the qualitative difference of “whether the track is visible or not.” As a dimensional check, $\hbar$ is in $\mathrm{MeV\,s}$ and $\Gamma$ in $\mathrm{MeV}$, so the quotient is in $\mathrm{s}$, which is correct.

Meaning. The essence of the story of the $\Omega^-$ is that the prediction of the mass (equal-spacing rule) and the prediction of the lifetime (selection rule) came out simultaneously from separate principles. The former comes from the assumption about how SU(3) is broken, the latter from the selection rule of strangeness conservation, and if either one had failed, the discovery would not have succeeded.

The argument “when a selection rule closes the path, the lifetime changes by orders of magnitude” appears in exactly the same form in materials science. In a direct-gap semiconductor (such as GaAs), momentum conservation is satisfied and the lifetime of radiative recombination is of order $\mathrm{ns}$, whereas in an indirect-gap one (Si), conservation of the wave number cannot be satisfied by the electron and the hole alone and the help of a phonon is needed, so the same recombination is slowed down to the $\mathrm{ms}$ level. When a conservation law forbids the main process, the system has no choice but to go through a weaker interaction (or a higher-order process), and as a result the lifetime is lengthened by many orders of magnitude. That the $\Omega^-$ left a track and that Si does not shine are different manifestations of the same logic.

Exercise 2.7: Counting colors with the $R$ ratio

Problem (restated)

Use the formula for the $R$ ratio in Chapter 2 of this book, $R=N_c\sum_iq_i^2$.

(1) Find $R$ with $N_c=3$ at $\sqrt s = 2.5\ \mathrm{GeV}$ (only $u,d,s$), $7\ \mathrm{GeV}$ ($+c$), and $30\ \mathrm{GeV}$ ($+b$).

(2) What happens if $N_c=1$? Compare with the measured values (about $2.2$, $3.6$, and $3.9$, respectively) and state which is supported.

(3) If there were an $e^+e^-$ collider with $\sqrt s > 2m_t = 345\ \mathrm{GeV}$, what would $R$ be?

(4) The first-order QCD correction is given by $R\to R(1+\alpha_s/\pi)$. Take $\alpha_s=0.14$ at $\sqrt s=30\ \mathrm{GeV}$, find the corrected value, and compare it with the measured $3.9$.

Solution

Strategy. $R$ counts “what the virtual photon can turn into,” weighted by the square of the charge. The sum runs over all quarks with $\sqrt s>2m_i$, that is, all quarks that can be pair-produced at that energy. The charges are $+2/3$ for the up-type quarks ($u,c,t$) and $-1/3$ for the down-type quarks ($d,s,b$); squaring gives $4/9$ and $1/9$, respectively.

(1) First we use the thresholds to decide which quarks enter the sum at each energy. Pair production requires $\sqrt s>2m_i$, so $c$ (from Table 2.11, $m_c=1.27\ \mathrm{GeV}$; the effective threshold for producing charm in the final state is $2m_D=3.73\ \mathrm{GeV}$) is not yet open at $2.5\ \mathrm{GeV}$ but is open at $7\ \mathrm{GeV}$. The $b$ quark ($m_b=4.18\ \mathrm{GeV}$, $2m_B=10.56\ \mathrm{GeV}$) is closed at $7\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and opens at $30\ \mathrm{GeV}$. The $t$ quark ($2m_t=345\ \mathrm{GeV}$) is far from open at any of these energies. This reproduces the assignment given in the problem statement. We then accumulate $\sum_iq_i^2$.

$\sqrt s=2.5\ \mathrm{GeV}$ ($u,d,s$):

$$ \sum_i q_i^2 = \frac49+\frac19+\frac19 = \frac69 = \frac23, \qquad R = 3\times\frac23 = 2 $$

$\sqrt s=7\ \mathrm{GeV}$ ($+c$, $q_c=+2/3$):

$$ \sum_i q_i^2 = \frac69+\frac49 = \frac{10}{9}, \qquad R = 3\times\frac{10}{9} = \frac{10}{3} = 3.33 $$

$\sqrt s=30\ \mathrm{GeV}$ ($+b$, $q_b=-1/3$):

$$ \sum_i q_i^2 = \frac{10}{9}+\frac19 = \frac{11}{9}, \qquad R = 3\times\frac{11}{9} = \frac{11}{3} = 3.67 $$

(2) For $N_c=1$, $R$ is simply equal to $\sum_iq_i^2$, so

$$ R = \frac23 = 0.67, \qquad \frac{10}{9} = 1.11, \qquad \frac{11}{9} = 1.22 $$

The measured values are about $2.2$, $3.6$, and $3.9$, respectively, so the $N_c=1$ prediction is $0.67/2.2=0.30$, $1.11/3.6=0.31$, and $1.22/3.9=0.31$ times the measured value; that is, in all three regions it comes out almost exactly $1/3$ of the measurement. A discrepancy of a factor of $3$ cannot possibly be made up by measurement error or correction terms. By contrast, the $N_c=3$ predictions $2$, $3.33$, and $3.67$ fall below the measurements by only $9\%$, $7\%$, and $6\%$, in that order, and this deviation is explained by the QCD correction $1+\alpha_s/\pi$ of (4)—the lower the energy, the larger $\alpha_s$ and hence the larger the correction, so even the trend that the deviation shrinks with increasing $\sqrt s$ is correct. Therefore $N_c=3$ is supported. Since $R$ is a ratio of cross sections, experimental normalization factors such as the accelerator luminosity and the detection efficiency almost entirely cancel, which makes it powerful: the number of colors can be counted without any calibration of absolute values.

(3) For $\sqrt s>2m_t$, all six quarks, up to the top, can be pair-produced. Splitting them into three up-type and three down-type quarks,

$$ \sum_i q_i^2 = 3\times\frac49 + 3\times\frac19 = \frac{12}{9}+\frac{3}{9} = \frac{15}{9} = \frac53 $$ $$ R = 3\times\frac53 = 5 $$

Note, however, that in reality near $\sqrt s=345\ \mathrm{GeV}$ the contribution of $Z$ boson exchange and the $\gamma$–$Z$ interference cannot be neglected, so this $R=5$ is “the value when only the electromagnetic contribution is counted.”

(4) The first-order QCD correction factor is

$$ 1+\frac{\alpha_s}{\pi} = 1+\frac{0.14}{3.1416} = 1+0.0446 = 1.0446 $$

Hence

$$ R_{\mathrm{corr}} = \frac{11}{3}\times1.0446 = 3.667\times1.0446 = 3.83 $$

The difference from the measured value $3.9$ is $(3.9-3.83)/3.9=1.8\%$, which agrees well within the measurement error. It is also qualitatively correct that the correction is positive (gluon emission is an additional open channel, so the cross section increases).

Verification. Checking with the steps rather than with the absolute value of $R$ gives a test that is insensitive to the experiment’s systematic errors. The jump when a new quark threshold is crossed is $\Delta R = N_cq^2$, so for $N_c=3$

$$ c\ \text{threshold:}\ \Delta R = 3\times\frac49 = \frac43 = 1.33, \qquad b\ \text{threshold:}\ \Delta R = 3\times\frac19 = \frac13 = 0.33 $$

The measured steps are $1.4$ for $2.2\to3.6$ and $0.3$ for $3.6\to3.9$. Both agree with the predictions. Moreover, the feature that the $c$ step is four times the $b$ step is exactly $q_c^2/q_b^2=(2/3)^2/(1/3)^2=4$, which independently supports the fractional charges of the quarks. As for dimensions, $R$ is a ratio of cross sections and hence dimensionless, and the right-hand side $N_c\sum q_i^2$ is also dimensionless, so the two are consistent.

Meaning. The $R$ ratio is a typical method that counts the number of internal degrees of freedom merely by measuring a ratio. We need not know at all how the final-state hadrons actually form (the details of hadronization); the counting works with only the picture that “the cross section is fixed at the moment the virtual photon creates a $q\bar q$ pair.”

The same argument appears throughout condensed matter physics. The Dulong–Petit $3R$ counts the vibrational degrees of freedom per atom; the low-temperature electronic specific-heat coefficient $\gamma$ counts the density of states at the Fermi level; and the conductance of a quantum point contact, which jumps in steps in units of $2e^2/h$, counts the number of channels times the spin degeneracy. All of these share the same structure: “the observable is proportional to the degeneracy, so reading off the steps counts the degrees of freedom.” One may regard the staircase of the $R$ ratio as the particle-physics version of the staircase of quantized conductance. And the counted $N_c=3$ was later found to be not a mere label but the gauge charge of the strong interaction, which led to QCD (Chapter 11).

Exercise 2.8: Numbers for positron annihilation spectroscopy

Problem (restated)

Let $m_ec^2=511\ \mathrm{keV}$; the atomic unit of momentum, $1\ \mathrm{a.u.}$, converted to energy is $3.729\ \mathrm{keV}$ ($=\hbar c/a_0$).

(1) When an $e^+e^-$ pair at rest annihilates into two photons, find the energy of each photon and the angle between them.

(2) For copper ($p_F=0.719\ \mathrm{a.u.}$ from Exercise 2.3), find the shift of the two-photon angular correlation, $\Delta\theta=p_T/(m_ec)$, and the Doppler shift, $\Delta E=p_Lc/2$, for annihilation with an electron at the edge of the Fermi surface.

(3) For aluminum ($\tau_b=166\ \mathrm{ps}$, $\tau_v=245\ \mathrm{ps}$), a mean lifetime $\bar\tau=180\ \mathrm{ps}$ was measured. Find the trapping rate $\kappa$ from the formula of the two-state trapping model in Chapter 2 of this book, and estimate the vacancy concentration $C_v$ with a specific trapping rate $\mu_v=2.0\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ (per atomic fraction).

(4) Using the Fano-factor formula of Chapter 2 of this book, $\Delta E_{\mathrm{FWHM}}=2.355\sqrt{F\epsilon E}$, examine the detector needed to resolve the Doppler shift in (2). Can high-purity Ge ($\epsilon=2.96\ \mathrm{eV}$, $F=0.13$) be used?

Solution

Strategy. (1) is four-momentum conservation in the rest frame; (2) amounts to substituting the $p_F$ of copper found in Exercise 2.3 into this chapter’s formulas for the Doppler shift and the angular correlation; (3) is algebra of the trapping model; and (4) is the resolution formula of a semiconductor detector. Note that the meaning of the conversion value $3.729\ \mathrm{keV}$ is that it is the factor that gives $pc$ in $\mathrm{keV}$ when the momentum $p$ is given in atomic units.

(1) The four-momentum of a stationary $e^+e^-$ pair is $P^\mu=(2m_ec^2,\bm 0)$. Let the final state be two photons $p_1^\mu,p_2^\mu$. Then

$$ \bm p_1 + \bm p_2 = \bm 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bm p_2 = -\bm p_1 $$

Since a photon has $E=\abs{\bm p}c$, $\abs{\bm p_1}=\abs{\bm p_2}$ gives $E_1=E_2$; combining this with energy conservation $E_1+E_2=2m_ec^2$ gives

$$ E_1 = E_2 = m_ec^2 = 511\ \mathrm{keV} $$

Because the momenta point in exactly opposite directions, the angle between the two photons is $180^\circ$.

Let us also check why a single photon will not do. The invariant mass of the initial state is $\sqrt{P^2}=2m_ec^2=1022\ \mathrm{keV}\ne0$, whereas a single real photon always has $p^2=0$. Therefore annihilation into one photon is kinematically forbidden. The foundation of all positron-annihilation measurements, “two $511\ \mathrm{keV}$ photons emerge back to back,” follows from this one remark.

(2) We convert the $p_F=0.719\ \mathrm{a.u.}$ of copper, found in Exercise 2.3, into energy:

$$ p_Fc = 0.719\times3.729\ \mathrm{keV} = 2.681\ \mathrm{keV} $$

The shift of the angular correlation (taking the transverse component $p_T=p_F$) is

$$ \Delta\theta = \frac{p_T}{m_ec} = \frac{p_Tc}{m_ec^2} = \frac{2.681}{511} = 5.25\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{rad} = 5.25\ \mathrm{mrad} $$

The Doppler shift (longitudinal component $p_L=p_F$) is

$$ \Delta E = \frac{p_Lc}{2} = \frac{2.681}{2}\ \mathrm{keV} = 1.34\ \mathrm{keV} $$

Since $p_L$ is distributed from $-p_F$ to $+p_F$, the overall broadening of the $511\ \mathrm{keV}$ peak is twice this, about $2.7\ \mathrm{keV}$.

(3) We insert the numbers into the formula of the two-state trapping model:

$$ \kappa = \frac{1}{\tau_b}\cdot\frac{\bar\tau-\tau_b}{\tau_v-\bar\tau} = \frac{1}{166\ \mathrm{ps}}\cdot\frac{180-166}{245-180} = \frac{1}{166\ \mathrm{ps}}\times\frac{14}{65} $$ $$ = \frac{0.2154}{166}\ \mathrm{ps^{-1}} = 1.297\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{ps^{-1}} = 1.30\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

(We used $1\ \mathrm{ps^{-1}}=10^{12}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$.) The vacancy concentration is

$$ C_v = \frac{\kappa}{\mu_v} = \frac{1.30\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}{2.0\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}} = 6.5\times10^{-6} $$

That is, about $6.5\ \mathrm{ppm}$. With the mean lifetime lengthened by a mere $14\ \mathrm{ps}$, monovacancies at a concentration of 6 to 7 per million atoms (that is, per $100$ ten-thousand atoms) can be quantified.

(4) We put $E=511\ \mathrm{keV}=5.11\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{eV}$ into high-purity Ge:

$$ \Delta E_{\mathrm{FWHM}} = 2.355\sqrt{F\epsilon E} = 2.355\sqrt{0.13\times2.96\ \mathrm{eV}\times5.11\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{eV}} $$ $$ = 2.355\times\sqrt{1.966\times10^{5}}\ \mathrm{eV} = 2.355\times443.4\ \mathrm{eV} = 1044\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.04\ \mathrm{keV} $$

Compared with the shift of $1.34\ \mathrm{keV}$ and the overall peak broadening of $2.7\ \mathrm{keV}$ found in (2), the resolution $1.04\ \mathrm{keV}$ is comparable to the shift and smaller than the total width by a factor of $2.5$. Therefore a Ge detector can resolve the Doppler broadening due to the Fermi motion in copper—barely, but reliably. In practice, electronic noise is added, giving about $1.2$–$1.3\ \mathrm{keV}$, but the measurement still works. This is why high-purity Ge is essential for Doppler spectroscopy of positron annihilation.

By contrast, an NaI(Tl) scintillator has a resolution at $511\ \mathrm{keV}$ of only $7\%$, that is, $36\ \mathrm{keV}$. The Doppler width of $2.7\ \mathrm{keV}$ is completely buried, and no information can be extracted.

Verification. We rebuild (4) starting again from the definition of the Fano factor. The number of electron-hole pairs that $511\ \mathrm{keV}$ creates in Ge is

$$ N = \frac{E}{\epsilon} = \frac{5.11\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{eV}}{2.96\ \mathrm{eV}} = 1.73\times10^{5}\ \text{pairs} $$

Its fluctuation is $\sigma_N=\sqrt{FN}=\sqrt{0.13\times1.73\times10^{5}}=150$, so the standard deviation converted to energy is $\sigma_E=\epsilon\sigma_N=2.96\times150=443\ \mathrm{eV}$, and the FWHM, $2.355$ times this, is $1044\ \mathrm{eV}$, in complete agreement with the value above. The dimensions also match: $F$ is dimensionless and $\epsilon$ and $E$ are both energies, so $\sqrt{F\epsilon E}$ is an energy.

We also check that (3) is physically reasonable. The monovacancy formation energy of Al is $E_f^v\approx0.67\ \mathrm{eV}$, so the temperature at which the thermal-equilibrium concentration $C_v=\ee^{-E_f^v/k_BT}$ becomes $6.5\times10^{-6}$ is

$$ k_BT = \frac{0.67\ \mathrm{eV}}{\ln(1/6.5\times10^{-6})} = \frac{0.67}{11.94}\ \mathrm{eV} = 0.056\ \mathrm{eV} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T = 651\ \mathrm{K} $$

This is $0.7$ times the melting point of Al, $933\ \mathrm{K}$, a perfectly natural value for the temperature range of annealing and quenching experiments. That a plausible temperature can be back-calculated from the measured value is corroborating evidence that the trapping model has been used correctly.

Meaning. This exercise shows the place where the three threads of this chapter—the antiparticle (the Dirac hole), the momentum distribution on the Fermi surface, and the detector material—meet at one point. The positron is the antiparticle demanded by the Dirac equation, and is a concept born of exactly the same logic as the hole in a semiconductor. When this positron is implanted into a material, its lifetime tells us the size of the open volume (down to monovacancies at the $\mathrm{ppm}$ level), and the Doppler broadening and angular correlation of the $511\ \mathrm{keV}$ line tell us the electron momentum density $n(\bm p)$. The latter is exactly the same physical quantity that the Compton profile of Exercise 4.6 (and Exercise 10.7) measures, so completely different experiments converge on the same $n(\bm p)$.

And as (4) shows, what ultimately determines what can be measured is the detector material. Without high-purity Ge, which satisfies the three conditions of a small band gap ($\epsilon=2.96\ \mathrm{eV}$), a small Fano factor ($F=0.13$), and the possibility of growing large single crystals with an impurity concentration of $10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ or less, the technique of Doppler spectroscopy of positron annihilation itself would not have existed. Detection technology in particle physics and materials science depend on each other; neither is a one-way street.

E.3 Solutions for Chapter 3: Dynamics of Elementary Particles — The Four Forces and Conservation Laws

Exercise 3.1: Making the coupling constants dimensionless

Problem (restated)

Following Section 3.1.2 of the main text, evaluate the dimensionless coupling constant of gravity. Use $G=6.674\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ and $\hbar c = 3.161\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{J\,m}$.

(1) Calculate $\alpha_G^{(e)} = Gm_e^2/(\hbar c)$ for the gravitational force between two electrons ($m_e = 9.109\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$).

(2) Find $\alpha/\alpha_G^{(e)}$ and compare it with the proton case ($1.2\times10^{36}$). Explain why the ratio is larger for electrons.

(3) What must the mass of a particle be for “gravity to become as strong as the electromagnetic force”? That is, find the $m$ that satisfies $Gm^2/(\hbar c)=\alpha$, and express it in GeV.

Solution

Strategy. We simply repeat what was done in Section 3.1.2 of the main text. That is, we divide the dimensionful quantity that expresses the strength of a force by $\hbar c$ to make it dimensionless. For the electromagnetic force the numerator is $e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$, and for gravity $Gm^2$ takes its place. This replacement is possible because the Coulomb force $\dfrac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\dfrac{e^2}{r^2}$ and the gravitational force $\dfrac{Gm^2}{r^2}$ both have the same form, $\dfrac{(\text{strength})}{r^2}$. The basis for the comparison is the main text’s

$$ \alpha = \frac{e^2}{4\pi\varepsilon_0\,\hbar c} = \frac{2.307\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{J\,m}}{3.161\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{J\,m}} = 7.298\times10^{-3} \simeq \frac{1}{137.036} $$

We use this value below.

(1) First we build the numerator. The square of the electron mass is

$$ m_e^2 = \left(9.109\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}\right)^2 = 8.2974\times10^{-61}\ \mathrm{kg^2} $$

Multiplying this by $G$ gives

$$ G m_e^2 = 6.674\times10^{-11}\times8.2974\times10^{-61} = 5.5377\times10^{-71}\ \mathrm{N\,m^2} $$

Let us check the units. Multiplying $[G]=\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}$ by $\mathrm{kg^2}$ gives $\mathrm{N\,m^2}=\mathrm{J\,m}$, which has exactly the same dimensions as $\hbar c$. The division therefore yields a dimensionless quantity:

$$ \alpha_G^{(e)} = \frac{G m_e^2}{\hbar c} = \frac{5.5377\times10^{-71}\ \mathrm{J\,m}}{3.161\times10^{-26}\ \mathrm{J\,m}} = 1.7519\times10^{-45} $$

That is, $\alpha_G^{(e)} = 1.75\times10^{-45}$.

(2) We take the ratio to the electromagnetic force:

$$ \frac{\alpha}{\alpha_G^{(e)}} = \frac{7.2974\times10^{-3}}{1.7519\times10^{-45}} = 4.165\times10^{42} $$

For the proton, from the main text’s $\alpha_G = Gm_p^2/(\hbar c) = 5.91\times10^{-39}$ we have

$$ \frac{\alpha}{\alpha_G^{(p)}} = \frac{7.2974\times10^{-3}}{5.910\times10^{-39}} = 1.235\times10^{36} $$

which is the main text’s $1.2\times10^{36}$. Taking the ratio of the two ratios gives

$$ \frac{\alpha/\alpha_G^{(e)}}{\alpha/\alpha_G^{(p)}} = \frac{\alpha_G^{(p)}}{\alpha_G^{(e)}} = \frac{m_p^2}{m_e^2} = \left(\frac{1.673\times10^{-27}}{9.109\times10^{-31}}\right)^2 = (1836.6)^2 = 3.373\times10^6 $$

Indeed, $4.165\times10^{42}/1.235\times10^{36}=3.37\times10^{6}$, in agreement.

The reason lies in the structure of the expressions themselves. The electron and the proton have electric charges of the same magnitude $e$, so $\alpha$ is common to both; but the “charge” of gravity, the mass, differs from particle to particle, and moreover $\alpha_G\propto m^2$. Since the electron is $1836$ times lighter than the proton, its gravitational coupling is smaller by a factor of $1836^2 = 3.4\times10^6$. As a result, between two electrons gravity is weaker than the electromagnetic force by as many as 42 orders of magnitude. The weakness of gravity is not a universal number; it changes by more than six orders of magnitude depending on which particle one is talking about, and this is the main point of this problem.

(3) Solving the condition $Gm^2/(\hbar c) = \alpha$ for $m$ gives

$$ m = \sqrt{\frac{\alpha\,\hbar c}{G}} $$

We insert the numbers. First, the numerator is

$$ \alpha\,\hbar c = 7.2974\times10^{-3}\times3.161\times10^{-26} = 2.3067\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{J\,m} $$

Dividing this by $G$ gives

$$ \frac{\alpha\,\hbar c}{G} = \frac{2.3067\times10^{-28}}{6.674\times10^{-11}} = 3.4562\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{kg^2} $$

(The unit is $\mathrm{J\,m}\div(\mathrm{N\,m^2/kg^2}) = \mathrm{kg^2}$.) Taking the square root,

$$ m = \sqrt{3.4562\times10^{-18}}\ \mathrm{kg} = 1.859\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{kg} $$

We convert this to a rest energy. Multiplying by $c^2 = 8.98755\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2}$,

$$ mc^2 = 1.859\times10^{-9}\times8.98755\times10^{16} = 1.671\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{J} $$

Dividing by $1\ \mathrm{GeV} = 1.6022\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J}$,

$$ mc^2 = \frac{1.671\times10^{8}}{1.6022\times10^{-10}} = 1.043\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

That is, $m = 1.86\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{kg} = 1.04\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{GeV}$. The same calculation with $\alpha$ dropped gives the Planck mass,

$$ M_{\mathrm{Pl}} = \sqrt{\frac{\hbar c}{G}} = \sqrt{4.7363\times10^{-16}}\ \mathrm{kg} = 2.176\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{kg} = 1.221\times10^{19}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

The ratio of the two is, obviously from the definitions, $\sqrt\alpha = 0.0854$, and $1.221\times10^{19}\times0.0854 = 1.043\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{GeV}$ returns us to the answer of (3).

Verification. We perform a double check of dimensions and consistency. As for dimensions, as seen in (1), both $Gm^2$ and $e^2/(4\pi\varepsilon_0)$ have the dimensions of $\mathrm{J\,m}$, and $\hbar c$ is also in $\mathrm{J\,m}$, so $\alpha$ and $\alpha_G$ are both pure numbers. This shows that the procedure of “dividing by $\hbar$ and $c$ to make the quantity dimensionless” is not an accident but a necessary consequence. As for consistency, the quotient of the two ratios computed independently in (2) agreed, to the second decimal place, with the square of the particle mass ratio, $(m_p/m_e)^2=3.37\times10^6$. Moreover, the answer to (3) reproduces the same number even via the analytic relation $m=\sqrt\alpha\,M_{\mathrm{Pl}}$. Since three routes independently arrive at the same conclusion, the calculation can be trusted.

Meaning. The result tells us two things. First, the reason why gravity can be ignored in the world of elementary particles has been fixed numerically. In a system of two electrons, gravity is only $10^{-43}$ of the electromagnetic force and is invisible in any precision experiment. This is why the gravitational constant $G$ never appears in first-principles calculations in materials science. That the Hamiltonian of density functional theory contains a Coulomb term but no gravitational term is not sloppiness; it is a justified approximation backed by a hierarchy of 42 orders of magnitude. Second, (3) shows that the mass scale at which gravity becomes comparable lies near the Planck mass, $10^{19}\ \mathrm{GeV}$. This is 15 orders of magnitude away from the energy reach of the LHC ($10^4\ \mathrm{GeV}$), which is the fundamental reason why quantum gravity cannot be studied in the laboratory. Note also that the mass dependence $\alpha_G\propto m^2$ is the flip side of the fact that gravity is a force whose “charge” has no sign and in which masses simply pile up. As stated in the Physical Meaning box of Section 3.1.2 of the main text, the reason gravity wins in everyday life is not that its coupling is strong, but that it is added up, unscreened, over $10^{51}$ particles.

Exercise 3.2: Mediator mass and range of the force

Problem (restated)

Use the range $R=\hbar c/(mc^2)$ of the Yukawa potential (derived in Section 3.1.3 of this book as $\phi(r) = \dfrac{g}{4\pi}\dfrac{\ee^{-mr}}{r}$).

(1) Find, in fm, the range of the force mediated by the $\rho$ meson ($m_\rho = 775.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$) and by the $Z^0$ ($m_Z=91.188\ \mathrm{GeV}$).

(2) Given that the range of the nuclear force is known experimentally to be about $1.4\ \mathrm{fm}$, estimate the mass of the mediator from Yukawa’s argument. Which actual particle is it?

(3) By what factor is the value of the Yukawa potential at $r = 2\ \mathrm{fm}$ smaller than that of the Coulomb potential ($m=0$) at the same position? Calculate it for the case of $\pi$ meson exchange ($R=1.41\ \mathrm{fm}$).

Solution

Strategy. There is only one tool to use: the conversion constant in natural units,

$$ \hbar c = 197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm} $$

which we use in two directions, as $R = \hbar c/(mc^2)$ and as $R = \hbar c/(\text{mass})$. Part (1) goes from mass to distance, and (2) is the inverse calculation from distance to mass. For (3) we use the fact that the ratio of the Yukawa potential to the Coulomb potential reduces to the exponential factor alone.

(1) For the $\rho$ meson, we put $m_\rho c^2 = 775.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$ in the denominator of $\hbar c$:

$$ R_\rho = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{775.3\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 0.2545\ \mathrm{fm} $$

For the $Z^0$, we need to match the units to MeV. Since $m_Z c^2 = 91.188\ \mathrm{GeV} = 91188\ \mathrm{MeV}$,

$$ R_Z = \frac{197.327}{91188}\ \mathrm{fm} = 2.164\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm} $$

That is, $R_\rho = 0.254\ \mathrm{fm}$ and $R_Z = 2.16\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}$. For reference, the value for the $W$ boson computed in the main text is $R_W = 197.327/80377 = 2.46\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}$, and the $Z$ is slightly shorter because it is heavier. The range of the $\rho$ is a little under one third of the proton radius ($\approx0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$), so it takes effect only when nucleons approach each other almost to contact. The range of the $Z$, on the other hand, is 1/400 of the proton radius, and it may be regarded as a contact interaction that acts effectively only at a point. This is the reason why the weak interaction at low energies could be written as Fermi’s four-fermion contact interaction (Section 3.2.3 of the main text).

(2) We solve the same formula in reverse. From $R = \hbar c/(mc^2)$,

$$ mc^2 = \frac{\hbar c}{R} = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{1.4\ \mathrm{fm}} = 140.9\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

That is, the nuclear force must be mediated by a particle with a mass of about $141\ \mathrm{MeV}$. The actual particle that fits is the $\pi$ meson. As in Table 3.7 of the main text, $m_{\pi^\pm} = 139.570\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $m_{\pi^0} = 134.977\ \mathrm{MeV}$, which differ by only 1% from the estimate of $141\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

Historically, the direction was the opposite. In 1935, Hideki Yukawa carried out this inverse calculation for a then-unknown mediator particle from a single experimental value, the range of the nuclear force, and predicted that there should exist a particle with a mass about 200 times that of the electron. The number “200 times” also comes out of the same formula. The range Yukawa adopted at the time was $2\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{cm} = 2\ \mathrm{fm}$, giving $197.327/2 = 98.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$; dividing this by the electron mass gives $98.7/0.511 = 193$ times, that is, about 200 times. Using the $1.4\ \mathrm{fm}$ of this problem gives $140.9/0.511 = 276$ times, which is even closer to the actual $\pi^\pm$ value of $139.570/0.511 = 273$ times. Merely tightening the estimate of the range from $2\ \mathrm{fm}$ to $1.4\ \mathrm{fm}$ shrinks a discrepancy of $3$ tenths to $1\ \%$. The accuracy of the inverse calculation is determined entirely by the accuracy of the input, the range. In 1947 the $\pi$ meson was discovered in cosmic rays, and the prediction was confirmed. This line of reasoning, guessing the mass of an undiscovered particle from a single number, is exactly the same type of inference as the prediction of the charm quark mass by the GIM mechanism in Section 3.4.4 of the main text.

(3) We take the ratio of the Yukawa potential to the Coulomb potential with the same source strength (the case $m=0$). Since the factor $1/r$ is common, it cancels neatly:

$$ \frac{\phi_{\text{Yukawa}}(r)}{\phi_{\text{Coulomb}}(r)} = \frac{\dfrac{g}{4\pi}\dfrac{\ee^{-mr}}{r}}{\dfrac{g}{4\pi}\dfrac{1}{r}} = \ee^{-mr} = \ee^{-r/R} $$

Putting in $R = 1.41\ \mathrm{fm}$ and $r = 2\ \mathrm{fm}$, the exponent first becomes

$$ \frac{r}{R} = \frac{2}{1.41} = 1.4184 $$

Therefore

$$ \ee^{-1.4184} = 0.2421 $$

That is, about $24\ \%$ of the Coulomb-type case. Using the more accurate $R = \hbar c/m_{\pi^\pm}c^2 = 197.327/139.570 = 1.4138\ \mathrm{fm}$ gives $\ee^{-2/1.4138} = \ee^{-1.4147} = 0.2430$, which is again $24\ \%$, so the conclusion does not change.

Verification. We check from three angles. First, dimensions: $\hbar c$ is in $\mathrm{MeV\,fm}$ and the mass energy is in $\mathrm{MeV}$, so the quotient is in $\mathrm{fm}$; the answers to (1) and (2) both have the correct dimensions of length and energy, respectively. Second, mutual consistency: putting the $141\ \mathrm{MeV}$ obtained in (2) back into the formula of (1) gives $197.327/141 = 1.40\ \mathrm{fm}$, which returns to the starting value of $1.4\ \mathrm{fm}$. Third, limits: the ratio $\ee^{-r/R}$ in (3) approaches $1$ as $m\to0$ ($R\to\infty$), reproducing the Coulomb potential itself. Also, it falls to $0$ as $r\to\infty$, which is consistent with the Yukawa force having a finite range. Furthermore, setting $r=R$ gives the ratio $\ee^{-1}=0.368$, which also agrees with the definition “the range is the distance over which the potential falls to $1/\ee$.”

Meaning. This exercise is practice in the relation “one reciprocal is one piece of physics,” which this book uses repeatedly. The reciprocal of the mediator mass is the range of the force; a heavy mediator gives a short-range force, and a massless mediator gives a force that reaches to infinity. What matters for materials scientists, as emphasized in Section 3.1.3 of the main text, is that exactly the same expression appears in the screened Coulomb interaction in a metal, $\ee^{-k_{\mathrm{TF}}r}/r$. There the Thomas–Fermi wave number $k_{\mathrm{TF}}$ occupies the place of $m$, and the screening length $1/k_{\mathrm{TF}}$ becomes the range. For copper the screening length is $1/k_{\mathrm{TF}}\approx0.55\ \AA$. Matching the units,

$$ 0.55\ \AA = 0.55\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m} = 5.5\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m} = 5.5\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{fm} $$

which is nearly 40,000 times the $\pi$ meson range of $1.41\ \mathrm{fm}$. If we subject this to exactly the same inverse calculation as in (2), we obtain the “effective mass of a photon in copper” as

$$ \frac{\hbar c}{1/k_{\mathrm{TF}}} = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{5.5\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{fm}} = 3.59\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{MeV} \approx 3.6\ \mathrm{keV} $$

A photon in vacuum is massless and reaches to infinity, but inside copper it is screened by the sea of electrons and, as far as the static Coulomb interaction is concerned, behaves as if it were a particle with a mass of $3.6\ \mathrm{keV}$. Compared with the $141\ \mathrm{MeV}$ of the $\pi$ meson it is lighter by a factor of $141/0.0036 = 3.9\times10^4$, and its range is longer by exactly the same factor of $3.9\times10^4$ ($5.5\times10^4/1.41 = 3.9\times10^4$). The fact that mass and range are reciprocals of each other shows up as the agreement of the two ratios. In other words, the very same calculation by which Yukawa predicted the $\pi$ meson in part (2) of this exercise is what materials scientists carry out every day in discussing screening lengths. The only difference is that in the former $m$ is a property of the vacuum, whereas in the latter $k_{\mathrm{TF}}$ is a property of matter, namely the electron density.

Exercise 3.3: Counting QED diagrams

Problem (restated)

Let time flow from left to right, and consider only lowest-order diagrams (those with the fewest vertices).

(1) Draw all the lowest-order diagrams for $e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-$. How many are there? Explain, from the properties of the vertex, why the $t$-channel and $u$-channel cannot be drawn.

(2) Draw all the lowest-order diagrams for $\gamma\gamma\to e^+e^-$ (the Breit–Wheeler process). How many are there?

(3) For light-by-light scattering $\gamma\gamma\to\gamma\gamma$, no diagram with two vertices can be drawn. The lowest order is a diagram in which the amplitude goes once around an electron loop, with four vertices. State the power of $\alpha$ to which the cross section of this process is proportional, and find its numerical value. Answer the question “Why do two laser beams pass straight through each other?”

Solution

Strategy. We apply, exactly as written, the three-step procedure given in the “Why?” box of Section 3.2.4 of the main text. That is, we ask in turn: (i) can the two incoming particles be collapsed into a single internal line (the $s$-channel)? (ii) can particle 1 and particle 3 be joined at a single vertex (the $t$-channel)? (iii) can particle 1 and particle 4 be joined at a single vertex (the $u$-channel)? Every criterion rests on the property of the fundamental vertex in Section 3.2.1 of the main text: “two fermion lines and one photon line meet at a point, and the incoming fermion and the outgoing fermion must be of the same kind.”

(1) The external lines are $e^+$ and $e^-$ on the incoming side and $\mu^+$ and $\mu^-$ on the outgoing side.

First we try the $s$-channel. Since $e^+$ and $e^-$ are a particle and its antiparticle, reading rule 5 of Section 3.2.2 of the main text ($e^+e^-\to\gamma$) lets us gather them at one vertex into a single photon line. The charge is $+1+(-1)=0$, which matches the photon charge $0$. If we open the other end of that photon line according to reading rule 6 ($\gamma\to\mu^+\mu^-$), then $\mu^+\mu^-$ comes out. In this way we obtain one diagram with two vertices and one internal line. The four-momentum carried by the internal line is $p_1+p_2$, so its square is $s=(p_1+p_2)^2$, and this is indeed the $s$-channel.

Next we try the $t$-channel. This requires the incoming $e^-$ and the outgoing $\mu^-$ to be joined directly at one vertex. However, at a QED vertex the incoming fermion and the outgoing fermion must be of the same kind. A vertex at which $e^-$ comes in and $\mu^-$ goes out, that is, a three-way junction $e^-\to\mu^-+\gamma$, does not exist. This is because the photon couples only to charge and has no ability to change the lepton flavor (generation). For the same reason the $u$-channel (joining the incoming $e^-$ and the outgoing $\mu^+$) cannot be drawn either.

Therefore there is only one lowest-order diagram, and it is the $s$-channel only. This corresponds to the last row of Table 3.3 of the main text.

This fact of “only one diagram” is very convenient theoretically. Because there is no interference term to consider, the cross section takes its simplest form, and $e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-$ is a reference process used for the absolute calibration of cross sections in accelerator experiments. The reason the coupling constant cancels cleanly in the $R$ ratio of Section 3.3.1 of the main text when the final state is simply changed from $\mu^+\mu^-$ to $q\bar q$ is also that both are described by the same single diagram.

(2) The external lines are two photons on the incoming side and $e^+$ and $e^-$ on the outgoing side.

We try the $s$-channel. To collapse the two incoming photons into a single internal line, we would need a vertex where two photons and one other line meet. The QED vertex consists of two fermions and one photon; a vertex with two incoming photons does not exist. Hence the $s$-channel cannot be drawn.

What remains is a diagram in which two vertices are joined by an internal fermion line. We need only assign one of the incoming photons (photon 1) to the vertex on the outgoing $e^+$ side and the other (photon 2) to the vertex on the outgoing $e^-$ side. There are two ways to decide which photon goes to which vertex, and these correspond to the $t$-channel and the $u$-channel. Concretely, the reading is as follows: at the first vertex photon 1 opens up and creates a real $e^+$ and a virtual electron (this is reading rule 6 of Section 3.2.2 of the main text, $\gamma\to e^++e^-$, with one leg made virtual), and that virtual electron absorbs photon 2 at the second vertex and becomes a real $e^-$ (reading rule 2, $e^-+\gamma\to e^-$). The line running through the interior is an electron off the mass shell, with $p^2\neq m_e^2$.

Therefore there are two lowest-order diagrams. This is nothing but the time reversal of the pair annihilation $e^+e^-\to\gamma\gamma$ of Figure 3.4(c)(d) of the main text. Because the two photons are identical bosons, we add the diagram with the photons exchanged with the same sign (the symmetrization rule of Section 3.2.4 of the main text).

(3) When the external lines are four photons, a diagram cannot be built with two vertices. A photon can only attach to a fermion line, so accommodating four photons requires four vertices, and since that fermion line cannot go out as an external line, it becomes a closed loop. That is, the diagram is a box that goes once around an electron loop.

Each vertex contributes a factor $e=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}$ to the amplitude, so the amplitude with four vertices is

$$ \mathcal{M} \propto e^4 = (4\pi\alpha)^2 $$

The cross section is proportional to the square of the amplitude, so

$$ \sigma \propto \abs{\mathcal{M}}^2 \propto e^8 \propto \alpha^4 $$

that is, it is proportional to the fourth power of $\alpha$. The numerical value is

$$ \alpha^4 = \left(7.2974\times10^{-3}\right)^4 $$

Computing step by step, $\alpha^2 = 5.3252\times10^{-5}$, and squaring this gives

$$ \alpha^4 = \left(5.3252\times10^{-5}\right)^2 = 2.836\times10^{-9} $$

Compared with the lowest-order QED process (two vertices, $\sigma\propto\alpha^2 = 5.33\times10^{-5}$), it is suppressed by a further factor of $\alpha^2 = 5.3\times10^{-5}$.

The answer to “why do two laser beams pass right through each other?” has two layers. First, as stated in Section 3.3.3 of the main text, the photon carries no charge, so there is no direct vertex among photons. The only fundamental vertex of QED is the three-way junction of two fermions and one photon; there are no vertices with three or four photons. Therefore light and light do not interact at all “at lowest order.” Second, the interaction is nevertheless not zero: scattering can occur indirectly through virtual electron–positron pairs (vacuum fluctuations). But the probability is only of order $\alpha^4 = 3\times10^{-9}$, that is, three parts in a billion. At laboratory laser intensities, even if scattering occurs with this probability there is no way to detect it, and the beams pass through each other. Note that in the strong interaction the situation is completely different: gluons carry color charge, so three-point and four-point self-coupling vertices exist from the lowest order on (Figure 3.5b,c of the main text). “Light passes through light, but gluons do not pass through gluons”—this single difference gives rise to asymptotic freedom and confinement.

Verification. We check both the consistency of the counting and the numerical value. For the counting: of the six processes listed in Table 3.3 of the main text, the two among the processes treated in this problem that appear in the table ($e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-$ with one diagram and $\gamma\gamma\to e^+e^-$ with two diagrams) agree with the “number of diagrams” column of the table ($\gamma\gamma\to\gamma\gamma$ is not listed in Table 3.3, so it cannot be compared). Moreover, the answer to (2) is related by time reversal to the pair annihilation $e^+e^-\to\gamma\gamma$ (two diagrams in Table 3.3), and reversing time should not change the number of diagrams, so the answer of two diagrams is automatically consistent with the table. For the numerical value, we compute $\alpha^4$ in two ways. Using $\alpha=1/137.036$, $\alpha^4 = 1/137.036^4 = 1/(3.5266\times10^{8}) = 2.836\times10^{-9}$, which agrees with the $2.836\times10^{-9}$ obtained directly from $(7.2974\times10^{-3})^4$. As for dimensions, the question asks not for the cross section itself but for “which power of $\alpha$,” so since $\alpha$ is dimensionless, it is the proportionality coefficient that carries the dimension of area (in fact the combination $\alpha^4/m_e^2$ appears).

Meaning. The lesson of this problem is that “the number of diagrams that can be drawn and the number of vertices alone fix the order of magnitude of a measurable quantity.” Without computing anything inside the matrix element, we can say at once that $\gamma\gamma\to\gamma\gamma$ occurs only $\alpha^2 = 5.33\times10^{-5}$ times as often as $\gamma\gamma\to e^+e^-$, that is, about one part in 20,000 (it is merely a tally: two more vertices bring two extra factors of $\alpha$). This is why, before entering the full-scale calculations from Chapter 8 on, this chapter trains us to “think in pictures.” Note that $\gamma\gamma\to\gamma\gamma$ is not forbidden in principle: in 2017 ATLAS obtained $4.4\sigma$ evidence in ultraperipheral collisions of lead ions (in which the strong electromagnetic field is regarded as a beam of photons), and in 2019 ATLAS ($8.2\sigma$) and CMS reached observations exceeding $5\sigma$. The connection to materials science is also clear. In vacuum the effective interaction between photons is suppressed to $\alpha^4$, but in matter the story is completely different. The Kerr effect and second-harmonic generation in nonlinear optics are nothing but an “effective photon–photon interaction” in which bound electrons mediate between the photons. Whereas the vacuum electron–positron pair requires an excitation energy equal to the mass $2m_e = 1.02\ \mathrm{MeV}$, valence electrons in a solid can be excited at the eV order, so the same mechanism becomes six orders of magnitude easier. The magnitude of the nonlinear optical constants can be read as measuring how much more “polarizable” the medium is than the vacuum.

Exercise 3.4: Color singlets and the eight gluons

Problem (restated)

Write the color states as $\ket{r},\ket{g},\ket{b}$ and the anticolors as $\ket{\bar r},\ket{\bar g},\ket{\bar b}$, and assume that these form an orthonormal system.

(1) Verify that $\ket{\psi_1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}(r\bar r+g\bar g+b\bar b)$, $\ket{\psi_2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(r\bar r-g\bar g)$, and $\ket{\psi_3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt6}(r\bar r+g\bar g-2b\bar b)$ are orthonormal.

(2) The number of gauge fields of $SU(N)$ is $N^2-1$. Find it for $N=2,3,5$. Also, how many would there be for $U(3)$?

(3) $\mathbf3\otimes\mathbf3 = \mathbf6\oplus\bar{\mathbf3}$ does not contain a singlet $\mathbf1$. Verify the dimension count $3\times3=6+3$, and from this conclude that “a particle made of only two quarks (a diquark) cannot exist on its own.” On the other hand, $\mathbf3\otimes\mathbf3\otimes\mathbf3$ is $\mathbf{10}\oplus\mathbf8\oplus\mathbf8\oplus\mathbf1$, with dimensions $27 = 10+8+8+1$. Since there is one singlet, baryons can exist.

Solution

Strategy. (1) is merely a linear algebra computation. Using the orthonormality $\braket{i\bar j|k\bar l} = \delta_{ik}\delta_{jl}$, we just take sums of products of coefficients. For (2) we apply the formula in the Math Note of Section 3.3.2 of the main text. (3) combines the addition of dimensions with an argument about what the invariant tensors of $SU(3)$ are.

(1) Each of the three states is a linear combination of the three mutually orthogonal basis states $r\bar r,\ g\bar g,\ b\bar b$, so it suffices to compute the inner products of the coefficient vectors. Writing the coefficients out,

$$ \ket{\psi_1}:\ \frac{1}{\sqrt3}(1,1,1),\qquad \ket{\psi_2}:\ \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,-1,0),\qquad \ket{\psi_3}:\ \frac{1}{\sqrt6}(1,1,-2) $$

Normalization. We check that the sum of the squares of the coefficients is 1 for each:

$$ \braket{\psi_1|\psi_1} = \frac{1}{3}\left(1^2+1^2+1^2\right) = \frac{3}{3} = 1 $$ $$ \braket{\psi_2|\psi_2} = \frac{1}{2}\left(1^2+(-1)^2\right) = \frac{2}{2} = 1 $$ $$ \braket{\psi_3|\psi_3} = \frac{1}{6}\left(1^2+1^2+(-2)^2\right) = \frac{1+1+4}{6} = \frac{6}{6} = 1 $$

Orthogonality. We take the sum of the products of the coefficients for each distinct pair:

$$ \braket{\psi_1|\psi_2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(1\cdot1 + 1\cdot(-1) + 1\cdot0\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}\left(1-1+0\right) = 0 $$ $$ \braket{\psi_1|\psi_3} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\left(1\cdot1+1\cdot1+1\cdot(-2)\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{18}}\left(1+1-2\right) = 0 $$ $$ \braket{\psi_2|\psi_3} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt6}\left(1\cdot1+(-1)\cdot1+0\cdot(-2)\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{12}}\left(1-1+0\right) = 0 $$

Hence the three form an orthonormal set. Note that all the coefficients are real, so taking the complex conjugate does not affect the result.

Physically, of these three only $\ket{\psi_1}$ is special. It is the combination that adds up the three colors on an equal footing, and it does not change at all under a relabeling of colors (an $SU(3)$ transformation). That is, it is a color singlet. The remaining $\ket{\psi_2},\ket{\psi_3}$ are asymmetric combinations, “the difference between $r$ and $g$” and “$b$ alone is left out,” so their form changes when the colors are rotated. As in Section 3.3.2 of the main text, the six off-diagonal states (such as $r\bar g$) together with these two make a total of eight forming an octet, and only $\ket{\psi_1}$ is pushed out of $SU(3)$.

(2) Applying the formula $N^2-1$:

$$ N=2:\ 2^2-1 = 3,\qquad N=3:\ 3^2-1 = 8,\qquad N=5:\ 5^2-1 = 24 $$

For $U(3)$ the condition that the determinant be 1 is not imposed, so the dimension is $N^2 = 9$. That is, there are nine.

Each of these has a physical counterpart. The three for $N=2$ are the gauge fields $W^1,W^2,W^3$ of $SU(2)_L$ (or, in condensed matter physics, the three generators $\sigma^x,\sigma^y,\sigma^z$ of spin $SU(2)$). The eight for $N=3$ are the gluons of QCD, whose generators are the Gell-Mann matrices $\lambda^a/2$ ($a=1,\ldots,8$). The 24 for $N=5$ is the number of gauge fields of the grand unification group $SU(5)$ mentioned in Section 3.6.3 of the main text, and its breakdown is the $8+3+1=12$ of the Standard Model plus the 12 of the new particles $X,Y$ that convert quarks into leptons. And the ninth one of $U(3)$ is the color-singlet gluon corresponding to $\ket{\psi_1}$ of (1). If it existed, being a color singlet it would not be confined, and a “second electromagnetic force” with infinite range would act among all hadrons, but no such force has been observed. That the gauge group of QCD is $SU(3)$ and not $U(3)$ is a requirement of experimental fact.

(3) First we confirm the dimension count. The states of $\mathbf3\otimes\mathbf3$ are the nine combinations $q_i q_j$ ($i,j = r,g,b$), so

$$ 3\times3 = 9 $$

Dividing these into the part symmetric under exchange of the indices and the antisymmetric part, the symmetric combinations, of the form $q_iq_j+q_jq_i$, number $3\cdot4/2 = 6$, and the antisymmetric combinations, of the form $q_iq_j-q_jq_i$, number $3\cdot2/2 = 3$. Altogether,

$$ 9 = 6 + 3 $$

and the dimensions indeed match those of $\mathbf3\otimes\mathbf3 = \mathbf6\oplus\bar{\mathbf3}$ (the three antisymmetric ones behave as the antifundamental representation $\bar{\mathbf3}$, in the form $\varepsilon_{ijk}q_jq_k$). Neither component has dimension 1, so no singlet $\mathbf1$ appears at all in this decomposition.

Why none appears becomes clearer in the language of invariant tensors. The invariant tensors of $SU(3)$ are only $\delta^i_{\ j}$ (one upper and one lower index) and $\varepsilon_{ijk},\ \varepsilon^{ijk}$ (three indices of the same kind). Making a singlet means contracting all the color indices completely with invariant tensors. Two quarks carry two lower indices, so $\delta$, which needs one upper and one lower index, cannot be used, and $\varepsilon$ needs three indices, so one is short. Hence they cannot be contracted completely, and a singlet cannot be made.

The principle of confinement (Section 3.3.6 of the main text) states that “particles appearing in nature must be color singlets.” Since a diquark $qq$ cannot be a color singlet, we conclude that it cannot be extracted into vacuum as a free-standing particle. A diquark is a correlation that has meaning only inside a baryon or a tetraquark, insofar as it combines with the remaining quarks to make the whole a singlet.

On the other hand, for $\mathbf3\otimes\mathbf3\otimes\mathbf3$ the number of states

$$ 3\times3\times3 = 27 = 10 + 8 + 8 + 1 $$

decomposes as shown, and one singlet appears at the end. This is the totally antisymmetric combination $\varepsilon_{ijk}\ket{i}\ket{j}\ket{k}/\sqrt6$, and it corresponds to the fact that the three indices can be contracted exactly and completely with $\varepsilon_{ijk}$. This is why baryons can exist. By the same counting, a meson, in $\mathbf3\otimes\bar{\mathbf3}$, can have its one upper and one lower index contracted with $\delta^i_{\ j}$, and is realized as the singlet in $9 = 8+1$.

Verification. We make three independent checks. First, the completeness in (1): $\ket{\psi_1},\ket{\psi_2},\ket{\psi_3}$ should be an orthonormal basis of the three-dimensional diagonal subspace, so the sum of the projection operators must equal the identity matrix. Adding the squares of the coefficients component by component, the $r\bar r$ component gives $1/3+1/2+1/6 = 2/6+3/6+1/6 = 1$, the $g\bar g$ component also gives $1/3+1/2+1/6 = 1$, and the $b\bar b$ component gives $1/3+0+4/6 = 1/3+2/3 = 1$; all are 1. Hence the three exhaust the diagonal subspace, and nothing is missing from the calculation. Second, the consistency of (2): the difference between the $9$ of $U(3)$ and the $8$ of $SU(3)$ is $1$, which agrees with the number of parameters removed by the determinant condition, and also with the number of singlets $\ket{\psi_1}$ in (1). Three ways of counting point to the same “1.” Third, the dimensions in (3): $6+3 = 9$ and $10+8+8+1 = 27$ agree with the left-hand sides $3^2$ and $3^3$, respectively. In a decomposition of representations the total dimension is always conserved, so this satisfies a necessary condition for the decomposition to be correct.

Meaning. This exercise shows that a single question, “can a singlet be made?”, decides which kinds of particles can exist in nature. $q\bar q$ and $qqq$ are allowed, and $qq$ is not. Tetraquarks $qq\bar q\bar q$ and pentaquarks $qqqq\bar q$ can form singlets and so are allowed, and indeed they have been discovered since 2003. What matters for materials scientists, as stated in Section 3.3.6 of the main text, is that for $SU(2)$ this contraction with $\varepsilon$ becomes the spin singlet $(\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}-\ket{\downarrow\uparrow})/\sqrt2$, that is, the valence-electron pair of a chemical bond itself. For $SU(2)$ the index of $\varepsilon_{\alpha\beta}$ has two slots, so two particles can make a singlet, whereas for $SU(3)$ the index of $\varepsilon_{ijk}$ has three slots, so three are needed. The two seemingly unrelated facts “a covalent bond is two electrons, a baryon is three quarks” have the same origin: the number of indices of the $\varepsilon$ tensor. And, as the main text points out, the method of extending $SU(2)$ to $SU(N)$ and doing a $1/N$ expansion in the RVB theory and in the mean-field theory of the Kondo lattice, and the large-$N_c$ expansion of 't Hooft, are literally the same expansion.

Exercise 3.5: Getting a feel for the string tension

Problem (restated)

Let the string tension be $\sigma = 0.9\ \mathrm{GeV/fm}$, the constituent mass of a light quark $m_q\approx0.33\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and $m_\pi = 0.140\ \mathrm{GeV}$.

(1) Find the energy required to pull a quark and an antiquark $1\ \mathrm{fm}$ apart, and compare it with the energy needed to create a $\pi^+\pi^-$ pair ($2m_\pi$).

(2) Find the distance at which the string stores enough energy ($2m_q$) to create a $q\bar q$ pair.

(3) Convert $\sigma$ to N (newtons) and find how many tonne-force it corresponds to. Do the same calculation for the line tension $T=\mu b^2/2$ of a dislocation in copper ($\mu=48\ \mathrm{GPa}$, $b=0.256\ \mathrm{nm}$), and find the ratio of the two. Summarize in your own words the warning in the main text about why the two must not be identified.

Solution

Strategy. Of the Cornell potential $V(r) = -\dfrac43\dfrac{\alpha_s\hbar c}{r} + \sigma r$ of Section 3.3.5, we use only the linear term $\sigma r$, which dominates at long distance.
