The quantity $\sigma$ is “energy per unit length” and at the same time a “force” ($F = -\dd V/\dd r = -\sigma$ is independent of distance). This double reading runs through the whole problem: we read parts (1) and (2) as energies and part (3) as a force.

(1) Using only the linear term, the energy required to pull $q$ and $\bar q$ apart to a distance $r$ is simply $E = \sigma r$. At $r = 1\ \mathrm{fm}$,

$$ E = 0.9\ \mathrm{GeV/fm}\times1\ \mathrm{fm} = 0.9\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

On the other hand, the minimum energy needed to create a $\pi^+\pi^-$ pair is

$$ 2m_\pi = 2\times0.140\ \mathrm{GeV} = 0.280\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Taking the ratio gives

$$ \frac{E}{2m_\pi} = \frac{0.9}{0.280} = 3.21 $$

That is, by the time the pair is separated by $1\ \mathrm{fm}$, 3.2 times the energy needed to create a $\pi$ meson pair has already been stored. There is plenty of energy to spare, so it is energetically favorable for the string to break and produce mesons. The operation of “pulling a quark away by $1\ \mathrm{fm}$” cannot actually be carried out, because the vacuum intervenes along the way and creates new particles.

(2) We now estimate using a constituent quark pair $q\bar q$ as the final state instead of $\pi$ mesons. The required energy is

$$ 2m_q = 2\times0.33\ \mathrm{GeV} = 0.66\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Solving $\sigma d = 2m_q$ for $d$ gives

$$ d = \frac{2m_q}{\sigma} = \frac{0.66\ \mathrm{GeV}}{0.9\ \mathrm{GeV/fm}} = 0.733\ \mathrm{fm} $$

That is, $d = 0.73\ \mathrm{fm}$. This is shorter than the radius of the proton ($\approx0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$). The string already breaks at the scale of the size of a hadron itself.

Note that, as stated in the caption of Figure 3.6 of the main text, including the Coulomb term lengthens this distance somewhat. Writing $V(d) = 2m_q$ with $\hbar c = 0.197327\ \mathrm{GeV\,fm}$,

$$ -\frac43\frac{\alpha_s\times0.197327}{d} + 0.9\,d = 0.66 $$

it suffices to solve the quadratic equation in $d$, $0.9d^2 - 0.66d - \frac43\alpha_s\times0.197327 = 0$. For $\alpha_s = 0.35$ the constant term is $-0.09209$, and

$$ d = \frac{0.66+\sqrt{0.66^2+4\times0.9\times0.09209}}{2\times0.9} = \frac{0.66+\sqrt{0.7671}}{1.8} = \frac{0.66+0.8759}{1.8} = 0.853\ \mathrm{fm} $$

This reproduces $r\approx0.85\ \mathrm{fm}$ of Figure 3.6 of the main text. Since the Coulomb term is attractive, the pair must be pulled farther apart to reach the same energy. The difference between $0.73\ \mathrm{fm}$ for the linear term alone and $0.85\ \mathrm{fm}$ with the Coulomb term is less than 20%, and as an estimate the conclusion is the same either way.

(3) First convert $\sigma$ to SI units. Since $1\ \mathrm{GeV} = 1.602\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J}$ and $1\ \mathrm{fm} = 10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}$,

$$ \sigma = \frac{0.9\times1.602\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J}}{10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}} = \frac{1.442\times10^{-10}}{10^{-15}}\ \mathrm{J/m} = 1.442\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N} $$

(Here $\mathrm{J/m} = \mathrm{N}$. Note that the reading as an energy density and the reading as a force are the same even in terms of units.) Next we convert this to a weight. Dividing by $g = 9.807\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ gives

$$ \frac{1.442\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N}}{9.807\ \mathrm{m/s^2}} = 1.470\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{kg} $$

That is, $14.7$ tonnes-force. This corresponds to the force needed to lift one medium-sized truck.

Next we put the line tension of a dislocation in copper on the same footing. Substituting numbers into $T = \mu b^2/2$, we first have

$$ b^2 = \left(0.256\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}\right)^2 = 6.554\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{m^2} $$ $$ T = \frac{48\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{Pa}\times6.554\times10^{-20}\ \mathrm{m^2}}{2} = \frac{3.146\times10^{-9}}{2}\ \mathrm{N} = 1.573\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{N} $$

(Since $\mathrm{Pa\cdot m^2} = \mathrm{N}$, the dimension is that of a force.) Taking the ratio,

$$ \frac{\sigma}{T} = \frac{1.442\times10^{5}}{1.573\times10^{-9}} = 9.17\times10^{13} $$

Taking the common logarithm, $\log_{10}(9.17\times10^{13}) = 13.96$; that is, there is a gap of about 14 orders of magnitude.

Summarizing in our own words the warning of Section 3.3.5 of the main text, we obtain the following. It is certainly true that the sentence “a line-like object has a tension and stores an energy proportional to its length” applies both to the QCD flux tube and to a dislocation in a crystal. But what agrees is only the form of the formula $V = \sigma r$, and the physics differs in four respects. First, the magnitudes differ by 14 orders of magnitude. Second, the origins differ: the line tension of a dislocation comes from the strain energy stored in an elastic continuum and in fact depends weakly on the size of the system through $\ln(R/r_0)$, whereas the QCD string tension is a nonperturbative property of the vacuum itself and is a constant independent of the size of the system. Third, the treatment of the ends differs: a dislocation line may terminate at a surface, a grain boundary, or a node, whereas a QCD string can terminate only on a color charge. Fourth, the consequences of breaking differ: when a dislocation breaks, no new particles are born, whereas in QCD the breaking of the string is itself particle production. Therefore, it is a mistake to import intuition about dislocations into QCD and draw physical conclusions from it, and this book does not use this comparison as an explanatory device. On the other hand, the correspondence of the renormalization group in Section 3.6.4 of the main text is a genuine correspondence, in the sense that the same differential equation is actually being solved, and it is important to distinguish the two.

Verification. We carry out three independent checks. First, the consistency of (1) and (2): since the energy is $0.9\ \mathrm{GeV}$ at $1\ \mathrm{fm}$, the distance at which $0.66\ \mathrm{GeV}$ is reached should be $0.66/0.9 = 0.73\ \mathrm{fm}$, which agrees with the answer to (2). Also, the distance at which $0.28\ \mathrm{GeV}$ ($2m_\pi$) is reached is $0.31\ \mathrm{fm}$, which is shorter than the $0.73\ \mathrm{fm}$ of (2). This accords with the intuition that the lighter $\pi$ pair can be created sooner. Second, the dimensions in (3): since $\mathrm{GeV/fm}$ is “energy/length”, it becomes $\mathrm{J/m} = \mathrm{N}$ and has the dimension of a force. On the dislocation side too, $\mathrm{Pa}\times\mathrm{m^2} = \mathrm{N}$ gives the same dimension, which justifies taking the ratio. Third, a check by an alternative route: Section 3.3.5 of the main text states the same $\sigma$ as “about 15 tonnes-force”, in agreement with the $14.7$ tonnes-force obtained in this problem. Also, expressing $\sigma$ in $\mathrm{GeV^2}$, $\sigma = 0.9\ \mathrm{GeV/fm}\times0.197327\ \mathrm{GeV\,fm} = 0.178\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$, which agrees with $\sigma\approx0.18\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ in the main text. It is reassuring to confirm that the two notations can be converted into each other.

Meaning. The heart of this exercise is that “confinement is not an infinite force but a finite force that never weakens.” The magnitude of the force itself is $14.7$ tonnes-force, not a cosmic number. But because this force is constant, independent of distance, the energy required to pull the quarks apart increases without limit, and along the way the vacuum is bound to break and new particles are created. Quarks are not observed in isolation not because the force is infinitely strong but because the force does not diminish even at large distances. The lesson for materials scientists lies in the second half of (3). An analogy between different fields is not justified merely because the forms of the formulas agree. Even for the same $V = \sigma r$, if the numerical values differ by 14 orders of magnitude, the origins differ, and the boundary conditions differ, the intuition from one must not be carried over to the other. Conversely, the correspondences that this book recognizes as genuine (the Yukawa potential and Thomas–Fermi screening, the renormalization group and Kondo scaling) are in every case ones where we can confirm that “the same equation is being solved with the same boundary conditions.” Acquiring a criterion for telling whether an analogy can be used is the other purpose of this problem.

Exercise 3.6: Two levels of Cabibbo suppression — decays of the $D^0$ meson

Problem (restated)

Consider the decay $c\to s+W^+$ (or $c\to d+W^+$) of $D^0=c\bar u$, combined with $W^+\to u\bar d$ (or $u\bar s$). Use the CKM matrix elements in Table 3.5.

(1) $D^0\to K^-\pi^+$ proceeds through $c\to s$, $W^+\to u\bar d$. Find the CKM factor $\abs{V_{cs}V_{ud}}^2$ that appears in the squared amplitude (Cabibbo-allowed).

(2) $D^0\to\pi^-\pi^+$ proceeds through $c\to d$, $W^+\to u\bar d$ (singly Cabibbo-suppressed), and $D^0\to K^+\pi^-$ proceeds through $c\to d$, $W^+\to u\bar s$ (doubly Cabibbo-suppressed). Find the CKM factor for each, and calculate the ratio to that in (1).

(3) The measured branching ratios are $\mathrm{BR}(K^-\pi^+)=3.95$%, $\mathrm{BR}(\pi^-\pi^+)=0.145$%, and $\mathrm{BR}(K^+\pi^-)=0.0150$%. Compare them with the predictions of (2) and state the degree of agreement.

Solution

Strategy. As in Section 3.4.3 of the main text, each time a $W$ vertex crosses generations, one CKM matrix element multiplies the amplitude. Every decay considered here uses a diagram with one $W$ and has two vertices (the $c$ side and the decay side of the $W$), so two CKM elements multiply the amplitude. Since the decay rate is the square of the amplitude, a factor of the form $\abs{V_{c\,q}V_{u\,q'}}^2$ appears. In every case the final state consists of two pseudoscalar mesons with similar masses, and the strong-interaction part (the hadronic matrix element) can be regarded as nearly common. Therefore we may expect that the ratios of branching ratios are determined roughly by the ratios of the CKM factors. The values needed from Table 3.5 of the main text are

$$ \abs{V_{cs}} = 0.975,\quad \abs{V_{ud}} = 0.97373,\quad \abs{V_{cd}} = 0.221,\quad \abs{V_{us}} = 0.2243 $$

.

(1) In the Cabibbo-allowed decay $D^0\to K^-\pi^+$, $V_{cs}$ attaches to $c\to s$ and $V_{ud}$ attaches to $W^+\to u\bar d$. The product is

$$ \abs{V_{cs}V_{ud}} = 0.975\times0.97373 = 0.94939 $$

Squaring,

$$ \abs{V_{cs}V_{ud}}^2 = (0.94939)^2 = 0.90134 $$

That is, $0.901$. Since both elements are diagonal elements and close to 1, there is almost no suppression.

(2) Singly suppressed ($D^0\to\pi^-\pi^+$). Since $c\to d$ crosses one generation, $V_{cs}$ is replaced by $V_{cd}$. The product is

$$ \abs{V_{cd}V_{ud}} = 0.221\times0.97373 = 0.21519 $$ $$ \abs{V_{cd}V_{ud}}^2 = (0.21519)^2 = 0.046309 $$

The ratio to (1) is

$$ \frac{0.046309}{0.90134} = 0.05138 = \frac{1}{19.5} $$

Since $V_{ud}$ cancels between numerator and denominator in this ratio, it can in fact be written as $\left(\abs{V_{cd}}/\abs{V_{cs}}\right)^2 = (0.221/0.975)^2 = (0.22667)^2 = 0.05138$. This is nearly the same number as $\tan^2\theta_C = (0.2243/0.97373)^2 = 0.0531 \approx 1/19$ in Section 3.4.3 of the main text, and it is exactly the standard degree of Cabibbo suppression: “crossing one generation costs a factor of about 20.”

Doubly suppressed ($D^0\to K^+\pi^-$). One generation is crossed at $c\to d$ and another at $W^+\to u\bar s$, two crossings in total. The product is

$$ \abs{V_{cd}V_{us}} = 0.221\times0.2243 = 0.049570 $$ $$ \abs{V_{cd}V_{us}}^2 = (0.049570)^2 = 0.0024572 $$

The ratio to (1) is

$$ \frac{0.0024572}{0.90134} = 0.0027262 = \frac{1}{367} $$

That is, about 1/400. This is nearly equal to the singly suppressed ratio $0.0514$ multiplied once more by $\tan^2\theta_C$ ($0.05138\times0.0531 = 0.00273$), confirming that the suppression is applied in two levels, quite literally.

(3) We take the ratios of the measured branching ratios, using the Cabibbo-allowed mode as the reference:

$$ \frac{\mathrm{BR}(\pi^-\pi^+)}{\mathrm{BR}(K^-\pi^+)} = \frac{0.145}{3.95} = 0.03671 $$ $$ \frac{\mathrm{BR}(K^+\pi^-)}{\mathrm{BR}(K^-\pi^+)} = \frac{0.0150}{3.95} = 0.0037975 $$

Comparing with the predictions of (2),

$$ \frac{0.03671}{0.05138} = 0.714, \qquad \frac{0.0037975}{0.0027262} = 1.393 $$

That is, the singly suppressed mode is $29\ \%$ smaller than the prediction, and the doubly suppressed mode is $39\ \%$ larger. Both are within a factor of 1.5. Considering that we looked only at the CKM factors and calculated no strong-interaction effects at all, this is remarkably good agreement.

What matters is that the order-of-magnitude structure is correctly reproduced. Against the prediction “Cabibbo-allowed $:$ singly suppressed $:$ doubly suppressed $= 1 : 1/19.5 : 1/367$,” the measurement is $1 : 1/27 : 1/263$. A hierarchy spanning three orders of magnitude is explained solely by multiplying elements of a $3\times3$ unitary matrix.

There are three causes of the remaining deviation within a factor of $1.5$. First, $SU(3)$ flavor symmetry breaking: because the $s$ quark is heavier than the $d$ quark, the hadronic matrix elements (decay constants and form factors) do not coincide between final states containing a $K$ and final states with only $\pi$. The $f_K/f_\pi = 1.19$ seen in Section 3.4.3 of the main text is precisely this effect, and its square is $1.42$, comparable to the deviation here. Second, the difference in phase space: since the sums of the final-state masses differ among $K^-\pi^+$, $\pi^-\pi^+$, and $K^+\pi^-$, the available kinematic space differs. Third, final-state interactions: before flying apart, the two produced mesons exchange strong interactions and change the magnitude and phase of the amplitude. All of these are effects originating in the strong interaction and are unrelated to the CKM matrix.

Verification. We check from three angles. First, a check of the upper limit: since the CKM matrix is unitary, no element has absolute value exceeding 1. Therefore $\abs{V_{cs}V_{ud}}^2 \le 1$ must hold, and the obtained $0.901$ satisfies this. Second, the self-consistency of the hierarchy: multiplying the singly suppressed ratio $0.05138$ by one more suppression factor $\left(\abs{V_{us}}/\abs{V_{ud}}\right)^2 = (0.2243/0.97373)^2 = 0.05306$ gives $0.05138\times0.05306 = 0.0027262$, which agrees with the $0.0027262$ calculated directly for the doubly suppressed mode. This confirms that the suppression multiplies as two independent levels. Third, a comparison with a known value: the degree of singly suppressed decay, $1/19.5$, agrees with $\tan^2\theta_C = 0.053 \approx 1/19$ that Section 3.4.3 of the main text derived from the Cabibbo angle. The same suppression rate is reproduced in a different system, the decay of the $D$ meson.

Meaning. What this exercise shows is that a measured quantity, the branching ratio of the weak interaction, can be predicted over three orders of magnitude by the surprisingly simple rule of multiplying elements of a $3\times3$ matrix. Moreover, the value of each element was determined independently from other experiments ($\beta$ decay, $K$ decay, $B$ decay, and so on), and in this problem we merely brought them in and applied them. It is a demonstration that a single structure, the CKM matrix, governs different decays of different particles across the board. At the same time, it is also important that the remaining deviation within a factor of 1.5 originates in the strong interaction. The weak-interaction part (CKM) and the strong-interaction part (the hadronic matrix element) can be treated as fundamentally separate. This has exactly the same structure as the argument in the example of $K\to\mu\nu$ versus $\pi\to\mu\nu$ in Section 3.4.3 of the main text, where $f_K/f_\pi = 1.19$ was extracted from the ratio and made to agree with the lattice QCD value $1.193$. In the language of materials science, it corresponds to a decomposition of the Wigner–Eckart theorem type, “dividing a matrix element into a part determined by symmetry and a part specific to the material.” What we are doing is the same as dividing a transition intensity into Clebsch–Gordan coefficients and reduced matrix elements in crystal field theory.

Exercise 3.7: Applying the selection rules

Problem (restated)

Using the quantum numbers in Table 3.7 and following the procedure of Section 3.5.2, determine for each of the following processes (i) whether it occurs, (ii) if it occurs, which interaction is responsible, and (iii) if it does not occur, which conservation law is violated.

  1. $\Sigma^-\to n+\pi^-$
  2. $\Delta^{++}\to p+\pi^+$
  3. $\mu^-\to e^-+e^++e^-$
  4. $n\to p+e^-$
  5. $K^+\to\pi^++\pi^0$
  6. $\Omega^-\to\Xi^0+\pi^-$
  7. $p+\bar p\to\pi^++\pi^-$
  8. $\Lambda\to n+\pi^0+\gamma$

Solution

Strategy. We apply the procedure of Section 3.5.2 of the main text mechanically. That is, we check in the order energy → charge $Q$ → baryon number $B$ → generation-by-generation lepton numbers $L_e,L_\mu,L_\tau$, and if even one of them is violated, we judge the process to be absolutely forbidden. If all are satisfied, we look at whether the flavor (here the strangeness $S$) is conserved and whether a photon or neutrino is involved, and decide which of the strong, electromagnetic, or weak interaction is responsible. The quantum numbers are taken from Table 3.7 of the main text. The $\Delta^{++}$ ($uuu$, $Q=+2$, $B=+1$, $S=0$, $m\approx1232\ \mathrm{MeV}$) and $\Xi^0$ ($uss$, $Q=0$, $B=+1$, $S=-2$, $m=1314.86\ \mathrm{MeV}$) are not listed in Table 3.7, but they follow immediately from the quark content by the rules of the main text ($B=+1/3$ per quark, $S=-(N_s-N_{\bar s})$).

1. $\Sigma^-\to n+\pi^-$.

Energy: $1197.45 > 939.565+139.570 = 1079.135$, and the $Q$ value is $118.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$. OK.

Charge: $-1 \to 0+(-1) = -1$. OK. Baryon number: $+1 \to +1+0 = +1$. OK. Lepton number: $0$ on both sides. OK.

Strangeness: $\Sigma^-$ ($dds$) has $S=-1$, and the final state consists of $n$ ($udd$, $S=0$) and $\pi^-$ ($d\bar u$, $S=0$), so $S=0$. Hence $\Delta S = +1$.

Verdict: it occurs; it is mediated by the weak interaction. Since $\abs{\Delta S}=1$, it can be realized by a diagram with a single $W$, and it is an $s\to u$ transition (the remaining $dd$ is a spectator). The measured lifetime is $\tau = 1.479\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{s}$, which falls squarely within the weak-decay band of Table 3.1 of the main text ($10^{-13}$–$10^{3}\ \mathrm{s}$). The branching ratio is almost $100\ \%$ ($99.85\ \%$).

2. $\Delta^{++}\to p+\pi^+$.

Energy: $1232 > 938.272+139.570 = 1077.842$, and the $Q$ value is $154\ \mathrm{MeV}$. OK.

Charge: $+2 \to +1+1 = +2$. OK. Baryon number: $+1 \to +1+0$. OK. Lepton number: $0$ on both sides. OK.

Strangeness: $\Delta^{++}$ is $uuu$, and the final state also contains no $s$ quark, so $0\to0$. Conserved.

Let us also check the angular momentum. The $\Delta^{++}$ has $J^P = 3/2^+$, and the final state consists of $p$ ($1/2^+$) and $\pi^+$ ($0^-$). With relative orbital angular momentum $\ell$, the total angular momentum can take values from $\abs{1/2-\ell}$ to $1/2+\ell$, so $\ell=1$ can produce $J=3/2$. The parity is $P_f = (+1)\times(-1)\times(-1)^\ell = +1$ (for $\ell=1$), which matches the parent’s $P=+1$. Therefore the decay is consistent as a $p\pi$ state with $\ell=1$.

Verdict: it occurs; it is mediated by the strong interaction. No photon or lepton appears and the flavor is conserved, so it is the strong interaction. As in Table 3.2 of the main text, $\Gamma = 117\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and converting to a lifetime gives $\tau = \hbar/\Gamma = 6.582\times10^{-22}/117 = 5.6\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{s}$, a typical value for a strong decay.

3. $\mu^-\to e^-+e^++e^-$.

Energy: $105.658 > 3\times0.511 = 1.533$. OK ($Q$ value $104\ \mathrm{MeV}$).

Charge: $-1 \to (-1)+(+1)+(-1) = -1$. OK. Baryon number: $0$ on both sides. OK.

We count the lepton numbers carefully. The $\mu^-$ has $L_\mu = +1$, $L_e = 0$. The final state has two $e^-$ (each with $L_e=+1$) and one $e^+$ ($L_e=-1$), so $L_e = +1+(-1)+1 = +1$ and $L_\mu = 0$. Therefore

$$ L_e:\ 0 \to +1\ (\text{violated}),\qquad L_\mu:\ +1 \to 0\ (\text{violated}) $$

If we look only at the total lepton number $L = L_e+L_\mu+L_\tau$, it is conserved ($+1\to+1$), but the absolute conservation law in Section 3.5.1 of the main text concerns the lepton numbers by generation.

Verdict: it does not occur; $L_e$ and $L_\mu$ are violated. It is forbidden in the Standard Model, and the experimental upper limit is $\mathrm{BR} < 1.0\times10^{-12}$. Strictly speaking, if neutrino oscillations (Chapter 14) are included it is not exactly zero, but the predicted branching ratio is about $10^{-54}$, which is unobservable. Therefore, if this decay were ever found, it would be direct evidence of physics beyond the Standard Model. It is a search of the same character as $\mu^-\to e^-\gamma$ (upper limit $\mathrm{BR}<3.1\times10^{-13}$, Table 3.8 of the main text).

4. $n\to p+e^-$.

Energy: $939.565 > 938.272+0.511 = 938.783$. The $Q$ value is $0.782\ \mathrm{MeV}$, small but positive, so the decay is energetically possible.

Charge: $0 \to +1+(-1) = 0$. OK. Baryon number: $+1 \to +1+0$. OK.

Lepton number: $L_e: 0 \to +1$. It is violated.

Furthermore, the angular momentum is also violated. The left-hand side has $J = 1/2$ (a half-integer). The right-hand side is a composite of $p$ ($1/2$) and $e^-$ ($1/2$), so the combined spin is $0$ or $1$; adding an integer orbital angular momentum $\ell$ to this, the total angular momentum is necessarily an integer. A half-integer and an integer cannot be equal.

Verdict: it does not occur; $L_e$ is violated (and so is angular momentum). The actual neutron decays as $n\to p+e^-+\bar\nu_e$. The $\bar\nu_e$ carries away $L_e=-1$, so the lepton number is conserved, and at the same time the presence of one more half-integer-spin particle makes the angular momentum consistent. Historically, it was precisely this double inconsistency that led Pauli to propose the existence of the neutrino (Chapter 2). The conclusion that “an invisible particle is emitted in $\beta$ decay” follows from the very procedure of judgment used in this problem.

5. $K^+\to\pi^++\pi^0$.

Energy: $493.677 > 139.570+134.977 = 274.547$, and the $Q$ value is $219.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$. OK.

Charge: $+1 \to +1+0$. OK. Baryon number: $0$ on both sides. OK. Lepton number: $0$ on both sides. OK.

Strangeness: $K^+$ ($u\bar s$) has $S=+1$, and both $\pi$ in the final state have $S=0$. Hence $\Delta S = -1$, that is, $\abs{\Delta S}=1$.

Verdict: it occurs; it is mediated by the weak interaction. The measured value is $\mathrm{BR} = 20.7\ \%$, and the $K^+$ lifetime is $1.238\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{s}$. Note that this decay is also the historical process in which parity violation first became an issue. The “$\theta$–$\tau$ puzzle”—that the same $K^+$ decays both to $2\pi$ (parity $+$) and to $3\pi$ (parity $-$)—led to the conclusion that the weak interaction does not conserve parity (Table 3.6 of the main text, Chapter 6).

6. $\Omega^-\to\Xi^0+\pi^-$.

Energy: the mass of $\Xi^0$ is $1314.86\ \mathrm{MeV}$ (Table 3.7 contains only $\Xi^-$, so we use the PDG value), so $1672.45 > 1314.86+139.570 = 1454.43$, and the $Q$ value is $218.0\ \mathrm{MeV}$. OK (even if we estimate with the $\Xi^-$ mass $1321.71$ from Table 3.7, we get $1461.28$, which is still comfortably lighter).

Charge: $-1 \to 0+(-1) = -1$. OK. Baryon number: $+1 \to +1+0$. OK. Lepton number: $0$ on both sides. OK.

Strangeness: $\Omega^-$ is $sss$ so $S=-3$, $\Xi^0$ is $uss$ so $S=-2$, and $\pi^-$ has $S=0$. Hence

$$ S:\ -3 \to -2, \qquad \Delta S = +1 $$

Verdict: it occurs; it is mediated by the weak interaction. Since $\abs{\Delta S}=1$, a diagram with a single $W$ suffices. The measured lifetime is $\tau = 8.21\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{s}$, which falls in the weak-decay band of the main text. The branching ratio is $23.6\ \%$.

Let us also confirm that it cannot occur through the strong interaction. The strong interaction conserves flavor, so we would need $\Delta S = 0$, and there is no decay path by which the $\Omega^-$ could drop to a lighter state while keeping $S=-3$ (no particle with $S=-3$ is lighter than the $\Omega^-$). Therefore the $\Omega^-$, although it is a baryon excitation that would otherwise vanish in $10^{-23}\ \mathrm{s}$, has no choice but to wait for a weak decay and lives as long as $10^{-10}\ \mathrm{s}$. It is precisely thanks to this “anomalously long lifetime” that the $\Omega^-$ was observed as a long track in the Brookhaven bubble chamber in 1964, decisively confirming Gell-Mann’s Eightfold Way (Chapter 2).

7. $p+\bar p\to\pi^++\pi^-$.

Energy: for a $p\bar p$ at rest, the center-of-mass energy is $2\times938.272 = 1876.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$, far above the final-state $2\times139.570 = 279.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$. OK.

Charge: $+1+(-1) = 0 \to +1+(-1) = 0$. OK.

Baryon number: $\bar p$ has $B=-1$, so $+1+(-1) = 0 \to 0+0 = 0$. OK. The point of this problem is not to forget the signs for antiparticles.

Lepton number: $0$ on both sides. OK. Strangeness: $0$ on both sides. Conserved.

Verdict: it occurs; it is mediated by the strong interaction. The flavor is conserved and no photon or lepton appears, so it is the strong interaction. Indeed, the $p\bar p$ annihilation cross section is of the millibarn class, and it is observed routinely in experiments using antiproton beams. Note that the two-body $\pi^+\pi^-$ mode is a minority channel compared with multiple $\pi$ production (about five pions on average), with a branching ratio of about $10^{-3}$, but it is allowed as far as the judgment of “whether it occurs or not” is concerned. Since the baryon number is conserved as $1+(-1)=0$, the annihilation of baryons does not violate the conservation law. In Section 3.5.1 of the main text we listed baryon number as an absolute conservation law, but that means that “the net number of baryons is conserved,” and it does not forbid in any way the disappearance of a particle–antiparticle pair.

8. $\Lambda\to n+\pi^0+\gamma$.

Energy: $1115.68 > 939.565+134.977 = 1074.542$, and the $Q$ value is $41.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$. The photon is massless, so there is no additional threshold. OK (although the margin is small).

Charge: $0 \to 0+0+0$. OK. Baryon number: $+1 \to +1$. OK. Lepton number: $0$ on both sides. OK.

Strangeness: $\Lambda$ ($uds$) has $S=-1$, and the final state all has $S=0$. Hence $\abs{\Delta S}=1$.

Verdict: it occurs; it is mediated by the weak interaction, but it is further suppressed by the emission of one extra photon. Since $\abs{\Delta S}=1$, only the weak interaction is possible. In addition, a photon is added to the final state, so the amplitude acquires one more vertex and the probability is smaller by a factor of $\alpha$. The reference is $\Lambda\to n+\pi^0$ without a photon ($\mathrm{BR} = 35.8\ \%$), from which we estimate

$$ \mathrm{BR} \sim 0.358\times\alpha = 0.358\times\frac{1}{137} = 2.6\times10^{-3} $$

that is, of order $10^{-3}$. In reality the $Q$ value is only $41\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and little momentum can be given to the photon, so the actual value is smaller still. The PDG does not list a branching ratio for this mode alone (it is hard to separate because $\pi^0\to\gamma\gamma$ acts as a background), but the analogous radiative decays that have been measured, $\Lambda\to n\gamma$ with $\mathrm{BR} = 1.75\times10^{-3}$ and $\Lambda\to p\pi^-\gamma$ with $\mathrm{BR} = 8.4\times10^{-4}$, are both of order $10^{-3}$. The estimate above is reasonable as an order of magnitude.

Verification. We carry out three independent checks. First, the sums of quantum numbers: if we make a table of $Q$, $B$, and $L_e$ summed on the left and right sides for all eight processes, only Nos. 3 and 4 mismatch in $L_e$ (and No. 3 also in $L_\mu$), and all the others agree. The places of violation correspond one-to-one with the verdicts. Second, corroboration by lifetimes: we compare the classification of Table 3.1 of the main text (strong $10^{-24}$–$10^{-22}\ \mathrm{s}$, electromagnetic $10^{-20}$–$10^{-16}\ \mathrm{s}$, weak $10^{-13}$–$10^{3}\ \mathrm{s}$) with the measured lifetime of each process. No. 2 is $5.6\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{s}$, in the strong-decay band; No. 1 is $1.48\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{s}$, No. 6 is $8.2\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{s}$, and No. 5 is $1.24\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{s}$, all in the weak-decay band. The verdicts derived from the quantum numbers correspond perfectly to the measured orders of magnitude. Third, confirmation by a different route: for No. 4, the prohibition follows from angular momentum independently of the violation of $L_e$, and the two reasons point to the same conclusion.

Meaning. What the eight problems show is that the information needed for the judgment is surprisingly small. The masses and the four integers (or fractions) $Q$, $B$, $L$, $S$ alone determine whether a process occurs or not and which force is responsible. We have computed neither a matrix element nor a cross section. And yet the result matches even the measured orders of magnitude of the lifetimes. As the connection to materials science in Section 3.5.3 of the main text states, this is exactly the same way of thinking as the selection rules of spectroscopy. We count the quantum numbers of the initial state, the final state, and the operator, and see whether the tensor product contains the totally symmetric component. That the $d$–$d$ transitions of transition-metal oxides are forbidden by the Laporte rule and hence the colors are pale, and that $\pi^0\to3\gamma$ is forbidden by $C$ parity and suppressed by seven orders of magnitude, are the same argument. And the two are even similar in that the prohibition is not complete but “leaks slightly.” The $d$–$d$ transitions leak through vibronic coupling, and the radiative decay of No. 8 leaks at first order in $\alpha$. Measuring the degree to which a prohibition is violated tells us the nature of the symmetry that imposes the prohibition—this use of the argument is precisely what one should take away from this problem.

Exercise 3.8: The running coupling constant and the Kondo temperature

Problem (restated)

Use the one-loop running (Section 3.3.4 of this book, $1/\alpha_s(\mu) = 1/\alpha_s(\mu_0) + \dfrac{b_0}{2\pi}\ln(\mu/\mu_0)$, $b_0 = 11-\frac23 n_f$). Let $\alpha_s(m_Z)=0.118$, $m_Z=91.188\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and $n_f=5$ ($b_0=23/3=7.667$).

(1) Find $\alpha_s$ at $\mu=10\ \mathrm{GeV}$. By what factor is it larger than the value at $m_Z$?

(2) Find the $\mu$ at which $1/\alpha_s(\mu)=0$ (that is, $\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}}$).

(3) Integrate the scaling equation of the Kondo problem, $\dd j/\dd\ln D = -2j^2$, and derive $1/j(D)=1/j(D_0)+2\ln(D/D_0)$. Then show that the scale at which $j$ diverges (the Kondo temperature) is given by $T_K = D_0\exp[-1/(2j_0)]$.

(4) For $D_0=3\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $j_0=\rho J=0.05$, find $T_K$ in both eV and K ($k_B = 8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/K}$).

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1) and (2) amount to substituting numbers into the one-loop running formula. The key point is that the quantity that runs is not $\alpha_s$ itself but its inverse $1/\alpha_s$, and that it is a linear function of $\ln\mu$. Because it is a straight line, both extrapolation and interpolation are easy, and the zero intercept gives $\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}}$. Part (3) builds exactly the same structure in the Kondo problem. If we rewrite the differential equation in terms of $1/j$, the right-hand side becomes a constant and the equation can be integrated at once. Part (4) puts numbers into the result of (3). As the correspondence table (Table 3.9) in the main text shows, (1)(2) and (3)(4) are two realizations of the same mathematics.

(1) Let $\mu_0 = m_Z = 91.188\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and $\mu = 10\ \mathrm{GeV}$. First we compute the logarithm:

$$ \ln\frac{\mu}{\mu_0} = \ln\frac{10}{91.188} = \ln(0.10967) = -2.2103 $$

It is negative because we are running to an energy lower than $m_Z$. Next we multiply by the coefficient:

$$ \frac{b_0}{2\pi}\ln\frac{\mu}{\mu_0} = \frac{7.6667}{6.28319}\times(-2.2103) = 1.22019\times(-2.2103) = -2.6970 $$

The starting point is

$$ \frac{1}{\alpha_s(m_Z)} = \frac{1}{0.118} = 8.4746 $$

Therefore

$$ \frac{1}{\alpha_s(10\ \mathrm{GeV})} = 8.4746 - 2.6970 = 5.7775 $$ $$ \alpha_s(10\ \mathrm{GeV}) = \frac{1}{5.7775} = 0.1731 $$

The ratio to the value at $m_Z$ is

$$ \frac{0.1731}{0.118} = 1.467 $$

That is, the coupling increases by a factor of about $1.47$. Lowering the energy by just one order of magnitude made the coupling almost 50% stronger. This is the flip side of asymptotic freedom. In the example of Section 3.3.4 of the main text we went the other way, from $m_Z$ up to $1\ \mathrm{TeV}$, and obtained $\alpha_s = 0.0877$. Comparing $0.173$ at $10\ \mathrm{GeV}$ with $0.0877$ at $1\ \mathrm{TeV}$, we see that over an energy difference of two orders of magnitude the coupling changes by a factor of two.

(2) We impose $1/\alpha_s(\mu) = 0$. From the running formula,

$$ 0 = \frac{1}{\alpha_s(m_Z)} + \frac{b_0}{2\pi}\ln\frac{\mu}{m_Z} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ln\frac{\mu}{m_Z} = -\frac{2\pi}{b_0\,\alpha_s(m_Z)} $$

We evaluate the right-hand side. The denominator is

$$ b_0\,\alpha_s(m_Z) = 7.6667\times0.118 = 0.90467 $$

so

$$ \ln\frac{\mu}{m_Z} = -\frac{6.28319}{0.90467} = -6.9453 $$

Exponentiating,

$$ \Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}} = m_Z\,\ee^{-6.9453} = 91.188\times9.632\times10^{-4} = 0.0878\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

That is, $\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}} \approx 88\ \mathrm{MeV}$. We obtained the same value as in the example of Section 3.3.4 of the main text.

That $1/\alpha_s$ vanishes at this point means that $\alpha_s$ itself diverges. Of course, this does not mean that a physical quantity really diverges; it means that the one-loop perturbative calculation breaks down there. Nevertheless, the very place where it breaks down has physical meaning. $88\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is of the same order as the mass of the $\pi$ meson ($140\ \mathrm{MeV}$), and it is nothing other than the hadron mass scale. From the dimensionless parameter $\alpha_s(m_Z) = 0.118$, a “mere number,” a quantity with the dimension of energy has welled up through the exponential function. This is what the main text calls dimensional transmutation. Note that this is a crude one-loop, five-flavor estimate: it is off by more than a factor of 3 from the actual value $\Lambda^{(3)}_{\overline{\mathrm{MS}}}\approx0.33\ \mathrm{GeV}$, which includes flavor thresholds and two-loop effects, but it is sufficient to show the structure of the order of magnitude.

(3) We rewrite the scaling equation of the Kondo problem

$$ \frac{\dd j}{\dd\ln D} = -2j^2 $$

by replacing the dependent variable with $1/j$. From the chain rule,

$$ \frac{\dd}{\dd\ln D}\left(\frac{1}{j}\right) = -\frac{1}{j^2}\frac{\dd j}{\dd\ln D} = -\frac{1}{j^2}\times\left(-2j^2\right) = 2 $$

The right-hand side has become a constant. This is a general feature of one-loop scaling equations: a $\beta$ function of the form $-\,(\text{constant})\times(\text{coupling})^2$ always becomes linear when we take the inverse. We can simply integrate with respect to $\ln D$. Integrating from $D_0$ to $D$,

$$ \frac{1}{j(D)} - \frac{1}{j(D_0)} = 2\left(\ln D - \ln D_0\right) = 2\ln\frac{D}{D_0} $$

that is,

$$ \frac{1}{j(D)} = \frac{1}{j(D_0)} + 2\ln\frac{D}{D_0} $$

This is the equation we were asked to show.

Next we find the scale at which $j$ diverges. Since $j\to\infty$ is the same as $1/j\to0$, we impose $1/j(D) = 0$. Writing $j_0 \equiv j(D_0)$, we have

$$ 0 = \frac{1}{j_0} + 2\ln\frac{T_K}{D_0} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ln\frac{T_K}{D_0} = -\frac{1}{2j_0} $$

Exponentiating,

$$ T_K = D_0\,\exp\!\left[-\frac{1}{2j_0}\right] $$

This is the equation we were asked to show. If $j_0 > 0$ (an antiferromagnetic exchange interaction), the exponent is negative, so $T_K$ is always smaller than $D_0$. As we lower $D$ (decrease $\ln D$), $1/j$ decreases and $j$ grows, and perturbation theory breaks down at $D = T_K$.

We also make the correspondence with (2) explicit. In (2), from $\ln(\mu/m_Z) = -2\pi/(b_0\alpha_s)$ we obtained $\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}} = m_Z\ee^{-2\pi/(b_0\alpha_s)}$. Now in (3), from $\ln(T_K/D_0) = -1/(2j_0)$ we obtained $T_K = D_0\ee^{-1/(2j_0)}$. Lining up the contents of the exponents,

$$ \frac{2\pi}{b_0\,\alpha_s} \qquad\longleftrightarrow\qquad \frac{1}{2\,j_0} $$

Both are “the inverse of the product of the coefficient of the $\beta$ function and the coupling constant.” If we write the $\beta$ function as $\dd g/\dd\ln(\text{scale}) = -Cg^2$, the divergence scale is in general $(\text{starting scale})\times\ee^{-1/(Cg_0)}$. In QCD, $C = b_0/(2\pi)$; in the Kondo problem, $C = 2$. The formulas of the two fields differ only in the value of this $C$.

(4) We put numbers into the formula of (3). First, the content of the exponent is

$$ -\frac{1}{2j_0} = -\frac{1}{2\times0.05} = -\frac{1}{0.1} = -10 $$

Therefore

$$ T_K = 3\ \mathrm{eV}\times\ee^{-10} = 3\times4.5400\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.362\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV} $$

We convert this to a temperature by dividing by $k_B = 8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/K}$:

$$ T_K = \frac{1.362\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}}{8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/K}} = 1.58\ \mathrm{K} $$

That is, $T_K = 1.36\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.6\ \mathrm{K}$. This is a perfectly realistic value for the Kondo temperature of a dilute Kondo alloy (such as iron in copper).

Let us get a feel for how the exponential function acts. If we double $j_0$ from $0.05$ to $0.1$, the exponent goes from $-10$ to $-5$, and $T_K = 3\times\ee^{-5} = 20.2\ \mathrm{meV} = 235\ \mathrm{K}$. Merely doubling the coupling raises the Kondo temperature by a factor of 150. Compared with the example of Section 3.6.4 of the main text with $D=1\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $j=0.1$ ($T_K = 78\ \mathrm{K}$), the bandwidth differs by a factor of 3, and $T_K$ differs by a factor of 3 accordingly, so the two are consistent. The fact that a slight difference in the coupling constant changes $T_K$ by orders of magnitude from material to material is a headache for experimentalists, and at the same time it is an advantage, because measuring $T_K$ determines $j$ precisely.

Verification. We check from three angles. First, the mutual consistency of (1) and (2): in (2) we obtained $\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}} = 0.0878\ \mathrm{GeV}$, so if we rewrite the running formula with $\Lambda$ as the starting point, it becomes $1/\alpha_s(\mu) = \dfrac{b_0}{2\pi}\ln(\mu/\Lambda)$. Putting in $\mu = 10\ \mathrm{GeV}$ gives $\ln(10/0.0878) = \ln(113.9) = 4.735$ and $1.22019\times4.735 = 5.777$, which agrees with the $5.7775$ obtained directly in (1). Two independent paths gave the same number. Second, limits and signs: since $b_0 > 0$, raising $\mu$ increases $1/\alpha_s$ and decreases $\alpha_s$. In (1) we lowered $\mu$, so $\alpha_s$ increased. This agrees with the direction of asymptotic freedom. Likewise, in the Kondo problem of (3), lowering $D$ increases $j$. In both cases the coupling is strong at low energy. Third, dimensions: the contents of the $\ln$ are the ratios $\mu/\mu_0$ and $D/D_0$, which are dimensionless, as they should be. $T_K$ is $D_0$ times a dimensionless factor, so it has the dimension of energy, and dividing by $k_B$ turns it into a temperature. The unit conversion in (4) is also dimensionally consistent.

Meaning. This problem is the most direct example of the proposition that this book asserts, namely that “particle physics and condensed matter physics share the same mathematical formulas.” The equation solved in (1)(2) and the equation solved in (3)(4) are mathematically identical, differing only in their coefficients, and their solutions have the same form. In both, a new scale with the dimension of energy is generated from a dimensionless coupling constant through the exponential function. In QCD it is $\Lambda_{\mathrm{QCD}} \approx 10^2\ \mathrm{MeV}$; in the Kondo problem it is $T_K \approx 1\ \mathrm{K}$. The two are 12 orders of magnitude apart, but the way they arise is identical. And in both cases, below that scale perturbation theory can no longer be used and nonperturbative methods are needed: lattice QCD for QCD and the numerical renormalization group for the Kondo problem. As the main text emphasizes, the person who created both of these was the same Kenneth Wilson, and moreover in the same years, 1974–75. The renormalization group that materials scientists use for the Kondo effect and critical phenomena is, neither as an analogy nor as a mere similarity, literally the same tool as the running coupling constant of particle physics. In contrast to the pairing of dislocations and strings, which Exercise 3.5 (3) warned us “must not be identified,” this one is a genuine correspondence. Whether the same equation is being solved under the same boundary conditions—that is the criterion that separates a true analogy from a false one.

E.4 Solutions for Chapter 4: Relativistic Kinematics

Exercise 4.1: Checking the additivity of rapidity numerically

Problem (restated)

Rocket A flies at $\beta_1=0.6$ relative to the Earth, and rocket B flies in the same direction at $\beta_2=0.8$ relative to A.

(1) Using $\eta=\frac12\ln\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}$, find $\eta_1=\mathrm{artanh}\,0.6$ and $\eta_2=\mathrm{artanh}\,0.8$ in logarithmic form (the values come out nicely).

(2) From $\eta_3=\eta_1+\eta_2$, find $\beta_3=\tanh\eta_3$ as a fraction.

(3) Confirm that it agrees with the result of a direct calculation using the velocity-composition law, and find $\gamma_3$.

(4) For the case $\beta_1=\beta_2=0.99$, find $\beta_3$ and confirm that it does not exceed $1$.

Solution

Strategy. We use only the definition of rapidity from Chapter 4 of this book, $\beta=\tanh\eta$, $\gamma=\cosh\eta$, $\gamma\beta=\sinh\eta$, and the composition law for boosts in the same direction, $\Lambda(\eta_1)\Lambda(\eta_2)=\Lambda(\eta_1+\eta_2)$. The velocity-composition law is used only at the end, as a “check of the answer.”

(1) Substitute directly into the defining formula. For $\beta_1=0.6$,

$$ \eta_1 = \frac12\ln\frac{1+0.6}{1-0.6} = \frac12\ln\frac{1.6}{0.4} = \frac12\ln 4 = \frac12\cdot 2\ln 2 = \ln 2 = 0.693147\cdots $$

For $\beta_2=0.8$,

$$ \eta_2 = \frac12\ln\frac{1+0.8}{1-0.8} = \frac12\ln\frac{1.8}{0.2} = \frac12\ln 9 = \frac12\cdot 2\ln 3 = \ln 3 = 1.098612\cdots $$

The numbers $0.6$ and $0.8$, which look quite ordinary, become the logarithms of the integers, $\ln2$ and $\ln3$, in terms of rapidity. This is no accident: a velocity of the form $\beta=(n^2-1)/(n^2+1)$ corresponds to $\eta=\ln n$ ($n=2$ for $\beta_1$ and $n=3$ for $\beta_2$).

(2) Since rapidity is additive for boosts in the same direction,

$$ \eta_3 = \eta_1+\eta_2 = \ln 2 + \ln 3 = \ln 6 = 1.791759\cdots $$

All that remains is to go back to the definition of $\tanh$. Since $\ee^{\eta_3}=6$ and $\ee^{-\eta_3}=1/6$,

$$ \beta_3 = \tanh(\ln 6) = \frac{\ee^{\ln 6}-\ee^{-\ln 6}}{\ee^{\ln 6}+\ee^{-\ln 6}} = \frac{6-\dfrac16}{6+\dfrac16} = \frac{36-1}{36+1} = \frac{35}{37} = 0.945946\cdots $$

We simply multiplied the numerator and denominator by $6$ and tidied up. In general $\beta=\tanh(\ln n)=(n^2-1)/(n^2+1)$, and here, too, $n=6$ gives $35/37$.

(3) Directly with the velocity-composition law,

$$ \beta_3 = \frac{\beta_1+\beta_2}{1+\beta_1\beta_2} = \frac{0.6+0.8}{1+0.6\times0.8} = \frac{1.4}{1.48} = \frac{140}{148} = \frac{35}{37} $$

which agrees exactly with (2). We can obtain $\gamma_3$ in two ways. From the rapidity,

$$ \gamma_3 = \cosh(\ln 6) = \frac{\ee^{\ln6}+\ee^{-\ln6}}{2} = \frac{6+\dfrac16}{2} = \frac{37}{12} = 3.083333\cdots $$

From the definition,

$$ \gamma_3 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta_3^2}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\left(\dfrac{35}{37}\right)^2}} = \frac{37}{\sqrt{37^2-35^2}} = \frac{37}{\sqrt{1369-1225}} = \frac{37}{\sqrt{144}} = \frac{37}{12} $$

which again agrees (factoring $37^2-35^2=(37-35)(37+35)=2\times72=144$ makes it easy to do in one’s head).

(4) For $\beta_1=\beta_2=0.99$, the rapidities are

$$ \eta_1=\eta_2=\frac12\ln\frac{1.99}{0.01}=\frac12\ln 199 = 2.646652\cdots, \qquad \eta_3 = 2\eta_1 = 5.293305\cdots $$

Calculating directly with the velocity-composition law,

$$ \beta_3 = \frac{0.99+0.99}{1+0.99\times0.99} = \frac{1.98}{1.9801} = 0.99994950\cdots $$

which is indeed below $1$. The gap from $1$ is

$$ 1-\beta_3 = \frac{1.9801-1.98}{1.9801} = \frac{0.0001}{1.9801} = 5.0502\times10^{-5} $$

which is still finite. The corresponding $\gamma_3$ is

$$ \gamma_3 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\beta_3^2}} = \frac{1+\beta^2}{1-\beta^2}\bigg|_{\beta=0.99} = \frac{1.9801}{0.0199} = 99.5025\cdots $$

(this can also be written $\gamma_3=\cosh 2\eta_1=2\cosh^2\eta_1-1=2\gamma_1^2-1$. Since $\gamma_1=1/\sqrt{1-0.99^2}=7.08881$, we get $2\times7.08881^2-1=99.5025$, which agrees).

Verification. Both $\beta$ and $\eta$ are dimensionless quantities, so the dimensions trivially match. A more meaningful check is the limits. The range of $\tanh$ is $(-1,1)$, so however large $\eta_1,\eta_2$ are, $\beta_3=\tanh(\eta_1+\eta_2)$ never reaches $1$. Indeed, in (4), despite the large rapidity $\eta_3=5.29$, we only get $\beta_3=0.99995$. Conversely, in the nonrelativistic limit $\beta_1,\beta_2\ll1$ we have $\eta\simeq\beta$ and $\tanh\eta\simeq\eta$, so $\beta_3\simeq\beta_1+\beta_2$, which recovers the Galilean addition of velocities. Moreover, the fact that (2) and (3) gave the same irreducible fraction $35/37$ by two independent paths serves as a mutual verification of the calculation itself.

Meaning. The conclusion of this problem is that “velocities cannot be added, but rapidities can.” The variable $\beta$ is what is at fault; the relativistic boost itself, as a hyperbolic rotation in the $(t,x)$ plane, is simply additive in $\eta$, which plays the role of the rotation angle. The composition law $\beta_3=(\beta_1+\beta_2)/(1+\beta_1\beta_2)$, which is hard to remember, is nothing but the addition theorem for $\tanh$. A feel for rapidity is also useful in practical materials science. For example, an electron in a transmission electron microscope with an accelerating voltage of $200\ \mathrm{kV}$ has $\gamma=1+200/511=1.391$, $\beta=0.695$, $\eta=0.858$, and in a $300\ \mathrm{kV}$ instrument this becomes $\beta=0.777$. In terms of $\beta$ it is “merely an increase from $0.70$ to $0.78$,” but in terms of rapidity the scale stretches naturally, $0.858\to1.037$. The electron wavelength and the relativistic correction factors are all determined by $\gamma$ (that is, $\cosh\eta$), so taking $\eta$ as the yardstick makes it easier to see the effect of the accelerating voltage.

Exercise 4.2: The photon Doppler effect and the GZK limit

Problem (restated)

The four-momentum of a photon traveling in the $+x$ direction is $k^\mu=\omega(1,1,0,0)$.

(1) Transform this photon by a boost of rapidity $\eta$ in the $+x$ direction, and show that $\omega'=\omega\,\ee^{-\eta}$.

(2) Show that $\ee^{-\eta}=\sqrt{(1-\beta)/(1+\beta)}$, and write down the relativistic Doppler formula. What happens for a photon approaching head-on ($k^\mu=\omega(1,-1,0,0)$)?

(3) For a cosmic-ray proton to undergo $p+\gamma\to p+\pi^0$ in a head-on collision with a photon of the cosmic microwave background (mean photon energy $\bar\omega\simeq6.3\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}$), it suffices that the photon energy in the proton rest frame exceed $144.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$ (verify this with the formula of Section 4.4.5 of the main text). In a head-on collision, $\omega_{\rm rest}\simeq2\gamma_p\bar\omega$. From this, estimate the upper limit of the proton energy.

Solution

Strategy. The four-momentum is also a four-vector, so we simply apply the Lorentz transformation matrix in the rapidity representation from Chapter 4 of this book. Since $k^2=0$ for a photon, $\abs{\bm{k}}=\omega$, and it is enough to look at a single component.

(1) The boost of rapidity $\eta$ in the $+x$ direction acts on $(k^0,k^1)$ as

$$ \begin{pmatrix} k'^0 \\ k'^1 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cosh\eta & -\sinh\eta \\ -\sinh\eta & \cosh\eta \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} k^0 \\ k^1 \end{pmatrix} $$

($k^2,k^3$ are unchanged). Now $k^\mu=\omega(1,1,0,0)$, that is, $k^0=k^1=\omega$, so

$$ k'^0 = \omega\cosh\eta - \omega\sinh\eta = \omega(\cosh\eta-\sinh\eta), $$ $$ k'^1 = -\omega\sinh\eta + \omega\cosh\eta = \omega(\cosh\eta-\sinh\eta) . $$

From the definitions of the hyperbolic functions, $\cosh\eta=(\ee^{\eta}+\ee^{-\eta})/2$ and $\sinh\eta=(\ee^{\eta}-\ee^{-\eta})/2$, we have $\cosh\eta-\sinh\eta=\ee^{-\eta}$, so

$$ k'^\mu = \omega\,\ee^{-\eta}\,(1,1,0,0), \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \omega' = \omega\,\ee^{-\eta} . $$

The result is that the whole of $k^\mu$ has merely been multiplied by the common factor $\ee^{-\eta}$. The direction remains $+x$, and $k'^2=0$ is also preserved. This property, that “under a boost in the same direction, the photon’s four-momentum is merely scaled,” means that the photon’s momentum is an eigenvector of the boost (with eigenvalue $\ee^{-\eta}$).

(2) Using $\gamma=\cosh\eta$ and $\gamma\beta=\sinh\eta$,

$$ \ee^{-\eta} = \cosh\eta-\sinh\eta = \gamma-\gamma\beta = \gamma(1-\beta) = \frac{1-\beta}{\sqrt{1-\beta^2}} = \frac{1-\beta}{\sqrt{(1-\beta)(1+\beta)}} = \sqrt{\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}} $$

Therefore the frequency seen by an observer receding (in the same direction as the photon) is

$$ \omega' = \omega\sqrt{\frac{1-\beta}{1+\beta}} \qquad(\text{redshift}) $$

This is the relativistic Doppler formula. On the other hand, for a photon approaching head-on, $k^\mu=\omega(1,-1,0,0)$, we have $k^0=\omega$ and $k^1=-\omega$, so

$$ k'^0 = \omega\cosh\eta + \omega\sinh\eta = \omega(\cosh\eta+\sinh\eta) = \omega\,\ee^{+\eta}, $$

that is,

$$ \omega' = \omega\,\ee^{+\eta} = \omega\sqrt{\frac{1+\beta}{1-\beta}} \qquad(\text{blueshift}) $$

For $\beta\to1$, $\ee^{\eta}=\gamma(1+\beta)\to2\gamma$, so $\omega'\simeq2\gamma\omega$. This is the content of the relation used in (3), “for a head-on collision, the energy is multiplied by $2\gamma$ in the rest frame.”

(3) First we verify the threshold $144.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Applying the fixed-target threshold formula of Chapter 4 of this book to the reaction $\gamma+p\to p+\pi^0$, with incident particle $a=\gamma$ ($m_a=0$) and target $b=p$, we obtain

$$ E_\gamma^{\rm thr} = \frac{(m_p+m_{\pi^0})^2-0-m_p^2}{2m_p} = \frac{m_{\pi^0}^2+2m_pm_{\pi^0}}{2m_p} = m_{\pi^0}\left(1+\frac{m_{\pi^0}}{2m_p}\right) $$

and inserting numbers,

$$ E_\gamma^{\rm thr} = 134.977\times\left(1+\frac{134.977}{2\times938.272}\right) = 134.977\times(1+0.0719285) = 144.69\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

(for details see Exercise 4.3(3)). In a head-on collision, the energy of a background-radiation photon seen in the proton rest frame is $\omega_{\rm rest}=\gamma_p(1+\beta_p)\bar\omega\simeq2\gamma_p\bar\omega$, so the condition for the reaction to occur is

$$ 2\gamma_p\bar\omega \ \ge\ E_\gamma^{\rm thr} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \gamma_p \ \ge\ \frac{E_\gamma^{\rm thr}}{2\bar\omega} = \frac{144.69\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV}}{2\times6.3\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}} = 1.148\times10^{11} $$

Converting to the proton energy,

$$ E_p = \gamma_p m_p = 1.148\times10^{11}\times9.383\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.08\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{eV} \simeq 1\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{eV} . $$

A proton with energy higher than this collides with background-radiation photons while traveling through space, produces $\pi^0$, and loses energy. Consequently, cosmic rays above $10^{20}\ \mathrm{eV}$ cannot reach us from far away (beyond $\sim50\ \mathrm{Mpc}$). This is the GZK limit.

Verification. First we verify the identity in (2) with concrete values. For $\beta=0.6$, Exercise 4.1 gives $\eta=\ln2$, so $\ee^{-\eta}=1/2$; on the other hand $\sqrt{(1-0.6)/(1+0.6)}=\sqrt{0.4/1.6}=\sqrt{0.25}=0.5$, which agrees. Next, as a consistency check between the two cases, the product of the factor $\ee^{-\eta}$ for the same-direction case and the factor $\ee^{+\eta}$ for the head-on case is $1$, which satisfies the requirement that “a boost in the opposite direction restores the original.” In the nonrelativistic limit, $\sqrt{(1-\beta)/(1+\beta)}\simeq1-\beta$, which reduces to the classical Doppler formula $\omega'\simeq\omega(1-v/c)$. (3) is also consistent dimensionally: $\gamma_p$ is dimensionless, and $E_p=\gamma_pm_p$ is an energy. Furthermore, $\bar\omega\simeq6.3\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}$ agrees exactly with the mean photon energy $\langle\omega\rangle=2.70\,k_BT=2.70\times2.35\times10^{-4}=6.3\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}$ of blackbody radiation at the cosmic microwave background temperature $T=2.725\ \mathrm{K}$ ($k_BT=2.35\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}$), so the input value itself is also reasonable.

Meaning. The single line stating that the photon energy is multiplied by $\ee^{\pm\eta}$ under a boost sets a ceiling on the highest energy of cosmic rays. Since the energy changes exponentially, under an extreme boost of $\gamma\sim10^{11}$ a background-radiation photon of less than a milli-eV turns, from the proton’s point of view, into a $\gamma$ ray capable of producing a $\pi$ meson. The same logic is at work in the field of materials science. For an electron with $\gamma\sim1.6\times10^4$ (an $8\ \mathrm{GeV}$ electron at SPring-8), the periodic magnetic field of an undulator at a synchrotron radiation facility looks like an electromagnetic wave contracted by a factor of $\gamma$; when this returns to the laboratory frame it is Doppler up-shifted once more, giving a hard X-ray with a total factor of $\sim2\gamma^2$. That light of Å wavelength emerges from a magnet array with a period of a few cm is nothing other than the result of using $\ee^{+\eta}\simeq2\gamma$ of (2) of this problem twice.

Exercise 4.3: The minimum invariant mass and the threshold condition

Problem (restated)

Consider the invariant mass $M_{\rm inv}=\sqrt{(\sum_ip_i)^2}$ of a system of $n$ particles.

(1) Show that $M_{\rm inv}=\sum_iE_i^*$ in the center-of-mass frame.

(2) Using $E_i^*\ge m_i$ (equality when the particle is at rest), show that $M_{\rm inv}\ge\sum_im_i$, and state the condition for equality. This is the proof of the threshold condition.

(3) For the reaction $\gamma+p\to p+\pi^0$ (photoproduction of the $\pi^0$), find the threshold photon energy for a proton at rest. Take $m_p=938.272$ and $m_{\pi^0}=134.977\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(4) Explain in one sentence, using the word recoil, why the answer to (3) is larger than $m_{\pi^0}$.

Solution

Strategy. Since $M_{\rm inv}$ is a Lorentz invariant, it may be computed in any frame. The key point is to evaluate it in the center-of-mass frame, where the calculation is easiest.

(1) Let the total four-momentum be $P^\mu\equiv\sum_ip_i^\mu$. The center-of-mass (CM) frame is, by definition, the frame in which the total momentum is zero, that is, the frame in which

$$ \bm{P}^* = \sum_i\bm{p}_i^* = \bm{0} $$

holds. In this frame $P^{*\mu}=(\sum_iE_i^*,\ \bm{0})$, so using the definition of the inner product from Chapter 4 of this book,

$$ M_{\rm inv}^2 = P\cdot P = P^*\cdot P^* = \Big(\sum_iE_i^*\Big)^2 - \abs{\bm{0}}^2 = \Big(\sum_iE_i^*\Big)^2 . $$

Since $E_i^*>0$, we take the positive sign of the square root and obtain

$$ M_{\rm inv} = \sum_i E_i^* $$

The step in the first line where we rewrite $P\cdot P=P^*\cdot P^*$ is precisely the benefit of using an invariant.

(2) Each particle is on its mass shell, so in the center-of-mass frame as well,

$$ E_i^* = \sqrt{\abs{\bm{p}_i^*}^2+m_i^2} \ \ge\ \sqrt{0+m_i^2} = m_i $$

and equality holds only when $\abs{\bm{p}_i^*}=0$, that is, when the particle is at rest in the center-of-mass frame. Substituting this into the sum in (1),

$$ M_{\rm inv} = \sum_i E_i^* \ \ge\ \sum_i m_i . $$

Equality holds when $\bm{p}_i^*=\bm{0}$ for all $i$, that is, when all the particles of the final state are at rest in the center-of-mass frame (seen in the laboratory frame, this corresponds to a state in which all the particles move forward together as one group with the same velocity). In a reaction $a+b\to1+2+\cdots+n$, by energy-momentum conservation the invariant mass of the whole final state equals $\sqrt{s}$, so it immediately follows that

$$ \sqrt{s} \ \ge\ \sum_f m_f $$

This is the threshold condition. The very simple fact that “the invariant mass has a lower bound, and that lower bound is the sum of the rest masses” turns out to be the true nature of the threshold.

(3) Insert into the general formula for the fixed-target threshold the incident particle $a=\gamma$ ($m_\gamma=0$), the target $b=p$, and the final state $\{p,\pi^0\}$:

$$ E_\gamma^{\rm thr} = \frac{(m_p+m_{\pi^0})^2 - m_\gamma^2 - m_p^2}{2m_p} = \frac{(m_p+m_{\pi^0})^2-m_p^2}{2m_p} . $$

Expanding the numerator gives $m_p^2+2m_pm_{\pi^0}+m_{\pi^0}^2-m_p^2=m_{\pi^0}(2m_p+m_{\pi^0})$, so

$$ E_\gamma^{\rm thr} = \frac{m_{\pi^0}(2m_p+m_{\pi^0})}{2m_p} = m_{\pi^0}\left(1+\frac{m_{\pi^0}}{2m_p}\right) . $$

Now insert numbers. Since $m_{\pi^0}/(2m_p) = 134.977/1876.544 = 0.0719285$,

$$ E_\gamma^{\rm thr} = 134.977\times1.0719285 = \underline{144.69\ \mathrm{MeV}} . $$

The mass of the $\pi^0$ we want to make is $134.977\ \mathrm{MeV}$, yet we are made to pay $9.71\ \mathrm{MeV}$ more.

(4) It is because of momentum conservation. The incident photon brings in a momentum of $144.69\ \mathrm{MeV}$, so the final state must take over that momentum, and the final state cannot be brought to rest. Therefore, besides “making the mass of the $\pi^0$,” kinetic energy to send the whole final state forward (the recoil energy) is always necessary. That portion is the excess $9.71\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

Let us check the breakdown. At threshold the $p$ and $\pi^0$ move together as one group, so their velocity is

$$ \beta = \frac{\abs{\bm{P}}}{E_{\rm tot}} = \frac{E_\gamma^{\rm thr}}{E_\gamma^{\rm thr}+m_p} = \frac{144.69}{1082.96} = 0.13360, \qquad \gamma = \frac{E_{\rm tot}}{m_p+m_{\pi^0}} = \frac{1082.96}{1073.25} = 1.009047 $$

Therefore the kinetic energies of the proton and the $\pi^0$ are, respectively,

$$ T_p = (\gamma-1)m_p = 0.009047\times938.272 = 8.49\ \mathrm{MeV}, \qquad T_{\pi^0} = (\gamma-1)m_{\pi^0} = 1.22\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

and their sum is $9.71\ \mathrm{MeV}$. This indeed agrees with the excess, and most of it ($87\ \%$) is carried by the heavy proton. In this sense, calling it the “kinetic energy of the recoiling proton” is accurate.

Verification. The dimensions obviously match (everything is an energy). Let us check by limits. In the limit $m_{\pi^0}/m_p\to0$ (an infinitely heavy target), $E_\gamma^{\rm thr}\to m_{\pi^0}$, which returns to the obvious result that “if recoil can be neglected, an energy equal to the mass suffices.” Conversely, the lighter the target, the larger the excess. As an independent check, let us directly verify that the center-of-mass energy at threshold is $\sqrt{s}=m_p+m_{\pi^0}$:

$$ \sqrt{s} = \sqrt{(E_\gamma+m_p)^2-E_\gamma^2} = \sqrt{1082.96^2-144.69^2} = \sqrt{1172802-20935} = \sqrt{1151867} = 1073.25\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

which agrees exactly with $m_p+m_{\pi^0}=938.272+134.977=1073.249\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Furthermore, this $144.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is itself the input value for the GZK limit in Exercise 4.2(3), so the fact that the two problems are tied together by the same number also serves as a consistency check.

Meaning. What (2) of this problem showed is that the question “is there enough energy?” reduces completely to the single line $\sqrt{s}\ge\sum_fm_f$. This one line simultaneously explains both why producing an antiproton requires $7m_p$ and why producing a $\pi^0$ requires $7\ \%$ more than $m_{\pi^0}$. Moreover, the viewpoint of (4), “who takes up the recoil?”, connects directly to measurements in materials science. In the Mössbauer effect, the recoil of the $\gamma$ ray is taken up not by a single atomic nucleus but by the whole crystal, so the effective target mass becomes practically infinite and the recoil energy becomes zero (corresponding to the $m_p\to\infty$ limit of this problem). Recoilless absorption occurs precisely because a term like the excess in (3), $m_{\pi^0}^2/(2m_p)$, vanishes. Merely by reinterpreting the target mass in the denominator of the recoil term as “whatever takes up the recoil,” the threshold in particle physics and recoilless absorption in solid-state physics can be described by the same formula.

Exercise 4.4: Counting Mandelstam variables and $e^-p$ elastic scattering

Problem (restated)

(1) Show, by counting degrees of freedom, that a $2\to2$ reaction has two independent Lorentz invariants. (Four four-momenta give $16$ components. Subtracting $4$ conservation laws and $4$ mass-shell conditions leaves $8$. We then remove the “orientation degrees of freedom” equal to the number of Lorentz-group parameters, $6$ (3 rotations plus 3 boosts).)

(2) For the elastic scattering $e^-p\to e^-p$ of a $1\ \mathrm{GeV}$ electron on a proton at rest, find $s$ and $\sqrt{s}$ (you may neglect $m_e$).

(3) Find the center-of-mass momentum $\abs{\bm{p}^*}$.

(4) Find $t$ at the center-of-mass scattering angle $\theta^*=90^\circ$, and determine $u$ from the sum rule.

Solution

Strategy. Part (1) is a pure counting problem. Parts (2)–(4) simply use, in turn, the Lab-frame expression for $s$, the formula for the CM momentum, the relation between $t$ and the scattering angle, and the sum rule $s+t+u=\sum_im_i^2$ from Chapter 4 of this book; no new tools are needed.

(1) We subtract constraints one at a time.

Starting point. The $2\to2$ reaction $1+2\to3+4$ involves four four-momenta $p_1,p_2,p_3,p_4$, so the total number of components is $4\times4=16$.

Conservation laws. Since $p_1+p_2=p_3+p_4$ is an equality of four-vectors, it gives $4$ conditions, one for each component. $16-4=12$.

Mass-shell conditions. Each particle satisfies $p_i^2=m_i^2$ ($i=1,2,3,4$), which gives $4$ conditions. $12-4=8$. We have now found that a “kinematic configuration that can actually occur” is specified by $8$ parameters.

Identify configurations that are related by a Lorentz transformation. Invariants do not change under Lorentz transformations, so configurations related by $\Lambda$ give “the same set of invariants.” The Lorentz group has rotations $3$ + boosts $3$ = $6$ parameters. $8-6=2$.

Hence there are $2$ independent Lorentz invariants. ∎

This counting looks more concrete if we redo it in the center-of-mass frame. A configuration in the CM frame consists of (a) the total energy $\sqrt{s}$, $1$ parameter, (b) the direction of the incident axis, $2$ parameters (polar and azimuthal angles), and (c) the scattering direction, $2$ parameters ($\theta^*$ and $\phi^*$), which makes $5$; adding (d) the boost from the CM frame to the Lab frame, $3$ parameters, gives a total of $8$. This indeed agrees with the $8$ found above. Of these, the ones that can be changed freely by a Lorentz transformation are the $2$ in (b), $1$ in (c) (the azimuthal angle $\phi^*$, a rotation about the incident axis), and the $3$ in (d), $6$ in all, so that only $\sqrt{s}$ and $\theta^*$, $2$ parameters, remain. These are none other than $(s,t)$ ($t$ is a function of $\theta^*$). Note that $u$ is not independent: it is determined from $s,t$ by the sum rule $s+t+u=\sum_im_i^2$.

(2) Since the target proton is at rest in the Lab frame, we use the expression from Chapter 4 of this book,

$$ s = m_1^2+m_2^2+2m_2E_1 $$

and substitute $m_1=m_e\to0$, $m_2=m_p=0.938272\ \mathrm{GeV}$, $E_1=E_e=1\ \mathrm{GeV}$:

$$ s = 0 + (0.938272)^2 + 2\times0.938272\times1.000 = 0.880354 + 1.876544 = \underline{2.756898\ \mathrm{GeV^2}} , $$ $$ \sqrt{s} = \sqrt{2.756898} = \underline{1.660391\ \mathrm{GeV}} . $$

Incidentally, as long as we read $E_1=1\ \mathrm{GeV}$ as the total energy of the electron, the only change from not dropping $m_e$ is that $m_e^2$ is added to $s$. Since $m_e=0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}=5.11\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{GeV}$,

$$ m_e^2 = 2.61\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{GeV^2}, \qquad s = 2.7568986\ \mathrm{GeV^2} $$

so only the seventh digit moves. The instruction to neglect $m_e$ is therefore justified.

Let us also read off the meaning. Of $\sqrt{s}=1.660\ \mathrm{GeV}$, the part $m_p=0.938\ \mathrm{GeV}$ is used up as the proton’s mass, so the center-of-mass kinetic energy available to the reaction is only $1.660-0.938=0.722\ \mathrm{GeV}$. Even though we fire a $1\ \mathrm{GeV}$ beam, only $0.72\ \mathrm{GeV}$ of it is in a “usable” form.

(3) We put $m_1=0$ and $m_2=m_p$ into the formula for the CM momentum. The Källén function becomes a perfect square, $\lambda(s,0,m_p^2)=s^2+0+m_p^4-0-0-2sm_p^2=(s-m_p^2)^2$, so

$$ \abs{\bm{p}^*} = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda(s,0,m_p^2)}}{2\sqrt{s}} = \frac{s-m_p^2}{2\sqrt{s}} = \frac{2.756898-0.880354}{2\times1.660391} = \frac{1.876544}{3.320782} = \underline{0.565091\ \mathrm{GeV}} . $$

While we are at it, let us also find the energy of each particle in the CM frame:

$$ E_e^* = \frac{s-m_p^2}{2\sqrt{s}} = 0.565091\ \mathrm{GeV}, \qquad E_p^* = \frac{s+m_p^2}{2\sqrt{s}} = \frac{3.637253}{3.320782} = 1.095300\ \mathrm{GeV} . $$

Since the electron is treated as massless, we can confirm that $E_e^*=\abs{\bm{p}^*}$.

(4) Putting $\theta^*=90^\circ$ ($\cos\theta^*=0$) into the relation between $t$ and the center-of-mass scattering angle gives

$$ t = -2\abs{\bm{p}^*}^2(1-\cos\theta^*) = -2\abs{\bm{p}^*}^2 = -2\times(0.565091)^2 = -2\times0.319328 = \underline{-0.638656\ \mathrm{GeV^2}} . $$

We determine $u$ from the sum rule. Since the scattering is elastic, $m_1=m_3=m_e\to0$ and $m_2=m_4=m_p$, so $\sum_im_i^2=2m_p^2$:

$$ u = 2m_p^2 - s - t = 2\times0.880354 - 2.756898 - (-0.638656) = 1.760709 - 2.756898 + 0.638656 = \underline{-0.357533\ \mathrm{GeV^2}} . $$

Indeed $t\le0$ and $u\le0$. However, the two statements differ in nature, so we discuss them separately.

$t\le0$ holds unconditionally. This is clear from $t=-2\abs{\bm{p}^*}^2(1-\cos\theta^*)=-4\abs{\bm{p}^*}^2\sin^2(\theta^*/2)$ in Chapter 4 of this book: in the physical region of the $s$-channel, $t=-Q^2\le0$ regardless of the scattering angle ($t=0$ in the forward direction $\theta^*=0$, and the minimum value is $t=-4\abs{\bm{p}^*}^2=-1.2773\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ in the backward direction $\theta^*=180^\circ$).

$u\le0$ does not hold unconditionally. From the sum rule, $u=2m_p^2-s-t$, so $u\le0$ is equivalent to $t\ge2m_p^2-s$, that is, to

$$ 2\abs{\bm{p}^*}^2(1-\cos\theta^*) \ \le\ s-2m_p^2 = 2.756898-1.760709 = 0.996189\ \mathrm{GeV^2} $$

Using $2\abs{\bm{p}^*}^2=0.638656\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$, we get $1-\cos\theta^*\le1.5598$, that is,

$$ \cos\theta^* \ \ge\ -0.5598 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \theta^* \ \le\ 124.0^\circ $$

The $\theta^*=90^\circ$ of this problem lies in this range, so $u<0$; but at, for example, $\theta^*=180^\circ$, we have $t=-1.2773$ and $u=1.760709-2.756898+1.277312=+0.2811\ \mathrm{GeV^2}>0$. In general, what is guaranteed in the physical region of the $s$-channel is $t\le(m_1-m_3)^2$ and $u\le(m_1-m_4)^2$. Here $m_1=m_3=0$, so $t\le0$ follows; but $m_1=0$ and $m_4=m_p$, so the upper limit of $u$ is only $m_p^2=0.880\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$. $u\le0$ holds unconditionally when the masses of the four particles are all equal, as in $pp$ elastic scattering ($u=4m^2-s-t$, and $t\ge-(s-4m^2)$ holds automatically). All that the sum rule $s+t+u=\sum_im_i^2$ says is that as $s$ grows, $t+u$ becomes correspondingly more negative.

Verification. The dimensions are all consistent: $\mathrm{GeV^2}$ for $s,t,u$ and $\mathrm{GeV}$ for $\sqrt{s}$ and $\abs{\bm{p}^*}$. As an independent check, we see whether the CM energies add up to $\sqrt{s}$: $E_e^*+E_p^*=0.565091+1.095300=1.660391\ \mathrm{GeV}=\sqrt{s}$, which agrees. Checking the proton’s mass-shell condition in the CM frame, $E_p^{*2}-\abs{\bm{p}^*}^2=1.199682-0.319328=0.880354=m_p^2$, which also agrees. The sum rule closes exactly as well: $s+t+u=2.756898-0.638656-0.357533=1.760709=2m_p^2$. Furthermore, computing $t$ independently from Lab-frame quantities should give the same result. For elastic scattering, $T_p=-t/(2m_p)$ (the same formula as in the discussion of the PKA in Chapter 4 of this book), so the proton’s recoil kinetic energy is $T_p=0.638656/(2\times0.938272)=0.340336\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and hence the Lab energy of the scattered electron is $E'=1.000-0.340=0.6597\ \mathrm{GeV}$. For a massless electron $t=-2E_eE'(1-\cos\theta_{\rm lab})$, so $\cos\theta_{\rm lab}=1+t/(2E_eE')=1-0.638656/(2\times0.6597)=0.5159$, that is, $\theta_{\rm lab}=58.9^\circ$. This also agrees with the relation “for a massless particle, $\cos\theta_{\rm lab}=\beta_{\rm CM}$ at $\theta^*=90^\circ$” ($\beta_{\rm CM}=E_e/(E_e+m_p)=1/1.938272=0.51592$). The two paths agree.

Meaning. The $-t=Q^2=0.639\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ of this problem is a typical momentum transfer when the proton form factor is measured in elastic electron scattering. Converting it to a length, $Q=0.799\ \mathrm{GeV}/c=4.05\ \mathrm{fm^{-1}}$, so the spatial resolution is $1/Q=0.247\ \mathrm{fm}$. This is smaller than the proton charge radius of $0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$, so at this $Q^2$ the internal structure of the proton is already visible. And this procedure of “varying $Q^2$ to measure the structure factor” follows exactly the same logic as measuring $S(\bm{Q},\omega)$ in condensed matter. If we sweep up to $Q\sim5\ \mathrm{\AA^{-1}}$ in neutron diffraction, we can see atomic arrangements with a resolution of $0.2\ \mathrm{\AA}$; if we sweep up to $Q\sim4\ \mathrm{fm^{-1}}$ in electron scattering, we can see the charge distribution inside the nucleus with a resolution of $0.2\ \mathrm{fm}$. The scales differ by only five orders of magnitude; the structure of what is being measured is the same. Fixing $s$ and scanning $t$ is the experimental practice common to both fields, and the Mandelstam variables are none other than that practice written in a Lorentz-invariant language.

Exercise 4.5: The Källén function and Heron’s formula

Problem (restated)

Consider $\lambda(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2+z^2-2xy-2yz-2zx$.

(1) Verify $\lambda(x,y,z)=[x-(\sqrt y+\sqrt z)^2][x-(\sqrt y-\sqrt z)^2]$ by expanding the right-hand side.

(2) Using Heron’s formula $16A^2=(a+b+c)(-a+b+c)(a-b+c)(a+b-c)$ for the area $A$ of a triangle with side lengths $a,b,c$, show that $\lambda(a^2,b^2,c^2)=-16A^2$. Hence “$a,b,c$ can form a triangle $\Leftrightarrow$ $\lambda<0$.”

(3) Rephrase the condition $\lambda(M^2,m_1^2,m_2^2)\ge0$ for the decay $M\to1+2$ to be possible, in the language of (2).

Solution

Strategy. Part (1) is a straightforward expansion. For (2), we only substitute $x=a^2,y=b^2,z=c^2$ into the factorization of (1) and compare with the four factors of Heron’s formula. The only point that needs care is where to pick up one sign.

(1) We expand the right-hand side. Setting $\alpha\equiv(\sqrt y+\sqrt z)^2$ and $\beta\equiv(\sqrt y-\sqrt z)^2$, the right-hand side has the form $x^2-(\alpha+\beta)x+\alpha\beta$. First, the sum is

$$ \alpha+\beta = (y+2\sqrt{yz}+z)+(y-2\sqrt{yz}+z) = 2(y+z) $$

where the $\sqrt{yz}$ terms cancel. Next, for the product, using $(\sqrt y+\sqrt z)(\sqrt y-\sqrt z)=y-z$,

$$ \alpha\beta = \left[(\sqrt y+\sqrt z)(\sqrt y-\sqrt z)\right]^2 = (y-z)^2 = y^2-2yz+z^2 . $$

Therefore

$$ [x-(\sqrt y+\sqrt z)^2][x-(\sqrt y-\sqrt z)^2] = x^2 - 2(y+z)x + y^2-2yz+z^2 = x^2+y^2+z^2-2xy-2xz-2yz $$

which is the very definition of $\lambda(x,y,z)$. ∎

This factorization is extremely useful in practice. For example, applying it to the formula for the two-body decay momentum in Chapter 4 of this book, we get

$$ \sqrt{\lambda(M^2,m_1^2,m_2^2)} = \sqrt{\left[M^2-(m_1+m_2)^2\right]\left[M^2-(m_1-m_2)^2\right]} $$

and we see at a glance that the quantity under the square root is positive only when $M>m_1+m_2$.

(2) Setting $x=a^2$, $y=b^2$, $z=c^2$ in (1) (since $a,b,c>0$, $\sqrt y=b$ and $\sqrt z=c$), we get

$$ \lambda(a^2,b^2,c^2) = \left[a^2-(b+c)^2\right]\left[a^2-(b-c)^2\right] . $$

We factor each factor further as a difference of squares:

$$ a^2-(b+c)^2 = (a-b-c)(a+b+c), \qquad a^2-(b-c)^2 = (a-b+c)(a+b-c) . $$

Therefore

$$ \lambda(a^2,b^2,c^2) = (a-b-c)(a+b+c)(a-b+c)(a+b-c) . $$

Here we pull the sign of the first factor outside. Since $(a-b-c) = -(-a+b+c)$,

$$ \lambda(a^2,b^2,c^2) = -(-a+b+c)(a+b+c)(a-b+c)(a+b-c) = -(a+b+c)(-a+b+c)(a-b+c)(a+b-c) . $$

By Heron’s formula, the product of the four factors on the right-hand side is exactly $16A^2$, so

$$ \lambda(a^2,b^2,c^2) = -16A^2 . $$

∎ When $a,b,c$ can form a triangle, the area $A$ takes a positive real value, so $-16A^2<0$, that is, $\lambda<0$. Conversely, when they cannot form a triangle, exactly one of the four factors becomes negative (if $a$ is the longest side, it is $-a+b+c$), so the whole product is negative and $\lambda=-(\text{negative})>0$. Therefore

$$ a,b,c\ \text{can form a triangle} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \lambda(a^2,b^2,c^2)<0 $$

The content of (2) is that “the sign of the Källén function decides whether the triangle inequalities hold.”

(3) In terms of (2), $\lambda(M^2,m_1^2,m_2^2)\ge0$ means

$$ \text{lengths}\ M,\ m_1,\ m_2\ \text{cannot form a triangle with these as its three sides (or it degenerates)} $$

Since a triangle cannot be formed (including the degenerate case) when “some one side is greater than or equal to the sum of the other two,” $\lambda\ge0$ splits into the three branches

$$ M\ge m_1+m_2, \qquad\text{or}\qquad m_1\ge M+m_2, \qquad\text{or}\qquad m_2\ge M+m_1 $$

This is unavoidable, because $\lambda$ is completely symmetric in its three variables. Of these, only the first branch actually allows the decay $M\to1+2$; the other two correspond to cases where the reverse process (such as $1\to M+2$) is allowed. That is, $\lambda\ge0$ alone is not enough; it becomes the condition for the decay only when we add the specification that “$M$ is the largest of the three”:

$$ M \ \ge\ m_1+m_2 . $$

This is none other than the two-body version of the threshold condition that “a parent particle cannot decay unless its mass is at least the sum of the masses of the daughter particles.” The equality $M=m_1+m_2$ is the case where the triangle collapses completely into a line segment; then $\lambda=0$, that is, $p=\sqrt\lambda/(2M)=0$. The daughter particles are produced at rest, and the decay is only just allowed kinematically.

Verification. We look at the dimensions. Since $\lambda(x,y,z)$ is quadratic in $x,y,z$, if we insert squares of energies such as $x=M^2$, then $\lambda$ has the dimension of energy to the fourth power. On the other hand, $16A^2$ is “the square of the square of a length” = length to the fourth power, and in the context where energies are read as lengths such as $a=M$, the two dimensions agree. The two-body decay momentum $p=\sqrt\lambda/(2M)$ is also correct: $(\text{energy}^4)^{1/2}/\text{energy}=\text{energy}$. We also check with concrete numbers. For an equilateral triangle $a=b=c=1$, $A=\sqrt3/4$ and $-16A^2=-16\times3/16=-3$. On the other hand $\lambda(1,1,1)=1+1+1-2-2-2=-3$, which agrees. Taking $a=2,b=c=1$ (a straight line) as a degenerate case, $A=0$ and $\lambda(4,1,1)=16+1+1-8-2-8=0$, which also agrees. For $a=3,b=c=1$, which does not form a triangle, $\lambda(9,1,1)=81+1+1-18-2-18=45>0$, which is indeed positive. We also check on the physics side: for $M\to1+2$ with $m_1=m_2=m$, $p=\sqrt{[M^2-4m^2][M^2-0]}/(2M)=\sqrt{M^2/4-m^2}$, which agrees with the value obtained from $E_1=M/2$ and the mass-shell condition $E_1^2-p^2=m^2$.

Meaning. The Källén function looks like a symmetric quadratic expression, but in substance it is the discriminant for the triangle inequalities. In particle physics, we can decide “whether a decay occurs” and “where the physical region of scattering lies” from the sign of $\lambda$ alone, without bringing in any angles or velocities. Moreover, because $\lambda$ is completely symmetric in its three variables, it is written in a form that does not depend on which particle we call the “parent.” This symmetry matters in the discussion of crossing symmetry, which moves back and forth between the $s$-channel and the $t$-channel. Note also that the picture in which the magnitude relations among three quantities decide whether the kinematics is allowed is not limited to particle physics. Consider the three-phonon scattering process $\bm{q}_1+\bm{q}_2\to\bm{q}_3$ in a crystal. Here we should be careful not to mistake where the constraint lies. Wave-vector conservation holds modulo a reciprocal lattice vector, so with $\bm{q}_3=\bm{q}_1+\bm{q}_2+\bm{G}$ it can always be satisfied for arbitrary $\bm{q}_1,\bm{q}_2$ (if Umklapp is allowed, the “triangle” always closes). What actually decides whether the scattering is allowed is energy conservation, $\omega(\bm{q}_1)+\omega(\bm{q}_2)=\omega(\bm{q}_3)$. Depending on the shape of the dispersion relation (for example, between upward-curving (convex-downward) acoustic branches), no set of wave vectors satisfies this equality, and the scattering phase space closes. Just as $\lambda\ge0$ decides whether a decay is possible through the triangle inequalities of three “masses,” here too it is the relation among three frequencies that decides whether the process is possible.

Exercise 4.6: Limits of Compton scattering and the resolution of profile measurements

Problem (restated)

(1) In the Compton formula, set $\theta=180^\circ$ (backscattering) and show that in the limit $\omega\to\infty$, $\omega'\to m_e/2=255.5\ \mathrm{keV}$.

(2) For the $\gamma$ rays of $^{137}\mathrm{Cs}$ ($662\ \mathrm{keV}$), find the scattered-photon energy at $\theta=180^\circ$ (the backscattering peak) and the energy the electron then gains (the Compton edge).

(3) In the Compton profile formula, for $\omega=662\ \mathrm{keV}$ and $\theta=160^\circ$, evaluate $\abs{\partial p_z/\partial\omega'}$. Using the atomic unit of momentum, $1\ \mathrm{a.u.}=\alpha m_ec=3.73\ \mathrm{keV}/c$, find the energy resolution required to obtain a momentum resolution of $0.4\ \mathrm{a.u.}$

(4) For the Compton profile of a free electron gas, verify that $\int_{-p_F}^{p_F}J(p_z)\dd p_z=1$, and express $J(0)$ in terms of $p_F$. Find $J(0)$ for aluminum ($p_F=0.926\ \mathrm{a.u.}$).

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1) and (2) are exactly the Compton formula of Chapter 4 of this book. In (3) we differentiate, with respect to $\omega'$, the expression for $p_z$ obtained by replacing the electron at rest with a moving electron; but the point at which the derivative is evaluated is exactly $p_z=0$ (the numerator vanishes), so the second term of the quotient rule drops out and the calculation simplifies. Part (4) is just a one-dimensional integral. Below we take $m_e=511\ \mathrm{keV}$.

(1) Insert $\theta=180^\circ$, that is, $\cos\theta=-1$ and $1-\cos\theta=2$, into the Compton formula:

$$ \omega' = \frac{\omega}{1+\dfrac{\omega}{m_e}(1-\cos\theta)} = \frac{\omega}{1+\dfrac{2\omega}{m_e}} . $$

Dividing the numerator and denominator by $\omega$ gives

$$ \omega' = \frac{1}{\dfrac{1}{\omega}+\dfrac{2}{m_e}} \ \xrightarrow[\ \omega\to\infty\ ]{}\ \frac{1}{0+\dfrac{2}{m_e}} = \frac{m_e}{2} = \frac{511}{2} = 255.5\ \mathrm{keV} . $$

However much we raise the incident energy, a photon returning straight backward cannot exceed $255.5\ \mathrm{keV}$. This is obvious in the reciprocal form $1/\omega'-1/\omega=(1-\cos\theta)/m_e$: even when $1/\omega\to0$, $1/\omega'$ merely settles at the finite value $2/m_e$.

(2) Substitute $\omega=662\ \mathrm{keV}$ and $\theta=180^\circ$.

$$ \frac{2\omega}{m_e} = \frac{2\times662}{511} = \frac{1324}{511} = 2.59100 $$

so that

$$ \omega' = \frac{662}{1+2.59100} = \frac{662}{3.59100} = \underline{184.4\ \mathrm{keV}} $$

This is the position of the backscattering peak that appears in the $\gamma$ ray spectrum. From energy conservation, the kinetic energy received by the recoil electron is

$$ T_e = \omega-\omega' = 662 - 184.4 = \underline{477.6\ \mathrm{keV}} $$
