and this is the Compton edge (the upper limit of the energy the electron can take). Of the total energy, $72.2\ \%$ is passed to the electron and $27.8\ \%$ returns as a photon. When we take the spectrum of a $^{137}\mathrm{Cs}$ source with a NaI or Ge detector, then besides the $662\ \mathrm{keV}$ photopeak there always appear a continuous distribution that cuts off at $478\ \mathrm{keV}$ (the Compton continuum) and a backscattering peak at $184\ \mathrm{keV}$. The relative positions of these three features are precisely the calculation of this problem.

(3) First we fix the reference point. We find $\omega'$ for an electron with $p_z=0$ (that is, with the same kinematics as an electron at rest) scattered through $\theta=160^\circ$. Since $\cos160^\circ=-0.939693$, we have $1-\cos\theta=1.939693$, and

$$ \frac{\omega}{m_e}(1-\cos\theta) = \frac{662}{511}\times1.939693 = 1.295499\times1.939693 = 2.512873, $$ $$ \omega' = \frac{662}{1+2.512873} = \frac{662}{3.512873} = 188.45\ \mathrm{keV} . $$

Next we find the magnitude of the momentum transfer:

$$ \abs{\bm{q}} = \sqrt{\omega^2+\omega'^2-2\omega\omega'\cos\theta} = \sqrt{662^2+188.45^2+2\times662\times188.45\times0.939693} . $$

Since the terms are $662^2=438244$, $188.45^2=35513$, and $2\times662\times188.45\times0.939693=234461$,

$$ \abs{\bm{q}} = \sqrt{438244+35513+234461} = \sqrt{708218} = 841.6\ \mathrm{keV} . $$

Now for the derivative. Writing the Compton profile expression of Chapter 4 of this book as

$$ p_z = \frac{N(\omega')}{\abs{\bm{q}}(\omega')}, \qquad N(\omega') = m_e(\omega-\omega')-\omega\omega'(1-\cos\theta) $$

the quotient rule gives

$$ \frac{\partial p_z}{\partial\omega'} = \frac{N'(\omega')}{\abs{\bm{q}}} - \frac{N(\omega')}{\abs{\bm{q}}^2}\frac{\partial\abs{\bm{q}}}{\partial\omega'} . $$

Here the point we are evaluating is precisely the point $p_z=0$, that is, $N(\omega')=0$, so the second term vanishes exactly. Therefore the first term alone suffices. Since $N'(\omega')=-m_e-\omega(1-\cos\theta)$,

$$ \left|\frac{\partial p_z}{\partial\omega'}\right| = \frac{m_e+\omega(1-\cos\theta)}{\abs{\bm{q}}} = \frac{511+662\times1.939693}{841.6} = \frac{511+1284.1}{841.6} = \frac{1795.1}{841.6} = \underline{2.133} . $$

This means “if $\omega'$ shifts by $1\ \mathrm{keV}$, $p_z$ shifts by $2.133\ \mathrm{keV}/c$.” Converting to atomic units of momentum, since $1\ \mathrm{a.u.}=3.73\ \mathrm{keV}/c$,

$$ \Delta p_z\,[\mathrm{a.u.}] = \frac{2.133}{3.73}\,\Delta\omega'\,[\mathrm{keV}] = 0.572\,\Delta\omega'\,[\mathrm{keV}] . $$

Hence, to obtain $\Delta p_z=0.4\ \mathrm{a.u.}$ we need an energy resolution of

$$ \Delta\omega' = \frac{0.4}{0.572} = \underline{0.70\ \mathrm{keV}} $$

Compared with the resolution of $500\text{--}600\ \mathrm{eV}$ of the Ge semiconductor detector quoted in Section 4.6.6, $0.7\ \mathrm{keV}$ is a level that Ge can reach.

However, a realistic experimental estimate calls for one more level of care. The value $500\text{--}600\ \mathrm{eV}$ refers to the energy band of the example in Section 4.6.6 (incident $100\ \mathrm{keV}$, scattered photon $72.5\ \mathrm{keV}$), and the resolution of Ge worsens with the energy being measured (at $662\ \mathrm{keV}$ the FWHM is about $1.3\text{--}1.5\ \mathrm{keV}$). The resolution we should evaluate here is that for the scattered photon entering the detector, $\omega'\simeq188\ \mathrm{keV}$, not for the incident $662\ \mathrm{keV}$. The FWHM of Ge in that band is $0.7\text{--}1.0\ \mathrm{keV}$, so

$$ \Delta p_z = 0.572\times(0.7\text{--}1.0) = 0.40\text{--}0.57\ \mathrm{a.u.} $$

which just barely reaches $0.4\ \mathrm{a.u.}$, with no margin to spare. Conversely, if we lower the incident energy to $100\ \mathrm{keV}$ at the same $\theta=160^\circ$, the coefficient increases to $1.11\ \mathrm{a.u./keV}$ because $\abs{\bm{q}}$ becomes smaller, but the resolution of Ge improves to $500\text{--}600\ \mathrm{eV}$, so $\Delta p_z\simeq0.6\ \mathrm{a.u.}$ This is the content of the statement in Section 4.6.6 that “about $0.6\ \mathrm{a.u.}$ is the limit.” In the end, $0.4\ \mathrm{a.u.}$ leaves no margin for Ge alone, and when higher resolution is needed, the practical solution is to combine high-energy X-rays from synchrotron radiation with a crystal spectrometer.

(4) We check the normalization. For $\abs{p_z}\le p_F$, $J(p_z)=\dfrac{3}{4p_F}\left(1-\dfrac{p_z^2}{p_F^2}\right)$, so

$$ \int_{-p_F}^{p_F}J(p_z)\dd p_z = \frac{3}{4p_F}\int_{-p_F}^{p_F}\left(1-\frac{p_z^2}{p_F^2}\right)\dd p_z = \frac{3}{4p_F}\left[p_z-\frac{p_z^3}{3p_F^2}\right]_{-p_F}^{p_F} . $$

The bracket takes the value $p_F-p_F/3=\dfrac{2p_F}{3}$ at the upper limit and $-p_F+p_F/3=-\dfrac{2p_F}{3}$ at the lower limit, so the difference is $\dfrac{4p_F}{3}$. Hence

$$ \int_{-p_F}^{p_F}J(p_z)\dd p_z = \frac{3}{4p_F}\cdot\frac{4p_F}{3} = 1 . $$

It is indeed normalized. The value at $p_z=0$ is

$$ J(0) = \frac{3}{4p_F} $$

For aluminum, $p_F=0.926\ \mathrm{a.u.}$, so

$$ J(0) = \frac{3}{4\times0.926} = \frac{3}{3.704} = \underline{0.810\ \mathrm{a.u.^{-1}}} . $$

Verification. We look at dimensions. The quantity $\abs{\partial p_z/\partial\omega'}$ in (3) is (momentum)/(energy), but in natural units $c=1$ both are energies, so it is dimensionless, and indeed a dimensionless number, $2.133$, came out. The division by $3.73\ \mathrm{keV}/c$ in converting to a.u. changes the unit of momentum from $\mathrm{keV}/c$ to a.u., which is consistent. The $J(p_z)$ in (4) has the dimension of (momentum)$^{-1}$, and $3/(4p_F)$ is exactly that. Check by limits: the $\omega'=184.4\ \mathrm{keV}$ of (2) is smaller than the saturation value $255.5\ \mathrm{keV}$ of (1). Since $662\ \mathrm{keV}$ is not yet $\omega\to\infty$, it is the correct behavior that the saturation value has not been reached (as $\omega$ is raised, it moves monotonically $184\to255.5\ \mathrm{keV}$, approaching the saturation value). The derivative in (3) can also be verified independently by numerical differentiation: computing $p_z$ directly at $\omega'=188.45\pm0.0001\ \mathrm{keV}$ and taking the difference gives $-2.1330$, which agrees with the analytic value $-2.133$. So the argument that the second term drops out at $N=0$ was correct. For (4) we can also make an order-of-magnitude check that $J(0)\times$(effective width of the distribution) should be about $1$: $0.810\times(4/3)\times0.926=1.00$, consistent with the fact that the area of a parabola is $2/3$ that of a rectangle of the same height.

Meaning. Parts (1) and (2) are precisely how to read the spectrum of a $\gamma$ ray detector: with a single formula we can tell which peaks are genuine $\gamma$ rays and which are spurious peaks of Compton origin. Parts (3) and (4), on the other hand, show that Compton scattering becomes “a microscope for measuring the electron momentum distribution.” The parabola in (4) is the momentum distribution of a free electron gas projected onto the $\bm{q}$ direction, and the kink where it cuts off sharply at $\abs{p_z}=p_F$ is a direct fingerprint of the Fermi surface. The value $J(0)=0.810\ \mathrm{a.u.^{-1}}$ for aluminum tells us what the peak height should be when the measured $J(p_z)$ is normalized, so it can be used as a check of the absolute calibration of the experiment. And what (3) answers is the instrument-design question of “what kind of detector is needed to see that kink.” Since we want to see structure at $p_F\sim1\ \mathrm{a.u.}$, a resolution of about $0.4\ \mathrm{a.u.}$ is desirable, and for that an energy resolution of $0.7\ \mathrm{keV}$ is required. In the verification workflow in which we obtain the momentum distribution of the Kohn–Sham orbitals from a first-principles calculation, predict $J(p_z)$, and compare it with measurement, this resolution estimate determines “up to which structures of the calculation can be compared with experiment.” With magnetic Compton scattering using circular polarization, only the spin magnetic moment can be singled out, so the same kinematics is also used to verify magnetism separately from the orbital component.

Exercise 4.7: PKA energies in fusion-reactor materials

Problem (restated)

You may approximate $\Lambda=4m_nM/(m_n+M)^2$ by $\Lambda=4A/(1+A)^2$, using the mass number $A$.

(1) Find $T_{\max}$ when a $2.45\ \mathrm{MeV}$ neutron produced in the D–D reaction hits tungsten ($A=184$). Compare it with the case of the $14.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$ neutron of D–T.

(2) For Si ($A=28$) and C ($A=12$) in SiC, find $T_{\max}$ for a $14.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$ neutron, and answer which sublattice receives the larger energy.

(3) Using the relativistic-correction formula, find the size of the relativistic correction to the values in (2). Confirm that for Si the $M\gg m_n$ approximation $E_n/2m_n$ is nearly sufficient, but for the light C the denominator term $2ME_n/(m_n+M)^2$ cannot be neglected.

(4) For the C PKA of (2), use the NRT model $N_d=0.8\,T/(2E_d)$ ($E_d\approx20\ \mathrm{eV}$ for the carbon sublattice of silicon carbide) to estimate an upper limit on the number of Frenkel pairs.

Solution

Strategy. We use the energy-transfer coefficient $T_{\max}=\Lambda E_n$ of Chapter 4 of this book, replacing the mass ratio by the mass-number ratio. Finally, we evaluate the correction factor with the ratio formula for the relativistic correction and connect to the NRT model.

(1) The transfer coefficient for tungsten is

$$ \Lambda_{\rm W} = \frac{4A}{(1+A)^2} = \frac{4\times184}{185^2} = \frac{736}{34225} = 0.021505 . $$

For the D–D neutron ($E_n=2.45\ \mathrm{MeV}$),

$$ T_{\max}^{\rm DD} = 0.021505\times2.45\ \mathrm{MeV} = 0.05269\ \mathrm{MeV} = \underline{52.7\ \mathrm{keV}} , $$

and for the D–T neutron ($E_n=14.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$),

$$ T_{\max}^{\rm DT} = 0.021505\times14.1\ \mathrm{MeV} = \underline{0.303\ \mathrm{MeV}} . $$

The ratio is $0.303/0.0527=5.76$, which is exactly the ratio of the incident neutron energies, $14.1/2.45=5.76$. This is natural, since $T_{\max}$ is proportional to $E_n$, but this single line carries the design implication that “in terms of the maximum recoil energy per neutron, D–T is about six times D–D, and for the same neutron flux the damage can be correspondingly more severe” (the actual dpa rate is determined by $\int\phi(E)\sigma(E)N_d(T_{\rm dam})\,\dd E$, so it also depends on the energy dependence of the elastic scattering cross section and on the partitioning of damage energy by the Lindhard factor. The ratio of $T_{\max}$ must not be read directly as the ratio of damage).

(2) We do the same calculation for silicon and carbon.

$$ \Lambda_{\rm Si} = \frac{4\times28}{29^2} = \frac{112}{841} = 0.13317, \qquad \Lambda_{\rm C} = \frac{4\times12}{13^2} = \frac{48}{169} = 0.28402 . $$

Multiplying by $E_n=14.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$,

$$ T_{\max}^{\rm Si} = 0.13317\times14.1 = \underline{1.88\ \mathrm{MeV}}, \qquad T_{\max}^{\rm C} = 0.28402\times14.1 = \underline{4.00\ \mathrm{MeV}} . $$

The ratio is $4.00/1.88=2.13$, so the lighter carbon sublattice receives 2.1 times as much energy. Since $\Lambda=4A/(1+A)^2\simeq4/A$ ($A\gg1$), the transfer coefficient is roughly inversely proportional to the mass number, and the lighter the element, the more energy it receives from the neutron. Even within the same compound SiC, the two sublattices are not damaged equally.

(3) The ratio formula for the relativistic correction is

$$ \frac{T_{\max}^{\rm rel}}{T_{\max}^{\rm NR}} = \frac{1+\dfrac{E_n}{2m_n}}{1+\dfrac{2ME_n}{(m_n+M)^2}} \ \simeq\ 1+\frac{E_n}{2m_n} \qquad(M\gg m_n) $$

Since $m_n=939.565\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $E_n=14.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$,

$$ \frac{E_n}{2m_n} = \frac{14.1}{2\times939.565} = \frac{14.1}{1879.13} = 0.00750 = \underline{0.75\ \%} . $$

That is, the correction is less than $1\ \%$. Estimated with this approximate value, it gives $1.88\to1.89\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for Si and $4.00\to4.03\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for C (for C the exact ratio below gives $4.02\ \mathrm{MeV}$). This is of the same size as the error from approximating $\Lambda$ by the mass-number ratio rather than the mass ratio, so it can be neglected in practice. Looking at that approximation error too, the values of $\Lambda=4m_nM/(m_n+M)^2$ with $M=A\times931.494\ \mathrm{MeV}$ inserted are $\Lambda_{\rm C}=0.28610$, $\Lambda_{\rm Si}=0.13425$, and $\Lambda_{\rm W}=0.021689$, and $4A/(1+A)^2$ underestimates these by $0.73\ \%$, $0.80\ \%$, and $0.85\ \%$, respectively. The cause is that $m_n=939.565\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is $0.9\ \%$ heavier than the atomic mass unit $931.494\ \mathrm{MeV}$, so the actual mass ratio $M/m_n$ is smaller than $A$ by that amount and $\Lambda$ comes out larger. Because the relativistic correction ($+0.75\ \%$) and the approximation error ($-0.8\ \%$) are of the same order and of opposite sign, discarding both together gives the clearest picture in practice.

However, it is worth checking how much the condition “$M\gg m_n$” matters. Using $M\simeq A\times931.494\ \mathrm{MeV}$, the denominator term $2ME_n/(m_n+M)^2$ is $0.00215$ for C ($M=11178\ \mathrm{MeV}$), $0.00101$ for Si ($M=26082\ \mathrm{MeV}$), and $0.00016$ for W ($M=171395\ \mathrm{MeV}$). Therefore the exact correction factors are

$$ \text{C}:\ \frac{1.00750}{1.00215}=1.00535\ (+0.53\ \%), \qquad \text{Si}:\ \frac{1.00750}{1.00101}=1.00649\ (+0.65\ \%), \qquad \text{W}:\ 1.00734\ (+0.73\ \%) $$

The heavier the element, the closer it comes to the asymptotic value $+0.75\ \%$; for a light element such as carbon the denominator term cannot be neglected, and the correction is smaller by about 30%, at $0.53\ \%$. In any case, the conclusion that it is less than $1\ \%$ does not change.

(4) We insert $T=T_{\max}^{\rm C}=4.00\ \mathrm{MeV}=4.00\times10^6\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $E_d=20\ \mathrm{eV}$ into the NRT model:

$$ N_d = \frac{0.8\,T}{2E_d} = \frac{0.8\times4.00\times10^6\ \mathrm{eV}}{2\times20\ \mathrm{eV}} = \frac{3.20\times10^6}{40} = \underline{8.0\times10^4\ \text{pairs}} . $$

That is, a single elastic scattering of one neutron can produce up to some $8$ ten-thousand (80,000) Frenkel pairs (vacancy + interstitial atom). This is an upper limit: in reality a considerable part of the PKA energy is “eaten” by electronic excitation (electronic stopping power), so the damage energy $T_{\rm dam}$ is smaller than $T$, and a correction through the Lindhard partition function is needed. Also, taking the average, for isotropic scattering in the center-of-mass frame $T$ is uniformly distributed over $[0,T_{\max}]$, so $\langle T\rangle=T_{\max}/2=2.0\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and the average $N_d$ is therefore half of this, about $4\times10^4$ pairs.

Verification. All dimensions are consistent ($\Lambda$ is dimensionless, $T_{\max}$ is an energy, and $N_d$ is dimensionless). We check by limits. For $A=1$ (hydrogen), $\Lambda=4\times1/2^2=1$, which agrees with the common knowledge of mechanics that “in a head-on collision between equal masses, the entire energy can be transferred.” This is why hydrogen-containing substances (water, polyethylene) are used as neutron moderators. Conversely, for $A\to\infty$, $\Lambda\to4/A\to0$, and an infinitely heavy target does not move. The orders of magnitude can also be checked against known values. For iron, which is listed in the table of Chapter 4 of this book, $\Lambda_{\rm Fe}=4\times56/57^2=0.0689$ and $T_{\max}=0.97\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and the $1.88\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for Si found in (2) sits at a reasonable position for an element with half the $A$ (from $\Lambda\simeq4/A$, $\Lambda_{\rm Si}/\Lambda_{\rm Fe}\simeq56/28=2$, and indeed $0.1332/0.0689=1.93$). Moreover, comparing the $N_d$ of (4) with the iron example in Chapter 4 of this book ($T\sim1\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $E_d=40\ \mathrm{eV}$, $N_d\sim1\times10^4$), carbon has $T$ four times larger and $E_d$ half as large, so it should be $8$ times larger, $8\times10^4$, and indeed it is.

Meaning. The formula $T_{\max}=\Lambda E_n$, which is the kinematics of two-body elastic collisions itself, is the starting point for the choice of materials for fusion reactors. What (1) says is that “once the reactor reaction (D–D or D–T) is chosen, the maximum recoil energy received by the material is almost determined,” and what (2) says is that “in a compound, the light sublattice is selectively struck hard.” That damage to the carbon sublattice dominates in SiC/SiC composites is determined first by kinematics, before one even discusses the strength of the bonds. And the $N_d$ of (4) is the very definition of dpa (displacements per atom), and the lifetime assessment of the reactor starts from here. That the relativistic correction in (3) is less than $1\ \%$ gives a practical guarantee that “in this field the nonrelativistic formula is sufficient,” but it also shows that this guarantee can be written in terms of the particle-physics quantity $E_n/2m_n$. The smallness of $\Lambda$ for tungsten ($0.0215$) is an advantage in that it is hard to damage as a plasma-facing material, and at the same time a drawback in that it is hard to slow neutrons down. The division of roles among multiplier, moderator, and structural materials is determined by the size of this single coefficient.

E.5 Solutions for Chapter 5: Symmetries, Groups, and Conservation Laws

Exercise 5.1: $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is a group; counting the generators

Problem (restated)

(1) Show that if $U_1,U_2\in\mathrm{SU}(2)$ then $U_1U_2\in\mathrm{SU}(2)$ (closure), and that $U^{-1}=U^\dagger\in\mathrm{SU}(2)$ (inverse element).

(2) By counting the number of parameters of an $N\times N$ complex matrix, show that the number of generators of $\mathrm{SU}(N)$ is $N^2-1$. Check that this gives 3 and 8 for $N=2,3$, respectively.

(3) Show that a general element of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ can be written, with real numbers $a,b,c,d$ ($a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2=1$), as $U=a\,\mathbb{1}-\ii(b\sigma_1+c\sigma_2+d\sigma_3)$. From this representation, explain why the manifold of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is the unit sphere $S^3$ in four-dimensional space.

Solution

Strategy. We use only the four group axioms of Section 5.1.1 of this book and the definition of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ in Section 5.3.1 ($U^\dagger U=\mathbb{1}$ and $\det U=1$). Part (1) needs just two facts: the multiplicativity of the determinant, $\det(AB)=\det A\det B$, and the reversal rule for the adjoint, $(AB)^\dagger=B^\dagger A^\dagger$. Part (2) is a simple subtraction: from the real degrees of freedom of the complex entries we subtract the number of independent real conditions. Part (3) merely rereads $U(\bm{n},\theta)=\cos\frac\theta2\,\mathbb{1}-\ii\sin\frac\theta2\,(\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma})$ of Section 5.3.2 of this book after renaming the parameters.

(1) First we show closure. If $U_1,U_2$ are both unitary, then by the reversal rule for the adjoint

$$ (U_1U_2)^\dagger (U_1U_2) = U_2^\dagger U_1^\dagger U_1 U_2 = U_2^\dagger\left(U_1^\dagger U_1\right)U_2 = U_2^\dagger\,\mathbb{1}\,U_2 = U_2^\dagger U_2 = \mathbb{1} $$

so $U_1U_2$ is also unitary. For the determinant, multiplicativity gives

$$ \det(U_1U_2) = \det U_1\cdot\det U_2 = 1\times 1 = 1 $$

so the condition $\det=1$ is preserved as well. Hence $U_1U_2\in\mathrm{SU}(2)$.

Next, the inverse element. Unitarity, $U^\dagger U=\mathbb{1}$, says precisely that $U^\dagger$ is a left inverse of $U$. For a $2\times2$ square matrix a left inverse is also a right inverse, so $UU^\dagger=\mathbb{1}$ holds too, and $U^{-1}=U^\dagger$. We now check that this $U^\dagger$ again belongs to $\mathrm{SU}(2)$. Unitarity follows from

$$ \left(U^\dagger\right)^\dagger U^\dagger = U U^\dagger = \mathbb{1} $$

and the determinant is $\det(U^\dagger)=\overline{\det U}=\bar 1=1$. Hence $U^{-1}=U^\dagger\in\mathrm{SU}(2)$.

The remaining two axioms also take one line each. The identity element is $\mathbb{1}$ itself, which satisfies $\mathbb{1}^\dagger\mathbb{1}=\mathbb{1}$ and $\det\mathbb{1}=1$, so it is an element of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$. Associativity holds automatically because matrix multiplication is associative to begin with. This shows that $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is a group.

(2) The entries of an $N\times N$ complex matrix $U$ are $N^2$ complex numbers, so there are $2N^2$ real parameters. We now subtract the conditions.

The first condition is unitarity, $U^\dagger U=\mathbb{1}$. Note that this does not give $N^2$ complex equations (that is, $2N^2$ real ones). The left-hand side $M\equiv U^\dagger U$ is automatically a Hermitian matrix ($M^\dagger = U^\dagger U = M$), and the right-hand side $\mathbb{1}$ is also Hermitian. That is, $M=\mathbb{1}$ is an equality between Hermitian matrices, and the number of independent real conditions equals the real degrees of freedom of an $N\times N$ Hermitian matrix. The diagonal elements are real, giving $N$ of them; among the off-diagonal elements only the upper triangle is independent, giving $N(N-1)/2$ complex numbers, that is, $N(N-1)$ real numbers. Hence

$$ N + N(N-1) = N^2 $$

Thus the unitarity condition imposes $N^2$ real conditions.

The second condition is $\det U=1$. Unitarity already implies $\abs{\det U}^2 = \det(U^\dagger)\det(U) = \det(U^\dagger U)=\det\mathbb{1}=1$, that is, $\abs{\det U}=1$. Hence only a phase $\det U=\ee^{\ii\varphi}$ remains, and what $\det U=1$ newly imposes is just the condition $\varphi=0$, which is one real condition.

Subtracting all of these, the number of real parameters of $\mathrm{SU}(N)$ (= the number of generators) is

$$ 2N^2 - N^2 - 1 = N^2 - 1 $$

For $N=2$ this is $4-1=3$, and for $N=3$ it is $9-1=8$. The former corresponds to the three Pauli matrices $\sigma_{1,2,3}$, the latter to the eight Gell-Mann matrices $\lambda^{1},\dots,\lambda^{8}$, in agreement with the values in Table 5.1 of this book. Note also that for $\mathrm{U}(N)$, where the condition $\det=1$ is dropped, there are $N^2$ generators; the one extra generator corresponds to the overall phase $\mathrm{U}(1)$ ($\mathrm{U}(2)\simeq\mathrm{SU}(2)\times\mathrm{U}(1)/\mathbb{Z}_2$).

(3) First we show that every element “can be written in that form.” In the closed expression for a general element of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ derived in Section 5.3.2 of this book,

$$ U(\bm{n},\theta) = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\,\mathbb{1} - \ii\,\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\,\left(\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma}\right) $$

define

$$ a \equiv \cos\frac{\theta}{2},\qquad (b,c,d)\equiv \bm{n}\,\sin\frac{\theta}{2} $$

Then $\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma}\,\sin\frac\theta2 = b\sigma_1+c\sigma_2+d\sigma_3$, so we immediately obtain the form $U=a\mathbb{1}-\ii(b\sigma_1+c\sigma_2+d\sigma_3)$. Moreover, since $\bm{n}$ is a unit vector ($\abs{\bm{n}}^2=1$),

$$ a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2 = \cos^2\frac{\theta}{2} + \abs{\bm{n}}^2\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2} = \cos^2\frac{\theta}{2}+\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2} = 1 $$

holds automatically.

Conversely, we check in components that the $U$ built from any real quadruple satisfying $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2=1$ really belongs to $\mathrm{SU}(2)$. Writing out $b\sigma_1+c\sigma_2+d\sigma_3$ gives

$$ b\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix} +c\begin{pmatrix}0&-\ii\\ \ii&0\end{pmatrix} +d\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix} d & b-\ii c\\ b+\ii c & -d\end{pmatrix} $$

so multiplying by $-\ii$ and adding $a\mathbb{1}$ yields

$$ U = \begin{pmatrix} a-\ii d & -c-\ii b\\ c-\ii b & a+\ii d\end{pmatrix} \equiv \begin{pmatrix} \alpha & \beta \\ -\bar\beta & \bar\alpha \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \alpha = a-\ii d,\quad \beta = -c-\ii b $$

(Indeed $-\bar\beta = -(-c+\ii b)=c-\ii b$ agrees with the lower-left entry.) A matrix of this form satisfies

$$ \det U = \abs{\alpha}^2+\abs{\beta}^2 = (a^2+d^2)+(c^2+b^2) = 1 $$ $$ U^\dagger U = \begin{pmatrix}\bar\alpha & -\beta\\ \bar\beta & \alpha\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \alpha & \beta \\ -\bar\beta & \bar\alpha \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\abs{\alpha}^2+\abs{\beta}^2 & \bar\alpha\beta-\beta\bar\alpha\\ \bar\beta\alpha - \alpha\bar\beta & \abs{\beta}^2+\abs{\alpha}^2\end{pmatrix} = \mathbb{1} $$

and so it is indeed an element of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$. That is, $\{U\in\mathrm{SU}(2)\}$ and $\{(a,b,c,d)\in\mathbb{R}^4 : a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2=1\}$ are in one-to-one correspondence.

The latter is, by its very definition, the unit sphere $S^3$ in four-dimensional Euclidean space. Therefore the group manifold of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is $S^3$. Counting dimensions, $S^3$ is a three-dimensional manifold, consistent with the three generators found in (2).

This geometry becomes important for simple connectivity. Any closed curve on $S^3$ can be slid along the sphere and contracted to a point ($\pi_1(S^3)=0$). On the other hand, since $U$ and $-U$ give the same spatial rotation, the group manifold of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is $S^3/\{\pm\}=\mathbb{RP}^3$, obtained by identifying antipodal points of $S^3$; a path connecting antipodal points cannot be contracted, so it is not simply connected ($\pi_1(\mathbb{RP}^3)=\mathbb{Z}_2$). This $\mathbb{Z}_2$ is the true nature of $U(\bm{n},2\pi)=-\mathbb{1}$ in Section 5.3.2 of this book, that is, of the two-valuedness of spinors. The statement “$\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is the universal cover of $\mathrm{SO}(3)$” is nothing other than a geometric rephrasing of the fact that $S^3$ is the simply connected double cover of $\mathbb{RP}^3$.

Verification. In the representation of (3), setting $\theta=0$ ($a=1$, $b=c=d=0$) gives $U=\mathbb{1}$, and setting $\theta=2\pi$ ($a=\cos\pi=-1$, $\bm{n}\sin\pi=0$) gives $U=-\mathbb{1}$, reproducing the result of Section 5.3.2 of this book. Also, for $\bm{n}=\hat{\bm{z}}$ and $\theta=\pi$ we have $a=0,\ (b,c,d)=(0,0,1)$ and $U=-\ii\sigma_3=\mathrm{diag}(-\ii,+\ii)$, which agrees with the value found independently in Exercise 5.3(2). If the counting in (2) is carried out in the same way for $\mathrm{SO}(N)$ (there are $N^2$ real entries, and the orthogonality condition is an equality of symmetric matrices, giving $N(N+1)/2$ conditions), it yields $N(N-1)/2$, which returns the known value 3 for $N=3$.

Meaning. The counting in (2) counts “the amount of information needed to specify the group.” That $\mathrm{SU}(3)_C$ has eight generators means directly that there are eight kinds of gluons (Chapter 11). For crystallographic point groups, the finite order plays this role: for $O_h$ one is done once the 48 elements are tabulated, whereas for a continuous group the measure of the size of the group is not “the number of elements” but “the number of generators.” In the context of condensed matter, the picture of $S^3$ in (3) appears as an object one step above the Bloch sphere ($S^2$). The operations acting on a two-level system (single-qubit gates) are elements of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$, that is, points on $S^3$. For states, too, a normalized vector in $\mathbb{C}^2$ lives on the same $S^3$ given by $\abs{c_1}^2+\abs{c_2}^2=1$, and only after dividing by the overall phase $\mathrm{U}(1)$, which has no physical effect, does it become the Bloch sphere $S^2$ (the Hopf bundle $S^3\to S^2$, with fiber $S^1$). The dimension difference $3-2=1$ accounts for that overall phase.

Exercise 5.2: Using Noether’s theorem

Problem (restated)

(1) Consider a point mass in a uniform gravitational field, $L=\frac12 m\dot z^2 - mgz$. How does $L$ change under the translation $z\to z+\varepsilon$? Is the momentum $p_z$ conserved? What about translations in the $x$ direction?

(2) For the two-dimensional isotropic harmonic oscillator $L=\frac12 m(\dot x^2+\dot y^2)-\frac12 m\omega^2(x^2+y^2)$, use Noether’s theorem of Section 5.1.3 of this book to verify that $L_z=xp_y-yp_x$ is conserved as a consequence of rotational invariance about the $z$ axis.

(3) Show that the Lagrangian for a complex field $\psi$ (the Schrödinger field)

$$ \Lag = \ii\psi^*\dot\psi - \frac{1}{2m}\nabla\psi^*\cdot\nabla\psi - V(\xx)\abs{\psi}^2 $$

is invariant under $\psi\to\ee^{\ii\alpha}\psi$ ($\alpha$ a constant), and show that the corresponding conserved quantity is $\int\abs{\psi}^2\dd^3x$ (the particle number, or the electric charge).

Solution

Strategy. We simply apply mechanically the statement derived in Section 5.1.3 of this book, “if $\delta L = 0$ then $I=\sum_i(\partial L/\partial\dot q_i)K_i$ is conserved.” The procedure is the same every time, in three steps: (i) write down the direction of the transformation $K$; (ii) compute $\delta L$ and see whether it is $0$; (iii) if it is $0$, write down $I$. Part (3) is the version lifted to field theory, in which $q_i$ is reread as “the value of the field at each point $\xx$” and $\partial L/\partial\dot q_i$ is replaced by $\partial\Lag/\partial\dot\psi$. We use natural units with $\hbar=1$.

(1) A translation in the $z$ direction has $K=1$, $\dot K=0$. By Step 1 of the derivation in Section 5.1.3 of this book,

$$ \delta L = \varepsilon\left[\frac{\partial L}{\partial z}K + \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot z}\dot K\right] = \varepsilon\left[(-mg)\cdot 1 + m\dot z\cdot 0\right] = -mg\,\varepsilon $$

Since $\delta L\ne0$, the hypothesis of Noether’s theorem is violated, and $p_z=\partial L/\partial\dot z=m\dot z$ is not conserved. Indeed, the Euler–Lagrange equation is

$$ \frac{\dd}{\dd t}(m\dot z) = \frac{\partial L}{\partial z} = -mg \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dot p_z = -mg \ne 0 $$

so the momentum decreases at a constant rate. The gravitational potential $mgz$ makes the physics depend on “where one takes the origin of height,” and thus explicitly breaks translation symmetry in the $z$ direction.

For the $x$ direction, it suffices to treat the point mass in three dimensions, $L=\frac12 m(\dot x^2+\dot y^2+\dot z^2)-mgz$. This $L$ does not contain $x$ explicitly, so $\partial L/\partial x = 0$, and together with $K_x=1$, $\dot K_x=0$ we obtain

$$ \delta L = \varepsilon\left[\frac{\partial L}{\partial x}\cdot1 + \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot x}\cdot 0\right] = 0 $$

Hence $p_x = m\dot x$ is conserved. Likewise $p_y$ is conserved. That the horizontal velocity stays constant in projectile motion is precisely a consequence of this horizontal translation symmetry.

Note that the way the symmetry is broken in the $z$ direction has a structure. $\delta L=-mg\varepsilon$ can be written as a total time derivative,

$$ \delta L = \varepsilon\frac{\dd\Lambda}{\dd t},\qquad \Lambda = -mgt $$

According to the supplement in Section 5.1.3 of this book, what is conserved in this case is $I=(\partial L/\partial\dot z)K-\Lambda$, that is,

$$ I = m\dot z + mgt $$

Checking, $\dot I = m\ddot z + mg = -mg+mg = 0$. This merely says that “the initial velocity $m\dot z(0)$ is conserved,” but it is the smallest example of the general rule that even when a symmetry is broken, as long as the way it is broken can be expressed as a total derivative, a modified conserved quantity remains.

(2) As in Example 2 of Section 5.1.4 of this book, an infinitesimal rotation about the $z$ axis has

$$ K_x = -y,\qquad K_y = x \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dot K_x = -\dot y,\quad \dot K_y = \dot x $$

The required partial derivatives are

$$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial x} = -m\omega^2 x,\quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial y} = -m\omega^2 y,\quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot x} = m\dot x,\quad \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot y} = m\dot y $$

Substituting these into the formula for the variation:

$$ \frac{\delta L}{\varepsilon} = \frac{\partial L}{\partial x}K_x + \frac{\partial L}{\partial y}K_y + \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot x}\dot K_x + \frac{\partial L}{\partial \dot y}\dot K_y $$ $$ = (-m\omega^2x)(-y) + (-m\omega^2 y)(x) + (m\dot x)(-\dot y) + (m\dot y)(\dot x) $$ $$ = m\omega^2 xy - m\omega^2 xy - m\dot x\dot y + m\dot x\dot y = 0 $$

The potential terms cancel among themselves, and the kinetic-energy terms cancel among themselves, each independently. The former reflects the invariance of $x^2+y^2$ under rotations, the latter the invariance of $\dot x^2+\dot y^2$ under rotations. Since we have shown $\delta L=0$, the conserved quantity is

$$ I = \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot x}K_x + \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot y}K_y = (m\dot x)(-y) + (m\dot y)(x) = x\,p_y - y\,p_x = L_z $$

that is, the $z$ component of the angular momentum.

Checking directly from the equations of motion gives the same result. Since $m\ddot x = -m\omega^2 x$ and $m\ddot y=-m\omega^2y$,

$$ \frac{\dd L_z}{\dd t} = \dot x p_y + x\dot p_y - \dot y p_x - y \dot p_x = m\dot x\dot y + x(-m\omega^2y) - m\dot y\dot x - y(-m\omega^2 x) = 0 $$

which agrees.

(3) First we show the invariance. Under $\psi\to\ee^{\ii\alpha}\psi$ we have $\psi^*\to\ee^{-\ii\alpha}\psi^*$, and since $\alpha$ is a constant it commutes with the time and space derivatives, so $\dot\psi\to\ee^{\ii\alpha}\dot\psi$ and $\nabla\psi\to\ee^{\ii\alpha}\nabla\psi$. Looking at each term of $\Lag$,

$$ \ii\psi^*\dot\psi \to \ii\,\ee^{-\ii\alpha}\psi^*\,\ee^{\ii\alpha}\dot\psi = \ii\psi^*\dot\psi,\qquad \nabla\psi^*\cdot\nabla\psi \to \nabla\psi^*\cdot\nabla\psi,\qquad \abs{\psi}^2 = \psi^*\psi \to \psi^*\psi $$

Every term contains exactly one $\psi$ and one $\psi^*$, so the phase factors $\ee^{\ii\alpha}$ and $\ee^{-\ii\alpha}$ cancel completely. Hence $\Lag$ is invariant.

Next we find the conserved quantity. Take the infinitesimal transformation with $\alpha=\varepsilon\ll1$:

$$ \delta\psi = \ii\varepsilon\psi,\qquad \delta\psi^* = -\ii\varepsilon\psi^* \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad K_\psi = \ii\psi,\quad K_{\psi^*}=-\ii\psi^* $$

The field-theory version of Noether’s theorem gives, for independent fields $\phi_A$ (here $\psi$ and $\psi^*$),

$$ j^{\mu} = \sum_A \frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi_A)}\,K_A, \qquad \partial_\mu j^\mu = 0 $$

This is the pointwise version of $I=\sum_i(\partial L/\partial\dot q_i)K_i$ of Section 5.1.3 of this book. Computing the required derivatives,

$$ \frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial\dot\psi} = \ii\psi^*,\qquad \frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial\dot\psi^*} = 0,\qquad \frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial(\nabla\psi)} = -\frac{1}{2m}\nabla\psi^*,\qquad \frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial(\nabla\psi^*)} = -\frac{1}{2m}\nabla\psi $$

(Since $\Lag$ does not contain $\dot\psi^*$, the second one is zero.) Therefore the time component is

$$ j^0 = \left(\ii\psi^*\right)\left(\ii\psi\right) + 0\cdot\left(-\ii\psi^*\right) = \ii^2\,\psi^*\psi = -\abs{\psi}^2 $$

which agrees with $j^0\propto-\abs{\psi}^2$ given in the hint. The spatial components are

$$ \bm{j} = \left(-\frac{1}{2m}\nabla\psi^*\right)\left(\ii\psi\right) +\left(-\frac{1}{2m}\nabla\psi\right)\left(-\ii\psi^*\right) = -\frac{\ii}{2m}\left(\psi\nabla\psi^* - \psi^*\nabla\psi\right) $$

The conserved quantity is the integral of $j^0$ over all space, that is,

$$ Q = \int j^0\,\dd^3x = -\int\abs{\psi}^2\,\dd^3x $$

The overall sign and normalization of the Noether current are free to the extent that the choice of $\varepsilon$ is arbitrary, so multiplying by $-1$ and writing

$$ N \equiv \int \abs{\psi}^2\,\dd^3 x = \text{const.} $$

we find that this is the particle number (the total probability in one-particle quantum mechanics, the particle number in a many-particle system). Multiplying by the charge $q$ gives the electric charge $Q_{\text{EM}}=qN$.

Verification. We compare the result of (3) with the conservation of probability that follows directly from the Schrödinger equation. First, writing the Euler–Lagrange equation for $\psi^*$,

$$ \frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial\psi^*} - \partial_t\frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial\dot\psi^*} - \nabla\cdot\frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial(\nabla\psi^*)} = \left(\ii\dot\psi - V\psi\right) - 0 + \frac{1}{2m}\nabla^2\psi = 0 $$

that is, $\ii\partial_t\psi = -\frac{1}{2m}\nabla^2\psi + V\psi$, which is indeed the Schrödinger equation (with $\hbar=1$). On the other hand, the probability current in quantum mechanics textbooks is $\bm{j}_{\text{prob}}=\frac{1}{2m\ii}(\psi^*\nabla\psi-\psi\nabla\psi^*)$; comparing with the $\bm{j}$ found above, $\bm{j}=-\bm{j}_{\text{prob}}$, and also $j^0=-\abs{\psi}^2=-\rho$. Therefore $\partial_\mu j^\mu=0$ becomes

$$ -\left(\frac{\partial\rho}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot\bm{j}_{\text{prob}}\right)=0 $$

that is, the continuity equation itself. Only a common overall factor $-1$ is attached, and the content agrees completely. Also, the result of (1) shows the natural behavior that in the limit $g\to0$ we have $\delta L\to0$ and the conservation of $p_z$ is restored. The result of (2) also holds for $\omega\to0$ (a free particle), consistent with the known fact that for a central force $L_z$ is conserved regardless of the form of $V$.

Meaning. The three subproblems show that “whether a symmetry is present or absent can be decided mechanically just by computing $\delta L$.” Part (1) in particular is the smallest example of what happens when a symmetry is broken. In a crystal, surfaces and interfaces break translation symmetry, and the momentum in that direction ceases to be a good quantum number (which is why a surface band structure cannot show dispersion in $k_\perp$ along the surface normal, and surface states appear). The gravitational field of (1) may be thought of as the one-dimensional version of this. The $\mathrm{U}(1)$ symmetry of (3) is, as we saw in the framework of Section 5.1.5 of this book, the origin of charge conservation, and it is also exactly the symmetry that is spontaneously broken in superconductivity. When the superconducting order parameter $\Delta=\abs{\Delta}\ee^{\ii\varphi}$ selects a particular $\varphi$, what is broken is nothing other than the property verified here, that “the origin of the phase is irrelevant to the physics.”

Exercise 5.3: Pauli matrices and rotation matrices

Problem (restated)

(1) Using $\sigma_a\sigma_b=\delta_{ab}\mathbb{1}+\ii\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c$ of Section 5.3.1 of this book, show that $(\bm{a}\cdot\bm{\sigma})(\bm{b}\cdot\bm{\sigma})=(\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b})\mathbb{1}+\ii(\bm{a}\times\bm{b})\cdot\bm{\sigma}$.

(2) Write $U=\exp(-\ii\theta\sigma_3/2)$ explicitly as a $2\times2$ matrix and find its values at $\theta=\pi,\,2\pi,\,4\pi$.

(3) Show that $U\sigma_1U^\dagger = \cos\theta\,\sigma_1+\sin\theta\,\sigma_2$, and verify that this corresponds to a rotation of the vector $\hat{\bm{x}}$ by the angle $\theta$ about the $z$ axis. Note that the angle in $U$ is $\theta/2$, yet the vector turns through $\theta$.

(4) Find the state obtained by rotating the spin-$1/2$ state $\ket{\uparrow}$ by $\theta$ about the $y$ axis, and show that the probability of obtaining spin up when the $z$-component of the spin is measured is $\cos^2(\theta/2)$.

Solution

Strategy. The starting point for everything is the basic identity of Section 5.3.1 of this book, $\sigma_a\sigma_b=\delta_{ab}\mathbb{1}+\ii\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c$. Part (1) just contracts it with indices. Parts (2) and (4) just substitute into the closed-form expression $U(\bm{n},\theta)=\cos\frac\theta2\mathbb{1}-\ii\sin\frac\theta2(\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma})$ of Section 5.3.2 of this book. For part (3), so that the mechanism “two half angles appear and combine into a full angle” is visible, we carry it out both by a component calculation and by an infinitesimal transformation.

(1) Write $\bm{a}\cdot\bm{\sigma}=a_a\sigma_a$ and $\bm{b}\cdot\bm{\sigma}=b_b\sigma_b$ (repeated indices are summed over $1,2,3$), and substitute the basic identity:

$$ (\bm{a}\cdot\bm{\sigma})(\bm{b}\cdot\bm{\sigma}) = a_a b_b\,\sigma_a\sigma_b = a_a b_b\left(\delta_{ab}\mathbb{1} + \ii\epsilon_{abc}\sigma_c\right) $$

The first term is $a_ab_b\delta_{ab}=a_ab_a=\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b}$. By the definition of the components of the cross product, $(\bm{a}\times\bm{b})_c=\epsilon_{cab}a_ab_b=\epsilon_{abc}a_ab_b$ (we used the cyclic symmetry of $\epsilon$, $\epsilon_{cab}=\epsilon_{abc}$), the second term is $\ii(\bm{a}\times\bm{b})_c\sigma_c=\ii(\bm{a}\times\bm{b})\cdot\bm{\sigma}$. Hence

$$ (\bm{a}\cdot\bm{\sigma})(\bm{b}\cdot\bm{\sigma}) = (\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b})\,\mathbb{1} + \ii\,(\bm{a}\times\bm{b})\cdot\bm{\sigma} $$

is shown. Setting $\bm{a}=\bm{b}=\bm{n}$ (a unit vector) and using $\bm{n}\times\bm{n}=0$, we obtain $(\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma})^2=\mathbb{1}$, which reproduces Step 1 of the derivation in Section 5.3.2 of this book.

(2) Since $\sigma_3=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1)$ is a diagonal matrix, the exponential can be computed component by component:

$$ U = \exp\left(-\ii\frac{\theta}{2}\sigma_3\right) = \exp\begin{pmatrix}-\ii\theta/2 & 0\\ 0 & +\ii\theta/2\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\ee^{-\ii\theta/2} & 0\\ 0 & \ee^{+\ii\theta/2}\end{pmatrix} $$

The same result follows from the closed-form expression of Section 5.3.2 of this book. For $\bm{n}=\hat{\bm{z}}$ we have $\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma}=\sigma_3$, so

$$ U = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\mathbb{1} - \ii\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\sigma_3 = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\frac\theta2-\ii\sin\frac\theta2 & 0\\ 0 & \cos\frac\theta2+\ii\sin\frac\theta2\end{pmatrix} = \mathrm{diag}\left(\ee^{-\ii\theta/2},\,\ee^{\ii\theta/2}\right) $$

and the two agree. The explicit values are

$$ \theta=\pi:\quad U = \mathrm{diag}\left(\ee^{-\ii\pi/2},\ee^{\ii\pi/2}\right) = \mathrm{diag}(-\ii,\,+\ii) = -\ii\,\sigma_3 $$ $$ \theta=2\pi:\quad U = \mathrm{diag}\left(\ee^{-\ii\pi},\ee^{\ii\pi}\right) = \mathrm{diag}(-1,-1) = -\mathbb{1} $$ $$ \theta=4\pi:\quad U = \mathrm{diag}\left(\ee^{-2\ii\pi},\ee^{2\ii\pi}\right) = \mathrm{diag}(+1,+1) = +\mathbb{1} $$

At $\theta=2\pi$ we get $-\mathbb{1}$, and only at $\theta=4\pi$ do we return to $+\mathbb{1}$. This is the check, for the simplest axis, of $U(\bm{n},2\pi)=-\mathbb{1}$ in Section 5.3.2 of this book. The period is $4\pi$, not $2\pi$.

(3) We compute by components, using the diagonal form from (2) as it stands. Since $\sigma_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, we first have

$$ U\sigma_1 = \begin{pmatrix}\ee^{-\ii\theta/2} & 0\\ 0 & \ee^{\ii\theta/2}\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0 & \ee^{-\ii\theta/2}\\ \ee^{\ii\theta/2} & 0\end{pmatrix} $$

Multiply this from the right by $U^\dagger=\mathrm{diag}(\ee^{\ii\theta/2},\ee^{-\ii\theta/2})$. Multiplying by a diagonal matrix from the right means “multiply the first column by $\ee^{\ii\theta/2}$ and the second column by $\ee^{-\ii\theta/2}$,” so

$$ U\sigma_1U^\dagger = \begin{pmatrix}0 & \ee^{-\ii\theta/2}\cdot\ee^{-\ii\theta/2}\\ \ee^{\ii\theta/2}\cdot\ee^{\ii\theta/2} & 0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0 & \ee^{-\ii\theta}\\ \ee^{\ii\theta} & 0\end{pmatrix} $$

Here is the key point. One half angle $\ee^{-\ii\theta/2}$ comes from $U$, and another $\ee^{-\ii\theta/2}$ comes from $U^\dagger$; they multiply together to give the full angle $\ee^{-\ii\theta}$. On the other hand, the right-hand side is

$$ \cos\theta\,\sigma_1 + \sin\theta\,\sigma_2 = \cos\theta\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix} + \sin\theta\begin{pmatrix}0&-\ii\\ \ii&0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0 & \cos\theta-\ii\sin\theta\\ \cos\theta+\ii\sin\theta & 0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0 & \ee^{-\ii\theta}\\ \ee^{\ii\theta} & 0\end{pmatrix} $$

and the two agree. Therefore $U\sigma_1U^\dagger=\cos\theta\,\sigma_1+\sin\theta\,\sigma_2$.

Let us look at the correspondence with the rotation of vectors. To a three-dimensional vector $\bm{a}$ we associate the matrix $\bm{a}\cdot\bm{\sigma}$ (this correspondence is one-to-one: we can recover $a_c=\frac12\Tr[\sigma_c(\bm{a}\cdot\bm{\sigma})]$). What we have just shown is that, for $\hat{\bm{x}}\cdot\bm{\sigma}=\sigma_1$,

$$ U\,(\hat{\bm{x}}\cdot\bm{\sigma})\,U^\dagger = (\cos\theta\,\hat{\bm{x}}+\sin\theta\,\hat{\bm{y}})\cdot\bm{\sigma} $$

The vector in parentheses on the right-hand side is precisely $\hat{\bm{x}}$ rotated by the angle $\theta$ about the $z$ axis. That is, the adjoint action $\bm{a}\cdot\bm{\sigma}\mapsto U(\bm{a}\cdot\bm{\sigma})U^\dagger$ realizes the $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ rotation $\bm{a}\mapsto R(\hat{\bm{z}},\theta)\bm{a}$.

Let us see the mechanism once more, with an infinitesimal transformation. For $\theta\ll1$, take $U\simeq\mathbb{1}-\ii\frac{\theta}{2}\sigma_3$. Then

$$ U(\bm{a}\cdot\bm{\sigma})U^\dagger \simeq \bm{a}\cdot\bm{\sigma} - \ii\frac{\theta}{2}\left[\sigma_3,\,a_j\sigma_j\right] = \bm{a}\cdot\bm{\sigma} - \ii\frac{\theta}{2}\,a_j\left(2\ii\epsilon_{3jk}\sigma_k\right) = \bm{a}\cdot\bm{\sigma} + \theta\,a_j\epsilon_{3jk}\sigma_k $$

The factors $\mp\ii\frac\theta2\sigma_3$ coming from $U$ and $U^\dagger$ combine into a commutator, and in the relation $[\sigma_3,\sigma_j]=2\ii\epsilon_{3jk}\sigma_k$ that enters there, the factor $2$ exactly cancels the $\frac12$, leaving $\theta$. Using $\epsilon_{312}=+1$ and $\epsilon_{321}=-1$ to write out the components,

$$ a_1 \to a_1 - \theta a_2,\qquad a_2\to a_2+\theta a_1,\qquad a_3\to a_3 $$

which is exactly the first-order expansion of the rotation by the angle $\theta$ about the $z$ axis. For $\bm{a}=\hat{\bm{x}}$ we get $\hat{\bm{x}}\to\hat{\bm{x}}+\theta\hat{\bm{y}}$, which agrees with the first-order expansion of $\cos\theta\,\hat{\bm{x}}+\sin\theta\,\hat{\bm{y}}$ obtained above.

(4) The rotation about the $y$ axis has $\bm{n}=\hat{\bm{y}}$, so we only need to set $\bm{n}\cdot\bm{\sigma}=\sigma_2$ in the expression of Section 5.3.2 of this book:

$$ U(\hat{\bm{y}},\theta) = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\mathbb{1}-\ii\sin\frac{\theta}{2}\sigma_2 $$

Since $-\ii\sigma_2 = -\ii\begin{pmatrix}0&-\ii\\ \ii&0\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}$,

$$ U(\hat{\bm{y}},\theta) = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\frac\theta2 & -\sin\frac\theta2\\[2pt] \sin\frac\theta2 & \cos\frac\theta2\end{pmatrix} $$

which is a real rotation matrix (but with the half angle). Acting on $\ket{\uparrow}=\begin{pmatrix}1\\0\end{pmatrix}$, it gives

$$ U(\hat{\bm{y}},\theta)\ket{\uparrow} = \begin{pmatrix}\cos\frac\theta2\\[2pt] \sin\frac\theta2\end{pmatrix} = \cos\frac{\theta}{2}\ket{\uparrow} + \sin\frac{\theta}{2}\ket{\downarrow} $$

The probability of finding spin up when the spin is measured along the $z$ direction is, by the Born rule, the absolute value squared of the amplitude:

$$ P(\uparrow) = \abs{\braket{\uparrow|U(\hat{\bm{y}},\theta)|\uparrow}}^2 = \cos^2\frac{\theta}{2}, \qquad P(\downarrow) = \sin^2\frac{\theta}{2} $$

The sum is $\cos^2\frac\theta2+\sin^2\frac\theta2=1$, so the normalization is also preserved.

Verification. We check (4) at special angles. For $\theta=0$, $P(\uparrow)=1$ (naturally, since nothing has been done); for $\theta=\pi$, $P(\uparrow)=\cos^2(\pi/2)=0$ (the spin is completely flipped); for $\theta=\pi/2$, $P(\uparrow)=\cos^2(\pi/4)=1/2$ (the spin points along the $x$ axis, so a $z$ measurement is fifty-fifty). All agree with intuition. Furthermore, computing the expectation value,

$$ \braket{\sigma_3} = P(\uparrow)-P(\downarrow) = \cos^2\frac\theta2-\sin^2\frac\theta2 = \cos\theta $$

which agrees exactly with the classical picture “the spin direction is tilted from $z$ by the angle $\theta$.” Here too the structure of (3), the state carries the half angle, the observed vector the full angle, appears as it is. Also, although $U=-\mathbb{1}$ at $\theta=2\pi$ in (2), the probability in (4) returns to its original value, $\cos^2(\pi)=1$. This is consistent with the remark in Section 5.3.2 of this book that the sign does not appear in probabilities and becomes visible only when we make states interfere.

Meaning. The $\cos^2(\theta/2)$ in (4) is precisely the transmission probability when two Stern–Gerlach apparatuses are connected in series, and the appearance of $\theta/2$ rather than $\theta$ is the direct experimental expression of the statement “spinors rotate by half angles.” In materials science, this expression appears as the very analysis formula of spin-resolved ARPES and spin-polarized tunneling spectroscopy. That the tunneling conductance between two ferromagnetic electrodes whose magnetization directions are tilted by the angle $\theta$ takes the form $G\propto1+P_1P_2\cos\theta$ (tunnel magnetoresistance) is also, traced back to its origin, this overlap integral. The relation in (3), “elements of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ carry half angles, the adjoint action carries full angles,” is also the reason why double groups are needed in the symmetry analysis of crystals with spin–orbit coupling (Section 5.5.4 of this book). Orbitals (vectors) return after $2\pi$, but spinors do not. Because there are two answers for the same rotation, we have no choice but to double the elements of the point group.

Exercise 5.4: Constructing the CG coefficients yourself ($1\otimes1=2\oplus1\oplus0$)

Problem (restated)

Combine two spin-1 particles. The dimension count is $3\times3=9=5+3+1$.

(1) Starting from the highest-weight state $\ket{2,2}=\ket{1,1}\ket{1,1}$, apply $J_-=J_-^{(1)}+J_-^{(2)}$ once to find $\ket{2,1}$.

(2) The $m=1$ space is two-dimensional. Construct the normalized state orthogonal to the $\ket{2,1}$ obtained in (1), and verify by applying $J_+$ that it is $\ket{1,1}_{\text{tot}}$ (the highest weight of the composite spin $J=1$).

(3) The $m=0$ space is three-dimensional. Find $\ket{2,0}$ and $\ket{1,0}_{\text{tot}}$ with the lowering operator, and construct $\ket{0,0}$ as the state orthogonal to both.

(4) Confirm the exchange-symmetry pattern: $J=2$ (symmetric), $J=1$ (antisymmetric), $J=0$ (symmetric).

Solution

Strategy. We apply, exactly as it stands, the procedure carried out for $\frac12\otimes\frac12$ in Section 5.3.4 of this book to $1\otimes1$. The only tools are the formula for the raising and lowering operators from Section 5.3.3 of this book

$$ J_\pm\ket{j,m} = \sqrt{j(j+1)-m(m\pm1)}\;\ket{j,m\pm1} $$

and $J_\pm = J_\pm^{(1)}+J_\pm^{(2)}$ for the composite system. There is no need to consult a table. To lighten the notation, we abbreviate the tensor-product state with particle 1 at $m_1$ and particle 2 at $m_2$ as $\ket{m_1,m_2}$ (we omit $j$ since both have $j=1$). States of the composite system are written $\ket{J,M}$ with capital letters.

First we prepare the raising and lowering coefficients for $j=1$. Since $j(j+1)=2$,

$$ J_-\ket{1,1}=\sqrt{2-1\cdot0}\,\ket{1,0}=\sqrt2\,\ket{1,0},\qquad J_-\ket{1,0}=\sqrt{2-0\cdot(-1)}\,\ket{1,-1}=\sqrt2\,\ket{1,-1} $$ $$ J_+\ket{1,-1}=\sqrt2\,\ket{1,0},\qquad J_+\ket{1,0}=\sqrt2\,\ket{1,1},\qquad J_-\ket{1,-1}=J_+\ket{1,1}=0 $$

For $j=1$ the raising and lowering coefficient is $\sqrt2$ at either step, and this is what makes the calculations of this problem so clean.

(1) The only tensor-product state that can make $M=m_1+m_2=2$ is $\ket{+1,+1}$. Therefore it is the highest-weight state, and

$$ \ket{2,2} = \ket{+1,+1} $$

Apply $J_-$ to both sides. Since the left-hand side has $J=2$, $M=2$,

$$ J_-\ket{2,2} = \sqrt{2\cdot3 - 2\cdot1}\;\ket{2,1} = \sqrt{4}\;\ket{2,1} = 2\,\ket{2,1} $$

On the right-hand side, letting $J_-=J_-^{(1)}+J_-^{(2)}$ act on each particle,

$$ \left(J_-^{(1)}+J_-^{(2)}\right)\ket{+1,+1} = \sqrt2\,\ket{0,+1} + \sqrt2\,\ket{+1,0} $$

Equating the two and dividing by $2$,

$$ \ket{2,1} = \frac{\sqrt2}{2}\left(\ket{+1,0}+\ket{0,+1}\right) = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(\ket{+1,0}+\ket{0,+1}\right) $$

This agrees with the hint’s $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{1,1}\ket{1,0}+\ket{1,0}\ket{1,1})$. The normalization is also correct: $\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)^2\times2=1$.

(2) The tensor-product states that make $M=1$ are the two states $\ket{+1,0}$ and $\ket{0,+1}$, so the $M=1$ subspace is two-dimensional. One dimension of it is occupied by the $\ket{2,1}$ of (1), so the remaining dimension is fixed by the orthogonality condition. Writing the state as $\alpha\ket{+1,0}+\beta\ket{0,+1}$ with coefficients $(\alpha,\beta)$, orthogonality to $\ket{2,1}$ gives $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\alpha+\beta)=0$, that is, $\beta=-\alpha$, and normalization gives $2\alpha^2=1$. Following the Condon–Shortley convention (the coefficient of the term with the largest $m_1$ is taken positive), we choose $\alpha=+1/\sqrt2$:

$$ \ket{1,1}_{\text{tot}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(\ket{+1,0}-\ket{0,+1}\right) $$

We verify with $J_+$ that this is really the highest weight of $J=1$. First, for each term,

$$ J_+\ket{+1,0} = \underbrace{J_+^{(1)}\ket{+1}}_{=0}\otimes\ket{0} + \ket{+1}\otimes\underbrace{J_+^{(2)}\ket{0}}_{=\sqrt2\ket{+1}} = \sqrt2\,\ket{+1,+1} $$ $$ J_+\ket{0,+1} = \sqrt2\,\ket{+1,+1} + 0 = \sqrt2\,\ket{+1,+1} $$

Therefore

$$ J_+\ket{1,1}_{\text{tot}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(\sqrt2\,\ket{+1,+1}-\sqrt2\,\ket{+1,+1}\right) = 0 $$

A $J_z$ eigenstate annihilated by $J_+$ is none other than the highest weight of the irreducible representation to which it belongs. At the highest weight $J=M$, so here $J=M=1$, and $\ket{1,1}_{\text{tot}}$ is the highest-weight state of total spin $J=1$. We can also pin this down by counting dimensions. The $M=2$ space is only the one-dimensional space of $\ket{+1,+1}$, and it is used up by $\ket{2,2}$. Of the two dimensions of $M=1$, the $J=2$ multiplet occupies one, so the remaining dimension must be the top of a new multiplet, and its $J$ can be nothing other than $1$.

(3) The tensor-product states that make $M=0$ are the three states $\ket{+1,-1}$, $\ket{0,0}$, and $\ket{-1,+1}$, so the subspace is three-dimensional. One $M=0$ component each of $J=2,1,0$ lives here.

$\ket{2,0}$. Apply $J_-$ to $\ket{2,1}$. The left-hand side is

$$ J_-\ket{2,1} = \sqrt{2\cdot3-1\cdot0}\;\ket{2,0} = \sqrt6\;\ket{2,0} $$

For the right-hand side, letting $J_-^{(1)}+J_-^{(2)}$ act on each tensor-product state,

$$ J_-\ket{+1,0} = \sqrt2\,\ket{0,0} + \sqrt2\,\ket{+1,-1},\qquad J_-\ket{0,+1} = \sqrt2\,\ket{-1,+1} + \sqrt2\,\ket{0,0} $$

so that

$$ J_-\ket{2,1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left[\sqrt2\ket{0,0}+\sqrt2\ket{+1,-1}+\sqrt2\ket{-1,+1}+\sqrt2\ket{0,0}\right] = \ket{+1,-1} + 2\ket{0,0} + \ket{-1,+1} $$

Equating the two and dividing by $\sqrt6$,

$$ \ket{2,0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}\left(\ket{+1,-1} + 2\,\ket{0,0} + \ket{-1,+1}\right) $$

The normalization is correct: $\frac16(1+4+1)=1$.

$\ket{1,0}_{\text{tot}}$. Apply $J_-$ to $\ket{1,1}_{\text{tot}}$. Since the left-hand side has $J=1,M=1$, $J_-\ket{1,1}_{\text{tot}}=\sqrt{2-0}\,\ket{1,0}_{\text{tot}}=\sqrt2\,\ket{1,0}_{\text{tot}}$. For the right-hand side, we use the same two formulas as above with the sign changed, to get

$$ \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left[\sqrt2\ket{0,0}+\sqrt2\ket{+1,-1}-\sqrt2\ket{-1,+1}-\sqrt2\ket{0,0}\right] = \ket{+1,-1}-\ket{-1,+1} $$

The characteristic feature is that the $\ket{0,0}$ terms cancel exactly. Hence

$$ \ket{1,0}_{\text{tot}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(\ket{+1,-1}-\ket{-1,+1}\right) $$

$\ket{0,0}$. The remaining one dimension is fixed by the orthogonality condition. The symbols collide between the composite state $\ket{J{=}0,M{=}0}$ and the tensor-product state $\ket{m_1{=}0,m_2{=}0}$, so below we write the tensor-product one as $\ket{0,0}_{\text{prod}}$. Let $\ket{0,0}=\alpha\ket{+1,-1}+\beta\ket{0,0}_{\text{prod}}+\gamma\ket{-1,+1}$. Then

$$ \braket{1,0|_{\text{tot}}\,0,0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\alpha-\gamma) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \gamma=\alpha $$ $$ \braket{2,0|0,0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}(\alpha+2\beta+\gamma) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2\alpha+2\beta=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \beta=-\alpha $$

From the normalization $\alpha^2+\beta^2+\gamma^2=3\alpha^2=1$ we get $\alpha=1/\sqrt3$. Hence

$$ \ket{0,0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\left(\ket{+1,-1} - \ket{0,0}_{\text{prod}} + \ket{-1,+1}\right) $$

This agrees with the expression in the hint. That this is $J=0$ can be confirmed by checking that it is annihilated by both $J_\pm$. For example,

$$ J_+\ket{+1,-1}=\sqrt2\ket{+1,0},\qquad J_+\ket{0,0}_{\text{prod}}=\sqrt2\ket{+1,0}+\sqrt2\ket{0,+1},\qquad J_+\ket{-1,+1}=\sqrt2\ket{0,+1} $$

give

$$ J_+\ket{0,0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt3}\left[\sqrt2\ket{+1,0}-\sqrt2\ket{+1,0}-\sqrt2\ket{0,+1}+\sqrt2\ket{0,+1}\right]=0 $$

and similarly $J_-\ket{0,0}=0$. Since it is annihilated by both raising and lowering, it is a one-dimensional irreducible representation, that is, $J=0$.

(4) We look at the behavior of each state under the exchange of the two particles, $P_{12}:\ket{m_1,m_2}\to\ket{m_2,m_1}$.

  • $J=2$: $\ket{2,2}=\ket{+1,+1}$ is obviously symmetric. $\ket{2,1}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{+1,0}+\ket{0,+1})$ is also invariant under exchange and symmetric. $\ket{2,0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt6}(\ket{+1,-1}+2\ket{0,0}_{\text{prod}}+\ket{-1,+1})$ is also symmetric, since only the first and third terms are interchanged. Hence all five states of $J=2$ are symmetric.
  • $J=1$: $\ket{1,1}_{\text{tot}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{+1,0}-\ket{0,+1})$ changes sign under exchange, so it is antisymmetric. $\ket{1,0}_{\text{tot}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{+1,-1}-\ket{-1,+1})$ is also antisymmetric.
  • $J=0$: $\ket{0,0}=\frac{1}{\sqrt3}(\ket{+1,-1}-\ket{0,0}_{\text{prod}}+\ket{-1,+1})$ is symmetric, since the first and third terms are interchanged and the second is invariant.

To summarize, $J=2$ is symmetric, $J=1$ is antisymmetric, and $J=0$ is symmetric. This is the case $j_1=j_2=1$ of the general rule

$$ P_{12}\ket{J,M} = (-1)^{j_1+j_2-J}\ket{J,M}\qquad(j_1=j_2=j\text{ when}) $$

and it agrees with the fact that $(-1)^{2-J}$ gives $+,-,+$ for $J=2,1,0$, respectively. The dimensions are also consistent. Of the $3\times3=9$ tensor-product states, $3\cdot4/2=6$ are symmetric and $3\cdot2/2=3$ are antisymmetric, and these split correctly as $6=5+1$ ($J=2$ and $J=0$) and $3$ ($J=1$).

Verification. The count of dimensions works out: $5+3+1=9=3\times3$. We can also confirm orthogonality by inner products. For example,

$$ \braket{2,0|1,0}_{\text{tot}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left[1\cdot1 + 2\cdot0 + 1\cdot(-1)\right] = 0 $$ $$ \braket{2,0|0,0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt6}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\left[1\cdot1+2\cdot(-1)+1\cdot1\right] = 0, \qquad \braket{1,0|_{\text{tot}}0,0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt3}\left[1\cdot 1 + 0\cdot(-1) + (-1)\cdot 1\right]=0 $$

Furthermore, we can check with the eigenvalues of the Casimir operator $\bm{J}^2=\bm{J}_1^2+\bm{J}_2^2+2\bm{J}_1\cdot\bm{J}_2$. Since $\bm{J}_1^2=\bm{J}_2^2=2$ ($j=1$), $\bm{J}_1\cdot\bm{J}_2 = \frac12\left[J(J+1)-4\right]$, which equals $+1,\,-1,\,-2$ for $J=2,1,0$, respectively. The sum of these weighted by their degeneracies (the trace) is $5\cdot1+3\cdot(-1)+1\cdot(-2)=0$, which agrees with $\Tr(\bm{J}_1\cdot\bm{J}_2)=0$ (each component is traceless).

Meaning. The three invariant combinations constructed here are in fact precisely the three kinds of tensors that can be built from two vectors. A spin-1 state transforms in the same way as a three-dimensional vector, so if we split the tensor product $a_ib_j$ (nine components) of $\bm{a}$ and $\bm{b}$ into pieces that do not mix under rotations, we obtain

$$ a_ib_j = \underbrace{\frac13(\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b})\delta_{ij}}_{J=0,\ 1\text{ component}} + \underbrace{\frac12\left(a_ib_j-a_jb_i\right)}_{J=1,\ 3\text{ components (}\bm{a}\times\bm{b}\text{)}} + \underbrace{\left[\frac12(a_ib_j+a_jb_i)-\frac13(\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b})\delta_{ij}\right]}_{J=2,\ 5\text{ components (symmetric traceless)}} $$

The state $\ket{0,0}$ corresponds to the dot product $\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b}$ (symmetric, scalar), $J=1$ to the cross product $\bm{a}\times\bm{b}$ (antisymmetric, pseudovector), and $J=2$ to the symmetric traceless tensor. That the pattern of exchange symmetry is $+,-,+$ is nothing other than the symmetry of this $1+3+5$ decomposition.

In materials science, we use this decomposition every day. It is the splitting of second-rank tensor properties (the permittivity $\varepsilon_{ij}$, the susceptibility, part of the elastic constants) into an isotropic component, an antisymmetric component, and a symmetric traceless component. The decomposition of the Raman tensor (the totally symmetric component is the isotropic part of the polarizability, the antisymmetric component appears in resonance Raman scattering, and the anisotropic symmetric component is the degenerate modes) and the classification of NMR chemical shift tensors and quadrupolar interactions are likewise written in the same language of $J=0,1,2$. The ranks $k=0,2,4,6$ that appear when we expand the crystal-field Hamiltonian in Stevens operators are also a consequence of the same irreducible tensor decomposition. The calculation that combines $\pi$ and $\pi$ in particle physics and the calculation that decomposes the dielectric tensor into irreducible parts consult the same table of CG coefficients.

Exercise 5.5: Predicting cross-section ratios from isospin

Problem (restated)

The deuteron $d$ is an isospin singlet ($I=0$), $\pi$ has $I=1$, and the nucleon has $I=1/2$.

(1) Which $\ket{I,I_3}$ are $\ket{pp}$ and $\ket{nn}$, respectively? Also expand $\ket{pn}$ in terms of $\ket{1,0}$ and $\ket{0,0}$.

(2) For the reactions $pp\to d\pi^+$ and $np\to d\pi^0$, express the transition matrix elements in terms of the isospin amplitude $A_1$ (the amplitude for $I=1$).

(3) Show that $\abs{\mathcal{M}(pp\to d\pi^+)}^2 / \abs{\mathcal{M}(np\to d\pi^0)}^2 = 2$.

(4) Find the decay branching ratio $\Gamma(\Delta^0\to n\pi^0)/\Gamma(\Delta^0\to p\pi^-)$ of the $\Delta^0$ using the CG coefficients constructed in Section 5.4.3.

Solution

Strategy. We use the statement of Section 5.4.3 of this book: “the amplitude of the strong interaction depends only on the total isospin $I$.” The procedure has three steps. (i) Expand the initial and final states in the basis $\ket{I,I_3}$. (ii) Pick out only the components with the same $I$ and take the product of their coefficients. (iii) Take the ratio while keeping the unknown amplitudes $A_I$; the $A_I$ then drop out. As in Section 5.4.1 of this book, the nucleons are $\ket{p}=\ket{\frac12,+\frac12}$ and $\ket{n}=\ket{\frac12,-\frac12}$.

(1) The two-nucleon system decomposes as $\frac12\otimes\frac12=1\oplus0$. We only need to reread the CG coefficients of $\frac12\otimes\frac12$ constructed in Section 5.3.4 of this book with the replacements $\ket{\uparrow}\to\ket{p}$ and $\ket{\downarrow}\to\ket{n}$.

The state $\ket{pp}$ has $I_3=\frac12+\frac12=+1$, and it is the only state that produces $I_3=+1$, so it is the highest-weight state:

$$ \ket{pp} = \ket{1,+1} $$

Similarly, $\ket{nn}$ is the only state with $I_3=-1$, so

$$ \ket{nn} = \ket{1,-1} $$

Both are pure $I=1$ (triplet) states.

The $I_3=0$ space is two-dimensional, spanned by $\ket{pn}$ (particle 1 is $p$, particle 2 is $n$) and $\ket{np}$. Transferring the result of Section 5.3.4 of this book as it stands, we have

$$ \ket{1,0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(\ket{pn}+\ket{np}\right), \qquad \ket{0,0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(\ket{pn}-\ket{np}\right) $$

Solving these in reverse (the matrix is a $2\times2$ orthogonal matrix, so we only need to transpose it) gives

$$ \ket{pn} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(\ket{1,0}+\ket{0,0}\right), \qquad \ket{np} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left(\ket{1,0}-\ket{0,0}\right) $$

This agrees with the Hint, $\ket{pn}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{1,0}+\ket{0,0})$. The point is that $pp$ and $nn$ are pure $I=1$, whereas $pn$ is an equal-weight superposition of $I=1$ and $I=0$, containing each component with probability $1/2$.

(2) We classify the final states. Since $d$ has $I=0$ and $\pi$ has $I=1$, the total isospin of the $d\pi$ system is $0\otimes1=1$; that is, it is necessarily $I=1$ (combining with a singlet changes nothing). Since $I_3$ is determined by that of the $\pi$,

$$ \ket{d\pi^+}=\ket{1,+1},\qquad \ket{d\pi^0}=\ket{1,0},\qquad \ket{d\pi^-}=\ket{1,-1} $$

Therefore the only independent amplitude that acts in this reaction is the $I=1$ one, which in the notation of Section 5.4.3 of this book can be written as

$$ \braket{1,I_3'|\Ham_{\text{strong}}|1,I_3} = A_1\,\delta_{I_3I_3'} $$

The $I=0$ component cannot contribute, because no $I=0$ state exists in the final state.

$pp\to d\pi^+$. By (1) the initial state is the pure $\ket{1,+1}$, and the final state is also $\ket{1,+1}$, so

$$ \mathcal{M}(pp\to d\pi^+) = \braket{1,+1|\Ham_{\text{strong}}|1,+1} = A_1 $$

$np\to d\pi^0$. By (1) the initial state is $\ket{np}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(\ket{1,0}-\ket{0,0})$. Only the $I=1$ component overlaps with the final state $\ket{d\pi^0}=\ket{1,0}$, so

$$ \mathcal{M}(np\to d\pi^0) = \bra{1,0}\Ham_{\text{strong}}\ket{np} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\bra{1,0}\Ham_{\text{strong}}\ket{1,0} - \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\bra{1,0}\Ham_{\text{strong}}\ket{0,0} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}A_1 $$

(The vanishing of the second term, $\bra{1,0}\Ham_{\text{strong}}\ket{0,0}=0$, follows from isospin conservation.) The sign depends on the choice of phase of the initial state (which nucleon is called particle 1), but only the absolute value is used below, so it has no effect. This agrees with the Hint, $\mathcal{M}(np\to d\pi^0)=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}A_1$.

(3) Taking the squares of the absolute values of the two expressions in (2) and forming the ratio, we get

$$ \frac{\abs{\mathcal{M}(pp\to d\pi^+)}^2}{\abs{\mathcal{M}(np\to d\pi^0)}^2} = \frac{\abs{A_1}^2}{\abs{\frac{1}{\sqrt2}A_1}^2} = \frac{\abs{A_1}^2}{\frac12\abs{A_1}^2} = 2 $$

The unknown $A_1$ cancels completely between numerator and denominator. Without knowing anything about the details of QCD, the nuclear-force potential, or the deuteron wave function, the ratio alone is fixed to be $2$.

The origin of this $2$ can be put in a single sentence: “half of $np$ is $I=0$, and that part cannot go to $d\pi$.” While $pp$ is entirely $I=1$, $np$ has an $I=1$ component of only $\abs{1/\sqrt2}^2=1/2$.

(4) The $\Delta^0$ is the $I_3=-1/2$ member of the $\Delta(1232)$ quartet ($I=3/2$), so $\ket{\Delta^0}=\ket{\frac32,-\frac12}$. We can simply use the CG coefficients constructed in Step 3 of the derivation in Section 5.4.3 of this book:

$$ \ket{\tfrac32,-\tfrac12} = \sqrt{\tfrac13}\,\ket{\pi^- p} + \sqrt{\tfrac23}\,\ket{\pi^0 n} $$

The Hamiltonian for the decay $\Delta^0\to N\pi$ is isospin invariant, so by the Wigner–Eckart theorem (Section 5.5.3 of this book) the reduced matrix element is common to both channels. Hence the decay width is proportional to the square of the CG coefficient:

$$ \Gamma(\Delta^0\to p\,\pi^-) \propto \left(\sqrt{\tfrac13}\right)^2 = \frac13, \qquad \Gamma(\Delta^0\to n\,\pi^0) \propto \left(\sqrt{\tfrac23}\right)^2 = \frac23 $$

Therefore

$$ \frac{\Gamma(\Delta^0\to n\,\pi^0)}{\Gamma(\Delta^0\to p\,\pi^-)} = \frac{2/3}{1/3} = 2 $$

This agrees with the value in the Hint. In the case of $\Delta^+$ (Section 5.5.3 of this book), $\ket{\frac32,+\frac12}=\sqrt{\frac23}\ket{\pi^0p}+\sqrt{\frac13}\ket{\pi^+n}$ gives $\Gamma(\Delta^+\to p\pi^0)/\Gamma(\Delta^+\to n\pi^+)=2$, which is again the same value. This is not a coincidence: it is because $\Delta^0$ and $\Delta^+$ are related by $I_3\to-I_3$ (corresponding to the interchange $u\leftrightarrow d$).

Verification. First we confirm that the expansion in (1) forms a complete set. We have $\abs{\braket{1,0|pn}}^2+\abs{\braket{0,0|pn}}^2 = \frac12+\frac12=1$, so the probabilities sum to $1$.

Next we check (4) using a sum rule for the whole quartet. Listing the branching ratios to $N\pi$ for each member of $I=3/2$ gives

$$ \Delta^{++}:\ \pi^+p\ (1),\qquad \Delta^+:\ \pi^0p\ \left(\tfrac23\right),\ \pi^+n\ \left(\tfrac13\right),\qquad \Delta^0:\ \pi^-p\ \left(\tfrac13\right),\ \pi^0n\ \left(\tfrac23\right),\qquad \Delta^-:\ \pi^-n\ (1) $$

and for every member the coefficients sum to $1$ ($\frac23+\frac13=1$). This reflects the normalization of the CG coefficients, $\sum_{m_1m_2}\abs{\braket{j_1m_1j_2m_2|jm}}^2=1$, and is consistent with the fact that “the $\Delta$ decays almost $100\%$ to $N\pi$ in every charge state” (measured: $99.4\%$).

For (3), we can check against experiment. The cross-section ratio of $pp\to d\pi^+$ to $np\to d\pi^0$, measured at the same center-of-mass energy, is reported to be about $2$, in agreement with the prediction. However, to treat the ratio of the cross sections themselves rigorously, one must correct for the statistical factor arising from the initial state $pp$ consisting of identical particles, and for the differences in phase space and incident flux. What is purely a consequence of isospin is the ratio of $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2$ shown here.

Meaning. This problem applies once more, to a completely different reaction, the same logic as the $\pi N$ scattering ($9:1:2$) of Section 5.4.3 of this book. In both cases only ratios can be predicted, not absolute values, because symmetry gives “the constraints that the dynamics must obey whatever it is,” but does not give the dynamics itself.

This same pattern carries over unchanged to materials science. Group theory tells us which phonon modes are Raman active and gives the ratios of the polarization dependences among modes belonging to the same irreducible representation, but the absolute value of the scattering intensity (the magnitude of the derivative of the polarizability) cannot be obtained without a first-principles calculation. The $A_{3/2}$ of Section 5.4.3 of this book and the reduced matrix element of the Raman tensor play exactly the same role. The division of labor “fix with group theory everything that group theory can fix, and compute only the rest” is a common practice in both particle physics and condensed matter physics.

Exercise 5.6: Weight diagrams of $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ and the $\Omega^-$

Problem (restated)

(1) Plot the three points $u,d,s$ in the $(I_3,Y)$ plane (Table 5.6) and verify that connecting them gives an equilateral triangle. Similarly plot $\bar u,\bar d,\bar s$ and show that they form an upside-down triangle.

(2) Write out all $9$ weights of $\bm{3}\otimes\bar{\bm{3}}$ as sums of a weight of $q$ and a weight of $\bar q$. Check that the origin $(0,0)$ appears three times, and explain that this is consistent with the decomposition $\bm{8}\oplus\bm{1}$.

(3) Use the equal-spacing rule of the decuplet to predict the mass of the $\Omega^-$, and compare it with the measured value $1672.45\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(4) Use the Gell-Mann–Nishijima relation $Q=I_3+Y/2$ to verify that the charge of the $\Omega^-$ ($I=0$, $B=1$, $S=-3$) is $-1$. Also verify that the charge of the $\Delta^{++}$ ($I_3=+3/2$, $B=1$, $S=0$) is $+2$.

Solution

Strategy. We start from the weights $(I_3,Y)$ of $\mathrm{SU}(3)_F$ introduced in Section 5.4.4 of this book and the quark quantum numbers in Table 5.6. Parts (1) and (2) need only addition and drawing; (3) is an application of the equal-spacing rule of Section 5.4.4 of this book; (4) is a substitution into the Gell-Mann–Nishijima relation. All the calculations close within the rational numbers, so we keep fractions as they are.

(1) From Table 5.6, the weights of the quarks are

$$ u:\ \left(I_3,Y\right)=\left(+\tfrac12,\ +\tfrac13\right),\qquad d:\ \left(-\tfrac12,\ +\tfrac13\right),\qquad s:\ \left(0,\ -\tfrac23\right) $$

(here $Y=B+S$, all of $u,d,s$ have $B=1/3$, and $S$ is $0,0,-1$ respectively). The sum of the hypercharges is $\frac13+\frac13-\frac23=0$, so the center of mass lies at the origin.

One caution is needed here. If $I_3$ and $Y$ are plotted on the same scale, the distance between $u$ and $d$ is $1$, while the distance between $u$ and $s$ is

$$ \sqrt{\left(\tfrac12\right)^2+\left(\tfrac13+\tfrac23\right)^2}=\sqrt{\tfrac14+1}=\frac{\sqrt5}{2}=1.118\cdots $$

The two do not agree, and the triangle is only isosceles. The triangle becomes equilateral when the vertical axis is taken not as $Y$ itself but as the diagonal generator $T^8=\frac{\sqrt3}{2}Y$ defined in Section 5.4.4 of this book. That is, writing the weights as $(T^3,T^8)=\left(I_3,\ \frac{\sqrt3}{2}Y\right)$, we have

$$ u:\left(\tfrac12,\ \tfrac{\sqrt3}{6}\right),\qquad d:\left(-\tfrac12,\ \tfrac{\sqrt3}{6}\right),\qquad s:\left(0,\ -\tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\right) $$

and the side lengths are

$$ \abs{u-d} = 1,\qquad \abs{u-s} = \sqrt{\left(\tfrac12\right)^2+\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{6}+\tfrac{\sqrt3}{3}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\tfrac14+\left(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}\right)^2} = \sqrt{\tfrac14+\tfrac34} = 1 $$

and $\abs{d-s}$ is also $1$ by symmetry. The three sides are equal, so the triangle is equilateral. This scale is natural because $T^3$ and $T^8$ are treated on an equal footing under the normalization of the generators, $\Tr\left(T^aT^b\right)=\frac12\delta^{ab}$. Figure 5.6(a) of this book is drawn with almost equal scales on the two axes (1 unit of $I_3$ is $80$ px, 1 unit of $Y$ is $75$ px), so strictly speaking it is an isosceles triangle with side ratio $1:1.06$ and only “looks nearly equilateral.” A strictly equilateral triangle is obtained only when drawn on the $(T^3,T^8)$ scale just seen. Below, when we say “weight,” we use $(I_3,Y)$ for the values and $(T^3,T^8)$ when drawing.

The antiquarks belong to the complex conjugate representation $\bar{\bm{3}}$, and the signs of all quantum numbers are reversed ($B,S$ are reversed, so $Y$ is reversed too, and $I_3$ is reversed as well):

$$ \bar u:\left(-\tfrac12,\ -\tfrac13\right),\qquad \bar d:\left(+\tfrac12,\ -\tfrac13\right),\qquad \bar s:\left(0,\ +\tfrac23\right) $$

This is the configuration obtained by rotating the three points of $\bm{3}$ by $180^\circ$ about the origin (that is, mapping them point-symmetrically), namely $(I_3,Y)\to(-I_3,-Y)$. On the other hand, “upside down” means the reflection about the horizontal axis, that is, the $I_3$ axis, $(I_3,Y)\to(I_3,-Y)$, and the two differ only in the sign of $I_3$. For the present three points, however, the upside-down reflection merely interchanges the labels, $u\to$ (the position of $\bar d$) and $d\to$ (the position of $\bar u$), so we obtain the same set of points. Hence it is fair to say that “$\bar{\bm{3}}$ is the upside-down triangle.” If $\bm{3}$ is a triangle that is “pointing down” ($s$ at the bottom), then $\bar{\bm{3}}$ is a triangle that is “pointing up” ($\bar s$ at the top).

(2) The weights of a tensor-product representation are the sums of the weights of the constituents (because both $I_3$ and $Y$ are additive quantities). We write out all nine $q\bar q$ combinations.

The nine weights of $\bm{3}\otimes\bar{\bm{3}}$
$q\bar q$$I_3$$Y$$Q=I_3+Y/2$Corresponding meson
$u\bar s$$+\tfrac12$$+1$$+1$$K^+$
$d\bar s$$-\tfrac12$$+1$$0$$K^0$
$u\bar d$$+1$$0$$+1$$\pi^+$
$d\bar u$$-1$$0$$-1$$\pi^-$
$u\bar u$$0$$0$$0$$\pi^0,\ \eta,\ \eta'$
$d\bar d$$0$$0$$0$
$s\bar s$$0$$0$$0$
$s\bar d$$+\tfrac12$$-1$$0$$\bar K^0$
$s\bar u$$-\tfrac12$$-1$$-1$$K^-$

For example, for $u\bar s$ we have $I_3 = \frac12+0=\frac12$ and $Y=\frac13+\frac23=+1$, in agreement with the $K^+$ ($Y=+1$) of Table 5.4. For $s\bar u$ we have $I_3=0-\frac12=-\frac12$ and $Y=-\frac23-\frac13=-1$, which is the $K^-$.

Counting, the weights other than the origin are the six $(\pm1,0)$, $(\pm\frac12,+1)$, $(\pm\frac12,-1)$, all distinct, and in the $(T^3,T^8)$ plane they form the vertices of a regular hexagon. The remaining three, $u\bar u,\,d\bar d,\,s\bar s$, all fall on $(0,0)$. That is, the origin is threefold degenerate. The total is $6+3=9$, which matches $3\times3$.

The consistency with $\bm{8}\oplus\bm{1}$ can be seen by comparing with the weight diagram of each irreducible representation. The octet $\bm{8}$ is “the six vertices of the hexagon plus a twofold degenerate center,” of dimension $6+2=8$, while the singlet $\bm{1}$ is just “the single point at the center,” of dimension $1$. Superposing the two gives the six points of the hexagon and a $2+1=3$-fold center, in complete agreement with the count above:

$$ \underbrace{6\ \text{(hexagon)} + 2\ \text{(center)}}_{\bm{8}} \ +\ \underbrace{1\ \text{(center)}}_{\bm{1}} \ =\ 6 + 3 = 9 $$

Physically, of the three orthogonal combinations at the center, two are members of the octet (for pseudoscalar mesons, $\pi^0\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(u\bar u-d\bar d)$ and $\eta_8\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt6}(u\bar u+d\bar d-2s\bar s)$), and the remaining one is the $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ singlet ($\eta_1\sim\frac{1}{\sqrt3}(u\bar u+d\bar d+s\bar s)$, the main component of the actual $\eta'$). The singlet combination contains the three flavors on an equal footing because it is invariant under $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ transformations.

(3) We list the masses of the decuplet in Figure 5.7(b), starting from the larger $Y$:

$$ \Delta\ (Y=1):\ 1232\ \mathrm{MeV},\quad \Sigma^*\ (Y=0):\ 1385,\quad \Xi^*\ (Y=-1):\ 1533,\quad \Omega\ (Y=-2):\ ? $$

Measuring the spacings from the three that have been measured, we get

$$ m_{\Sigma^*}-m_{\Delta} = 1385-1232 = 153\ \mathrm{MeV},\qquad m_{\Xi^*}-m_{\Sigma^*} = 1533-1385 = 148\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

They are well matched (the difference is $5\ \mathrm{MeV}$, or $3\%$). Assuming the equal-spacing rule, and supposing that the last spacing is equal to the preceding value $148\ \mathrm{MeV}$, we get

$$ m_{\Omega} \simeq m_{\Xi^*} + \left(m_{\Xi^*}-m_{\Sigma^*}\right) = 1533 + 148 = 1681\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

Comparing with the measured value $1672.45\ \mathrm{MeV}$,

$$ \Delta m = 1681 - 1672.45 = 8.55\ \mathrm{MeV}, \qquad \frac{\abs{\Delta m}}{m_\Omega^{\text{exp}}} = \frac{8.55}{1672.45} = 5.11\times10^{-3} = 0.51\% $$

The prediction is correct to an accuracy of $0.5\%$. For reference, if we make a least-squares fit of the form $m=\alpha+\beta Y$ using all three points, we obtain $\alpha=1383.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $\beta=-150.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$, which gives $m_\Omega = 1383.3+2\times150.5 = 1684.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$ at $Y=-2$ (error $0.71\%$). Either extrapolation leads to the same conclusion, about $1680\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

Note that the statement in Figure 5.7(b) of this book that the mass changes “by about $147\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for each decrease of $Y$ by 1” refers to the average of the three spacings obtained from the four measured points after the $\Omega^-$ was found,

$$ 153,\qquad 148,\qquad m_\Omega - m_{\Xi^*} = 1672-1533 = 139\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

namely $\frac{153+148+139}{3}=146.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$. At the time of the prediction only the first two above were available, so it is natural to adopt the preceding spacing $148\ \mathrm{MeV}$; in fact that result ($1681\ \mathrm{MeV}$) is hardly different from the one using the average ($1533+147=1680\ \mathrm{MeV}$). The slight tendency of the spacing to shrink ($153\to148\to139$) shows that the equal-spacing rule is not exact and that higher-order effects of the $\mathrm{SU}(3)_F$ breaking remain.

(4) We substitute into the Gell-Mann–Nishijima relation $Q=I_3+\frac{Y}{2}$, $Y=B+S$.

$\Omega^-$. Since $I=0$, only $I_3=0$ is possible ($2I+1=1$). Since $B=1$ and $S=-3$,

$$ Y = B+S = 1+(-3) = -2, \qquad Q = I_3 + \frac{Y}{2} = 0 + \frac{-2}{2} = -1 $$

The charge is indeed $-1$. This also agrees with the row of the $\Omega^-$ in Table 5.4 ($Y=-2$).

$\Delta^{++}$. Since $I_3=+\frac32$, $B=1$, and $S=0$,

$$ Y = 1+0 = 1, \qquad Q = \frac32 + \frac12 = 2 $$

The charge is indeed $+2$. The $\Delta^{++}$ is the $I_3=+3/2$ end of the $I=3/2$ quartet, and it sits at the right end of the $Y=1$ row (the row of the $\Delta$).

“Why the relation can be written this way” can also be stated in a single sentence in the language of weights. $I_3$ and $Y$ are none other than the two diagonal generators of $\mathrm{SU}(3)_F$ (the Cartan subalgebra), $T^3,\,T^8$ ($I_3=T^3$, $Y=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}T^8$), and the Gell-Mann–Nishijima relation amounts to the statement that the charge operator is a linear combination of them:

$$ Q = T^3 + \frac{1}{\sqrt3}T^8 $$

Writing this out in the fundamental representation, $T^3=\frac12\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,0)$ and $\frac{1}{\sqrt3}T^8=\frac16\mathrm{diag}(1,1,-2)$, so

$$ Q = \mathrm{diag}\left(\tfrac12+\tfrac16,\ -\tfrac12+\tfrac16,\ -\tfrac13\right) = \mathrm{diag}\left(+\tfrac23,\ -\tfrac13,\ -\tfrac13\right) $$

which gives exactly the charges of $u,d,s$. Moreover, $\Tr Q = \frac23-\frac13-\frac13 = 0$, which expresses the fact that $Q$ is a generator of $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ (not of $\mathrm{U}(3)$), that is, traceless. That the quark charges take the fractional values $\frac23,\,-\frac13$ is nothing other than a consequence of this group-theoretic constraint that “the sum of the charges of the three flavors must be zero.”

Verification. We check independently of the quark model. The $\Omega^-$ is $sss$, so adding three copies of $Q_s=-\frac13$ from Table 5.6 gives $Q=3\times(-\frac13)=-1$ ✓. The strangeness is also $S=3\times(-1)=-3$ ✓, and the baryon number is $B=3\times\frac13=1$ ✓. The $\Delta^{++}$ is $uuu$, so $Q=3\times(+\frac23)=+2$ ✓ and $I_3=3\times(+\frac12)=+\frac32$ ✓.
