As a check of (2), it suffices to see that the values of $Q$ listed in the table all agree with the charges of the actual mesons ($K^+:+1$, $K^0:0$, $\pi^\pm:\pm1$, $\pi^0:0$, $\bar K^0:0$, $K^-:-1$). Also, the baryon number $B$ of a $q\bar q$ state is $\frac13-\frac13=0$, so it follows automatically that mesons carry no baryon number.

Check of (1): the sum of the three weights, $\left(\frac12-\frac12+0,\ \frac13+\frac13-\frac23\right)=(0,0)$, is a direct consequence of the generators being traceless ($\Tr T^a=0$, Section 5.3.1 of this book). It is no accident that the center of the equilateral triangle lies at the origin.

Meaning. The prediction of the $\Omega^-$ in (3) is a historical case in which symmetry correctly predicted “the mass of a particle not yet seen.” Moreover, as explained in Section 5.4.4 of this book, the equal-spacing rule holds only for the decuplet, where, because of the relation $I=1+Y/2$, even the $I$-dependent term of the mass formula turns into a term linear in $Y$. In other words, “symmetry constrains even the form of the breaking.”

This structure has the same form as Landau theory in materials science. In a structural phase transition of a crystal, the powers of the order parameter that can be written in the free energy are determined by the irreducible representation (whether a cubic term is allowed or not decides whether the transition is first or second order), and which subgroup the system drops to is restricted. In both cases, which irreducible representation the symmetry-breaking perturbation belongs to determines everything. That the main culprit breaking $\mathrm{SU}(3)_F$ is the mass of the $s$ quark (a component belonging to $\bm{8}$), and that the driving force of a structural phase transition is the irreducible representation to which the soft mode belongs, are the same story in the same formalism.

The structure in (2), “the origin is threefold degenerate and splits into $8+1$,” also has the same form as crystal-field splitting. The splitting of the fivefold degeneracy of $\ell=2$ into $E_g\oplus T_{2g}$ in $O_h$, and the splitting of the nine dimensions of $q\bar q$ into $\bm{8}\oplus\bm{1}$, are both the same operation of “decomposing a reducible representation into irreducible ones” (Section 5.5.1 of this book).

Exercise 5.7: Irreducible decomposition in a crystallographic point group — Vibrational modes of $\mathrm{NH_3}$

Problem (restated)

$\mathrm{NH_3}$ is trigonal-pyramidal and belongs to the point group $C_{3v}=\{E,\,2C_3,\,3\sigma_v\}$ (order 6). The character table is $A_1=(1,1,1)$, $A_2=(1,1,-1)$, $E=(2,-1,0)$. The translations transform as $z\to A_1$, $(x,y)\to E$, and the rotations as $R_z\to A_2$, $(R_x,R_y)\to E$.

(1) Count the atoms left unmoved by each operation and derive $\chi_{\text{total}}=(12,\,0,\,2)$.

(2) Use the reduction formula to decompose $\Gamma_{\text{total}}$ into irreducible representations.

(3) Subtract the translations and rotations to obtain $\Gamma_{\text{vib}}$, and check that its dimension is $3N-6=6$.

(4) List the infrared-active and Raman-active modes. Also state, in two or three lines, what is the same and what is different between this calculation and the calculation of the $\pi N$ scattering cross-section ratios carried out in Section 5.4.3.

Solution

Strategy. We apply the five steps carried out for $\mathrm{H_2O}$ ($C_{2v}$) in Section 5.5.2 of this book directly to $\mathrm{NH_3}$ ($C_{3v}$). The tools are just the two relations

$$ \chi_{\text{total}}(g) = N_{\text{unmoved}}(g)\times\chi_{\text{vec}}(g), \qquad n_a = \frac{1}{\abs{G}}\sum_{g\in G}\chi^{(a)}(g)^*\,\chi(g) $$

The elements of $C_{3v}$ are one $E$, two $C_3$ ($C_3$ and $C_3^2$), and three $\sigma_v$, six in all, so the order is $\abs{G}=6$. Since the characters are fixed class by class for the three classes ($E$, $2C_3$, $3\sigma_v$), the sum in the reduction formula becomes “a three-term sum weighted by the number of elements in each class.”

(1) First we find $\chi_{\text{vec}}$, that is, the trace as a three-dimensional orthogonal matrix. For a proper rotation (angle $\theta$) it is $1+2\cos\theta$, and for a reflection (improper rotation $S_1$, $\theta=0$) it is $-1+2\cos0=+1$.

$$ \chi_{\text{vec}}(E) = 1+2\cos0^\circ = 3,\qquad \chi_{\text{vec}}(C_3) = 1+2\cos120^\circ = 1+2\left(-\tfrac12\right) = 0,\qquad \chi_{\text{vec}}(\sigma_v) = 1 $$

Next we count the atoms left unmoved by each operation (atoms that are mapped onto their own positions). $\mathrm{NH_3}$ is a trigonal pyramid with N at the apex and the three H atoms forming an equilateral triangle as the base; the $C_3$ axis passes through N perpendicular to the base, and each of the three $\sigma_v$ planes contains the $C_3$ axis and one H atom.

  • $E$: nothing is moved, so all four atoms are unmoved. $N_{\text{unmoved}}=4$.
  • $C_3$: the three H atoms are cyclically permuted. Only N, which lies on the axis, is unmoved. $N_{\text{unmoved}}=1$.
  • $\sigma_v$: this mirror plane contains N and one H atom (which lies in the plane) and interchanges the remaining two H atoms. Hence two atoms, N and its H atom, are unmoved. $N_{\text{unmoved}}=2$.

Multiplying, we obtain

$$ \chi_{\text{total}}(E) = 4\times3 = 12,\qquad \chi_{\text{total}}(C_3) = 1\times0 = 0,\qquad \chi_{\text{total}}(\sigma_v) = 2\times1 = 2 $$

that is, $\chi_{\text{total}}=(12,\,0,\,2)$. That $\chi_{\text{total}}(E)=12=3N$ (with $N=4$ atoms) confirms the general rule that the character of the identity operation equals the dimension of the representation.

(2) We substitute into the reduction formula. The numbers of elements in the classes are $(1,2,3)$, and since the characters are real, no complex conjugation is needed.

$$ n_{A_1} = \frac16\left[1\cdot1\cdot12 + 2\cdot1\cdot0 + 3\cdot1\cdot2\right] = \frac16\left[12+0+6\right] = \frac{18}{6} = 3 $$ $$ n_{A_2} = \frac16\left[1\cdot1\cdot12 + 2\cdot1\cdot0 + 3\cdot(-1)\cdot2\right] = \frac16\left[12+0-6\right] = \frac{6}{6} = 1 $$ $$ n_{E} = \frac16\left[1\cdot2\cdot12 + 2\cdot(-1)\cdot0 + 3\cdot0\cdot2\right] = \frac16\left[24+0+0\right] = \frac{24}{6} = 4 $$

Therefore

$$ \Gamma_{\text{total}} = 3A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus 4E $$

Counting dimensions, $3\times1 + 1\times1 + 4\times2 = 3+1+8 = 12$, which agrees with $3N=12$. That $n_{A_1},\,n_{A_2},\,n_E$ all came out as non-negative integers is itself strong evidence that the calculation is correct (if the result of the reduction formula were not an integer, there would be a mistake somewhere in the characters or in the counting of unmoved atoms).

(3) As given in the problem statement, the translations are $z\to A_1$ and $(x,y)\to E$, so

$$ \Gamma_{\text{trans}} = A_1\oplus E\qquad(\text{dimension }1+2=3\ \checkmark) $$

The rotations are $R_z\to A_2$ and $(R_x,R_y)\to E$, so

$$ \Gamma_{\text{rot}} = A_2\oplus E\qquad(\text{dimension }1+2=3\ \checkmark) $$

Subtracting these, we obtain

$$ \Gamma_{\text{vib}} = \left(3A_1 \oplus A_2 \oplus 4E\right) - \left(A_1\oplus E\right) - \left(A_2\oplus E\right) = 2A_1 \oplus 2E $$

The dimension is $2\times1 + 2\times2 = 2+4 = 6$, which agrees with $3N-6 = 12-6 = 6$ ($\mathrm{NH_3}$ is a nonlinear molecule, so it has three rotational degrees of freedom).

The actual normal modes of $\mathrm{NH_3}$ are two of $A_1$ (the symmetric stretch $\nu_1\simeq3337\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and the umbrella bend $\nu_2\simeq950\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) and two of $E$ (the antisymmetric stretch $\nu_3\simeq3444\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ and the bend $\nu_4\simeq1627\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, both twofold degenerate), so the group-theoretical prediction $2A_1\oplus2E$ corresponds exactly to the four observed fundamental frequencies.

(4) Infrared activity. Infrared absorption is an electric dipole transition, so a mode is active if it belongs to the same irreducible representation as the dipole moment $(x,y,z)$. In $C_{3v}$ we have $z\to A_1$ and $(x,y)\to E$, so both $A_1$ and $E$ are infrared active. Since $\Gamma_{\text{vib}}=2A_1\oplus2E$ contains only these two kinds, all four modes (all six degrees of freedom) are infrared active.

Raman activity. Raman scattering is governed by the polarizability tensor, that is, a mode is active if it belongs to the same irreducible representation as the quadratic forms $x^2,y^2,z^2,xy,yz,zx$. In $C_{3v}$,

$$ A_1:\ \left(x^2+y^2,\ z^2\right),\qquad A_2:\ \text{none},\qquad E:\ \left(x^2-y^2,\ xy\right)\ \text{and}\ \left(xz,\ yz\right) $$

so both $A_1$ and $E$ are Raman active, and again all four modes are Raman active.

That is, all the normal modes of $\mathrm{NH_3}$ are active in both the infrared and Raman spectra. This is because $\mathrm{NH_3}$ has no inversion center ($C_{3v}$ is noncentrosymmetric), so the rule of mutual exclusion that holds in centrosymmetric crystals (infrared-active modes are Raman inactive, and vice versa) does not operate. Note that $A_2$ is a “silent mode” that appears in neither the infrared nor the Raman spectrum, but it is not contained in $\Gamma_{\text{vib}}$ ($A_2$ is used up by the rotation $R_z$), so $\mathrm{NH_3}$ has no silent mode.

Comparison with the $\pi N$ scattering calculation. What is the same is the framework of Section 5.5.2 of this book itself: the four stages are completely common, namely (i) regard the space spanned by the states as a reducible representation of the symmetry group, (ii) decompose it into irreducible representations, (iii) use Schur’s lemma to compress the dynamics into one constant per irreducible representation, and (iv) fix the ratios of observables by the geometric coefficients alone. There are three differences. First, the groups differ (the finite group $C_{3v}$ versus the continuous group $\mathrm{SU}(2)_I$), so the decomposition tool splits into the reduction formula (a finite sum) or the CG coefficients (raising and lowering operators). Second, the space on which the group acts differs: position space (atomic displacements) versus internal space (isospin). Third, what we obtained in this problem is mainly a selection rule, “active or inactive” ($0$ or non-$0$), whereas in $\pi N$ we compared coefficients within a multiplet, and so a numerical ratio $9:1:2$ emerged. If several states belonging to the same irreducible representation are compared, numerical ratios can be obtained even for finite groups, as in the polarization dependence of Raman scattering.

Verification. The decomposition in (2) can also be checked by reconstructing the characters without using the reduction formula. The characters of $3A_1\oplus A_2\oplus 4E$ are

$$ E:\ 3\cdot1 + 1\cdot1 + 4\cdot2 = 12\ \checkmark,\qquad C_3:\ 3\cdot1 + 1\cdot1 + 4\cdot(-1) = 0\ \checkmark,\qquad \sigma_v:\ 3\cdot1 + 1\cdot(-1) + 4\cdot0 = 2\ \checkmark $$

which correctly reproduce $\chi_{\text{total}}=(12,0,2)$. In addition, the sum of the squares of the dimensions of the irreducible representations is $1^2+1^2+2^2=6=\abs{G}$, which confirms that these three exhaust the irreducible representations of $C_{3v}$ ($\sum_a d_a^2=\abs{G}$ of Section 5.5.1 of this book).

The dimension bookkeeping also works out threefold: $\Gamma_{\text{total}}$ has $12=3N$, $\Gamma_{\text{trans}}$ and $\Gamma_{\text{rot}}$ each have $3$, and $\Gamma_{\text{vib}}$ has $6=3N-6$. Furthermore, that $\mathrm{NH_3}$ has four observed fundamentals (two of which are twofold degenerate, for six degrees of freedom in all) agrees with the measured infrared and Raman spectra.

Meaning. The calculation carried out here is exactly the task of classifying $\Gamma$-point phonons into irreducible representations in a first-principles calculation. For a crystal, one only has to replace $C_{3v}$ by the point-group part of the space group and $N$ by the number of atoms in the unit cell, and the same formulas work as they are. And, as Section 5.5.2 of this book emphasizes, this calculation is procedurally identical to the calculation of the cross-section ratios of the $\Delta$ resonance.

$\mathrm{NH_3}$ has one more famous phenomenon that group theory cannot capture. Moving along the umbrella bending mode $\nu_2$ ($A_1$, $950\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$), the nitrogen pushes through the hydrogen plane and reaches the inverted structure (another equivalent minimum). The tunneling splitting of the double well splits the vibrational ground state by $0.79\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ (since $1\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}=29.98\ \mathrm{GHz}$, this is $23.8\ \mathrm{GHz}$, in the microwave region). Among these inversion transitions, the line of the rotational level $(J,K)=(3,3)$ ($23.87\ \mathrm{GHz}$) became the oscillation line of the ammonia maser in 1954. Group theory determines only that the mode belongs to $A_1$; it determines neither the depth of the well nor the size of the tunneling splitting. This is exactly the same division of labor as for $A_1$ (the isospin amplitude) in Exercise 5.5, which group theory did not determine.

Exercise 5.8: Double groups and optical spin injection (GaAs)

Problem (restated)

At the $\Gamma$ point of GaAs, the valence band consists of $\Gamma_8$ ($j=3/2$, fourfold) and $\Gamma_7$ ($j=1/2$, twofold, lying $\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}=341\ \mathrm{meV}$ below), and the conduction band is $\Gamma_6$ ($j=1/2$, twofold).

(1) Verify, using the composition law of Section 5.3.4 of this book, that combining spin $1/2$ with a $p$-like orbital ($\ell=1$) gives $j=3/2$ and $j=1/2$. Also verify that the number of states matches, $3\times2=4+2$.

(2) Take the photon energy in the range $E_g < \hbar\omega < E_g+\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}$. Then no excitation from $\Gamma_7$ occurs. Why?

(3) When $\sigma^+$ circularly polarized light ($\Delta m_j=+1$) drives the $\Gamma_8\to\Gamma_6$ transition, there are two paths, $m_j=-3/2\to-1/2$ and $m_j=-1/2\to+1/2$. By the Wigner–Eckart theorem, the ratio of their transition probabilities is $3:1$. Find the degree of spin polarization of the conduction electrons produced,

$$ P = \frac{n_{-1/2}-n_{+1/2}}{n_{-1/2}+n_{+1/2}} $$

.

(4) In a material where $\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}$ is sufficiently small (for example, Si, with $44\ \mathrm{meV}$), discuss qualitatively how this upper limit of $50\%$ changes.

Solution

Strategy. Part (1) is a direct application of the composition law $j_1\otimes j_2 = \abs{j_1-j_2}\oplus\cdots\oplus(j_1+j_2)$ of Section 5.3.4 of this book. Part (2) is a matter of energy conservation alone. In (3) we need only substitute the given $3:1$ into the definition of the polarization, but we first derive for ourselves where that $3:1$ comes from, using the Wigner–Eckart theorem of Section 5.5.3 of this book. In (4) we add the contribution of $\Gamma_7$ to the framework of (3) and see quantitatively what happens.

(1) The $p$ orbital has $\ell=1$, and the electron spin is $s=1/2$. By the composition law,

$$ 1\otimes\tfrac12 = \abs{1-\tfrac12}\ \oplus\ \left(1+\tfrac12\right) = \tfrac12\ \oplus\ \tfrac32 $$

(Since the value runs in steps of 1 from $\abs{j_1-j_2}=1/2$ to $j_1+j_2=3/2$, it ends with the two terms $1/2$ and $3/2$.) Counting the number of states,

$$ (2\ell+1)(2s+1) = 3\times2 = 6, \qquad (2\cdot\tfrac32+1)+(2\cdot\tfrac12+1) = 4+2 = 6\ \checkmark $$

so they match. In a crystal, this $j=3/2$ quartet appears as $\Gamma_8$ (heavy holes with $m_j=\pm3/2$ and light holes with $m_j=\pm1/2$), and the $j=1/2$ doublet appears as $\Gamma_7$ (the split-off band). This is the content of Figure 5.8(b) in Section 5.5.4 of this book, and it is “the composition law of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ translated into the language of crystallographic point groups.”

(2) The answer follows from energy accounting alone. Taking the top of $\Gamma_8$ as the valence-band maximum ($E=0$), $\Gamma_7$ lies $\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}$ below it ($E=-\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}$). The bottom of the conduction band $\Gamma_6$ is at $E=E_g$. Therefore

$$ \Gamma_8\to\Gamma_6\ \text{threshold}: \hbar\omega \ge E_g, \qquad \Gamma_7\to\Gamma_6\ \text{threshold}: \hbar\omega \ge E_g+\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}} $$

If $\hbar\omega$ is chosen in the window $E_g < \hbar\omega < E_g+\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}$, excitation from $\Gamma_8$ is possible, but excitation from $\Gamma_7$ does not occur, because the photon energy falls short by the extra binding energy $\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}$ of $\Gamma_7$. It is energy conservation that forbids it, not symmetry.

Putting in numbers for GaAs, with $E_g=1.42\ \mathrm{eV}$ at room temperature and $\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}=0.341\ \mathrm{eV}$, the window is

$$ 1.42\ \mathrm{eV} < \hbar\omega < 1.761\ \mathrm{eV} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 704\ \mathrm{nm} < \lambda < 873\ \mathrm{nm} $$

(we used $hc=1239.8\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$). A window as wide as $170\ \mathrm{nm}$ is extremely convenient experimentally. Here lies the practical reason why GaAs has become the standard material for optical spin injection.

(3) First we verify the $3:1$ ourselves. The absorption of $\sigma^+$ circularly polarized light is a transition caused by the spherical component $q=+1$ of the dipole operator (one component of an irreducible tensor operator of rank $k=1$). By the Wigner–Eckart theorem of Section 5.5.3 of this book,

$$ \bra{j'\,m'}T^1_{+1}\ket{j\,m} = \braket{j\,m;\,1\,{+}1\,|\,j'\,m'}\times\braket{j'\,\|T^1\|\,j} $$

The two transitions being compared both go from $j=3/2$ ($\Gamma_8$) to $j'=1/2$ ($\Gamma_6$); since $j,j'$ are the same, the reduced matrix element is common. Therefore the ratio is determined solely by the ratio of the squares of the CG coefficients. The required CG coefficients are

$$ \braket{\tfrac32,-\tfrac32;\,1,+1\,|\,\tfrac12,-\tfrac12} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}, \qquad \braket{\tfrac32,-\tfrac12;\,1,+1\,|\,\tfrac12,+\tfrac12} = \frac{1}{\sqrt6} $$

(they can be constructed by the lowering-operator procedure of Section 5.3.4 of this book), and squaring and taking the ratio gives

$$ \frac{\abs{\mathcal{M}\left(-\tfrac32\to-\tfrac12\right)}^2}{\abs{\mathcal{M}\left(-\tfrac12\to+\tfrac12\right)}^2} = \frac{1/2}{1/6} = 3 $$

It is indeed $3:1$. What is important here is that for $\sigma^+$ ($\Delta m_j=+1$), only two of the four states of $\Gamma_8$, namely $m_j=-3/2$ and $m_j=-1/2$, can be used. From $m_j=+1/2$ one would have to go to $m_j=+3/2$, but the conduction band $\Gamma_6$ has only $m_j=\pm1/2$, so no final state exists. The same holds for $m_j=+3/2$.

Therefore, with a common constant of proportionality, the numbers of conduction electrons produced are

$$ n_{-1/2} \propto 3\ \ (m_j=-\tfrac32\ \text{, from a heavy hole}), \qquad n_{+1/2} \propto 1\ \ (m_j=-\tfrac12\ \text{, from a light hole}) $$

The polarization is

$$ P = \frac{n_{-1/2}-n_{+1/2}}{n_{-1/2}+n_{+1/2}} = \frac{3-1}{3+1} = \frac{2}{4} = +0.5 $$

that is, $50\%$. This is the theoretical upper limit of optical spin injection, and, as stated in Section 5.5.4 of this book, its direct origin is that $\Gamma_8$ is a four-dimensional irreducible representation with $j=3/2$. If $\Gamma_8$ did not exist and the valence band were only a $j=1/2$ doublet, there would be only one path that $\sigma^+$ could excite, and $\abs{P}=100\%$ would have been possible (in this definition only the single path $m_j=-1/2\to+1/2$ remains, so $P=-100\%$). The number $50\%$ expresses the fact that “inside $\Gamma_8$, the path through the light hole, which produces the opposite spin, is mixed in with a weight.”

(4) To state the conclusion first, $50\%$ is no longer reached. The reason is that excitation from $\Gamma_7$ occurs at the same time. To estimate how much the polarization drops, we need to compare the transition strengths of $\Gamma_8$ and $\Gamma_7$ on a common scale. However, the two have different $j$ (initial state), so we cannot compare only the CG coefficients as in (3) (the reduced matrix elements are different). We therefore use the fact that $\Gamma_8$ and $\Gamma_7$ are both made from the same composition of the $p$ orbital and the spin, and return to the basis $\ket{\ell=1,m_\ell}\ket{s_z}$ to calculate. The conduction band $\Gamma_6$ is $s$-like ($\ell=0$), and the dipole operator does not act on the spin, so the transition amplitude is proportional to “the coefficient of the $\ket{\ell=1,m_\ell=-1}\ket{s_z}$ component of the valence-band state” (because $\sigma^+$ raises $m_\ell$ as $-1\to0$). The expansion of $1\otimes\frac12$ constructed by the procedure of Section 5.3.4 of this book is

$$ \ket{\tfrac32,-\tfrac32} = \ket{1,-1}\ket{\downarrow},\qquad \ket{\tfrac32,-\tfrac12} = \sqrt{\tfrac13}\,\ket{1,-1}\ket{\uparrow} + \sqrt{\tfrac23}\,\ket{1,0}\ket{\downarrow} $$ $$ \ket{\tfrac12,-\tfrac12} = -\sqrt{\tfrac23}\,\ket{1,-1}\ket{\uparrow} + \sqrt{\tfrac13}\,\ket{1,0}\ket{\downarrow} $$

so by taking the square of the $\ket{1,-1}$ component we can read off the relative transition strengths:

$$ \Gamma_8\ (m_j=-\tfrac32) \to \Gamma_6\ (\downarrow):\ 1, \qquad \Gamma_8\ (m_j=-\tfrac12) \to \Gamma_6\ (\uparrow):\ \tfrac13, \qquad \Gamma_7\ (m_j=-\tfrac12) \to \Gamma_6\ (\uparrow):\ \tfrac23 $$

Multiplying all by 3 gives $3:1:2$. The ratio of the first two is $3:1$, consistent with (3). Now if we take $\hbar\omega > E_g+\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}$ and excite all three equally,

$$ n_{-1/2}\propto 3, \qquad n_{+1/2}\propto 1+2 = 3 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad P = \frac{3-3}{3+3} = 0 $$

and the polarization vanishes completely. The contribution of $\Gamma_7$ (weight 2), together with the contribution of the light hole (weight 1), exactly cancels the contribution of the heavy hole (weight 3). This is no accident: it expresses the requirement that in the limit $\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}\to0$ the spin and the orbital are completely decoupled, and light acts only on the orbital, so there is no way a spin polarization can be produced.

Therefore, in a material with small $\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}$, $P$ falls to an intermediate value between $50\%$ ($\Gamma_7$ completely frozen out) and $0\%$ ($\Gamma_7$ excited equally). Which side it approaches depends on whether the window $\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}$ of (2) is sufficiently wide compared with the effective blurring due to the linewidth of the light source, thermal broadening, and the nonparabolicity of the bands. The $\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}=44\ \mathrm{meV}$ of Si is only $1.7$ times the room-temperature thermal energy $k_BT=25.9\ \mathrm{meV}$ ($300\ \mathrm{K}$). In contrast, the $341\ \mathrm{meV}$ of GaAs is $13$ times. In Si it is difficult to separate the window from the thermal broadening, and even at low temperature the window itself, $44\ \mathrm{meV}$, is narrow. In addition, since Si is an indirect-gap semiconductor, injecting electrons by a vertical transition at the $\Gamma$ point is in itself inefficient.

As a general rule, the heavier the element, the stronger the spin–orbit coupling ($\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}$ increases steeply with atomic number), which is favorable for optical spin injection. Indeed, $\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}$ is Si $44\ \mathrm{meV}$, Ge $290\ \mathrm{meV}$, GaAs $341\ \mathrm{meV}$, InSb $810\ \mathrm{meV}$, so it is larger the heavier the constituent elements of the material (Figure 5.8(b) of this book). There is, however, a trade-off. The same spin–orbit coupling also speeds up the spin relaxation of conduction electrons (the D’yakonov–Perel and Elliott–Yafet mechanisms), so the more easily spins are injected into a material, the faster the injected spins are lost. The spin diffusion length of Si is extremely long precisely because $\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}$ is small. That “injection efficiency” and “retention time” are opposite functions of the same parameter is the central dilemma of semiconductor spintronics.

Verification. The CG coefficients in (3) can also be checked from normalization. $\ket{\frac32,-\frac32}$ is the single state $\ket{1,-1}\ket{\downarrow}$, so the square of its coefficient is $1$; for $\ket{\frac32,-\frac12}$ the sum of the squares of the expansion coefficients is $\frac13+\frac23=1$, and for $\ket{\frac12,-\frac12}$ it is $\frac23+\frac13=1$, so all are normalized. The orthogonality of $\ket{\frac32,-\frac12}$ and $\ket{\frac12,-\frac12}$ follows from $\sqrt{\frac13}\cdot\left(-\sqrt{\frac23}\right)+\sqrt{\frac23}\cdot\sqrt{\frac13}=0$ ✓.

The weights $3:1:2$ in (4) can also be checked from another viewpoint. The valence-band states that $\sigma^+$ can excite are only the two states $\ket{1,-1}\ket{\uparrow}$ and $\ket{1,-1}\ket{\downarrow}$ ($m_\ell=-1$ is required). By completeness, the total “distribution” of these two states among $\Gamma_8,\Gamma_7$ must be

$$ \ket{1,-1}\ket{\downarrow}:\ 1 = 1, \qquad \ket{1,-1}\ket{\uparrow}:\ \tfrac13+\tfrac23 = 1 $$

and indeed it is. The sum of the normalized weights is $1+1=2$, and in the representation multiplied by 3 it is $3+(1+2)=6$, which is consistent. And that the total weights of spin $\uparrow$ and $\downarrow$ are equal ($3$ each) is the direct basis for $P\to0$ as $\Delta_{\mathrm{SO}}\to0$.

The numerical value in (2) can also be checked by dimensions. The wavelength corresponding to $\hbar\omega=1.42\ \mathrm{eV}$ is $1239.8/1.42 = 873\ \mathrm{nm}$, which agrees with the well-known value of the GaAs emission wavelength (near infrared, about $870\ \mathrm{nm}$).

Meaning. This problem most directly illustrates the theme of the whole book, “the elementary-particle toolbox and the materials-science toolbox are the same.” From literally the same Wigner–Eckart theorem and the same table of CG coefficients that gave the branching ratios of the $\Delta$ resonance, the upper limit $50\%$ on the spin-injection efficiency of GaAs follows. The only difference is whether $j$ is the total angular momentum in position space or isospin.

And the number $50\%$ does not depend at all on material-specific parameters (effective mass, permittivity, defect density). What it depends on is a fact fixed by symmetry alone: that “the valence-band maximum is a $j=3/2$ quartet.” From the standpoint of device design, to exceed this limit one cannot improve the material; one can only lift the degeneracy of $\Gamma_8$ by some other means. If one confines along the $z$ direction in a quantum well and separates heavy holes from light holes, the path through the light hole (weight 1) can be closed, and $P$ can in principle approach $100\%$. Indeed, polarizations exceeding $90\%$ have been reported in strained quantum wells and quantum dots. A symmetry argument not only tells us the upper limit but also tells us what must be broken in order to break that limit.

E.6 Solutions for Chapter 6: Discrete Symmetries — P, C, T and the CPT Theorem

Exercise 6.1: Parity selection rules

Problem (restated)

Take the intrinsic parities to be $\eta_\pi=-1$, $\eta_\gamma=-1$, $\eta_p=\eta_n=+1$, $\eta_{\bar p}=-1$.

(1) Is $\omega\,(J^{P}=1^{-})\to\pi^+\pi^-$ allowed by the strong interaction? Answer by computing the parity and the angular momentum of the final state.

(2) An antiproton $\bar p$ at rest is trapped by deuterium and $\bar p\,d\to n\,\pi^0$ occurs. Assuming that the $\bar p$ is captured from the $1s$ orbit ($\ell=0$), compare the parities of the initial and final states and determine whether the relative orbital angular momentum $\ell'$ of the final state is even or odd.

(3) Determine, from both parity and Bose statistics, whether a hypothetical particle $X$ with $J^{P}=0^{+}$ can decay to $\pi^0\pi^0$ and whether it can decay to $\pi^0\pi^0\pi^0$.

Solution

Strategy. The only tools we use are the three principles of parity calculation from Chapter 6 of this book: (i) the parity of a composite system is the product of the intrinsic parities of its constituents, (ii) each unit of relative orbital angular momentum $\ell$ contributes a factor $(-1)^\ell$, and (iii) parity is conserved in the strong interaction. To these we add angular-momentum conservation and Bose statistics / the Pauli exclusion principle for identical particles. The procedure is the same every time, in three steps: “fix $\ell$ by matching the angular momentum of the final state to the spin of the parent $\to$ compute the parity for that $\ell$ $\to$ compare with the parity of the parent.”

(1) Both particles in the final state $\pi^+\pi^-$ have spin $0$. Therefore only the orbital part contributes to the total angular momentum of the final state, and

$$ J_{\text{final}} = \ell $$

The parent $\omega$ has $J=1$, so angular-momentum conservation fixes $\ell=1$ uniquely. The parity of the final state is then, by the composition law,

$$ \eta_{\pi^+\pi^-} = \eta_{\pi^+}\,\eta_{\pi^-}\,(-1)^{\ell} = (-1)\times(-1)\times(-1)^{1} = -1 $$

The intrinsic parity of the $\omega$ is $-1$ from $J^P=1^-$, and the two agree. Therefore the decay is allowed from the standpoint of parity and angular momentum.

Note that $\pi^+$ and $\pi^-$ are distinct particles, so the restriction that Bose statistics places on the parity of $\ell$ does not operate here. The key point is that the situation differs from the decay $\rho^0\to\pi^0\pi^0$ (two identical bosons), which is forbidden.

(2) First we assemble the initial state. The deuteron $d$ is a proton and a neutron bound with $\ell=0$, so

$$ \eta_d = \eta_p\,\eta_n\,(-1)^{0} = (+1)(+1)(+1) = +1 $$

(this is why Table 6.2 in Chapter 6 of this book gives $J^P=1^+$ for $d$). The $\bar p$ is captured from the $1s$ orbit, so the relative orbital angular momentum is $\ell=0$. Hence

$$ \eta_{\text{initial}} = \eta_{\bar p}\,\eta_d\,(-1)^{0} = (-1)\times(+1)\times(+1) = -1 $$

Next we write the parity of the final state $n\,\pi^0$, denoting the relative orbital angular momentum by $\ell'$:

$$ \eta_{\text{final}} = \eta_n\,\eta_{\pi^0}\,(-1)^{\ell'} = (+1)\times(-1)\times(-1)^{\ell'} = -(-1)^{\ell'} $$

Since parity is conserved in the strong interaction, $\eta_{\text{initial}}=\eta_{\text{final}}$, that is,

$$ -1 = -(-1)^{\ell'} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad (-1)^{\ell'} = +1 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ell' = 0,2,4,\dots\ (\text{even}) $$

The relative orbital angular momentum $\ell'$ of the final state must be even.

(3) First consider $X\to\pi^0\pi^0$. The $\pi^0$ are identical bosons, so the total wave function must be symmetric under exchange of the two particles. The $\pi^0$ has spin $0$ and hence no spin part, so the symmetry is determined solely by the spatial part $(-1)^{\ell}$, and $\ell$ is restricted to even values. On the other hand, the total angular momentum of the final state is $J=\ell$, and matching the parent’s $J=0$ requires $\ell=0$. This is even, so it is compatible with Bose statistics. The parity is then

$$ \eta_{\pi^0\pi^0} = (-1)\times(-1)\times(-1)^{0} = +1 $$

which agrees with the parity $+1$ of $X$. $X\to\pi^0\pi^0$ is allowed.

Next consider $X\to3\pi^0$. In a three-body system there are two relative coordinates, and the orbital factor of the parity is $(-1)^{\ell_1+\ell_2}$ ($\ell_1$ is the relative orbital angular momentum of the two $\pi^0$, and $\ell_2$ is the relative orbital angular momentum between that pair and the third $\pi^0$). For the total angular momentum to be $J=0$, $\bm{\ell}_1$ and $\bm{\ell}_2$ must cancel each other, which requires $\ell_1=\ell_2$. Therefore

$$ (-1)^{\ell_1+\ell_2} = (-1)^{2\ell_1} = +1 $$

so the orbital factor is always $+1$, regardless of the value of $\ell_1$. Hence

$$ \eta_{3\pi^0} = (-1)^3\times(+1) = -1 \neq +1 = \eta_X $$

$X\to3\pi^0$ is forbidden by parity. Bose statistics poses no obstacle, since a completely symmetric state with $\ell_1=\ell_2=0$ can be constructed. That is, in this case it is parity alone, not statistics, that does the forbidding.

Verification. All three results can be checked by independent routes.

(1) can be checked with $C$ parity. Acting with $\hat{\mathcal{C}}$ on the $\pi^+\pi^-$ system interchanges $\pi^+$ and $\pi^-$, which is the same as exchanging the two particles, so $C(\pi^+\pi^-)=(-1)^{\ell}$. By Table 6.2 of Chapter 6 of this book, the $\omega$ is $1^{--}$ with $C=-1$, so $\ell$ is odd, that is, $\ell=1$. This agrees exactly with the conclusion obtained from parity.

(2) can be checked by counting angular momentum. The initial state is the $\bar p$ of spin $1/2$ and the $d$ of spin $1$ combined with $\ell=0$, so $J=1/2$ or $3/2$. The final state combines the spin $1/2$ of the $n$ with the orbital $\ell'$, giving $J=\abs{\ell'\pm1/2}$. For $\ell'=0$ we get $J=1/2$, and for $\ell'=2$ we get $J=3/2,5/2$, so with even $\ell'$ both $J=1/2$ and $3/2$ can be reached. There is no need anywhere to assume an odd $\ell'$. The results are consistent.

(3) can be checked against a known decay. Applying the same calculation to $\eta\,(0^{-+})\to3\pi^0$, the orbital factor is again $+1$ and the parity is $(-1)^3=-1$, which agrees with the parity $-1$ of the $\eta$, so the decay is allowed. In fact the branching ratio of this decay is $32.6\%$ (Worked Example 6.3 in Chapter 6 of this book). The same tool correctly sorts “forbidden” from “allowed.”

Meaning. What the three problems have in common is the structure that the parity (even or odd) of the number of pseudoscalar particles in the final state directly reads out the parity of the parent. Each $\pi$ meson carries one factor $(-1)$, and each unit of orbital angular momentum carries another $(-1)$. This is what a multiplicative quantum number is: the selection rule follows without any knowledge of the details of the interaction.

One more point deserves emphasis: the result “allowed” in (1) does not mean “occurs often.” The measured branching ratio of $\omega\to\pi^+\pi^-$ is only $1.5\%$, and the main decay of the $\omega$ is to $3\pi$. The cause of the suppression is not parity but isospin (the $\omega$ has $I=0$, whereas a $\pi\pi$ state with $\ell=1$ has $I=1$). Symmetry states “forbidden” exactly, but for “allowed” it gives only an upper limit. This division of roles holds equally in crystal physics. For example, a non-centrosymmetric point group is a necessary condition for SHG to appear, but the magnitude of $\chi^{(2)}$ itself cannot be known without a calculation of the electronic structure. Symmetry decides “zero or not,” and dynamics decides the magnitude.

Exercise 6.2: $C$ parity and the photon-number selection rule

Problem (restated)

Use $C(\gamma)=-1$ and, for a fermion pair, $C(f\bar f)=(-1)^{L+S}$ and $P(f\bar f)=(-1)^{L+1}$.

(1) Find $J^{PC}$ of the first excited state $2^{3}P_{2}$ ($L=1,S=1,J=2$) of positronium. Into how many photons can this state decay?

(2) Verify from $C$ that $\eta\,(0^{-+})$ can decay to $2\gamma$ (measured branching ratio $39.4\%$). Also show that $\eta\to3\gamma$ is forbidden.

(3) The $J/\psi$ is the $^3S_1$ state of $c\bar c$. Find $J^{PC}$ and explain why it can be produced directly in $e^+e^-$ collisions (because it has the same quantum numbers as a virtual photon).

(4) Is $\omega\,(1^{--})\to\pi^0\gamma$ allowed? Decide using $C$ alone.

Solution

Strategy. We apply mechanically the two formulas derived in Chapter 6 of this book, $C(f\bar f)=(-1)^{L+S}$ and $P(f\bar f)=(-1)^{L+1}$, together with $C(n\gamma)=(-1)^n$ for photons. Since $C$ is a multiplicative quantum number, for a final state of several particles it suffices to take the product of the $C$ of the individual particles. Do not forget, however, that a $C$ eigenvalue can be defined only for neutral systems in which the electric charge, baryon number, lepton number, and strangeness all vanish.

(1) The state $2^{3}P_{2}$ has $L=1$, $S=1$, $J=2$. We substitute directly into the formulas:

$$ C = (-1)^{L+S} = (-1)^{1+1} = (-1)^{2} = +1 $$ $$ P = (-1)^{L+1} = (-1)^{1+1} = (-1)^{2} = +1 $$

Therefore

$$ J^{PC} = 2^{++} $$

For the number of photons, matching $C(n\gamma)=(-1)^n$ with $C=+1$ gives $(-1)^n=+1$, that is, $n$ must be even. The case $n=0$ is not a decay, so the minimum is $n=2$. The decay of a $J=2$ state into $2\gamma$ is also allowed kinematically (the Landau–Yang theorem, which says that a $J=1$ state cannot decay into $2\gamma$, does not extend to $J=2$). Hence the answer is an even number of photons, at least $2\gamma$.

In reality, however, the $2^3P_2$ state decays far faster by an electric dipole (E1) transition to $1^{3}S_1$ (ortho-positronium) than by falling to $2\gamma$. The E1 transition occurs at low order in $\alpha$, and the phase space is also favorable. That symmetry allows a process is a separate matter from whether it is the dominant channel.

(2) The $\eta$ has $J^{PC}=0^{-+}$, that is, $C(\eta)=+1$. The $C$ of the final state $2\gamma$ is

$$ C(2\gamma) = (-1)^2 = +1 = C(\eta) $$

These agree, so $\eta\to2\gamma$ is allowed from the standpoint of $C$. The electromagnetic interaction conserves $C$, so this decay can occur electromagnetically. The measured branching ratio $39.4\%$ is consistent with this.

For $3\gamma$, on the other hand,

$$ C(3\gamma) = (-1)^3 = -1 \neq +1 = C(\eta) $$

which does not agree. In the $C$-conserving electromagnetic interaction, $\eta\to3\gamma$ is strictly forbidden. This is exactly the same logic as that by which $\pi^0\to3\gamma$ is forbidden (Theorem 6.2 in Chapter 6 of this book), and in the case of the $\pi^0$ it has been confirmed as a strong suppression, with an experimental upper limit of $3.1\times10^{-8}$.

(3) The $J/\psi$ is the $^{3}S_1$ state of $c\bar c$, that is, $L=0$, $S=1$, $J=1$. Substituting into the formulas,

$$ C = (-1)^{L+S} = (-1)^{0+1} = -1, \qquad P = (-1)^{L+1} = (-1)^{0+1} = -1 $$

Therefore

$$ J^{PC} = 1^{--} $$

Looking now at Table 6.2 in Chapter 6 of this book, the quantum numbers of the photon are also $1^{--}$. In an $e^+e^-$ collision, the electron and positron undergo pair annihilation into a single virtual photon, from which the final state is formed. The virtual photon carries $J^{PC}=1^{--}$, so the resonant states that can be produced directly by this route are limited to those with $1^{--}$. The $J/\psi$ has exactly these quantum numbers, so it appears as a huge peak in the total cross section of $e^+e^-$. Conversely, $\eta_c\,(0^{-+})$ and $\chi_{cJ}\,(J^{++})$ are not $1^{--}$, so they cannot be produced directly in $e^+e^-$ collisions and can only be produced by way of, for example, transitions from $\psi$ states.

(4) The $\omega$ is $1^{--}$, so $C(\omega)=-1$. For the final state $\pi^0\gamma$, the $C$ is obtained as follows: the $\pi^0$ is $0^{-+}$ with $C(\pi^0)=+1$ and the photon has $C(\gamma)=-1$, so

$$ C(\pi^0\gamma) = (+1)\times(-1) = -1 = C(\omega) $$

These agree. $\omega\to\pi^0\gamma$ is allowed from the standpoint of $C$. The measured branching ratio is $8.3\%$.

As in (1), we should stress that $C$ is merely saying “allowed.” Checking angular momentum and parity independently as well: the $\omega$ is $1^{-}$ and the $\pi^0$ is $0^{-}$, and for the pair with one photon the parity is $\eta_{\pi^0}\eta_\gamma(-1)^{\ell}=(-1)(-1)(-1)^{\ell}=(-1)^{\ell}$. To make $J=1$ we can use $\ell=1$, and then $(-1)^1=-1=\eta_\omega$, which agrees. Thus $C$, $P$, and $J$ all allow the decay, and it does in fact occur as a magnetic-dipole-type ($V\to P\gamma$) electromagnetic transition with the large branching ratio of $8.3\%$. Note that since this decay is electromagnetic, it is suppressed by one power of $\alpha$, which is not inconsistent with the fact that the main decay of the $\omega$ is the strong-interaction decay to $3\pi$ ($89\%$).

Verification. We check by applying the same rules to other decays whose answers are known.

First, we examine $\omega\to\pi^0\pi^0$. We have $C(\pi^0\pi^0)=(+1)(+1)=+1$, which does not agree with $C(\omega)=-1$. Therefore it is forbidden. In fact this decay has not been observed. (From the side of parity as well, with two identical bosons $\ell$ must be even, whereas $J=1$ requires $\ell=1$, a contradiction. It is doubly forbidden.)

Second, we apply the same formulas as in (1) to the ground states of positronium. The $1^{1}S_0$ has $L=0,S=0$ and $C=(-1)^{0+0}=+1$, so it decays into an even number of photons, and the $1^{3}S_1$ has $L=0,S=1$ and $C=(-1)^{0+1}=-1$, so it decays into an odd number of photons. This agrees with Table 6.3 in Chapter 6 of this book. The lifetimes differ by more than a factor of $1100$, being $125.14\ \mathrm{ps}$ and $142.05\ \mathrm{ns}$, because this difference in parity produces a difference of one photon, that is, one factor of $\alpha$. The formulas function correctly.

Meaning. $C$ parity is a multiplicative quantum number that takes only the values $\pm1$, and it directly specifies whether the number of photons in the final state is even or odd. This mere piece of information, “the quantum number is $\pm1$,” changes lifetimes by three orders of magnitude and determines which particles can be seen at $e^+e^-$ accelerators.

Materials science has a phenomenon of the same type. Monolayer $\mathrm{MoS_2}$ has no inversion center, so SHG appears; when two layers are stacked an inversion center arises and the SHG disappears; with three layers it appears again. This oscillation, in which the parity (even or odd) of the number of layers determines the presence or absence of the signal, is the same as seeing a multiplicative quantum number $(-1)^n$ with the naked eye in the laboratory (Exercise 6.7(3)). Counting the parity of the photon number in particle physics and counting the parity of the layer number in a crystal use exactly the same algebra.

Exercise 6.3: Constructing Table 6.7 yourself

Problem (restated)

For each of the following quantities, derive the sign under $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{T}$ from the transformation properties of its constituents.

(1) The Poynting vector $\bm{S}_{\text{P}}=\bm{E}\times\bm{H}$

(2) The energy density of the electromagnetic field, $u=\frac{1}{2}(\varepsilon_0E^2+B^2/\mu_0)$

(3) The Rashba term $(\bm{\sigma}\times\bm{k})\cdot\hat{\bm{z}}$ ($\hat{\bm z}$ is the interface normal, a polar vector)

(4) The spin–orbit interaction $\bm{L}\cdot\bm{S}$

(5) The Dzyaloshinskii–Moriya interaction $\bm{D}\cdot(\bm{S}_1\times\bm{S}_2)$ ($\bm{D}$ is a constant vector determined by the crystal structure and, like $\bm{S}_1\times\bm{S}_2$, is an axial vector. Note that the inversion operation interchanges sites 1 and 2.)

(6) Explain why (2) and (4) above are allowed in any crystal. Also state what kind of symmetry breaking is needed for (3) and (5) to appear.

Solution

Strategy. We need to remember only the basic ingredients of Table 6.7 of Chapter 6 of this book. $\bm{x}$ has $(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{T})=(-,+)$; $\bm{p}$ and $\kk$ have $(-,-)$; $\bm{L},\bm{S},\bm{\sigma}$ have $(+,-)$; $\bm{E}$ and $\bm{P}$ have $(-,+)$; and $\bm{B}$, $\bm{H}$, and $\bm{M}$ have $(+,-)$. After that, we simply multiply the signs each time we take a product. For the purpose of counting signs, the dot product and the cross product are both just products, and no distinction is needed. (The cross product appears to “change the $\mathcal{P}$ sign each time it is taken” only because the $\mathcal{P}$ sign of $\bm{a}\times\bm{b}$ is the product of the two; for two $\mathcal{P}$-odd quantities, $(-)(-)=+$, and the result is axial, nothing more.)

(1) The Poynting vector $\bm{S}_{\text{P}}=\bm{E}\times\bm{H}$. $\bm{E}$ has $(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{T})=(-,+)$, and $\bm{H}$ transforms like $\bm{B}$, with $(+,-)$. Taking the product,

$$ \mathcal{P}:\ (-)\times(+) = -, \qquad \mathcal{T}:\ (+)\times(-) = - $$

that is, $\bm{S}_{\text{P}}$ is $\mathcal{P}$-odd and $\mathcal{T}$-odd. That it is $\mathcal{T}$-odd is physically very natural: the Poynting vector is a flow of energy, so if a film is played backward the flow also reverses direction.

(2) The energy density $u=\frac{1}{2}(\varepsilon_0E^2+B^2/\mu_0)$. $E^2=\bm{E}\cdot\bm{E}$ is a product of the same quantity, so the sign is applied twice:

$$ \mathcal{P}:\ (-)^2=+,\qquad \mathcal{T}:\ (+)^2=+ $$

Likewise for $B^2$: $\mathcal{P}:(+)^2=+$ and $\mathcal{T}:(-)^2=+$. Therefore $u$ is $\mathcal{P}$-even and $\mathcal{T}$-even. Energy is a quantity without direction, so this too is a natural result.

(3) The Rashba term $(\bm{\sigma}\times\kk)\cdot\hat{\bm z}$. We compute in two stages. First we form the cross-product part. $\bm{\sigma}$ has $(+,-)$ and $\kk$ has $(-,-)$, so

$$ \bm{\sigma}\times\kk:\quad \mathcal{P}:\ (+)\times(-)=-, \qquad \mathcal{T}:\ (-)\times(-)=+ $$

that is, $\bm{\sigma}\times\kk$ is $\mathcal{P}$-odd and $\mathcal{T}$-even. Next, taking the dot product of this with $\hat{\bm z}$ (a polar vector, so $(-,+)$),

$$ (\bm{\sigma}\times\kk)\cdot\hat{\bm z}:\quad \mathcal{P}:\ (-)\times(-)=+, \qquad \mathcal{T}:\ (+)\times(+)=+ $$

that is, the term as a whole is $\mathcal{P}$-even and $\mathcal{T}$-even. A term in the Hamiltonian must be $\mathcal{P}$-even and $\mathcal{T}$-even, so this term satisfies the requirement of symmetry.

(4) The spin–orbit interaction $\bm{L}\cdot\bm{S}$. Both $\bm{L}$ and $\bm{S}$ are axial vectors with $(+,-)$. Taking the product,

$$ \mathcal{P}:\ (+)\times(+)=+, \qquad \mathcal{T}:\ (-)\times(-)=+ $$

that is, $\mathcal{P}$-even and $\mathcal{T}$-even. The key point is that under $\mathcal{T}$ both $\bm{L}$ and $\bm{S}$ change sign, so they cancel in the product.

(5) The DM interaction $\bm{D}\cdot(\bm{S}_1\times\bm{S}_2)$. First we evaluate the cross product of the spins. $\bm{S}_1,\bm{S}_2$ both have $(+,-)$, so

$$ \bm{S}_1\times\bm{S}_2:\quad \mathcal{P}:\ (+)\times(+)=+, \qquad \mathcal{T}:\ (-)\times(-)=+ $$

that is, $\bm{S}_1\times\bm{S}_2$ is $\mathcal{P}$-even and $\mathcal{T}$-even. Following the instruction in the problem, take $\bm{D}$ to be a constant axial vector determined by the crystal structure ($\mathcal{P}$-even, and even also under $\mathcal{T}$ since it is a coefficient determined by the structure). Then the term as a whole is

$$ \mathcal{P}:\ (+)\times(+)=+, \qquad \mathcal{T}:\ (+)\times(+)=+ $$

that is, $\mathcal{P}$-even and $\mathcal{T}$-even, and from sign counting alone it appears, as with (2) and (4), to be allowed in any crystal. This, however, leads to a wrong conclusion. The key is that the inversion operation interchanges the site labels. Suppose there is an inversion center at the midpoint of the bond $1$–$2$. This inversion operation maps site $1$ and site $2$ onto each other. Spins are axial vectors, so their directions do not change, but since the labels are interchanged,

$$ \bm{S}_1\times\bm{S}_2\ \longrightarrow\ \bm{S}_2\times\bm{S}_1 = -\,\bm{S}_1\times\bm{S}_2 $$

On the other hand, $\bm{D}$ is a constant vector determined by the crystal structure alone, and since the inversion is a symmetry operation of the crystal, the structure is invariant and therefore $\bm{D}$ is also invariant. The interaction term therefore changes sign, and for it to be invariant we must have

$$ \bm{D}\cdot(\bm{S}_1\times\bm{S}_2) = -\,\bm{D}\cdot(\bm{S}_1\times\bm{S}_2) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \bm{D} = \bm{0} $$

This is Moriya’s rule: “the DM interaction vanishes when there is an inversion center at the bond midpoint.” The DM interaction arises only in an environment where inversion symmetry is broken. Some references adopt a notation that regards $\bm{D}$ as a “$\mathcal{P}$-odd polar vector,” but that absorbs the sign associated with this site interchange into the transformation property of $\bm{D}$, and the conclusion is the same. Note also that the Heisenberg exchange term $\bm{S}_1\cdot\bm{S}_2$ is symmetric under the interchange, so this sign does not appear, and it is allowed in any crystal.

(6) Summarized in a table, the results are as follows.

Table E.6.1: $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{T}$ transformation properties of the terms in Exercise 6.3, and the conditions for their existence
Quantity$\mathcal{P}$$\mathcal{T}$Condition required for existence
(1) $\bm{E}\times\bm{H}$$-$$-$It is a quantity of the field itself, not a material constant, so it is not constrained by crystal symmetry (a state with finite $\bm{S}_{\text{P}}$ is one in which the field side breaks $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{T}$)
(2) $u$$+$$+$No condition (allowed in any crystal)
(3) $(\bm{\sigma}\times\kk)\cdot\hat{\bm z}$$+$$+$$\hat{\bm z}\neq0$, that is, breaking of structural inversion symmetry
(4) $\bm{L}\cdot\bm{S}$$+$$+$No condition (allowed in any crystal)
(5) $\bm{D}\cdot(\bm{S}_1\times\bm{S}_2)$$+$ (but the sign flips if inversion exchanges sites 1 and 2)$+$The bond midpoint must not be an inversion center

Why (2) and (4) are allowed in any crystal. These two are true scalars that are $\mathcal{P}$-even and $\mathcal{T}$-even. A true scalar is invariant under every one of rotation, inversion, and time reversal, and it is contained in the identity representation of any point group or magnetic point group. Neumann’s principle (the physical properties of a crystal must not have lower symmetry than the crystal itself) imposes no constraint in this case. That is why the spin–orbit interaction exists even in inversion-symmetric $\mathrm{Si}$, and why the energy density of the electromagnetic field is found everywhere. Conversely, the mere existence of $\bm{L}\cdot\bm{S}$ does not imply any symmetry breaking. It is a common misconception, but spin splitting does not occur just because a spin–orbit interaction is present. For splitting, a separate breaking of $\mathcal{P}$ or $\mathcal{T}$ is required, as in (3).

The breaking required for (3). The term itself is $\mathcal{P}$-even and $\mathcal{T}$-even, so the signs balance, but it contains $\hat{\bm z}$, a $\mathcal{P}$-odd structural vector. By Theorem 6.1, if the crystal (or the environment near the interface) is inversion-symmetric, the material vector corresponding to $\hat{\bm z}$ vanishes. Therefore structural inversion asymmetry (SIA) is required for the Rashba term to appear. Interfaces, surfaces, asymmetric quantum wells, and polar bulk materials (such as $\mathrm{BiTeI}$) are where it arises. On the other hand, $\mathcal{T}$ need not be broken. Rashba splitting occurs even in nonmagnetic materials.

The breaking required for (5). As seen above, the bond midpoint must not be an inversion center. Note that this does not require the crystal as a whole to be noncentrosymmetric. Even if the crystal has an inversion center, as long as it does not sit at the midpoint of a particular bond, $\bm{D}\neq0$ is allowed for that bond. The interfacial DM interaction in a magnetic thin film in contact with an interface (the source of skyrmion formation) is exactly this situation.

Verification. (1) and (2) can be verified together by using Poynting’s theorem

$$ \frac{\partial u}{\partial t} + \nabla\cdot\bm{S}_{\text{P}} = -\,\bm{j}\cdot\bm{E} $$

We count the transformation properties of the three terms independently. First term: $u$ is $(+,+)$ and $\partial/\partial t$ is $\mathcal{P}$-even and $\mathcal{T}$-odd, so $\partial u/\partial t$ is $(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{T})=(+,-)$. Second term: $\nabla$ is an operator with the dimension of the inverse of $\bm{x}$ and is $(-,+)$, and $\bm{S}_{\text{P}}$ is $(-,-)$ as found above, so the divergence is $(-)(-)=+$ and $(+)(-)=-$, that is, $(+,-)$. Third term: $\bm{j}$ is $(-,-)$ and $\bm{E}$ is $(-,+)$, so $\bm{j}\cdot\bm{E}$ is $(-)(-)=+$ and $(-)(+)=-$, that is, $(+,-)$. All three terms are $\mathcal{P}$-even and $\mathcal{T}$-odd, in complete agreement. Had we gotten even one sign wrong in (1) or (2), this equation would have failed in terms of transformation properties. This is an independent confirmation that the Maxwell equations are consistent with $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{T}$.

For (3), (4), and (5), it suffices to compare with Table 6.7 of Chapter 6 of this book and the description of the Rashba term in Section 6.6.2; the result agrees with the statement in the main text that $\bm{\sigma}\times\kk$ is “$\mathcal{P}$-odd and $\mathcal{T}$-even.”

Meaning. What this exercise teaches is the habit of separating “which terms can be written in the Hamiltonian” from “the condition for such a term to be nonzero.” The former is a bookkeeping problem of being $\mathcal{P}$-even and $\mathcal{T}$-even; the latter is a problem of Neumann’s principle, namely whether the material vector in the coefficient ($\hat{\bm z}$, $\bm{D}$, $\bm{P}$, $\bm{M}$) vanishes. When we treated the EDM term $\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{E}$ in particle physics, we made exactly the same two-stage argument. The materials design strategies “to get Rashba splitting, build an interface” and “to get skyrmions, break inversion symmetry” in crystals are written in the same grammar as the statement in particle physics that “an EDM requires the breaking of $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{T}$.”

Exercise 6.4: Proof and applications of Kramers degeneracy

Problem (restated)

(1) For $\hat{\mathcal{T}}=-\ii\sigma_y K$ acting on spin $1/2$, verify component by component that $\hat{\mathcal{T}}\sigma_i\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{-1}=-\sigma_i$ ($i=x,y,z$) (use the fact that $\sigma_x,\sigma_z$ are real and $\sigma_y$ is purely imaginary).

(2) Show that for a system of $N$ electrons, $\hat{\mathcal{T}}^2=(-1)^N$. Hence Kramers degeneracy is guaranteed only when $N$ is odd.

(3) Place $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ ($3d^9$, one unpaired electron) and $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$ ($3d^8$, two unpaired electrons) in a crystal field. For which of the two is the degeneracy of the ground state never completely lifted, however low the symmetry of the crystal field? Also state how this affects the measurability by ESR (electron spin resonance).

(4) Show that a magnetic field lifts the Kramers degeneracy, using the commutation relation between $\hat{\mathcal{T}}$ and the Zeeman term $-\bm{\mu}\cdot\bm{B}$.

Solution

Strategy. (1) needs only Pauli matrix algebra. When conjugating by the antiunitary operator $\hat{\mathcal{T}}=UK$, we need to be careful about just one point: when $K$ is passed to the right, the matrix elements are complex conjugated. (2) is a product of the $-1$ attached to each electron. (3) and (4) are problems of checking whether the premises of Theorem 6.5 (Kramers) are satisfied.

(1) We write out explicitly, as a matrix, $\hat{\mathcal{T}}=-\ii\sigma_y K$ as introduced in an equation of Chapter 6 of this book:

$$ U \equiv -\ii\sigma_y = -\ii\begin{pmatrix}0&-\ii\\ \ii&0\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\ 1&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad U^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{pmatrix} = +\ii\sigma_y $$

Since $U$ is a real matrix, $U^{*}=U$. Now $K$ is the complex conjugation operator ($K^2=1$, $KAK^{-1}=A^{*}$), so for an arbitrary matrix $A$,

$$ \hat{\mathcal{T}}A\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{-1} = (UK)\,A\,(UK)^{-1} = U\,(KAK^{-1})\,U^{-1} = U A^{*} U^{-1} $$

Note that $U^{-1}=-U$ (indeed $U^2=-\mathbb{1}$, so $U^{-1}=-U$); alternatively, we may rewrite $UAU^{-1}=\sigma_y A\sigma_y$ (because $(-\ii)$ and $(+\ii)$ cancel). In what follows we use $\hat{\mathcal{T}}A\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{-1}=\sigma_y A^{*}\sigma_y$.

For $\sigma_x$. Since $\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is a real matrix, $\sigma_x^{*}=\sigma_x$. Since $\sigma_y$ and $\sigma_x$ anticommute ($\sigma_y\sigma_x=-\sigma_x\sigma_y$) and $\sigma_y^2=\mathbb{1}$,

$$ \hat{\mathcal{T}}\sigma_x\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{-1} =\sigma_y\sigma_x\sigma_y =-\sigma_x\sigma_y\sigma_y =-\sigma_x $$

We may also check directly with matrices:

$$ \begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&1\end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix} =-\sigma_x $$

For $\sigma_y$. Since $\sigma_y=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\ii\\ \ii&0\end{pmatrix}$ is purely imaginary, $\sigma_y^{*}=-\sigma_y$. Hence

$$ \hat{\mathcal{T}}\sigma_y\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{-1} =\sigma_y\,\sigma_y^{*}\,\sigma_y =\sigma_y(-\sigma_y)\sigma_y =-\left(\sigma_y\sigma_y\right)\sigma_y =-\mathbb{1}\cdot\sigma_y =-\sigma_y $$

This is the most delicate component, and the mechanism is as follows: since $\sigma_y$ commutes with $\sigma_y$, the rotation does not change its sign, but the complex conjugation $K$ flips the sign for us.

For $\sigma_z$. Since $\sigma_z=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$ is real, $\sigma_z^{*}=\sigma_z$, and it anticommutes with $\sigma_y$, so

$$ \hat{\mathcal{T}}\sigma_z\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{-1}=\sigma_y\sigma_z\sigma_y=-\sigma_z $$

For all three components, $\hat{\mathcal{T}}\sigma_i\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{-1}=-\sigma_i$ holds. That is, spin correctly reverses its direction under time reversal. The rotation by $\sigma_y$ acts on $\sigma_x,\sigma_z$, and the complex conjugation acts on $\sigma_y$; this division of roles is why the form $-\ii\sigma_y K$ is necessary.

(2) For a system of $N$ electrons, the time-reversal operator can be written as the product of the tensor product of the $U_i=-\ii\sigma_y^{(i)}$ acting on the spin space of each electron and a single complex conjugation operator $K$ acting on the whole:

$$ \hat{\mathcal{T}} = \left(\prod_{i=1}^{N}U_i\right)K \equiv \mathcal{U}K, \qquad \mathcal{U}=U_1\otimes U_2\otimes\cdots\otimes U_N $$

We compute the square. When the first $K$ is passed to the right, $\mathcal{U}$ is complex conjugated ($K\mathcal{U}=\mathcal{U}^{*}K$), so

$$ \hat{\mathcal{T}}^2 = \mathcal{U}K\,\mathcal{U}K = \mathcal{U}\,\mathcal{U}^{*}\,K^2 = \mathcal{U}\,\mathcal{U}^{*} $$

Since the tensor product factorizes component by component,

$$ \mathcal{U}\,\mathcal{U}^{*} = \bigotimes_{i=1}^{N}\left(U_iU_i^{*}\right) $$

For a single electron, $U_i=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$ is a real matrix, so $U_i^{*}=U_i$, and hence

$$ U_iU_i^{*} = U_i^2 = \begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}^2=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}=-\mathbb{1} $$

That is, each electron contributes one factor of $-1$. Taking the product of $N$ of them,

$$ \hat{\mathcal{T}}^2 = (-1)^{N}\,\mathbb{1} $$

What was decisive in the proof of Theorem 6.5 was $\hat{\mathcal{T}}^2=-1$. If $N$ is even, then $\hat{\mathcal{T}}^2=+1$, step (ii) of the proof does not work, and the possibility remains that $\hat{\mathcal{T}}\ket{\psi}$ is proportional to $\ket{\psi}$. Kramers degeneracy is guaranteed only when $N$ is odd, that is, when the total spin is a half-integer.

(3) We count the parity of the electron number. $\mathrm{Cu}$ has $Z=29$, so the electron number of $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ is $29-2=27$, which is odd (counting by the $3d^9$ subshell gives the same conclusion: closed shells contain an even number of electrons, so the parity is determined by the number of $d$ electrons, and $9$ is odd). $\mathrm{Ni}$ has $Z=28$, so $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$ has $28-2=26$, which is even ($3d^8$).

  • $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ is a Kramers ion. Since $N$ is odd (total spin $S=1/2$), as long as $\hat{\mathcal{T}}$ is a symmetry, the lowest level is always twofold degenerate however low the symmetry of the applied crystal field. This is because the crystal field is an electrostatic potential and does not break $\mathcal{T}$.
  • $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$ is a non-Kramers ion. Since $N$ is even ($S=1$), Kramers’ theorem does not apply, and a low-symmetry crystal field can split the triplet completely.

Therefore, the ion whose degeneracy is never completely lifted however low the symmetry is $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$.

The effect on ESR is as follows. For $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$, the ground Kramers doublet is exactly degenerate at zero field, so when a magnetic field is applied, the Zeeman splitting $h\nu=g\mu_{\text{B}}B$ grows continuously from zero. The resonance condition is easily satisfied even in standard X-band ESR ($\nu=9.5\ \mathrm{GHz}$), and $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ becomes one of the ions most readily seen by ESR. For $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$, on the other hand, the $S=1$ triplet is split even at zero field by the crystal field, by $D$ (the zero-field splitting constant). In a typical $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$ complex, $\abs{D}$ reaches several $\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, whereas the photon energy in the X band is

$$ h\nu = 4.136\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}\times9.5\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} = 3.93\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV} = 0.317\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}} $$

only. Since $\abs{D}\gg h\nu$, the allowed transitions are out of reach, and $\mathrm{Ni^{2+}}$ is often “invisible” (ESR silent) in ordinary X-band ESR. This is why high-frequency, high-field ESR (several hundred $\mathrm{GHz}$, over ten $\mathrm{T}$) is needed. The $\pm1$ information of whether the electron number is odd or even affects even the choice of measuring instrument.

(4) We write the Zeeman term. The magnetic moment is proportional to the spin ($\bm{\mu}=-g\mu_{\text{B}}\bm{S}/\hbar$ and so on; the sign of the proportionality constant is not essential), so

$$ \Ham_{\text{Z}} = -\bm{\mu}\cdot\bm{B} \propto \bm{S}\cdot\bm{B} $$

Here $\bm{B}$ is a fixed parameter supplied from outside and not a dynamical degree of freedom of the system. Therefore $\hat{\mathcal{T}}$ does not act on $\bm{B}$ but only on $\bm{S}$:

$$ \hat{\mathcal{T}}\,\Ham_{\text{Z}}\,\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{-1} \propto \left(\hat{\mathcal{T}}\bm{S}\hat{\mathcal{T}}^{-1}\right)\cdot\bm{B} = (-\bm{S})\cdot\bm{B} = -\,\Ham_{\text{Z}} $$

That is,

$$ \hat{\mathcal{T}}\Ham_{\text{Z}} = -\Ham_{\text{Z}}\hat{\mathcal{T}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad [\hat{\mathcal{T}},\ \Ham_{\text{Z}}] = 2\,\hat{\mathcal{T}}\Ham_{\text{Z}} \neq 0 $$

The commutator does not vanish. The premise of Theorem 6.5, “$[\hat{\mathcal{T}},\Ham]=0$,” breaks down, so the guarantee of Kramers degeneracy disappears. In fact, the $S=1/2$ doublet splits into

$$ E_\pm = \pm\frac{1}{2}g\mu_{\text{B}}B $$

and the splitting is $\Delta E=g\mu_{\text{B}}B$. Putting in $g=2$ and $B=1\ \mathrm{T}$,

$$ \Delta E = 2\times5.788\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/T}\times1\ \mathrm{T} = 1.158\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV} = 0.116\ \mathrm{meV} $$

The important point is that what cannot be split by a crystal field ($\mathcal{T}$-even), however low its symmetry, is split the moment a magnetic field ($\mathcal{T}$-odd) is applied. Since what protects the degeneracy is not spatial symmetry but time-reversal symmetry, the degeneracy remains as long as this symmetry is not broken.

Verification. The result of (1) is consistent with the computation of $\hat{\mathcal{T}}^2$. We get $\hat{\mathcal{T}}^2=(-\ii\sigma_y K)(-\ii\sigma_y K)=(-\ii\sigma_y)(+\ii\sigma_y^{*})=(-\ii)(+\ii)\sigma_y(-\sigma_y)=-\sigma_y^2=-\mathbb{1}$, which agrees with the result $-1$ obtained by setting $S=1/2$ in $\hat{\mathcal{T}}^2=(-1)^{2S}$ of Chapter 6 of this book. The case $N=1$ of (2) is exactly this.

(4) can be verified against an experimental value. Solving the splitting formula $h\nu=g\mu_{\text{B}}B$ for the X band ($\nu=9.5\ \mathrm{GHz}$) and $g=2$ gives

$$ B = \frac{h\nu}{g\mu_{\text{B}}} = \frac{4.136\times10^{-15}\times9.5\times10^{9}}{2\times5.788\times10^{-5}}\ \mathrm{T} = 0.339\ \mathrm{T} $$

This agrees precisely with the laboratory rule of thumb that the resonance field of X-band ESR is about $3400\ \mathrm{G}=0.34\ \mathrm{T}$. The reasoning of time-reversal symmetry directly predicts the magnet setting of the instrument.

Meaning. Kramers degeneracy is an extremely strong statement: whether the degeneracy is protected is determined solely by the $\pm1$ information of whether the number of electrons is odd or even. Moreover, its basis is $\hat{\mathcal{T}}^2=-1$, that is, the geometric fact that a spinor changes sign under a rotation by $2\pi$.

As we saw in Section 6.6.6 of Chapter 6 of this book, this $\hat{\mathcal{T}}^2=-1$ is also the reason for the existence of $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological insulators. That bands necessarily form Kramers pairs at the time-reversal invariant momenta (TRIM), and that the pairs open a gap only through magnetic impurities (breaking of $\mathcal{T}$), are nothing other than (3) and (4) translated into the language of band structure. The opening of a gap at the Dirac point in $\mathrm{Cr}$-doped $(\mathrm{Bi},\mathrm{Sb})_2\mathrm{Te_3}$ is exactly the same phenomenon as the splitting of the Kramers doublet of $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$ by a magnetic field. Symmetry protects, so if the symmetry is broken, the protection disappears.

Exercise 6.5: Oscillation of neutral $K$ mesons

Problem (restated)

Suppose that a pure $\ket{K^0}$ is produced at $t=0$. Let $\ket{K^0}=(\ket{K_S}+\ket{K_L})/\sqrt2$ (ignore $\mathcal{CP}$ violation), and let the time evolution of $K_{S,L}$ be $\ee^{-\ii m_{S,L}t-\Gamma_{S,L}t/2}$.

(1) Show that the probability of finding $\bar K^0$ at time $t$ is

$$ P_{\bar K^0}(t)=\frac{1}{4}\left[\ee^{-\Gamma_S t}+\ee^{-\Gamma_L t}-2\ee^{-(\Gamma_S+\Gamma_L)t/2}\cos(\Delta m\,t)\right] $$

(with $\Delta m=m_L-m_S$).

(2) Compute the dimensionless parameter $x\equiv\Delta m/\Gamma_S=\Delta m\,\tau_S$ from $\Delta m=5.29\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $\tau_S=8.954\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{s}$.

(3) Is it favorable or unfavorable for experiments that $x$ is around $1$? Discuss what happens in the cases $x\ll1$ and $x\gg1$.

Solution

Strategy. $K_S$ and $K_L$ are eigenstates of time evolution, and $K^0$ and $\bar K^0$ are superpositions of them. Therefore the process “produce as $K^0$, observe as $\bar K^0$” is itself the interference of two beams. It suffices to write the amplitude for $\bar K^0$ in terms of the expansion in $K_S$ and $K_L$ and take the absolute value squared. We use natural units ($\hbar=c=1$).

(1) First we expand $\bar K^0$ in terms of $K_{S,L}$. From $\ket{K^0}=(\ket{K_S}+\ket{K_L})/\sqrt2$ in the problem statement and the orthogonality of $K^0$ and $\bar K^0$ ($\braket{K^0|\bar K^0}=0$), the normalized orthogonal partner is the one with a single sign changed, so

$$ \ket{\bar K^0}=\frac{\ket{K_S}-\ket{K_L}}{\sqrt2} $$

can be taken (because of the freedom of the overall phase, $-(\ket{K_S}-\ket{K_L})/\sqrt2$ would also do; it does not affect the probability).

Step 1: Time evolution. Since $K_S$ and $K_L$ are eigenstates with masses $m_{S,L}$ and decay widths $\Gamma_{S,L}$, respectively, each decays while its phase rotates independently:

$$ \ket{\psi(t)} =\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left[ \ee^{-\ii m_S t-\Gamma_S t/2}\ket{K_S} +\ee^{-\ii m_L t-\Gamma_L t/2}\ket{K_L} \right] $$

Below we abbreviate $f_{S}(t)\equiv\ee^{-\ii m_S t-\Gamma_S t/2}$ and $f_{L}(t)\equiv\ee^{-\ii m_L t-\Gamma_L t/2}$.

Step 2: Project onto the $\bar K^0$ component. Multiplying by $\bra{\bar K^0}=(\bra{K_S}-\bra{K_L})/\sqrt2$ and using $\braket{K_S|K_S}=\braket{K_L|K_L}=1$ and $\braket{K_S|K_L}=0$, we obtain

$$ \braket{\bar K^0|\psi(t)} =\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\left[f_S(t)-f_L(t)\right] =\frac{1}{2}\left[f_S(t)-f_L(t)\right] $$

Step 3: Take the absolute value squared.

$$ P_{\bar K^0}(t)=\abs{\braket{\bar K^0|\psi(t)}}^2 =\frac{1}{4}\left(f_S-f_L\right)\left(f_S-f_L\right)^{*} =\frac{1}{4}\left[\abs{f_S}^2+\abs{f_L}^2-f_Sf_L^{*}-f_S^{*}f_L\right] $$

Step 4: Write out each term. First, for the diagonal terms, the absolute value of the phase factor is $1$, so only the decay factor remains:

$$ \abs{f_S}^2=\ee^{-\Gamma_S t},\qquad \abs{f_L}^2=\ee^{-\Gamma_L t} $$

The cross term is

$$ f_Sf_L^{*} =\ee^{-\ii m_S t-\Gamma_S t/2}\cdot\ee^{+\ii m_L t-\Gamma_L t/2} =\ee^{-(\Gamma_S+\Gamma_L)t/2}\,\ee^{\ii(m_L-m_S)t} =\ee^{-(\Gamma_S+\Gamma_L)t/2}\,\ee^{\ii\Delta m\,t} $$

(where we used $\Delta m=m_L-m_S$). Its complex conjugate is $f_S^{*}f_L=\ee^{-(\Gamma_S+\Gamma_L)t/2}\ee^{-\ii\Delta m t}$, so the sum of the two is

$$ f_Sf_L^{*}+f_S^{*}f_L =\ee^{-(\Gamma_S+\Gamma_L)t/2}\left(\ee^{\ii\Delta m t}+\ee^{-\ii\Delta m t}\right) =2\,\ee^{-(\Gamma_S+\Gamma_L)t/2}\cos(\Delta m\,t) $$

Step 5: Put it together.

$$ P_{\bar K^0}(t)=\frac{1}{4}\left[ \ee^{-\Gamma_S t}+\ee^{-\Gamma_L t} -2\,\ee^{-(\Gamma_S+\Gamma_L)t/2}\cos(\Delta m\,t)\right] $$

This is the required expression. ∎

The reading of this expression is clear. The first and second terms are the contributions from the simple decay of $K_S$ and $K_L$, and the third term is the interference term, which carries the oscillation $\cos(\Delta m\,t)$. The oscillation frequency is determined only by the mass difference $\Delta m$, and the interference term decays as $\ee^{-(\Gamma_S+\Gamma_L)t/2}$, the “geometric mean of the two decays.” At $t=0$, $\cos=1$ and the three terms cancel, giving $P_{\bar K^0}(0)=\frac{1}{4}(1+1-2)=0$, which correctly reproduces the initial condition “initially a pure $K^0$.”

(2) Multiply as defined:

$$ x = \Delta m\,\tau_S = \left(5.29\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\right)\times\left(8.954\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{s}\right) $$ $$ = 5.29\times8.954\times10^{9-11} = 47.37\times10^{-2} = 0.4737 $$

That is,

$$ \boxed{\ x = 0.474\ } $$

(to 3 significant figures). We can also confirm that it is a dimensionless quantity ($\mathrm{s^{-1}}\times\mathrm{s}$ is dimensionless).

(3) We relate the condition for the interference term to be observable to the value of $x$. The interference term is $\ee^{-(\Gamma_S+\Gamma_L)t/2}\cos(\Delta m\,t)$. Since $\Gamma_L/\Gamma_S=\tau_S/\tau_L=8.954\times10^{-11}/5.116\times10^{-8}=1.75\times10^{-3}$ is very small, the decay acts almost as $\ee^{-\Gamma_S t/2}$, that is, with time constant $2\tau_S$. Meanwhile, the phase accumulates at the rate $\Delta m\,t = x\,(t/\tau_S)$. Therefore $x$ itself determines “how much phase accumulates while the interference term survives.”

  • The case $x\ll1$. Almost no phase difference develops before the $K_S$ has died out. Since the interference term vanishes while $\cos(\Delta m\,t)\approx1$ still holds, the production of $\bar K^0$ does not show up as an oscillation; it looks like a merely monotonic rise. To measure $\Delta m$ one would have to follow the tiny curvature that comes from expanding $\cos$ as $1-(\Delta m\,t)^2/2$, and the sensitivity drops hopelessly.
  • The case $x\gg1$. Conversely, the oscillation is too fast. If it goes around dozens of times during the $K_S$ lifetime of $89.5\ \mathrm{ps}$, one period cannot be resolved by the experiment’s time resolution (or by the position resolution of the tracks), and the oscillation is averaged out inside the detector and disappears. Again $\Delta m$ cannot be read off.
  • The case $x\sim0.5$ (reality). Right in between the two, a clearly visible phase accumulates during the time window in which the interference term is still alive. Let us check this numerically. Evaluating $P_{\bar K^0}(t)$ as a function of $t/\tau_S$, we find $P=0.176$ at $t=2\tau_S$, $P=0.245$ at $t=3\tau_S$, and the maximum $P_{\bar K^0}=0.279$ at $t=4.74\tau_S$. The phase $\Delta m\,t$ reaches $\pi$ (half a period) at $t=\pi/x\cdot\tau_S=6.63\,\tau_S$, and even then $P=0.266$ is still large. In other words, a huge oscillation in which the strangeness is reversed to almost $3$ tenths (about 30%) fits snugly inside an experimentally convenient time window (several $K_S$ lifetimes, a flight distance of several tens of $\mathrm{cm}$ in the laboratory frame).

Therefore $x\sim0.5$ is extremely favorable. In fact, $\Delta m$ is one of the most precisely measured mass differences in particle physics: the tiny mass difference $\Delta m/m_{K^0}\sim7\times10^{-15}$ has been measured to a precision of $0.2\%$ (PDG: $\Delta m=(0.5293\pm0.0009)\times10^{10}\,\hbar\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$). It is fair to say that nature has provided favorable conditions.

Verification. We carry out three independent checks.

First, we check the consistency of the formula in (1) through the sum of probabilities. Doing the same calculation with $\bra{K^0}=(\bra{K_S}+\bra{K_L})/\sqrt2$, only the sign of the cross term changes, and we obtain

$$ P_{K^0}(t)=\frac{1}{4}\left[\ee^{-\Gamma_S t}+\ee^{-\Gamma_L t}+2\ee^{-(\Gamma_S+\Gamma_L)t/2}\cos(\Delta m\,t)\right] $$

Adding the two, the interference term cancels and

$$ P_{K^0}(t)+P_{\bar K^0}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\left[\ee^{-\Gamma_S t}+\ee^{-\Gamma_L t}\right] $$

results, which is exactly the picture “$K_S$ and $K_L$ each exist with probability $1/2$ and decay independently.” It equals $1$ at $t=0$ and $0$ as $t\to\infty$, which is physically correct.

Second, we check the numerical value of $\Delta m$ by another route. Table 6.4 in Chapter 6 of this book gives $\Delta m=3.484\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Dividing by $\hbar=6.582\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{MeV\,s}$ gives

$$ \frac{3.484\times10^{-12}}{6.582\times10^{-22}} = 5.29\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

which agrees with the value in the problem statement. The unit conversion is consistent as well.

Third, we pin down the size of the phase with concrete numbers. The phase at $t=\tau_S$ is $\Delta m\,\tau_S=x=0.474\ \mathrm{rad}$ (about $27^\circ$), which is only $7.5\%$ of one period $2\pi$. The phase reaches half a period $\pi$ at $t=6.63\,\tau_S$. The “phase difference of about half a period” mentioned in the hint in the main text is acquired not within a single $K_S$ lifetime but when the time window in which the interference term is alive (time constant $2\tau_S$, effectively $t\lesssim7\tau_S$) has been used up. The conclusion ($x\sim0.5$ is optimal for the experiment) is unchanged.

Meaning. The mathematics of this problem is not at all specific to particle physics. A state built by superposing two eigenstates of different energies oscillates with the phase difference $\Delta E\,t/\hbar$—this is a universal phenomenon called a quantum beat. Free induction decay in nuclear magnetic resonance, coherent-phonon beats in ultrafast spectroscopy, Larmor precession of a spin, Rabi oscillations of a two-level system, and the beating of coupled modes between optical waveguides (Exercise 6.8) are all described by the same formula. The only difference is whether the identity of $\Delta E$ is a “mass difference,” a “Zeeman splitting,” or a “phonon frequency difference.”

The presence of damping is also common to all of them. For the neutral $K$, as we saw in Section 6.4.5 of Chapter 6 of this book, the time evolution is described by the non-Hermitian effective Hamiltonian $\mathcal{H}_{\text{eff}}=M-\frac{\ii}{2}\Gamma$. The structure in which the difference of the real parts of the eigenvalues gives $\Delta m$ (the frequency) and the difference of the imaginary parts gives $\Delta\Gamma$ (the difference of decay rates) is exactly the general theory of a dissipative two-level system. For those who deal with exciton polaritons and non-Hermitian bands in materials science, the neutral $K$ meson system is worth referring to as “the oldest and most precisely measured example.”

Exercise 6.6: Estimating the sensitivity of a neutron EDM search

Problem (restated)

In a neutron EDM experiment, a magnetic field $\bm{B}$ and an electric field $\bm{E}$ are applied to ultracold neutrons, parallel or antiparallel, and the difference in the Larmor precession frequency is measured.

(1) Show from $H=-\bm{d}\cdot\bm{E}$ that, when the EDM is $d_n$, the energy difference on reversing the direction of the electric field is $\Delta E = 2 d_n E$.

(2) Find $\Delta E$ in eV for $d_n = 1.8\times10^{-26}\ e\,\mathrm{cm}$ and $E=10\ \mathrm{kV/cm}$.

(3) Find the corresponding frequency $\Delta\nu=\Delta E/h$ (with $h=4.136\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}$).

(4) Find the minimum observation time $T\sim1/\Delta\nu$ needed to measure this frequency, and discuss whether a single measurement suffices or whether statistics must be accumulated.

Solution

Strategy. As we saw in Section 6.5.5 of Chapter 6 of this book, the EDM of a spin-$1/2$ particle is necessarily parallel to the spin and can be written $\bm{d}=d_n\bm{S}/\abs{\bm{S}}$. In the experiment, the spins are polarized by the magnetic field $\bm{B}$, and the Larmor precession frequencies are compared between the case where $\bm{E}$ is applied parallel to $\bm{B}$ and the case where it is applied antiparallel. The unit $e\,\mathrm{cm}$ is “the product of the charge $e$ and the distance $\mathrm{cm}$,” so multiplying by $\mathrm{V/cm}$ automatically gives $\mathrm{eV}$. Exploiting this convenient compatibility of units, the calculation takes one line.

(1) The interaction energy is $H=-\bm{d}\cdot\bm{E}$. Let the spin direction be $\hat{\bm{s}}=\bm{S}/\abs{\bm{S}}$, and write $\bm{d}=d_n\hat{\bm s}$ and $\bm{E}=E\hat{\bm e}$. Then

$$ H = -d_n E\,(\hat{\bm s}\cdot\hat{\bm e}) $$

In the experiment, the spin is polarized by the magnetic field $\bm{B}$, and the electric field is applied parallel to it ($\hat{\bm e}=+\hat{\bm b}$) or antiparallel to it ($\hat{\bm e}=-\hat{\bm b}$). Reversing only the electric field while keeping the spin direction fixed gives

$$ H_{\uparrow\uparrow} = -d_n E, \qquad H_{\uparrow\downarrow} = +d_n E $$

The difference between the two is the measured quantity, and

$$ \Delta E = H_{\uparrow\downarrow}-H_{\uparrow\uparrow} = (+d_nE)-(-d_nE) = 2\,d_n E $$

That is, when the electric field is reversed, the level shift changes by $2d_nE$. The factor $2$ comes from the “round trip due to the reversal.” The reason for taking this difference experimentally is that the much larger Zeeman energy due to the magnetic field ($\sim2\mu_nB$) does not change under reversal of $\bm{E}$, so it can be eliminated by taking the difference. This is a standard way of removing systematic errors.

(2) We substitute the numbers. Here $E=10\ \mathrm{kV/cm}=10^{4}\ \mathrm{V/cm}$.

$$ \Delta E = 2 d_n E = 2\times\left(1.8\times10^{-26}\ e\,\mathrm{cm}\right)\times\left(10^{4}\ \mathrm{V/cm}\right) $$

Since $e\,\mathrm{cm}\times\mathrm{V/cm}=e\,\mathrm{V}=\mathrm{eV}$ (the energy when a charge $e$ passes through a potential difference of $1\ \mathrm{V}$ is $1\ \mathrm{eV}$), the unit is simply $\mathrm{eV}$.

$$ \Delta E = 2\times1.8\times10^{4-26}\ \mathrm{eV} = 3.6\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{eV} $$

That is, $\Delta E = 3.6\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{eV}$. For reference, compared with the thermal energy at room temperature, $k_BT=2.6\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{eV}$, it is smaller by as much as $20$ orders of magnitude.

(3) The corresponding frequency is

$$ \Delta\nu = \frac{\Delta E}{h} = \frac{3.6\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{eV}}{4.136\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}} = \frac{3.6}{4.136}\times10^{-22+15}\ \mathrm{Hz} = 0.8704\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{Hz} $$

that is,

$$ \Delta\nu = 8.70\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{Hz} = 87.0\ \mathrm{nHz} $$

That is, $87$ nanohertz. For comparison, in the static magnetic field $B\sim1\ \mu\mathrm{T}$ used in actual nEDM experiments, the Larmor frequency of the neutron is $2\abs{\mu_n}B/h\approx29.2\ \mathrm{Hz}$. What we are trying to measure is the relative shift

$$ \frac{8.70\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{Hz}}{29.2\ \mathrm{Hz}} = 3.0\times10^{-9} $$

riding on top of this $29.2\ \mathrm{Hz}$. This corresponds to reading the frequency to nine digits of precision.

(4) Simply put, the time needed to distinguish one period of the frequency $\Delta\nu$ is

$$ T \sim \frac{1}{\Delta\nu} = \frac{1}{8.70\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{Hz}} = 1.15\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s} $$

Converting to days,

$$ \frac{1.15\times10^{7}}{86400} = 133\ \mathrm{days} \approx 4.4\ \text{months} $$

This means that a single neutron would have to be observed continuously for more than four months. This is completely impossible, for two reasons. First, the neutron undergoes $\beta$ decay and disappears with a lifetime of $\tau_n=878\ \mathrm{s}$ (about $15$ minutes). Second, the time for which ultracold neutrons (UCN) can be stored in a container is, owing also to losses at the walls, only $T_{\text{store}}\sim100$–$300\ \mathrm{s}$ in practice. It falls far short of $4$ months.

Therefore we have no choice but to accumulate statistics. If $N$ neutrons are measured simultaneously, the precision of the phase measurement improves as $1/\sqrt{N}$. When a free precession time $T_{\text{free}}$ is secured by Ramsey’s separated oscillatory fields method, the accumulated phase difference is $\Delta\phi=\Delta E\,T_{\text{free}}/\hbar = 2d_nET_{\text{free}}/\hbar$, and since the statistical error of the phase is $1/\sqrt{N}$, the measurement precision of $d_n$ is

$$ \sigma_{d} = \frac{\hbar}{2\,E\,T_{\text{free}}\sqrt{N}} $$

Let us insert realistic experimental values. With $E=10\ \mathrm{kV/cm}=10^{6}\ \mathrm{V/m}$, $T_{\text{free}}=200\ \mathrm{s}$, and $N=10^{4}$ neutrons per cycle, the sensitivity of one cycle is
