$$ \sigma_d^{(1\text{cycle})} =\frac{1.055\times10^{-34}}{2\times10^{6}\times200\times\sqrt{10^{4}}}\ \mathrm{C\,m} =2.64\times10^{-45}\ \mathrm{C\,m} =1.65\times10^{-24}\ e\,\mathrm{cm} $$

To reach the target $1.8\times10^{-26}\ e\,\mathrm{cm}$, we need $(1.65\times10^{-24}/1.8\times10^{-26})^2=8.4\times10^{3}$ cycles. If one cycle takes $300\ \mathrm{s}$ (filling, polarizing, precession, counting), then

$$ 8.4\times10^{3}\times300\ \mathrm{s} = 2.5\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{s} \approx 29\ \text{days} $$

is the net data-taking time. In practice, the duty cycle of the apparatus, the drift of the magnetic field, and the evaluation of systematic errors such as leakage currents and geometric phases accompanying the reversal of $\bm{E}$ require a much longer time than this. This is why the PSI experiment took several years to produce the upper limit of $1.8\times10^{-26}\ e\,\mathrm{cm}$.

Verification. We confirm that the two estimates are consistent. From the phase argument in (4), the time needed for the phase difference to reach $1\ \mathrm{rad}$ with $N=1$ is

$$ T_{\text{1rad}}=\frac{\hbar}{2d_nE} =\frac{1.055\times10^{-34}}{2\times2.884\times10^{-47}\times10^{6}}\ \mathrm{s} =1.83\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{s} = 21\ \text{days} $$

(we used $d_n=1.8\times10^{-26}\ e\,\mathrm{cm}=2.884\times10^{-47}\ \mathrm{C\,m}$). On the other hand, the naive estimate in (4), $T=1/\Delta\nu=h/(2d_nE)$, was $1.15\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}$. The ratio of the two is

$$ \frac{h/(2d_nE)}{\hbar/(2d_nE)} = \frac{h}{\hbar} = 2\pi = 6.28 $$

Indeed $1.15\times10^{7}/1.83\times10^{6}=6.28$. We have confirmed that the difference between “one period” and “one radian” appears correctly as $2\pi$, and that the two estimates merely express the same physics in different units. Whichever we use, the conclusion that a single neutron is hopeless is unchanged.

Let us also check the size of $\Delta E$ from another angle. Section 6.5.5 of Chapter 6 of this book states that $d_n=1.8\times10^{-26}\ e\,\mathrm{cm}$ corresponds to “a displacement between the positive and negative charges of only about $1\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ even if the neutron were enlarged to the size of the Earth.” Indeed, multiplying $1.8\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{m}/(0.8\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m})=2.25\times10^{-13}$ by the Earth’s radius $6.4\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m}$ gives $1.4\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$ (the main text rounds the relative displacement to $2\times10^{-13}$ and so obtains $1.3\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$; both lead to the same conclusion of about $1\ \mu\mathrm{m}$). The same smallness appears as $10^{-22}\ \mathrm{eV}$ in energy and as $10^{-7}\ \mathrm{Hz}$ in frequency.

Meaning. What this exercise conveys is a feel for why “precision experiments” in particle physics take so long. Since the quantity we wish to measure is of the order of $10^{-22}\ \mathrm{eV}$, a single measurement is in principle insufficient and we must rely on $\sqrt{N}$. And to gain by $\sqrt{N}$ also means that improving the sensitivity by one order of magnitude requires a hundred times the measurement time. So experiments progress not by “measuring longer” but by improvements on the apparatus side: “raise $E$,” “extend $T_{\text{free}}$,” and “strengthen the UCN source to increase $N$.”

The same structure appears on the materials science side. In measurements of the magnetoelectric effect, the magnetization induced by an electric field (or the polarization induced by a magnetic field) must be separated from a far larger background and read out. The technique used there is likewise a lock-in measurement that reverses the external field and takes the difference. The experimental practice for measuring the small coefficient $\alpha_{\perp}\approx1\ \mathrm{ps/m}$ of $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ (even the maximal $\alpha_{\parallel}$ is only about $4\ \mathrm{ps/m}$) is essentially the same as that of the nEDM experiment. And what the two are looking for, as Table 6.7 in Chapter 6 of this book shows, is exactly the same question: whether a $\mathcal{P}$-odd and $\mathcal{T}$-odd quantity is nonzero.

Exercise 6.7: Determining material properties from the crystallographic point group

Problem (restated)

Answer using Table 6.8 and Theorem 6.1.

(1) Of $\mathrm{Si}$ ($m\bar3m$), $\mathrm{GaAs}$ ($\bar43m$), and $\mathrm{LiNbO_3}$ ($3m$), which show SHG in the bulk? Which show piezoelectricity?

(2) SHG is observed at the surface of $\mathrm{Si}$ and at the $\mathrm{Si/SiO_2}$ interface. Explain why an effect forbidden in the bulk appears at the interface.

(3) Monolayer $\mathrm{MoS_2}$ has point group $\bar6m2$ (no inversion center), and bilayer $2H$-stacked $\mathrm{MoS_2}$ has $\bar3m$ (with an inversion center). Predict whether the SHG signal “appears / does not appear” for the number of layers $n=1,2,3,4$.

(4) The magnetic point group of $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ is $\bar3'm'$. Does this material (i) have a spontaneous polarization, (ii) have a spontaneous magnetization, (iii) show a linear magnetoelectric effect? Answer each with reasons.

Solution

Strategy. All parts reduce to a single statement of Theorem 6.1: “if the symmetry operation is a symmetry operation of the crystal, then a quantity that is odd under that operation must vanish.” This is called Neumann’s principle. The necessary transformation properties can be picked up from Table 6.7 in Chapter 6 of this book: $\bm{P}$ is $(\mathcal{P},\mathcal{T})=(-,+)$, $\bm{M}$ is $(+,-)$, $\alpha_{ij}$ is $(-,-)$, and $\chi^{(2)}_{ijk}$ and $d_{ijk}$ are third-rank polar tensors that are $\mathcal{P}$-odd.

(1) We sort the three point groups according to whether they contain the inversion center $\bar1$.

  • $\mathrm{Si}$ ($m\bar3m$). The symbol contains $\bar3$ (threefold rotoinversion), and $m\bar3m$ is a centrosymmetric point group (it is also cited in the main text as a representative example of the 11 “centrosymmetric” groups in Table 6.8). Since both $\chi^{(2)}_{ijk}$ and $d_{ijk}$ are odd-rank (third-rank) polar tensors, they change sign under inversion. By Theorem 6.1, both vanish. Both SHG and piezoelectricity are forbidden.
  • $\mathrm{GaAs}$ ($\bar43m$). It has the zincblende structure and no inversion center. It belongs to the 20 “piezoelectric” groups of Table 6.8. SHG is allowed, and piezoelectricity is present. However, it is not a polar point group ($\bar43m$ does not allow a polar vector), so there is no spontaneous polarization.
  • $\mathrm{LiNbO_3}$ ($3m$). It has no inversion center, and moreover it belongs to the polar point groups (the 10 “polar (pyroelectric)” groups of Table 6.8). SHG is allowed, piezoelectricity is present, and in addition it has a spontaneous polarization $\bm{P}_s\neq0$ (it is a ferroelectric).

To summarize, $\mathrm{GaAs}$ and $\mathrm{LiNbO_3}$ show SHG, and $\mathrm{GaAs}$ and $\mathrm{LiNbO_3}$ also show piezoelectricity, while $\mathrm{Si}$ shows neither. Only $\mathrm{LiNbO_3}$ is in addition ferroelectric.

Let us recall here one caveat about Table 6.8. There is exactly one noncentrosymmetric point group that shows neither piezoelectricity nor SHG ($432$). Hence, strictly speaking, it is not “noncentrosymmetric $\Rightarrow$ piezoelectric” but “noncentrosymmetric and not $432$ $\Rightarrow$ piezoelectric.” Since neither $\bar43m$ nor $3m$ is $432$, the above determination stands.

(2) Bulk $\mathrm{Si}$ shows no SHG because the crystal, as an infinitely continuing periodic structure, has an inversion center. However, a surface or an interface breaks that very assumption. Standing at the surface and looking outward, there is vacuum (or $\mathrm{SiO_2}$); looking inward, there is $\mathrm{Si}$. Clearly “up” and “down” are not equivalent, and a polar vector, the interface normal $\hat{\bm z}$, can be defined. Since the inversion operation sends $\hat{\bm z}\to-\hat{\bm z}$, the environment of the interface is not inversion symmetric.

Therefore $\chi^{(2)}\neq0$ is allowed only within a range of a few atomic layers from the interface, and SHG is generated there. Since the contribution from the bulk is zero, the observed SHG signal originates almost purely from the interface. This is why SHG (and sum-frequency generation, SFG) works as an interface-selective probe. It is used for evaluating defects, strain, and electric fields at the $\mathrm{Si}/\mathrm{SiO_2}$ interface, for determining the molecular orientation of adsorbed species on catalyst surfaces, for nondestructive observation of buried interfaces, and so on.

This logic has exactly the same structure as the discussion of the Rashba term in Exercise 6.3. Both rest on the single point that “a $\mathcal{P}$-odd structural vector, the interface normal $\hat{\bm z}$, becomes nonzero only at the interface.” The breaking of inversion symmetry produces SHG in one case and spin splitting in the other.

(3) In $2H$-stacked $\mathrm{MoS_2}$, adjacent layers are stacked rotated by $180^\circ$ relative to each other. As a result,

  • odd numbers of layers ($n=1,3,5,\dots$): the whole has no inversion center (the monolayer is $\bar6m2$). $\chi^{(2)}\neq0$ is allowed. SHG appears.
  • even numbers of layers ($n=2,4,6,\dots$): the bilayer becomes $\bar3m$ and an inversion center arises. By Theorem 6.1, $\chi^{(2)}=0$. SHG disappears.

Therefore the prediction is

$$ n=1:\ \text{appears},\quad n=2:\ \text{does not appear},\quad n=3:\ \text{appears},\quad n=4:\ \text{does not appear} $$

An even-odd oscillation appears, in which the signal switches on and off according to the parity of the number of layers. This behavior has been confirmed experimentally, and SHG is used as a simple way of counting the layers of $\mathrm{MoS_2}$.

Strictly speaking, even for an even number of layers the environments of the topmost and bottommost layers at the surfaces are not equivalent, so a very weak signal originating from the interfaces may remain. However, it is smaller by orders of magnitude than the bulk-like signal for odd numbers of layers (which grows in proportion to the number of layers), and experimentally it may be said to “disappear.”

(4) We begin by deciphering the symbol of the magnetic point group $\bar3'm'$. A primed operation means that “the operation alone is not a symmetry, but it becomes one when combined with time reversal $\mathcal{T}$.” Therefore in $\bar3'm'$

  • Unitary (unprimed) symmetry operations: a $3$-fold rotation and a $2$-fold rotation perpendicular to it, that is, the operations of the point group $32$.
  • Antiunitary (primed) symmetry operations: inversion $\bar1$ or reflection $m$ multiplied by $\mathcal{T}$. In particular, $\bar1\cdot\mathcal{T}$ ($=\mathcal{PT}$) is a symmetry operation.
  • On the other hand, $\bar1$ alone and $\mathcal{T}$ alone are not symmetry operations.

Once we have these three points, all that remains is to multiply by the signs in Table 6.7.

(i) Spontaneous polarization $\bm{P}_s$. Since $\bm{P}$ is $\mathcal{P}$-odd and $\mathcal{T}$-even, under $\mathcal{PT}$ we have

$$ \bm{P}\ \xrightarrow{\ \mathcal{PT}\ }\ (-1)\times(+1)\,\bm{P} = -\bm{P} $$

Since $\mathcal{PT}$ is a symmetry operation, Theorem 6.1 gives $\bm{P}_s=\bm{0}$. There is no spontaneous polarization. (The unitary part alone gives the same conclusion. The point group $32$ has a $2$-fold axis perpendicular to the $3$-fold axis, so it is a nonpolar point group that does not allow a polar vector. It is forbidden twice over.)

(ii) Spontaneous magnetization $\bm{M}$. Since $\bm{M}$ is $\mathcal{P}$-even and $\mathcal{T}$-odd, under $\mathcal{PT}$ we have

$$ \bm{M}\ \xrightarrow{\ \mathcal{PT}\ }\ (+1)\times(-1)\,\bm{M} = -\bm{M} $$

Again by Theorem 6.1, $\bm{M}=\bm{0}$. There is no spontaneous magnetization. Indeed, $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ is an antiferromagnet (Néel temperature $307\ \mathrm{K}$) and its net magnetization is zero. The reason that no macroscopic magnetization appears even though magnetic order exists is that $\mathcal{PT}$ forbids it.

(iii) Linear magnetoelectric effect $\alpha_{ij}$. As we saw in Section 6.6.5 of Chapter 6 of this book, matching how the two sides of $P_i=\alpha_{ij}H_j$ transform shows that $\alpha_{ij}$ must be $\mathcal{P}$-odd and $\mathcal{T}$-odd. Under $\mathcal{PT}$ we have

$$ \alpha_{ij}\ \xrightarrow{\ \mathcal{PT}\ }\ (-1)\times(-1)\,\alpha_{ij} = +\alpha_{ij} $$

so it is invariant. Even though $\mathcal{PT}$ is a symmetry operation, $\alpha_{ij}$ does not drop to zero. And since neither $\bar1$ alone nor $\mathcal{T}$ alone is a symmetry operation, the prohibitions they would impose do not operate either. Therefore $\alpha_{ij}\neq0$ is allowed, and the material exhibits a linear magnetoelectric effect. Indeed, $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ was the first material in which the magnetoelectric effect was demonstrated, in 1960; $\alpha_{\parallel}$ has a maximum of about $4\ \mathrm{ps/m}$ near $T\approx260\ \mathrm{K}$, and $\alpha_{\perp}$ is about $1\ \mathrm{ps/m}$ (Astrov 1960, Rado–Folen 1961; both given in SI units of $\mathrm{s/m}$).

This is the key point of the problem. What is required is that $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{T}$ be broken individually; the product $\mathcal{PT}$ may well be preserved. Rather, it is precisely because $\mathcal{PT}$ is preserved that this selective situation is realized, in which neither $\bm{P}_s$ nor $\bm{M}$ appears and only $\alpha_{ij}$ survives.

Verification. Reorganizing the answer to (4) as a table of how $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{T}$ are broken confirms the logical consistency.

Table E.6.2: Which physical quantities are allowed in $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ ($\bar3'm'$)
Quantity$\mathcal{P}$$\mathcal{T}$$\mathcal{PT}$Since $\mathcal{PT}$ is a symmetry operation
Spontaneous polarization $\bm{P}_s$$-$$+$$-$Zero
Spontaneous magnetization $\bm{M}$$+$$-$$-$Zero
Magnetoelectric tensor $\alpha_{ij}$$-$$-$$+$Nonzero is allowed
Toroidal moment $\bm{T}\propto\bm{P}\times\bm{M}$$-$$-$$+$Not forbidden by $\mathcal{PT}$, but $\bm{T}=\bm{0}$ because the unitary subgroup $32$ does not allow a polar vector ($\alpha_{ij}$ has only diagonal elements)

A quantity with $-$ in the $\mathcal{PT}$ column is necessarily zero. A quantity with $+$, on the other hand, is merely not forbidden by $\mathcal{PT}$; whether it actually becomes nonzero must be decided separately by the remaining operations (here, the unitary subgroup $32$ and the antiunitary $m'$)—being $\mathcal{PT}$-even is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one. The toroidal row of the table is exactly such an example: $\bm{T}$ is a polar vector that is $\mathcal{P}$-odd and $\mathcal{T}$-odd, so it vanishes under the nonpolar point group $32$ (for the same reason, only the diagonal elements $\alpha_{xx}=\alpha_{yy}$ and $\alpha_{zz}$ of $\alpha_{ij}$ survive). Also, the signs in this table agree exactly with the corresponding rows ($\bm{P}$, $\bm{M}$, $\alpha_{ij}$) of Table 6.7 in Chapter 6 of this book.

Let us also check the consistency of (1) and (3). $\mathrm{LiNbO_3}$ ($3m$) has a polar point group, so $\bm{P}_s\neq0$ is allowed, which agrees with the experimental fact (a ferroelectric, $P_s\approx0.7\ \mathrm{C/m^2}$). On the other hand, $\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$ has $\bm{P}_s=0$, as we saw above. Even under the same “breaking of $\mathcal{P}$,” the physical properties that appear are entirely different between the case where $\mathcal{P}$ alone is broken ($\mathrm{LiNbO_3}$) and the case where $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{T}$ are broken at the same time while $\mathcal{PT}$ remains ($\mathrm{Cr_2O_3}$). This contrast shows well how important it is to distinguish carefully which symmetries are broken.

Meaning. What we did in this exercise was to decide whether a physical property is allowed from the point-group symbol alone, without any first-principles calculation or experiment. Moreover, the only basis was Theorem 6.1, the same theorem used in particle physics to conclude parity violation from $\braket{\bm{J}\cdot\bm{p}_e}\neq0$. As Table 6.9 in Chapter 6 of this book shows, the Wu experiment and SHG measurements are literally the same experiment in that both “measure whether the expectation value of a $\mathcal{P}$-odd quantity is zero or not.”

The practical benefits are also large. When a candidate for a new material appears, examining the magnetic point group first tells us, before any calculation, “whether an anomalous Hall effect appears,” “whether a magnetoelectric effect is allowed,” and “whether SHG appears.” We avoid wasting computational resources searching for forbidden properties; conversely, if we meet a situation in which “symmetry allows it but experiments do not see it,” that means the effect is dynamically small, which gives guidance on what should be improved. Symmetry decides strictly whether a quantity is zero or not, and dynamics decides its magnitude—the division of roles described in Exercise 6.1 applies directly in the practice of materials design.

Exercise 6.8: A $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric two-level system and exceptional points

Problem (restated)

The effective Hamiltonian of two coupled waveguides with balanced gain and loss is

$$ \mathcal{H}=\begin{pmatrix}\ii\gamma & \kappa\\ \kappa & -\ii\gamma\end{pmatrix} \qquad(\gamma,\kappa>0\ \text{real numbers}) $$

.

(1) Verify that $\mathcal{H}$ is not Hermitian but is $\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric ($\mathcal{P}=\sigma_x$ interchanges the two waveguides, and $\mathcal{T}=K$ takes the complex conjugate). That is, show that $(\sigma_x K)\mathcal{H}(\sigma_x K)^{-1}=\mathcal{H}$.

(2) Show that the eigenvalues are $E_\pm=\pm\sqrt{\kappa^2-\gamma^2}$, and verify that they are real for $\gamma<\kappa$ and purely imaginary for $\gamma>\kappa$.

(3) Show that at $\gamma=\kappa$ (the exceptional point) the two eigenvectors coalesce. Describe how this differs from the degeneracy of a Hermitian matrix.

(4) Let $\kappa=\gamma(1+\delta)$ ($\delta\ll1$), expand $E_\pm$, and show that the splitting of the eigenvalues is $\propto\sqrt{\delta}$. Explain why this is said to be advantageous for a sensor.

Solution

Strategy. The calculation is just a careful solution of a $2\times2$ matrix eigenvalue problem, but it is essential not to overlook the phenomenon peculiar to non-Hermitian matrices (the coalescence of eigenvectors). Since $\mathcal{PT}=\sigma_xK$ is an antilinear operator, when it acts on a matrix $A$ we have $(\sigma_xK)A(\sigma_xK)^{-1}=\sigma_xA^{*}\sigma_x$ (the same rule as in Exercise 6.4(1)).

(1) First we examine Hermiticity. The Hermitian conjugate is the operation of transposing and taking the complex conjugate, so

$$ \mathcal{H}^\dagger =\begin{pmatrix}\ii\gamma & \kappa\\ \kappa & -\ii\gamma\end{pmatrix}^{\dagger} =\begin{pmatrix}(\ii\gamma)^{*} & \kappa^{*}\\ \kappa^{*} & (-\ii\gamma)^{*}\end{pmatrix} =\begin{pmatrix}-\ii\gamma & \kappa\\ \kappa & +\ii\gamma\end{pmatrix} \neq\mathcal{H} $$

The signs of the diagonal elements are reversed (as long as $\gamma\neq0$). $\mathcal{H}$ is not Hermitian. Physically, $+\ii\gamma$ represents gain (the amplitude grows exponentially) and $-\ii\gamma$ represents loss (it decays); this corresponds to an open system in which probability is not conserved.

Next we verify $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry. We have $\sigma_x=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $\sigma_x^{-1}=\sigma_x$, and $K^{-1}=K$. From the conjugation rule for antilinear operators,

$$ (\sigma_xK)\mathcal{H}(\sigma_xK)^{-1} = \sigma_x\left(K\mathcal{H}K^{-1}\right)\sigma_x = \sigma_x\,\mathcal{H}^{*}\,\sigma_x $$

First we take the complex conjugate:

$$ \mathcal{H}^{*}=\begin{pmatrix}-\ii\gamma & \kappa\\ \kappa & +\ii\gamma\end{pmatrix} $$

Next we sandwich it between $\sigma_x$ on the left and right. Since $\sigma_xM\sigma_x$ exchanges rows and columns at the same time, for a $2\times2$ matrix the diagonal elements are exchanged with each other and the off-diagonal elements are exchanged with each other:

$$ \sigma_x\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\ c&d\end{pmatrix}\sigma_x =\begin{pmatrix}d&c\\ b&a\end{pmatrix} $$

Applying this, we obtain

$$ \sigma_x\mathcal{H}^{*}\sigma_x =\begin{pmatrix}+\ii\gamma & \kappa\\ \kappa & -\ii\gamma\end{pmatrix} =\mathcal{H} $$

$\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry holds. ∎ The mechanism is clear: $K$ changes the sign as $\ii\gamma\to-\ii\gamma$, and $\sigma_x$ exchanges the gain side and the loss side and restores the original. The very structure “gain and loss are balanced between left and right” is the content of $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry. This is nothing other than the discretization to two waveguides of the condition $n^{*}(-x)=n(x)$ in Section 6.6.4 of Chapter 6 of this book (the real part of the refractive index is an even function and the imaginary part is an odd function).

(2) The eigenvalue equation is $\det(\mathcal{H}-E\mathbb{1})=0$. First we record the invariants:

$$ \Tr\mathcal{H} = \ii\gamma+(-\ii\gamma) = 0, \qquad \det\mathcal{H} = (\ii\gamma)(-\ii\gamma)-\kappa^2 = \gamma^2-\kappa^2 $$

Since the characteristic equation of a $2\times2$ matrix is $E^2-(\Tr\mathcal{H})E+\det\mathcal{H}=0$,

$$ E^2 + (\gamma^2-\kappa^2) = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E^2 = \kappa^2-\gamma^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E_\pm = \pm\sqrt{\kappa^2-\gamma^2} $$

This is the desired result. Considering the cases separately:

  • $\gamma<\kappa$ ($\mathcal{PT}$-symmetric phase): Since $\kappa^2-\gamma^2>0$, $E_\pm$ are real. This is the phenomenon pointed out by Bender and Boettcher, that the eigenvalues are real even though the Hamiltonian is non-Hermitian. Physically, light goes back and forth between the two waveguides, beating, and gain and loss cancel on average.
  • $\gamma>\kappa$ ($\mathcal{PT}$-broken phase): Since $\kappa^2-\gamma^2<0$, $E_\pm=\pm\ii\sqrt{\gamma^2-\kappa^2}$, which are purely imaginary and moreover form a mutually complex-conjugate pair. One mode is amplified exponentially and the other decays exponentially. This is the state in which the coupling $\kappa$ is too weak for the light to go back and forth between the gain side and the loss side.

Why there are only these two possibilities, real eigenvalues and complex-conjugate pairs, is explained by the argument in Section 6.6.4 of Chapter 6 of this book. Since $[\mathcal{H},\mathcal{PT}]=0$ and $\mathcal{PT}$ is antilinear, applying $\mathcal{PT}$ to both sides of $\mathcal{H}\ket{\psi}=E\ket{\psi}$ gives $\mathcal{H}(\mathcal{PT}\ket{\psi})=E^{*}(\mathcal{PT}\ket{\psi})$. If the eigenvector itself is an eigenstate of $\mathcal{PT}$, then $E=E^{*}$, so the eigenvalue is real; otherwise $E$ and $E^{*}$ appear as a pair. The former is the symmetric phase and the latter is the broken phase.

(3) Substituting $\gamma=\kappa$, we obtain

$$ \mathcal{H}_{\text{EP}}=\gamma\begin{pmatrix}\ii&1\\ 1&-\ii\end{pmatrix} $$

. Since both the trace and the determinant are zero ($\det=\gamma^2-\gamma^2=0$), the eigenvalue is the double root $E_+=E_-=0$. Let us find the eigenvectors. Writing $\mathcal{H}_{\text{EP}}\bm{v}=0$ in components,

$$ \ii\gamma v_1 + \gamma v_2 = 0, \qquad \gamma v_1 - \ii\gamma v_2 = 0 $$

The first equation gives $v_2=-\ii v_1$. Substituting into the second gives $\gamma v_1-\ii\gamma(-\ii v_1)=\gamma v_1-\gamma v_1=0$, which is identically satisfied. The two equations that should be there are effectively only one. Therefore the eigenvector is

$$ \bm{v} \propto \begin{pmatrix}1\\ -\ii\end{pmatrix} $$

—only one—and the eigenspace is only one-dimensional. As a matrix, it is a defective matrix: its algebraic multiplicity is $2$ but its geometric multiplicity is $1$. Indeed, the rank of $\mathcal{H}_{\text{EP}}$ is $1$ (the two rows are proportional).

Finding the eigenvectors for general $\gamma<\kappa$ makes the way they coalesce easy to see. Let $\gamma=\kappa\sin\theta$ ($0\le\theta<\pi/2$); then $E_\pm=\pm\kappa\cos\theta$, and the eigenvectors are

$$ \bm{v}_\pm \propto \begin{pmatrix}1\\ \pm\ee^{\mp\ii\theta}\end{pmatrix} \qquad\left(\text{second component}=\frac{E_\pm-\ii\gamma}{\kappa}\right) $$

. In the limit $\theta\to\pi/2$ (that is, $\gamma\to\kappa$), $\ee^{-\ii\theta}\to-\ii$ and $-\ee^{+\ii\theta}\to-\ii$, so the two eigenvectors are sucked into the same vector $(1,-\ii)^{T}$. This is the exceptional point (EP).

Difference from degeneracy of Hermitian matrices. For a Hermitian matrix (or, in general, a normal matrix), even when eigenvalues are degenerate, there always exist as many independent eigenvectors as the degeneracy, and they can be chosen mutually orthogonal. For example, the $2\times2$ zero matrix $\mathcal{H}=0$ has the double eigenvalue $0$, but its eigenspace is two-dimensional and any two orthogonal vectors serve as eigenvectors. A spectral decomposition is always possible, and the matrix can always be diagonalized.

In contrast, at an EP not only the eigenvalues but even the eigenvectors coalesce into one. Since the eigenvectors cannot span a basis, the matrix is not diagonalizable and can be brought only to Jordan normal form (the form $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$). This is a phenomenon peculiar to non-Hermitian systems that never occurs in Hermitian systems. It is closer to the truth to call it a “branch point” than a “degeneracy point”; as we see in (4), the eigenvalues behave as a $\sqrt{\ }$ branch point.

(4) We substitute $\kappa=\gamma(1+\delta)$ into the expression for the eigenvalues.

$$ E_\pm = \pm\sqrt{\kappa^2-\gamma^2} = \pm\sqrt{\gamma^2(1+\delta)^2-\gamma^2} = \pm\gamma\sqrt{(1+\delta)^2-1} $$

Expanding the inside of the square root, $(1+\delta)^2-1=1+2\delta+\delta^2-1=2\delta+\delta^2$, so

$$ E_\pm = \pm\gamma\sqrt{2\delta+\delta^2} = \pm\gamma\sqrt{2\delta}\sqrt{1+\frac{\delta}{2}} $$

For $\delta\ll1$, expanding $\sqrt{1+\delta/2}\approx1+\delta/4$ gives

$$ E_\pm \approx \pm\gamma\sqrt{2\delta}\left(1+\frac{\delta}{4}\right) = \pm\left[\gamma\sqrt{2\delta}+\frac{\gamma\delta}{4}\sqrt{2\delta}\right]+\cdots $$

Therefore, to lowest order,

$$ \boxed{\ E_\pm \approx \pm\gamma\sqrt{2\delta}\ }, \qquad \Delta E \equiv E_+-E_- = 2\gamma\sqrt{2\delta}\ \propto\ \sqrt{\delta} $$

The splitting is proportional to the $1/2$ power of the perturbation.

Why it is advantageous as a sensor. In an ordinary Hermitian system, when a perturbation of magnitude $\epsilon$ is applied to a degenerate two-level system, first-order perturbation theory gives a splitting $\Delta E\propto\epsilon$, which is linear. Near an EP, however, $\Delta E\propto\sqrt{\epsilon}$. In the regime $\epsilon\ll1$ we have $\sqrt{\epsilon}\gg\epsilon$, so the response to a tiny perturbation becomes larger than usual by orders of magnitude.

Let us get a feel for the numbers. For $\delta=10^{-4}$, a linear response would give a signal of only $10^{-4}$, but at an EP we get $\sqrt{2\delta}=1.41\times10^{-2}$, which is $141$ times larger. For $\delta=10^{-6}$, $\sqrt{2\delta}=1.41\times10^{-3}$, and the ratio widens to $1414$ times. The smaller the perturbation, the greater the advantage; this is the appeal as a sensor. Experiments have been reported in which a microtoroid resonator is tuned to an EP and the tiny perturbation caused by a single nanoparticle or virus attached to its surface is read out as a mode splitting.

A caveat is necessary, however. Near an EP the eigenvectors become degenerate and lose orthogonality, so noise is amplified at the same time. Whether there is a true gain in the sense of the signal-to-noise ratio is a point that requires careful discussion, as we note here (Section 6.6.4 of Chapter 6 of this book carries a caveat to the same effect).

Verification. We check from three angles.

First, we confirm the eigenvalues with concrete numbers. For $\kappa=1$ and $\gamma=0.6$, $E_\pm=\pm\sqrt{1-0.36}=\pm\sqrt{0.64}=\pm0.8$, which is indeed real. For $\gamma=1.4$, $E_\pm=\pm\sqrt{1-1.96}=\pm\ii\sqrt{0.96}=\pm0.980\,\ii$, which is indeed a purely imaginary conjugate pair. This agrees with the case analysis in (2).

Second, we check the relation between $\mathcal{PT}$ symmetry and the eigenvectors. For $\gamma=0.6,\kappa=1$ (that is, $\sin\theta=0.6$, $\cos\theta=0.8$), the eigenvector for $E_+=0.8$ is $\bm{v}_+\propto(1,\ \ee^{-\ii\theta})=(1,\ 0.8-0.6\ii)$. Acting on it with $\mathcal{PT}=\sigma_xK$ gives $\sigma_x(1,\ 0.8+0.6\ii)^{T}=(0.8+0.6\ii,\ 1)^{T}$, which equals $(0.8+0.6\ii)\times(1,\ 0.8-0.6\ii)^{T}$ (we used $(0.8+0.6\ii)(0.8-0.6\ii)=0.64+0.36=1$). The eigenvector is indeed an eigenstate of $\mathcal{PT}$ (with eigenvalue a phase factor of absolute value $1$), and that is why the eigenvalue is real. On the other hand, trying the same thing in the broken phase $\gamma>\kappa$, $\mathcal{PT}$ maps one eigenvector to the other and so it is not an eigenstate. The general argument given in (2) has thus been confirmed concretely.

Third, we compare the expansion in (4) with the exact expression. For $\delta=10^{-4}$ and $\gamma=1$, the exact value is $E_+=\sqrt{2\times10^{-4}+10^{-8}}=1.41425\times10^{-2}$, while the approximate expression gives $\sqrt{2\delta}=1.41421\times10^{-2}$, so the relative difference is $2.5\times10^{-5}$ (that is, $\delta/4$). This agrees with the fact that the next term of the expansion is a relative correction of $\delta/4$, so the calculation contains no error.

Meaning. This problem is the most concrete appearance of the keyword “$\mathcal{PT}$” that has appeared many times throughout Chapter 6 of this book. And what is important is that exactly the same mathematics also appears in particle physics. The effective Hamiltonian of the neutral $K$ meson that we saw in Section 6.4.5 of Chapter 6 of this book,

$$ \mathcal{H}_{\text{eff}} = M-\frac{\ii}{2}\Gamma $$

is a $2\times2$ matrix of exactly the same type as $\mathcal{H}$ in this problem: $M$ and $\Gamma$ are both Hermitian but their combination is non-Hermitian. The structure is also common in that the difference of the real parts of the eigenvalues gives the oscillation frequency ($\Delta m$) and the difference of the imaginary parts gives the difference of decay rates ($\Delta\Gamma$). The $K^0$–$\bar K^0$ oscillation that we solved in Exercise 6.5 and the beat between the two waveguides in this problem are merely different faces of the same equation.

On the materials science side, this framework is spreading rapidly. Exciton polaritons, dissipative cavity QED, acoustic metamaterials, $RLC$ circuits, the non-Hermitian skin effect, and the complex winding number of topological bands—all share the same starting point, that “the effective Hamiltonian of an open system becomes non-Hermitian.” Bender and Boettcher’s observation that Hermiticity is a sufficient condition for real eigenvalues but not a necessary one has created a field in a little over twenty years. The training in thinking of $\mathcal{P}$ and $\mathcal{T}$ separately in particle physics becomes, just as it is, a tool for non-Hermitian physics.

E.7 Solutions for Chapter 7: Bound States — From Hydrogen to Hadrons

Exercise 7.1: Calculating the fine-structure splitting

Problem (restated)

Use the fine-structure formula of Chapter 7 of this book. Take $\alpha^2 = 5.3251\times10^{-5}$ and $\mathrm{Ry}=13.606\ \mathrm{eV}$.

(1) Find the fine-structure correction for $n=1$ ($1S_{1/2}$) in eV. What is the energy of the ground state including the correction?

(2) The $n=3$ level splits into three levels, $j=1/2,3/2,5/2$. Find the energy difference between $3D_{5/2}$ and $3P_{1/2}$ in GHz.

(3) State how the size of the fine structure scales with $n$ (the ratio of the maximum splittings for $n=2$ and $n=3$).

Solution

Strategy. We simply apply the fine-structure formula derived in Chapter 7 of this book,

$$ E_{nj} = E_n\left[1 + \frac{\alpha^2}{n^2}\left(\frac{n}{j+\tfrac12}-\frac34\right)\right], \qquad E_n = -\frac{\mathrm{Ry}}{n^2} $$

mechanically. There are three key points. First, the correction term depends on neither $\ell$ nor $s$; it is a function of the total angular momentum $j$ alone (this is the result of the $\ell$ dependences of the relativistic correction, the spin–orbit coupling, and the Darwin term canceling one another). Second, since $E_n$ itself is negative, if the content of the square brackets is positive, the correction is downward (in the direction of deeper binding). Third, to convert an energy into a frequency we divide by the Planck constant $h = 4.13567\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}$. We use these three points repeatedly below.

(1) For $n=1$ only $\ell=0$ exists, so there is only the single level $j=1/2$. The correction part inside the square brackets is

$$ \frac{\alpha^2}{n^2}\left(\frac{n}{j+\tfrac12}-\frac34\right) = \frac{5.3251\times10^{-5}}{1}\left(\frac{1}{1}-\frac34\right) = 5.3251\times10^{-5}\times 0.25 = 1.3313\times10^{-5} $$

Multiplying by $E_1 = -13.606\ \mathrm{eV}$, the correction due to the fine structure is

$$ \Delta E_{1,\,1/2} = E_1\times1.3313\times10^{-5} = -13.606\times1.3313\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV} = -1.8113\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV} $$

Since it is negative, the ground state becomes slightly deeper. The energy including the correction is

$$ E(1S_{1/2}) = -13.606 - 0.00018113 = -13.606181\ \mathrm{eV} $$

That is, the effect is of a size that first shows up in the sixth significant figure, and its relative size is $1.33\times10^{-5}$, which is of the order of $\alpha^2$ itself. Converted to a frequency, it corresponds to $1.8113\times10^{-4}/4.13567\times10^{-15} = 4.38\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{Hz} = 43.8\ \mathrm{GHz}$. Note that for $n=1$ there is no partner level to split from, so this is not a “splitting width” but a shift of the whole Bohr level.

(2) For $n=3$ we have $\ell=0,1,2$, and hence three levels, $j=1/2,3/2,5/2$. First we prepare the common factors:

$$ E_3 = -\frac{13.606}{9} = -1.51178\ \mathrm{eV}, \qquad \frac{\alpha^2}{n^2} = \frac{5.3251\times10^{-5}}{9} = 5.9168\times10^{-6} $$

Next we compute $\left(\dfrac{n}{j+\frac12}-\dfrac34\right)$ in the square brackets for each $j$:

$$ j=\tfrac12:\ \frac{3}{1}-\frac34 = 2.25, \qquad j=\tfrac32:\ \frac{3}{2}-\frac34 = 0.75, \qquad j=\tfrac52:\ \frac{3}{3}-\frac34 = 0.25 $$

Therefore the correction for each level is

$$ \Delta E(3P_{1/2}) = -1.51178\times5.9168\times10^{-6}\times2.25 = -2.0126\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV} $$ $$ \Delta E(3D_{5/2}) = -1.51178\times5.9168\times10^{-6}\times0.25 = -2.2362\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{eV} $$

The required difference is

$$ E(3D_{5/2})-E(3P_{1/2}) = (-2.2362\times10^{-6})-(-2.0126\times10^{-5}) = 1.7890\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV} $$

and $3D_{5/2}$ is higher (the larger $j$ is, the smaller the correction, and the higher the level lies). Converted to a frequency,

$$ \nu = \frac{1.7890\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV}}{4.13567\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}} = 4.326\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{Hz} = 4.33\ \mathrm{GHz} $$

In terms of wavelength, $c/\nu = 6.9\ \mathrm{cm}$, a microwave, and the frequency is lower than the $10.95\ \mathrm{GHz}$ (wavelength $2.7\ \mathrm{cm}$) for $n=2$.

(3) For general $n$, the maximum splitting width is the difference between the smallest value of $j$, $1/2$, and the largest value, $n-1/2$. Taking the difference of the square brackets gives

$$ \left(\frac{n}{1}-\frac34\right)-\left(\frac{n}{n}-\frac34\right) = n-1 $$

so the $3/4$ term cancels in the difference. Therefore

$$ \Delta E_{\max}(n) = \abs{E_n}\frac{\alpha^2}{n^2}(n-1) = \mathrm{Ry}\,\alpha^2\,\frac{n-1}{n^4} $$

Taking the ratio for $n=2$ and $n=3$,

$$ \frac{\Delta E_{\max}(2)}{\Delta E_{\max}(3)} = \frac{(2-1)/2^4}{(3-1)/3^4} = \frac{1/16}{2/81} = \frac{81}{32} = 2.53125 $$

Let us also check this numerically. For $n=2$, $\Delta E_{\max} = 13.606\times5.3251\times10^{-5}\times1/16 = 4.5283\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV}$ ($= 10.95\ \mathrm{GHz}$), and for $n=3$ it is the $1.7890\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV}$ obtained in (2). The ratio is $4.5283/1.7890 = 2.531$, in complete agreement with the formula.

For large $n$, $\Delta E_{\max}\simeq \mathrm{Ry}\,\alpha^2/n^3$, which shrinks as $n^{-3}$, one power faster than the level spacing $\abs{E_n}\propto n^{-2}$. That is, the higher the level, the smaller the fine structure, in both absolute and relative terms. This is why the fine structure is hard to see in Rydberg states.

Verification. We check the dimensions and the order of magnitude independently. The fine structure is a quantity of order $O(\alpha^4 m_e)$, with $\alpha^4m_ec^2 = 1.449\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}$. On the other hand, the $n=1$ correction $1.81\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}$ obtained in (1) agrees exactly with $\alpha^4m_ec^2/8 = 1.81\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}$. Indeed, $\mathrm{Ry}\,\alpha^2 = \tfrac12\alpha^2m_ec^2\times\alpha^2 = \tfrac12\alpha^4m_ec^2$, and multiplying this by $0.25$ gives $\tfrac18\alpha^4 m_ec^2$. The same number came out of an order-of-magnitude estimate without going through the formula. Furthermore, the $n=2$ value $10.95\ \mathrm{GHz}$ from (3) agrees to within $0.2\%$ with the numerical example in Chapter 7 of this book and with the measured value $10.969\ \mathrm{GHz}$, which confirms that the calculation path is correct.

Meaning. The fine structure leaves behind a strong degeneracy in which “levels are distinguished only by $j$.” For the same $n$ and the same $j$, the energy is exactly the same even if $\ell$ differs (for example, $2S_{1/2}$ and $2P_{1/2}$). What breaks this remaining degeneracy is the Lamb shift, that is, the quantum fluctuations of the vacuum, which is the subject of Exercise 7.2. The attitude of reading hierarchically “which degeneracy is broken by which physics” is exactly the same as the way crystal-field splitting is read in materials science. A cubic-symmetry field splits the $d$ orbitals into $t_{2g}$ and $e_g$, and a Jahn–Teller distortion then splits $t_{2g}$ further. The structure in which a new interaction makes its appearance at each step is shared with the hydrogen atom.

Exercise 7.2: Vacuum polarization and the Lamb shift

Problem (restated)

Use the Uehling potential of Chapter 7 of this book.

(1) Find the vacuum-polarization shift of the hydrogen $1S$ state in MHz. How does it depend on $n$?

(2) The shift due to the finite size of the proton is given by $\Delta E = \tfrac{2\pi\alpha}{3}r_p^2\abs{\psi(0)}^2$ (because the Coulomb potential becomes shallower inside the proton). Taking $r_p = 0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$, find the shift of the hydrogen $2S$ state in MHz.

(3) Find the same quantity for muonic hydrogen ($\mu^-p$). Note that with $\mu\to185.8\,m_e$, $\abs{\psi(0)}^2$ is multiplied by $(185.8)^3$. Explain why muonic hydrogen is used for the precise determination of $r_p$.

Solution

Strategy. (1) and (2) have the same form. In both, the effective potential is a contact term of the $\delta^3(\bm{r})$ type, and the expectation value merely picks out $\abs{\psi(0)}^2$. As in Chapter 7 of this book,

$$ \abs{\psi_{n00}(0)}^2 = \frac{1}{\pi n^3 a^3}, \qquad a = \frac{1}{\mu\alpha} $$

and since $\psi(0)=0$ for $\ell\ne0$, it acts only on $s$ waves. We compute in natural units ($\hbar=c=1$) and at the end convert to practical units with $\hbar c = 0.197327\ \mathrm{GeV\,fm}$ and $h = 4.13567\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}$. The key point is that the expectation value of a contact term is proportional to the cube of the reduced mass through $\abs{\psi(0)}^2\propto\mu^3$. Part (3) comes down to this single point.

(1) The Uehling term was

$$ \delta V_{\text{VP}}(\bm{r}) = -\frac{4\alpha^2}{15\,m_e^2}\,\delta^3(\bm{r}) $$

We take the expectation value. Since $\mu\simeq m_e$ and $a = 1/(m_e\alpha)$, we have $\abs{\psi_{n00}(0)}^2 = m_e^3\alpha^3/(\pi n^3)$, and

$$ \Delta E_{\text{VP}} = -\frac{4\alpha^2}{15 m_e^2}\cdot\frac{m_e^3\alpha^3}{\pi n^3} = -\frac{4}{15\pi}\,\frac{\alpha^5 m_e}{n^3} $$

We use $\alpha^5m_ec^2 = 1.05742\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV}$ and the coefficient $4/(15\pi) = 0.084883$. For $n=1$,

$$ \Delta E_{\text{VP}}(1S) = -0.084883\times1.05742\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV} = -8.9756\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{eV} $$ $$ \nu = \frac{8.9756\times10^{-7}}{4.13567\times10^{-15}} = 2.170\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{Hz} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \Delta E_{\text{VP}}(1S) = -217.0\ \mathrm{MHz} $$

The $n$ dependence follows immediately from the form of the expression: $\Delta E_{\text{VP}}\propto n^{-3}$. This is simply $\abs{\psi_{n00}(0)}^2\propto n^{-3}$, a dependence common to all contact-type interactions. As a check, for $n=2$ we get $-217.0/8 = -27.1\ \mathrm{MHz}$, which agrees with the $2S$ value in Chapter 7 of this book.

We should also confirm that the sign is negative, that is, that vacuum polarization lowers the $s$-wave levels. The virtual $e^+e^-$ pairs of the vacuum screen the nuclear charge, so the closer one approaches the nucleus, the more the screening is stripped away and the bare charge becomes visible, which increases the attraction. Therefore, with respect to the $2S$–$2P_{1/2}$ Lamb shift ($2S$ above), vacuum polarization acts in the opposite direction. The main contributors that build up the net $+1058\ \mathrm{MHz}$ are the self-energy term ($+1010\ \mathrm{MHz}$) and the anomalous magnetic moment ($+68\ \mathrm{MHz}$), to which are added the higher-order corrections ($+7\ \mathrm{MHz}$) and the finite size of the proton ($+0.15\ \mathrm{MHz}$, calculated in (2)). As in Table 7.1 of Chapter 7 of this book, the sum is $1010+68+7-27.1+0.15 = 1058.1\ \mathrm{MHz}$, which agrees with the measured $1057.845(9)\ \mathrm{MHz}$. Keep in mind that vacuum polarization is the only contribution with a different sign.

(2) First let us confirm where the given formula comes from. If we regard the proton not as a point charge but as an extended charge distribution, the Coulomb potential inside it becomes shallower than $-\alpha/r$. The difference $\delta V = V_{\text{finite}}-V_{\text{point}}$ acts only inside the proton, so from the viewpoint of the scale of the electron wave function ($a_0\sim10^5\ \mathrm{fm}$) it is a perfect contact term. For a general charge distribution,

$$ \Delta E = \abs{\psi(0)}^2\int\dd^3r\,\delta V(\bm{r}) = \frac{2\pi\alpha}{3}\braket{r^2}\abs{\psi(0)}^2 $$

where $r_p^2\equiv\braket{r^2}$ is the mean-square charge radius. Substituting the expectation value gives

$$ \Delta E = \frac{2\pi\alpha}{3}\,r_p^2\cdot\frac{m_e^3\alpha^3}{\pi n^3} = \frac{2}{3}\,\frac{\alpha^4 m_e^3 r_p^2}{n^3} $$

which reproduces the form of the hint. Now we insert numbers. In natural units,

$$ r_p = 0.84\ \mathrm{fm} = \frac{0.84}{0.197327}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-1}} = 4.2569\ \mathrm{GeV^{-1}}, \qquad r_p^2 = 18.121\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}} $$ $$ m_e = 5.10999\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{GeV}, \qquad m_e^3 = 1.33434\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{GeV^3}, \qquad \alpha^4 = 2.83571\times10^{-9} $$

Substituting $n=2$,

$$ \Delta E = \frac{2}{3}\times\frac{2.83571\times10^{-9}\times1.33434\times10^{-10}\times18.121}{8}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 5.714\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$ $$ = 5.714\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{eV} = \frac{5.714\times10^{-10}}{4.13567\times10^{-15}}\ \mathrm{Hz} = 1.38\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{Hz} = 0.14\ \mathrm{MHz} $$

The sign is positive (shallower means weaker binding, which means the level rises). This corresponds to the “proton finite size $+0.15\ \mathrm{MHz}$” in Table 7.1 of Chapter 7 of this book. Its share of the total Lamb shift of $1058\ \mathrm{MHz}$ is $0.14/1058 = 1.3\times10^{-4}$, that is, only one part in ten thousand.

(3) For muonic hydrogen the reduced mass is

$$ \mu = \frac{m_\mu m_p}{m_\mu+m_p} = \frac{105.658\times938.272}{105.658+938.272}\ \mathrm{MeV} = 94.96\ \mathrm{MeV} = 185.8\,m_e $$

Since the contact term is proportional to $\abs{\psi(0)}^2\propto\mu^3$, the shift is simply multiplied by $(185.8)^3 = 6.414\times10^{6}$:

$$ \Delta E(\mu^-p,\ 2S) = 5.714\times10^{-10}\times6.414\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV} = 3.665\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV} = 3.67\ \mathrm{meV} $$ $$ \nu = \frac{3.665\times10^{-3}}{4.13567\times10^{-15}} = 8.86\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{Hz} = 0.89\ \mathrm{THz} $$

What is essential here is that not only does the absolute value grow by a factor of $6.4\times10^{6}$, but its share of the splitting being measured jumps up. The $2S$–$2P_{1/2}$ splitting (Lamb shift) of muonic hydrogen is about $202\ \mathrm{meV}$, of which the proton-size term accounts for $3.7\ \mathrm{meV}$, that is, $1.8\%$. In ordinary hydrogen it is only $0.14/1058 = 0.013\%$. Taking the ratio,

$$ \frac{1.8\ \%}{0.013\ \%} \simeq 1.4\times10^{2} $$

so with spectroscopy of the same relative precision, $r_p^2$ is determined about $10^2$ times more precisely. The physical reason is simple: the muon Bohr radius $a_\mu = a_0/185.8 = 285\ \mathrm{fm}$ comes closer to the proton radius $0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$ by a factor of nearly $200$, so the fraction of time the muon spends inside the proton is larger by orders of magnitude.

Indeed, the muonic-hydrogen laser spectroscopy of Pohl et al. in $2010$ gave $r_p = 0.8418\ \mathrm{fm}$, which disagreed at the $5\sigma$ level with the CODATA value $0.8768\ \mathrm{fm}$ then based on ordinary hydrogen and electron scattering. This is the proton radius puzzle. Subsequently, new $2S$–$4P$ spectroscopy of ordinary hydrogen and reanalyses of electron scattering supported the smaller value, and the currently recommended value has moved toward the muonic-hydrogen side.

Verification. We check in three ways. First, the $n=2$ value $-27.1\ \mathrm{MHz}$ in (1) agrees with the derivation in Chapter 7 of this book and with the literature value. Second, we compare the result of (2) with an empirical formula from the literature. The finite-size term of muonic hydrogen is known to be $\Delta E = 5.226\,r_p^2\ \mathrm{meV\,fm^{-2}}$, and for $r_p=0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$ this gives $5.226\times0.7056 = 3.69\ \mathrm{meV}$. The nonrelativistic calculation of this problem, $3.67\ \mathrm{meV}$, agrees to within $0.6\%$. Third, we look at the dimensions. $\alpha^4m_e^3r_p^2$ has dimensions $[\text{mass}]^3\times[\text{length}]^2 = [\text{mass}]^3[\text{mass}]^{-2} = [\text{mass}]$, which indeed is the dimension of energy.

Meaning. The lesson of this exercise comes down to a single phrase: “push the probe’s wave function into the object you want to measure.” Since the contact term is proportional to $\abs{\psi(0)}^2\propto\mu^3$, using a heavy probe makes the sensitivity grow as the cube. Examples in which exactly the same logic operates in materials science are $\mu$SR (muon spin rotation) and Mössbauer spectroscopy. The Mössbauer isomer shift is $\delta\propto\abs{\psi(0)}^2\Delta\braket{r_N^2}$, reading out the change in nuclear radius through the electron density. That only $s$ electrons contribute, and that the “internal structure” of nuclear size is read by spectroscopy, are both the same structure as in this problem. The proton radius puzzle of particle physics and the Mössbauer measurement that determines the oxidation state of Fe are different uses of the same formula.

Exercise 7.3: Positronium lifetimes and annihilation channels

Problem (restated)

(1) Starting from $\Gamma(\text{para}) = \tfrac12\alpha^5 m_e$, find the lifetime in ps ($\hbar = 6.582\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}$).

(2) What is the annihilation lifetime of para-Ps with $n=2$ ($2^1S_0$)? Use $\abs{\psi_{n00}(0)}^2\propto n^{-3}$.

(3) When a magnetic field is applied, the $m=0$ component of $1^3S_1$ mixes with $1^1S_0$, and part of the ortho state comes to decay into $2\gamma$ (magnetic quenching). Let $\theta$ be the mixing angle, and explain why the $2\gamma$ decay rate of the mixed state is $\Gamma_{2\gamma}\sin^2\theta$. Then explain why this is an effect similar to the shortening of the lifetime of o-Ps in matter (pick-off annihilation).

(4) Using the $C$ quantum number, state in one line why para-Ps cannot decay into $3\gamma$ and ortho-Ps cannot decay into $2\gamma$.

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1) and (2) are simply unit conversion and scaling. The single fact that the annihilation rate is proportional to $\abs{\psi(0)}^2$ settles (2). Part (3) is the mixing of a two-level system, the tool used most often in quantum mechanics. The key point is the selection rule that “only the singlet component has an amplitude to the $2\gamma$ final state,” which is nothing other than the $C$ conservation of (4). That is, (3) and (4) are two sides of the same physics.

(1) As in Chapter 7 of this book,

$$ \Gamma(\text{para}) = 4\pi\frac{\alpha^2}{m_e^2}\abs{\psi(0)}^2 = \frac{1}{2}\alpha^5 m_e $$

First let us check how the right-hand side follows from the middle expression. The Bohr radius of Ps is fixed by the reduced mass $\mu = m_e/2$, so $a_{\text{Ps}} = 1/(\mu\alpha) = 2/(m_e\alpha)$, which is $2$ times larger than for hydrogen. Therefore

$$ \abs{\psi_{100}(0)}^2 = \frac{1}{\pi a_{\text{Ps}}^3} = \frac{1}{\pi}\left(\frac{m_e\alpha}{2}\right)^3 = \frac{\alpha^3m_e^3}{8\pi} $$

Substituting this gives

$$ 4\pi\frac{\alpha^2}{m_e^2}\cdot\frac{\alpha^3m_e^3}{8\pi} = \frac{4}{8}\,\alpha^5m_e = \frac12\alpha^5m_e $$

which indeed agrees. The same structure as the contact term of Exercise 7.2 is at work here: the annihilation rate picks up $\abs{\psi(0)}^2\propto\mu^3$. Next we insert numbers. Since $\alpha^5 m_ec^2 = (7.29735\times10^{-3})^5\times5.10999\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.05742\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV}$,

$$ \Gamma = \frac12\times1.05742\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV} = 5.2871\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{eV} $$

The lifetime is $\tau = \hbar/\Gamma$ (in natural units $\tau = 1/\Gamma$; when we return to practical units, $\hbar$ appears):

$$ \tau(\text{para}) = \frac{6.582\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}}{5.2871\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{eV}} = 1.2449\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{s} = 124.5\ \mathrm{ps} $$

This agrees with the measured $125.14(2)\ \mathrm{ps}$ to $0.5\%$. The residual is explained by the $O(\alpha)$ QED correction. The one-loop correction for para-Ps is

$$ \Gamma = \Gamma_0\left[1-\left(5-\frac{\pi^2}{4}\right)\frac{\alpha}{\pi}+\cdots\right], \qquad 5-\frac{\pi^2}{4} = 2.5326 $$

Since $\alpha/\pi = 2.3228\times10^{-3}$, the correction is $2.5326\times2.3228\times10^{-3} = 5.883\times10^{-3}$; that is, it lowers $\Gamma$ by $0.59\%$ and lengthens the lifetime by the same amount:

$$ \tau = \frac{124.49\ \mathrm{ps}}{1-5.883\times10^{-3}} = 125.23\ \mathrm{ps} $$

The difference from the measured $125.14\ \mathrm{ps}$ shrinks to $0.07\%$. Adding just one power of $\alpha$ reduced the discrepancy by a factor of $7$, confirming that the perturbative expansion works as expected. Incidentally, the breakdown of the exponent in $\Gamma\propto\alpha^5$ is the product of $\abs{\psi(0)}^2\propto(\mu\alpha)^3$ (the strength of the binding) and the factor $\alpha^2$ on the annihilation cross-section side (two photon vertices).

(2) Annihilation requires the $e^+$ and the $e^-$ to be at the same point, so the decay rate is always proportional to $\abs{\psi(0)}^2$. On the other hand, $\abs{\psi_{n00}(0)}^2 = 1/(\pi n^3 a_{\text{Ps}}^3)\propto n^{-3}$. The factor $\alpha^2/m_e^2$ (the part that comes from the annihilation cross section of a free $e^+e^-$ pair) does not depend on the details of the bound state, so the ratio is simply

$$ \frac{\Gamma(2^1S_0)}{\Gamma(1^1S_0)} = \frac{\abs{\psi_{200}(0)}^2}{\abs{\psi_{100}(0)}^2} = \frac{2^{-3}}{1^{-3}} = \frac{1}{8} $$

Therefore

$$ \tau(2^1S_0) = 8\times124.5\ \mathrm{ps} = 996\ \mathrm{ps} \simeq 1.0\ \mathrm{ns} $$

Incidentally, by the same logic, for ortho with $n=2$ we get $8\times138.7\ \mathrm{ns} = 1.11\ \mu\mathrm{s}$. Note also that the $2S$ state is a metastable state for which the electric dipole transition to $1S$ is forbidden, and since the path of falling to $1S$ by radiative decay is suppressed, this “pure annihilation lifetime” is the quantity that is actually observed.

(3) Origin of the mixing. In a uniform magnetic field $\bm{B} = B\hat{z}$, the Zeeman term acting on the spin of Ps is

$$ H_Z = -(\bm{\mu}_{e^-}+\bm{\mu}_{e^+})\cdot\bm{B} = g\mu_B B\left(S_z^{(-)}-S_z^{(+)}\right) $$

Since the $e^-$ and $e^+$ have opposite charges, their magnetic moments have opposite signs, and the crucial point is that the difference of the two spin operators appears. The difference operator is antisymmetric under exchange of the two particles, so it connects the symmetric triplet and the antisymmetric singlet. Indeed,

$$ \left(S_z^{(-)}-S_z^{(+)}\right)\ket{\uparrow\downarrow} = +\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}, \qquad \left(S_z^{(-)}-S_z^{(+)}\right)\ket{\downarrow\uparrow} = -\ket{\downarrow\uparrow} $$

so for $\ket{1,0} = (\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}+\ket{\downarrow\uparrow})/\sqrt2$ and $\ket{0,0} = (\ket{\uparrow\downarrow}-\ket{\downarrow\uparrow})/\sqrt2$ we have

$$ \bra{0,0}H_Z\ket{1,0} = g\mu_B B $$

The triplet components with $m=\pm1$ have no partner and therefore do not mix. In the two-dimensional subspace $\{\ket{1,0},\ket{0,0}\}$ the Hamiltonian is the $2\times2$ matrix

$$ H = \begin{pmatrix} E_t & g\mu_B B \\ g\mu_B B & E_s \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \Delta E_{\text{hf}} = E_t-E_s = \tfrac{7}{12}\alpha^4m_e $$

and the eigenstate can be written as

$$ \ket{+} = \cos\theta\ket{1,0}+\sin\theta\ket{0,0}, \qquad \tan2\theta = \frac{2g\mu_B B}{\Delta E_{\text{hf}}} = \frac{4\mu_B B}{\Delta E_{\text{hf}}}\quad(g=2) $$

Here $\theta$ is the required mixing angle.

Why the decay rate is proportional to $\sin^2\theta$. The $2\gamma$ final state has $C=+1$. Since the electromagnetic interaction conserves $C$, the matrix element of the transition operator $T_{2\gamma}$ is nonzero only from an initial state with $C=+1$:

$$ \bra{2\gamma}T\ket{1,0} = 0 \qquad(\because\ C(\ket{1,0})=-1), \qquad \bra{2\gamma}T\ket{0,0} \ne 0 $$

Therefore the amplitude of the mixed state is

$$ \bra{2\gamma}T\ket{+} = \cos\theta\underbrace{\bra{2\gamma}T\ket{1,0}}_{=0} + \sin\theta\,\bra{2\gamma}T\ket{0,0} = \sin\theta\,\bra{2\gamma}T\ket{0,0} $$

and since the rate is the square of the amplitude,

$$ \Gamma_{2\gamma}(\ket{+}) = \abs{\sin\theta}^2\,\Gamma_{2\gamma}(\text{para}) = \Gamma_{2\gamma}\sin^2\theta $$

follows. Since the $2\gamma$ and $3\gamma$ final states are orthogonal, they do not interfere, and the total decay rate is simply the sum $\Gamma = \sin^2\theta\,\Gamma_{2\gamma}+\cos^2\theta\,\Gamma_{3\gamma}$.

Inserting numbers. With $\mu_B = 5.7884\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/T}$ and $\Delta E_{\text{hf}} = 8.453\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}$, at $B=1\ \mathrm{T}$

$$ \tan2\theta = \frac{4\times5.7884\times10^{-5}}{8.453\times10^{-4}} = 0.2739 \ \Longrightarrow\ \theta = 0.1337\ \mathrm{rad}, \quad \sin^2\theta = 1.78\times10^{-2} $$ $$ \Gamma = 0.0178\times\frac{1}{124.5\ \mathrm{ps}}+0.9822\times\frac{1}{138.7\ \mathrm{ns}} \ \Longrightarrow\ \tau = 6.7\ \mathrm{ns} $$

With only $1.8\%$ of singlet admixture, the lifetime shrinks by a factor of $20$, from $138.7\ \mathrm{ns}$ to $6.7\ \mathrm{ns}$. This is because the decay rate of the singlet is $1100$ times larger.

Analogy with pickoff annihilation. In matter, the $e^+$ in an o-Ps meets and annihilates with a wall electron instead of its partner $e^-$. In this case the spin states of the $e^+$ and the external electron are uncorrelated, so statistically the pair is in a singlet configuration with probability $1/4$, and that configuration disappears rapidly into $2\gamma$. That is,

$$ \Gamma_{\text{pick-off}} \simeq \frac14\,\Gamma_{2\gamma}^{\text{free}}\times(\text{overlap with the wall electron density}) $$

In magnetic quenching, a singlet component $\sin^2\theta$ arises in the internal state with the same partner, whereas in pickoff a singlet component $1/4$ arises in the combination with a different partner. The origins differ, but in both cases the effect is that “the fast $2\gamma$ channel opens through a small singlet weight,” and it appears in the same form as a shortening of the observed o-Ps lifetime. What the Tao–Eldrup formula (Exercise 7.4) gives as a function of the void radius $R$ is precisely this “overlap” part.

(4) A state of $n$ photons has $C = (-1)^n$, and an $e^+e^-$ bound state has $C = (-1)^{L+S}$. For $1S$, $C(\text{para}) = (-1)^{0+0} = +1 = C(2\gamma)$ and $C(\text{ortho}) = (-1)^{0+1} = -1 = C(3\gamma)$, and since the electromagnetic interaction conserves $C$, para can decay only into an even number of photons and ortho only into an odd number (the $1\gamma$ decay of ortho is forbidden by momentum conservation, so the minimum is $3\gamma$).

Let us fill in what lies behind this one line. $C(\gamma)=-1$ because the electromagnetic field couples to the current $j^\mu$, and $C$ reverses the sign of the electric charge so that $j^\mu\to-j^\mu$. Hence an $n$-photon system has $(-1)^n$. On the other hand, $C=(-1)^{L+S}$ for a fermion–antifermion pair follows from the fact that the operation of exchanging particle and antiparticle is the product of “spatial inversion $(-1)^L$,” “exchange of the spins $(-1)^{S+1}$,” and “the sign of fermion exchange $(-1)$” (Chapter 6). The product is $(-1)^{L+S+2}=(-1)^{L+S}$.

In other words, the selection rule of this problem asserts that the discrete symmetry $C$ alone completely separates the two decay channels, and the lifetime difference of one power of $\alpha$ (the factor of $1100$) is merely a consequence of it. The degree of the prohibition is also constrained experimentally: an upper limit at the $10^{-6}$ level is placed on the $2\gamma$ branching ratio of o-Ps. Precisely because this separation is exact, the argument of (3) that “only the singlet admixture $\sin^2\theta$ opens $2\gamma$” holds, and in PALS the long-lived $\tau_3$ component can be identified as originating from o-Ps.

Verification. Let us derive the lifetime ratio independently of the $\Gamma$ of (1). The ratio of $\Gamma(\text{ortho}) = 0.06151\,\alpha^6m_e$ from Chapter 7 of this book to $\Gamma(\text{para}) = 0.5\,\alpha^5m_e$ is

$$ \frac{\tau_{\text{ortho}}}{\tau_{\text{para}}} = \frac{0.5}{0.06151\times\alpha} = \frac{0.5}{0.06151\times7.2974\times10^{-3}} = 1114 $$

so $124.5\ \mathrm{ps}\times1114 = 138.7\ \mathrm{ns}$, in agreement with the value in Table 7.2. Also, in the numerical example of (3), letting $B\to0$ gives $\theta\to0$ and $\tau\to138.7\ \mathrm{ns}$ again, while for $B\to\infty$ we get $\theta\to\pi/4$ and $\sin^2\theta\to1/2$, so that $\tau\to2\times124.5\ \mathrm{ps} = 249\ \mathrm{ps}$ and it saturates. Both limits are physically correct behavior.

Meaning. The QED hierarchy in which a single extra power of $\alpha$ changes the lifetime by a factor of $10^3$ directly becomes the resolution of a materials measurement. The $125\ \mathrm{ps}$ of para is buried in the time resolution of the apparatus ($150$–$200\ \mathrm{ps}$ FWHM), but the $142\ \mathrm{ns}$ of ortho can be separated with ease. This is why the free volume of polymers and porous materials can be read out on its own as the “third component $\tau_3$.” Moreover, the magnetic quenching of (3) is a technique that is also used in practice: by applying a magnetic field and seeing whether the $\tau_3$ component shortens, one can judge whether that long-lived component really originates from o-Ps or from some other trapping state. A selection rule of particle physics thus becomes, as it stands, a tool for eliminating systematic errors in a measurement.

Exercise 7.4: Finding defect concentrations and free volumes with PALS

Problem (restated)

(1) A PALS measurement on neutron-irradiated iron gave $\tau_1 = 80\ \mathrm{ps}$, $\tau_2 = 175\ \mathrm{ps}$, $I_2 = 0.45$. Taking the lifetime of the perfect crystal to be $\tau_b = 106\ \mathrm{ps}$, find the trapping rate $\kappa$ from the formulas of the two-state trapping model of Chapter 7 of this book.

(2) Taking the specific trapping rate of iron to be $\mu_v = 1.1\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ (per atomic fraction), find the monovacancy concentration $C_v$ in ppm.

(3) Check whether $\tau_1 = 1/(\lambda_b+\kappa)$ is consistent with the $\kappa$ of (1).

(4) In another polymer sample, a third component with $\tau_3 = 2.5\ \mathrm{ns}$, $I_3 = 22\%$ was observed. Solve the Tao–Eldrup formula numerically to find the radius $R$ of the free volume and its volume $\tfrac43\pi R^3$.

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1)–(3) simply apply the two-state trapping model of Chapter 7 of this book,

$$ \tau_1 = \frac{1}{\lambda_b+\kappa}, \qquad \tau_2 = \frac{1}{\lambda_v} = \tau_v, \qquad \kappa = \frac{I_2}{I_1}\left(\frac{1}{\tau_b}-\frac{1}{\tau_v}\right) = \mu_v C_v $$

to the given numbers. What the measurement gives directly are the three quantities $(\tau_1,\tau_2,I_2)$, and $\tau_b$ is supplied separately (from a defect-free reference sample or from a theoretical calculation). Note that $\tau_1$ is the bulk component “eaten by trapping,” so necessarily $\tau_1<\tau_b$. Therefore (3) serves as an independent consistency check. Part (4) is a transcendental equation, so we solve it numerically.

(1) First, $I_1 = 1-I_2 = 0.55$. The value $\tau_2 = \tau_v = 175\ \mathrm{ps}$ is the monovacancy lifetime (it coincides exactly with $\tau_{1V}=175\ \mathrm{ps}$ for Fe in Table 7.3, so the defect can be identified as a monovacancy). We compute the annihilation rates:

$$ \lambda_b = \frac{1}{\tau_b} = \frac{1}{106\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{s}} = 9.4340\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$ $$ \lambda_v = \frac{1}{\tau_v} = \frac{1}{175\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{s}} = 5.7143\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$ $$ \lambda_b-\lambda_v = 3.7197\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

Since the intensity ratio is $I_2/I_1 = 0.45/0.55 = 0.81818$,

$$ \kappa = 0.81818\times3.7197\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} = 3.043\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

Note that $\kappa$ and $\lambda_b$ are of the same order ($\kappa/\lambda_b = 0.32$). Annihilation from the bulk ($\lambda_b$) and trapping into vacancies ($\kappa$) compete, so the fraction of trapped positrons is not the ratio but $\kappa/(\lambda_b+\kappa)=3.04/12.48=0.24$, that is, about one quarter (the second-component intensity $I_2=0.45$ is not itself the trapped fraction; it is a different combination, $I_2=\kappa/(\lambda_b-\lambda_v+\kappa)$).

(2) The trapping rate is proportional to the vacancy concentration ($\kappa = \mu_v C_v$), so

$$ C_v = \frac{\kappa}{\mu_v} = \frac{3.043\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}{1.1\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}} = 2.767\times10^{-6} = 2.8\ \mathrm{ppm} $$

That is, about 3 vacancies per $100$ ten-thousand (one million) atoms. Let us also check the units. Since $\mu_v$ is a specific trapping rate “per atomic fraction,” $\kappa/\mu_v$ comes out as an atomic fraction, that is, a dimensionless quantity. To convert to $\mathrm{ppm}$, multiply by $10^6$. Multiplying by the atomic density of iron, $8.5\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, gives a volume concentration of $2.4\times10^{17}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$.

We check the plausibility of this value from two directions. The first is the window of measurable concentrations. The two-state trapping model carries information only when $\kappa$ is comparable to $\lambda_b$. If $\kappa\ll\lambda_b$, then $\tau_1\simeq\tau_b$ and the trapped component is invisible; conversely, if $\kappa\gg\lambda_b$, all the positrons are trapped (saturation trapping), only $\tau_2$ remains, and the information on the concentration is lost. The center of the window is

$$ C_v \sim \frac{\lambda_b}{\mu_v} = \frac{9.43\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}{1.1\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}} = 8.6\times10^{-6} \simeq 9\ \mathrm{ppm} $$

and one to two orders of magnitude around it, roughly $0.1$–$100\ \mathrm{ppm}$, is the practical range of PALS. The $2.8\ \mathrm{ppm}$ of this problem lies right near the middle of that range, in the region where the concentration is determined most precisely (indeed, the consistency in (3) held to $0.2\%$).

The second is the comparison with the thermal-equilibrium concentration. Taking the vacancy formation energy of iron to be $E_f\simeq1.8\ \mathrm{eV}$, the vacancy concentration in thermal equilibrium is given by $C_v^{\text{eq}} = \ee^{-E_f/k_BT}$:

$$ T = 300\ \mathrm{K}:\ \ \ee^{-1.8/0.0259} = 6\times10^{-31}, \qquad T = 1811\ \mathrm{K}\ (\text{melting point}):\ \ \ee^{-1.8/0.156} = 1\times10^{-5} $$

The room-temperature equilibrium value of $10^{-31}$ is so small that no method could measure it. On the other hand, the $2.8\ \mathrm{ppm} = 2.8\times10^{-6}$ just obtained means that an amount of vacancies comparable to the equilibrium concentration just below the melting point is frozen in at room temperature. This is precisely the nonequilibrium nature of irradiation damage, and the value of this method lies in the fact that a state $25$ orders of magnitude away from equilibrium can be quantified at room temperature.

(3) We put the $\kappa$ obtained in (1) back into the model formula:

$$ \tau_1 = \frac{1}{\lambda_b+\kappa} = \frac{1}{9.4340\times10^{9}+3.043\times10^{9}}\ \mathrm{s} = \frac{1}{1.2477\times10^{10}}\ \mathrm{s} = 8.015\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{s} = 80.1\ \mathrm{ps} $$

This agrees with the measured value $\tau_1 = 80\ \mathrm{ps}$ to $0.2\%$. It is consistent.

This agreement is not trivial. The $\kappa$ was obtained from $(I_2/I_1,\tau_b,\tau_v)$, whereas $\tau_1$ comes out of the spectrum fit independently. Their agreement simultaneously guarantees that (i) there is only one kind of trapping site, (ii) detrapping (escape) after trapping is negligible, and (iii) the value of $\tau_b$ is appropriate. When they do not agree, one must include three or more components or reconsider $\tau_b$. In practice this check is always performed.

(4) We solve the Tao–Eldrup formula

$$ \tau_{o\text{-Ps}}[\mathrm{ns}] = \frac{1}{2}\left[1-\frac{R}{R+\Delta R}+\frac{1}{2\pi}\sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi R}{R+\Delta R}\right)\right]^{-1}, \qquad \Delta R = 0.1656\ \mathrm{nm} $$

for $R$ with $\tau_{o\text{-Ps}} = 2.5\ \mathrm{ns}$. Denoting the content of the square brackets by $f(R)$, the condition is

$$ f(R) = \frac{1}{2\tau} = \frac{1}{2\times2.5} = 0.200 $$

Since $f$ is a monotonically decreasing function of $R$, it can be solved by bracketing. Letting $x\equiv R/(R+\Delta R)$, we tabulate:

Table E.7.1: Numerical solution of the Tao–Eldrup formula ($\Delta R = 0.1656\ \mathrm{nm}$)
$R$ (nm)$x = R/(R+\Delta R)$$1-x$$\sin(2\pi x)/2\pi$$f(R)$$\tau$ (ns)
$0.300$$0.64433$$0.35567$$-0.12535$$0.23032$$2.171$
$0.320$$0.65898$$0.34102$$-0.13383$$0.20719$$2.413$
$0.325$$0.66245$$0.33755$$-0.13568$$0.20187$$2.477$
$\bm{0.3268}$$0.66369$$0.33631$$-0.13632$$\bm{0.19999}$$\bm{2.500}$
$0.330$$0.66586$$0.33414$$-0.13743$$0.19671$$2.542$
$0.350$$0.67882$$0.32118$$-0.14350$$0.17768$$2.814$

Therefore

$$ R = 0.327\ \mathrm{nm} = 3.27\ \AA $$

Assuming the free volume is a sphere,

$$ V_h = \frac43\pi R^3 = \frac43\pi\times(3.27)^3\ \AA^3 = \frac43\pi\times34.97\ \AA^3 = 146\ \AA^3 $$

In Table 7.4, $R=0.29\ \mathrm{nm}$ (polystyrene) gave $102\ \AA^3$ and $R=0.35\ \mathrm{nm}$ gave $180\ \AA^3$, so this value lies exactly in between: a relatively soft polymer close to a rubbery one.

$I_3 = 22\%$ is an indicator of the Ps formation probability and is used to estimate the free-volume fraction:

$$ f_v = C\,I_3\,V_h $$

Taking the empirical proportionality constant $C\simeq1.5\times10^{-3}\ \AA^{-3}$ (the usual convention of entering $I_3$ in units of $\%$), we get $f_v \simeq 1.5\times10^{-3}\times22\times146 = 4.8\ \%$, which is consistent with the typical free-volume fraction of polymers (a few $\%$). Since $C$ is a quantity that must be calibrated for each material system, the accepted practice is that it is more reliable to read the kink in the temperature dependence $f_v(T)$ (the glass transition point $T_g$) than the absolute value.

Verification. We check at three points. First, (3) is already an independent consistency check ($80.1$ against the measured $80\ \mathrm{ps}$). Second, putting the solution of (4) back into the formula gives $f(0.3268) = 0.19999$ and $\tau = 0.5/0.19999 = 2.500\ \mathrm{ns}$, which indeed satisfies the condition. Third, we look at the limits. For $R\to\infty$, $x\to1$, $1-x\to0$, and $\sin(2\pi x)\to0$, so $f\to0$ and $\tau\to\infty$. In an infinitely large void there are no walls, so o-Ps should approach its vacuum value of $142\ \mathrm{ns}$, and both the sign and the direction are right (the Tao–Eldrup formula gives only the pickoff component, so in practice one combines it as $1/\tau = 1/\tau_{\text{TE}}+1/142\ \mathrm{ns}$, but in the $\mathrm{ns}$ range pickoff is overwhelming). Conversely, for $R\to0$, $x\to0$, $f\to1$, and $\tau\to0.5\ \mathrm{ns}$, which is exactly the inverse of the spin-averaged annihilation rate $2\ \mathrm{ns^{-1}}$ within the electron layer.

Meaning. This exercise shows that numbers found in a particle-physics textbook become, as they stand, the scale of an instrument for materials characterization. The metal vacancy measurements of (1)–(3) use the fact that the positron annihilation rate, which is fixed by $\alpha^5$, is proportional to the electron density, and read a vacancy, a “place where electrons are thin,” as a lengthening of the lifetime. There are almost no other methods that can quantify point defects at the ppm level nondestructively, and PALS is actually used for evaluating the irradiation embrittlement of reactor pressure vessel steel and for detecting the precursor processes of fatigue cracks. The polymer side, (4), would not work without the long lifetime of $142\ \mathrm{ns}$ for ortho-Ps. The selection rule of $C$ conservation provides a yardstick that measures free volume with a resolution of $\AA^3$.

Exercise 7.5: Estimating levels with the Cornell potential

Problem (restated)

Use the variational energy of Chapter 7 of this book.

(1) For the purely linear potential $V=ar$, ignoring the Coulomb term, minimize $E(\lambda) = \dfrac{1}{2\mu\lambda^2}+\dfrac{3a\lambda}{2}$ and express $\lambda_{\min}$ and $E_{\min}$ in terms of $\mu,a$.

(2) From the result of (1), show that $E_{\min}\propto \mu^{-1/3}a^{2/3}$. Verify by dimensional analysis that, in general, for $V\propto r^p$ one has $E\propto\mu^{-p/(p+2)}$, and show that the $\mu$ dependence disappears for $p\to0$ (the logarithmic potential).

(3) Insert $\mu = m_c/2 = 0.75\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and $a=0.18\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ into (1) and find $E_{\min}$ in GeV. Do the same for $\mu=m_b/2=2.35\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and check whether the ratio $E_{b\bar b}/E_{c\bar c}$ agrees with the prediction $(\mu_b/\mu_c)^{-1/3}$ of (2).

(4) Using $\hbar c = 0.197327\ \mathrm{GeV\,fm}$, convert $\lambda_{\min}$ to fm.

Solution

Strategy. This is the standard procedure of the variational method. Take the hydrogen-like trial function $\psi_\lambda(r) = (\pi\lambda^3)^{-1/2}\ee^{-r/\lambda}$. As in Chapter 7 of this book, $\braket{T} = 1/(2\mu\lambda^2)$ and $\braket{r} = 3\lambda/2$, so the expectation value of the linear potential is $a\braket{r} = 3a\lambda/2$. What remains is a minimization over the single variable $\lambda$. The generalization in (2) can be checked twice over, since both the virial theorem and dimensional analysis give the same answer. Everything is done in natural units ($\hbar=c=1$), and at the end we multiply by $\hbar c$ to return to fm.

(1) For the given energy functional

$$ E(\lambda) = \frac{1}{2\mu\lambda^2}+\frac{3a\lambda}{2} $$

the kinetic energy diverges as $\lambda^{-2}$ for $\lambda\to0$, and the potential diverges linearly for $\lambda\to\infty$, so there is always a minimum at a finite $\lambda$. Differentiating gives

$$ \frac{\dd E}{\dd\lambda} = -\frac{1}{\mu\lambda^3}+\frac{3a}{2} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda^3 = \frac{2}{3a\mu} $$ $$ \boxed{\ \lambda_{\min} = \left(\frac{2}{3a\mu}\right)^{1/3}\ } $$

We substitute this into $E$. A clever rewriting makes the calculation easy. From $\mu\lambda_{\min}^3 = 2/(3a)$ we get $\mu\lambda_{\min}^2 = 2/(3a\lambda_{\min})$, so

$$ \braket{T} = \frac{1}{2\mu\lambda_{\min}^2} = \frac{3a\lambda_{\min}}{4} $$

That is, at the minimum the kinetic energy is exactly half of the potential term $3a\lambda/2$. Therefore

$$ E_{\min} = \frac{3a\lambda_{\min}}{4}+\frac{3a\lambda_{\min}}{2} = \frac{9}{4}a\,\lambda_{\min} = \frac{9}{4}a\left(\frac{2}{3a\mu}\right)^{1/3} $$

Collecting the powers of $a$ gives

$$ E_{\min} = \frac94\left(\frac23\right)^{1/3}a^{2/3}\mu^{-1/3} = 1.9656\,a^{2/3}\mu^{-1/3} $$

(here $\tfrac94(2/3)^{1/3} = 2.25\times0.87358 = 1.9656$). Note that $E_{\min}$ is positive. Because the linear potential diverges at infinity, a bound state always exists, but since we take $V(0)=0$ as the reference, the energy is positive. The mass of the quarkonium is read off as $M = 2m_q+E_{\min}$.

(2) From the final form of (1) we can immediately read off $E_{\min}\propto \mu^{-1/3}a^{2/3}$. Let us generalize. Let $V(r) = A r^p$ ($p>-2$). The variational energy takes the form

$$ E(\lambda) = \frac{c_1}{\mu\lambda^2}+c_2 A\lambda^p $$

($c_1,c_2$ are pure numbers determined by the trial function alone). Minimizing gives

$$ -\frac{2c_1}{\mu\lambda^3}+p\,c_2A\lambda^{p-1} = 0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda^{p+2} = \frac{2c_1}{p\,c_2\,\mu A} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \lambda_{\min}\propto(\mu A)^{-1/(p+2)} $$

Substituting this back into $E$, both terms give the same scaling, so

$$ E_{\min}\propto A\lambda_{\min}^p \propto A\,(\mu A)^{-p/(p+2)} = A^{2/(p+2)}\,\mu^{-p/(p+2)} $$

that is,

$$ \boxed{\ E_{\min}\propto \mu^{-p/(p+2)}A^{2/(p+2)}\ } $$

holds.

So far we have gone through a specific trial function, but this exponent is an exact result that depends neither on the variational method nor on the trial function. Let us confirm it by the dimensional analysis that the problem asks for (more precisely, by the scaling of the Schrödinger equation). In natural units $[\mu]=M$, $[r]=M^{-1}$, $[E]=M$, so for $V=Ar^p$ to have the dimension of energy we must have $[A]=M^{p+1}$. Now we apply the length-scale transformation $\bm{r} = s\bm{\rho}$ to the Hamiltonian:

$$ H = -\frac{\nabla_r^2}{2\mu}+Ar^p = \frac{1}{2\mu s^2}\left(-\nabla_\rho^2\right)+As^p\rho^p $$

We choose $s$ so that the coefficients of the two terms coincide, that is,

$$ \frac{1}{2\mu s^2} = As^p \quad\Longrightarrow\quad s^{p+2} = \frac{1}{2\mu A} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad s = (2\mu A)^{-1/(p+2)} $$

and the Hamiltonian can then be written as

$$ H = \frac{1}{2\mu s^2}\left[-\nabla_\rho^2+\rho^p\right] $$

Neither $\mu$ nor $A$ remains inside the square brackets. In other words, all the material constants are factored out into the common prefactor, and the content of the brackets is a purely numerical eigenvalue problem. If we denote its eigenvalues by $\varepsilon_n$ (dimensionless numbers), then $E_n = \varepsilon_n/(2\mu s^2)$, and

$$ E_n \propto \frac{1}{\mu}s^{-2} \propto \frac{1}{\mu}(2\mu A)^{2/(p+2)} \propto \mu^{-1+\frac{2}{p+2}}A^{\frac{2}{p+2}} = \mu^{-\frac{p}{p+2}}A^{\frac{2}{p+2}} $$

follows exactly. This agrees perfectly with the exponent obtained by the variational method. As a by-product, we also learn that the level ratio $E_n/E_m = \varepsilon_n/\varepsilon_m$ depends on neither $\mu$ nor $A$. This fact becomes important in the second half of (2) and in (3).

As a check, let us apply the result to known cases.

  • $p=1$ (linear): $E\propto\mu^{-1/3}A^{2/3}$. This agrees with (1).
  • $p=-1$ (Coulomb, $A=-\kappa$): $E\propto\mu^{-(-1)/1}A^{2/1} = \mu\,\kappa^2$. This agrees with the Bohr formula $E = -\tfrac12\mu\kappa^2$.
  • $p=2$ (harmonic oscillator): $E\propto\mu^{-1/2}A^{1/2}$. Indeed $E = \tfrac32\omega$ with $\omega=\sqrt{2A/\mu}$ ($A = \tfrac12\mu\omega^2$), so $E\propto\mu^{-1/2}A^{1/2}$. They agree.

Now take the limit $p\to0$. The exponent of $\mu$, $-p/(p+2)\to0$, so the dependence on $\mu$ disappears. For $p\to0$ the potential is expanded as $A r^p = A(1+p\ln r+\cdots)$, and if we drop the constant term we obtain $Ap\ln r$, that is, a logarithmic potential $V = B\ln r$. For a logarithmic potential the level spacings do not depend on the reduced mass at all:

$$ E_n - E_m = (\text{constant independent of $\mu$})\times B $$

This explains the experimental fact stated in Chapter 7 of this book, that “the $2S$–$1S$ spacings of $c\bar c$ and $b\bar b$ are almost equal.” Indeed $M_{\psi(2S)}-M_{J/\psi} = 3686.1-3096.9 = 589\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $M_{\Upsilon(2S)}-M_{\Upsilon(1S)} = 10023.3-9460.3 = 563\ \mathrm{MeV}$, so although the reduced masses differ by a factor of $3.1$, the spacings differ by only $5\%$. In the region of $0.2$–$0.5\ \mathrm{fm}$ probed by $c\bar c$ and $b\bar b$, the Cornell potential happens to be approximated very well by $\ln r$ (a point made by Quigg and Rosner).

(3) Charmonium ($\mu = 0.75\ \mathrm{GeV}$, $a = 0.18\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$):

$$ 3a\mu = 3\times0.18\times0.75 = 0.405\ \mathrm{GeV^3}, \qquad \lambda_{\min} = \left(\frac{2}{0.405}\right)^{1/3} = (4.9383)^{1/3} = 1.7029\ \mathrm{GeV^{-1}} $$ $$ E_{\min} = \frac94\times0.18\times1.7029 = 0.405\times1.7029 = 0.6897\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Bottomonium ($\mu = 2.35\ \mathrm{GeV}$):

$$ 3a\mu = 3\times0.18\times2.35 = 1.269\ \mathrm{GeV^3}, \qquad \lambda_{\min} = \left(\frac{2}{1.269}\right)^{1/3} = (1.5760)^{1/3} = 1.1637\ \mathrm{GeV^{-1}} $$ $$ E_{\min} = 0.405\times1.1637 = 0.4713\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Taking the ratio,

$$ \frac{E_{\min}(b\bar b)}{E_{\min}(c\bar c)} = \frac{0.4713}{0.6897} = 0.6834 $$

On the other hand, the prediction of (2) is

$$ \left(\frac{\mu_b}{\mu_c}\right)^{-1/3} = \left(\frac{\mu_c}{\mu_b}\right)^{1/3} = \left(\frac{0.75}{2.35}\right)^{1/3} = (0.31915)^{1/3} = 0.6834 $$

which agrees to four decimal places. This is only natural, since the formula is built so that $E_{\min}\propto\mu^{-1/3}$ holds exactly. What matters here is the direction, that “the heavier the quark, the smaller the binding energy (the contribution of the linear term),” and the sluggish dependence that even when $\mu$ increases by a factor of $3.1$, $E$ decreases only by a factor of $0.68$. For a Coulomb system we would have $E\propto\mu$, which would increase by a factor of $3.1$, whereas here the change goes in the opposite direction and is weak. This is a characteristic of linear confinement.

(4) Since $1\ \mathrm{GeV^{-1}} = \hbar c/(1\ \mathrm{GeV}) = 0.197327\ \mathrm{fm}$,

$$ \lambda_{\min}(c\bar c) = 1.7029\times0.197327\ \mathrm{fm} = 0.3360\ \mathrm{fm} $$ $$ \lambda_{\min}(b\bar b) = 1.1637\times0.197327\ \mathrm{fm} = 0.2296\ \mathrm{fm} $$

The mean radius is $\braket{r} = \tfrac32\lambda$, so it is $0.504\ \mathrm{fm}$ for $c\bar c$ and $0.344\ \mathrm{fm}$ for $b\bar b$. These are larger than the values $\braket{r} = 0.40\ \mathrm{fm}$ ($c\bar c$) and $0.26\ \mathrm{fm}$ ($b\bar b$) for the Cornell potential of Chapter 7 of this book (with the Coulomb term included). Since dropping the Coulomb attraction lets the system spread out more loosely, this is the correct direction.

Let us also look at the ratio. We have $\lambda_{\min}(b\bar b)/\lambda_{\min}(c\bar c) = 0.2296/0.3360 = 0.683$, which is exactly the same $(\mu_c/\mu_b)^{1/3}$ as the energy ratio. This is natural from $\lambda_{\min}\propto(a\mu)^{-1/3}$ in (1), because $E_{\min} = \tfrac94a\lambda_{\min}$ ties the two directly together. Both the size and the energy move with the same $\mu^{-1/3}$, which is much more sluggish than the shrinking $\propto\mu^{-1}$ of the size of a Coulomb system. Even if we bring in a heavier quark, the system does not become small so easily.

We also check that the orders of magnitude are reasonable. The values $0.23$–$0.34\ \mathrm{fm}$ are clearly smaller than the proton radius of $0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$, consistent with the picture that quarkonium is an especially compact system even among hadrons. Let us also get a feel for the size of the string tension $a$. In natural units, $a=0.18\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ is an “energy per unit length,” so dividing by $\hbar c$ gives

$$ a = \frac{0.18\ \mathrm{GeV^2}}{0.197327\ \mathrm{GeV\,fm}} = 0.912\ \mathrm{GeV/fm} = \frac{0.912\times1.602\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J}}{10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}} = 1.46\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N} $$

that is, about $15$ tonne-force, which reproduces the statement of Chapter 7 of this book. The energy required to pull the pair apart by the distance $\lambda_{\min}$ is $a\lambda_{\min} = 0.18\times1.703 = 0.31\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and for $1\ \mathrm{fm}$ it is $0.91\ \mathrm{GeV}$.
