The latter corresponds to the mass of one meson. The more we stretch, the more energy is needed, but at some point it becomes cheaper to create one $q\bar q$ pair and cut the string—this is the quantitative content of the fact that quarks cannot be extracted singly.

Verification. We make three checks. First, the virial theorem. For $V\propto r^p$ the virial theorem reads $2\braket{T} = p\braket{V}$. Inserting $\braket{T} = \tfrac34a\lambda$ and $\braket{V} = \tfrac32a\lambda$ obtained in (1), we get $2\times\tfrac34a\lambda = \tfrac32a\lambda = 1\times\tfrac32a\lambda$, so the virial theorem for $p=1$ is properly satisfied. Second, comparison with the exact solution. The exact $s$-wave solution of the linear potential can be written with Airy functions, and the ground state is $E_1^{\text{exact}} = \abs{a_1}(a^2/(2\mu))^{1/3}$ ($a_1=-2.33811$ is the first zero of the Airy function). Inserting numbers for $c\bar c$, $(0.18^2/1.5)^{1/3} = (0.0216)^{1/3} = 0.27850$ and $E_1^{\text{exact}} = 2.33811\times0.27850 = 0.6512\ \mathrm{GeV}$. The variational value $0.6897\ \mathrm{GeV}$ is $5.9\%$ larger than this, which does not contradict the principle that the variational method gives an upper bound. Third, dimensions. $a^{2/3}\mu^{-1/3}$ has dimension $[\text{mass}^2]^{2/3}[\text{mass}]^{-1/3} = [\text{mass}]^{4/3-1/3} = [\text{mass}]$, which is indeed an energy.

Meaning. The result of (2), that “the power $p$ of the potential determines the mass dependence,” is a powerful indicator for classifying bound systems. For Coulomb ($p=-1$) we have $E\propto\mu$, for linear ($p=1$) $E\propto\mu^{-1/3}$, and for the logarithm in between, it is independent of $\mu$. By measuring the mass dependence of the level spacings, one can conversely read off the shape of the potential, and this is the reasoning that makes quarkonium a “microscope for QCD.” The same logic works in materials science. For example, the fact that the mean-square amplitude of the zero-point vibration of a phonon, $\braket{u^2}$, is $\propto M^{-1/2}$ (harmonic, $p=2$) is the starting point of the analysis of the isotope effect, and in systems with strong anharmonicity this power deviates. The approach of reading the form of the bonding from the exponent of the power law is common to both.

Exercise 7.6: Calculating baryon magnetic moments in the quark model

Problem (restated)

Let $\mu_u = \tfrac23(m_p/m_u)\mu_N$ and so on, and use $m_u=m_d=336\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_s=510\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_p = 938.272\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(1) Find $\mu_u,\mu_d,\mu_s$ in units of $\mu_N$.

(2) Calculate the magnetic moment of $\Sigma^+ = uus$ (the $uu$, not the $ud$, pair forms the spin-1 pair) from $\mu_{\Sigma^+} = \tfrac43\mu_u-\tfrac13\mu_s$, and compare it with the measured $+2.458\,\mu_N$.

(3) The magnetic moment of $\Omega^- = sss$ ($J=3/2$, all three spins parallel) is $3\mu_s$. Compare it with the measured $-2.02\,\mu_N$, and find what $m_s$ becomes if it is redetermined from this single point.

(4) Explain why $\mu_n/\mu_p = -2/3$ does not depend on the constituent quark mass. Also consider how this prediction would change if the quarks were not point particles with $g=2$.

Solution

Strategy. If we regard a quark as a point Dirac particle with $g=2$, then, as in Chapter 7 of this book, $\mu_q = e_q/(2m_q)$. Dividing by the nuclear magneton $\mu_N = e/(2m_p)$ gives

$$ \frac{\mu_q}{\mu_N} = \frac{e_q}{e}\cdot\frac{m_p}{m_q} $$

which is an easy-to-remember form: the product of the charge ratio and the inverse mass ratio. The magnetic moment of a baryon is obtained simply by multiplying these quark magnetic moments by the coefficients that come from taking the expectation value of $\sum_i\mu_i\sigma_z^{(i)}$ in the spin-flavor wave function. The calculation itself ends with the four arithmetic operations, and the point of this problem is to identify in (4) “what is a parameter and what is a prediction.”

(1) We use $e_u = +2/3$ and $e_d = e_s = -1/3$.

$$ \mu_u = \frac23\cdot\frac{m_p}{m_u}\mu_N = \frac23\times\frac{938.272}{336}\mu_N = \frac23\times2.79248\,\mu_N = +1.8617\,\mu_N $$ $$ \mu_d = -\frac13\cdot\frac{m_p}{m_d}\mu_N = -\frac13\times2.79248\,\mu_N = -0.9308\,\mu_N $$ $$ \mu_s = -\frac13\cdot\frac{m_p}{m_s}\mu_N = -\frac13\times\frac{938.272}{510}\mu_N = -\frac13\times1.83975\,\mu_N = -0.6132\,\mu_N $$

To be safe, let us reproduce $\mu_p$ and $\mu_n$ from these:

$$ \mu_p = \frac43\mu_u-\frac13\mu_d = \frac43(1.8617)-\frac13(-0.9308) = 2.4822+0.3103 = 2.7925\,\mu_N $$ $$ \mu_n = \frac43\mu_d-\frac13\mu_u = \frac43(-0.9308)-\frac13(1.8617) = -1.2411-0.6206 = -1.8617\,\mu_N $$

Since $m_u$ was chosen to match the measured value $2.7928$ of $\mu_p$, the agreement is natural (this is the fit point). For $\mu_n$, the measured value is $-1.9130$, so there is a $2.7\%$ deviation, and this is a parameter-free prediction. Also, $\mu_s$ was fitted by choosing $m_s$ to match the measured $\Lambda$ moment $\mu_\Lambda=-0.613$, so this too is a fit point. Keep in mind the fact that only two points are being fitted as we proceed to (2) and (3).

(2) In $\Sigma^+ = uus$, the $uu$ form spin 1 (symmetric), and the $s$ couples to it to give total $J=1/2$. This is the same structure as in the proton $uud$, where the $uu$ pair up, so the coefficients can be carried over as they are:

$$ \mu_{\Sigma^+} = \frac43\mu_u-\frac13\mu_s $$

(this is the formula for $p$ with $d\to s$ substituted). Inserting numbers,

$$ \mu_{\Sigma^+} = \frac43\times1.8617 - \frac13\times(-0.6132) = 2.4822 + 0.2044 = +2.6866\,\mu_N $$

Comparing with the measured value $+2.458\,\mu_N$,

$$ \frac{2.6866-2.458}{2.458} = +0.0930 = +9.3\ \% $$

so the prediction is $9\%$ too large. The sign and the order of magnitude are correct, and the accuracy is at the level of about ten percent. The main cause of the deviation is the breaking of $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ flavor symmetry: in systems containing an $s$ quark, the constituent quark mass depends slightly on the environment (on which baryon the quark sits in). This is the price of carrying the $m_s=510\ \mathrm{MeV}$ determined from the $\Lambda$ over to the $\Sigma$ as it is. In addition, the fact that the quarks actually move relativistically and the contribution of the meson cloud also play a role.

(3) Since $\Omega^-=sss$ has $J=3/2$ with all three spins parallel, the expectation value is simply a sum:

$$ \mu_{\Omega^-} = 3\mu_s = 3\times(-0.6132) = -1.8397\,\mu_N $$

Relative to the measured $-2.02\,\mu_N$,

$$ \frac{\abs{-1.8397}-\abs{-2.02}}{\abs{-2.02}} = -0.089 = -8.9\ \% $$

it is $9\%$ too small. We therefore redetermine $m_s$ from the single point of the $\Omega^-$. From $3\mu_s = -2.02\,\mu_N$,

$$ \mu_s = -\frac{2.02}{3}\,\mu_N = -0.67333\,\mu_N $$

Inserting this into $\abs{\mu_s} = \tfrac13(m_p/m_s)\mu_N$ and solving for $m_s$ gives

$$ m_s = \frac{m_p}{3\abs{\mu_s}/\mu_N} = \frac{938.272}{3\times0.67333} = \frac{938.272}{2.02} = 464.5\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

This differs from the $510\ \mathrm{MeV}$ obtained from the $\Lambda$ by

$$ \frac{510-464.5}{510} = 8.9\ \% $$

The same quantity, the “constituent mass of the $s$ quark,” fluctuates by $9\%$ depending on which baryon it is determined from, and here the limit of the nonrelativistic quark model is clearly visible. The constituent quark mass is not a fundamental constant but an effective parameter for a particular state. Nevertheless, $464$ and $510$ are within $10\%$ of each other, and the qualitative picture that “the $s$ is $130$–$170\ \mathrm{MeV}$ heavier than $u,d$” ($464.5-336 = 128.5$, $510-336 = 174\ \mathrm{MeV}$) is robust.

(4) Why it does not depend on the mass. From isospin symmetry set $m_u = m_d\equiv m_q$, and write $\mu_0\equiv e/(2m_q)$, so that $\mu_u = \tfrac23\mu_0$ and $\mu_d = -\tfrac13\mu_0$. Then

$$ \mu_p = \frac43\left(\frac23\mu_0\right)-\frac13\left(-\frac13\mu_0\right) = \left(\frac89+\frac19\right)\mu_0 = \mu_0 $$ $$ \mu_n = \frac43\left(-\frac13\mu_0\right)-\frac13\left(\frac23\mu_0\right) = -\left(\frac49+\frac29\right)\mu_0 = -\frac23\mu_0 $$

and taking the ratio, $\mu_0$ cancels and disappears:

$$ \frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p} = -\frac23 $$

In short, both $\mu_p$ and $\mu_n$ are proportional to the same single scale $\mu_0 = e/(2m_q)$, and only rational numbers coming from the spin-flavor wave function (how the quark charges and spins are combined) remain in the ratio. This is the sense in which the answer comes out without knowing the value of $m_q$. The measured value is $-1.91304/2.79285 = -0.6850$, an agreement to $2.7\%$.

What happens if $g\ne2$. If the quarks are not point Dirac particles but have an anomalous magnetic moment, the magnetic moment can be written as

$$ \mu_q = \frac{g_q\,e_q}{4m_q} $$

(this returns to the original for $g_q=2$). If $g$ is common to $u$ and $d$ ($g_u=g_d\equiv g$) and $m_u=m_d$, then $\mu_0\to (g/2)\mu_0$ merely replaces everything by the same factor, so the ratio still remains

$$ \frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p} = -\frac23 $$

unchanged. What changes is the absolute value, and the constituent quark mass determined from $\mu_p$ shifts as $m_q\to(g/2)m_q$. On the other hand, if $g$ is flavor-dependent ($g_u\ne g_d$), the situation changes. Setting $\mu_u = \tfrac23 r_u\mu_0$ and $\mu_d = -\tfrac13 r_d\mu_0$ ($r_q\equiv g_q/2$), we get

$$ \frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p} = \frac{-\tfrac49 r_d-\tfrac29 r_u}{\tfrac89 r_u+\tfrac19 r_d} = -\frac{4r_d+2r_u}{8r_u+r_d} $$

which returns to $-2/3$ only when $r_u=r_d$. For example, if $r_d/r_u = 1.1$, the ratio is $-6.4/9.1 = -0.7033$, which deviates from $-2/3$ by $5.5\%$. Thus $\mu_n/\mu_p=-2/3$ amounts to a test that “the $g$-factor of the quarks does not depend on flavor.” The $2.7\%$ deviation from experiment can be read as placing an upper limit on the flavor dependence of $g$, but, more naturally, it can be read as indicating the size of the relativistic corrections and of the $\mathrm{SU}(3)$ breaking.

Verification. First, comparison with Table 7.7. The values $\mu_{\Sigma^+}=+2.687$ and $\mu_{\Omega^-}=-1.840$ obtained in this problem both agree with the predicted values in the table. Next, we make an independent check with a sum rule. From the quark-model formulas, $\mu_{\Sigma^+}+\mu_{\Sigma^-} = \tfrac43(\mu_u+\mu_d)-\tfrac23\mu_s$, and inserting $\mu_u+\mu_d = \tfrac13\mu_0 = \tfrac13\times2.7925 = 0.9308$ and $\mu_s=-0.6132$ gives $\tfrac43\times0.9308+\tfrac23\times0.6132 = 1.2411+0.4088 = 1.6499$. On the other hand, $\mu_p+\mu_n = 2.7925-1.8617 = 0.9308$. The measured value is $\mu_{\Sigma^+}+\mu_{\Sigma^-} = 2.458-1.160 = 1.298$, so the model overestimates by $27\%$, whereas for $\mu_p+\mu_n$ the model gives $0.9308$ against the measured $2.7928-1.9130 = 0.8798$, a $6\%$ deviation. This is consistent with the trend in Table 7.7 that the deviation is larger for systems containing $s$. Finally, a check of units: $\mu_q/\mu_N$ is dimensionless and $m_p/m_q$ is also dimensionless, so the formula is consistent.

Meaning. The quark-model magnetic moments are a historic calculation that cleanly separated “rational numbers fixed by symmetry” from “a scale fixed by dynamics.” The number $-2/3$ comes only from the spin-flavor wave function (the structure of $\mathrm{SU}(6)$), so it can be stated without knowing the details of the dynamics. The absolute value of $\mu_p$, on the other hand, requires a dynamical quantity, $m_q$. The counterpart in materials science is, for example, the $g$-factor of a transition-metal ion in a crystal field. The ratio of the quenching of the orbital angular momentum to the $g$ shift due to spin–orbit coupling is fixed by group theory (the irreducible representations of the point group), while the absolute value requires a dynamical quantity, the crystal-field splitting $\Delta$. The division “ratios from symmetry, absolute values from dynamics” is a strategy that is effective across fields.

Exercise 7.7: Comparing excitons and positronium

Problem (restated)

Use the exciton formulas of Chapter 7 of this book.

(1) Find the exciton binding energy and Bohr radius of CdSe ($m_e^*=0.13\,m_0$, $m_h^*=0.45\,m_0$, $\epsilon_r=9.6$). Is the exciton stable at room temperature ($k_BT=25.9\ \mathrm{meV}$)?

(2) Using the $a_X$ obtained in (1), determine whether a CdSe nanocrystal of diameter $4\ \mathrm{nm}$ lies in the “strong-confinement” regime or the “weak-confinement” regime.

(3) For the yellow exciton series of Cu$_2$O ($E_b=98\ \mathrm{meV}$, $a_X = 1.1\ \mathrm{nm}$), find the radius $a_Xn^2$ and the binding energy $E_b/n^2$ of the $n=25$ state. Compare the latter with $k_BT$ and explain why cryogenic temperatures are needed for this observation.

(4) Verify that substituting positronium ($\mu=m_e/2$, $\epsilon_r=1$) into the exciton formulas of Chapter 7 of this book gives $6.80\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $1.06\ \AA$. State in one line the physical factors that distinguish excitons from positronium.

Solution

Strategy. The exciton formulas derived in Chapter 7 of this book,

$$ E_b = 13.606\ \mathrm{eV}\times\frac{\mu/m_0}{\epsilon_r^2}, \qquad a_X = 0.0529\ \mathrm{nm}\times\frac{\epsilon_r}{\mu/m_0}, \qquad \frac{1}{\mu} = \frac{1}{m_e^*}+\frac{1}{m_h^*} $$

are just the Rydberg formula of the hydrogen atom with “the mass replaced by the reduced effective mass and the square of the charge replaced by $e^2/\epsilon_r$.” Once we have the two scalings $E_b\propto\mu/\epsilon_r^2$ and $a_X\propto\epsilon_r/\mu$ in hand, all that remains is substitution. The criterion for strong versus weak confinement in (2) is the comparison of the dot radius $R$ with $a_X$ or, equivalently, the comparison of the confinement energy $\pi^2/(2\mu R^2)$ with $E_b$.

(1) First we find the reduced effective mass:

$$ \mu = \frac{m_e^*m_h^*}{m_e^*+m_h^*} = \frac{0.13\times0.45}{0.13+0.45}\,m_0 = \frac{0.0585}{0.58}\,m_0 = 0.10086\,m_0 $$

The hole is $3.5$ times heavier than the electron, so $\mu$ is close to the lighter mass $m_e^*=0.13$ ($0.101$). Next, the binding energy:

$$ E_b = 13.606\ \mathrm{eV}\times\frac{0.10086}{9.6^2} = 13.606\times\frac{0.10086}{92.16}\ \mathrm{eV} = 13.606\times1.0944\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV} = 1.489\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{eV} $$

That is, $E_b = 14.9\ \mathrm{meV}$. The Bohr radius is

$$ a_X = 0.0529\ \mathrm{nm}\times\frac{9.6}{0.10086} = 0.0529\times95.18\ \mathrm{nm} = 5.035\ \mathrm{nm} $$

Comparison with room temperature:

$$ \frac{E_b}{k_BT} = \frac{14.9}{25.9} = 0.575 < 1 $$

Since $E_b<k_BT$, excitons in bulk CdSe are easily dissociated thermally at room temperature. Estimating with the Boltzmann factor, the weight by which the bound state is favored over the dissociated state is only about $\ee^{+E_b/k_BT}=\ee^{0.575}\approx1.8$ times, and indeed the exciton peak is not distinct in the room-temperature absorption spectrum of bulk CdSe. If we cool to $77\ \mathrm{K}$ ($k_BT=6.6\ \mathrm{meV}$), then $E_b/k_BT = 2.3$, and a sharp exciton absorption line appears.

(2) The nanocrystal has a diameter of $4\ \mathrm{nm}$, so its radius is $R = 2.0\ \mathrm{nm}$. Comparing with $a_X = 5.035\ \mathrm{nm}$,

$$ \frac{R}{a_X} = \frac{2.0}{5.035} = 0.40 < 1 $$

that is, $R<a_X$, and we are in the strong-confinement regime. Comparing in terms of energy makes the verdict even clearer. Evaluating the confining term of the Brus formula of Chapter 7 of this book (with $\hbar^2/(2m_0) = (\hbar c)^2/(2m_0c^2) = (197.327\ \mathrm{eV\,nm})^2/(2\times5.10999\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{eV}) = 0.03810\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}$),

$$ E_{\text{conf}} = \frac{\pi^2}{2\mu R^2} = \frac{\pi^2\times0.03810}{0.10086\times(2.0)^2}\ \mathrm{eV} = \frac{0.37603}{0.40345}\ \mathrm{eV} = 0.932\ \mathrm{eV} $$

The Coulomb term is

$$ -1.786\frac{e^2}{4\pi\epsilon_0\epsilon_r R} = -1.786\times\frac{1.440\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{9.6\times2.0\ \mathrm{nm}} = -0.134\ \mathrm{eV} $$

so the confinement is $7$ times larger than the Coulomb term and $63$ times larger than the exciton binding energy $E_b=0.0149\ \mathrm{eV}$. The electron and hole are no longer bound as an exciton; each is confined independently in the box, and the Coulomb interaction is a perturbation—this is the picture. This is the very definition of strong confinement.

The net blueshift comes out as $0.932-0.134 = 0.80\ \mathrm{eV}$. The emission of an actual $4\ \mathrm{nm}$ CdSe dot is around $2.1\ \mathrm{eV}$, and the shift from the bulk band gap of $1.74\ \mathrm{eV}$ is about $0.3$–$0.4\ \mathrm{eV}$, so the Brus formula, which assumes infinite barriers, overestimates by about a factor of $2$. The main causes are that the barrier is finite, so the wave function leaks outside, and the nonparabolicity of the bands. Even so, it correctly captures both the design principle that “changing the particle size changes the emission color” and the $1/R^2$ scaling.

(3) For $n=25$ in the yellow series of Cu$_2$O:

$$ r_{25} = a_X n^2 = 1.1\ \mathrm{nm}\times625 = 687.5\ \mathrm{nm} \simeq 0.69\ \mu\mathrm{m} $$ $$ E_{25} = \frac{E_b}{n^2} = \frac{98\ \mathrm{meV}}{625} = 0.157\ \mathrm{meV} $$

The size is extraordinary: the radius is comparable to the wavelength of visible light ($0.4$–$0.7\ \mu\mathrm{m}$). A “giant hydrogen atom” of diameter $1.4\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ is floating inside the crystal.

Converting to temperature,

$$ T = \frac{E_{25}}{k_B} = \frac{0.157\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}}{8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/K}} = 1.82\ \mathrm{K} $$

Therefore, for $T\gtrsim2\ \mathrm{K}$ we have $k_BT>E_{25}$, and the $n=25$ state is thermally ionized. This is why the experiment (Kazimierczuk et al., 2014) was carried out at $1.2\ \mathrm{K}$ in liquid helium under reduced pressure. Moreover, the level spacing between adjacent $n$ is

$$ E_{24}-E_{25} = 98\ \mathrm{meV}\times\left(\frac{1}{24^2}-\frac{1}{25^2}\right) = 98\times(1.7361\times10^{-3}-1.6000\times10^{-3})\ \mathrm{meV} = 1.33\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{meV} $$

which is only $13\ \mu\mathrm{eV}$, so to resolve these levels the spectral linewidth must be kept below the $\mu\mathrm{eV}$ level. Cryogenic temperatures are also essential in the sense of suppressing the thermal broadening of the linewidth (phonon scattering). “To resolve levels, make both $k_BT$ and the linewidth smaller than the level spacing”—this basic principle of spectroscopy applies directly.

(4) Positronium is $e^+e^-$ in vacuum, so $\epsilon_r=1$ and $\mu = m_e/2 = 0.5\,m_0$. Substituting,

$$ E_b = 13.606\ \mathrm{eV}\times\frac{0.5}{1^2} = 6.803\ \mathrm{eV} $$ $$ a_X = 0.0529\ \mathrm{nm}\times\frac{1}{0.5} = 0.1058\ \mathrm{nm} = 1.058\ \AA $$

Indeed, the positronium values of Chapter 7 of this book, $6.803\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $1.058\ \AA$ ($=2a_0$), are reproduced. The exciton formulas are merely a rewriting of the hydrogen formulas, so it is only natural that setting $\epsilon_r=1$ returns us to the two-body problem in vacuum.

What distinguishes excitons from positronium. Just two things: only the dielectric screening $\epsilon_r$ and the reduced effective mass $\mu$. In CdSe we divide by $\epsilon_r^2 = 92$ and multiply by $\mu/m_0 = 0.10$, so $E_b$ becomes $460$ times smaller, from $6.80\ \mathrm{eV}$ for Ps to $14.9\ \mathrm{meV}$, and the radius becomes $48$ times larger, from $1.06\ \AA$ to $50\ \AA$. Not a single character of the equation itself has changed.

Verification. We check in three ways. First, the consistency of the scalings. We have $E_b a_X^2\propto (\mu/\epsilon_r^2)(\epsilon_r/\mu)^2 = 1/\mu$, so $E_b a_X^2$ should not depend on $\epsilon_r$. For CdSe, $E_ba_X^2 = 1.4891\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{eV}\times(5.035\ \mathrm{nm})^2 = 0.37751\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}$, and for Ps, $6.803\ \mathrm{eV}\times(0.1058\ \mathrm{nm})^2 = 0.07615\ \mathrm{eV\,nm^2}$. Taking the ratio gives $0.37751/0.07615 = 4.957$, which agrees to four digits with $\mu_{\text{Ps}}/\mu_{\text{CdSe}} = 0.5/0.10086 = 4.957$. Second, comparison with Table 7.8. For the Cu$_2$O entry, with $\mu/m_0=0.363$ and $\epsilon_r=7.5$, we get $E_b = 13.606\times0.363/56.25 = 87.8\ \mathrm{meV}$ and $a_X = 0.0529\times7.5/0.363 = 1.09\ \mathrm{nm}$, which agree with the table values $87.8\ \mathrm{meV}$ and $1.1\ \mathrm{nm}$. The same computational path returns the correct values for another material as well. Third, units. $E_b$ is $\mathrm{Ry}$ times a dimensionless quantity, and $a_X$ is $a_0$ times a dimensionless quantity, so the dimensions match automatically.

Meaning. This problem is a fitting close to this chapter. What runs through an energy scale spanning $11$ orders of magnitude is one and the same Schrödinger equation, in which only the two inputs $\mu$ and $V(r)$ are swapped. What (1)–(2) show is the fact that materials design is nothing other than manipulating these two inputs. If we lower $\epsilon_r$ (or weaken the screening by going to two dimensions), $E_b$ rises and the exciton survives at room temperature. This is the reasoning behind the $E_b\sim0.5\ \mathrm{eV}$ of monolayer $\mathrm{MoS_2}$ and the room-temperature exciton emission of organic and perovskite systems. Conversely, if we make $R$ smaller than $a_X$, confinement dominates and the emission color is determined by the particle size (quantum dots). The Rydberg exciton of (3), in the opposite limit, has reached the point of “making an atom of $\mu\mathrm{m}$ size in a solid.” And as (4) drives home, all of this is just another parameter point of the same equation as that of positronium in vacuum. There are few examples that show so succinctly that elementary particles and materials share the same equation.

E.8 Solutions for Chapter 8: The Feynman Rules — Decay Rates and Scattering Cross Sections

Exercise 8.1: Partial widths of the $Z^0$ boson and the number of neutrino generations

Problem (restated)

The total width of the $Z^0$ is $\Gamma_{\text{tot}}=2.4952\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and the branching ratios are $\mathrm{BR}(e^+e^-)=3.363\%$ and $\mathrm{BR}(\text{invisible})=20.00\%$ (Table 8.1).

(1) Find the lifetime $\tau$ of the $Z^0$ in seconds. Also compute $c\tau$ and compare it with the proton diameter $1.7\ \mathrm{fm}$.

(2) Find the partial width $\Gamma(Z\to e^+e^-)$ in MeV.

(3) The Standard Model predicts a partial width per neutrino generation of $\Gamma_{\nu\bar\nu}=167.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$ (the predicted invisible width $\Gamma_{\text{inv}}^{\text{SM}}=501.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$ divided by 3). Find the number of neutrino generations $N_\nu$ from the invisible width.

Solution

Strategy. We use only two tools from Section 8.1 of this book. One is the relation between decay rate and lifetime, $\tau=1/\Gamma$ ($\tau=\hbar/\Gamma$ when SI units are restored); the other is the definition of the branching ratio, $\mathrm{BR}_i=\Gamma_i/\Gamma_{\text{tot}}$, that is, $\Gamma_i=\mathrm{BR}_i\times\Gamma_{\text{tot}}$. No new physics is needed; unit conversion and multiplication carry us all the way. Yet the conclusion that emerges is the single line that fixed the generation structure of the Standard Model: “there are only three kinds of light neutrinos.”

(1) In natural units, $\tau=1/\Gamma$. To convert to seconds we multiply by $\hbar$: $$ \tau = \frac{\hbar}{\Gamma_{\text{tot}}}. $$ Using $\hbar = 6.582\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{MeV\,s} = 6.582\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{GeV\,s}$ and substituting $\Gamma_{\text{tot}}=2.4952\ \mathrm{GeV}$, we obtain $$ \tau = \frac{6.582\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{GeV\,s}}{2.4952\ \mathrm{GeV}} = 2.638\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{s}. $$ Next we find $c\tau$. Since $c=2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$, $$ c\tau = 2.998\times10^{8}\times2.638\times10^{-25} = 7.91\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{m} = 7.91\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{fm}. $$ The same number follows in one line from $\hbar c = 197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$: $$ c\tau = \frac{\hbar c}{\Gamma_{\text{tot}}} = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{2495.2\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 7.908\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{fm}. $$ The ratio to the proton diameter, $1.7\ \mathrm{fm}$, is $$ \frac{1.7\ \mathrm{fm}}{0.0791\ \mathrm{fm}} = 21.5 $$ That is, even traveling at the speed of light, the $Z^0$ decays after covering only $1/21$ of a proton diameter. In principle, no track is left. Hence the lifetime of the $Z^0$ cannot be measured from a track length; instead we sweep the center-of-mass energy of $e^+e^-$ and measure it as the width of the invariant-mass distribution (the Breit–Wigner FWHM, Section 8.7.4 of this book). This is why Table 8.1 lists $\Gamma$ rather than $\tau$ in the entry for the $Z^0$.

(2) The partial width is just the branching ratio times the total width. Since $\Gamma_{\text{tot}}=2.4952\ \mathrm{GeV}=2495.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $$ \Gamma(Z\to e^+e^-) = \mathrm{BR}(e^+e^-)\times\Gamma_{\text{tot}} = 0.03363\times 2495.2\ \mathrm{MeV} = 83.91\ \mathrm{MeV}\ \simeq\ 83.9\ \mathrm{MeV}. $$ This is also consistent with the PDG 2022 value $\Gamma(Z\to\ell^+\ell^-)=83.984\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Note that this $83.9\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is “the rate at which the $Z$ decays into $e^+e^-$,” not “the lifetime of the $Z$ until it decays into $e^+e^-$.” What determines the lifetime is always the total width $\Gamma_{\text{tot}}$; a partial width is merely one term in the sum $\Gamma_{\text{tot}}=\sum_i\Gamma_i$ (Section 8.1.2 of this book). If the $Z$ decayed only into $e^+e^-$, its lifetime would be $\hbar/83.9\ \mathrm{MeV}=7.84\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{s}$, about 30 times longer than the actual value $2.64\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{s}$. The more channels there are, the shorter the lifetime—this is the foundation of the argument in (3).

It helps to check two more things here. The first is lepton universality. The value $\mathrm{BR}(\ell^+\ell^-)=3.37\%$ in Table 8.1 is the same for each of $e,\mu,\tau$, and in terms of the partial width, $$ \Gamma(Z\to\ell^+\ell^-) = 0.0337\times2495.2\ \mathrm{MeV} = 84.1\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ which agrees, within rounding, with the value $\Gamma(Z\to e^+e^-)=83.9\ \mathrm{MeV}$ just obtained. The $Z$ does not distinguish generations. The total for the three charged leptons is $3\times84.1=252\ \mathrm{MeV}$, exactly $10.1\%$ of the total width.

The second is the ratio to the value $\Gamma_{\nu\bar\nu}=167.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$ used in (3): $$ \frac{\Gamma_{\nu\bar\nu}}{\Gamma(Z\to e^+e^-)} = \frac{167.2}{83.9} = 1.99 . $$ A single neutrino species appears to couple to the $Z$ almost twice as strongly as the electron. This is no accident. The coupling of the $Z$ is governed by $\Gamma\propto g_V^2+g_A^2$; for the electron, $g_V=-\tfrac12+2\sin^2\theta_W = -0.038$ is nearly zero thanks to $\sin^2\theta_W\simeq0.231$, so effectively only $g_A^2=1/4$ contributes. For the neutrino, on the other hand, $g_V=g_A=\tfrac12$, so $g_V^2+g_A^2=1/2$. The ratio is $(1/2)/(1/4)=2$ (including $g_V^2=0.0014$, it is $0.5/0.2514=1.99$)—the structure of the weak neutral current, which we derive in Chapter 12, shows up in this single number.

(3) We obtain the invisible width by the same procedure: $$ \Gamma_{\text{inv}} = 0.2000\times2495.2\ \mathrm{MeV} = 499.0\ \mathrm{MeV}. $$ “Invisible” means a final state that leaves no signal whatsoever in the detector, that is, $Z\to\nu\bar\nu$. If there are $N_\nu$ kinds of neutrinos, each contributes $\Gamma_{\nu\bar\nu}$, and rates add (the relation $\Gamma_{\text{tot}}=\sum_i\Gamma_i$ of Section 8.1.2 of this book), so $$ \Gamma_{\text{inv}} = N_\nu\,\Gamma_{\nu\bar\nu} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad N_\nu = \frac{\Gamma_{\text{inv}}}{\Gamma_{\nu\bar\nu}} = \frac{499.0\ \mathrm{MeV}}{167.2\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 2.984. $$ Within the measurement error, $N_\nu = 3$.

Verification. We check whether the branching ratios in Table 8.1 sum to $1$. The hadrons contribute $69.91\%$, the invisible channel $20.00\%$, and each of the three charged leptons $3.37\%$, so $$ 69.91 + 20.00 + 3\times3.37 = 100.02\ \% $$ which satisfies $\sum_i\mathrm{BR}_i=1$ (Section 8.1.2 of this book) within rounding error. We also check the dimensions. Since $[\hbar]=$ energy $\times$ time and $[\Gamma]=$ energy, $[\hbar/\Gamma]=$ time, as it should be. And $N_\nu$ is a ratio of widths, hence dimensionless, which is also consistent.

Meaning. The one line in (3) is the greatest result that LEP produced over several years starting in 1989. One produces a large number of $Z^0$, measures the total width, and subtracts the widths of all the visible final states; what remains is the width of the “nothing is seen” channel. Dividing it by the Standard Model prediction per generation gives $3$. That is, there are exactly three kinds of neutrinos light enough for the $Z$ to decay into them ($m_\nu<m_Z/2$) in the universe. Many experiments have searched for fourth-generation quarks and leptons, but this $N_\nu=3$ remains one of the strongest constraints.

The procedure itself is exactly the same as the analysis of a phosphor in materials science. Measuring the luminescence lifetime $\tau$ gives $\Gamma_{\text{tot}}$, and measuring the luminescence quantum yield gives the branching ratio of the “visible channel.” What remains is the rate of the nonradiative process (thermal relaxation to the lattice), which cannot be measured directly and so can only be obtained by subtraction. The invisible width of the $Z$ and the nonradiative relaxation rate of a phosphor are quantities that are the same even in the way they are measured.

Exercise 8.2: The barn, luminosity, and event counts

Problem (restated)

(1) Express $1\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$ in barns. Also express $1\ \mathrm{fm^2}$ in barns.

(2) Using $\sigma(e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-) = 4\pi\alpha^2/(3s) = 86.9\ \mathrm{nb}/s\,[\mathrm{GeV^2}]$, find $\sigma(e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-)$ in nb at $\sqrt{s}=10\ \mathrm{GeV}$. How many events are obtained when an integrated luminosity of $1\ \mathrm{ab^{-1}}$ ($=10^{18}\ \mathrm{barn^{-1}}$) is accumulated?

(3) Using the result of Worked Example 8.1 ($7.7\times10^6$ Higgs bosons in LHC Run 2), find the number of $H\to\gamma\gamma$ events ($\mathrm{BR}=0.227\%$). If the product of the detection efficiency and the selection efficiency is $30\%$, how many events finally remain?

Solution

Strategy. Everything we need is the definition of the barn in Section 8.1.4 of this book together with $(\hbar c)^2 = 0.3894\ \mathrm{GeV^2\,mbarn}$, and $N=\mathcal{L}_{\text{int}}\sigma$ from Section 8.1.5. Particle-physics experiments are planned with these two equations—“what is the cross section of this process?” and “how many $\mathrm{fb^{-1}}$ must be accumulated to get how many events?” The calculation itself is only a change of units, but an error in the order of magnitude would make the experiment infeasible, so we write out the path of conversion explicitly.

(1) In natural units, length is identified with $1/$energy. The conversion factor is $\hbar c$: $$ \hbar c = 197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm} = 0.197327\ \mathrm{GeV\,fm}. $$ Squaring both sides gives $$ (\hbar c)^2 = (0.197327)^2\ \mathrm{GeV^2\,fm^2} = 0.038938\ \mathrm{GeV^2\,fm^2}. $$ In natural units $\hbar c = 1$ is understood, so this equation may be read as “$1\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}} = 0.038938\ \mathrm{fm^2}$.” It remains to convert $\mathrm{fm^2}$ to barns. The definition of the barn (Section 8.1.4 of this book) is $1\ \mathrm{barn}=10^{-28}\ \mathrm{m^2}$, while $1\ \mathrm{fm}=10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}$, so $$ 1\ \mathrm{fm^2} = 10^{-30}\ \mathrm{m^2} = \frac{10^{-30}}{10^{-28}}\ \mathrm{barn} = 10^{-2}\ \mathrm{barn} = 10\ \mathrm{mbarn}. $$ This is the answer to the second half of (1). Using it, $$ 1\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}} = 0.038938\ \mathrm{fm^2} = 0.038938\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{barn} = 3.894\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{barn} = 0.3894\ \mathrm{mbarn}. $$ The expression $(\hbar c)^2 = 0.3894\ \mathrm{GeV^2\,mbarn}$ in the main text is these two lines compressed into one.

(2) $\sqrt{s}=10\ \mathrm{GeV}$ means $s = 100\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$. Substituting into the given formula, $$ \sigma(e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-) = \frac{86.9\ \mathrm{nb}}{100} = 0.869\ \mathrm{nb}. $$ The number of events is $N=\mathcal{L}_{\text{int}}\sigma$. We match the units. Since $1\ \mathrm{ab}=10^{-18}\ \mathrm{barn}$, $1\ \mathrm{ab^{-1}}=10^{18}\ \mathrm{barn^{-1}}$, and since $1\ \mathrm{nb}=10^{-9}\ \mathrm{barn}$, this can be read as $1\ \mathrm{ab^{-1}} = 10^{9}\ \mathrm{nb^{-1}}$. Therefore $$ N = 0.869\ \mathrm{nb}\times 10^{9}\ \mathrm{nb^{-1}} = 8.69\times10^{8}\ \text{events}. $$ This is about 900 million events. The $B$ factory (Belle II) aims at several tens of $\mathrm{ab^{-1}}$ (design goal $50\ \mathrm{ab^{-1}}$) at $\sqrt{s}=10.58\ \mathrm{GeV}$ precisely to obtain statistics of this order of magnitude.

(3) Of the Higgs bosons produced, those that decay into $\gamma\gamma$ number, after multiplying by the branching ratio, $$ N_{\gamma\gamma}^{\text{produced}} = 7.7\times10^{6}\times 0.00227 = 1.75\times10^{4}\ \text{decays}. $$ Of these, those that are recorded by the detector and survive the selection are obtained by multiplying by the efficiency $30\%$: $$ N_{\gamma\gamma}^{\text{observed}} = 1.75\times10^{4}\times0.30 = 5.2\times10^{3}\ \text{events}. $$

Verification. We reproduce the coefficient $86.9\ \mathrm{nb}$ of (2) ourselves, using the conversion factor built in (1). With $\alpha=1/137.036$, $$ \frac{4\pi\alpha^2}{3} = \frac{4\pi}{3\times(137.036)^2} = \frac{12.566}{56337} = 2.2306\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}. $$ Multiplying by $0.3894\ \mathrm{mbarn/GeV^{-2}}$ gives $$ 2.2306\times10^{-4}\times0.3894\ \mathrm{mbarn} = 8.686\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{mbarn} = 86.9\ \mathrm{nb} $$ (where we used $1\ \mathrm{mbarn}=10^{6}\ \mathrm{nb}$). This agrees with the $86.9\ \mathrm{nb}$ in the main text. In fact, the true value is $86.85\ \mathrm{nb}$ (obtained with the more precise $(\hbar c)^2=0.389379\ \mathrm{GeV^2\,mbarn}$), exactly on the borderline; the $86.8$ in Appendix B is its truncation and the $86.9$ in Chapter 8 and Appendix D is its rounding up, and both refer to the same quantity. Thus the formula $\sigma=4\pi\alpha^2/(3s)$ and the numerical form $86.9\ \mathrm{nb}/s[\mathrm{GeV^2}]$ are the same thing, and we have confirmed that the conversion factor of (1) is used correctly.

Meaning. The relation “cross section $\times$ integrated luminosity $=$ number of events” is the very design principle of particle-physics experiments. The figure of $5.2\times10^{3}$ events left in (3) is by no means comfortable, considering that the $\gamma\gamma$ continuum background rides on it at more than $10^2$ times that level. This is exactly why the Higgs search is carried out not by “counting events” but by looking for a narrow peak standing on the $\gamma\gamma$ invariant-mass distribution. To keep the signal from being buried under the background, improving the mass resolution (= the energy resolution of the electromagnetic calorimeter) is decisive, and there the choice of materials such as crystal scintillators and liquid argon makes or breaks the physics.

The same relation is used as it is on the materials-science side. In estimating activation and damage by neutron irradiation, one multiplies the neutron fluence $\Phi$ ($\mathrm{n/cm^2}$) by the cross section $\sigma$ (barn) of the nuclide to obtain the number of reactions per atom. The fact that the $\sigma_a$ listed in Table 8.2 differ by orders of magnitude translates directly into the decision of “which elements may be put into a reactor.” The luminosity of an accelerator and the fluence of an irradiation facility are quantities that play the same role.

Exercise 8.3: Momentum in two-body decay (the Källén function)

Problem (restated)

A particle of mass $M$ at rest decays into two particles of masses $m_1$ and $m_2$.

(1) Starting from energy conservation $E_1+E_2=M$ and momentum conservation $\abs{\pp_1}=\abs{\pp_2}\equiv\abs{\pp}$, derive $$ \abs{\pp} = \frac{1}{2M}\sqrt{\big[M^2-(m_1+m_2)^2\big]\big[M^2-(m_1-m_2)^2\big]}. $$

(2) Find the momentum of the muon in $\pi^+\to\mu^+\nu_\mu$ ($m_{\pi}=139.570\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_\mu=105.658\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_\nu\simeq0$).

(3) Find the momentum of the proton in $\Lambda\to p+\pi^-$ ($m_\Lambda=1115.683$, $m_p=938.272$, $m_{\pi^-}=139.570\ \mathrm{MeV}$).

Solution

Strategy. No dynamics appears in this problem at all. All we use is energy-momentum conservation and $E^2=\abs{\pp}^2+m^2$ ($p^2=m^2$ under the metric $g^{\mu\nu}=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$). The resulting $\abs{\pp}$ is the Källén function of Section 8.2.4 of this book itself, a purely kinematic quantity that does not depend at all on the content of the interaction ($\mathcal{M}$). This is exactly why the value of $\abs{\pp}$ does not change whatever theory one brings in.

(1) We work in the rest frame of the parent particle. Since the three-momentum of the initial state is zero, momentum conservation tells us that the two daughter particles have momenta of equal magnitude in exactly opposite directions: $$ \pp_2 = -\pp_1, \qquad \abs{\pp_1}=\abs{\pp_2}\equiv\abs{\pp}. $$ Their energies are $$ E_1 = \sqrt{\abs{\pp}^2+m_1^2}, \qquad E_2 = \sqrt{\abs{\pp}^2+m_2^2} $$ and energy conservation is $E_1+E_2=M$.

Step 1 (find $E_1$). Write $E_2=M-E_1$ and square both sides: $$ E_2^2 = M^2 - 2ME_1 + E_1^2. $$ Substituting $E_2^2=\abs{\pp}^2+m_2^2$ on the left-hand side and $\abs{\pp}^2+m_1^2$ for $E_1^2$ on the right-hand side, we get $$ \abs{\pp}^2+m_2^2 = M^2-2ME_1+\abs{\pp}^2+m_1^2. $$ The key point is that $\abs{\pp}^2$ cancels on both sides. What remains is a linear equation in $E_1$: $$ 2ME_1 = M^2+m_1^2-m_2^2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad E_1 = \frac{M^2+m_1^2-m_2^2}{2M}. $$ Note that $E_1$ is completely determined by the masses alone. The energy of a daughter particle in a two-body decay is monochromatic.

Step 2 (compute $\abs{\pp}^2$). Substitute into $\abs{\pp}^2=E_1^2-m_1^2$: $$ \abs{\pp}^2 = \left(\frac{M^2+m_1^2-m_2^2}{2M}\right)^2 - m_1^2 = \frac{\big(M^2+m_1^2-m_2^2\big)^2 - 4M^2m_1^2}{4M^2}. $$

Step 3 (factor the numerator). The numerator has the form $X^2-Y^2$ (with $X=M^2+m_1^2-m_2^2$, $Y=2Mm_1$), so $$ X^2-Y^2 = \big(M^2+m_1^2-2Mm_1-m_2^2\big)\big(M^2+m_1^2+2Mm_1-m_2^2\big) = \big[(M-m_1)^2-m_2^2\big]\big[(M+m_1)^2-m_2^2\big]. $$ Expanding each of these further as a difference of squares, $$ = (M-m_1-m_2)(M-m_1+m_2)\,(M+m_1-m_2)(M+m_1+m_2). $$ We regroup the four factors. Pairing the first and fourth factors gives $$ (M-m_1-m_2)(M+m_1+m_2) = M^2-(m_1+m_2)^2, $$ and pairing the second and third factors gives $$ (M-m_1+m_2)(M+m_1-m_2) = \big[M-(m_1-m_2)\big]\big[M+(m_1-m_2)\big] = M^2-(m_1-m_2)^2. $$ Therefore $$ \abs{\pp}^2 = \frac{\big[M^2-(m_1+m_2)^2\big]\big[M^2-(m_1-m_2)^2\big]}{4M^2}, $$ $$ \abs{\pp} = \frac{1}{2M}\sqrt{\big[M^2-(m_1+m_2)^2\big]\big[M^2-(m_1-m_2)^2\big]} $$ This is the desired formula. Expanding the brackets, $$ \abs{\pp} = \frac{1}{2M}\sqrt{M^4+m_1^4+m_2^4-2M^2m_1^2-2M^2m_2^2-2m_1^2m_2^2} = \frac{\sqrt{\lambda(M^2,m_1^2,m_2^2)}}{2M} $$ which agrees with the form of the Källén function $\lambda(x,y,z)=x^2+y^2+z^2-2xy-2yz-2zx$ of Section 8.2.4 of this book. The first factor $M^2-(m_1+m_2)^2$ vanishes at $M=m_1+m_2$, so one can see at a glance that the threshold is built into this formula. For $M<m_1+m_2$ the quantity under the root is negative and $\abs{\pp}$ is imaginary; that is, the decay cannot occur.

(2) For $m_\nu=0$ the formula simplifies remarkably. Setting $m_2=0$, both brackets become $M^2-m_1^2$, so the square root comes off directly: $$ \abs{\pp} = \frac{M^2-m_1^2}{2M}. $$ We apply this to $\pi^+\to\mu^+\nu_\mu$. Since $m_\pi=139.570\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $m_\mu=105.658\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $$ m_\pi^2 = 19479.78\ \mathrm{MeV^2}, \qquad m_\mu^2 = 11163.61\ \mathrm{MeV^2}, $$ $$ \abs{\pp} = \frac{19479.78-11163.61}{2\times139.570} = \frac{8316.17}{279.14} = 29.79\ \mathrm{MeV}. $$ Both the muon and the neutrino fly off with momentum of magnitude $29.79\ \mathrm{MeV}$ in opposite directions.

(3) In $\Lambda\to p+\pi^-$ all three masses are finite, so we use the factored form as it is. With $M=1115.683$, $m_1=m_p=938.272$, and $m_2=m_{\pi^-}=139.570\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $$ M^2 = 1.244749\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{MeV^2}, $$ $$ (m_p+m_{\pi})^2 = (1077.842)^2 = 1.161743\times10^{6}, \qquad (m_p-m_{\pi})^2 = (798.702)^2 = 6.379249\times10^{5}. $$ Taking the differences, $$ M^2-(m_p+m_\pi)^2 = 8.30052\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{MeV^2}, \qquad M^2-(m_p-m_\pi)^2 = 6.068237\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{MeV^2}. $$ The product is $5.03695\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{MeV^4}$, and its square root is $2.24432\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{MeV^2}$. Dividing by $2M=2231.366\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $$ \abs{\pp} = \frac{2.24432\times10^{5}}{2231.366} = 100.58\ \mathrm{MeV}. $$ Both the proton and the $\pi^-$ fly off with momentum $100.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

Verification. We check in three ways.

First, for (2) we verify energy conservation directly. With $E_\mu=\sqrt{(29.79)^2+(105.658)^2}=109.78\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $E_\nu=\abs{\pp}=29.79\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $$ E_\mu+E_\nu = 109.78+29.79 = 139.57\ \mathrm{MeV} = m_\pi $$ which matches exactly.

Second, for (3) we compute independently from the formula of Step 1. $$ E_p = \frac{M^2+m_p^2-m_\pi^2}{2M} = 943.65\ \mathrm{MeV}, \qquad \abs{\pp}=\sqrt{E_p^2-m_p^2}=\sqrt{(943.65)^2-(938.272)^2}=100.58\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ which agrees with the answer from the factored formula. Also, from $E_\pi = M-E_p = 172.04\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $\sqrt{E_\pi^2-m_\pi^2}=100.58\ \mathrm{MeV}$ gives the same value.

Third, we compare with the nonrelativistic approximation. The $Q$ value of the $\Lambda$ decay is $Q=M-m_p-m_\pi=37.84\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and the reduced mass is $\mu = m_pm_\pi/(m_p+m_\pi)=121.50\ \mathrm{MeV}$, so nonrelativistically $\abs{\pp}\simeq\sqrt{2\mu Q}=95.9\ \mathrm{MeV}$. This differs from the exact value $100.58\ \mathrm{MeV}$ by only $5\%$. Since the $\pi$ meson is somewhat relativistic ($E_\pi/m_\pi=1.23$), the size of this deviation is reasonable.

Meaning. In a two-body decay, both the energy and the momentum of the daughter particles are determined by the masses alone. That is, the spectrum of a two-body decay is a monochromatic line. This is decisive in experiments. In hypernuclear experiments the decay of the $\Lambda$ can be identified because a proton (or $\pi^-$) with the definite momentum $100.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$ emerges, and for the same reason a $29.8\ \mathrm{MeV}$ muon (kinetic energy $4.12\ \mathrm{MeV}$) can be used to check the purity of a $\pi^+$ beam. Conversely, when the decay is into three or more bodies, the sharing of momentum acquires degrees of freedom and the spectrum becomes a continuous distribution. That Pauli postulated the neutrino from the continuity of the electron spectrum in $\beta$ decay was an argument based on nothing other than this kinematics: “monochromatic for two bodies, continuous for three.”

On the materials-science side, too, the same logic is used routinely. That $\alpha$ decay gives a monochromatic line spectrum, and that characteristic X-ray lines and Mössbauer lines are sharp, are both because the final state is effectively two-body. From the position of a measured peak one can work backward to how many bodies the reaction involved—kinematics tells us what can be said without knowing the dynamics.

Exercise 8.4: Lifetime in the ABC model (a different set of masses)

Problem (restated)

Let $m_A=5\ \mathrm{GeV}$, $m_B=2\ \mathrm{GeV}$, $m_C=1\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and $g=0.5\ \mathrm{GeV}$.

(1) Find $\abs{\pp}$.

(2) Find $\Gamma(A\to B+C)$ in MeV and the lifetime $\tau$ in seconds.

(3) If only $m_B$ is increased from $2\ \mathrm{GeV}$ to $3.9\ \mathrm{GeV}$ (just barely reaching the threshold $m_B+m_C=4.9\ \mathrm{GeV}$), by what factor does $\Gamma$ change? Confirm how the phase-space suppression works.

Solution

Strategy. This is a complete replay of Section 8.4 of this book. The amplitude is $\mathcal{M}=-g$ (one vertex, external-line factors equal to 1, no internal lines), so $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2=g^2$ and there is no angular dependence. We simply insert the $\abs{\pp}$ derived in Exercise 8.3 into the two-body decay formula $\Gamma=S\abs{\pp}\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2/(8\pi m_A^2)$. Since $B$ and $C$ in the final state are different kinds of particles, the statistical factor is $S=1$. Part (3) asks how strongly the phase-space factor $\abs{\pp}$ acts when only the masses are moved and the amplitude is left completely unchanged.

(1) Insert $M=m_A=5$, $m_1=m_B=2$, $m_2=m_C=1\ \mathrm{GeV}$ into the formula of Exercise 8.3(1). Since $m_B+m_C=3$ and $m_B-m_C=1$, $$ \abs{\pp} = \frac{1}{2\times5}\sqrt{(25-9)(25-1)} = \frac{1}{10}\sqrt{16\times24} = \frac{\sqrt{384}}{10} = \frac{19.5959}{10} = 1.9596\ \mathrm{GeV}. $$ The threshold is $m_B+m_C=3\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and $m_A=5\ \mathrm{GeV}$ is well above it. There is ample phase space.

Let us check that the daughter-particle energies give the same value. Inserting $M=5$, $m_1=m_B=2$, $m_2=m_C=1$ into the formula of Step 1 of Exercise 8.3 gives $$ E_B = \frac{25+4-1}{10} = 2.8\ \mathrm{GeV}, \qquad E_C = \frac{25+1-4}{10} = 2.2\ \mathrm{GeV} $$ and the sum $E_B+E_C=5.0\ \mathrm{GeV}=m_A$ satisfies energy conservation. The momenta are $$ \sqrt{E_B^2-m_B^2} = \sqrt{7.84-4} = \sqrt{3.84} = 1.9596\ \mathrm{GeV}, \qquad \sqrt{E_C^2-m_C^2} = \sqrt{4.84-1} = \sqrt{3.84} = 1.9596\ \mathrm{GeV} $$ so both give the same $\abs{\pp}$. Since $\abs{\pp}/m_A = 0.39$ and $E_C/m_C=2.2$, the particle $C$ flies out fairly relativistically.

(2) Substitute into the formula of Section 8.4.2 of this book, $$ \Gamma(A\to B+C) = \frac{g^2\,\abs{\pp}}{8\pi m_A^2} $$ With $g^2=(0.5\ \mathrm{GeV})^2=0.25\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ and $8\pi m_A^2 = 8\pi\times25 = 628.32\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$, $$ \Gamma = \frac{0.25\times1.9596}{628.32}\ \mathrm{GeV} = \frac{0.48990}{628.32}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 7.797\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 0.7797\ \mathrm{MeV}. $$ Now convert to a lifetime. Using $\hbar=6.582\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{MeV\,s}$, $$ \tau = \frac{\hbar}{\Gamma} = \frac{6.582\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{MeV\,s}}{0.7797\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 8.44\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{s}. $$ That is, $\Gamma=0.780\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $\tau=8.44\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{s}$.

(3) Changing to $m_B=3.9\ \mathrm{GeV}$, we have $m_B+m_C=4.9$ and $m_B-m_C=2.9$, so $$ \abs{\pp}' = \frac{1}{10}\sqrt{\big(25-(4.9)^2\big)\big(25-(2.9)^2\big)} = \frac{1}{10}\sqrt{(25-24.01)(25-8.41)} = \frac{1}{10}\sqrt{0.99\times16.59} $$ $$ = \frac{\sqrt{16.4241}}{10} = \frac{4.0527}{10} = 0.4053\ \mathrm{GeV}. $$ The decisive point here is that the amplitude has not changed at all. $\mathcal{M}=-g$ does not depend on the masses, and neither $g$ nor $m_A$ has been moved. Therefore the ratio of the decay rates is exactly the ratio of $\abs{\pp}$: $$ \frac{\Gamma'}{\Gamma} = \frac{\abs{\pp}'}{\abs{\pp}} = \frac{0.4053}{1.9596} = 0.2068 \qquad\left(=\frac{1}{4.84}\right). $$ In numbers, $\Gamma' = 0.2068\times0.7797 = 0.1613\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and the lifetime correspondingly lengthens to $\tau'=4.08\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{s}$. The rate drops to about $1/4.8$, that is, roughly one fifth.

Why it drops so much becomes clear if we rewrite the first factor: $$ m_A^2-(m_B+m_C)^2 = \big(m_A-m_B-m_C\big)\big(m_A+m_B+m_C\big) = 0.1\times9.9 = 0.99\ \mathrm{GeV^2}. $$ The margin above threshold, $\Delta\equiv m_A-m_B-m_C$, has decreased from $2\ \mathrm{GeV}$ to $0.1\ \mathrm{GeV}$, which reduces the first factor $16\to0.99\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$, a decrease by a factor of about $16$ (the sum factor $m_A+m_B+m_C$ grows $8\to9.9$, so the decrease is slightly milder than the ratio $1/20$ of $\Delta$). Because $\abs{\pp}$ contains a square root, it decreases in proportion to $\sqrt{\Delta}$—this is the threshold law.

Verification. First, look at the dimensions. $[g^2]=$ mass$^2$, $[\abs{\pp}]=$ mass, and $[m_A^2]=$ mass$^2$, so $[\Gamma]=$ mass$^{2+1-2}=$ mass$^1$, which is correct. On the amplitude side as well, $[\mathcal{M}]=[g]=$ mass$^1$ agrees with the general rule $[\mathcal{M}]=$ mass$^{4-n}$ for a process with $n=3$ external lines (Section 8.2.1 of this book).

Next, we check the validity of perturbation theory. The coupling constant has mass dimension, so the dimensionless ratio that measures its smallness is $g/m_A = 0.5/5 = 0.1$, or, more precisely, the criterion of Section 8.4.2 of this book, $g^2/(16\pi^2m_A^2) = 0.25/(16\pi^2\times25)=6.3\times10^{-5}$. Both are far smaller than $1$, so it is legitimate to calculate only at lowest order. Also, $\Gamma/m_A = 0.780/5000 = 1.6\times10^{-4}$, so this $A$ is a narrow resonance whose width is only $0.016\%$ of its mass (comparable to the $2\times10^{-4}$ of Worked Example 8.2).

Finally, we verify the threshold law independently. In the limit $\Delta\ll m_A$, $$ \abs{\pp}\simeq\frac{1}{2m_A}\sqrt{\Delta\,(m_A+m_B+m_C)\big[m_A^2-(m_B-m_C)^2\big]} $$ so $\abs{\pp}\propto\sqrt{\Delta}$. We therefore rewrite the ratio $\abs{\pp}'/\abs{\pp}$ as a product of three factors. $$ \frac{\abs{\pp}'}{\abs{\pp}} = \sqrt{\frac{\Delta'}{\Delta}}\times \sqrt{\frac{(m_A+m_B'+m_C)}{(m_A+m_B+m_C)}}\times \sqrt{\frac{m_A^2-(m_B'-m_C)^2}{m_A^2-(m_B-m_C)^2}} . $$ Inserting numbers, $\Delta$ goes from $2\to0.1$, that is, by $1/20$, giving $\sqrt{1/20}=0.2236$; the sum of the masses goes from $8\to9.9$, giving $\sqrt{9.9/8}=1.1124$; and the second factor goes from $24\to16.59$, giving $\sqrt{16.59/24}=0.8314$. Multiplying them together, $$ 0.2236\times1.1124\times0.8314 = 0.2068 $$ which agrees to the fourth decimal place with the $0.2068$ obtained by the direct calculation in (3). The crude estimate from the threshold law, “$\sqrt{1/20}=0.224$ times,” differs slightly from the actual factor $0.207$ because the two factors other than $\Delta$ (the sum factor, which grows by a factor of $1.11$, and the second factor, which shrinks by a factor of $0.83$) nearly cancel each other while leaving a slight net decrease. The $\sqrt{\Delta}$ law is an asymptotic law that becomes exact only in the immediate neighborhood of the threshold, and in the present problem, with $\Delta/m_A=0.02$, it is the correct picture that a correction of this size appears.

Meaning. The claim of this problem can be put in one sentence: a decay can be slow for only two reasons: the force is weak, or the phase space is narrow (Section 8.2.2 of this book). Here, without touching the force ($g$) at all, the rate dropped to one fifth through phase space alone. The same holds for real particles: the neutron lifetime of about $878\ \mathrm{s}$ is extraordinarily long not only because the weak interaction is weak, but also because the $Q$ value is only $0.78\ \mathrm{MeV}$, so the phase space is extremely narrow (the $\beta$-decay rate is proportional to $Q^5$).

In materials science, too, the same “threshold law” shows up everywhere. The direct-transition absorption edge of a semiconductor rises as $\alpha\propto\sqrt{\hbar\omega-E_g}$ because the joint density of states of the final states is of the $\sqrt{E}$ type, which is exactly the same origin as that of $\abs{\pp}\propto\sqrt{\Delta}$ in this problem (Section 8.7.2 of this book). The reason absorption rises from zero even though the transition matrix element is nearly constant near the band edge is that “the places one can go are few.” The phase-space suppression in particle physics and the shape of the optical absorption edge are different faces of the same formula.

Exercise 8.5: $A+B\to A+B$ scattering ($s$-channel and $u$-channel)

Problem (restated)

Consider $A+B\to A+B$ in the ABC model at lowest order (two vertices). Let the incoming particles be $A(p_1)$, $B(p_2)$ and the outgoing particles $A(p_3)$, $B(p_4)$.

(1) Draw all the diagrams that can be drawn. Verify that there are two diagrams whose internal line is $C$, and state for each whether $q^2$ of the internal line is $s$ or $u$. Also explain why a $t$-channel diagram cannot be drawn.

(2) Write down the invariant amplitude $\mathcal{M}$.

(3) Under what condition can the denominator $s-m_C^2$ of the $s$-channel propagator vanish? State what happens then, relating it to Section 8.7.4.

(4) What is the statistical factor $S$? Write down $\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega$.

Solution

Strategy. We simply apply the Feynman rules of Section 8.3.2 of this book in order, but the pitfall is Rule 1 (do not miss a single diagram that can be drawn). So rather than counting by intuition, we first fix the skeleton of the diagrams with the counting formulas $I=(3V-E)/2$ and $L=I-V+1$ of Section 8.6.1 of this book, and then examine the assignments of external lines exhaustively. In this way we can argue that “there are only two.”

(1) At lowest order there are $V=2$ vertices and $E=4$ external lines. Every vertex of the ABC model has three lines, so there are $3V=6$ line ends in all; four of them are ends of external lines, and the remaining two pair up to form an internal line: $$ I = \frac{3V-E}{2} = \frac{6-4}{2} = 1, \qquad L = I-V+1 = 1-2+1 = 0 . $$ That is, there is one internal line, there are no loops, and every diagram is a tree diagram.

What remains is to count the ways of distributing the four external lines two each to the two vertices. There are only the following three distributions.

(i) $\{A(p_1),B(p_2)\}$ and $\{A(p_3),B(p_4)\}$. Each vertex has one $A$ and one $B$, so if the remaining line is taken to be $C$ we get an $A$–$B$–$C$ three-pronged junction, which is allowed as a vertex of the model. The internal line is $C$. The four-momentum of the internal line is $q=p_1+p_2$ from conservation at the left vertex, and $$ q^2 = (p_1+p_2)^2 = s . $$ This is the $s$-channel. Physically, it is the process in which $A$ and $B$ merge into a single $C$, and that $C$ splits again into $A+B$.

(ii) $\{A(p_1),B(p_4)\}$ and $\{B(p_2),A(p_3)\}$. Here too each vertex has one $A$ and one $B$, so connecting them with an internal line of $C$ is allowed. The momentum of the internal line is $q=p_1-p_4$, and $$ q^2 = (p_1-p_4)^2 = u . $$ This is the $u$-channel. It is the exchange diagram in which the incoming $A$ emits $B(p_4)$ and becomes $C$, and that $C$ is absorbed by the other $B(p_2)$, which becomes $A(p_3)$.

(iii) $\{A(p_1),A(p_3)\}$ and $\{B(p_2),B(p_4)\}$. In this assignment, two $A$ lines gather at one vertex. Whatever particle we take for the internal line, that vertex would have the form $A$–$A$–$X$. The interaction of the ABC model is only the single term $\Lag_{\text{int}}=-g\,\phi_A\phi_B\phi_C$, and an $A$–$A$–$X$ vertex does not exist. Hence this diagram cannot be drawn. The momentum of the internal line is $q=p_1-p_3$, with $q^2=t$, so this model has no $t$-channel.

From the above, there are exactly two lowest-order diagrams, the $s$-channel and the $u$-channel. Which channels appear is determined solely by the forms of the vertices the model has—this is exactly the reverse of the same argument by which no $s$-channel appeared for $A+A\to B+B$ in Section 8.5.1 of this book.

(2) We apply the rules to the $s$-channel diagram. The two vertices give $(-\ii g)^2=-g^2$, the internal line (mass $m_C$) gives $\ii/(q^2-m_C^2)$, there are two $\delta$ functions for momentum conservation at the vertices, and there is one integral $\int\dd^4q/(2\pi)^4$ for the one internal line. By exactly the same procedure as in Section 8.5.2 of this book, one $\delta$ function enforces $q=p_1+p_2$ and eliminates the integral, and the other remains as the overall $(2\pi)^4\delta^4(p_1+p_2-p_3-p_4)$. Following Rule 8, we strip off the overall $\delta$ function and $(2\pi)^4$ and multiply by $-\ii$, which gives $$ \mathcal{M}_s = (-\ii)\times(-g^2)\times\frac{\ii}{s-m_C^2} = (-\ii)(\ii)\times\frac{-g^2}{s-m_C^2} = \frac{-g^2}{s-m_C^2} $$ (we used $(-\ii)(\ii)=-\ii^2=+1$). For the $u$-channel, only the momentum of the internal line changes to $q=p_1-p_4$, and the coefficient is exactly the same. Following Rule 9, we add the two diagrams with the same sign: $$ \mathcal{M} = -g^2\left[\frac{1}{s-m_C^2} + \frac{1}{u-m_C^2}\right]. $$

(3) The denominator vanishes when $$ s = m_C^2, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad \sqrt{s} = m_C $$ On the other hand, the physical region of this reaction is where $A$ and $B$ can be prepared as real particles in the initial state, that is, $$ \sqrt{s}\ \ge\ m_A+m_B $$ Therefore the pole can be reached only when $$ m_C \ \ge\ m_A+m_B $$ that is, only when $C$ is heavy enough to decay into $A+B$.

What happens then? If we collide the particles with $\sqrt{s}=m_C$, the exchanged $C$ is produced not as a virtual particle but as a real particle, lives for a while, and then decays into $A+B$. This is a resonance. In the lowest-order expression as it stands, the cross section would become infinite, but this is due to the approximation of assuming that $C$ is stable. As we saw in Section 8.6.4 of this book, if $C$ can decay then the self-energy has an imaginary part, and by the argument of Section 8.7.4 the denominator of the propagator is replaced by $$ s-m_C^2\ \longrightarrow\ s-m_C^2+\ii\,m_C\Gamma_C $$ Since the pole is displaced from the real axis by $\Gamma_C$, the cross section does not diverge but becomes a finite Breit–Wigner-type peak, $$ \abs{\mathcal{M}}^2 \propto \frac{1}{(s-m_C^2)^2+m_C^2\Gamma_C^2} $$ The height of the peak is proportional to $1/(m_C\Gamma_C)^2$, and the full width at half maximum (measured in $\sqrt{s}$) is $\Gamma_C$.

Note that in this situation ($m_C>m_A+m_B$) we have $m_A<m_B+m_C$, so the decay $A\to B+C$ calculated in Section 8.4 of this book is forbidden. The “model in which $A$ decays” and the “model in which $C$ appears as a resonance” are two mutually exclusive parameter regions of the same ABC model.

(4) The statistical factor $S$ is obtained by multiplying by $1/k!$ for each set of $k$ identical particles in the final state (Section 8.2.2 of this book). The present final state has one $A$ and one $B$, and there are no sets of identical particles. Therefore $$ S = 1 . $$ Furthermore, since both the initial and final states are $A$ and $B$ pairs with the same masses (elastic scattering), the formula of Section 8.2.4 of this book gives $\abs{\pp_f}=\abs{\pp_i}$, and the ratio factor is $1$. Inserting into the two-body scattering formula of Section 8.2.6 of this book, $$ \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd\Omega} = \frac{S\,\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}{64\pi^2 s}\frac{\abs{\pp_f}}{\abs{\pp_i}} = \frac{g^4}{64\pi^2 s}\left[\frac{1}{s-m_C^2}+\frac{1}{u-m_C^2}\right]^2 . $$ Here $u$ can be written as a function of $\cos\theta$ from $u = 2m_A^2+2m_B^2-s-t$, as in Section 8.5.3 of this book. Let us write it out explicitly. Since the scattering is elastic, the magnitude of the momentum in the CM frame is the same before and after: $$ \abs{\pp} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{s}}\sqrt{\big[s-(m_A+m_B)^2\big]\big[s-(m_A-m_B)^2\big]} $$ (the formula of Exercise 8.3 with $M\to\sqrt{s}$). Taking the scattering angle to be the angle $\theta$ between $\pp_1$ and $\pp_3$, $$ t = (p_1-p_3)^2 = 2m_A^2-2\big(E_1^2-\abs{\pp}^2\cos\theta\big) = -2\abs{\pp}^2\,(1-\cos\theta), $$ $$ u = 2m_A^2+2m_B^2-s-t = 2m_A^2+2m_B^2-s+2\abs{\pp}^2(1-\cos\theta) $$ (we used $E_1^2=m_A^2+\abs{\pp}^2$). That $t$ vanishes in the forward direction $\theta=0$ and equals $-4\abs{\pp}^2$ in the backward direction $\theta=\pi$ is a property peculiar to elastic scattering. Inserting this into the formula of (4), $\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega$ becomes a number at any energy and any angle.

Verification. We check at three points.

First, the dimensions. $[g^2]=$ mass$^2$ and $[s-m_C^2]=$ mass$^2$, so $[\mathcal{M}]=$ mass$^0$, that is, dimensionless. This agrees with the general rule $[\mathcal{M}]=$ mass$^{4-n}=$ mass$^0$ for a process with $n=4$ external lines (Section 8.2.1 of this book). Therefore $[\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega]=[\mathcal{M}]^2/[s]=$ mass$^{-2}$, which has the dimension of an area.

Second, the identity for the Mandelstam variables. Inserting the present external-line masses $m_A^2+m_B^2+m_A^2+m_B^2$ into $s+t+u=\sum_i m_i^2$ of Section 8.5.1 of this book gives $s+t+u=2m_A^2+2m_B^2$, the same right-hand side as in the case $A+A\to B+B$. This is because the sum of the squared masses does not change whether the external lines are $A,B,A,B$ or $A,A,B,B$.

Third, we take the limit of a heavy mediator. If $m_C^2\gg s,\abs{u}$, then $1/(s-m_C^2)\to-1/m_C^2$ and $1/(u-m_C^2)\to-1/m_C^2$, so $$ \mathcal{M}\ \longrightarrow\ -g^2\left(-\frac{2}{m_C^2}\right) = \frac{2g^2}{m_C^2} $$ which is a constant independent of both angle and energy. Then $\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega\propto1/s$, and the total cross section also falls as $\sigma\propto1/s$. This is just as in the general statement of Section 8.2.6 of this book, “if the amplitude is a dimensionless constant, then $\sigma\propto1/s$,” and it is also a prototype of the argument of Chapter 12 that integrating out a heavy mediator yields a four-point contact interaction (of the Fermi type).

Meaning. Even for the same model and the same coupling constant, the energy dependence of the cross section is completely different depending on which channel is open. The $s$-channel raises a sharp peak at a particular energy (resonance), while the $t$/$u$-channels, whose denominators never vanish, make a smooth background (exchange force). The peak seen when the energy is swept in an experiment and the continuum lying beneath it have different origins in this way.

On the materials-science side, too, the same two types coexist. In the scattering of neutrons by atomic nuclei, the $6.67\ \mathrm{eV}$ resonance of $^{238}\mathrm{U}$ (Table 8.7) corresponds to an $s$-channel-type compound-nucleus resonance, and smooth potential scattering corresponds to the $t$-channel-type background. The Fano resonance is the asymmetric line shape that appears when the two interfere, and it is observed routinely in optical absorption spectra of solids and in scanning tunneling spectroscopy. The practice of this problem, thinking of resonance and background separately, is directly the practice of analyzing spectroscopic data.

Exercise 8.6: The Yukawa potential and the Thomas–Fermi screening length

Problem (restated)

(1) Verify by direct differentiation that $V(r)=\ee^{-\kappa r}/(4\pi r)$ satisfies the equation $(-\nabla^2+\kappa^2)V=0$ for $r\neq0$ (the spherically symmetric Laplacian is $\nabla^2 f = \frac{1}{r}\frac{\dd^2}{\dd r^2}(rf)$). Explain why this constitutes an alternative proof of the Fourier-transform formula of Section 8.7.3 of this book.

(2) The conduction electron density of aluminum is $n=1.81\times10^{29}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ (three electrons per atom). From $k_F=(3\pi^2n)^{1/3}$ and $\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}^2=4k_F/(\pi a_0)$ ($a_0=0.529\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}}$), find the screening length $\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}=1/\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}$ and compare it with the value for Cu ($0.55\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}}$).

(3) Examine the statement “a photon in a metal has an effective mass $\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}$.” For Al, find $\hbar c\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}$ in eV and compare it with the plasma energy $\hbar\omega_p=\hbar\sqrt{ne^2/(\varepsilon_0 m)}$ (about $15\ \mathrm{eV}$ for Al). Discuss why they differ by more than two orders of magnitude, and which of the two deserves to be called the “mass of a photon in a metal.”

Solution

Strategy. Part (1) is a restatement in terms of Green functions. The Fourier-transform relation shown by a residue calculation in Section 8.7.3 of this book is, written in position space, nothing but the statement that “$V$ is the Green function of the operator $-\nabla^2+\kappa^2$.” Hence verifying the differential equation directly shows the same thing. Parts (2) and (3) are numerical calculations and are practice in using natural units (a wave number is directly an energy).

(1) For $V(r)=\ee^{-\kappa r}/(4\pi r)$, forming $rV$ cancels the factor $r$, leaving $$ r\,V(r) = \frac{\ee^{-\kappa r}}{4\pi} $$ a mere exponential function. Differentiating it twice gives $$ \frac{\dd}{\dd r}(rV) = -\frac{\kappa\,\ee^{-\kappa r}}{4\pi}, \qquad \frac{\dd^2}{\dd r^2}(rV) = \frac{\kappa^2\,\ee^{-\kappa r}}{4\pi} = \kappa^2\,(rV). $$ Substituting into the formula for the spherically symmetric Laplacian, for $r\neq0$ we obtain $$ \nabla^2 V = \frac{1}{r}\frac{\dd^2}{\dd r^2}(rV) = \frac{1}{r}\,\kappa^2\,(rV) = \kappa^2 V, $$ $$ (-\nabla^2+\kappa^2)V = -\kappa^2V+\kappa^2V = 0 \qquad (r\neq0). $$ The property that an exponential function “returns to itself when differentiated twice” is precisely the reason why $\ee^{-\kappa r}/r$ satisfies the screened Poisson equation.

The singularity at the origin. The calculation above is valid only for $r\neq0$. At the origin $V\sim1/(4\pi r)$ diverges, and a $\delta$ function is hidden there. Let us check this by integrating over a small sphere of radius $\varepsilon$. By Gauss’s theorem, $$ \int_{r<\varepsilon}(-\nabla^2V)\,\dd^3x = -\oint_{r=\varepsilon}\nabla V\cdot\dd\bm{S} = -4\pi\varepsilon^2\left.\frac{\dd V}{\dd r}\right|_{r=\varepsilon}. $$ The derivative is $$ \frac{\dd V}{\dd r} = \frac{\dd}{\dd r}\left(\frac{\ee^{-\kappa r}}{4\pi r}\right) = -\frac{\ee^{-\kappa r}}{4\pi r^2}-\frac{\kappa\,\ee^{-\kappa r}}{4\pi r} = -\frac{(1+\kappa r)\,\ee^{-\kappa r}}{4\pi r^2} $$ so that $$ -4\pi\varepsilon^2\left.\frac{\dd V}{\dd r}\right|_{\varepsilon} = (1+\kappa\varepsilon)\,\ee^{-\kappa\varepsilon} \ \xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\to0\ }\ 1 . $$ On the other hand, the contribution of $\kappa^2V$ is $$ \int_{r<\varepsilon}\kappa^2 V\,\dd^3x = \kappa^2\int_0^\varepsilon \frac{\ee^{-\kappa r}}{4\pi r}\,4\pi r^2\,\dd r = \kappa^2\int_0^{\varepsilon} r\,\ee^{-\kappa r}\,\dd r \ \xrightarrow{\ \varepsilon\to0\ }\ 0 $$ which vanishes. Therefore the integral over the small sphere converges to $1$, and altogether $$ (-\nabla^2+\kappa^2)\,V(r) = \delta^3(\bm{r}) $$ holds.

Why is this an alternative proof? Transfer this differential equation to momentum space. Expanding $V(\bm{r})=\int\dd^3q/(2\pi)^3\ \tilde V(\qq)\ee^{\ii\qq\cdot\bm{r}}$ replaces $-\nabla^2\to \abs{\qq}^2$, and since $\delta^3(\bm{r})=\int\dd^3q/(2\pi)^3\ \ee^{\ii\qq\cdot\bm{r}}$, that is, the Fourier coefficient of the $\delta$ function is $1$, we obtain $$ \big(\abs{\qq}^2+\kappa^2\big)\,\tilde V(\qq) = 1 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \tilde V(\qq) = \frac{1}{\abs{\qq}^2+\kappa^2}. $$ In other words, the statement “$V=\ee^{-\kappa r}/(4\pi r)$ satisfies $(-\nabla^2+\kappa^2)V=\delta^3(\bm{r})$” and the statement “the Fourier transform of $1/(\abs{\qq}^2+\kappa^2)$ is $\ee^{-\kappa r}/(4\pi r)$” are two ways of saying the same claim. Since the solution that decays to zero at infinity is unique, proving one implies the other. In Section 8.7.3 of this book we carried out the integral by the residue theorem; the point of this problem is that, if one knows the answer, it can be verified by differentiation alone. The same calculation also shows that for $\kappa\to0$ we recover $-\nabla^2 (1/4\pi r)=\delta^3(\bm{r})$, the familiar Green function of the Poisson equation in electromagnetism.

(2) First we find the Fermi wave number. Since $3\pi^2 = 29.609$, $$ 3\pi^2 n = 29.609\times1.81\times10^{29} = 5.359\times10^{30}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}, $$ $$ k_F = \big(5.359\times10^{30}\big)^{1/3} = (5.359)^{1/3}\times10^{10} = 1.750\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}} = 1.750\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}^{-1}}. $$ Next comes the Thomas–Fermi wave number. Using $a_0 = 0.529\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}} = 0.529\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$, $$ \kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}^2 = \frac{4k_F}{\pi a_0} = \frac{4\times1.750\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}}{\pi\times0.529\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}} = \frac{7.000\times10^{10}}{1.6619\times10^{-10}} = 4.212\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-2}}, $$ $$ \kappa_{\mathrm{TF}} = 2.052\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}} = 2.052\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}^{-1}}. $$ The screening length is its reciprocal: $$ \lambda_{\mathrm{TF}} = \frac{1}{\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}} = 4.873\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m} = 0.487\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}}. $$ Compared with $0.55\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}}$ for Cu, Al is shorter by about $12\%$. Since Al contributes three electrons per atom, its conduction-electron density is $2.1$ times that of Cu; the more electrons there are, the more strongly the screening acts and the shorter the screening length becomes, which is the direction we expected.

(3) In natural units $\hbar=c=1$, so a wave number (an inverse length) is directly an energy (a mass). The conversion factor for restoring SI units is $\hbar c$, with $$ \hbar c = 197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm} = 1973.27\ \mathrm{eV\,\mathring{A}} $$ (from $1\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm} = 10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV}\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}} = 10\ \mathrm{eV\,\mathring{A}}$). Hence the energy corresponding to the screening wave number of Al is $$ \hbar c\,\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}} = 1973.27\ \mathrm{eV\,\mathring{A}}\times2.052\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}^{-1}} = 4.05\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{eV} = 4.05\ \mathrm{keV}. $$ This is an effective mass in the sense that the static Coulomb potential is screened inside Al into the same form as a “Yukawa potential due to the exchange of a particle of mass $4\ \mathrm{keV}$.” The range $R=\hbar/(mc)$ of the Yukawa potential and the screening length $\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}=1/\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}$ stand in the same place in the same formula. On the other hand, the plasma energy is $$ \hbar\omega_p = \hbar\sqrt{\frac{ne^2}{\varepsilon_0 m}} = 1.0546\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}\times2.400\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} = 15.8\ \mathrm{eV} $$ (the measured value is about $15\ \mathrm{eV}$), and the ratio is $$ \frac{\hbar c\,\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}}{\hbar\omega_p} = \frac{4.05\times10^{3}}{15.8} = 256 $$ This ratio is not a coincidence. Taking the ratio of $\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}^2=3ne^2/(2\varepsilon_0E_F)$ and $\omega_p^2=ne^2/(\varepsilon_0 m)$ gives $$ \frac{\hbar c\,\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}}{\hbar\omega_p} = \sqrt{\frac{3mc^2}{2E_F}} = \sqrt{\frac{3\times5.110\times10^{5}}{2\times11.67}} = 256 $$ ($E_F=\hbar^2k_F^2/2m=11.67\ \mathrm{eV}$), and the two are separated by more than two orders of magnitude because of the factor $\sqrt3\,c/v_F$. The physical reason for the difference is that the two quantities look at different components of the field and at different frequencies. $\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}$ is the wave number at which a static ($\omega=0$) longitudinal field (an electric field) is screened, and it corresponds to the Debye mass of plasma physics. It does not appear in the dispersion relation of the photon, which is a transverse wave. What sets the threshold below which an electromagnetic wave can no longer propagate in a metal is $\omega_p$, which is the mass term in the dispersion relation of the transverse wave, $\omega^2=\omega_p^2+c^2k^2$. Therefore what deserves to be called the “photon mass in a metal” is $\hbar\omega_p\approx15\ \mathrm{eV}$, not $4\ \mathrm{keV}$. Indeed, X rays of $4\ \mathrm{keV}$ pass almost straight through Al. The statement “the photon has an effective mass $\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}$” is a rephrasing valid only for the static longitudinal response (the box “Caution: How far does ‘the same’ go?” in Section 8.7.3 of this book).

Verification. We check in three ways.

First, dimensions. $[\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}^2]=[k_F]/[a_0]=\mathrm{m^{-1}}/\mathrm{m}=\mathrm{m^{-2}}$, which is correct for the square of a wave number. Also $[\hbar c\,\kappa]=\mathrm{eV\,\mathring{A}}\times\mathrm{\mathring{A}^{-1}}=\mathrm{eV}$, so it is indeed an energy.

Second, we check whether the same procedure reproduces the value for Cu in Section 8.7.3 of this book. Inserting $n=8.47\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ gives $$ k_F = 1.359\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}^{-1}}, \qquad \kappa_{\mathrm{TF}} = 1.808\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}^{-1}}, \qquad \lambda_{\mathrm{TF}} = 0.553\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}} $$ in agreement with the text’s $k_F=1.36\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}^{-1}}$, $\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}=1.81\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}^{-1}}$, and $\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}=0.55\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}}$. This confirms that there is no error in the calculation procedure.

Third, we check with the power of the density dependence. Since $k_F\propto n^{1/3}$ and $\kappa_{\mathrm{TF}}\propto k_F^{1/2}\propto n^{1/6}$, $$ \lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}\propto n^{-1/6}. $$ The density ratio of Al to Cu is $1.81\times10^{29}/8.47\times10^{28}=2.137$, and its $1/6$ power is $2.137^{1/6}=1.135$. Therefore $$ \lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}^{\mathrm{Al}} = \frac{0.553}{1.135} = 0.487\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}} $$ in perfect agreement with the direct calculation in (2). It is also important that the power $n^{-1/6}$ is a weak one: even if the electron density is doubled, $2^{-1/6}=0.891$, that is, the screening length shrinks by only $11\%$. Even a tenfold increase in the electron density gives $10^{-1/6}=0.68$, a reduction of a little over 30%. This is why the screening length of a metal falls around $0.5\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}}$ for almost every metal.

Meaning. $\lambda_{\mathrm{TF}}=0.49\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}}$ is $1/5.9$, that is, about $1/6$, of the nearest-neighbor interatomic distance of Al, $2.86\ \mathrm{\mathring{A}}$. That is, even if a single impurity ion is placed in a metal, its charge is almost completely hidden before it reaches the nearest-neighbor atoms. It is thanks to this short screening length that first-principles calculations of alloys and defects can use finite-size supercells that ignore the influence of distant ions. Conversely, in a semiconductor the conduction-electron density is lower by orders of magnitude, so the screening length is tens of $\mathrm{\mathring{A}}$ or more, and the long-distance Coulomb field of the dopant must be treated carefully. Estimating the screening length is also a way of deciding the cell size of the calculation.

And as (3) shows, the statement “the photon mass in a metal” must be accompanied by which component and which frequency of the response is meant. The screening of the static longitudinal field ($4\ \mathrm{keV}$) and the threshold of the transverse wave ($15\ \mathrm{eV}$) are different quantities. The Anderson–Higgs mechanism of Chapter 13 concerns the side on which the transverse photon acquires a mass inside a superconductor, and as a result the magnetic field is screened over the London penetration depth (the Meissner effect). The nuclear force, the weak interaction, the screening in a metal, and the Debye length of an electrolyte listed in Table 8.5 are all different faces of one and the same formula, $1/(\abs{\qq}^2+\kappa^2)\to\ee^{-\kappa r}/(4\pi r)$.

Exercise 8.7: The Breit–Wigner width and the $Q$ value

Problem (restated)

(1) For the Lorentzian function $f(E)=1/[(E-M)^2+\Gamma^2/4]$ of Section 8.7.4 of this book, find the values of $E$ at which it falls to half its peak value, and show that the full width at half maximum is $\Gamma$.

(2) The width of the $\Delta(1232)$ is $\Gamma=117\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Find its lifetime $\tau$ in seconds and compare it with the time light takes to cross the proton diameter $1.7\ \mathrm{fm}$.

(3) Find $Q=M/\Gamma$ for the $\rho(770)$, the $J/\psi$, and the optical phonon of Si ($520\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, FWHM $3.0\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$), and state how they compare in size.

(4) For the damped oscillator $\chi(\omega)=(1/m)/(\omega_0^2-\omega^2-\ii\gamma\omega/m)$, show that the FWHM of $\mathrm{Im}\,\chi$ near the resonance is $\gamma/m$, and state its correspondence with the $\Gamma$ of an elementary particle.

Solution

Strategy. The claim of this problem comes down to this: “a resonance of an elementary particle and a damped oscillator in matter are described by the same Lorentzian function.” Parts (1) and (4) show this identity in formulas, and (2) and (3) line up elementary particles and solids on the same yardstick ($\Gamma$ and $Q$). All we use in the calculation is $\tau=\hbar/\Gamma$ and the elementary properties of the Lorentzian function.

(1) $f(E)=1/[(E-M)^2+\Gamma^2/4]$ is maximal where the denominator is minimal. The denominator $(E-M)^2+\Gamma^2/4$ takes its minimum value $\Gamma^2/4$ at $E=M$, so $$ f_{\max} = f(M) = \frac{4}{\Gamma^2}. $$ We look for the $E$ at which the function is half the peak value: $$ \frac{1}{(E-M)^2+\Gamma^2/4} = \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{4}{\Gamma^2} = \frac{2}{\Gamma^2}. $$ Taking reciprocals, $$ (E-M)^2+\frac{\Gamma^2}{4} = \frac{\Gamma^2}{2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (E-M)^2 = \frac{\Gamma^2}{2}-\frac{\Gamma^2}{4} = \frac{\Gamma^2}{4}, $$ $$ E = M \pm \frac{\Gamma}{2}. $$ The separation between the two half-maximum points, that is, the full width at half maximum, is $$ \text{FWHM} = \left(M+\frac{\Gamma}{2}\right)-\left(M-\frac{\Gamma}{2}\right) = \Gamma $$ This makes completely clear why the decay rate $\Gamma$ is called the “width.” The exponential decay $\ee^{-\Gamma t}$ in the time domain and the Lorentzian peak in the frequency domain are one and the same thing, connected by a Fourier transform, and the faster the decay, the broader the peak.

(2) Inserting $\hbar=6.582\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{MeV\,s}$ and $\Gamma=117\ \mathrm{MeV}$ into $\tau=\hbar/\Gamma$: $$ \tau = \frac{6.582\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{MeV\,s}}{117\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 5.63\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{s}. $$ On the other hand, the time light takes to cross the proton diameter, $1.7\ \mathrm{fm}$, is $$ t_{\text{cross}} = \frac{1.7\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}}{2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}} = 5.67\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{s}. $$ The two are almost the same (the ratio is $0.99$). That is, the $\Delta(1232)$ exists only for as long as it takes light to cross a single hadron, barely long enough to say that it was “formed.” The same can be said in terms of $c\tau$: $$ c\tau = \frac{\hbar c}{\Gamma} = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{117\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 1.69\ \mathrm{fm} $$ which is exactly the proton diameter. This is why there is no clear answer to the question of whether the $\Delta$ is a “particle” or a “resonance in $\pi N$ scattering.” The lifetimes of resonances that decay through the strong interaction all cluster around this scale of $10^{-23}\text{--}10^{-24}\ \mathrm{s}$.

(3) We compute $Q=M/\Gamma$ for the three cases (using the values in Tables 8.1 and 8.7). $$ Q(\rho) = \frac{775.26\ \mathrm{MeV}}{149.1\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 5.20, $$ $$ Q(J/\psi) = \frac{3096.90\ \mathrm{MeV}}{92.6\ \mathrm{keV}} = \frac{3096.90}{0.0926} = 3.34\times10^{4}, $$ $$ Q(\text{Si phonon}) = \frac{520\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}}{3.0\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}} = 1.7\times10^{2}. $$ Since $Q$ is a ratio, for the phonon we may divide the wave numbers ($\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$) as they are. Their ordering is $$ Q(J/\psi)\ \gg\ Q(\text{Si phonon})\ \gg\ Q(\rho) $$ so the $J/\psi$ is 200 times sharper than the optical phonon of Si, and the $\rho$ is more than 30 times broader than the phonon.

$Q$ has an even more definite reading. In natural units the lifetime is $\tau=1/\Gamma$ and the “internal angular frequency of oscillation” of the resonance is $M$ (so the period is $2\pi/M$, or $h/Mc^2$ when SI units are restored), hence $$ Q = \frac{M}{\Gamma} = M\tau = \frac{\tau}{2\pi/M}\times2\pi = 2\pi\times(\text{number of oscillations before decay}), $$ that is, $Q/2\pi$ counts “how many times it can oscillate before it dies.” For the $\rho$, $Q/2\pi=0.83$—it decays before completing even a single oscillation. The $J/\psi$ makes $5.3\times10^{3}$ oscillations, and the optical phonon of Si makes $173/2\pi=27.6$. The last number can be checked immediately. The frequency of $520\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ is $\nu = 520\times2.998\times10^{10} = 1.559\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{Hz}$, and the period is $64.1\ \mathrm{fs}$. Dividing the phonon lifetime $1.77\ \mathrm{ps}$, found in the verification below, by this gives $(1.77\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{s})/(64.1\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{s}) = 27.6$, in agreement with $Q/2\pi$. The $Q$ value and the lifetime merely say the same thing in different units.

(4) We expand the response function of the damped oscillator $$ \chi(\omega) = \frac{1/m}{\omega_0^2-\omega^2-\ii\gamma\omega/m} $$ near the resonance ($\omega\simeq\omega_0$). The real part of the denominator is $$ \omega_0^2-\omega^2 = (\omega_0-\omega)(\omega_0+\omega) \simeq 2\omega_0(\omega_0-\omega), $$ and the coefficient of the imaginary part can be approximated as $\gamma\omega/m\simeq\gamma\omega_0/m$.
