Therefore $$ \chi(\omega) \simeq \frac{1/m}{2\omega_0(\omega_0-\omega)-\ii\,\gamma\omega_0/m} = \frac{1}{2m\omega_0}\cdot\frac{1}{(\omega_0-\omega)-\ii\,\gamma/(2m)}. $$ Multiplying numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator, $$ \chi(\omega) \simeq \frac{1}{2m\omega_0}\cdot \frac{(\omega_0-\omega)+\ii\,\gamma/(2m)}{(\omega-\omega_0)^2+\big(\gamma/2m\big)^2} $$ (in the denominator we used $(\omega_0-\omega)^2=(\omega-\omega_0)^2$). Extracting only the imaginary part, $$ \mathrm{Im}\,\chi(\omega) \simeq \frac{1}{2m\omega_0}\cdot \frac{\gamma/(2m)}{(\omega-\omega_0)^2+\big(\gamma/2m\big)^2}. $$ Defining $\Gamma\equiv\gamma/m$ here, $$ \mathrm{Im}\,\chi(\omega) \simeq \frac{1}{2m\omega_0}\cdot \frac{\Gamma/2}{(\omega-\omega_0)^2+\Gamma^2/4} $$ which coincides exactly with the Lorentzian function $f$ treated in (1) under the replacements $\omega\leftrightarrow E$ and $\omega_0\leftrightarrow M$. Therefore the result of (1) can be used as it stands, and the full width at half maximum of $\mathrm{Im}\,\chi$ is $$ \text{FWHM} = \Gamma = \frac{\gamma}{m} $$ The correspondence is as follows. The resonance mass $M$ corresponds to the natural frequency $\omega_0$, the decay width $\Gamma$ to the damping rate $\gamma/m$, the lifetime $\tau=1/\Gamma$ to the relaxation time $m/\gamma$, and $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2$ (Breit–Wigner) to the absorption spectrum $\mathrm{Im}\,\chi$ (Table 8.6). The stronger the friction, the broader the resonance and the faster the relaxation—in the language of elementary particles, the more decay channels are open, the wider the width and the shorter the lifetime.

Verification. We check in two ways.

First, we apply the procedure of (3) to another resonance listed in Table 8.7 and look for consistency. For the $\Delta(1232)$, $Q=1232/117=10.5$, which agrees with the $10.5$ in Table 8.7. The $5.2$ of the $\rho$ and the $3.3\times10^{4}$ of the $J/\psi$ also agree with the table.

Second, we check the correspondence in (4) numerically for the Si phonon. Since $1\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}} = 0.12398\ \mathrm{meV}$, the FWHM of $3.0\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$ in energy is $$ \Gamma = 3.0\times0.12398 = 0.372\ \mathrm{meV} = 3.72\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}. $$ Applying $\tau=\hbar/\Gamma$ ($\hbar=6.582\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}$) to this gives $$ \tau = \frac{6.582\times10^{-16}}{3.72\times10^{-4}} = 1.77\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{s} = 1.8\ \mathrm{ps}. $$ This yields a picosecond-order value, which is reasonable for the lifetime of an optical phonon in Si. It is confirmed numerically that the same formula $\tau=\hbar/\Gamma$ used for elementary-particle resonances works as it stands as the formula that gives the phonon lifetime from the linewidth of a Raman peak.

Meaning. When lined up on the single yardstick of the $Q$ value, the resonances of elementary particles and the elementary excitations of solids appear in the same table (Table 8.7). The $Q=5$ of the $\rho$ is so broad that one hesitates to call it a resonance—the width of the peak is as much as $2$ tenths of its center value. The $Q=3\times10^4$ of the $J/\psi$ rivals the sharpness of a quartz oscillator, and it was this abnormal narrowness that surprised physicists at its discovery in 1974. A narrow resonance always has a reason (a selection rule) that hinders its decay. For the $J/\psi$ it is the OZI suppression (Chapter 11).

On the materials-science side as well, measuring a linewidth is measuring a lifetime, and measuring a lifetime is asking “what is responsible for the relaxation.” The width of a Raman peak directly gives the strength of phonon–phonon scattering due to anharmonic interactions (three-phonon and four-phonon processes), and following its temperature dependence tells which process is at work. Formally, too, the correspondence is complete: the fact that the imaginary part of the phonon self-energy $\Sigma$ gives the linewidth and the real part gives the frequency shift has exactly the same structure as the fact that the imaginary part of $\Pi(p^2)$ in Section 8.6.4 of this book gives $\Gamma$ and the real part gives the mass shift. The phonon linewidth treated in first-principles calculations of thermal conductivity and the decay width of an elementary particle are different names for the same quantity.

E.9 Solutions for Chapter 9: The Dirac Equation and Spinors

Exercise 9.1: Contraction identities for $\gamma$ matrices

Problem (restated)

Using only the Clifford algebra $\{\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu\}=2g^{\mu\nu}$ and $g^\mu{}_\mu=4$, show the following.

(1) $\gamma^\mu\gamma_\mu = 4$

(2) $\gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\gamma_\mu = -2\slashed{a}$

(3) $\gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\gamma_\mu = 4\,(a\cdot b)$

(4) $\gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\gamma_\mu = -2\,\slashed{c}\slashed{b}\slashed{a}$

Solution

Strategy. The only tool we use is the Clifford algebra of Chapter 9 of this book, $\{\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu\}=2g^{\mu\nu}\mathbb{1}$. We read it as the rewriting rule “$\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu=2g^{\mu\nu}-\gamma^\nu\gamma^\mu$: each time the leftmost $\gamma$ is passed one place to the right, the sign flips and a remainder $2g^{\mu\nu}$ appears.” This gives a staircase structure in which (1) produces (2), (2) produces (3), and (3) produces (4), so the whole problem is settled by induction. Here $a^\mu,b^\mu,c^\mu$ are four-vectors of ordinary numbers that commute with the $\gamma$ matrices, and $\slashed{a}=\gamma^\nu a_\nu$. Below we omit the $\mathbb{1}_4$ on the right-hand sides.

(1) Since $\gamma^\mu\gamma_\mu$ is summed over $\mu$, we can lower the index with the metric and write $\gamma^\mu\gamma_\mu = g_{\mu\nu}\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu$. Because $g_{\mu\nu}$ is symmetric under the exchange $\mu\leftrightarrow\nu$, the quantity it is contracted with contributes only through its symmetric part. That is,

$$ \gamma^\mu\gamma_\mu = g_{\mu\nu}\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu = g_{\mu\nu}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\left(\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu+\gamma^\nu\gamma^\mu\right) = \frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}\left\{\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu\right\} $$

Substituting the Clifford algebra here, we obtain

$$ \gamma^\mu\gamma_\mu = \frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu}\cdot 2g^{\mu\nu} = g_{\mu\nu}g^{\mu\nu} = g^\mu{}_\mu = 4 $$

Finally, note that this is not $g^\mu{}_\mu=\mathrm{tr}\,\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$ but $g_{\mu\nu}g^{\mu\nu}=\delta^\mu{}_\mu=4$ (the dimension of spacetime). If spacetime has $d$ dimensions, only this value changes to $d$.

(2) First we compute the form with free indices, $\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma_\mu$, and multiply by $a_\nu$ at the end. Passing the leftmost $\gamma^\mu$ to the right of $\gamma^\nu$ with the rewriting rule gives

$$ \gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma_\mu = \left(2g^{\mu\nu}-\gamma^\nu\gamma^\mu\right)\gamma_\mu = 2g^{\mu\nu}\gamma_\mu - \gamma^\nu\left(\gamma^\mu\gamma_\mu\right) $$

The first term is $2\gamma^\nu$ because $g^{\mu\nu}\gamma_\mu=\gamma^\nu$. In the second term, $\gamma^\mu\gamma_\mu=4$ by (1), so it is $-4\gamma^\nu$. Hence

$$ \gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma_\mu = 2\gamma^\nu-4\gamma^\nu = -2\gamma^\nu $$

Multiplying both sides by $a_\nu$ and summing, we obtain $\gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\gamma_\mu=-2\slashed{a}$. $\blacksquare$

(3) We use the same move just once. In $\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma_\mu$, pass the leftmost $\gamma^\mu$ to the right of $\gamma^\nu$:

$$ \gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma_\mu = \left(2g^{\mu\nu}-\gamma^\nu\gamma^\mu\right)\gamma^\rho\gamma_\mu = 2\gamma^\rho\gamma^\nu - \gamma^\nu\left(\gamma^\mu\gamma^\rho\gamma_\mu\right) $$

In the first term we used $g^{\mu\nu}\gamma^\rho\gamma_\mu=\gamma^\rho\gamma^\nu$ (this merely raises the index of $\gamma_\mu$ with $g^{\mu\nu}$). The parenthesis in the second term has already been computed in (2) and equals $-2\gamma^\rho$. Therefore

$$ \gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma_\mu = 2\gamma^\rho\gamma^\nu + 2\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho = 2\left\{\gamma^\nu,\gamma^\rho\right\} = 4g^{\nu\rho} $$

Multiplying by $a_\nu b_\rho$ and summing gives $\gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\gamma_\mu = 4g^{\nu\rho}a_\nu b_\rho = 4\,(a\cdot b)$. $\blacksquare$

(4) We climb just one more step.

$$ \gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma\gamma_\mu = \left(2g^{\mu\nu}-\gamma^\nu\gamma^\mu\right)\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma\gamma_\mu = 2\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma\gamma^\nu - \gamma^\nu\left(\gamma^\mu\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma\gamma_\mu\right) $$

The contents of the parenthesis are exactly the result of (3), namely $4g^{\rho\sigma}$. Hence

$$ \gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma\gamma_\mu = 2\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma\gamma^\nu - 4g^{\rho\sigma}\gamma^\nu $$

All that remains is to expand $\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma$ in the first term once more with the rewriting rule, $\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma = 2g^{\rho\sigma}-\gamma^\sigma\gamma^\rho$:

$$ 2\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma\gamma^\nu = 4g^{\rho\sigma}\gamma^\nu - 2\gamma^\sigma\gamma^\rho\gamma^\nu $$

Substituting this, the terms $4g^{\rho\sigma}\gamma^\nu$ cancel exactly, leaving

$$ \gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma\gamma_\mu = -2\,\gamma^\sigma\gamma^\rho\gamma^\nu $$

Multiplying by $a_\nu b_\rho c_\sigma$ and summing, we obtain, corresponding to the reversal of the index order from $\nu\rho\sigma$ to $\sigma\rho\nu$,

$$ \gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\gamma_\mu = -2\,\slashed{c}\slashed{b}\slashed{a} $$

$\blacksquare$

Verification. We reduce to special cases and check consistency. First, set $b=a$ in (3). Since $\slashed{a}\slashed{a}=a^\mu a^\nu\gamma_\mu\gamma_\nu=\frac12 a^\mu a^\nu\{\gamma_\mu,\gamma_\nu\}=a^2$ is a number, the left-hand side is $\gamma^\mu(a^2)\gamma_\mu = a^2\cdot4$, and the right-hand side is $4(a\cdot a)=4a^2$, so they agree. Next, set $c=b$ in (4). Using $\slashed{b}\slashed{b}=b^2$, the left-hand side becomes $b^2\,\gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\gamma_\mu = -2b^2\slashed{a}$ (using (2)), and the right-hand side is $-2\slashed{b}\slashed{b}\slashed{a}=-2b^2\slashed{a}$, which again agree. The coefficients also appear alternately as $4,\,-2,\,4,\,-2$, as expected from the recursive structure (1)→(2)→(3)→(4).

Meaning. In the cross-section calculations from Chapter 10 onward, these identities are the tools for shortening the long products of $\gamma$ matrices that appear after the spin sums are taken. For example, in QED Compton scattering and Møller scattering, a “block sandwiched between the same index,” $\gamma^\mu\cdots\gamma_\mu$, always appears inside $\Tr[\cdots]$, and each time the formulas of this exercise shorten the product by two. Moreover, if the spacetime dimension is generalized to $d$, (1) becomes $d$ and (2) becomes $-(d-2)\slashed{a}$. Using this “deviation from 4” as a control parameter is dimensional regularization, which is the groundwork for the renormalization of Chapter 10. On the materials-science side too, exactly the same kind of algebra appears when one contracts the spin structure $\sigma^i\cdots\sigma^i$ in many-body perturbation theory ($\sigma^i\sigma^i=3$, $\sigma^i\sigma^j\sigma^i=-\sigma^j$, and so on). The only differences are whether the dimension is 3 or 4 and whether the metric is Euclidean or Minkowskian; the skeleton of the calculation is the same.

Exercise 9.2: Normalization and completeness relation of the $v$ spinor

Problem (restated)

For $v(p,s)$ as normalized in Chapter 9 of this book, follow the calculation for $u$ in the main text and show the following.

(1) $\bar v(p,s)v(p,s)=-2m$, $v^\dagger(p,s)v(p,s)=2E$.

(2) $\displaystyle\sum_{s}v(p,s)\bar v(p,s) = \slashed{p}-m$.

(3) $\bar u(p,s)v(p,s')=0$ (for the same four-momentum $p$).

Solution

Strategy. We treat the explicit forms of Chapter 9 of this book

$$ u(p,s)=\sqrt{E+m}\begin{pmatrix}\chi_s\\[4pt] \lambda\chi_s\end{pmatrix}, \qquad v(p,s)=\sqrt{E+m}\begin{pmatrix}\lambda\eta_s\\[4pt] \eta_s\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \lambda\equiv\frac{\bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp}{E+m} $$

as $2\times2$ blocks throughout. Only three properties are key. First, $\lambda$ is Hermitian (because $\bm{\sigma}$ is Hermitian and $\pp$ is a real vector). Second,

$$ \lambda^2=\frac{(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp)^2}{(E+m)^2}=\frac{\pp^2}{(E+m)^2} =\frac{(E+m)(E-m)}{(E+m)^2}=\frac{E-m}{E+m} $$

(we applied the identity $(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{a})(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{b})=\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b}+\ii\bm{\sigma}\cdot(\bm{a}\times\bm{b})$ with $\bm{a}=\bm{b}=\pp$ and substituted the dispersion relation $\pp^2=E^2-m^2$). Third, $\gamma^0=\mathrm{diag}(\mathbb{1}_2,-\mathbb{1}_2)$ flips the sign of the lower two components. We also take $\chi_s,\eta_s$ to be orthonormal bases of two-component spinors, with $\chi_s^\dagger\chi_{s'}=\eta_s^\dagger\eta_{s'}=\delta_{ss'}$ and $\sum_s\eta_s\eta_s^\dagger=\mathbb{1}_2$.

(1) First we construct the adjoint spinor. We have $v^\dagger=\sqrt{E+m}\left(\eta_s^\dagger\lambda,\ \eta_s^\dagger\right)$ (using $\lambda^\dagger=\lambda$), and multiplying by $\gamma^0$ from the right flips the sign of the lower block:

$$ \bar v = v^\dagger\gamma^0 = \sqrt{E+m}\left(\eta_s^\dagger\lambda,\ -\eta_s^\dagger\right) $$

Therefore

$$ \bar v v = (E+m)\left[\eta_s^\dagger\lambda\cdot\lambda\eta_s - \eta_s^\dagger\eta_s\right] = (E+m)\left[\lambda^2-1\right] $$

Substituting $\lambda^2=(E-m)/(E+m)$ here, we get

$$ \bar v v = (E+m)\left[\frac{E-m}{E+m}-1\right] = (E-m)-(E+m) = -2m $$

For $u$ we had $\bar u u=(E+m)[1-\lambda^2]=+2m$, so the content of the calculation is that the sign flips because the direction of the subtraction between $\lambda^2$ and $1$ is reversed. Similarly, the inner product without $\gamma^0$ is

$$ v^\dagger v = (E+m)\left[\lambda^2+1\right] = (E-m)+(E+m) = 2E $$

This is the same $2E$ as for $u$. $\blacksquare$

(2) Since $v\bar v$ is the product of a column vector and a row vector, it is a $4\times4$ matrix, which in block form reads

$$ v\bar v = (E+m) \begin{pmatrix} \lambda\eta_s\eta_s^\dagger\lambda & -\lambda\eta_s\eta_s^\dagger\\[4pt] \eta_s\eta_s^\dagger\lambda & -\eta_s\eta_s^\dagger \end{pmatrix} $$

Now summing over spin and using the completeness of two-component spinors, $\sum_s\eta_s\eta_s^\dagger=\mathbb{1}_2$, we obtain

$$ \sum_s v\bar v = (E+m) \begin{pmatrix} \lambda^2 & -\lambda\\[4pt] \lambda & -\mathbb{1} \end{pmatrix} $$

We simplify each block.

Upper left: $(E+m)\lambda^2 = (E+m)\dfrac{E-m}{E+m}=E-m$.

Upper right: $-(E+m)\lambda = -(E+m)\dfrac{\bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp}{E+m}=-\bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp$.

Lower left: $+(E+m)\lambda = +\bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp$.

Lower right: $-(E+m)\mathbb{1}$.

Collecting these,

$$ \sum_s v\bar v = \begin{pmatrix} E-m & -\bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp\\[4pt] \bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp & -(E+m) \end{pmatrix} $$

On the other hand, subtracting $m\mathbb{1}_4$ from the block representation of Chapter 9 of this book, $\slashed{p}=\begin{pmatrix}E&-\bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp\\ \bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp&-E\end{pmatrix}$, gives

$$ \slashed{p}-m = \begin{pmatrix} E-m & -\bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp\\[4pt] \bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp & -E-m \end{pmatrix} $$

and all four blocks coincide. Hence $\sum_s v\bar v=\slashed{p}-m$. $\blacksquare$

The only difference from the $u$ case is that $m$ enters the diagonal blocks with a $-$ rather than a $+$ sign, which has the same origin as the sign flip we saw in (1).

(3) We construct the adjoint of $u$ by exactly the same procedure as for $\bar v$. Multiplying $u^\dagger=\sqrt{E+m}\left(\chi_s^\dagger,\ \chi_s^\dagger\lambda\right)$ by $\gamma^0$ flips the sign of the lower block, so $\bar u = \sqrt{E+m}\left(\chi_s^\dagger,\ -\chi_s^\dagger\lambda\right)$. We multiply this by $v=\sqrt{E+m}\left(\lambda\eta_{s'},\ \eta_{s'}\right)^T$. We simply add the product of the first block of the row vector with the first block of the column vector and the product of the second blocks, so

$$ \bar u(p,s)v(p,s') = (E+m)\left[\chi_s^\dagger\,\lambda\eta_{s'} \;-\; \chi_s^\dagger\lambda\,\eta_{s'}\right] = 0 $$

The two terms are literally the same expression with opposite signs, so they cancel exactly. Since this does not depend at all on the contents of $s$ and $s'$, the result is zero for both $s=s'$ and $s\ne s'$. $\blacksquare$

The origin of this cancellation lies in $\gamma^0$. The sign of the lower two components is flipped when $\bar u$ is constructed, and because the lower component of $u$ and the upper component of $v$ each carry exactly one factor of $\lambda$, the two terms have the same form.

Verification. Take the trace of both sides of (2). The right-hand side is $\Tr[\slashed{p}-m]=p_\mu\Tr\gamma^\mu - m\Tr\mathbb{1}_4 = 0-4m=-4m$ (using $\Tr\gamma^\mu=0$). For the left-hand side, using the interchange of column and row vectors, $\Tr[v\bar v]=\bar v v$, we get $\sum_s\bar v v = 2\times(-2m)=-4m$ ($s$ takes two values). The two agree. Doing the same check for $u$, $\Tr[\slashed{p}+m]=4m$ and $\sum_s\bar u u=2\times2m=4m$ again agree. Moreover, (2) must be consistent with the equation that $v$ must satisfy, $(\slashed{p}+m)v=0$, and indeed

$$ (\slashed{p}+m)\sum_s v\bar v = (\slashed{p}+m)(\slashed{p}-m) = \slashed{p}\slashed{p}-m^2 = p^2-m^2 = 0 $$

so there is no contradiction ($\slashed{p}\slashed{p}=p^2$ follows from the Clifford algebra). The fact that in the limit $m\to0$ both $\sum_su\bar u$ and $\sum_sv\bar v$ become degenerate to $\slashed{p}$ also agrees with the fact that, for massless particles, the spin structures of the particle and the antiparticle are the same.

Meaning. The completeness relation is the device that reduces the square of a scattering amplitude to a trace calculation without ever writing out the components of the spinors. If the amplitude has the form $\mathcal{M}=\bar u\,\Gamma\,v$, then $\sum_{\text{spins}}\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2=\Tr[(\slashed{p}_1+m)\Gamma(\slashed{p}_2-m)\bar\Gamma]$, and the rest can be handled mechanically with the contraction formulas of Exercise 9.1 and the trace theorems. The $-m$ that appears on the $v$ side is the reason the sign of the interference term differs between particle and antiparticle, and it bears directly, for example, on the angular distribution of $\ee^+\ee^-$ pair annihilation (Chapter 10). On the solid-state side, in the Bogoliubov–de Gennes (BdG) equation of superconductivity (Exercise 9.8), the electron branch and the hole branch play the same roles, and the coherence factors $u^2$ and $v^2$ correspond precisely to the weights of the $u$-type and $v$-type solutions here.

Exercise 9.3: The Pauli equation and the ESR resonance frequency

Problem (restated)

Reproduce the derivation of Section 9.3.5 of the main text yourself, and carry it through to numerical values.

(1) Derive the identity $(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{a})(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{b})=\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b}+\ii\bm{\sigma}\cdot(\bm{a}\times\bm{b})$ from $\sigma^i\sigma^j=\delta^{ij}+\ii\varepsilon^{ijk}\sigma^k$.

(2) For $\bm{\pi}=\pp-q\bm{A}$, show that $\bm{\pi}\times\bm{\pi}=\ii q\bm{B}$. Explain in a single sentence why, for a classical numerical vector, $\bm{\pi}\times\bm{\pi}=0$, yet here it does not vanish.

(3) For the electron ($q=-e$), verify that the spin term of the Pauli equation (with $\hbar$ restored) is $+\dfrac{e\hbar}{2m}\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{B}=g\mu_B\bm{S}\cdot\bm{B}/\hbar$ (with $\mu_B=e\hbar/2m$ and $\bm{S}=\hbar\bm{\sigma}/2$), and read off $g=2$.

(4) The resonance condition of electron spin resonance (ESR) is $h\nu = g\mu_B B$. Find $\nu$ for $g=2.0023$ (free electron) and $B=0.34\ \mathrm{T}$.

Solution

Strategy. Part (1) is a mere contraction of the Pauli-matrix product formula; in (2) the only essential point is that “the momentum operators do not commute”; (3) is a reading-off of the coefficient of the spin term in the Pauli equation; (4) is a numerical substitution. The point is to confirm, through (1) and (2), the route by which $g=2$ emerges necessarily from the commutation relations of quantum mechanics.

(1) Writing $\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{a}=\sigma^ia^i$ and $\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{b}=\sigma^jb^j$ (summed over $i,j$), we have

$$ (\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{a})(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{b}) = a^ib^j\,\sigma^i\sigma^j $$

Here we do not change the order of $a^i$ and $b^j$ (because we will later use them as operators). Substituting the given product formula $\sigma^i\sigma^j=\delta^{ij}+\ii\varepsilon^{ijk}\sigma^k$ gives

$$ (\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{a})(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{b}) = a^ib^j\delta^{ij} + \ii\,\varepsilon^{ijk}a^ib^j\,\sigma^k $$

The first term is $a^ib^i=\bm{a}\cdot\bm{b}$. For the second term, using the cyclic symmetry of the Levi-Civita symbol, $\varepsilon^{ijk}=\varepsilon^{kij}$, we have $\varepsilon^{ijk}a^ib^j=\varepsilon^{kij}a^ib^j=(\bm{a}\times\bm{b})^k$. Therefore

$$ (\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{a})(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{b}) = \bm{a}\cdot\bm{b} + \ii\,\bm{\sigma}\cdot(\bm{a}\times\bm{b}) $$

follows. $\blacksquare$ Incidentally, the given product formula itself is obtained by adding $\{\sigma^i,\sigma^j\}=2\delta^{ij}$ and $[\sigma^i,\sigma^j]=2\ii\varepsilon^{ijk}\sigma^k$ and dividing by 2. The crucial point, which leads to (2) below, is that the commutativity of $\bm{a}$ and $\bm{b}$ is used nowhere in the derivation.

(2) Let $\bm{\pi}=\pp-q\bm{A}=-\ii\nabla-q\bm{A}$ and let it act on an arbitrary test function $f$. Expanding the cross product component by component, we get

$$ (\bm{\pi}\times\bm{\pi})f = \underbrace{(\pp\times\pp)f}_{=0} - q\left[\pp\times(\bm{A}f) + \bm{A}\times(\pp f)\right] + q^2\underbrace{(\bm{A}\times\bm{A})}_{=0}f $$

The first term vanishes because the components of $\pp$ commute with one another ($[\partial_i,\partial_j]=0$), and the third term vanishes because it is the cross product of a numerical vector with itself. We now compute the remaining term. Using the vector-analysis formula $\nabla\times(f\bm{A})=f(\nabla\times\bm{A})+(\nabla f)\times\bm{A}=f(\nabla\times\bm{A})-\bm{A}\times(\nabla f)$, and $\pp=-\ii\nabla$, we obtain

$$ \pp\times(\bm{A}f) = -\ii\nabla\times(\bm{A}f) = -\ii(\nabla\times\bm{A})f + \ii\,\bm{A}\times(\nabla f) = -\ii\bm{B}f - \bm{A}\times(\pp f) $$

(In the last step we used $\ii\nabla=-\pp$ and $\bm{B}=\nabla\times\bm{A}$.) Putting this into the square brackets above, the terms $\bm{A}\times(\pp f)$ cancel and we are left with

$$ \pp\times(\bm{A}f)+\bm{A}\times(\pp f) = -\ii\bm{B}f $$

Therefore

$$ (\bm{\pi}\times\bm{\pi})f = -q\left(-\ii\bm{B}f\right) = \ii q\bm{B}f \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \bm{\pi}\times\bm{\pi} = \ii q\bm{B} $$

$\blacksquare$

Why it does not vanish. In a word, it is because the components of $\bm{\pi}$ are not mutually commuting numbers but non-commuting operators. For a classical numerical vector $\bm{v}$, $(\bm{v}\times\bm{v})^k=\varepsilon^{kij}v^iv^j$, where $\varepsilon^{kij}$ is antisymmetric under $i\leftrightarrow j$ and $v^iv^j$ is symmetric, so the result is necessarily zero. For operators, however, the symmetry of $v^iv^j$ is broken, and the antisymmetric part, that is, the commutator, survives. Indeed,

$$ (\bm{\pi}\times\bm{\pi})^k = \varepsilon^{kij}\pi^i\pi^j = \frac{1}{2}\varepsilon^{kij}\left[\pi^i,\pi^j\right] $$

and substituting $[\pi^i,\pi^j]=-q\left([p^i,A^j]+[A^i,p^j]\right)=-q\left(-\ii\partial^iA^j+\ii\partial^jA^i\right)=\ii q\,\varepsilon^{ijl}B^l$ gives $\frac12\varepsilon^{kij}\varepsilon^{ijl}\,\ii qB^l=\frac12\cdot2\delta^{kl}\,\ii qB^l=\ii qB^k$, the same answer as above.

(3) Combining (1) and (2), we have $(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{\pi})^2=\bm{\pi}^2+\ii\bm{\sigma}\cdot(\ii q\bm{B})=\bm{\pi}^2-q\,\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{B}$, and the spin term of the Pauli equation in Chapter 9 of this book is $-\dfrac{q}{2m}\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{B}$. Since the electron has $q=-e$ ($e>0$),

$$ -\frac{q}{2m}\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{B} \;\longrightarrow\; +\frac{e}{2m}\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{B} $$

so the sign is indeed reversed and becomes positive. Section 9.3.5 of this book is written in natural units with $\hbar=1$, so we first read off the coefficient in those units. The spin operator is $\bm{S}=\bm{\sigma}/2$, that is, $\bm{\sigma}=2\bm{S}$, so

$$ +\frac{e}{2m}\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{B} = \frac{e}{2m}\cdot 2\,\bm{S}\cdot\bm{B} = \frac{e}{m}\,\bm{S}\cdot\bm{B} $$

On the other hand, the defining expression that leaves the $g$-factor undetermined is, using $\mu_B=e/2m$ (the Bohr magneton for $\hbar=1$),

$$ g\,\mu_B\,\bm{S}\cdot\bm{B} = g\,\frac{e}{2m}\,\bm{S}\cdot\bm{B} $$

Equating the two gives $\dfrac{e}{m}=g\dfrac{e}{2m}$, that is, $1=g/2$, and hence

$$ g = 2 $$

For orbital angular momentum we had $\bm{\mu}=(q/2m)\bm{L}$, that is, $g_L=1$, so only the spin is doubled. $\blacksquare$

The form with $\hbar$ restored. When we write in practical units, the spin term of the Pauli equation is $-\dfrac{q\hbar}{2m}\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{B}$, which for the electron becomes $+\dfrac{e\hbar}{2m}\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{B}=\mu_B\,\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{B}$ ($\mu_B=e\hbar/2m$). In this case $\bm{S}=\dfrac{\hbar}{2}\bm{\sigma}$, that is, $\bm{\sigma}=2\bm{S}/\hbar$, so

$$ \mu_B\,\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{B} = 2\mu_B\,\frac{\bm{S}\cdot\bm{B}}{\hbar} = g\,\mu_B\,\frac{\bm{S}\cdot\bm{B}}{\hbar}, \qquad g=2 $$

which is the form in the problem statement. If one naively places the $\hbar=1$ expression $+\dfrac{e}{2m}\bm{\sigma}\cdot\bm{B}$ obtained above next to the expression with $\hbar$ restored, the bookkeeping of $\hbar$ appears not to match, so it is safer to decide first in which system of units one is reading and then to compare. The conclusion $g=2$ is, of course, independent of the system of units.

Let us also state the physical reading of the sign. The magnetic moment of the electron is $\bm{\mu}=-\dfrac{e}{m}\bm{S}$, in the opposite direction to the spin, and the energy is $-\bm{\mu}\cdot\bm{B}=+\dfrac{e}{m}\bm{S}\cdot\bm{B}$, which agrees with the expression above. Therefore, in a magnetic field, the state with the spin parallel to the field ($m_s=+1/2$) has the higher energy.

(4) The resonance condition is the equation stating that the energy difference $\Delta E=g\mu_BB$ between $m_s=+1/2$ and $m_s=-1/2$ equals the energy $h\nu$ of a single photon. We substitute in turn the given values $g=2.0023$, $\mu_B=9.274\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J/T}$, $B=0.34\ \mathrm{T}$, and $h=6.626\times10^{-34}\ \mathrm{J\,s}$.

$$ g\mu_B = 2.0023\times9.274\times10^{-24} = 1.8569\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/T} $$ $$ \Delta E = g\mu_B B = 1.8569\times10^{-23}\times0.34 = 6.3136\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{J} $$ $$ \nu = \frac{\Delta E}{h} = \frac{6.3136\times10^{-24}}{6.626\times10^{-34}} = 9.5285\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{Hz} = 9.53\ \mathrm{GHz} $$

This agrees with the value $9.53\ \mathrm{GHz}$ in the hint in the main text. Converted to a vacuum wavelength, $\lambda=c/\nu=(2.998\times10^{8})/(9.5285\times10^{9})=3.15\ \mathrm{cm}$, which is the X band of the microwave region. As an energy, it is a mere $\Delta E=3.94\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV}=39.4\ \mathrm{\mu eV}$, and converted to a temperature, $\Delta E/k_B=0.46\ \mathrm{K}$. $\blacksquare$

Verification. Check the dimensions: $[\mu_B B/h]=(\mathrm{J/T})\cdot\mathrm{T}/(\mathrm{J\,s})=\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, which is indeed a frequency. As an alternative numerical route, it is quick to form the electron gyromagnetic ratio first:

$$ \frac{g\mu_B}{h} = \frac{1.8569\times10^{-23}}{6.626\times10^{-34}} = 2.802\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{Hz/T} = 28.02\ \mathrm{GHz/T} $$

This is a value widely used for mental arithmetic in the field of ESR (for $g=2$ it is about $28\ \mathrm{GHz/T}$; in other words, for an instrument with $\nu=9.5\ \mathrm{GHz}$ the resonance field is about $0.34\ \mathrm{T}=3400\ \mathrm{G}$), and $28.02\times0.34=9.53\ \mathrm{GHz}$ agrees with the result above. Comparing with the proton value in nuclear magnetic resonance, $42.58\ \mathrm{MHz/T}$,

$$ \frac{28.02\times10^{9}}{42.58\times10^{6}} = 658 $$

times. Let us also decompose what lies inside this number $658$. The gyromagnetic ratio is proportional to $g\mu/h$; the electron has the Bohr magneton $\mu_B=e\hbar/2m_e$ and $g_e=2.0023$, and the proton has the nuclear magneton $\mu_N=e\hbar/2m_p$ and $g_p=5.586$, so

$$ \frac{g_e\mu_B}{g_p\mu_N} = \frac{g_e}{g_p}\cdot\frac{m_p}{m_e} = \frac{2.0023}{5.586}\times1836 = 0.3585\times1836 = 658 $$

It is often said that “the electron-to-proton mass ratio $1836$ is what counts,” but this is not exactly correct: the mass ratio $1836$ is multiplied by the ratio of $g$-factors, $g_e/g_p=0.36$, to give $658$. The large deviation of the proton’s $g_p=5.586$ from $2$ is because the proton is not a point particle but a composite state of quarks, and it is also direct evidence that Dirac’s prediction $g=2$ does not hold for composite particles (the $g=2$ of Chapter 9 is a prediction only for a structureless, pointlike Dirac particle).

Meaning. For materials scientists, ESR (EPR) measurement is a setting in which Dirac’s prediction $g=2$ is put to work every day. What matters is that the measured $g$ value deviates from $2.0023$. When orbital angular momentum is slightly admixed in a crystal field (through spin–orbit coupling), $g$ has a deviation determined by the crystal-field splitting $\Delta_{\text{cf}}$ and the spin–orbit coupling constant $\lambda$, as in $g\simeq2.0023\pm\kappa\lambda/\Delta_{\text{cf}}$, and moreover this deviation is anisotropic with respect to the crystal axes. Hence, by measuring the principal values and principal axes of the $g$ tensor, one can determine the valence, spin state, and coordination environment (octahedral or tetrahedral, whether there is a Jahn–Teller distortion) of a transition-metal ion. The same holds for organic radicals and defect centers (for example, the $E'$ center in silicon and the NV center in diamond). The deviation from $g=2$ also includes the quantum-electrodynamic correction $a_e=(g-2)/2=\alpha/2\pi+\cdots=1.16\times10^{-3}$, and the trailing $23$ of the free-electron $2.0023$ is precisely this radiative correction (Chapter 10). The deviations of $g$ values in matter (typically $10^{-2}$ to $10^{-1}$) are larger than this by a further one to two orders of magnitude.

Exercise 9.4: Chirality projection operators

Problem (restated)

For $P_{L,R}=(1\mp\gamma^5)/2$, show the following.

(1) $P_L^2=P_L$, $P_R^2=P_R$, $P_LP_R=0$, $P_L+P_R=1$.

(2) $\gamma^\mu P_L = P_R\gamma^\mu$, $\bar\psi_L=\bar\psi P_R$.

(3) $\bar\psi\psi = \bar\psi_L\psi_R+\bar\psi_R\psi_L$.

(4) For the $V-A$ current of the weak interaction, show that $\bar\psi\gamma^\mu(1-\gamma^5)\psi = 2\,\bar\psi_L\gamma^\mu\psi_L$.

Solution

Strategy. We use only three properties, all proved in Chapter 9 of this book: $(\gamma^5)^2=\mathbb{1}$, $\gamma^{5\dagger}=\gamma^5$, and $\{\gamma^5,\gamma^\mu\}=0$ (for all $\mu$). The last, anticommutation, yields the rule that runs through this entire problem: “passing through $\gamma^\mu$ interchanges $L$ and $R$.” The definitions are $P_L=(1-\gamma^5)/2$, $P_R=(1+\gamma^5)/2$, $\psi_{L}=P_L\psi$, and $\psi_R=P_R\psi$.

(1) We expand the squares directly.

$$ P_L^2 = \frac{(1-\gamma^5)^2}{4} = \frac{1-2\gamma^5+(\gamma^5)^2}{4} = \frac{1-2\gamma^5+1}{4} = \frac{2(1-\gamma^5)}{4} = \frac{1-\gamma^5}{2}=P_L $$

For $P_R$, the same calculation with only the sign of $\gamma^5$ changed gives $P_R^2=P_R$. The product is

$$ P_LP_R = \frac{(1-\gamma^5)(1+\gamma^5)}{4} = \frac{1-(\gamma^5)^2}{4} = \frac{1-1}{4}=0 $$

($P_RP_L$ is likewise zero. In the course of the expansion, the commutation of $\gamma^5$ with $1$ is trivial, so there is no need to worry about the order.) The sum is

$$ P_L+P_R = \frac{(1-\gamma^5)+(1+\gamma^5)}{2} = \frac{2}{2} = \mathbb{1} $$

It follows that $P_{L,R}$ is a complete set of mutually orthogonal projection operators, and any spinor can be uniquely decomposed as $\psi=P_L\psi+P_R\psi=\psi_L+\psi_R$. $\blacksquare$

(2) The first half uses the anticommutation $\gamma^\mu\gamma^5=-\gamma^5\gamma^\mu$ just once.

$$ \gamma^\mu P_L = \gamma^\mu\frac{1-\gamma^5}{2} = \frac{\gamma^\mu - \gamma^\mu\gamma^5}{2} = \frac{\gamma^\mu + \gamma^5\gamma^\mu}{2} = \frac{(1+\gamma^5)}{2}\gamma^\mu = P_R\gamma^\mu $$

Similarly, $\gamma^\mu P_R=P_L\gamma^\mu$. That is, each time we pass through a $\gamma^\mu$, $L$ and $R$ are interchanged.

For the second half, we first check that $P_L$ is Hermitian: $P_L^\dagger=\dfrac{(1-\gamma^5)^\dagger}{2}=\dfrac{1-\gamma^{5\dagger}}{2}=\dfrac{1-\gamma^5}{2}=P_L$. Therefore

$$ \bar\psi_L = (P_L\psi)^\dagger\gamma^0 = \psi^\dagger P_L^\dagger\gamma^0 = \psi^\dagger P_L\gamma^0 $$

Here $\gamma^0$ is also one of the $\gamma^\mu$, so the rule of the first half applies and $P_L\gamma^0=\gamma^0P_R$. Hence

$$ \bar\psi_L = \psi^\dagger\gamma^0P_R = \bar\psi P_R $$

Similarly, $\bar\psi_R=\bar\psi P_L$. This is the property, easy to confuse but crucially important, that putting on the bar interchanges the labels $L$ and $R$. $\blacksquare$

(3) We insert the completeness relation $P_L+P_R=\mathbb{1}$ of (1) between $\bar\psi$ and $\psi$.

$$ \bar\psi\psi = \bar\psi\left(P_L+P_R\right)\psi = \bar\psi P_L\psi + \bar\psi P_R\psi $$

We rewrite the first term. Since $P_L$ is idempotent, we split it into two as $P_L=P_LP_L$, and using the second half of (2), $\bar\psi P_L=\bar\psi_R$, we obtain

$$ \bar\psi P_L\psi = \bar\psi P_L\,P_L\psi = \left(\bar\psi P_L\right)\left(P_L\psi\right) = \bar\psi_R\,\psi_L $$

The second term goes through in exactly the same way: $\bar\psi P_R\psi=\left(\bar\psi P_R\right)\left(P_R\psi\right)=\bar\psi_L\psi_R$. Therefore

$$ \bar\psi\psi = \bar\psi_L\psi_R + \bar\psi_R\psi_L $$

$\blacksquare$ Applying the same procedure to the vector current changes the result. In $\bar\psi\gamma^\mu\psi=\bar\psi P_L\gamma^\mu\psi+\bar\psi P_R\gamma^\mu\psi$, we split the first term into two as $P_L=P_LP_L$, as above, and then pass only the right-hand $P_L$ to the other side of $\gamma^\mu$ using the rule of (2):

$$ \bar\psi P_L\gamma^\mu\psi = \bar\psi P_L\,P_L\gamma^\mu\,\psi = \bar\psi P_L\,\gamma^\mu P_R\,\psi = \left(\bar\psi P_L\right)\gamma^\mu\left(P_R\psi\right) = \bar\psi_R\,\gamma^\mu\psi_R $$

Whereas the indices disagreed in the mass term, $\bar\psi_R\psi_L$, here in $\bar\psi_R\gamma^\mu\psi_R$ they are both $R$ and match. This is because passing through one $\gamma^\mu$ causes one extra interchange, which exactly cancels the interchange due to the bar. Likewise, the second term is $\bar\psi_L\gamma^\mu\psi_L$, and $L$ and $R$ do not mix. The conclusion of Chapter 9 of this book, “the mass term mixes; the current term does not mix,” is this difference.

(4) Since $1-\gamma^5=2P_L$, we first have

$$ \gamma^\mu\left(1-\gamma^5\right) = 2\gamma^\mu P_L = 2P_R\gamma^\mu $$

(In the last step we used (2).) Sandwiching this between the conjugate spinor and the spinor gives

$$ \bar\psi\gamma^\mu\left(1-\gamma^5\right)\psi = 2\,\bar\psi P_R\gamma^\mu\psi = 2\,\bar\psi_L\gamma^\mu\psi $$

(We used the second half of (2), $\bar\psi P_R=\bar\psi_L$.) What remains is to show that the $\psi$ on the right can be restricted to its left-handed component alone. Inserting completeness and splitting $\psi=\psi_L+\psi_R$, we get

$$ \bar\psi_L\gamma^\mu\psi = \bar\psi_L\gamma^\mu\psi_L + \bar\psi_L\gamma^\mu\psi_R $$

We evaluate the second term. Returning to the definitions, $\bar\psi_L=\bar\psi P_R$ and $\psi_R=P_R\psi$, so

$$ \bar\psi_L\gamma^\mu\psi_R = \bar\psi\,P_R\gamma^\mu P_R\,\psi = \bar\psi\,\gamma^\mu P_LP_R\,\psi = 0 $$

On the way we used $P_R\gamma^\mu=\gamma^\mu P_L$ from (2), and at the end $P_LP_R=0$ from (1). Therefore

$$ \bar\psi\gamma^\mu\left(1-\gamma^5\right)\psi = 2\,\bar\psi_L\gamma^\mu\psi_L $$

$\blacksquare$ Although the $V-A$ current is written as if it contained the whole of $\psi$, it actually picks out only the left-handed chirality component.

Verification. We check using the rank of the projection operators. First we show $\Tr\gamma^5=0$. From $(\gamma^0)^2=\mathbb{1}$ and the cyclicity of the trace, $\Tr\gamma^5=\Tr\left[\gamma^0\gamma^5\gamma^0\right]$, and by $\{\gamma^5,\gamma^0\}=0$ the right-hand side equals $\Tr\left[-\gamma^5\gamma^0\gamma^0\right]=-\Tr\gamma^5$. From $\Tr\gamma^5=-\Tr\gamma^5$ it can only be zero. Using this,

$$ \Tr P_L = \frac{\Tr\mathbb{1}_4-\Tr\gamma^5}{2} = \frac{4-0}{2}=2, \qquad \Tr P_R = 2 $$

Since the trace of a projection operator equals the dimension of its image, $P_L$ and $P_R$ are each operators that project onto a two-dimensional subspace of the four-dimensional spinor space, and $2+2=4$ is consistent with $P_L+P_R=\mathbb{1}$. We can also check with a concrete example: as seen in Chapter 9 of this book, a massless spinor of helicity $\lambda=+1$ satisfies $\gamma^5u=+u$, so $P_Ru=u$ and $P_Lu=0$, which does not contradict $P_LP_R=0$ of (1). Furthermore, applying the replacement $\gamma^5\to-\gamma^5$ ($L\leftrightarrow R$) to the result of (4) gives $\bar\psi\gamma^\mu(1+\gamma^5)\psi=2\bar\psi_R\gamma^\mu\psi_R$, and adding the two gives $2\bar\psi\gamma^\mu\psi=2(\bar\psi_L\gamma^\mu\psi_L+\bar\psi_R\gamma^\mu\psi_R)$, that is, the decomposition of the vector current stated in the second half of (3) is reproduced.

Meaning. (4) is the mathematical expression of the central fact of the Standard Model that “the weak interaction acts only on left-handed particles” (Chapter 12). At the same time, (3) says that “the mass term mixes left and right,” and combining these two yields an important consequence: although there is a mass term that does not preserve chirality, the weak interaction selects chirality, so mass and gauge interactions are, naively, incompatible. The resolution of this contradiction is the Higgs mechanism (Chapter 13).

The connection to materials science is also clear. In a Weyl semimetal, the massless four-component Dirac equation decomposes, by $P_L$ and $P_R$, into two $2\times2$ equations, each of which appears as a Weyl point of opposite chirality at a separate position in momentum space. The relation $P_LP_R=0$ of this problem gives the algebraic backing for the fact that the two Weyl points are independent (and therefore that one of them alone cannot be eliminated by a local perturbation). And only the mass term (a perturbation that merges the two Weyl points in momentum space) mixes left and right and opens a gap. The slogan of Chapter 9 of this book, “mass is an interaction that changes chirality,” can be translated into the language of band structure in real materials such as TaAs.

Exercise 9.5: The “wrong chirality” contained in a helicity state

Problem (restated)

Consider a particle of mass $m$, momentum $\pp$ (in the $z$ direction), energy $E$, and helicity $+1$. The spinor is the normalized $u(p,s)$ of Chapter 9 of this book, with $\chi$ chosen so that $\sigma_z\chi=+\chi$.

(1) Writing $a\equiv\sqrt{E+m}$ and $b\equiv\abs{\pp}/\sqrt{E+m}$, verify that $u=(a\chi,\ b\chi)^T$, and show that $u^\dagger u=a^2+b^2=2E$.

(2) Compute $P_{R}u$ and $P_Lu$, and show that $\abs{P_Ru}^2=(a+b)^2/2$ and $\abs{P_Lu}^2=(a-b)^2/2$.

(3) Using $ab=\abs{\pp}$, show that the fraction of the left-handed chirality component is $\dfrac{\abs{P_Lu}^2}{u^\dagger u}=\dfrac{1-v}{2}$ (with $v=\abs{\pp}/E$).

(4) For an electron with $E=10\ \mathrm{MeV}$ ($m_e=0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$), find this fraction numerically. Also show that $(1-v)/2\simeq m^2/(4E^2)$ as $v\to1$, and confirm that the numerical values agree.

Solution

Strategy. In the Dirac–Pauli representation, $\gamma^5=\begin{pmatrix}0&\mathbb{1}_2\\ \mathbb{1}_2&0\end{pmatrix}$ is the matrix that “swaps the upper and lower two components.” Hence the projections $P_{R,L}=(1\pm\gamma^5)/2$ are nothing but operations that form the sum and difference of the upper and lower components. The problem essentially reduces to comparing the squares of the sum and difference of two numbers $a,b$.

(1) Take the momentum to be $\pp=(0,0,\abs{\pp})$, so that $\bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp=\abs{\pp}\,\sigma_z$. Since $\chi$ has been chosen to satisfy $\sigma_z\chi=+\chi$ (that is, $\chi=(1,0)^T$), we have $(\bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp)\chi=\abs{\pp}\chi$. Substituting this into the $u$ of Chapter 9 of this book gives

$$ u = \sqrt{E+m}\begin{pmatrix}\chi\\[4pt] \dfrac{\bm{\sigma}\cdot\pp}{E+m}\chi\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}\sqrt{E+m}\,\chi\\[4pt] \dfrac{\abs{\pp}}{\sqrt{E+m}}\chi\end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix}a\chi\\[4pt] b\chi\end{pmatrix} $$

which confirms the stated form. Here we simplified the coefficient of the lower components as $\sqrt{E+m}\cdot\dfrac{\abs{\pp}}{E+m}=\dfrac{\abs{\pp}}{\sqrt{E+m}}=b$. For the norm, noting that $\chi^\dagger\chi=1$,

$$ u^\dagger u = a^2\chi^\dagger\chi + b^2\chi^\dagger\chi = a^2+b^2 = (E+m) + \frac{\pp^2}{E+m} = \frac{(E+m)^2+\pp^2}{E+m} $$

Inserting the dispersion relation $\pp^2=E^2-m^2$ into the numerator gives

$$ (E+m)^2+E^2-m^2 = E^2+2Em+m^2+E^2-m^2 = 2E^2+2Em = 2E(E+m) $$

Therefore $u^\dagger u = 2E(E+m)/(E+m)=2E$. This agrees with the convention $u^\dagger u=2E$ of Chapter 9 of this book. $\blacksquare$

(2) Since $\gamma^5$ swaps the upper and lower blocks, $\gamma^5u=(b\chi,\ a\chi)^T$. Thus

$$ P_Ru = \frac{u+\gamma^5u}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}(a+b)\chi\\ (a+b)\chi\end{pmatrix} = \frac{a+b}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\chi\\ \chi\end{pmatrix} $$ $$ P_Lu = \frac{u-\gamma^5u}{2} = \frac{1}{2}\begin{pmatrix}(a-b)\chi\\ -(a-b)\chi\end{pmatrix} = \frac{a-b}{2}\begin{pmatrix}\chi\\ -\chi\end{pmatrix} $$

Now we compute the norms. In both cases the upper and lower blocks are proportional to $\chi$, and $\chi^\dagger\chi=1$, so the squared norm of the column vector $(\chi,\pm\chi)^T$ is $1+1=2$. Therefore

$$ \abs{P_Ru}^2 = \left(\frac{a+b}{2}\right)^2\times 2 = \frac{(a+b)^2}{2}, \qquad \abs{P_Lu}^2 = \left(\frac{a-b}{2}\right)^2\times 2 = \frac{(a-b)^2}{2} $$

$\blacksquare$ Adding them gives $\dfrac{(a+b)^2+(a-b)^2}{2}=\dfrac{2a^2+2b^2}{2}=a^2+b^2=u^\dagger u$, consistent with (1) (the cross terms $\pm2ab$ cancel). This is a concrete manifestation of the fact that the images of $P_L$ and $P_R$ are orthogonal, that is, of $P_LP_R=0$ from Exercise 9.4.

(3) First we compute $ab$.

$$ ab = \sqrt{E+m}\cdot\frac{\abs{\pp}}{\sqrt{E+m}} = \abs{\pp} $$

Using this together with $a^2+b^2=2E$,

$$ \frac{\abs{P_Lu}^2}{u^\dagger u} = \frac{(a-b)^2/2}{a^2+b^2} = \frac{a^2+b^2-2ab}{2(a^2+b^2)} = \frac{2E-2\abs{\pp}}{2\cdot 2E} = \frac{E-\abs{\pp}}{2E} = \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{\abs{\pp}}{E}\right) = \frac{1-v}{2} $$

$\blacksquare$ By the same calculation the fraction of the right-handed component is $\dfrac{(a+b)^2/2}{2E}=\dfrac{1+v}{2}$, and the two fractions sum to $1$. As $v\to1$ (ultrarelativistic) the left-handed fraction approaches $0$, and as $v\to0$ (at rest) it approaches $1/2$. For a particle at rest, left and right are exactly half and half, and the distinction by chirality loses its meaning.

(4) First we find the momentum and the velocity. For $m=0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $E=10\ \mathrm{MeV}$ we have $m^2=0.261121\ \mathrm{MeV^2}$, so

$$ \abs{\pp} = \sqrt{E^2-m^2} = \sqrt{100-0.261121} = \sqrt{99.738879} = 9.98694\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ $$ v = \frac{\abs{\pp}}{E} = \frac{9.98694}{10} = 0.998694 $$

Therefore the fraction of the left-handed chirality component is

$$ \frac{\abs{P_Lu}^2}{u^\dagger u} = \frac{1-v}{2} = \frac{1-0.998694}{2} = \frac{1.30646\times10^{-3}}{2} = 6.532\times10^{-4} $$

that is, about $0.065\ \%$.

Next we derive the ultrarelativistic approximation. We have $v=\dfrac{\sqrt{E^2-m^2}}{E}=\sqrt{1-\dfrac{m^2}{E^2}}$, and when $m^2/E^2\ll1$ we use $\sqrt{1-x}\simeq1-x/2$ to obtain

$$ v \simeq 1-\frac{m^2}{2E^2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{1-v}{2} \simeq \frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{m^2}{2E^2} = \frac{m^2}{4E^2} $$

Inserting the numbers,

$$ \frac{m^2}{4E^2} = \frac{0.261121}{4\times100} = \frac{0.261121}{400} = 6.528\times10^{-4} $$

The exact value $6.532\times10^{-4}$ and the approximate value $6.528\times10^{-4}$ indeed agree to 3 significant figures. The size of the discrepancy can also be predicted from the expansion. Letting $x\equiv m^2/E^2$, we have $\sqrt{1-x}=1-\dfrac{x}{2}-\dfrac{x^2}{8}-\cdots$, so

$$ \frac{1-v}{2} = \frac{x}{4}+\frac{x^2}{16}+\cdots = \frac{x}{4}\left(1+\frac{x}{4}+\cdots\right), \qquad x=\frac{m^2}{E^2}=2.6112\times10^{-3} $$

That is, the absolute size of the second term is $x^2/16=(2.6112\times10^{-3})^2/16=4.26\times10^{-7}$, and its relative size compared with the first term is $x/4=6.53\times10^{-4}$. The actual difference is $6.5322\times10^{-4}-6.5280\times10^{-4}=4.2\times10^{-7}$ (relative $0.065\ \%$), in precise agreement with this prediction. $\blacksquare$

Verification. We perform three independent checks. First, the two fractions in (2) sum to $\dfrac{1-v}{2}+\dfrac{1+v}{2}=1$, which corresponds to conservation of probability. Numerically, $6.532\times10^{-4}+0.9993468=1.0000000$. Second, the formula of (3) in the rest limit $\abs{\pp}\to0$ ($v\to0$) gives $1/2$, which agrees with the direct calculation that the spinor at rest is $u=\sqrt{2m}(\chi,0)^T$ and the norms of $P_Lu$ and $P_Ru$ are equal ($a=\sqrt{2m}$ and $b=0$, so $(a\pm b)^2/2$ are both $m$). Third, in the massless limit $m\to0$ we get $v\to1$ and the left-handed component vanishes exactly; that is, the helicity $+1$ state becomes a pure right-handed chirality state, which reproduces the theorem of Chapter 9 of this book that “for zero mass, chirality = helicity.”

Meaning. Even for an electron of helicity $+1$, as long as it has mass, a left-handed chirality fraction of $(1-v)/2$ is always mixed in. The most famous consequence of this in particle physics is the decay ratio of the charged pion. In $\pi^+\to\ell^+\nu_\ell$, because a spin-0 parent undergoes a two-body decay, the chirality demanded by the weak interaction and the helicity demanded by angular-momentum conservation collide, and the amplitude becomes proportional to the admixture fraction of the “wrong chirality,” that is, to $m_\ell^2$. As a result the light electron mode is more strongly suppressed, and the counterintuitive ratio $\Gamma(\pi\to e\nu)/\Gamma(\pi\to\mu\nu)\sim10^{-4}$ is realized (Chapter 12).

On the materials-science side, the same structure appears in the surface states of topological insulators. The surface Dirac cone of Bi$_2$Se$_3$ is described by the two-dimensional Dirac equation with $m=0$, and spin and momentum are in a fixed relation (spin–momentum locking). Here $v=1$, that is, “always pure chirality,” and thanks to this the $180^\circ$ backscattering is forbidden by the vanishing spin overlap, so that the surface conduction is robust against impurities. However, when magnetic impurities are introduced, or when the sample is made an ultrathin film so that the top and bottom surfaces couple, an effective mass $m$ opens in the surface states. Then the “wrong chirality” corresponding to $(1-v)/2$ in this problem is admixed, backscattering revives, and the conduction deteriorates. The particle-physics statement that “once mass enters, the chirality protection breaks down” shows up directly in measurements as the degradation of surface conduction.

Exercise 9.6: The Dirac equation of graphene

Problem (restated)

Let $H=\hbar v_F(\sigma_xq_x+\sigma_yq_y)+\Delta\sigma_z$ with $\hbar v_F=0.658\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$ ($v_F=1.0\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s}$).

(1) Show that the eigenvalues are $E=\pm\sqrt{\hbar^2v_F^2q^2+\Delta^2}$, using $(\bm{d}\cdot\bm{\sigma})^2=\abs{\bm{d}}^2$.

(2) For $\Delta=0$, verify that the eigenvectors are $\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,\pm\ee^{\ii\theta_q})^T$, and show that the overlap integral for $\qq\to-\qq$ (backscattering) vanishes.

(3) For $\Delta=0$ and a degeneracy of 4 (spin 2 × valley 2), show that the density of states per unit area is $\rho(E)=\dfrac{2\abs{E}}{\pi\hbar^2v_F^2}$.

(4) For $E_F=0.10\ \mathrm{eV}$, find the carrier density $n=E_F^2/(\pi\hbar^2v_F^2)$ and the density of states $\rho(E_F)$ in units of $\mathrm{cm^{-2}}$ and $\mathrm{eV^{-1}cm^{-2}}$.

Solution

Strategy. This Hamiltonian can be squeezed into the form $H=\bm{d}\cdot\bm{\sigma}$, a “linear combination of Pauli matrices.” Then both the eigenvalues and the eigenvectors are settled algebraically. The density of states follows the standard procedure of counting states in two dimensions (dividing the area in $\kk$ space by $(2\pi)^2$). Note that in this section we have restored $\hbar$, and treating $\hbar v_F=0.658\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$ as a single constant makes the numerical calculation easier. The wavevector $\qq$ is measured from the Dirac point ($K$ point).

(1) The given Hamiltonian can be written as

$$ H = \hbar v_F q_x\,\sigma_x + \hbar v_F q_y\,\sigma_y + \Delta\,\sigma_z = \bm{d}\cdot\bm{\sigma}, \qquad \bm{d}\equiv\left(\hbar v_Fq_x,\ \hbar v_Fq_y,\ \Delta\right) $$

Note that $\bm{d}$ is not an operator but a real numerical vector ($\qq$ is a good quantum number). Applying the identity of Exercise 9.3(1) with $\bm{a}=\bm{b}=\bm{d}$, and using $\bm{d}\times\bm{d}=0$,

$$ H^2 = (\bm{d}\cdot\bm{\sigma})(\bm{d}\cdot\bm{\sigma}) = \bm{d}\cdot\bm{d} + \ii\bm{\sigma}\cdot(\bm{d}\times\bm{d}) = \abs{\bm{d}}^2\,\mathbb{1}_2 $$

Therefore an eigenvalue $E$ satisfies $E^2=\abs{\bm{d}}^2$, so $E=\pm\abs{\bm{d}}$. Moreover, since all the Pauli matrices are traceless, $\Tr H=0$; that is, the sum of the two eigenvalues must be zero. Hence as long as $\abs{\bm{d}}\ne0$ the two eigenvalues are $+\abs{\bm{d}}$ and $-\abs{\bm{d}}$, and neither of them can appear twice (only for $\qq=0$ and $\Delta=0$ do we have $H=0$, in which case the two eigenvalues are both degenerate at zero; this is the Dirac point). Written explicitly,

$$ E_\pm = \pm\abs{\bm{d}} = \pm\sqrt{\hbar^2v_F^2\left(q_x^2+q_y^2\right)+\Delta^2} = \pm\sqrt{\hbar^2v_F^2q^2+\Delta^2} $$

$\blacksquare$ This is exactly the relativistic formula $E=\pm\sqrt{c^2p^2+m^2c^4}$ with the replacements $c\to v_F$ and $mc^2\to\Delta$.

(2) Let $\Delta=0$ and $\qq=q(\cos\theta_q,\sin\theta_q)$. Then

$$ H = \hbar v_F\begin{pmatrix}0 & q_x-\ii q_y\\ q_x+\ii q_y & 0\end{pmatrix} = \hbar v_Fq\begin{pmatrix}0 & \ee^{-\ii\theta_q}\\ \ee^{\ii\theta_q} & 0\end{pmatrix} $$

(we used $q_x\pm\ii q_y=q\ee^{\pm\ii\theta_q}$). Let it act on the candidates $\ket{\psi_\pm}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(1,\pm\ee^{\ii\theta_q})^T$:

$$ H\ket{\psi_\pm} = \frac{\hbar v_Fq}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}\ee^{-\ii\theta_q}\cdot(\pm\ee^{\ii\theta_q})\\ \ee^{\ii\theta_q}\cdot1\end{pmatrix} = \frac{\hbar v_Fq}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}\pm1\\ \ee^{\ii\theta_q}\end{pmatrix} = \pm\hbar v_Fq\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1\\ \pm\ee^{\ii\theta_q}\end{pmatrix} $$

In the last equality we used the fact that factoring out $\pm1$ turns the lower component into $\pm\ee^{\ii\theta_q}$ (since $1/(\pm1)=\pm1$). Therefore $\ket{\psi_\pm}$ is an eigenvector with eigenvalue $E_\pm=\pm\hbar v_Fq$. The normalization is also correct: $\braket{\psi_\pm|\psi_\pm}=\frac12(1+1)=1$. $\blacksquare$

Next we consider scattering straight backward. Since $\qq\to-\qq$ is a reversal of direction, $\theta_q\to\theta_q+\pi$. The overlap between states in the same band (same sign $\pm$) is

$$ \braket{\psi_\pm(\theta_q+\pi)|\psi_\pm(\theta_q)} = \frac{1}{2}\left[1^*\cdot1 + \left(\pm\ee^{\ii(\theta_q+\pi)}\right)^*\left(\pm\ee^{\ii\theta_q}\right)\right] = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 + \ee^{-\ii(\theta_q+\pi)}\ee^{\ii\theta_q}\right] $$ $$ = \frac{1}{2}\left[1+\ee^{-\ii\pi}\right] = \frac{1}{2}\left[1-1\right] = 0 $$

which is exactly zero (since $(\pm1)^*(\pm1)=1$, the sign of the band drops out). $\blacksquare$ Physically, because the pseudospin is locked to the direction of $\qq$, reversing the momentum also reverses the pseudospin, and the two states become orthogonal. For scatterers that do not act on the pseudospin, such as lattice disorder, this overlap multiplies the matrix element, so $180^\circ$ backscattering is forbidden.

(3) We count the states in a two-dimensional system whose wavenumber magnitude is at most $q$. The area of a circle of radius $q$ in $\qq$ space is $\pi q^2$, and the density of states per unit area of the sample is counted with the volume element $1/(2\pi)^2$ of $\qq$ space. Multiplying further by the degeneracy of 4 (spin 2 × valley 2), the number of states per unit area is

$$ n(q) = 4\times\frac{\pi q^2}{(2\pi)^2} = \frac{4\pi q^2}{4\pi^2} = \frac{q^2}{\pi} $$

For $\Delta=0$ we have $\abs{E}=\hbar v_Fq$, that is, $q=\abs{E}/(\hbar v_F)$, so

$$ n(E) = \frac{1}{\pi}\left(\frac{\abs{E}}{\hbar v_F}\right)^2 = \frac{E^2}{\pi\hbar^2v_F^2} $$

The density of states is the derivative of this with respect to energy, and on the $E>0$ side

$$ \rho(E) = \frac{\dd n}{\dd E} = \frac{2E}{\pi\hbar^2v_F^2} $$

The same counting holds on the $E<0$ side (the valence band) as well; since we differentiate in the direction in which $\abs{E}$ increases, we write, with the sign included,

$$ \rho(E) = \frac{2\abs{E}}{\pi\hbar^2v_F^2} $$

$\blacksquare$ Thanks to the absolute value, the density of states vanishes at $E=0$ (the Dirac point). This is the hallmark of a “semimetal,” which is neither a metal nor an insulator.

(4) First we collect the constants.

$$ \left(\hbar v_F\right)^2 = (0.658)^2 = 0.43296\ \mathrm{eV^2\,nm^2}, \qquad \pi\left(\hbar v_F\right)^2 = 3.1416\times0.43296 = 1.3602\ \mathrm{eV^2\,nm^2} $$

The carrier density is

$$ n = \frac{E_F^2}{\pi\hbar^2v_F^2} = \frac{(0.10)^2}{1.3602} = \frac{0.0100}{1.3602} = 7.352\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{nm^{-2}} $$

We convert the units. Since $1\ \mathrm{nm}=10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm}$, we have $1\ \mathrm{nm^{-2}}=10^{14}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}}$. Therefore

$$ n = 7.352\times10^{-3}\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}} = 7.35\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}} $$

The density of states is

$$ \rho(E_F) = \frac{2E_F}{\pi\hbar^2v_F^2} = \frac{2\times0.10}{1.3602} = 0.1470\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}nm^{-2}} = 1.47\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}cm^{-2}} $$

$\blacksquare$ These agree with the values in the hint in the main text ($7.3\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}}$ and $1.5\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}cm^{-2}}$).

Verification. We check in three ways. First, a direct calculation from the Fermi wavenumber. We have $q_F=E_F/(\hbar v_F)=0.10/0.658=0.1520\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}$, and putting it into $n=q_F^2/\pi$ of (3) gives $0.1520^2/3.1416=7.35\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{nm^{-2}}$, in agreement. Incidentally, $q_F$ is a mere $0.9\ \%$ of the distance from the $\Gamma$ point to the $K$ point ($\abs{\bm{K}}=4\pi/(3\sqrt3\,a_{\mathrm{CC}})=4\pi/(3\times1.732\times0.142)=17.0\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}}$, where $a_{\mathrm{CC}}=0.142\ \mathrm{nm}$ is the C–C bond length), so the premise of the linear expansion near the $K$ point holds well. Second, between $n$ and $\rho$ there should be the relation $\rho(E_F)=\dd n/\dd E_F=2n/E_F$, and $2\times7.352\times10^{-3}/0.10=0.147\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}nm^{-2}}$ agrees with the above. Third, dimensions: $[E^2]/[E^2L^2]=L^{-2}$, which is indeed an areal density.

Meaning. The form of the result is decisively different from that of an ordinary two-dimensional electron gas (2DEG). In a 2DEG with a parabolic band, the density of states $\rho=m^*/(\pi\hbar^2)$ is a constant that is independent of energy, and the carrier density grows linearly as $n\propto E_F$. In graphene, however, $\rho\propto\abs{E}$ and $n\propto E_F^2$. Therefore, when $E_F$ is moved by the gate voltage, the density of states itself moves. Conversely, $E_F=\hbar v_F\sqrt{\pi n}$, so $n$ must be increased fourfold for $E_F$ to double.

The bridge to experiment is the gate capacitance. In a field-effect-transistor-type sample, $n=C_gV_g/e$ holds. For typical graphene on $300\ \mathrm{nm}$ of SiO$_2$, $C_g=\varepsilon_0\varepsilon_r/d=8.854\times10^{-12}\times3.9/(300\times10^{-9})=1.15\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{F/m^2}$, so that $C_g/e=7.18\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}V^{-1}}$. Therefore the gate voltage required to create the $n=7.35\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}}$ of this problem is

$$ V_g = \frac{n}{C_g/e} = \frac{7.35\times10^{11}}{7.18\times10^{10}} = 10.2\ \mathrm{V} $$

which is all that is needed. With a voltage of a few batteries one can “move the Fermi energy of a Dirac particle by $0.1\ \mathrm{eV}$,” and this is the strength of graphene that is impossible with the Dirac equation of particle physics. The value of the density of states, $1.47\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}cm^{-2}}$, can also be measured through the quantum capacitance $C_q=e^2\rho$. If $\rho$ is measured in $\mathrm{eV^{-1}m^{-2}}$, we can write $C_q=e\times\rho$, so

$$ C_q = 1.602\times10^{-19}\times1.47\times10^{17} = 2.36\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{F/m^2} $$

This is about $200$ times the $C_g=1.15\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{F/m^2}$ above, and in the series combination $1/C=1/C_g+1/C_q$ the contribution of $C_q$ stays at about $0.5\ \%$. Therefore in an ordinary gate structure the geometric capacitance is the limiting factor, and the simple relation $n=C_gV_g/e$ is a good approximation. However, very close to the Dirac point $\rho\to0$, that is, $C_q\to0$, so only there does the quantum capacitance matter and the proportionality between $V_g$ and $n$ breaks down.

Exercise 9.7: Transmission probability of Klein tunneling

Problem (restated)

We study the transmission probability of Klein tunneling in Chapter 9 of this book, $T(\phi)=\dfrac{\cos^2\phi}{1-\cos^2(q_xD)\sin^2\phi}$.

(1) Show that $T=1$ for $\phi=0$ (normal incidence). Confirm that it does not depend on the barrier height $V_0$ or the width $D$.

(2) Show that $T=1$ for all angles of incidence when $q_xD=n\pi$ ($n$ an integer) (Fabry–Pérot resonance).

(3) For $\phi=45^\circ$, find the maximum and minimum values of $T$ as $q_xD$ is varied.

(4) Let $E=80\ \mathrm{meV}$, $V_0=200\ \mathrm{meV}$, $D=100\ \mathrm{nm}$, and $\phi=30^\circ$. Compute $k=E/(\hbar v_F)$, $k_y=k\sin\phi$, and $q_x=\sqrt{(E-V_0)^2/(\hbar v_F)^2-k_y^2}$, and find $T$ numerically (with $\hbar v_F=0.658\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$). Note that the formula above is the limiting formula for $\abs{V_0}\gg\abs{E}$, and here $V_0/E=2.5$ is only moderately large, so the approximation is crude (the correction arising because the pseudospin angle inside the barrier, $\theta=\arcsin(k_y\hbar v_F/\abs{E-V_0})=19.5^\circ$, differs from the incidence angle $\phi$ is significant, and the general formula of Katsnelson et al. gives $T\simeq0.49$). Here you may compute with the approximate formula as it stands.

Solution

Strategy. The given $T(\phi)$ has the structure that the numerator is determined by the incident angle alone, while the denominator contains $q_xD$, the “phase inside the barrier,” in the form of a $\cos^2$. Therefore, regarding it as a function of the two variables $\phi$ and $q_xD$, we first settle the limits and special values, and finally insert the numbers. Here $q_x$ is the $x$ component of the wavenumber inside the barrier, and $k_y$ is the transverse wavenumber, which is conserved both outside and inside the barrier (by translational symmetry).

(1) Substituting $\phi=0$, we have $\cos^2 0=1$ and $\sin^2 0=0$, so

$$ T(0) = \frac{1}{1-\cos^2(q_xD)\times 0} = \frac{1}{1-0} = 1 $$

$\blacksquare$ What matters here is that the only route by which $V_0$ and $D$ enter $T$ is through the combination $q_xD$, and that this $q_xD$ is multiplied by $\sin^2\phi$. At $\phi=0$ we have $\sin^2\phi=0$, so whatever the value of $\cos^2(q_xD)$ may be, the denominator stays equal to $1$. That is, no matter how high or how thick the barrier is, there is perfect transmission at normal incidence. For the Schrödinger equation, $T\sim\ee^{-2\kappa D}$ decays exponentially with thickness, so this is a dramatic difference.

(2) If $q_xD=n\pi$ ($n$ an integer), then $\cos(q_xD)=(-1)^n$, that is, $\cos^2(q_xD)=1$. Substituting this,

$$ T = \frac{\cos^2\phi}{1-1\cdot\sin^2\phi} = \frac{\cos^2\phi}{1-\sin^2\phi} = \frac{\cos^2\phi}{\cos^2\phi} = 1 $$

so there is perfect transmission regardless of the incident angle, as long as $\phi\ne\pi/2$ (that is, as long as $\cos^2\phi\ne0$). $\blacksquare$ This is a Fabry–Pérot resonance, in which the waves reflected at the two ends of the barrier reinforce each other with round-trip phase $2q_xD=2n\pi$ and the net reflection vanishes; the mechanism is exactly the same as that of an antireflection coating in optics. The difference is that in graphene the perfect transmission at normal incidence in (1) holds independently of the resonance condition.

(3) At $\phi=45^\circ$ we have $\cos^2\phi=\sin^2\phi=1/2$. Abbreviating $c^2\equiv\cos^2(q_xD)$,

$$ T = \frac{1/2}{1-c^2/2} = \frac{1}{2-c^2} $$

If $q_xD$ is varied freely over the reals, $c^2$ takes all values from $0$ to $1$. Since $T=1/(2-c^2)$ is monotonically increasing in $c^2$,

  • Maximum: when $c^2=1$ (that is, $q_xD=n\pi$), $T_{\max}=\dfrac{1}{2-1}=1$.
  • Minimum: when $c^2=0$ (that is, $q_xD=(n+\tfrac12)\pi$), $T_{\min}=\dfrac{1}{2-0}=\dfrac{1}{2}$.

This completes the proof. $\blacksquare$ The minimum value $1/2$ equals $\cos^2 45^\circ$. In general, $T=\cos^2\phi$ when $c^2=0$ and $T=1$ when $c^2=1$, so $T$ oscillates between $\cos^2\phi$ and $1$ as $q_xD$ varies. Even at a relatively large angle such as $45^\circ$, at least half is transmitted even in the worst case.

(4) We work out the numbers in order. We have $\hbar v_F=0.658\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$, $E=0.080\ \mathrm{eV}$, $V_0=0.200\ \mathrm{eV}$, $D=100\ \mathrm{nm}$, and $\phi=30^\circ$.

First, the wave number outside the barrier:

$$ k = \frac{E}{\hbar v_F} = \frac{0.080}{0.658} = 0.12158\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}} $$

The transverse component (conserved at the boundary):

$$ k_y = k\sin30^\circ = 0.12158\times0.5 = 0.060790\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}} $$

The energy inside the barrier is $E-V_0=0.080-0.200=-0.120\ \mathrm{eV}$, which is negative; that is, the state lies on the valence-band (hole) side. The corresponding total wave number is

$$ \frac{E-V_0}{\hbar v_F} = \frac{-0.120}{0.658} = -0.18237\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}} $$

The $x$ component is

$$ q_x = \sqrt{\left(\frac{E-V_0}{\hbar v_F}\right)^2 - k_y^2} = \sqrt{(0.18237)^2-(0.060790)^2} = \sqrt{0.033259-0.003695} $$ $$ = \sqrt{0.029564} = 0.171941\ \mathrm{nm^{-1}} $$

The fact that $q_x$ is real is the heart of Klein tunneling. For a Schrödinger particle it would be imaginary here, and only decaying waves would exist. The phase accumulated inside the barrier is

$$ q_xD = 0.171941\times100 = 17.194\ \mathrm{rad} $$

Dividing this by $2\pi$ leaves a remainder of $17.194-2\times2\pi=17.194-12.566=4.6277\ \mathrm{rad}$. This lies in the third quadrant ($\pi<4.6277<3\pi/2$) and is very close to the boundary $3\pi/2=4.7124$, so the cosine should be negative and small in absolute value. Indeed,

$$ \cos(q_xD) = \cos(4.6277) = -0.08457, \qquad \cos^2(q_xD) = 7.1525\times10^{-3} $$

Finally we assemble the transmission probability. Since $\cos^2 30^\circ=3/4=0.75$ and $\sin^2 30^\circ=1/4=0.25$,

$$ T = \frac{0.75}{1-7.1525\times10^{-3}\times0.25} = \frac{0.75}{1-1.7881\times10^{-3}} = \frac{0.75}{0.998212} = 0.7513 $$

That is, $T\simeq0.75$. $\blacksquare$ This agrees with the value $0.751$ in the hint in the main text. According to the approximate formula, $75\ \%$ of the electrons incident at $30^\circ$ pass through a barrier of height $200\ \mathrm{meV}$ and width $100\ \mathrm{nm}$. As the note in the problem statement says, at $V_0/E=2.5$ the mismatch between the pseudospin angle $\theta=\arcsin(0.060790/0.18237)=19.5^\circ$ and $\phi=30^\circ$ matters, and the general formula gives $T\simeq0.49$, about half. Even so, about $50\ \%$ is transmitted, and this remains a value that is impossible for a Schrödinger particle, whose transmission decays exponentially with the barrier width.

Verification. First we check unitarity. For the denominator, $1-c^2\sin^2\phi\ge1-\sin^2\phi=\cos^2\phi$ holds (because $c^2\le1$), so we always have $T\le\cos^2\phi/\cos^2\phi=1$. The formula thus satisfies the physical requirement that the transmission probability not exceed $1$. Next, repeating the argument of (3) at $\phi=30^\circ$, $T$ should oscillate between $\cos^2 30^\circ=0.750$ and $1$ as $q_xD$ varies. The value $T=0.7513$ of this problem lies just above the lower end of this interval, which is consistent with $\cos^2(q_xD)=0.0072$ being nearly zero (close to antiresonance). In other words, the present $D=100\ \mathrm{nm}$ is close to the “hardest to transmit” condition, and still $75\ \%$ is transmitted. Finally, as $\phi\to90^\circ$ (grazing incidence), the numerator $\cos^2\phi\to0$ and $T\to0$, in agreement with the description of the limits in Chapter 9 of this book. Also, if we choose $D$ so that $q_xD=n\pi$, that is, $D=n\pi/0.171941=18.27n\ \mathrm{nm}$, then $T=1$: $D=91.4\ \mathrm{nm}$ for $n=5$ and $D=109.6\ \mathrm{nm}$ for $n=6$ are the resonances on either side of the $100\ \mathrm{nm}$ of this problem. The value $100\ \mathrm{nm}$ lies between them ($8.6\ \mathrm{nm}$ from $91.4$ and $9.6\ \mathrm{nm}$ from $109.6$), which is exactly why it came out near antiresonance, as seen above. That $T$ swings from $0.751$ to $1$ when the barrier width changes by only about $9\ \mathrm{nm}$ is also an important property of this formula.

Meaning. Klein tunneling was pointed out by Oskar Klein in 1929 as an interpretational difficulty of the Dirac equation. To test it in vacuum, one would have to apply a potential difference of $2m_ec^2\simeq1\ \mathrm{MeV}$ over a distance of about the Compton wavelength, $386\ \mathrm{fm}$, which requires an electric field of order $10^{18}\ \mathrm{V/m}$ (the Schwinger limit). In graphene, on the other hand, $c$ is replaced by $v_F\simeq c/300$ and the mass scale becomes $\mathrm{meV}$, so the same condition is met by an electrostatic barrier of about $100\ \mathrm{meV}$ created with a gate electrode. A phenomenon that is unreachable in particle physics can be reproduced with a semiconductor process near room temperature.

From the viewpoint of materials-science applications, this is a double-edged sword. Because of Klein tunneling, a graphene field-effect transistor does not turn off: even if a barrier is raised with the gate, electrons pass straight through, so the on/off ratio stays at about $10$ and the device cannot be used as a logic element. The only way to avoid this is to open a gap, and the $\Delta\sigma_z$ term of Exercise 9.6 (matching to an h-BN substrate, a perpendicular electric field on bilayer graphene, and so on) has been studied for this purpose. On the other hand, the strong dependence of the transmission on the angle of incidence can also be exploited actively. It has been proposed, and demonstrated experimentally, that a $p$–$n$ junction acts as a medium with a negative refractive index for electrons (a Veselago lens), and that angular filters can be built using the resonance condition.

Exercise 9.8: The BdG equation, coherence factors, and the Majorana condition

Problem (restated)

Consider $H_{\text{BdG}}=\xi\tau_z+\Delta\tau_x$ ($\Delta$ real).

(1) Show that the eigenvalues are $E=\pm\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2}$, using only the fact that $\tau_z$ and $\tau_x$ anticommute.

(2) Writing the positive-energy eigenvector as $(u,v)^T$, show that $u^2=\frac12(1+\xi/E)$ and $v^2=\frac12(1-\xi/E)$. State what $(u,v)$ becomes in the three limits $\xi\to+\infty$, $\xi\to-\infty$, and $\xi=0$, and interpret them physically.

(3) For $\Xi=\tau_y\mathcal{K}$ ($\mathcal{K}$ is complex conjugation), show that $\Xi H\Xi^{-1}=-H$, and conclude that the spectrum is symmetric about $E=0$.

(4) For Al ($T_c=1.20\ \mathrm{K}$, $v_F=2.03\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s}$), find the gap in $\mathrm{meV}$ from the BCS weak-coupling relation $\Delta=1.764\,k_BT_c$. Furthermore, noting that the quantity in superconductivity corresponding to the “Compton wavelength $\hbar/mc$ for the mass $m$” in the Dirac equation is the “coherence length $\xi_0=\hbar v_F/(\pi\Delta)$,” find $\xi_0$.

(5) Find the ratio of the electron rest energy $511\ \mathrm{keV}$ to the gap in (4), and state “how many orders of magnitude of scale the same equation spans.”

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1)–(3) need only $2\times2$ algebra. The key is that $\tau_x,\tau_y,\tau_z$ obey the same algebra as the Pauli matrices (mutually anticommuting, squaring to $\mathbb{1}$). Here, however, the two-component space is not spin but Nambu space, that is, the space in which “electron” and “hole” are placed side by side. Parts (4) and (5) are numerical substitutions, and they let us verify with our own hands the claim of Chapter 9 of this book about the number of orders of magnitude over which the same equation extends.

(1) We compute the square of $H=\xi\tau_z+\Delta\tau_x$.

$$ H^2 = \left(\xi\tau_z+\Delta\tau_x\right)^2 = \xi^2\tau_z^2 + \Delta^2\tau_x^2 + \xi\Delta\left(\tau_z\tau_x+\tau_x\tau_z\right) = \xi^2\tau_z^2 + \Delta^2\tau_x^2 + \xi\Delta\left\{\tau_z,\tau_x\right\} $$

By the anticommutation $\{\tau_z,\tau_x\}=0$ the cross term vanishes, and using $\tau_z^2=\tau_x^2=\mathbb{1}$ we obtain

$$ H^2 = \left(\xi^2+\Delta^2\right)\mathbb{1} $$

Hence the eigenvalue $E$ satisfies $E^2=\xi^2+\Delta^2$. Moreover, from $\Tr\tau_z=\Tr\tau_x=0$ we get $\Tr H=0$; that is, the sum of the two eigenvalues is zero. Therefore

$$ E = \pm\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2} $$

$\blacksquare$ The result is fixed by this one point alone, the vanishing of the cross term, and this is exactly the same mechanism as the one by which $\{\alpha^i,\beta\}=0$ was effective when $E^2=\pp^2+m^2$ follows from $\Ham=\bm{\alpha}\cdot\pp+\beta m$ in the Dirac equation. We can also read off that a gap $\abs{E}=\abs{\Delta}$ remains even at $\xi=0$ (on the Fermi surface).

(2) In matrix form, $H=\begin{pmatrix}\xi&\Delta\\ \Delta&-\xi\end{pmatrix}$. The eigenvector $(u,v)^T$ with positive energy $E=+\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2}$ satisfies

$$ \xi u + \Delta v = E u \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{v}{u} = \frac{E-\xi}{\Delta} $$

(The second row, $\Delta u-\xi v=Ev$, gives $u/v=(E+\xi)/\Delta$, but since $(E-\xi)(E+\xi)=E^2-\xi^2=\Delta^2$, the two are the same condition.) Imposing the normalization condition $u^2+v^2=1$ gives

$$ u^2\left[1+\left(\frac{E-\xi}{\Delta}\right)^2\right]=1 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad u^2 = \frac{\Delta^2}{\Delta^2+(E-\xi)^2} $$

We simplify the denominator. Using $\Delta^2=E^2-\xi^2$,

$$ \Delta^2+(E-\xi)^2 = \left(E^2-\xi^2\right)+\left(E^2-2E\xi+\xi^2\right) = 2E^2-2E\xi = 2E(E-\xi) $$

Also, the numerator factors as $\Delta^2=(E-\xi)(E+\xi)$, so

$$ u^2 = \frac{(E-\xi)(E+\xi)}{2E(E-\xi)} = \frac{E+\xi}{2E} = \frac{1}{2}\left(1+\frac{\xi}{E}\right) $$

Therefore

$$ v^2 = 1-u^2 = \frac{1}{2}\left(1-\frac{\xi}{E}\right) $$

$\blacksquare$ These are the BCS coherence factors.

Three limits.

  • $\xi\to+\infty$: $E\to\xi$, so $\xi/E\to+1$; hence $u^2\to1$ and $v^2\to0$, that is, $(u,v)\to(1,0)$. Far above the Fermi surface (deep in the conduction band), the quasiparticle is a pure electron. The superconducting gap has no effect, and this is an ordinary one-electron excitation.
  • $\xi\to-\infty$: $E\to\abs{\xi}=-\xi$, so $\xi/E\to-1$; hence $(u,v)\to(0,1)$. Far below the Fermi surface, the quasiparticle is a pure hole. It is nothing other than the excitation obtained by removing one electron from an occupied level.
  • $\xi=0$ (on the Fermi surface): $u^2=v^2=1/2$, and choosing the phase to be real, $(u,v)=(1,1)/\sqrt2$. The quasiparticle is a superposition of exactly half electron and half hole. It is not an eigenstate of charge, and its average charge is zero. Moreover, the creation operator takes the form $\gamma^\dagger=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}(c^\dagger+c)$, and in a situation where the indices can be dropped, $\gamma=\gamma^\dagger$; that is, the Majorana condition is satisfied.

These three limits are the superconducting version of the structure in the Dirac equation in which the large and small components are nearly equal when $\abs{\pp}\gg m$ and the small component vanishes when $\abs{\pp}\ll m$. The essence of superconductivity is that “electron character” and “hole character” mix completely on the Fermi surface, and $\Delta$ plays the same role as the mass, which mixes particle and antiparticle.

(3) $\Xi=\tau_y\mathcal{K}$ is an antiunitary operator. First we find the inverse operator. Using $\mathcal{K}\tau_y=\tau_y^*\mathcal{K}=-\tau_y\mathcal{K}$ ($\tau_y$ has purely imaginary components, so $\tau_y^*=-\tau_y$) and $\mathcal{K}^2=\mathbb{1}$, we get

$$ \Xi^2 = \tau_y\mathcal{K}\,\tau_y\mathcal{K} = \tau_y\left(-\tau_y\right)\mathcal{K}^2 = -\tau_y^2 = -\mathbb{1} $$

Hence $\Xi^{-1}=-\Xi$. Using this,

$$ \Xi H\Xi^{-1} = \tau_y\mathcal{K}\,H\,\left(-\tau_y\mathcal{K}\right) = -\tau_y\left(\mathcal{K}H\right)\tau_y\mathcal{K} = -\tau_y H^*\left(\mathcal{K}\tau_y\mathcal{K}\right) = -\tau_y H^*\left(-\tau_y\right) = \tau_y H^*\tau_y $$

Along the way we used $\mathcal{K}H=H^*\mathcal{K}$ and $\mathcal{K}\tau_y\mathcal{K}=\tau_y^*=-\tau_y$. Now, since $\xi$ and $\Delta$ are both real, $H^*=H$, and using the Pauli-matrix relations $\tau_y\tau_z\tau_y=-\tau_z$ and $\tau_y\tau_x\tau_y=-\tau_x$ (distinct Pauli matrices anticommute, and $\tau_y^2=\mathbb{1}$), we obtain

$$ \tau_yH\tau_y = \xi\,\tau_y\tau_z\tau_y + \Delta\,\tau_y\tau_x\tau_y = -\xi\tau_z-\Delta\tau_x = -H $$

Therefore

$$ \Xi H\Xi^{-1} = -H $$

$\blacksquare$

Symmetry of the spectrum. Suppose $H\ket{\psi}=E\ket{\psi}$ ($E$ real). Apply $\Xi$ to both sides from the left. Since $\Xi$ is antiunitary, it passes complex numbers through as their complex conjugates, but $E$ is real, so $\Xi E\ket{\psi}=E\,\Xi\ket{\psi}$. On the other hand, $\Xi H=-H\Xi$ (the relation above written without multiplying by $\Xi^{-1}$), so

$$ \Xi H\ket{\psi} = -H\,\Xi\ket{\psi} = E\,\Xi\ket{\psi} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad H\left(\Xi\ket{\psi}\right) = -E\left(\Xi\ket{\psi}\right) $$

That is, whenever there is an eigenstate of energy $E$, there necessarily exists an eigenstate $\Xi\ket{\psi}$ of energy $-E$. The spectrum is exactly symmetric about $E=0$. $\blacksquare$ This is the complete counterpart of the fact that, in the Dirac equation, the $u$ solutions (positive energy) and the $v$ solutions (negative energy) are linked by charge conjugation and come in pairs. Note that in the $2\times2$ form of this problem (the spin-singlet $s$-wave case, which preserves spin-rotation symmetry, contracted onto the Nambu basis $(c_\uparrow,c^\dagger_\downarrow)$), $\Xi^2=-\mathbb{1}$, which corresponds to class C of the Altland–Zirnbauer classification. In the $4\times4$ Nambu basis that retains the spin degree of freedom, $\Xi=\tau_x\mathcal{K}$ and $\Xi^2=+\mathbb{1}$, which gives class D, and it is this class that supports Majorana zero modes (classes D and DIII both have $\Xi^2=+\mathbb{1}$, and what distinguishes them is the presence or absence of time-reversal symmetry). Since the sign of $\Xi^2$ determines which class one falls into, it is important to state explicitly in which basis $\Xi$ is written.

(4) We substitute directly into the BCS weak-coupling relation. With $k_B=8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/K}$ and $T_c=1.20\ \mathrm{K}$,

$$ \Delta = 1.764\,k_BT_c = 1.764\times8.617\times10^{-5}\times1.20 $$ $$ = 1.764\times1.03404\times10^{-4} = 1.8240\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV} = 0.1824\ \mathrm{meV} $$

That is, about $0.18\ \mathrm{meV}$. Next we find the coherence length. Using $\hbar=6.582\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}$ and $v_F=2.03\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s}$, the numerator is

$$ \hbar v_F = 6.582\times10^{-16}\times2.03\times10^{6} = 1.3361\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{eV\,m} $$

and the denominator is

$$ \pi\Delta = 3.1416\times1.8240\times10^{-4} = 5.7303\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV} $$

Therefore

$$ \xi_0 = \frac{\hbar v_F}{\pi\Delta} = \frac{1.3361\times10^{-9}}{5.7303\times10^{-4}} = 2.332\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m} = 2.33\ \mathrm{\mu m} $$

$\blacksquare$ The literature value of the BCS coherence length of Al is about $1.6\ \mathrm{\mu m}$, which is of the same order (the difference comes from the choice of the value of $v_F$ and from the nonspherical shape of the Fermi surface). It is exceptionally long for a superconductor, and this is one of the reasons why “clean” Josephson devices and superconducting qubits are easy to make from Al.

(5) The ratio of the electron rest energy to the gap is

$$ \frac{m_ec^2}{\Delta} = \frac{511\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{eV}}{1.8240\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV}} = 2.802\times10^{9} $$

Since $\log_{10}(2.802\times10^{9})=9.45$, this is about nine and a half orders of magnitude. Equations of the same form (the $E=\pm\sqrt{p^2c^2+m^2c^4}$ of Chapter 9 of this book and $E=\pm\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2}$) hold across both the $\mathrm{keV}$ world and the $\mathrm{\mu eV}$ world.

On the other hand, comparing length scales gives a different picture. The Compton wavelength of the electron is $\lambda_C=\hbar/(m_ec)=3.862\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{m}=386\ \mathrm{fm}$, and its ratio to $\xi_0=2.332\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}$ from (4) is

$$ \frac{\xi_0}{\lambda_C} = \frac{2.332\times10^{-6}}{3.862\times10^{-13}} = 6.04\times10^{6} $$

that is, $\log_{10}(6.04\times10^{6})=6.78$ orders of magnitude, which does not agree with the $9.45$ orders of the energy ratio. The difference is $9.45-6.78=2.67$ orders (the amount that the hint in the chapter rounds off as “three orders of magnitude”). Where this comes from is immediately clear if we write the ratio analytically.

$$ \frac{\xi_0}{\lambda_C} = \frac{\hbar v_F/(\pi\Delta)}{\hbar/(m_ec)} = \frac{v_F\,m_ec}{\pi\Delta} = \frac{v_F}{c}\cdot\frac{m_ec^2}{\pi\Delta} $$

Inserting numbers, $v_F/c = (2.03\times10^{6})/(2.998\times10^{8})=6.77\times10^{-3}$ and $m_ec^2/(\pi\Delta)=(2.802\times10^{9})/3.1416=8.92\times10^{8}$, and the product is $6.77\times10^{-3}\times8.92\times10^{8}=6.04\times10^{6}$, which agrees with the direct calculation. Counting in orders of magnitude,

$$ \log_{10}\frac{c}{v_F} = \log_{10}147.7 = 2.17, \qquad \log_{10}\pi = 0.50, \qquad 2.17+0.50 = 2.67 $$

Because $v_F$ rather than $c$ plays the role of the “speed of light,” the factor $v_F/c\simeq1/148$ eats up $2.17$ orders, and the $1/\pi$ that enters the definition of the coherence length eats up another $0.50$ orders. Together, these $2.67$ orders are the true origin of the discrepancy between the energy ratio and the length ratio. $\blacksquare$

Verification. We check in three ways. First, converting the gap in (4) into a temperature gives $\Delta/k_B=(1.8240\times10^{-4})/(8.617\times10^{-5})=2.117\ \mathrm{K}$, which agrees with $1.764\times T_c=1.764\times1.20=2.117\ \mathrm{K}$ (this is of course expected since it is the very definition, but it confirms that there is no error in the orders of magnitude). Relatedly, the universal BCS ratio $2\Delta/(k_BT_c)=2\times1.764=3.53$ is also reproduced. Second, the dimensions of $\xi_0$: $[\hbar v_F/\Delta]=(\mathrm{eV\,s})(\mathrm{m/s})/\mathrm{eV}=\mathrm{m}$, which is indeed a length. Third, we independently check $\lambda_C$.

$$ \lambda_C = \frac{\hbar c}{m_ec^2} = \frac{(6.582\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{eV\,s})(2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s})}{5.11\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{eV}} = \frac{1.973\times10^{-7}}{5.11\times10^{5}}\ \mathrm{m} = 3.86\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{m} $$

which agrees with the $386\ \mathrm{fm}$ used above.

Meaning. This problem condenses the theme of Chapter 9 of this book into a single number. The Dirac equation and the BdG equation are the same equation, and the same structure operates in worlds separated by nine and a half orders of magnitude in energy and nearly seven in length. The gap $\Delta$ plays the role of the mass $m$, the Fermi velocity $v_F$ the role of the speed of light $c$, electrons and holes the role of particles and antiparticles, and the particle–hole symmetry $\Xi$ the role of charge conjugation $C$.

The most important point for practical applications is the limit $\xi=0$ of (2). A zero-energy state with $u=v$ satisfies $\gamma=\gamma^\dagger$, that is, the Majorana condition, and this is literally the same equation as the condition $\psi=\psi^c$ for a Majorana neutrino treated in Chapter 14.
