In particle physics, whether the neutrino satisfies it is the question posed by the search for neutrinoless double-beta decay, whereas on the condensed-matter side the search continues in composite systems of semiconductor nanowires and $s$-wave superconductors (InAs or InSb with Al), at interfaces between topological insulators and superconductors, in the vortex cores of the iron-based superconductor FeTe$_{0.55}$Se$_{0.45}$, and elsewhere. That Al was chosen as the subject of this problem is not a coincidence: Al has a long $\xi_0$ and clean thin films are easy to make, so it is in fact the material most often used as the parent superconductor in contact with nanowires. That such Majorana zero modes obey non-Abelian statistics is the principle of topological quantum computation, and a single line of Dirac’s in 1928 has become a design guideline for quantum-computing materials in the 2020s.

E.10 Solutions for Chapter 10: Quantum Electrodynamics

Exercise 10.1: Using the trace theorems

Problem (restated)

(1) Derive $\Tr\left[\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\right]=4\left[(a\!\cdot\! b)(c\!\cdot\! d)-(a\!\cdot\! c)(b\!\cdot\! d)+(a\!\cdot\! d)(b\!\cdot\! c)\right]$ from T4 of Table 10.3.

(2) Show directly that $\Tr\left[\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\right]=0$, using only the anticommutation relations rather than the general argument with $\gamma^5$ (T2).

(3) Compute the following trace ($m$ is a scalar).

$$ \Tr\left[(\slashed{p}+m)\,\gamma^\mu\,(\slashed{p}'+m)\,\gamma_\mu\right] $$

(4) Explain why $\Tr\left[\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\gamma^5\right]$ vanishes when $a,b,c,d$ are linearly dependent (that is, when at most three of the four vectors are independent and they do not span four-dimensional space).

Solution

Strategy. The only tools we use are the trace theorems of Table 10.3 in Chapter 10 of this book (T1, T3, T4, T7), the contraction formulas C1 and C2, the cyclicity of the trace $\Tr(AB)=\Tr(BA)$, and the Clifford algebra $\{\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu\}=2g^{\mu\nu}\mathbb{1}$. Part (2) requires that $\gamma^5$ not be used at all, so we push through with a single move: insert a $\gamma$ with a different index and pass it through by anticommutation.

(1) Substitute the definition of the Feynman slash, $\slashed{a}=a_\mu\gamma^\mu$, directly. The coefficients $a_\mu,b_\nu,c_\rho,d_\sigma$ are just numbers, so they can be taken outside the trace:

$$ \Tr\left[\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\right] = a_\mu b_\nu c_\rho d_\sigma\,\Tr\left[\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma\right] $$

Insert T4 here, that is, $\Tr\left[\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma\right]=4\left(g^{\mu\nu}g^{\rho\sigma}-g^{\mu\rho}g^{\nu\sigma}+g^{\mu\sigma}g^{\nu\rho}\right)$:

$$ =4\left[a_\mu b_\nu g^{\mu\nu}\,c_\rho d_\sigma g^{\rho\sigma} -a_\mu c_\rho g^{\mu\rho}\,b_\nu d_\sigma g^{\nu\sigma} +a_\mu d_\sigma g^{\mu\sigma}\,b_\nu c_\rho g^{\nu\rho}\right] $$

Contracting indices with the metric is just the inner product ($a_\mu b_\nu g^{\mu\nu}=a_\mu b^\mu=a\!\cdot\! b$), so

$$ \Tr\left[\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\right] =4\left[(a\!\cdot\! b)(c\!\cdot\! d)-(a\!\cdot\! c)(b\!\cdot\! d)+(a\!\cdot\! d)(b\!\cdot\! c)\right] $$

This is T9. Its structure is "list the three ways of pairing the four vectors two at a time, and give a negative sign only to the pairing that is not adjacent (the pair $ac$ and $bd$)"; this is a remnant of the factor $(-1)$ that appears from anticommutation each time a $\gamma$ matrix is moved one place over.

(2) First we show that the one-matrix trace $\Tr(\gamma^\alpha)$ vanishes. Take one index value $\beta$ different from $\alpha$ (this is always possible since the space is four-dimensional). We have $\gamma^\beta\gamma^\beta=g^{\beta\beta}\mathbb{1}$ (no sum over $\beta$), and $g^{\beta\beta}=\pm1\neq0$. Insert this and pass the right-hand $\gamma^\beta$ to the right of $\gamma^\alpha$. Since $\alpha\neq\beta$, we may use $\gamma^\beta\gamma^\alpha=-\gamma^\alpha\gamma^\beta$, and obtain

$$ g^{\beta\beta}\Tr(\gamma^\alpha)=\Tr\left(\gamma^\beta\gamma^\beta\gamma^\alpha\right) =-\Tr\left(\gamma^\beta\gamma^\alpha\gamma^\beta\right) \stackrel{\text{cyclicity}}{=}-\Tr\left(\gamma^\beta\gamma^\beta\gamma^\alpha\right) =-g^{\beta\beta}\Tr(\gamma^\alpha) $$

Dividing by $g^{\beta\beta}\neq0$ gives $\Tr(\gamma^\alpha)=0$.

Exactly the same argument works for three matrices. Let $T\equiv\Tr\left[\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\right]$, and take an index $\lambda$ with a value different from all of $\mu,\nu,\rho$. The distinct values among $\mu,\nu,\rho$ number at most three, and the index takes four values $0,1,2,3$, so such a $\lambda$ always exists. Since $\gamma^\lambda$ anticommutes with all of $\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu,\gamma^\rho$, passing $\gamma^\lambda$ through three matrices produces $(-1)^3=-1$:

$$ g^{\lambda\lambda}T=\Tr\left[\gamma^\lambda\gamma^\lambda\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\right] =(-1)^3\Tr\left[\gamma^\lambda\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma^\lambda\right] \stackrel{\text{cyclicity}}{=}-\Tr\left[\gamma^\lambda\gamma^\lambda\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\right] =-g^{\lambda\lambda}T $$

Hence $T=-T$, that is, $\Tr\left[\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\right]=0$. We have used only the anticommutation relations and cyclicity.

Note also that the naive route, "carry $\gamma^\mu$ to the right end by anticommutation and return it by cyclicity," does not close for an odd number of matrices. Indeed,

$$ \gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho=2g^{\mu\nu}\gamma^\rho-2g^{\mu\rho}\gamma^\nu+\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma^\mu $$

and since $\gamma^\mu$ has passed through two $\gamma$'s, the sign is $(-1)^2=+1$. Taking the trace and using cyclicity, the last term on the right returns to $T$ itself, and we get

$$ T=2g^{\mu\nu}\Tr(\gamma^\rho)-2g^{\mu\rho}\Tr(\gamma^\nu)+T $$

that is, we obtain only the identity $0=2g^{\mu\nu}\Tr(\gamma^\rho)-2g^{\mu\rho}\Tr(\gamma^\nu)$, which does not determine $T$ itself (this identity is automatically satisfied by $\Tr(\gamma^\alpha)=0$ shown above). Therefore the statement in the hint in the main text, "carrying $\gamma^\mu$ to the right end and returning it by cyclicity gives the form $T=-T+(\text{two traces})$," does not hold, because, as we have just seen, the sign does not flip. We must adopt the $\lambda$-insertion method above. The fact that the sign does not flip for an odd number of matrices is precisely why the general proof needs the move T2, which inserts $\gamma^5$. The $\lambda$-insertion method above can be used only when the number of $\gamma$'s is at most three, so that a "spare index" can be secured.

(3) First eliminate the inner contraction. Using the contraction formula C2 $\left(\gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\gamma_\mu=-2\slashed{a}\right)$ and C1 $\left(\gamma^\mu\gamma_\mu=4\right)$, we have

$$ \gamma^\mu\left(\slashed{p}'+m\right)\gamma_\mu =\gamma^\mu\slashed{p}'\gamma_\mu+m\,\gamma^\mu\gamma_\mu =-2\slashed{p}'+4m $$

Therefore the trace we want is

$$ \Tr\left[(\slashed{p}+m)\left(-2\slashed{p}'+4m\right)\right] =-2\Tr\left[\slashed{p}\slashed{p}'\right]+4m\Tr\left[\slashed{p}\right] -2m\Tr\left[\slashed{p}'\right]+4m^2\Tr\left[\mathbb{1}\right] $$

The trace of an odd number (one) of $\gamma$ matrices is 0 as shown in (2), so the second and third terms drop out. Inserting T8 $\left(\Tr\left[\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\right]=4\,a\!\cdot\! b\right)$ and T1 $\left(\Tr\mathbb{1}=4\right)$ into the rest, we obtain

$$ \Tr\left[(\slashed{p}+m)\,\gamma^\mu\,(\slashed{p}'+m)\,\gamma_\mu\right] =-8\,p\!\cdot\! p'+16\,m^2 $$

(4) Contracting T7, we get

$$ \Tr\left[\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\gamma^5\right] =a_\mu b_\nu c_\rho d_\sigma\,\Tr\left[\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu\gamma^\rho\gamma^\sigma\gamma^5\right] =-4\ii\,\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}a_\mu b_\nu c_\rho d_\sigma $$

Here $\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ is the totally antisymmetric tensor (this book uses $\epsilon^{0123}=+1$), so its definition is precisely the "sign of the permutation." That is, for the $4\times4$ matrix whose rows are the covariant components of the four vectors,

$$ M=\begin{pmatrix} a_0&a_1&a_2&a_3\\ b_0&b_1&b_2&b_3\\ c_0&c_1&c_2&c_3\\ d_0&d_1&d_2&d_3 \end{pmatrix} $$

the quantity $\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}a_\mu b_\nu c_\rho d_\sigma$ is exactly the Leibniz expansion of the determinant, $\sum_\pi \mathrm{sgn}(\pi)\,a_{\pi(0)}b_{\pi(1)}c_{\pi(2)}d_{\pi(3)}$, and equals $\det M$. Hence

$$ \Tr\left[\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\gamma^5\right]=-4\ii\,\det M $$

Now suppose that at most three of $a,b,c,d$ are linearly independent; then, for example, we can write $d=\lambda a+\mu b+\nu c$. Since the determinant is linear in each row and changes sign under an exchange of rows (it is 0 if two rows are the same),

$$ \det M=\lambda\det\begin{pmatrix}a\\ b\\ c\\ a\end{pmatrix} +\mu\det\begin{pmatrix}a\\ b\\ c\\ b\end{pmatrix} +\nu\det\begin{pmatrix}a\\ b\\ c\\ c\end{pmatrix}=0 $$

that is, the trace is zero. Geometrically, $\abs{\det M}$ is the four-dimensional volume of the four-dimensional parallelepiped spanned by the four vectors, and if the spanned space is at most three-dimensional, that volume is simply 0.

Verification. (1) can be checked by setting $a=b=c=d=p$. The formula gives $4\left[(p^2)^2-(p^2)^2+(p^2)^2\right]=4(p^2)^2$. On the other hand, $\slashed{p}\slashed{p}=p^2\mathbb{1}$, so $\slashed{p}^4=(p^2)^2\mathbb{1}$, and the direct trace gives $\Tr=4(p^2)^2$, in agreement. (3) can also be checked in the opposite order, expanding the product first and then contracting: dropping the traces of an odd number of matrices leaves $\Tr\left[\slashed{p}\gamma^\mu\slashed{p}'\gamma_\mu\right]+m^2\Tr\left[\gamma^\mu\gamma_\mu\right]$; the former, using C2 on the inside, becomes $-2p_\alpha p'_\beta\Tr\left[\gamma^\alpha\gamma^\beta\right]=-8\,p\!\cdot\! p'$, and the latter is $m^2\Tr\left[4\,\mathbb{1}\right]=16m^2$, giving the same answer. The dimensions also match, since both terms are the square of a mass. Furthermore, setting $p'=p$, $p^2=m^2$ gives $-8m^2+16m^2=8m^2$, which is finite and positive, and as $m\to0$ it connects smoothly to the massless limit $-8\,p\!\cdot\! p'$.

Meaning. The expression $-8\,p\!\cdot\! p'+16m^2$ in (3) is the form that actually appears in Chapter 10 of this book when taking the spin sums for $e^-\mu^-\to e^-\mu^-$ and $e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-$. It is important that the result is written using only the four-momentum inner product $p\!\cdot\! p'$ and the mass; this reflects the requirement that only Lorentz-invariant quantities survive, and it also serves as a detector of computational mistakes. Part (4) has a more practical meaning. In two-body $\to$ two-body scattering there are four external momenta, but by momentum conservation $p_1+p_2=p_3+p_4$ only three of them are independent. Therefore $\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}p_{1\mu}p_{2\nu}p_{3\rho}p_{4\sigma}=0$ holds identically, and terms in which a single $\epsilon^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}$ appears vanish identically. This is why an interference term in which $\gamma^5$ enters only one of the traces, as in QED, does not contribute to the unpolarized cross section, and T7 has no role in cross-section calculations. On the other hand, when $\gamma^5$ enters both traces, as in the $V-A$ interaction of Chapter 12, the contraction of $\epsilon^{\alpha\mu\beta\nu}\epsilon_{\gamma\mu\delta\nu}$ becomes a product of metric tensors and survives. Therefore parity nonconservation can be observed even in unpolarized two-body $\to$ two-body processes, as in the unpolarized cross section of two-body $\to$ two-body processes such as $\nu_\mu e\to\mu\,\nu_e$ (the interchange of $s^2$ and $u^2$ between $\nu$ and $\bar\nu$ is the effect of this term) and in the forward–backward asymmetry $A_{\rm FB}$ of $e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-$. Introducing polarization (the spin four-vector) or looking at final states with three or more bodies is merely one means of raising the sensitivity. Note also that the argument "the contraction of a totally antisymmetric tensor is a determinant, and a determinant is a volume" has exactly the same structure as writing the unit-cell volume in crystallography as $V=\bm a\cdot(\bm b\times\bm c)=\epsilon_{ijk}a_ib_jc_k$, and it is the four-dimensional version of the obvious fact that $V=0$ if the basis vectors lie in a common plane.

Exercise 10.2: Contraction formulas and gauge invariance

Problem (restated)

(1) Starting from C3, show the contraction formula C4 $\left(\gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\gamma_\mu=-2\slashed{c}\slashed{b}\slashed{a}\right)$.

(2) Going one step further, show that

$$ \gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\gamma_\mu =2\left(\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\slashed{a}+\slashed{a}\slashed{d}\slashed{c}\slashed{b}\right) $$

.

(3) For the second term of the Compton amplitude of Chapter 10 of this book (the expression for the sum of the two diagrams), verify that replacing $\epsilon_2\to p_2$ gives $-g_e^2\,\bar u(4)\slashed{\epsilon}_3^{\,*}u(1)$, and show that together with the first term (already computed in the main text) this gives $\mathcal{M}=0$.

(4) The result of (3) means that “the amplitude is not gauge-invariant unless both diagrams are added.” From this, explain why two diagrams are needed at lowest order for $\gamma e^-\to\gamma e^-$, from a viewpoint other than counting the powers of $g_e^2$.

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1) and (2) are a recursion: using $\gamma^\mu\slashed{a}=2a^\mu-\slashed{a}\gamma^\mu$ (an intermediate step of C2), send the leftmost $\gamma^\mu$ to the right one matrix at a time, and apply the next-lower formula to the remaining contraction. Part (3) is pushed through using only momentum conservation and the Dirac equation of the external spinor, $\bar u(4)(\slashed{p}_4-m)=0$.

(1) First, $\gamma^\mu\slashed{a}=a_\nu\gamma^\mu\gamma^\nu=a_\nu\left(2g^{\mu\nu}-\gamma^\nu\gamma^\mu\right)=2a^\mu-\slashed{a}\gamma^\mu$. Using this at the left end, we get

$$ \gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\gamma_\mu =2a^\mu\,\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\gamma_\mu-\slashed{a}\left(\gamma^\mu\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\gamma_\mu\right) $$

In the first term, $a^\mu$ is just a number, so it can slip past $\slashed{b}\slashed{c}$ and be contracted with $\gamma_\mu$, giving $2a^\mu\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\gamma_\mu=2\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\left(a^\mu\gamma_\mu\right)=2\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{a}$. In the parentheses of the second term we can use C3 $\left(\gamma^\mu\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\gamma_\mu=4\,b\!\cdot\! c\right)$. Hence

$$ \gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\gamma_\mu=2\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{a}-4(b\!\cdot\! c)\,\slashed{a} $$

Finally, substituting $2(b\!\cdot\! c)=\{\slashed{b},\slashed{c}\}=\slashed{b}\slashed{c}+\slashed{c}\slashed{b}$, we obtain

$$ =2\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{a}-2\left(\slashed{b}\slashed{c}+\slashed{c}\slashed{b}\right)\slashed{a} =-2\,\slashed{c}\slashed{b}\slashed{a} $$

that is, C4. The characteristic feature is that the order is reversed, a consequence of passing through an odd number (three) of matrices.

(2) We repeat exactly the same procedure one level up:

$$ \gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\gamma_\mu =2a^\mu\,\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\gamma_\mu-\slashed{a}\left(\gamma^\mu\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\gamma_\mu\right) $$

As before, the first term is $2\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\slashed{a}$. The parentheses in the second term have exactly the form of C4 proved in (1), so $\gamma^\mu\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\gamma_\mu=-2\slashed{d}\slashed{c}\slashed{b}$. Therefore

$$ \gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\gamma_\mu =2\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\slashed{a}-\slashed{a}\left(-2\slashed{d}\slashed{c}\slashed{b}\right) =2\left(\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\slashed{a}+\slashed{a}\slashed{d}\slashed{c}\slashed{b}\right) $$

For an even number (four) of matrices, the form is asymmetric: in one term the order is preserved and $\slashed{a}$ is moved to the end, while in the other the order is reversed. C1–C4 together with this formula exhaust the contractions needed to connect external lines and do tree-level calculations in four dimensions (when treating one loop in dimensional regularization, one must replace them by their $d$-dimensional versions, such as $\gamma^\mu\gamma_\mu=d$ and $\gamma^\mu\slashed a\gamma_\mu=-(d-2)\slashed a$).

(3) The Compton amplitude of Chapter 10 of this book is

$$ \mathcal{M}= g_e^2\,\bar u(4)\left[ \frac{\slashed{\epsilon}_3^{\,*}\left(\slashed{p}_1+\slashed{p}_2+m\right)\slashed{\epsilon}_2}{2p_1\!\cdot\! p_2} -\frac{\slashed{\epsilon}_2\left(\slashed{p}_1-\slashed{p}_3+m\right)\slashed{\epsilon}_3^{\,*}}{2p_1\!\cdot\! p_3} \right]u(1) $$

(with $p_1$ the incoming electron, $p_2$ the incoming photon, $p_3$ the outgoing photon, and $p_4$ the outgoing electron). Here we set $\epsilon_2\to p_2$.

First term (recap of the main text). Using $\slashed{p}_2\slashed{p}_2=p_2^2=0$ and $\slashed{p}_1\slashed{p}_2=2p_1\!\cdot\! p_2-\slashed{p}_2\slashed{p}_1$, and letting $\left(\slashed{p}_1-m\right)u(1)=0$ act on $u(1)$, we get

$$ \left(\slashed{p}_1+\slashed{p}_2+m\right)\slashed{p}_2u(1) =\left(2p_1\!\cdot\! p_2\right)u(1)-\slashed{p}_2\left(\slashed{p}_1-m\right)u(1) =\left(2p_1\!\cdot\! p_2\right)u(1) $$

This cancels exactly against the denominator $2p_1\!\cdot\! p_2$, and the first term becomes $+g_e^2\,\bar u(4)\slashed{\epsilon}_3^{\,*}u(1)$.

Second term. The numerator is $\slashed{p}_2\left(\slashed{p}_1-\slashed{p}_3+m\right)\slashed{\epsilon}_3^{\,*}$. Using momentum conservation $p_1+p_2=p_3+p_4$ in the form $p_1-p_3=p_4-p_2$, the numerator can be written as $\slashed{p}_2\left(\slashed{p}_4-\slashed{p}_2+m\right)\slashed{\epsilon}_3^{\,*}$. Focusing on $\bar u(4)$ at the left end, we process the three terms in turn:

$$ \bar u(4)\slashed{p}_2\slashed{p}_4 =\bar u(4)\left(2p_2\!\cdot\! p_4-\slashed{p}_4\slashed{p}_2\right) =2\left(p_2\!\cdot\! p_4\right)\bar u(4)-m\,\bar u(4)\slashed{p}_2 $$

(In the last step we used $\bar u(4)\slashed{p}_4=m\,\bar u(4)$.) Also, since $\slashed{p}_2\slashed{p}_2=p_2^2=0$, the second term vanishes, and the third term is simply $+m\,\bar u(4)\slashed{p}_2$. Adding the three, the terms proportional to $\slashed{p}_2$ cancel completely, and

$$ \bar u(4)\,\slashed{p}_2\left(\slashed{p}_4-\slashed{p}_2+m\right) =2\left(p_2\!\cdot\! p_4\right)\bar u(4) $$

Next we look at the relation to the denominator. Expanding both sides of $\left(p_1-p_3\right)^2=\left(p_4-p_2\right)^2$ and using $p_1^2=p_4^2=m^2$, $p_2^2=p_3^2=0$, we obtain

$$ m^2-2p_1\!\cdot\! p_3=m^2-2p_2\!\cdot\! p_4 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad p_1\!\cdot\! p_3=p_2\!\cdot\! p_4 $$

Therefore the numerator $2p_2\!\cdot\! p_4$ cancels exactly against the denominator $2p_1\!\cdot\! p_3$, and the second term (including the leading $-$) becomes

$$ -g_e^2\,\bar u(4)\slashed{\epsilon}_3^{\,*}u(1) $$

This is what we wanted. Adding it to the first term,

$$ \mathcal{M}\Big|_{\epsilon_2\to p_2} =g_e^2\,\bar u(4)\slashed{\epsilon}_3^{\,*}u(1)-g_e^2\,\bar u(4)\slashed{\epsilon}_3^{\,*}u(1)=0 $$

Gauge invariance has been verified. Note that with only one of the diagrams, a nonzero quantity $\pm g_e^2\bar u(4)\slashed{\epsilon}_3^{\,*}u(1)$ remains.

(4) Independently of the counting of powers (two vertices, hence $g_e^2$), we can say that gauge invariance itself demands two diagrams. There are three ways of putting the reason.

First, gauge invariance is a requirement on the exact amplitude, so it must hold separately at each order of the perturbative expansion. The condition that the amplitude be unchanged under the replacement $\epsilon_2\to\epsilon_2+\lambda p_2$ ($\lambda$ an arbitrary number) is an identity that holds whatever value the coupling constant $g_e$ takes. If we regard the amplitude as a power series in $g_e$, $\mathcal{M}=g_e^2\mathcal{M}^{(2)}+g_e^4\mathcal{M}^{(4)}+\cdots$, then since $g_e$ is a formally freely adjustable parameter, each coefficient $\mathcal{M}^{(2n)}$ must individually vanish under $\epsilon_2\to p_2$. Therefore the "set of diagrams of order $g_e^2$" alone must be gauge invariant in closed form, and as (3) shows, both diagrams are needed for that.

Second, there is a physical reason. The photon field $A_\mu$ has four components, but the physical polarizations are only the two transverse waves. The property that the amplitude vanishes under $\epsilon\to p$ is exactly what guarantees that the remaining longitudinal and timelike components do not contribute to probabilities. If we take only one diagram, unphysical polarizations contaminate the cross section, states of negative norm appear in the probabilities, and unitarity (conservation of probability) is broken. "Adding all the diagrams" is a requirement of the consistency of the theory itself.

Third, there is the viewpoint of Bose symmetry. The incoming photon $p_2$ and the outgoing photon $p_3$ are identical bosons coming from the same field, and under the crossing operation $p_2\leftrightarrow-p_3$, $\epsilon_2\leftrightarrow\epsilon_3^{\,*}$, Figure (c-1) and Figure (c-2) are transformed into each other. For the amplitude to have this symmetry, the two diagrams can exist only as a pair. A theory with only one of them would, to begin with, break the exchange symmetry of the photons.

Verification. We check (2) by taking the traces of both sides. By cyclicity, the left-hand side is $\Tr\left[\gamma_\mu\gamma^\mu\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\right]=4\Tr\left[\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\right]$. The right-hand side is $2\Tr\left[\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\slashed{a}\right]+2\Tr\left[\slashed{a}\slashed{d}\slashed{c}\slashed{b}\right]$; by cyclicity the first term equals $\Tr\left[\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\right]$, and applying T9 to the second term gives $4\left[(a\!\cdot\! d)(c\!\cdot\! b)-(a\!\cdot\! c)(d\!\cdot\! b)+(a\!\cdot\! b)(d\!\cdot\! c)\right]$, which is the same value. Hence the trace of the right-hand side is $4\Tr\left[\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{c}\slashed{d}\right]$, in agreement with the left-hand side. Also, setting $a=b=c=d$, the left-hand side is $(a^2)^2\gamma^\mu\gamma_\mu=4(a^2)^2$ and the right-hand side is $2\left[(a^2)^2+(a^2)^2\right]=4(a^2)^2$, which agree. (1) can be checked by setting $c=a$: the formula gives $-2\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{a}$. On the other hand, $\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{a}=\left(2a\!\cdot\! b-\slashed{b}\slashed{a}\right)\slashed{a}=2(a\!\cdot\! b)\slashed{a}-a^2\slashed{b}$, so using C2 twice directly gives $2(a\!\cdot\! b)(-2\slashed{a})-a^2(-2\slashed{b})=-4(a\!\cdot\! b)\slashed{a}+2a^2\slashed{b}$, which agrees with the expansion of $-2\slashed{a}\slashed{b}\slashed{a}$.

Meaning. The lesson that "to respect a conservation law, one must add all the diagrams of the same order" is not limited to QED. The exact counterpart in condensed matter is the Ward–Takahashi identity and the discussion of conserving approximations (Baym–Kadanoff). When computing the polarization function in linear response, unless one includes vertex corrections consistent with the diagrams put into the self-energy $\Sigma$, charge conservation $q_\mu\Pi^{\mu\nu}=0$ is violated. As a result, unphysical answers arise, such as a finite conductivity at $\omega\to0$ in an insulator, or a failure of the $f$-sum rule. It is the same situation that leads to the statement that "the $GW$ approximation is not a conserving approximation with $GW$ alone, and becomes consistent only when one goes to $GW\Gamma$." The calculation in this problem’s Compton amplitude, "with one diagram, $\bar u(4)\slashed{\epsilon}_3^{\,*}u(1)$ remains," is the smallest example of this. And in practical terms, substituting $\epsilon\to p$ and seeing whether the result is 0 is the strongest check, one that can be done without knowing the answer.

Exercise 10.3: Cross section for $\tau$ pair production

Problem (restated)

Consider $e^+e^-\to\tau^+\tau^-$. Take $m_\tau=1776.86\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(1) Find the threshold energy $\sqrt{s}_{\mathrm{th}}$ for production.

(2) Find $\beta$ at $\sqrt{s}=4.00\ \mathrm{GeV}$.

(3) Find the total cross section at the same energy in nb. By what percentage does it deviate from the value obtained when the mass effect is neglected ($4\pi\alpha^2/3s$)?

(4) Compare the angular distribution $2-\beta^2+\beta^2\cos^2\theta$ at this energy for $\theta=0^\circ$ and $\theta=90^\circ$. State how it differs from the high-energy limit ($1+\cos^2\theta$, in which the forward direction ($0^\circ$) is twice the sideways direction ($90^\circ$)).

Solution

Strategy. Simply by replacing $\mu$ with $\tau$, the result for $e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-$ derived in Chapter 10 of this book can be used as it stands (the $\tau$ is also a spin-$1/2$ point particle of charge $-1$, and the QED vertex does not depend on the type of lepton). We use the following two formulas, which retain the mass:

$$ \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd\Omega}=\frac{\alpha^2\beta}{4s}\left(2-\beta^2+\beta^2\cos^2\theta\right), \qquad \sigma=\frac{4\pi\alpha^2}{3s}\,\beta\,\frac{3-\beta^2}{2}, \qquad \beta=\sqrt{1-\frac{4m_\tau^2}{s}} $$

together with the numerical conversion from Chapter 10 of this book, $4\pi\alpha^2/3s=86.9\ \mathrm{nb}/s[\mathrm{GeV^2}]$. The numbers below were computed with $\alpha=1/137.036$.

(1) The threshold is where the final-state $\tau^+\tau^-$ are both at rest in the center-of-mass frame, that is, where the invariant mass equals $2m_\tau$. The condition $\beta=0$, $s=4m_\tau^2$, gives the same thing:

$$ \sqrt{s}_{\mathrm{th}}=2m_\tau=2\times1.77686\ \mathrm{GeV}=3.55372\ \mathrm{GeV} \simeq3.554\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

It is worth recalling that when the $\tau$ was discovered at SPEAR in 1975, the $e^+e^-$ center-of-mass energy was being swept right around this value.

(2) We have $\sqrt{s}=4.00\ \mathrm{GeV}$, that is, $s=16.00\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$. First,

$$ 4m_\tau^2=4\times(1.77686)^2=4\times3.157231=12.62892\ \mathrm{GeV^2} $$ $$ \frac{4m_\tau^2}{s}=\frac{12.62892}{16.00}=0.789308 $$

Therefore

$$ \beta=\sqrt{1-0.789308}=\sqrt{0.210692}=0.45901 $$

For reference, at this energy each $\tau$ has energy $E=\sqrt{s}/2=2.000\ \mathrm{GeV}$, momentum $p=\beta E=0.918\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}=1.126$. That $\beta$ already rises to 0.46 when the energy is raised only 13% above the threshold value of 3.554 GeV, to 4.00 GeV, is due to the square-root behavior $\beta\propto\sqrt{s-4m_\tau^2}$.

(3) The value with mass neglected is

$$ \sigma_0=\frac{4\pi\alpha^2}{3s}=\frac{86.86\ \mathrm{nb}}{16.00}=5.4287\ \mathrm{nb} $$

The mass correction factor is

$$ \beta\,\frac{3-\beta^2}{2}=0.45901\times\frac{3-0.210692}{2} =0.45901\times1.394654=0.640163 $$

Therefore

$$ \sigma=5.4287\times0.640163=3.4752\ \mathrm{nb}\simeq3.48\ \mathrm{nb} $$

The deviation from the value with mass neglected is

$$ \frac{3.4752-5.4287}{5.4287}=-0.3598 $$

that is, the cross section is smaller by about 36%. Since we are only 13% above the threshold, it is only natural that the mass effect exceeds 30%. The main cause of the suppression is the factor $\beta$ in the correction factor, that is, the final-state phase space (the small momentum of the outgoing $\tau$).

(4) Since $\beta^2=0.210692$, we have $2-\beta^2=1.789308$. The angular distribution $f(\theta)=2-\beta^2+\beta^2\cos^2\theta$ gives

$$ f(0^\circ)=1.789308+0.210692\times1=2.000,\qquad f(90^\circ)=1.789308+0=1.789 $$

The forward-to-transverse ratio is

$$ \frac{f(0^\circ)}{f(90^\circ)}=\frac{2.000}{1.789}=1.118 $$

That is, the forward direction is only about 12% stronger than the transverse direction, and the distribution is nearly isotropic. In the high-energy limit $\beta\to1$, on the other hand, $f\to1+\cos^2\theta$, so that $f(0^\circ)/f(90^\circ)=2/1=2.00$; that is, the forward direction is twice the transverse direction. The magnitude of the anisotropy is proportional to $\beta^2$ (the coefficient of the $\cos^2\theta$-dependent part of $f$ is precisely $\beta^2$), and as $\beta\to0$ it degenerates into a completely isotropic distribution.

Physically, this is because near the threshold the final-state fermion pair can be produced only with orbital angular momentum $L=0$ ($S$ wave). The $S$ wave does not depend on angle. The virtual photon has $J=1$, so the only way to make $J=1$ from an $S$ wave is to use the spin-triplet state $S=1$ of the pair ($^3S_1$); this has a spherically symmetric orbital part, so the angular distribution is flat. At high energies helicity conservation takes effect and $L$ and $S$ mix, and the overlap of Wigner’s $d^1_{\pm1,\pm1}(\theta)=\tfrac12(1\pm\cos\theta)$, explained in Chapter 10 of this book, produces $1+\cos^2\theta$.

Verification. We check the two limits of the correction factor $\beta(3-\beta^2)/2$. For $\beta\to1$ it gives $1\times(3-1)/2=1$, correctly returning to the massless formula, and for $\beta\to0$ it goes $\to0$, so that the cross section vanishes continuously at the threshold. We can also check that integrating the differential cross section over angle reproduces the total cross section. Using $\int\dd\Omega=4\pi$ and $\int\cos^2\theta\,\dd\Omega=4\pi/3$, we get

$$ \sigma=\frac{\alpha^2\beta}{4s}\left[\left(2-\beta^2\right)4\pi+\beta^2\frac{4\pi}{3}\right] =\frac{\pi\alpha^2\beta}{s}\left(2-\beta^2+\frac{\beta^2}{3}\right) =\frac{\pi\alpha^2\beta}{s}\cdot\frac{2\left(3-\beta^2\right)}{3} =\frac{4\pi\alpha^2}{3s}\,\beta\,\frac{3-\beta^2}{2} $$

which indeed agrees. The dimensions are also correct, since $\alpha^2/s$ is in $\mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$ (an area). Numerically, for $\sqrt{s}=10\ \mathrm{GeV}$ we have $4m_\tau^2/s=0.12629$, $\beta=\sqrt{0.87371}=0.93472$, and the correction factor is $\beta(3-\beta^2)/2=0.93472\times1.06314=0.99375$. That is, the correction is $0.63$%, which is five orders of magnitude larger than in the case of the $\mu$ in the main text (where the correction is $10^{-7}$). Expanding in the small quantity $x\equiv4m^2/s$, we have $\beta(3-\beta^2)/2=\sqrt{1-x}\left(1+x/2\right)=1-\tfrac38x^2+O(x^3)$, which acts only at order $x^2$ (for the $\mu$, $x=4.5\times10^{-4}$, so $\tfrac38x^2=7.5\times10^{-8}$; for the $\tau$, $x=0.1263$, so $\tfrac38x^2=6.0\times10^{-3}$). Because the $\tau$ is heavy, a mass effect of 0.6% remains even in the $B$-factory region.

Meaning. The rise $\sigma\propto\beta$ at the threshold is not specific to QED; it is a consequence of the three-dimensional final-state phase space having $\dd^3p\propto p^2\dd p\propto p\,\dd E$. The same square-root onset appears, in materials science, directly in the absorption edge of a direct-gap semiconductor. The joint density of states for parabolic bands is $J(\hbar\omega)\propto\sqrt{\hbar\omega-E_g}$, and the onset of the absorption coefficient as $\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}\propto\sqrt{\hbar\omega-E_g}$ is exactly the same counting of three-dimensional phase space as the onset of the $e^+e^-\to\tau^+\tau^-$ cross section at threshold as $\propto\beta=\sqrt{1-4m_\tau^2/s}$ (an $M_0$-type critical point). This is the basis of the familiar procedure of reading off the band gap by fitting $(\alpha_{\mathrm{abs}}\hbar\omega)^2$ to a straight line against $\hbar\omega$ in a Tauc plot. Just as on the particle-physics side “the $\beta$ dependence at threshold tells us the spin and orbital angular momentum of the produced particles,” on the solid-state side “the exponent of the absorption edge ($1/2$, $3/2$, or $2$) tells us whether the transition is direct or indirect, and allowed or forbidden.” In both cases, what we are looking at is the phase space and the angular-momentum dependence of the matrix element.

Exercise 10.4: From Mott scattering to Rutherford scattering

Problem (restated)

Generalizing the Mott cross-section formula of Chapter 10 of this book to a heavy target of charge $Ze$ (the vertex factor is multiplied by $Z$) gives

$$ \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd\Omega}=\frac{Z^2\alpha^2}{4p^2\beta^2\sin^4(\theta/2)}\left[1-\beta^2\sin^2\tfrac\theta2\right] $$

.

(1) Show that in the limit $\beta\ll1$ it reduces to Rutherford’s formula $\left(Z\alpha/4E_{\mathrm{kin}}\right)^2/\sin^4(\theta/2)$.

(2) For an electron of kinetic energy $100\ \mathrm{keV}$, find $p$, $E$, and $\beta$.

(3) Find the differential cross section for scattering at $\theta=90^\circ$ off an aluminum nucleus ($Z=13$) in barn/sr. (Conversion: $1\ \mathrm{MeV^{-2}}=389.4\ \mathrm{barn}$.)

(4) Evaluate the Mott factor $\left[1-\beta^2\sin^2(\theta/2)\right]$ at $\theta=90^\circ$ and $180^\circ$, and state by what percentage it deviates from Rutherford.

Solution

Strategy. We compute to the end in natural units ($\hbar=c=1$) and at the end convert to an area using $1\ \mathrm{MeV^{-2}}=389.4\ \mathrm{barn}$. The relativistic kinematics consists of just three relations: $E=m_e+T$, $p=\sqrt{E^2-m_e^2}$, and $\beta=p/E$. We use $m_e=0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $\alpha=1/137.036$.

(1) For $\beta\ll1$, the term $\beta^2\sin^2(\theta/2)$ inside the square brackets is negligible compared with $1$, and the Mott factor becomes $1$. Only the prefactor remains. In the nonrelativistic limit, $E\to m_e$, $p\to m_ev$, and $\beta\to v$, so

$$ p^2\beta^2=\frac{p^4}{E^2}\;\longrightarrow\;\frac{(m_ev)^4}{m_e^2}=m_e^2v^4=\left(m_ev^2\right)^2 $$

Here the nonrelativistic kinetic energy is $E_{\mathrm{kin}}=\tfrac12m_ev^2$, so $m_ev^2=2E_{\mathrm{kin}}$, and

$$ p^2\beta^2\;\longrightarrow\;4E_{\mathrm{kin}}^2, \qquad 4p^2\beta^2\;\longrightarrow\;16E_{\mathrm{kin}}^2 $$

Therefore

$$ \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd\Omega}\;\longrightarrow\; \frac{Z^2\alpha^2}{16E_{\mathrm{kin}}^2\sin^4(\theta/2)} =\left(\frac{Z\alpha}{4E_{\mathrm{kin}}}\right)^2\frac{1}{\sin^4(\theta/2)} $$

This is Rutherford’s formula. The expression written in 1911 without using spin, relativity, or field theory has been reproduced as the $\beta\to0$ limit of QED.

(2) From $T=0.100\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $m_e=0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$,

$$ E=m_e+T=0.511+0.100=0.611\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ $$ p=\sqrt{E^2-m_e^2}=\sqrt{0.611^2-0.511^2}=\sqrt{0.373321-0.261121}=\sqrt{0.112200}=0.334963\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

(Writing $p=\sqrt{T(T+2m_e)}=\sqrt{0.100\times1.122}$ gives the same result.)

$$ \beta=\frac pE=\frac{0.334963}{0.611}=0.548220, \qquad \beta^2=0.300546, \qquad \gamma=\frac{E}{m_e}=\frac{0.611}{0.511}=1.1957 $$

An electron at $100\ \mathrm{kV}$, a standard accelerating voltage for transmission electron microscopy, is already traveling at 55% of the speed of light. From $\lambda=2\pi/p$ the wavelength is $3.70\ \mathrm{pm}$, far shorter than the interatomic distance.

(3) First, the coupling part.

$$ Z\alpha=\frac{13}{137.036}=0.0948656 $$

Next we put the prefactor into the form $\left(Z\alpha/2p\beta\right)^2$.

$$ 2p\beta=2\times0.334963\times0.548220=0.367267\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ $$ \left(\frac{Z\alpha}{2p\beta}\right)^2=\left(\frac{0.0948656}{0.367267}\right)^2 =(0.258299)^2=0.0667197\ \mathrm{MeV^{-2}} $$

At $\theta=90^\circ$, $\sin(\theta/2)=\sin45^\circ=1/\sqrt2$, so $\sin^4(\theta/2)=1/4=0.250000$. Dividing by this, the Rutherford part (before multiplying by the Mott factor) is

$$ \frac{Z^2\alpha^2}{4p^2\beta^2\sin^4(\theta/2)}=\frac{0.0667197}{0.250000}=0.266879\ \mathrm{MeV^{-2}} $$

The Mott factor is

$$ 1-\beta^2\sin^2\tfrac{90^\circ}{2}=1-0.300546\times\tfrac12=1-0.150273=0.849727 $$

Therefore

$$ \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd\Omega}=0.266879\times0.849727=0.226774\ \mathrm{MeV^{-2}} $$

Finally, we convert to an area.

$$ \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd\Omega}=0.226774\times389.4\ \mathrm{barn/sr}=88.3\ \mathrm{barn/sr} $$

To get a feel for the magnitude, $88\ \mathrm{barn/sr}=8.8\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{m^2/sr}$. This is nearly 90 times the geometric cross section of an atomic nucleus ($\sim1\ \mathrm{barn}$), which shows how strongly electrons are scattered in matter. This is the reason that specimens for transmission electron microscopy must be thinned to below $100\ \mathrm{nm}$.

(4) We evaluate the Mott factor $F(\theta)=1-\beta^2\sin^2(\theta/2)$ at two points. Here $\beta^2=0.300546$.

$$ F(90^\circ)=1-0.300546\times\sin^245^\circ=1-0.300546\times0.500000=1-0.150273=0.8497 $$ $$ F(180^\circ)=1-0.300546\times\sin^290^\circ=1-0.300546\times1=0.6995 $$

That is, compared with Rutherford’s prediction, which neglects spin, the cross section is 15.0% lower at $\theta=90^\circ$ and 30.1% lower at $\theta=180^\circ$ (straight back). The further backward, the stronger the suppression. In the ultrarelativistic limit $\beta\to1$, $F(180^\circ)\to0$, that is, scattering straight backward vanishes completely. A $100\ \mathrm{keV}$ electron is partway along this path.

Verification. We check from three angles. (i) Dimensions: $\alpha$ is dimensionless, and $p^2\beta^2$ is in $\mathrm{MeV^2}$ from $p$ and $\beta$, so $\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega$ is in $\mathrm{MeV^{-2}}$, that is, it has the dimension of an area. The conversion $1\ \mathrm{MeV^{-2}}=389.4\ \mathrm{barn}$ is the same as $(\hbar c)^2=0.3894\ \mathrm{GeV^2\,mb}$ ($1\ \mathrm{MeV^{-2}}=10^6\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}=0.3894\times10^6\ \mathrm{mb}=389.4\ \mathrm{b}$), so it is consistent. (ii) Comparison with the nonrelativistic formula: inserting $E_{\mathrm{kin}}=T=0.100\ \mathrm{MeV}$ directly into Rutherford’s formula from (1) gives

$$ \left(\frac{Z\alpha}{4T}\right)^2\frac{1}{\sin^4 45^\circ} =\left(\frac{0.0948656}{0.400}\right)^2\times4=0.0562467\times4=0.224987\ \mathrm{MeV^{-2}} =87.6\ \mathrm{barn/sr} $$

This differs from the relativistically correct value $88.3\ \mathrm{barn/sr}$ by only $0.8$%. The breakdown is interesting. The relativistic denominator $4p^2\beta^2=0.1349\ \mathrm{MeV^2}$ is 16% smaller than the nonrelativistic $16E_{\mathrm{kin}}^2=0.1600\ \mathrm{MeV^2}$, which makes the prefactor 19% larger. Meanwhile the Mott factor lowers it by 15%. The two nearly cancel each other. This is a coincidence, but it is why the naive Rutherford formula works surprisingly well around $100\ \mathrm{keV}$. (iii) Limits: it is also correct that the Mott factor $\to1$ as $\beta\to0$, and that as $\theta\to0$ the cross section diverges because of $\sin^{-4}(\theta/2)$ (a reflection of the infinite range of the Coulomb force; it becomes finite once screening is included).

Meaning. This calculation is the very foundation of image contrast in electron microscopy. First, the $Z^2$ dependence. The fact that backscattered-electron (BSE) images in scanning electron microscopy and high-angle annular dark-field images in scanning transmission electron microscopy (HAADF-STEM) give the Z-contrast in which “heavier elements appear brighter” is due precisely to this $\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega\propto Z^2$ (effectively about $Z^{1.6\text{--}2}$ because of multiple scattering and screening). This formula is the basis of the everyday task of reading the chemical species of an atomic column from its brightness in atomic-resolution HAADF-STEM. Second, $\sin^{-4}(\theta/2)$, that is, the $1/q^2$ dependence of the photon propagator. This is the prefactor of the Mott–Bethe formula $f^{e}(q)=2m_e\alpha\left[Z-f^{X}(q)\right]/q^2$ described in Chapter 10 of this book, and is the reason that the atomic scattering factor in electron diffraction, unlike that of X-rays, rises steeply at low angles. Third, the Mott factor itself. This is a factor specific to spin $1/2$, and it does not appear if the target has spin 0. The same procedure by which Hofstadter divided the measured cross section by the Mott cross section to extract the form factor $F(q^2)$ is carried out every day in crystallography, in the form of “dividing the measured diffraction intensity by the atomic scattering factor to extract the structure factor.” The “point-particle cross section” of particle physics plays the role of a calibration constant in condensed-matter measurements.

Exercise 10.5: The running coupling constant and the Landau pole

Problem (restated)

Take the formula for the running coupling constant of Chapter 10 of this book,

$$ \alpha(Q^2)=\frac{\alpha}{1-\dfrac{\alpha}{3\pi}\left(\ln\dfrac{Q^2}{m_e^2}-\dfrac53\right)} $$

as the starting point.

(1) Without expanding the denominator, show that $1/\alpha(Q^2)$ is a linear function of $\ln Q^2$.

(2) Considering only the electron loop, evaluate $\alpha(Q^2)$ numerically at $Q=1\ \mathrm{GeV}$.

(3) Find the energy at which the denominator of the above formula vanishes (the Landau pole). Compare this value with the Planck mass $1.22\times10^{19}\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and explain why QED is said not to break down “in practice.”

(4) In Section 10.4.4 of this book we used $\alpha=1/137$ at $\sqrt{s}=10\ \mathrm{GeV}$. If we use $\alpha(Q^2=s)$ instead, by what percentage does the cross section change (take $\alpha(10\ \mathrm{GeV})\simeq1/132.1$, including all fermions)?

Solution

Strategy. Part (1) only requires taking the reciprocal of the expression. Parts (2) and (3) simply substitute numbers into the resulting linear expression; since an exponential function is involved, we convert to common logarithms and track the orders of magnitude. Part (4) uses the fact that the cross section is proportional to $\alpha^2$. We use $\alpha\equiv\alpha(0)=1/137.036$ and $m_e=0.511\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GeV}$.

(1) Take the reciprocal of both sides of the given expression. There is no need at all to expand the denominator:

$$ \frac{1}{\alpha(Q^2)}=\frac{1}{\alpha}\left[1-\frac{\alpha}{3\pi}\left(\ln\frac{Q^2}{m_e^2}-\frac53\right)\right] =\frac{1}{\alpha}-\frac{1}{3\pi}\left(\ln\frac{Q^2}{m_e^2}-\frac53\right) $$

Splitting $\ln(Q^2/m_e^2)=\ln Q^2-\ln m_e^2$ and collecting the constant terms, we obtain

$$ \frac{1}{\alpha(Q^2)} =\underbrace{\left[\frac{1}{\alpha}+\frac{1}{3\pi}\ln m_e^2+\frac{5}{9\pi}\right]}_{\text{constant}} -\frac{1}{3\pi}\,\ln Q^2 $$

That is, $1/\alpha(Q^2)$ is a linear function of $\ln Q^2$, with slope $-1/(3\pi)$. Written in differential form, the same statement reads

$$ \frac{\dd}{\dd\ln Q^2}\left(\frac{1}{\alpha}\right)=-\frac{1}{3\pi} \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \frac{\dd\alpha}{\dd\ln Q^2}=\frac{\alpha^2}{3\pi} $$

This is the one-loop QED $\beta$ function. What deserves attention is that the slope $-1/(3\pi)$ is a pure number that depends on neither $\alpha$ nor $m_e$. What runs is not $\alpha$ but $1/\alpha$, and how it runs is determined only by the species and charges of the particles in the loop (in general a factor $\sum_f N_c^{(f)}Q_f^2$ multiplies the coefficient). “If you plot $1/\alpha$ on semilog paper you get a straight line, and its slope counts the charged particles”: this is the structure at one loop.

(2) Let $Q=1\ \mathrm{GeV}$. The logarithm is

$$ \ln\frac{Q^2}{m_e^2}=2\ln\frac{1}{5.11\times10^{-4}}=2\ln\left(1956.95\right)=2\times7.57914=15.1583 $$ $$ \ln\frac{Q^2}{m_e^2}-\frac53=15.1583-1.6667=13.4916 $$

The coefficient is

$$ \frac{\alpha}{3\pi}=\frac{7.29735\times10^{-3}}{9.42478}=7.74273\times10^{-4} $$

Hence the vacuum polarization contribution is

$$ \hat\Pi=7.74273\times10^{-4}\times13.4916=1.04462\times10^{-2} $$

Substituting directly into the linear expression of (1), we get

$$ \frac{1}{\alpha(Q^2)}=137.036\times\left(1-0.0104462\right)=137.036\times0.989554=135.604 $$ $$ \alpha(1\ \mathrm{GeV})=\frac{1}{135.60}=7.3744\times10^{-3} $$

The increase from $\alpha(0)=1/137.036$ is only 1.06%. Even when the momentum scale is raised 2000-fold from $m_e$ to 1 GeV, the coupling moves only this much. This is what it means to run only logarithmically.

(3) The condition for the denominator to vanish is

$$ 1-\frac{\alpha}{3\pi}\left(\ln\frac{Q^2}{m_e^2}-\frac53\right)=0 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \ln\frac{Q^2}{m_e^2}=\frac{3\pi}{\alpha}+\frac53 $$

Substituting numbers, we find

$$ \frac{3\pi}{\alpha}=3\pi\times137.036=9.42478\times137.036=1291.53 $$ $$ \ln\frac{Q^2}{m_e^2}=1291.53+1.67=1293.20 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \ln\frac{Q}{m_e}=\frac{1293.20}{2}=646.60 $$

That is, $Q=m_e\,\ee^{646.60}$. To obtain the order of magnitude, we convert to common logarithms.

$$ \log_{10}\ee^{646.60}=\frac{646.60}{2.302585}=280.815, \qquad \log_{10}\left(5.11\times10^{-4}\right)=-3.292 $$ $$ \log_{10}Q\,[\mathrm{GeV}]=280.815-3.292=277.523 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad Q_{\mathrm{Landau}}\simeq3.3\times10^{277}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Comparing with the Planck mass $M_{\mathrm{Pl}}=1.22\times10^{19}\ \mathrm{GeV}$ ($\log_{10}M_{\mathrm{Pl}}=19.09$), we have

$$ \log_{10}\frac{Q_{\mathrm{Landau}}}{M_{\mathrm{Pl}}}=277.52-19.09=258.43 $$

That is, the Landau pole lies as much as 258 orders of magnitude above the Planck mass. This is why it is said that “QED does not break down in practice.” To begin with, beyond $M_{\mathrm{Pl}}$ the quantum effects of gravity dominate, and the very premise of a field theory on flat spacetime breaks down. Moreover, at $\sim10^2\ \mathrm{GeV}$ QED is unified into the electroweak theory, and at still higher scales unknown physics enters. In other words, the Landau pole has meaning only in the fictitious setting of “pushing QED up to infinite energy in a world with nothing else.” QED is an effective field theory, and as long as it is used with its range of applicability stated explicitly, there is no problem at all. Note also that extrapolating the one-loop formula all the way to the region $\alpha(Q^2)\sim1$ is itself an abuse of perturbation theory, so the numerical position of the pole has no meaning either.

(4) The cross section of $e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-$ is $\sigma=4\pi\alpha^2/3s$, which is proportional to $\alpha^2$. Therefore, replacing $\alpha(0)=1/137.036$ by $\alpha(10\ \mathrm{GeV})=1/132.1$, we obtain

$$ \frac{\sigma\left[\alpha(s)\right]}{\sigma\left[\alpha(0)\right]} =\left(\frac{\alpha(10\ \mathrm{GeV})}{\alpha(0)}\right)^2 =\left(\frac{137.036}{132.1}\right)^2=(1.03736)^2=1.0761 $$

That is, the cross section increases by about 7.6%. The value $0.869\ \mathrm{nb}$ in the main text becomes $0.935\ \mathrm{nb}$. In modern measurements, where the statistical error of an experiment falls below 1%, this is a correction that can by no means be neglected.

Verification. Let us see whether the procedure of (2) reproduces the $\alpha(m_Z)$ of the main text (electron loop only). Taking $Q=m_Z=91.188\ \mathrm{GeV}$,

$$ \ln\frac{Q^2}{m_e^2}=2\ln\frac{91.188}{5.11\times10^{-4}}=2\times12.0921=24.1841, \qquad 24.1841-1.6667=22.5175 $$ $$ \hat\Pi=7.74273\times10^{-4}\times22.5175=0.0174347, \qquad \frac{1}{\alpha(m_Z)}=137.036\times0.982565=134.65 $$

This agrees exactly with the $1/134.65$ of the main text. The property of the linear expression in (1) can also be checked. When $Q$ is raised from $1\ \mathrm{GeV}$ to $m_Z$, $\ln Q^2$ increases by $24.184-15.158=9.026$, and $1/\alpha$ decreases by $135.604-134.647=0.957$. Taking the ratio gives $0.957/9.026=0.1060$, which agrees with the predicted slope $1/(3\pi)=0.10610$. As for dimensions, it suffices to confirm that the argument of the logarithm, $Q^2/m_e^2$, is a dimensionless quantity and that $\hat\Pi$ is also dimensionless.

Meaning. The idea that “the coupling constant depends on the scale of observation” is used as it stands in first-principles calculations in materials science. The most direct correspondence is $W=v/(1-v\chi_0)$, discussed in Section 10.7.2 of this book. The vacuum polarization $\hat\Pi$ corresponds to the polarization function $\chi_0$ of the solid, and the running $\alpha$ corresponds to the screened Coulomb interaction $W$; both are solutions of the same Dyson series. In QED, the higher $Q^2$ is raised (the shorter the distance), the less effective the screening becomes and the larger $\alpha$ grows; in a solid, the higher $q$ is raised, the more $\epsilon(q)\to1$ and the more we return to the bare $v(q)$. It is the same diagram.

A more practical correspondence is the determination of the parameters of low-energy effective models. When the $U$ of the Hubbard model is determined by the constrained random phase approximation (cRPA), the value of $U$ obtained depends on how the energy window is chosen, that is, which bands are kept in the model and which bands are allowed to screen. If the window is taken wide, fewer agents are left to do the screening and $U$ becomes larger; if it is taken narrow, $U$ becomes smaller. This is logically identical to “the value of $\alpha$ changes depending on where $Q^2$ is taken,” and both are manifestations of a single principle: “the parameters of an effective theory are quantities that belong to the scale at which that theory was defined.” The question “what is the correct value of $U$?” has no meaning without specifying the scale, just as “what is the correct value of $\alpha$?” cannot be settled without specifying $Q^2$.

Exercise 10.6: Measuring vacancies by positron annihilation (silicon)

Problem (restated)

Use the PALS formula of Chapter 10 of this book and $\pi r_e^2c=7.48\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$. The positron lifetime in a perfect Si crystal is $\tau_b=219\ \mathrm{ps}$, and in a monovacancy it is $\tau_v=265\ \mathrm{ps}$.

(1) Verify the value of $\pi r_e^2c$ by computing it yourself from $r_e=2.818\ \mathrm{fm}$.

(2) From $\tau_b$ and $\tau_v$, find the effective electron density $n_{\mathrm{eff}}$ felt by the positron in each case.

(3) Calculate the valence electron density of Si (diamond structure, $a=5.431\ \mathrm{\AA}$, 8 atoms per unit cell, 4 valence electrons per atom) and compare it with (2). Explain why the ratio is not 1.

(4) In a certain sample a mean lifetime $\bar\tau=230\ \mathrm{ps}$ was measured. From the two-state trapping model formula

$$ \kappa=\frac{1}{\tau_b}\,\frac{\bar\tau-\tau_b}{\tau_v-\bar\tau} $$

find the trapping rate $\kappa$, and, taking the trapping-rate coefficient to be $\mu=1.0\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, find the vacancy concentration $C_v$ in ppm.

Solution

Strategy. All we use is the single line for the annihilation rate derived from Dirac’s annihilation cross section, $\lambda=1/\tau=\pi r_e^2c\,n_{\mathrm{eff}}$. We work throughout in SI units, with lengths in m and times in s.

(1) We have $r_e=2.818\ \mathrm{fm}=2.818\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}$ and $c=2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}$.

$$ r_e^2=\left(2.818\times10^{-15}\right)^2=7.9411\times10^{-30}\ \mathrm{m^2} $$ $$ \pi r_e^2=3.14159\times7.9411\times10^{-30}=2.49478\times10^{-29}\ \mathrm{m^2} $$ $$ \pi r_e^2c=2.49478\times10^{-29}\times2.998\times10^{8}=7.4793\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}} $$

This agrees with the given $7.48\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$. The dimensions also work: $\mathrm{m^2}\times\mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}=\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}$, and multiplying this by an electron density in $\mathrm{m^{-3}}$ gives $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, that is, the annihilation rate. Note also that $\pi r_e^2=0.2495\ \mathrm{b}$, which is $3/8$ of the Thomson cross section $\sigma_T=8\pi r_e^2/3=0.665\ \mathrm{b}$. Both use the same “QED area” $r_e^2$ as their unit.

(2) Solving $\lambda=1/\tau=\pi r_e^2c\,n_{\mathrm{eff}}$ in reverse gives $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=1/\left(\tau\,\pi r_e^2c\right)$.

Perfect crystal ($\tau_b=219\ \mathrm{ps}=2.19\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{s}$):

$$ n_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(b)}=\frac{1}{2.19\times10^{-10}\times7.4793\times10^{-21}} =\frac{1}{1.6379\times10^{-30}}=6.105\times10^{29}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}} $$

Monovacancy ($\tau_v=265\ \mathrm{ps}=2.65\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{s}$):

$$ n_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(v)}=\frac{1}{2.65\times10^{-10}\times7.4793\times10^{-21}} =\frac{1}{1.9820\times10^{-30}}=5.045\times10^{29}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}} $$

The ratio is $5.045/6.105=0.826$; that is, the electron density felt by a positron trapped in a vacancy is 83% of its value in the perfect crystal. This 17% reduction lengthens the lifetime by 21%, from 219 ps to 265 ps (as it must, since $\tau\propto1/n$).

(3) The cubic unit cell of the diamond structure contains 8 Si atoms, and each atom has 4 valence electrons, so there are $8\times4=32$ valence electrons per unit cell. Since the lattice constant is $a=5.431\ \mathrm{\AA}=5.431\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$,

$$ a^3=\left(5.431\right)^3\ \mathrm{\AA^3}=160.19\ \mathrm{\AA^3}=1.6019\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{m^3} $$ $$ n_{\mathrm{val}}=\frac{32}{160.19\ \mathrm{\AA^3}}=0.1998\ \mathrm{\AA^{-3}} =\frac{32}{1.6019\times10^{-28}}=1.998\times10^{29}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}} $$

The ratio to the effective value in the perfect crystal is

$$ \frac{n_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(b)}}{n_{\mathrm{val}}}=\frac{6.105\times10^{29}}{1.998\times10^{29}}=3.06 $$

There are two reasons why the ratio is not 1. First, the positron annihilates not only with valence electrons but also with core electrons (the $1s,2s,2p$ electrons of Si, 10 per atom). Core electrons are strongly localized near the nucleus, so their overlap with the positron is small, but their density is higher by orders of magnitude, so the contribution cannot be neglected. Second, and this is the main factor, there is the enhancement factor $\gamma$. Because the positron has positive charge, it attracts electrons around itself (electron–positron correlation). Therefore the local electron density at the position of the positron is several times higher than the average density. In the language of particle physics, this corresponds to the Sommerfeld factor due to the Coulomb interaction in the final state. In the Al example of the main text the effective density was 4.5 times the valence electron density, whereas in Si it is 3.06 times. This reflects the fact that in covalent Si the valence electrons are concentrated at the middle of the bonds, so the electron density in the interstitial region that the positron can enter is relatively low. In any case, the QED formula $\lambda=\pi r_e^2cn_e$ itself is correct, and “what to put in for $n_e$” is entirely a condensed matter problem.

(4) First we find the bulk annihilation rate.

$$ \frac{1}{\tau_b}=\frac{1}{219\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{s}}=4.5662\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

Next we compute the lifetime-ratio part.

$$ \frac{\bar\tau-\tau_b}{\tau_v-\bar\tau}=\frac{230-219}{265-230}=\frac{11}{35}=0.314286 $$

Hence the trapping rate is

$$ \kappa=4.5662\times10^{9}\times0.314286=1.4351\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

Using the trapping rate coefficient $\mu=1.0\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ (per atomic fraction), the vacancy concentration is

$$ C_v=\frac{\kappa}{\mu}=\frac{1.4351\times10^{9}}{1.0\times10^{15}}=1.435\times10^{-6} \simeq1.4\ \mathrm{ppm} $$

The atomic density of Si is $8/a^3=4.995\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, so this corresponds, in terms of the vacancy number density, to $7.2\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}=7.2\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$.

Verification. Part (4) can be checked by going back to the original formula of the two-state trapping model. The expression for the mean lifetime was $\bar\tau=\left(1+\kappa\tau_v\right)/\left(1/\tau_b+\kappa\right)$. Substituting the value $\kappa=1.4351\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ that we found, we get

$$ \kappa\tau_v=1.4351\times10^{9}\times2.65\times10^{-10}=0.38030 $$ $$ \bar\tau=\frac{1+0.38030}{4.5662\times10^{9}+1.4351\times10^{9}} =\frac{1.38030}{6.0013\times10^{9}}=2.3000\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{s}=230.0\ \mathrm{ps} $$

This correctly reproduces the measured value of 230 ps. The dimensions are also consistent: $\kappa$ is in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ and $\mu$ is in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ (per atomic fraction), so $C_v=\kappa/\mu$ is dimensionless. The limiting behavior is also correct: $\kappa\to0$ as $\bar\tau\to\tau_b$ (no vacancies), and $\kappa\to\infty$ as $\bar\tau\to\tau_v$ (the saturation regime in which all positrons are trapped); we can also read off that as saturation is approached, the precision with which $\kappa$ can be determined drops rapidly. While we are at it, let us estimate the intensity of the vacancy component:

$$ I_v=\frac{\kappa}{1/\tau_b-1/\tau_v+\kappa} =\frac{1.4351}{4.5662-3.7736+1.4351}=\frac{1.4351}{2.2277}=0.644 $$

That is, with only 1.4 ppm of vacancies, 64% of the positrons are trapped.

Meaning. This last number captures the essence of the PALS technique. A defect present at only one in a million atoms captures two thirds of the positrons. The reason is that, because the positron has positive charge, it is expelled from the positive ion cores and diffuses into, and falls into, the free volume where the electron density is low (the diffusion length $L_+=\sqrt{D_+\tau_b}$ is about $200\ \mathrm{nm}$ in Si). A defect at ppm concentration does not even show up in the widths of the diffraction lines in X-ray diffraction, and it barely enters the field of view of a transmission electron microscope. Only the positron actively goes out and seeks the defects.

And the prefactor $\pi r_e^2c$ that produces this sensitivity is the one derived in Section 10.2.4 of this book from Dirac’s annihilation cross section $\sigma_{2\gamma}=\pi r_e^2/\beta$, and its content is only $r_e=\alpha/m_e$, that is, the fine-structure constant and the electron mass. A purely QED quantity works as a calibration constant for the quality control of silicon wafers. Indeed, PALS is routinely used to evaluate vacancy-type defects in Czochralski-grown Si (COPs), as well as residual vacancies and vacancy–oxygen complexes (VO centers) after ion implantation. A picosecond measurement, “the lifetime increased by just 11 ps, from 219 ps to 230 ps,” is translated into a defect concentration in ppm.

Exercise 10.7: The Klein–Nishina cross section and the Compton profile

Problem (restated)

Use the Klein–Nishina formula of Chapter 10 of this book:

$$ \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd\Omega}=\frac{r_e^2}{2}\left(\frac{\omega'}{\omega}\right)^2 \left[\frac{\omega}{\omega'}+\frac{\omega'}{\omega}-\sin^2\theta\right] $$

Take $m_e=0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $r_e=2.818\ \mathrm{fm}$.

(1) Show that in the limit $\omega\ll m_e$ it reduces to Thomson’s formula $\left(r_e^2/2\right)\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)$, and compute $\sigma_T=8\pi r_e^2/3$ in barn.

(2) For the $\gamma$ ray of $^{137}\mathrm{Cs}$ ($\omega=662\ \mathrm{keV}$), find the scattered-photon energy at $\theta=180^\circ$ (the backscattering peak) and the maximum kinetic energy received by the electron (the Compton edge).

(3) Compute the differential cross section for the same $\gamma$ ray at $\theta=180^\circ$ and compare it with the Thomson value.

(4) Verify that the Compton profile of a free-electron gas, $J(p_z)=\left(3/4p_F\right)\left[1-(p_z/p_F)^2\right]$, is normalized to $\int J\,\dd p_z=1$, and find $J(0)$ for Al ($p_F=0.926$ a.u.). Then state the main reason why the measured $J(0)$ is larger than in the free-electron model, and, using $J(p_z)=2\pi\int_{\abs{p_z}}^{\infty}n(p)\,p\,\dd p$, explain where the quasiparticle weight (renormalization factor) $Z$ appears in the Compton profile (in the height of $J(0)$, or in the kink at $p_z=\pm p_F$).

Solution

Strategy. For (1)–(3), the Klein–Nishina formula and the Compton relation $1/\omega'-1/\omega=(1-\cos\theta)/m_e$ are all we need. Part (4) requires only an elementary integral and the geometry of the Fermi sphere.

(1) Solving the Compton relation for $\omega'$ gives

$$ \omega'=\frac{\omega}{1+\dfrac{\omega}{m_e}\left(1-\cos\theta\right)} $$

For $\omega\ll m_e$ the denominator approaches $1$ at every scattering angle, so $\omega'\to\omega$; that is, $\omega'/\omega\to1$ and $\omega/\omega'\to1$. Hence the square bracket becomes

$$ \frac{\omega}{\omega'}+\frac{\omega'}{\omega}-\sin^2\theta\;\longrightarrow\;1+1-\sin^2\theta=2-\left(1-\cos^2\theta\right)=1+\cos^2\theta $$

Together with the prefactor $(\omega'/\omega)^2\to1$, this gives

$$ \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd\Omega}\;\longrightarrow\;\frac{r_e^2}{2}\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right) $$

This is the Thomson formula (it is precisely the dipole-radiation intensity of an oscillating free electron in classical electromagnetism). Using the same angular integration as in Section 10.4 of this book, $\int\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)\dd\Omega=16\pi/3$, the total cross section is

$$ \sigma_T=\frac{r_e^2}{2}\cdot\frac{16\pi}{3}=\frac{8\pi}{3}r_e^2 $$

Numerically,

$$ \sigma_T=\frac{8\times3.14159}{3}\times\left(2.818\times10^{-15}\right)^2 =8.37758\times7.9411\times10^{-30}=6.6527\times10^{-29}\ \mathrm{m^2} $$ $$ =6.6527\times10^{-29}/10^{-28}\ \mathrm{barn}=0.6653\ \mathrm{barn} $$

That is $0.665\ \mathrm{b}$ per electron. This is the starting point for the absolute calibration of all intensities in X-ray scattering experiments.

(2) At $\theta=180^\circ$ we have $1-\cos\theta=2$, so

$$ \omega'=\frac{\omega}{1+\dfrac{2\omega}{m_e}} $$

With $\omega=662\ \mathrm{keV}=0.662\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $m_e=0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$,

$$ \frac{2\omega}{m_e}=\frac{2\times0.662}{0.511}=\frac{1.324}{0.511}=2.59100, \qquad 1+\frac{2\omega}{m_e}=3.59100 $$ $$ \omega'=\frac{662}{3.59100}=184.35\ \mathrm{keV}\simeq184\ \mathrm{keV} $$

This is the backscattering peak. The kinetic energy received by the electron is $T_e=\omega-\omega'$, and it is maximal at $\theta=180^\circ$, so

$$ T_e^{\max}=662-184.35=477.65\ \mathrm{keV}\simeq478\ \mathrm{keV} $$

This is the Compton edge. If we use the unrounded values ($\omega=661.657\ \mathrm{keV}$, $m_e=510.999\ \mathrm{keV}$), we obtain $2\omega/m_e=2.58966$, $\omega'=661.657/3.58966=184.32\ \mathrm{keV}$, and $T_e^{\max}=477.33\ \mathrm{keV}$, which agree with the 184 keV / 477 keV quoted in the main text (the 478 keV above arose because we rounded to $\omega=662$ and $m_e=0.511$). When a real $^{137}\mathrm{Cs}$ source is measured with a NaI or HPGe detector, then in addition to the 662 keV photopeak there always appear a small peak near 184 keV (photons that were backscattered outside the detector and then entered it) and a continuum that cuts off sharply at 477 keV (events in which the photon Compton-scattered inside the detector and the scattered photon escaped). Anyone who has done radiation measurements will find this spectrum familiar, and its features are fixed by these two lines of calculation.

(3) From (2), $\omega'/\omega=1/3.59100=0.278474$ and $\omega/\omega'=3.59100$. At $\theta=180^\circ$ we have $\sin^2\theta=0$, so the square bracket is

$$ \frac{\omega}{\omega'}+\frac{\omega'}{\omega}-0=3.59100+0.278474=3.869474 $$

The prefactor is

$$ \left(\frac{\omega'}{\omega}\right)^2=(0.278474)^2=0.0775478 $$

Therefore

$$ \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd\Omega}=\frac{r_e^2}{2}\times0.0775478\times3.869474=0.15003\,r_e^2 $$

Since $r_e^2=7.9411\times10^{-30}\ \mathrm{m^2}=7.9411\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{barn}$,

$$ \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd\Omega}=0.15003\times7.9411\times10^{-2}=1.191\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{barn/sr} $$

On the other hand, the Thomson value at $\theta=180^\circ$ is $\left(r_e^2/2\right)\left(1+\cos^2180^\circ\right)=\left(r_e^2/2\right)\times2=r_e^2=7.94\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{barn/sr}$. The ratio is

$$ \frac{\left(\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega\right)_{\mathrm{KN}}}{\left(\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega\right)_{\mathrm{Thomson}}}=0.150 $$

That is, at 662 keV backscattering is suppressed to 15% of the Thomson prediction. The main cause of the suppression is the prefactor $(\omega'/\omega)^2$, which is the direct effect of the decrease in the scattered-photon energy due to recoil (since $\omega'/\omega$ is 0.28, its square drops to 0.078, and this cannot be made up even though the square bracket increases to 3.87). The most important consequence of the Klein–Nishina formula is that higher-energy $\gamma$ rays are scattered more strongly forward; shielding design for $\gamma$ rays and dose calculations for medical linacs rest on this angular dependence.

(4) We verify the normalization directly. Since the function is nonzero only for $\abs{p_z}<p_F$,

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}J(p_z)\,\dd p_z =\frac{3}{4p_F}\int_{-p_F}^{p_F}\left(1-\frac{p_z^2}{p_F^2}\right)\dd p_z =\frac{3}{4p_F}\left[p_z-\frac{p_z^3}{3p_F^2}\right]_{-p_F}^{p_F} $$ $$ =\frac{3}{4p_F}\left[\left(p_F-\frac{p_F}{3}\right)-\left(-p_F+\frac{p_F}{3}\right)\right] =\frac{3}{4p_F}\cdot\frac{4p_F}{3}=1 $$

Indeed, it is normalized to one per electron. Inserting $p_F=0.926$ a.u. for Al gives

$$ J(0)=\frac{3}{4p_F}=\frac{3}{4\times0.926}=\frac{3}{3.704}=0.8099\ \text{a.u.}\simeq0.810\ \text{a.u.} $$

The measured Compton profile of Al has $J(0)\simeq0.85$, somewhat larger than the free-electron-model value.

Here we state precisely what it is that measures $Z$. In an interacting electron system, the momentum distribution $n(\pp)$ is smaller than $1$ inside the Fermi sphere and has a tail outside it. The size of the jump of $n$ across $p_F$ is exactly the quasiparticle weight (renormalization factor) $Z$ of Section 10.7.1 of this book ($Z=1$ for free electrons). The Compton profile satisfies the relation

$$ J(p_z)=2\pi\int_{\abs{p_z}}^{\infty}n(p)\,p\,\dd p \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{\dd J}{\dd p_z}=-2\pi p_z\,n(p_z)\quad(p_z>0) $$

so the jump of $n$ appears not as a jump of $J$ itself but as a discontinuity in the slope of $J$ (a kink), and its size is proportional to the product of $2\pi p_F$ and the jump of $n$, that is, to $Z$. For a free-electron gas ($Z=1$), $\dd J/\dd p_z=-3p_z/(2p_F^3)$ just inside $p_z=p_F$ and $0$ outside, so the size of the kink is

$$ \left|\frac{\dd J}{\dd p_z}\right|_{p_z\to p_F^-}=\frac{3}{2p_F^2} =\frac{3}{2\times(0.926)^2}=\frac{3}{1.71495}=1.749\quad(\text{a.u.}) $$

If the measured kink is smaller than this, the ratio gives $Z$ directly. “Measuring $Z$ by Compton scattering” means measuring the sharpness of this kink.

One more point deserves a note here. Both electron correlation and core electrons contribute to the difference from experiment, but it is not correct to explain the upward shift of the height $J(0)$ by correlation alone. If, with the normalization $\int J\,\dd p_z=1$ held fixed, correlation leaks weight outside $p_F$, then $J(0)=2\pi\int_0^\infty n(p)\,p\,\dd p$ picks up the weight at large $p$ only with the first power of $p$ (the normalization picks it up with $p^2$), so $J(0)$ moves in the direction of a slight decrease. The main reasons why the measured $J(0)$ comes out larger than in the free-electron model are two: (i) the measured total profile includes a broad component from the core electrons (the $1s,2s,2p$ electrons of Al), which raises the whole profile, including $p_z=0$, like a pedestal; and (ii) the actual Fermi surface is not a sphere, and has higher momentum components (umklapp components) due to the lattice potential. In short, correlation ($Z$) shows up in the blunting of the kink at $p_z=\pm p_F$, not in the height of $J(0)$. This is exactly what the main text means when it says that “measuring the size of the jump is equivalent to measuring $Z$.”

Verification. Parts (1)–(3) can be checked in three ways. First, the limit: in (1) we confirmed that putting $\omega\to0$ in the Klein–Nishina formula returns the Thomson formula; conversely, comparing the numerical value in (3) with the $\omega\to0$ limit, we can read off the size of the suppression, a factor of $0.150$. Second, kinematic consistency: substituting $\omega'=184.35\ \mathrm{keV}$ from (2) back into the Compton relation gives $1/\omega'-1/\omega=1/184.35-1/662=5.42446\times10^{-3}-1.51057\times10^{-3}=3.91389\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{keV^{-1}}$, which agrees to six digits with the right-hand side $(1-\cos180^\circ)/m_e=2/\left(511\ \mathrm{keV}\right)=3.91389\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{keV^{-1}}$ (if we substitute the four-significant-figure value $184.4\ \mathrm{keV}$, we get $3.9124\times10^{-3}$, which agrees only to three digits, so use the unrounded value for the check). Third, dimensions: $r_e^2$ is an area, and the square bracket and $(\omega'/\omega)^2$ are dimensionless, so $\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega$ is area per solid angle. For (4), we have confirmed that $\int J\dd p_z=1$ holds independently of $p_F$ (that is, for arbitrary $p_F\to$ values), and the inverse proportionality $J(0)\propto1/p_F$ (the larger the Fermi sphere, the lower and broader the profile) is also just what the normalization requires.

Meaning. This problem shows, in two stages, the structure by which a QED cross section serves as a calibration constant for condensed-matter measurements. The first stage is (1)–(3): the Klein–Nishina cross section is the exact QED prediction for “a single free electron at rest,” and is determined solely by a particle-physics quantity, $r_e^2=(\alpha/m_e)^2$. The second stage is (4): when a real material is measured, the double differential cross section factorizes into the product “Klein–Nishina cross section × $J(p_z)$” (the impulse approximation). The former is a known number independent of the material, and the latter is the information about the material that we want. This is exactly the same logic as in Section 10.5 of this book, where we stated that “dividing the measured cross section by the Mott cross section leaves the form factor”; Hofstadter’s measurement of the proton radius, structure factors in crystallography, and Compton-profile measurements all belong to this single pattern.

The resulting $J(p_z)$ is one of the few experimental quantities that can be compared directly with the $n(\pp)$ obtained from band calculations. Whereas ARPES reads $Z$ from the height of the quasiparticle peak, Compton scattering reads $Z$ from the jump in the momentum-space occupation number. The two are complementary: the former is surface-sensitive, the latter bulk-sensitive. To borrow the words of Section 10.7 of this book, the wave-function renormalization constant that particle physics calls $Z_2$ is routinely measured in X-ray scattering experiments at synchrotron radiation facilities.

E.11 Solutions for Chapter 11: Quark Electrodynamics and Chromodynamics

Exercise 11.1: Counting colors from the $R$ ratio

Problem (restated)

(1) Find $R$ at an energy where the five flavors $u,d,s,c,b$ can be produced, for both $N_c=3$ and $N_c=1$.

(2) Suppose that fourth-generation quarks $t'$ (charge $+2/3$) and $b'$ (charge $-1/3$) exist and that $\sqrt{s}$ exceeds their threshold (eight flavors including $t$). What is $R$?

(3) Find $R$ at $\sqrt{s}=30$ GeV including the QCD correction (you may use $\alpha_s(30\ \mathrm{GeV})=0.14$), and from it find the hadron production cross section in nb.

(4) Suppose the positron beam intensity is sufficient and the luminosity is $\mathcal{L}=10^{31}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}s^{-1}}$. Under the conditions of (3), how many hadron production events occur per day?

Solution

Strategy. We use $R=N_c\sum_i q_i^2$ from Chapter 11 of this book, its QCD-corrected form $R=N_c\sum_i q_i^2(1+\alpha_s/\pi)$, and the practical form of the $\mu$-pair cross section, $\sigma_{\mu\mu}\simeq86.9\ \mathrm{nb}/(s/\mathrm{GeV^2})$. In the last step we merely apply the basic formula of particle-physics experiments, “cross section $\times$ luminosity $\times$ time $=$ number of events,” paying attention to the units.

(1) The quark charges are $q_u=q_c=q_t=+2/3$ and $q_d=q_s=q_b=-1/3$. Among the five flavors $u,d,s,c,b$ there are two with $+2/3$ ($u,c$) and three with $-1/3$ ($d,s,b$), so

$$ \sum_i q_i^2 = 2\times\left(\frac23\right)^2 + 3\times\left(\frac13\right)^2 = 2\times\frac49 + 3\times\frac19 = \frac89+\frac39 = \frac{11}{9} $$

Therefore

$$ R(N_c=3) = 3\times\frac{11}{9} = \frac{11}{3} = 3.667, \qquad R(N_c=1) = 1\times\frac{11}{9} = \frac{11}{9} = 1.222 $$

The measured value is $3.6$–$3.9$ for $\sqrt{s}=11$–$40$ GeV, which agrees with the $N_c=3$ prediction $3.67$ to within a few percent, but disagrees with the $N_c=1$ prediction $1.22$ by a factor of three. The claim of Chapter 11 of this book, that the $R$ ratio is a counting experiment for the number of colors, is condensed into this single-line comparison.

(2) For the eight flavors $u,d,s,c,b,t,t',b'$, there are four with charge $+2/3$ ($u,c,t,t'$) and four with charge $-1/3$ ($d,s,b,b'$). Hence

$$ \sum_i q_i^2 = 4\times\frac49 + 4\times\frac19 = \frac{16}{9}+\frac49 = \frac{20}{9} $$ $$ R = 3\times\frac{20}{9} = \frac{20}{3} = 6.667 $$

What deserves attention here is that adding one fourth-generation pair raises $R$ as $\frac{11}{3}\to\frac{20}{3}$, an increase of $3$. In general, adding one generation (a pair with charges $+2/3$ and $-1/3$) increases it by

$$ \Delta R = 3\left(\frac49+\frac19\right) = 3\times\frac59 = \frac53 = 1.667 $$

each time. The $b'$ alone contributes $3\times\frac19=\frac13$, and the $t'$ alone contributes $3\times\frac49=\frac43$. Indeed $\frac{20}{3}-\frac{11}{3}=3=\frac43+\frac13+\frac43$, which is the contribution of three quarks: $t$ (not yet counted) and $t',b'$. That is, the height of each step of the staircase in $R$ itself measures the charge of the new quark, and the number of steps measures the number of flavors. The $R$ ratio is thus an experiment that “counts flavors” as well as one that “counts colors.”

(3) Since $\sqrt{s}=30$ GeV is above the $b$ threshold and far below the $t$ threshold, this is the five-flavor case of (1). Including the QCD correction,

$$ R = 3\sum_i q_i^2\left(1+\frac{\alpha_s}{\pi}\right) = \frac{11}{3}\times\left(1+\frac{0.14}{3.1416}\right) = 3.6667\times(1+0.04456) = 3.6667\times1.04456 = 3.830 $$

Next comes the $\mu$-pair cross section. Since $s=(30\ \mathrm{GeV})^2=900\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$,

$$ \sigma_{\mu\mu} = \frac{86.9\ \mathrm{nb}}{900} = 0.09656\ \mathrm{nb} $$

Therefore

$$ \sigma_{\rm had} = R\,\sigma_{\mu\mu} = 3.830\times0.09656\ \mathrm{nb} = 0.3698\ \mathrm{nb} $$

This is about $0.37$ nb. Without the QCD correction we would have $3.6667\times0.09656=0.3540$ nb, so the correction amounts to an increase of $4.5\%$. It is precisely because the measurement accuracy of $R$ has reached this level that $\alpha_s$ can be extracted backward from $R$.

(4) The number of events is $N=\sigma\,\mathcal{L}\,T$. We first make the units consistent. $1\ \mathrm{nb}=10^{-9}\ \mathrm{barn}=10^{-9}\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{cm^2}=10^{-33}\ \mathrm{cm^2}$, and one day is $T=24\times3600=8.64\times10^4$ s. Hence

$$ N = 0.3698\times10^{-33}\ \mathrm{cm^2}\times10^{31}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}s^{-1}}\times8.64\times10^4\ \mathrm{s} $$

Multiplying in order, $0.3698\times10^{-33}\times10^{31}=3.698\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, and multiplying this by $8.64\times10^4$ s gives

$$ N = 3.20\times10^{2} \approx 3.2\times10^{2}\ \text{events/day} $$

That is about $320$ events per day. Let us now see whether the presence or absence of color can be distinguished statistically. In what follows we use $N_3=320$ events/day. For $N_c=1$ the cross section is $1/3$ as large, so $N_1=N_3/3=107$ events/day. Over $t$ days of measurement, the difference in the number of events and the statistical fluctuation under the $N_c=3$ hypothesis (the standard deviation is $\sqrt{N_3t}$ because of the Poisson distribution) are

$$ \Delta N = (N_3-N_1)\,t = 213\,t, \qquad \delta N = \sqrt{N_3\,t} = \sqrt{320\,t} $$

The significance is

$$ S(t) = \frac{\Delta N}{\delta N} = \frac{213\,t}{\sqrt{320\,t}} = \frac{213}{\sqrt{320}}\sqrt{t} = 11.9\sqrt{t} $$

so it grows in proportion to $\sqrt{t}$. For $t=1$ day, $S=11.9$, that is, about 12 standard deviations in one day. The time needed to reach $5\sigma$ follows from solving $S(t)=5$:

$$ t = \left(\frac{5}{11.9}\right)^2 = \frac{25\times320}{213^2} = 0.176\ \text{days} = 4.2\ \text{hours} $$

That is, measuring for as little as half a day settles that there are three colors. The fact that the significance grows only as $\sqrt{t}$ is important: going from $5\sigma$ to $10\sigma$ requires four times the measurement time. Conversely, it is because the size of the “discrepancy between the predictions,” the factor of $3$, is so large that even a luminosity of $10^{31}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}s^{-1}}$ (modest by modern standards) settles the question in half a day.

Verification. We check both the dimensions and the normalization. First the dimensions: $[\sigma][\mathcal{L}][T]=\mathrm{cm^2}\cdot\mathrm{cm^{-2}s^{-1}}\cdot\mathrm{s}=$ dimensionless, which is consistent with the number of events (dimensionless). Next the absolute value of $\sigma_{\mu\mu}$: substituting $\alpha=1/137.036$ and $s=1\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ into $\sigma=4\pi\alpha^2/3s$ of Chapter 11 of this book gives $\frac{4\pi}{3}\times5.3251\times10^{-5}=2.2306\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$, and multiplying by $(\hbar c)^2=0.3894\ \mathrm{GeV^2\,mbarn}$ gives $8.686\times10^{-5}$ mbarn $=86.9$ nb. This agrees with the mental-arithmetic formula’s $86.9$ nb. Finally the value of $R$: the QCD-corrected $3.83$ agrees with the $30$ GeV row of Table 11.2 and also agrees with the measured value $\approx3.9$ to within a few percent.

Meaning. The Feynman rules of QCD do not appear anywhere in the discussion of the $R$ ratio. All we used were QED’s $e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-$ and the counting of charges and colors in the final state. Even so, the foundation of QCD, “there are three colors,” emerges as an experimental value. This is the same logic as compositional analysis in materials science. For example, the intensity of incoherent scattering (Compton scattering or incoherent neutron scattering) is proportional to the number of scatterers, so measuring the absolute intensity tells us the number of atoms per unit cell (the intensity of Bragg reflections, by contrast, is proportional to the square of the structure factor, $\abs{F_{hkl}}^2$, so the number and arrangement of the atoms enter in an intertwined way). By measuring the “number of final states” for a single probe, the virtual photon, the $R$ ratio directly reads out the number of an internal degree of freedom, the color multiplicity. Furthermore, the estimate in (4) is exactly the practical business of accelerator-experiment design, which is determined by the product of luminosity, cross section, and measurement time; it is precisely the same accounting as estimating the S/N of a synchrotron-radiation experiment from the flux, the scattering cross section, and the integration time.

Exercise 11.2: Mass-producing color factors with Casimir’s trick

Problem (restated)

Use the formula of Casimir’s trick from Chapter 11 of this book, $\braket{\bm{T}_1\cdot\bm{T}_2}=\frac12\big[C_2(R_{\rm tot})-C_2(R_1)-C_2(R_2)\big]$, together with $C_2(p,q)=\frac13(p^2+q^2+pq+3p+3q)$.

(1) Find the color factor of each channel of quark–gluon scattering ($3\otimes8=3\oplus\bar6\oplus15$). Here $\bar6=(0,2)$ and $15=(2,1)$.

(2) Do the same for gluon–gluon scattering ($8\otimes8=1\oplus8_S\oplus8_A\oplus10\oplus\overline{10}\oplus27$). Here $10=(3,0)$ and $27=(2,2)$. Which channel is the most strongly attractive? What does this predict?

(3) Verify that multiplying the color factors obtained in (1) and (2) by the dimension of each representation and summing gives $0$. Explain why it is $0$.

Solution

Strategy. Casimir’s trick is a tool that says “once the labels of the representations are known, no computation of matrix elements is needed.” The only work required is to substitute into $C_2(p,q)$, and this completely replaces the direct calculation that lays out eight $3\times3$ matrices (Sections 11.4.3 and 11.4.4 of Chapter 11 of this book). The trace identity in (3) provides a powerful check for a table of color factors.

(1) First we compute the necessary Casimir eigenvalues in turn from $C_2(p,q)=\frac13(p^2+q^2+pq+3p+3q)$.

$$ \begin{aligned} C_2(\bm{3})&=C_2(1,0)=\tfrac13(1+0+0+3+0)=\tfrac43\\ C_2(\bm{8})&=C_2(1,1)=\tfrac13(1+1+1+3+3)=\tfrac93=3\\ C_2(\bar{\bm{6}})&=C_2(0,2)=\tfrac13(0+4+0+0+6)=\tfrac{10}{3}\\ C_2(\bm{15})&=C_2(2,1)=\tfrac13(4+1+2+6+3)=\tfrac{16}{3} \end{aligned} $$

The quark is a $\bm{3}$ and the gluon is an $\bm{8}$, so the common part is $C_2(R_1)+C_2(R_2)=\frac43+3=\frac{13}{3}$. Therefore

$$ \braket{\bm{T}_q\cdot\bm{T}_g} = \frac12\left[C_2(R_{\rm tot})-\frac{13}{3}\right] $$

Substituting into each channel,
