$$ \begin{aligned} \bm{3}\ \text{channel}&:\ \tfrac12\left(\tfrac43-\tfrac{13}{3}\right)=\tfrac12\times\left(-\tfrac93\right)=-\tfrac32\\ \bar{\bm{6}}\ \text{channel}&:\ \tfrac12\left(\tfrac{10}{3}-\tfrac{13}{3}\right)=\tfrac12\times\left(-1\right)=-\tfrac12\\ \bm{15}\ \text{channel}&:\ \tfrac12\left(\tfrac{16}{3}-\tfrac{13}{3}\right)=\tfrac12\times1=+\tfrac12 \end{aligned} $$

The attractive (negative) channels are $\bm{3}$ and $\bar{\bm{6}}$, and the repulsive (positive) one is $\bm{15}$. The most attractive is the $\bm{3}$ channel, that is, the channel carrying the same color as a single quark, and its value $-3/2$ is even stronger than the $-4/3$ of the $q\bar q$ singlet. This suggests that a quark and a gluon can bind to form a “composite that behaves like a quark,” and it is the seed of the existence of hybrid mesons ($q\bar qg$). The dimension count $3\times8=24=3+6+15$ checks out.

(2) For two gluons, the common part is $C_2(R_1)+C_2(R_2)=3+3=6$. The remaining Casimir eigenvalues are

$$ C_2(\bm{1})=C_2(0,0)=0,\qquad C_2(\bm{10})=C_2(3,0)=\tfrac13(9+0+0+9+0)=6,\qquad C_2(\bm{27})=C_2(2,2)=\tfrac13(4+4+4+6+6)=8 $$

(and $\overline{\bm{10}}=(0,3)$ has the same $C_2=6$). Substituting into $\braket{\bm{T}_1\cdot\bm{T}_2}=\frac12[C_2(R_{\rm tot})-6]$, we obtain

$$ \begin{aligned} \bm{1}&:\ \tfrac12(0-6)=-3 & \bm{8}_S,\ \bm{8}_A&:\ \tfrac12(3-6)=-\tfrac32\\ \bm{10},\ \overline{\bm{10}}&:\ \tfrac12(6-6)=0 & \bm{27}&:\ \tfrac12(8-6)=+1 \end{aligned} $$

The dimensions check out as $8\times8=64=1+8+8+10+10+27$. The most attractive is the singlet channel, with $-3$, which is $2.25$ times the $-4/3$ of the $q\bar q$ singlet. The decuplet has a color factor of exactly $0$, so no force acts at the level of one-gluon exchange.

What is predicted from this? If two gluons can form a color singlet, a strong attraction acts, so it follows that a bound state made of gluons alone, a glueball, is allowed to exist. Lattice QCD predicts a scalar glueball ($J^{PC}=0^{++}$) at $1.6$–$1.7$ GeV. However, because it mixes quantum-mechanically with ordinary mesons of the same quantum numbers (the $f_0$ family), the experimental identification of “this is the glueball” remains unsettled even now. In the language of condensed matter, this is the same difficulty as the situation in which, when two excitations of the same symmetry lie at nearby energies, the eigenstates hybridize and one can no longer say which is the “original” excitation—for example, hybrid modes of phonons and magnons (such as electromagnons in multiferroics), or the hybridization of $d$ orbitals with ligand orbitals.

(3) We sum with the dimensions as weights. For quark–gluon,

$$ 3\times\left(-\frac32\right) + 6\times\left(-\frac12\right) + 15\times\left(+\frac12\right) = -\frac92 - 3 + \frac{15}{2} = -4.5-3+7.5 = 0 $$

For gluon–gluon, counting $\bm{8}_S$ and $\bm{8}_A$ together as $16$ and $\bm{10}$ and $\overline{\bm{10}}$ together as $20$,

$$ 1\times(-3) + 16\times\left(-\frac32\right) + 20\times0 + 27\times(+1) = -3 - 24 + 0 + 27 = 0 $$

Both are zero. Reason. When $R_1\otimes R_2$ is decomposed into irreducible components, within each irreducible component $R$ the value $\braket{\bm{T}_1\cdot\bm{T}_2}$ is a constant (depending only on $R$). Therefore, when the operator $\bm{T}_1\cdot\bm{T}_2$ is traced over the entire product space, each irreducible component contributes its constant $\times$ its dimension:

$$ \sum_R d_R\braket{\bm{T}_1\cdot\bm{T}_2}_R = \Tr_{R_1\otimes R_2}\big(\bm{T}_1\cdot\bm{T}_2\big) $$

On the other hand, since the right-hand side is a trace over the product space, it factorizes into two factors:

$$ \Tr_{R_1\otimes R_2}\left(\sum_a T_1^aT_2^a\right) = \sum_a \Tr_{R_1}(T^a)\,\Tr_{R_2}(T^a) $$

But the generators of $SU(3)$ are traceless ($\Tr T^a=0$; this is precisely the condition $\det U=1$), so every term on the right-hand side vanishes. Hence the sum is zero.

Verification. We apply the same identity to the color factors already computed directly in Chapter 11 of this book. For $q\bar q$ ($3\otimes\bar3=1\oplus8$),

$$ 1\times\left(-\frac43\right) + 8\times\left(+\frac16\right) = -\frac43+\frac86 = -\frac43+\frac43 = 0 $$

and for $qq$ ($3\otimes3=\bar3\oplus6$),

$$ 3\times\left(-\frac23\right) + 6\times\left(+\frac13\right) = -2+2 = 0 $$

Both vanish, confirming that the direct calculation via the Fierz identity and Casimir’s trick are independently consistent. In addition, the value $-3/2$ of the $\bm{3}$ channel can also be written, using $C_2(\bm{3})=C_F=4/3$ and $C_2(\bm{8})=C_A=3$, as $\frac12(C_F-C_F-C_A)=-\frac{C_A}{2}=-\frac32$, and it is also consistent that the same number $C_A=3$ appearing in the $\beta$ function shows up here.

Meaning. This verification identity states that “the sum over attractive channels always balances the sum over repulsive channels.” Averaged over color, the force is zero; the attraction is simply concentrated in particular channels. In the language of magnetism, this has exactly the same structure as the fact that the weighted average of the eigenvalues of the exchange interaction $-2J\bm{S}_1\cdot\bm{S}_2$ is zero ($1\times(-\frac34)+3\times(+\frac14)=0$). The triplet loses exactly as much as the singlet gains by dropping into the singlet. That “only color singlets appear in nature” in QCD, and that “the ground state becomes a spin singlet” in the Kondo problem, are answers to the same question of how the system exploits this lopsidedness of the allocation. And the glueball of (2) corresponds, for a materials scientist, to a “bound state of excitations made of the lattice alone”—a situation in which mediator particles bind to each other to form a new particle—and shares its idea with the two-phonon bound state discussed when the anharmonic interaction between phonons is strong.

Exercise 11.3: Running $\alpha_s$

Problem (restated)

Start from $\alpha_s(m_Z)=0.118$ and $m_Z=91.188$ GeV.

(1) Keeping $n_f=5$ ($\beta_0=23/3$), find $\alpha_s(10\ \mathrm{GeV})$.

(2) Find $\Lambda^{(5)}$ from $\Lambda=\mu\exp[-2\pi/(\beta_0\alpha_s(\mu^2))]$ of Chapter 11 of this book. Then substitute $Q=10$ GeV into $\alpha_s(Q^2)=4\pi/[\beta_0\ln(Q^2/\Lambda^2)]$ and verify that it agrees with (1).

(3) For $n_f=3$ ($\beta_0=9$) and $\Lambda^{(3)}=143$ MeV, find the $Q$ at which $\alpha_s(Q)=1$. What is this in terms of a length?

(4) Discuss the length obtained in (3) by comparing it with $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^{-1}\approx1$ fm and with the size of a hadron.

Solution

Strategy. We use the integrated form of the one-loop renormalization group equation, that is, the equation of Chapter 11 of this book:

$$ \frac{1}{\alpha_s(Q^2)} = \frac{1}{\alpha_s(\mu^2)} + \frac{\beta_0}{4\pi}\ln\frac{Q^2}{\mu^2} $$

The whole content of the one-loop approximation is that $1/\alpha_s$ is a linear function of $\ln Q^2$, and every calculation reduces to “extrapolating a straight line.”

(1) First we obtain the coefficient. For $n_f=5$, $\beta_0=11-\frac23\times5=11-\frac{10}{3}=\frac{23}{3}=7.6667$, so

$$ \frac{\beta_0}{4\pi} = \frac{7.6667}{12.5664} = 0.61009 $$

For the logarithm, with $Q^2=100\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ and $m_Z^2=91.188^2=8315.25\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$,

$$ \ln\frac{Q^2}{m_Z^2} = \ln\frac{100}{8315.25} = \ln(1.20261\times10^{-2}) = -4.42068 $$

(Computing it as $2\ln(10/91.188)=2\times(-2.21034)=-4.42068$ gives the same result.) Hence

$$ \frac{1}{\alpha_s(10\ \mathrm{GeV})} = \frac{1}{0.118} + 0.61009\times(-4.42068) = 8.47458 - 2.69703 = 5.77755 $$ $$ \alpha_s(10\ \mathrm{GeV}) = \frac{1}{5.77755} = 0.17308 $$

The value $0.118$ at $m_Z$ has grown to $0.173$ merely by lowering the energy by one order of magnitude. We have $(0.17308-0.118)/0.118=0.467$, that is, an increase of $47\%$.

(2) We put $\mu=m_Z$ into the definition of $\Lambda$. The exponent is

$$ \frac{2\pi}{\beta_0\alpha_s(m_Z^2)} = \frac{6.28319}{7.66667\times0.118} = \frac{6.28319}{0.904667} = 6.94530 $$ $$ \Lambda^{(5)} = 91.188\ \mathrm{GeV}\times\ee^{-6.94530} = 91.188\times9.6315\times10^{-4} = 0.08783\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

That is, $\Lambda^{(5)}=87.8$ MeV. Next we use this to recompute $\alpha_s(10\ \mathrm{GeV})$. Since $\Lambda^2=(0.087827)^2=7.7137\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$,

$$ \ln\frac{Q^2}{\Lambda^2} = \ln\frac{100}{7.7137\times10^{-3}} = \ln(1.29639\times10^{4}) = 9.46993 $$ $$ \alpha_s(10\ \mathrm{GeV}) = \frac{4\pi}{\beta_0\ln(Q^2/\Lambda^2)} = \frac{12.5664}{7.66667\times9.46993} = \frac{12.5664}{72.6028} = 0.17308 $$

This agrees with the $0.17308$ of (1) to the fifth decimal place. Of course it must: the definition of $\Lambda$ is “the point where the straight line of $1/\alpha_s$ crosses $0$,” and the line is the same whether it is drawn from the reference point $m_Z$ or from the intercept $\Lambda$. Concretely,

$$ \frac{1}{\alpha_s(Q^2)} = \frac{\beta_0}{4\pi}\ln\frac{Q^2}{\Lambda^2} $$

is the relation connecting the two, and indeed $0.61009\times9.46993=5.7775$ agrees with the $1/\alpha_s=5.77755$ of (1) (within the accuracy of a calculation with the coefficient rounded to five digits).

(3) For $n_f=3$, $\beta_0=11-\frac23\times3=11-2=9$. Requiring $\alpha_s(Q)=1$ gives

$$ 1 = \frac{4\pi}{9\ln(Q^2/\Lambda^2)} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \ln\frac{Q^2}{\Lambda^2} = \frac{4\pi}{9} = \frac{12.5664}{9} = 1.39626 $$

Since $\ln(Q^2/\Lambda^2)=2\ln(Q/\Lambda)$, we have $\ln(Q/\Lambda)=0.69813$, that is,

$$ \frac{Q}{\Lambda} = \ee^{0.69813} = 2.0100 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad Q = 0.143\ \mathrm{GeV}\times2.0100 = 0.2874\ \mathrm{GeV} = 287\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

We now convert this into a length. Since $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$,

$$ r = \frac{\hbar c}{Q} = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{287.4\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 0.687\ \mathrm{fm} $$

This is about $0.69$ fm.

(4) We line up three lengths to compare.

  • Distance at which $\alpha_s=1$: $0.69$ fm (part (3) of this exercise)
  • Inverse of $\Lambda^{(3)}$: $\hbar c/\Lambda^{(3)}=197.327/143=1.38$ fm (using the one-loop value $\Lambda^{(3)}=143$ MeV; for the often-quoted $\Lambda\approx200$ MeV it is $0.99$ fm)
  • Charge radius of the proton: $0.8409$ fm (this book, Chapter 11, Section 11.2.3). The typical size of a meson is also $0.6$–$0.8$ fm.

All three fall within the range $0.7$–$1.4$ fm, so they agree completely as orders of magnitude. It is clear from the formula that the distance at which $\alpha_s=1$ and $\Lambda^{-1}$ differ only by a constant factor (a factor of $\ee^{-2\pi/\beta_0}$, that is, $1/2.01$ for $\beta_0=9$), but it is not obvious that both of them agree with the measured sizes of hadrons. This amounts to the statement that it is $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}$ itself that determines the size of a hadron. The quark masses ($m_u\sim2$ MeV, $m_d\sim5$ MeV) play no role at all in setting this scale, and both the size and the mass of the proton arise solely from the running of the dimensionless parameter $\alpha_s$.

Verification. We check in three ways. (i) Dimensions: since $\Lambda=\mu\,\ee^{-\text{dimensionless}}$, $\Lambda$ has the dimension of energy and $\hbar c/Q$ has the dimension of length. These are consistent. (ii) Limits: for $Q\to\infty$, $\ln(Q^2/\Lambda^2)\to\infty$, so $\alpha_s\to0$ (asymptotic freedom), and for $Q\to\Lambda^+$, $\alpha_s\to+\infty$ (breakdown of perturbation theory). Both agree with the description in Chapter 11 of this book. (iii) Comparison with a known value: if we compute $\alpha_s(m_c=1.27\ \mathrm{GeV})$ with the same one-loop formula for $n_f=3$ and $\Lambda^{(3)}=0.143$ GeV, then $\ln(1.27^2/0.143^2)=2\ln(8.881)=4.3679$ and $\alpha_s=12.5664/(9\times4.3679)=0.3197$, which agrees with the value $\alpha_s(m_c)=0.319$ obtained in the threshold-matching calculation of Chapter 11, Section 11.6.4 of this book. Since $\Lambda^{(3)}=143$ MeV is precisely the value back-calculated from that $\alpha_s(m_c)$, this is a check that the circle closes.

Meaning. The running of $\alpha_s$ boils down, in essence, to the single statement that “$1/\alpha_s$ is a straight line in $\ln Q^2$.” We have merely named $\Lambda$ the point where this line crosses $0$, and the single measured value $\alpha_s(m_Z)$ and the single scale $\Lambda$ carry the same information. A dimensionless coupling constant has been translated into a scale with dimensions—this is dimensional transmutation. The closest analogues for a materials scientist are the relation between $N(0)V$ and the gap $\Delta$ in BCS theory, or between $\rho J$ and $T_K$ in the Kondo problem (Exercise 11.7). In both, a “dimensionless coupling” and a “dynamically generated energy scale” are connected by an exponential function, so measuring one fixes the other. As a further practical lesson, what (2) shows is the renormalization-group invariance that “the result is the same wherever the reference point is taken,” which is exactly the same property as the check, in first-principles calculations, that physical quantities do not change when the cutoff or the energy reference is changed.

Exercise 11.4: The Callan–Gross relation and the parton spin

Problem (restated)

(1) Suppose the partons were scalar particles of spin $0$. Since there is no magnetic scattering, $W_1=0$. What then becomes of $F_2/(2xF_1)$? What becomes of the longitudinal-to-transverse ratio $R_L=\sigma_L/\sigma_T$?

(2) Show that $R_L=(F_2-2xF_1)/(2xF_1)$ (you may neglect corrections of order $M^2/Q^2$).

(3) For the experimental value $R_L=0.15$, what is $F_2/(2xF_1)$? By what percentage does it deviate from the Callan–Gross relation?

(4) Using the parton-model expression $F_2(x)=\sum_i e_i^2\,x f_i(x)$, predict the value of $F_2^{ep}(x)/F_2^{en}(x)$ at $x\to1$. Assume that at $x\to1$ the $u$ quark dominates among the valence quarks ($d/u\to0$).

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1), (3), and (4) need only the parton-model expressions $F_2=\sum_i e_i^2xf_i$, $F_1=\frac12\sum_ie_i^2f_i$ of Chapter 11 of this book and their ratio. Only (2) requires carrying out a calculation whose result alone was stated in the main text: sandwiching the hadronic tensor $W^{\mu\nu}$ between virtual-photon polarization vectors.

(1) If $W_1=0$, then $F_1=MW_1=0$. Therefore

$$ \frac{F_2}{2xF_1} \longrightarrow \infty \qquad(\text{denominator vanishes}) $$

The ratio diverges. For $R_L$, using $R_L=F_2/(2xF_1)-1$, which we show in (2), we get $R_L\to\infty$. Physically, since $\sigma_T\propto W_1=0$, the situation is that transversely polarized photons are not absorbed at all, and only longitudinally polarized photons are absorbed. The reason is simple: a spin-$0$ particle has no magnetic moment, so it cannot couple to the magnetic component of the virtual photon (the transverse component, which carries helicity $\pm1$).

Let us contrast this with the spin-$1/2$ case. There the Callan–Gross relation $F_2=2xF_1$ holds, so

$$ \frac{F_2}{2xF_1}=1,\qquad R_L=0 $$

That is, $1$ versus $\infty$, and $0$ versus $\infty$—the predictions for spin $0$ and spin $1/2$ could hardly be farther apart. The measured value is $F_2/(2xF_1)\approx1.1$–$1.2$, so the verdict is immediate: the charged constituents inside the proton have spin $1/2$.

(2) As stated in Chapter 11 of this book, Lorentz invariance and current conservation $q_\mu W^{\mu\nu}=0$ alone allow the hadronic tensor to be expanded in only two structures:

$$ W^{\mu\nu} = W_1\left(-g^{\mu\nu}+\frac{q^\mu q^\nu}{q^2}\right) + \frac{W_2}{M^2}\,\tilde P^\mu\tilde P^\nu, \qquad \tilde P^\mu \equiv P^\mu - \frac{P\cdot q}{q^2}q^\mu $$

The photon absorption cross section is proportional to this $W^{\mu\nu}$ sandwiched between polarization vectors, $\sigma_i\propto \varepsilon^{(i)*}_\mu\varepsilon^{(i)}_\nu W^{\mu\nu}$ (the proportionality factor is the flux factor of the virtual photon, which is common to the longitudinal and transverse polarizations and therefore cancels in the ratio). In the laboratory frame, take $P^\mu=(M,\bm{0})$, $q^\mu=(\nu,0,0,q_z)$, $q_z=\sqrt{\nu^2+Q^2}$, and $q^2=-Q^2$.

Transverse component. For $\varepsilon^\mu=(0,1,0,0)$, the sandwiched quantity is $W^{11}$. Since $-g^{11}=+1$, $q^1=0$, and $\tilde P^1=0$,

$$ \varepsilon_\mu\varepsilon_\nu W^{\mu\nu} = W^{11} = W_1 $$

Longitudinal component. For $\varepsilon_L^\mu=\frac{1}{\sqrt{Q^2}}(q_z,0,0,\nu)$, we have $\varepsilon_L\cdot q=\frac{1}{\sqrt{Q^2}}(q_z\nu-\nu q_z)=0$, so the transversality condition is satisfied. (A note on normalization: the transverse polarization has $\varepsilon_T\cdot\varepsilon_T=-1$, whereas the longitudinal polarization has $\varepsilon_L\cdot\varepsilon_L=(q_z^2-\nu^2)/Q^2=+1$. Since the virtual-photon momentum is spacelike ($q^2=-Q^2<0$), the three-dimensional subspace orthogonal to it contains one timelike direction, and that corresponds to the longitudinal polarization. For a real photon, $q^2\to0$, this degree of freedom disappears and $\sigma_L\to0$, so $R_L\to0$ holds automatically.) We prepare the necessary components. From $P\cdot q=M\nu$ and $q^2=-Q^2$,

$$ \tilde P^0 = M+\frac{M\nu^2}{Q^2}=M\left(1+\frac{\nu^2}{Q^2}\right), \qquad \tilde P^3 = \frac{M\nu q_z}{Q^2} $$

Abbreviating $A\equiv1+\nu^2/Q^2$ and $B\equiv\nu^2/Q^2$ (so $A=1+B$), we obtain

$$ \begin{aligned} W^{00}&=-W_1A + W_2A^2,\\ W^{33}&=-W_1B + W_2\frac{\nu^2q_z^2}{Q^4},\\ W^{03}&=-W_1\frac{\nu q_z}{Q^2} + W_2A\frac{\nu q_z}{Q^2} \end{aligned} $$

Here the coefficients of the first structure were evaluated, noting that $q^2=-Q^2$, as

$$ -g^{00}+\frac{(q^0)^2}{q^2} = -1+\frac{\nu^2}{-Q^2} = -\left(1+\frac{\nu^2}{Q^2}\right) = -A, \qquad -g^{33}+\frac{(q^3)^2}{q^2} = +1+\frac{\nu^2+Q^2}{-Q^2} = -\frac{\nu^2}{Q^2} = -B, $$ $$ -g^{03}+\frac{q^0q^3}{q^2} = 0-\frac{\nu q_z}{Q^2} $$

Noting that $\varepsilon_{L\mu}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{Q^2}}(q_z,0,0,-\nu)$, we compute

$$ \varepsilon_{L\mu}\varepsilon_{L\nu}W^{\mu\nu} = \frac{1}{Q^2}\left[q_z^2W^{00} - 2q_z\nu\,W^{03} + \nu^2W^{33}\right] $$

Collecting the $W_1$ terms and using $q_z^2=\nu^2+Q^2$,

$$ -\frac{W_1}{Q^2}\left[q_z^2A - 2\frac{q_z^2\nu^2}{Q^2} + \frac{\nu^4}{Q^2}\right] = -\frac{W_1}{Q^2}\left[q_z^2 - \frac{q_z^2\nu^2}{Q^2} + \frac{\nu^4}{Q^2}\right] = -\frac{W_1}{Q^2}\left[\nu^2+Q^2 - \frac{\nu^4}{Q^2}-\nu^2 + \frac{\nu^4}{Q^2}\right] = -W_1 $$

For the $W_2$ terms, the bracket is the perfect square $A^2-2BA+B^2=(A-B)^2=1$, so

$$ \frac{W_2}{Q^2}\,q_z^2\left(A-B\right)^2 = \frac{W_2q_z^2}{Q^2} = W_2\frac{\nu^2+Q^2}{Q^2} = W_2A $$

Therefore

$$ \varepsilon_{L\mu}\varepsilon_{L\nu}W^{\mu\nu} = \left(1+\frac{\nu^2}{Q^2}\right)W_2 - W_1, \qquad\text{that is}\qquad R_L = \frac{\sigma_L}{\sigma_T} = \frac{(1+\nu^2/Q^2)W_2 - W_1}{W_1} $$

Finally, we translate into the language of structure functions. Neglecting corrections of order $M^2/Q^2$ means that, at fixed $x$, $\nu^2/Q^2=Q^2/(4M^2x^2)\gg1$, so we may set $1+\nu^2/Q^2\simeq\nu^2/Q^2$. Substituting $F_1=MW_1$ and $F_2=\nu W_2$,

$$ R_L = \frac{\nu^2}{Q^2}\cdot\frac{W_2}{W_1} - 1 = \frac{\nu^2}{Q^2}\cdot\frac{F_2/\nu}{F_1/M} - 1 = \frac{M\nu}{Q^2}\cdot\frac{F_2}{F_1} - 1 $$

Here, from the definition of the Bjorken variable $x=Q^2/(2M\nu)$, we have $M\nu/Q^2=1/(2x)$, so

$$ R_L = \frac{F_2}{2xF_1} - 1 = \frac{F_2-2xF_1}{2xF_1} $$

which is what was to be shown.

(3) We simply solve the above relation in reverse.

$$ \frac{F_2}{2xF_1} = 1 + R_L = 1+0.15 = 1.15 $$

Since the Callan–Gross relation predicts $F_2/(2xF_1)=1$, the deviation is

$$ \frac{1.15-1}{1}\times100 = 15\ \% $$

In the opposite direction, we can also write $2xF_1/F_2=1/1.15=0.870$.

We can also read this number as a breakdown of the absorbed virtual photons. The fraction of longitudinal polarization in the total absorption is

$$ \frac{\sigma_L}{\sigma_L+\sigma_T} = \frac{R_L}{1+R_L} = \frac{0.15}{1.15} = 0.130 $$

so $13\%$ of the absorbed virtual photons are longitudinally polarized and $87\%$ are transversely polarized. For spin-$1/2$ partons, longitudinal polarization should not be absorbed at all ($0\%$), so this $13\%$ is the true nature of the “violation of the Callan–Gross relation.”

This $15\%$ is not an error: it is a QCD effect arising from the quark mass, the transverse momentum $k_T$, and gluon emission ($\gamma^*g\to q\bar q$), and it is a calculable quantity. All of these are processes that do not conserve the parton helicity, and they open a path that couples to the longitudinal component of the virtual photon. In fact, $R_L$ decreases with $Q^2$ in proportion to $\alpha_s(Q^2)$ (a consequence of asymptotic freedom) and returns to $R_L\to0$ as $Q^2\to\infty$. As a matter of measurement practice as well, the value of $R_L$ is indispensable for separating $F_2$ and $F_1$ experimentally: one must measure at the same $x$ and $Q^2$ with different beam energies, changing the degree of polarization of the virtual photon to separate the longitudinal and transverse components. This is exactly the same logic as the Rosenbluth separation of Chapter 11 of this book (separating $G_E$ and $G_M$ by linearizing in $\tan^2(\theta/2)$).

We also check the sensitivity. If $R_L=0.5$ had been measured, we would have $F_2/(2xF_1)=1.5$, a deviation of $50\%$, and for $R_L=1$ it would be $100\%$. We see that the very fact that the measured value falls at $0.15$ is itself a strong constraint. Considering that the difference from the spin-$0$ prediction ($R_L=\infty$) is infinite, a deviation of $15\%$ is small enough that we may say “the relation holds.”

(4) We write down the parton-model expressions for the proton and the neutron. Using isospin symmetry (the $u$ distribution of the proton equals the $d$ distribution of the neutron, and so on), and keeping only the valence quarks on the assumption that the sea quarks and the $s$ quark are negligible at $x\to1$, we have

$$ F_2^{ep}(x) = x\left[\frac49u(x)+\frac19d(x)\right], \qquad F_2^{en}(x) = x\left[\frac49d(x)+\frac19u(x)\right] $$

Taking the ratio, $x$ and $\frac19$ cancel:

$$ \frac{F_2^{ep}}{F_2^{en}} = \frac{4u+d}{4d+u} = \frac{4+d/u}{4(d/u)+1} $$

If $d/u\to0$ at $x\to1$, then

$$ \frac{F_2^{ep}}{F_2^{en}} \longrightarrow \frac{4+0}{0+1} = 4 $$

that is, $(4/9)/(1/9)=4$. The measured value in this limit stays at only $\approx2.5$. Solving the above expression for $2.5$,

$$ \frac{4+r}{4r+1}=2.5 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad 4+r = 10r+2.5 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = \frac{d}{u} = \frac{1.5}{9} = 0.167 = \frac16 $$

so even at $x\to1$ the $d$ quark remains at about $1/6$ of the $u$ quark. For reference, several competing theoretical predictions exist for the value of $d/u$: $SU(6)$ spin-flavor symmetry gives $d/u=1/2$ (ratio $1.5$), scalar-diquark dominance gives $d/u\to0$ (ratio $4$), and the helicity-conservation rule of perturbative QCD gives $d/u\to1/5$ (ratio $2.33$). The measured $2.5$ is close to the last picture.

Verification. We check at three points. (i) Upper and lower bounds on the ratio: $\frac{4+r}{4r+1}$ is a monotonically decreasing function of $r$, taking the value $4$ at $r=0$, $1$ at $r=1$ ($u=d$), and $1/4$ as $r\to\infty$. Therefore $F_2^{ep}/F_2^{en}$ must always lie within $[1/4,\,4]$, and both the measured $2.5$ and the value $\approx1$ in the sea-quark-dominated region $x\to0$ fall within this range. If the parton model broke down, the ratio would leave this band, so this is a test of the model itself. (ii) Consistency of the limits: in the limit $R_L\to0$, the expression in (2) reduces to $F_2=2xF_1$, reproducing the Callan–Gross relation. Also, in the limit $F_1\to0$, $R_L\to\infty$, which is consistent with (1). (iii) Consistency with the momentum sum rule: from $U+D=0.54$ and $U-D=0.18$ obtained in Chapter 11 of this book, $U/D=0.36/0.18=2$, so averaged over all $x$, $d/u\approx1/2$. The conclusion of (4) that $d/u$ falls to $1/6$ at $x\to1$ is not inconsistent with the picture that $u$ becomes more dominant at large $x$.

Meaning. The value of the Callan–Gross relation is that the unknown functions (the parton distributions $f_i$) and the unknown constants (the charges $e_i$) all cancel, so that only a single discrete property, the spin, remains. Taking a ratio of measured quantities erases the details of the system and extracts a quantity that depends only on symmetry or spin—this method is central in materials science as well. For example, when we separate magnetic scattering from nuclear scattering by polarization analysis in inelastic neutron scattering, or separate the spin angular momentum from the orbital angular momentum with the sum rules of X-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD), we are doing the same thing. In both cases the strategy is to “eliminate the unknown normalization factor by measuring a ratio rather than an absolute value.” Moreover, the longitudinal–transverse separation in (2) is a matter of selection rules based on the polarization of light, and its logic is the same as determining the symmetry of a mode from polarization measurements in infrared and Raman spectroscopy. The fact that longitudinally polarized photons are not absorbed is nothing other than a selection rule for massless chiral fermions.

Exercise 11.5: The form factor of a Gaussian charge distribution

Problem (restated)

Consider the normalized Gaussian charge distribution

$$ \rho(r) = \frac{1}{(2\pi b^2)^{3/2}}\,\ee^{-r^2/2b^2} $$

.

(1) Show that the form factor is $F(q)=\ee^{-q^2b^2/2}$.

(2) Show that $\braket{r^2}=3b^2$, and find the $b$ for which $\sqrt{\braket{r^2}}=0.84$ fm.

(3) Compute $F$ at $Q^2=1\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ (that is, $q=1\ \mathrm{GeV}/c$) and compare it with the value of the dipole form $G_E=(1+Q^2/0.71\,\mathrm{GeV^2})^{-2}$. Which falls faster?

(4) From this result, is the proton’s charge distribution closer to Gaussian or exponential? What does this imply about the “tail” of the charge distribution?

Solution

Strategy. We carry out the definition of the form factor in Chapter 11 of this book, $F(\qq)=\int\rho(\bm{r})\ee^{\ii\qq\cdot\bm{r}}\dd^3r$, directly for the Gaussian distribution. The Gaussian function separates completely in Cartesian coordinates, so the key point is that the three-dimensional integral becomes the cube of a one-dimensional integral. At the end we compare numerically with the dipole form of Chapter 11, Section 11.2.3 of this book.

(1) Since $r^2=x^2+y^2+z^2$, the integrand factorizes completely in Cartesian coordinates:

$$ F(\qq) = \int \frac{\ee^{-(x^2+y^2+z^2)/2b^2}}{(2\pi b^2)^{3/2}}\,\ee^{\ii(q_xx+q_yy+q_zz)}\,\dd x\,\dd y\,\dd z = \prod_{j=x,y,z} \left[\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi b^2}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\ee^{-u^2/2b^2}\ee^{\ii q_ju}\,\dd u\right] $$

We handle the one-dimensional integral by completing the square. Combining the exponents,

$$ -\frac{u^2}{2b^2}+\ii q_ju = -\frac{1}{2b^2}\left(u^2 - 2\ii b^2q_ju\right) = -\frac{1}{2b^2}\left[(u-\ii b^2q_j)^2 + b^4q_j^2\right] = -\frac{(u-\ii b^2q_j)^2}{2b^2} - \frac{b^2q_j^2}{2} $$

(the second term comes out as a real constant). Therefore

$$ \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi b^2}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\ee^{-u^2/2b^2}\ee^{\ii q_ju}\,\dd u = \ee^{-b^2q_j^2/2}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi b^2}}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\ee^{-(u-\ii b^2q_j)^2/2b^2}\,\dd u = \ee^{-b^2q_j^2/2} $$

(shifting the contour in the complex plane parallel to the real axis by $\ii b^2q_j$ does not change the value by Cauchy’s theorem, because the Gaussian function decays rapidly at infinity, and the remaining integral equals $\sqrt{2\pi b^2}$). Taking the product of the three components,

$$ F(\qq) = \ee^{-b^2(q_x^2+q_y^2+q_z^2)/2} = \ee^{-q^2b^2/2} $$

which is what was to be shown. As a check of the normalization, $F(0)=1$, that is, $\int\rho\,\dd^3r=1$, is satisfied.

(2) We compute the mean-square radius by its definition. Since the distribution is spherically symmetric, the angular integration gives $4\pi$:

$$ \braket{r^2} = \int r^2\rho(r)\,\dd^3r = \frac{4\pi}{(2\pi b^2)^{3/2}}\int_0^\infty r^4\,\ee^{-r^2/2b^2}\,\dd r $$

We use the formula $\int_0^\infty u^4\ee^{-u^2/2b^2}\dd u = 3b^5\sqrt{\pi/2}$. This is obtained by putting $n=2$ and $a=1/2b^2$ into $\int_0^\infty u^{2n}\ee^{-au^2}\dd u=\frac{(2n-1)!!}{2(2a)^n}\sqrt{\pi/a}$. Substituting,

$$ \braket{r^2} = \frac{4\pi\cdot3b^5\sqrt{\pi/2}}{2^{3/2}\pi^{3/2}b^3} = \frac{12\pi\, b^2\,\pi^{1/2}2^{-1/2}}{2^{3/2}\pi^{3/2}} = \frac{12b^2}{2^{2}} = 3b^2 $$

As a simpler alternative solution, one may expand the result of (1) for small $q$. Putting $F=\ee^{-q^2b^2/2}=1-\frac{q^2b^2}{2}+\cdots$ into $\braket{r^2}=-6\,\dd F/\dd q^2|_{q^2=0}$ of Chapter 11 of this book gives

$$ \braket{r^2} = -6\times\left(-\frac{b^2}{2}\right) = 3b^2 $$

the same answer. Requiring $\sqrt{\braket{r^2}}=\sqrt3\,b=0.84$ fm gives

$$ b = \frac{0.84\ \mathrm{fm}}{\sqrt3} = \frac{0.84}{1.73205} = 0.4850\ \mathrm{fm} $$

(3) First we convert $q$ to fm$^{-1}$. Since $\hbar c=0.197327\ \mathrm{GeV\,fm}$,

$$ q = 1\ \mathrm{GeV}/c = \frac{1}{0.197327\ \mathrm{fm}} = 5.0677\ \mathrm{fm^{-1}} $$

Therefore

$$ qb = 5.0677\times0.4850 = 2.4577, \qquad \frac{q^2b^2}{2} = \frac{(2.4577)^2}{2} = \frac{6.0404}{2} = 3.0202 $$ $$ F_{\rm Gauss}(1\ \mathrm{GeV}) = \ee^{-3.0202} = 0.0488 $$

On the other hand, the dipole form at $Q^2=1\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ gives

$$ G_E = \frac{1}{(1+1/0.71)^2} = \frac{1}{(1+1.40845)^2} = \frac{1}{(2.40845)^2} = \frac{1}{5.8006} = 0.1724 $$

The ratio is $0.1724/0.0488=3.53$. That is, the Gaussian falls $3.5$ times faster.

This comparison depends hardly at all on the choice of $b$. For example, if we give the Gaussian the same root-mean-square radius as the dipole form, $0.811$ fm, then $b=0.811/\sqrt3=0.4682$ fm, $qb=2.3728$, and $F=\ee^{-2.8152}=0.0599$, which is still only $1/2.9$ of the dipole-form value $0.172$. The conclusion is robust.

(4) Since the measured $G_E$ follows the dipole form well for $Q^2\lesssim1\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$, the charge distribution of the proton is close to the exponential form $\rho\propto\ee^{-r/a}$. This is because, as we saw in Chapter 11, Section 11.2.3 of this book, the Fourier transform of an exponential form is exactly the dipole form $1/(1+q^2a^2)^2$.

What can be said about the “tail”? The way the form factor falls at large $q$ reflects what the density looks like far from the origin in position space.

  • Gaussian form: $F\sim\ee^{-q^2b^2/2}$—it falls off exponentially in the square of $q$. In position space it is $\ee^{-r^2/2b^2}$, and beyond a certain radius the density is effectively zero. This is a distribution with a sharp edge.
  • Exponential form: $F\sim1/(q^2a^2)^2\propto q^{-4}$—it falls off only as a power law. In position space it is $\ee^{-r/a}$, which has a far longer tail than the Gaussian form. This is a distribution with a fuzzy edge.

That the form factor falls off only as a power law in momentum space and that the density has a long tail in position space are two sides of the same fact (the cusped, non-analytic shape of $\rho$ at $r=0$ produces the power-law tail of $F$). The proton is not a “sphere of radius $0.84$ fm” but a cloud with no edge, dense at the center and fading smoothly outward.

Verification. We perform three independent checks. (i) Limit: as $q\to0$, $F\to1$ (total charge $1$), which both form factors satisfy. (ii) Dimensions: $qb$ is (momentum) $\times$ (length) $=$ dimensionless, so it can appear in an exponent. The conversion of $q=1\ \mathrm{GeV}/c$ to $5.07\ \mathrm{fm^{-1}}$ is also the standard one, using $\hbar c=197\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$. (iii) Comparison with known values: using $b=0.485$ fm obtained in (2) and comparing the slopes at small $Q^2$, the Gaussian form gives $\dd F/\dd Q^2|_0=-b^2/2=-0.1176\ \mathrm{fm^2}$, while the dipole form gives $-2/\Lambda_D^2=-2/0.71\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}=-2.817\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}=-2.817\times0.03894\ \mathrm{fm^2}=-0.1097\ \mathrm{fm^2}$, which differ by only $7\%$ (this $7\%$ is not due to the difference in the shape of the distribution but to having given the Gaussian form a radius of $0.84$ fm and the dipole form a different radius of $0.811$ fm. The slope at $Q^2\to0$ is $-\braket{r^2}/6$, determined by the radius alone regardless of shape, and indeed $(0.84/0.811)^2=1.07$). That is, the two are almost indistinguishable at $Q^2\to0$, yet differ by a factor of $3.5$ at $Q^2\sim1\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$. Measuring the radius alone does not determine the shape of the distribution; the shape is fixed only by measuring out to high $Q^2$—this is the very essence of form-factor measurements.

Meaning. This problem may be the particle-physics problem closest to home for a materials scientist. In quantum chemistry, the correct asymptotic form of an atomic orbital is known to be the Slater form $\ee^{-\zeta r}$ (the solution for a bound state in a Coulomb potential has this form). However, because two-electron integrals are easy to compute, Gaussian basis functions $\ee^{-\alpha r^2}$ are used in actual calculations. Hence a device is needed, as in STO-3G, of contracting several Gaussian functions to reproduce the long tail of the Slater form. What we saw in (3) is precisely this fact, “the Gaussian form has too little tail,” quantified in a different system, the proton. The same thing happens with the atomic form factor in X-ray diffraction: the intensities of high-angle (large $q$) reflections fall off more slowly than expected, reflecting the sharp distribution of the inner-shell electrons—a cusp in position space. The correspondence between “a cusp in position space” and “a long tail in reciprocal space” is a universal fact common to all fields that use the Fourier transform.

Exercise 11.6: The Cornell potential and string breaking

Problem (restated)

Let $V(r)=-\dfrac{4\alpha_s}{3r}+\sigma r$, with $\sigma=0.18\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ and $\alpha_s=0.3$.

(1) Convert $\sigma$ to GeV/fm and to N (newtons). Also, to the weight of an object of how many kilograms does it correspond?

(2) Find the distance $r_0$ at which the Coulomb term and the confining term are equal in magnitude.

(3) Let the constituent quark mass be $m_q\approx330$ MeV. If the string breaks when the energy $\sigma r$ stored in it reaches $2m_q$, what is the breaking distance?

(4) From the results of (2) and (3), discuss which term dominates the physics inside the hadron ($r\lesssim0.3$ fm) and outside it ($r\gtrsim0.7$ fm).

Solution

Strategy. Everything reduces to converting between natural units and SI. We use only two facts: $\hbar c=0.197327\ \mathrm{GeV\,fm}$ and $1\ \mathrm{GeV}=1.602\times10^{-10}$ J. The quantity $\sigma$ has the dimension $[\mathrm{GeV^2}]$, that is, (energy)$^2$; in natural units (energy)$/$(length)$=$(energy)$^2$, so this is the dimension of a force.

(1) First we convert to GeV/fm. Since $1\ \mathrm{GeV}=1/(0.197327\ \mathrm{fm})=5.0677\ \mathrm{fm^{-1}}$,

$$ \sigma = 0.18\ \mathrm{GeV^2} = 0.18\ \mathrm{GeV}\times5.0677\ \mathrm{fm^{-1}} = 0.9122\ \mathrm{GeV/fm} $$

(Equivalently, one may write it as the division $\sigma=0.18/0.197327=0.912$ GeV/fm.) Next we convert to SI. Since $1\ \mathrm{GeV}=1.602177\times10^{-10}$ J and $1\ \mathrm{fm}=10^{-15}$ m,

$$ \sigma = 0.9122\times\frac{1.602177\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J}}{10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}} = 0.9122\times1.602177\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N} = 1.461\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N} $$

Dividing this by the gravitational acceleration $g=9.807\ \mathrm{m/s^2}$ gives the mass of an object that exerts the same force:

$$ m = \frac{1.461\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{N}}{9.807\ \mathrm{m/s^2}} = 1.490\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{kg} \approx 15\ \text{tonnes} $$

This is about $1.5\times10^4$ kg, that is, the force needed to hold up a 15-tonne object. Moreover, it is a constant force independent of distance (the confining part of $F=-\dd V/\dd r$ is $-\sigma$, which does not depend on $r$). Two particles in a world of size $10^{-15}$ m are, in effect, constantly lifting one large truck.

(2) The condition for the two terms to have equal magnitude is

$$ \frac{4\alpha_s}{3r_0} = \sigma r_0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r_0^2 = \frac{4\alpha_s}{3\sigma} $$

Substituting numbers: in natural units, with $\alpha_s=0.3$ and $\sigma=0.18\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$,

$$ r_0^2 = \frac{4\times0.3}{3\times0.18} = \frac{1.2}{0.54} = 2.2222\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r_0 = 1.4907\ \mathrm{GeV^{-1}} $$

Converting this to fm:

$$ r_0 = 1.4907\ \mathrm{GeV^{-1}}\times0.197327\ \mathrm{GeV\,fm} = 0.2942\ \mathrm{fm} $$

This is about $0.29$ fm. At this point the value of the potential itself is

$$ V(r_0) = -\frac{4\alpha_s}{3r_0}+\sigma r_0 = -\sigma r_0 + \sigma r_0 = 0 $$

so this is also the point where $V$ changes sign ($V<0$ for $r<r_0$, $V>0$ for $r>r_0$). Note that the same $r_0$ marks the boundary for the forces as well: the magnitude of the Coulomb force, $4\alpha_s/(3r^2)$, equals the confining force $\sigma$ when $r^2=4\alpha_s/(3\sigma)=r_0^2$. That the balance point of the potentials and the balance point of the forces coincide is a coincidence peculiar to the combination of $1/r$ and $r$.

(3) The condition is $\sigma r = 2m_q = 2\times0.330\ \mathrm{GeV} = 0.66$ GeV. Using $\sigma$ converted to GeV/fm,

$$ r = \frac{0.66\ \mathrm{GeV}}{0.9122\ \mathrm{GeV/fm}} = 0.7235\ \mathrm{fm} $$

Calculating in natural units gives the same result: $r=0.66/0.18=3.6667\ \mathrm{GeV^{-1}}=3.6667\times0.197327=0.7235$ fm. The string breaks at about $0.72$ fm.

The string-breaking distance from lattice QCD is somewhat larger, $1.2$–$1.3$ fm. The reason for the difference is that the energy required for breaking is not “the constituent quark mass $2\times330$ MeV” but in fact the energy required to create two heavy–light mesons. The energy corresponding to $r=1.25$ fm is $\sigma r=0.912\times1.25=1.14$ GeV, that is, $570$ MeV per side, which is a reasonable size for the contribution of one light quark to the mass of a heavy–light meson (the constituent mass plus the binding energy and kinetic energy). In short, the $330$ MeV of the constituent quark model underestimates the threshold for breaking.

(4) We line up the two distances obtained: $r_0=0.29$ fm and the breaking distance $0.72$ fm ($1.2$ fm on the lattice).

  • Inside ($r\lesssim0.3$ fm): since $r<r_0$, the Coulomb term $-4\alpha_s/3r$ dominates. The physics in this region can be described by one-gluon exchange, that is, perturbative QCD. The Bohr radii of heavy quarkonia ($J/\psi$, $\Upsilon$) lie in this region, so their spectra can be computed in the same way as for the hydrogen atom, and indeed charmonium spectroscopy is an important source of information for determining $\alpha_s$ and $\sigma$.
  • Outside ($r\gtrsim0.7$ fm): the confining term $\sigma r$ dominates, and at this distance the string breaks. This is the nonperturbative region, and nonperturbative methods such as lattice QCD and string models are required. As we saw in Exercise 11.3, it is also from around this $0.69$ fm that $\alpha_s$ exceeds $1$.

What is important is that the boundary between these two regions ($0.3$–$0.7$ fm) is exactly the size of a hadron. The charge radius of the proton, $0.84$ fm, lies just outside this band, so light hadrons live “right at the boundary between perturbation theory and nonperturbative theory.” It is precisely because of this placement that calculating the properties of light hadrons from first principles is difficult.

Verification. (i) Dimensions: $\sigma$ is in $\mathrm{GeV^2}$ and $r$ is in $\mathrm{GeV^{-1}}$, so $\sigma r$ is in GeV (energy) and can be compared with $2m_q$. $4\alpha_s/(3r)$ is also in $\mathrm{GeV}$, confirming that the two terms have the same dimension. (ii) Agreement between independent conversion paths: we computed (3) in two ways, one “via GeV/fm” and the other “calculating in natural units with $\mathrm{GeV^{-1}}$ and converting to fm at the end,” and both gave $0.7235$ fm. This confirms that the conversion factors were used correctly. (iii) Comparison with known values: $\sigma\approx0.91$ GeV/fm $\approx1.46\times10^5$ N $\approx15$ tonne-force given in Section 11.5.1 of Chapter 11 of this book agrees perfectly with $0.9122$ GeV/fm, $1.461\times10^5$ N, and $1.49\times10^4$ kg in (1) of this problem. Also, from the argument in Section 11.2.3 that $197$ MeV$/c$ is needed to resolve $1$ fm, resolving $0.3$ fm requires $660$ MeV$/c$, so $r_0=0.294$ fm is consistent with the typical momentum scale of charmonium spectroscopy.

Meaning. The sheer strangeness of the number 15 tonnes captures the essence of QCD. In electromagnetism, the farther apart we pull charges, the weaker the force becomes, and in the end they separate into a free electron and an ion. In QCD this does not happen: the energy required to pull them apart grows without bound, and eventually a new pair is created from the vacuum. This picture—“when we pull, the field energy grows linearly, and at a certain threshold a new defect is created and relaxation occurs”—shares its skeleton with several phenomena in materials science. In the plastic deformation of crystals, when the stress reaches a critical value, dislocations are generated one after another from Frank–Read sources and the stress relaxes. When a magnetic field is applied to a type-II superconductor, quantized flux lines penetrate at a certain critical field and “cut” the field. In a vacuum in a strong electric field, Schwinger pair production occurs. In every case it is the combination of two elements: “a thin tube that stores energy” and “relaxation by defect creation at a threshold.” In fact, the leading picture of confinement is the dual superconductor model—the Meissner effect of the color electric field in a vacuum in which magnetic monopoles have condensed—and the QCD string and the flux quantum of a type-II superconductor are described by the same mathematics, not merely by analogy.

Exercise 11.7: The correspondence between $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}$ and the Kondo temperature

Problem (restated)

Compare the two expressions $k_BT_K=D_0\exp[-1/(2\rho J_0)]$ of Chapter 11 of this book and $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}=\mu\exp[-2\pi/(\beta_0\alpha_s(\mu))]$.

(1) By equating the exponents, find the dimensionless coupling of the Kondo problem that corresponds to the QCD $\alpha_s$ (write it in a form containing $\beta_0$).

(2) For $\beta_0=9$ ($n_f=3$), find numerically the $\alpha_s$ that corresponds to $\rho J=0.1$.

(3) For $\alpha_s(m_Z)=0.118\pm0.001$, find the relative uncertainty $\delta\Lambda/\Lambda$ of $\Lambda^{(5)}$. What percentage of $\Lambda$ does a $1\%$ uncertainty in $\alpha_s$ become?

(4) What does the result of (3) suggest about the difficulty of predicting $T_K$ or $\Delta_{\rm BCS}$ by first-principles calculations?

Solution

Strategy. Both share the same skeleton, $(\text{cutoff scale})\times\ee^{-1/(\text{coupling})}$. Parts (1) and (2) involve only the algebra of equating the exponents, and (3) is the logarithmic derivative of an exponential function (error propagation). For error propagation, the shortest route is to differentiate $\ln\Lambda$ with respect to $\alpha_s$, starting from the form $\Lambda=\mu\,\ee^{-c/\alpha_s}$.

(1) We equate the two exponents:

$$ \frac{2\pi}{\beta_0\alpha_s} = \frac{1}{2\rho J} $$

Solving this for $\alpha_s$ gives

$$ \alpha_s = \frac{4\pi\,\rho J}{\beta_0} \qquad\text{or conversely}\qquad \rho J = \frac{\beta_0\,\alpha_s}{4\pi} $$

The reversed form $\rho J=\beta_0\alpha_s/(4\pi)$ is suggestive. Comparing the renormalization group equations of Chapter 11 of this book,

$$ \frac{\dd\alpha_s}{\dd\ln Q^2} = -\frac{\beta_0}{4\pi}\alpha_s^2, \qquad \frac{\dd J}{\dd\ln D} = -2\rho J^2 $$

we see that the “effective coupling” on the QCD side is not $\alpha_s$ itself but the combination $\beta_0\alpha_s/(4\pi)$, which corresponds exactly to $\rho J$ on the Kondo side. That is, $\beta_0/4\pi$ is the conversion factor that turns $\alpha_s$ into the “natural unit of the RG”. In Table 11.7 the dimensionless coupling on the Kondo side was written as $2\rho J$; this notation absorbs the difference of a factor of $2$ arising because the Kondo-side RG is written in terms of $\ln D$ (not $\ln D^2$).

(2) We substitute $\beta_0=9$ and $\rho J=0.1$:

$$ \alpha_s = \frac{4\pi\times0.1}{9} = \frac{12.5664\times0.1}{9} = \frac{1.25664}{9} = 0.1396 $$

This is about $0.14$. By coincidence this is nearly equal to $\alpha_s(30\ \mathrm{GeV})=0.14$ (the value used in Exercise 11.1). A Kondo system with $\rho J\approx0.1$, regarded as “typical” in condensed matter, runs with about the same coupling strength as an $e^+e^-$ collision at $\sqrt{s}\sim30$ GeV in QCD. In terms of coupling strength, dilute magnetic alloys and the PETRA energy region live in the same world.

Let us also look at the correspondence in the opposite direction. Putting $n_f=5$ ($\beta_0=23/3$) and $\alpha_s(m_Z)=0.118$ into $\rho J=\beta_0\alpha_s/(4\pi)$ gives

$$ \rho J = \frac{7.6667\times0.118}{12.5664} = \frac{0.904667}{12.5664} = 0.0720 $$

that is, QCD at $m_Z$ corresponds to a Kondo system with $\rho J\approx0.072$. This is weaker than $\rho J=0.1$, which fits the sense that it is “still sufficiently perturbative.”

The correspondence holds even down to the ratio of the generated scales. Since the exponent is the common $1/(2\rho J)$ for both, the ratio of the cutoff scale to the generated scale is

$$ \frac{\mu}{\Lambda} = \frac{D_0}{k_BT_K} = \ee^{1/2\rho J} $$

For $\rho J=0.1$ this is $\ee^{5}=148.4$, and for $\rho J=0.0720$ it is $\ee^{6.945}=1038$. The latter is none other than $m_Z/\Lambda^{(5)}=91.188/0.08783=1038$ obtained in Exercise 11.3 (2) (because the exponent $1/(2\rho J)=1/0.14398=6.945$ is the same number as $2\pi/(\beta_0\alpha_s)=6.945$ there). Reading the former on the Kondo side, for a bandwidth $D_0=5$ eV we get $k_BT_K=5\,\ee^{-5}=5/148.4=0.0337$ eV, that is, $T_K=0.0337/(8.617\times10^{-5})=391$ K. The estimate in Section 11.7.1 of Chapter 11 of this book, that the “typical value” $\rho J=0.1$ gives a Kondo temperature of several hundred kelvin, has been reproduced from this single formula.

(3) Taking the logarithm of $\Lambda=\mu\,\ee^{-2\pi/(\beta_0\alpha_s)}$ gives

$$ \ln\Lambda = \ln\mu - \frac{2\pi}{\beta_0\alpha_s} $$

Differentiating with respect to $\alpha_s$,

$$ \frac{\dd\ln\Lambda}{\dd\alpha_s} = +\frac{2\pi}{\beta_0\alpha_s^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \frac{\delta\Lambda}{\Lambda} = \frac{2\pi}{\beta_0\alpha_s^2}\,\delta\alpha_s $$

Since $n_f=5$, we substitute $\beta_0=23/3=7.6667$, $\alpha_s=0.118$, and $\delta\alpha_s=0.001$. First, $\alpha_s^2=0.013924$ and $\beta_0\alpha_s^2=7.6667\times0.013924=0.106751$, so

$$ \frac{\delta\Lambda}{\Lambda} = \frac{6.28319}{0.106751}\times0.001 = 58.86\times0.001 = 0.0589 $$

That is, for $\delta\alpha_s=0.001$ (relative error $0.85\%$), the relative error of $\Lambda$ is $5.9\%$. If the uncertainty of $\alpha_s$ is $1\%$, that is, $\delta\alpha_s=0.01\times0.118=0.00118$, then

$$ \frac{\delta\Lambda}{\Lambda} = 58.86\times0.00118 = 0.0695 = 6.9\ \% $$

which is about $7\%$. In other words, the uncertainty is magnified about sevenfold.

This “sevenfold” has a clear meaning. Rewriting the above formula as a relation between relative errors,

$$ \frac{\delta\Lambda}{\Lambda} = \frac{2\pi}{\beta_0\alpha_s}\cdot\frac{\delta\alpha_s}{\alpha_s} $$

we see that the magnification factor is the exponent itself, $L\equiv2\pi/(\beta_0\alpha_s)$. And since $\Lambda=\mu\ee^{-L}$, we have $L=\ln(\mu/\Lambda)$, that is,

$$ \frac{\delta\Lambda}{\Lambda} = \ln\!\left(\frac{\mu}{\Lambda}\right)\cdot\frac{\delta\alpha_s}{\alpha_s} $$

Indeed $\ln(91.188/0.0878)=\ln(1038.6)=6.945$, which agrees with the exponent $6.945$ computed in Exercise 11.3 (2). The magnification factor is “the logarithm of the separation between the reference point and the scale.” Since we extrapolate from $m_Z$ down to $\Lambda$ across nearly three orders of magnitude, a sevenfold magnification is unavoidable.

(4) The same structure holds just as well for $T_K$ and $\Delta_{\rm BCS}$. Let us look at BCS. The logarithmic derivative of $\Delta=2\hbar\omega_D\,\ee^{-1/N(0)V}$ is

$$ \frac{\delta\Delta}{\Delta} = \frac{1}{N(0)V}\cdot\frac{\delta[N(0)V]}{N(0)V} $$

and the magnification factor is $1/N(0)V=\ln(2\hbar\omega_D/\Delta)$. As a concrete example, take $\hbar\omega_D=30$ meV and $N(0)V=0.30$:

$$ \Delta = 2\times30\times\ee^{-1/0.30} = 60\times0.03567 = 2.14\ \mathrm{meV} $$

If $N(0)V$ were $10\%$ larger, $0.33$, then

$$ \Delta = 60\times\ee^{-1/0.33} = 60\times0.04830 = 2.90\ \mathrm{meV} $$

that is, $\Delta$ increases by as much as $35\%$. The magnification factor is $35/10=3.5$, in good agreement with $1/N(0)V=3.3$. The same holds for the Kondo temperature: in the example of Section 11.7.1 of Chapter 11 of this book, merely changing $\rho J_0$ from $0.1$ to $0.066$ (a $34\%$ change) moved $T_K$ by more than an order of magnitude, from $390$ K to $30$ K, and this is precisely a manifestation of this magnification.

What this suggests is clear. Even if DFT could calculate the electron–phonon coupling constant $\lambda\sim N(0)V$ to an accuracy of a few percent, the accuracy of the prediction of $T_c$ would remain at a few tens of percent. Conversely, to get $T_c$ right to $10\%$ one must obtain the coupling constant to an accuracy of $3\%$ or better, which is an extremely demanding requirement considering the treatment of exchange–correlation functionals, pseudopotentials, anisotropy, and anharmonicity. Here lies the fundamental reason why first-principles prediction of the superconducting transition temperature has long remained a hard problem. For the same reason, on the particle-physics side, improving the measurement accuracy of $\alpha_s$ is itself the most important task for narrowing down $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}$. Note also that predicting not the absolute value of $T_c$ but the ratio of $T_c$ between materials of the same type, or the direction of its change with pressure, is far more reliable, because for two materials calculated with the same functional and the same pseudopotential the systematic errors in $\lambda$ enter in the same direction and that part cancels when the ratio is taken. Since $\delta\ln(T_{c1}/T_{c2})=\delta\lambda_1/\lambda_1^2-\delta\lambda_2/\lambda_2^2$, we should note that statistically independent errors instead add up. The cancellation works only when the errors are strongly correlated. This is an extremely useful way out in practice.

Verification. We check in three ways. (i) Dimensions: $\rho J$ is (density of states) $\times$ (energy) $=$ dimensionless, and $\alpha_s$ is also dimensionless, so the equation in (1) relates dimensionless quantities and is consistent. $\delta\Lambda/\Lambda$ and $\delta\alpha_s/\alpha_s$ are also dimensionless, and the relation in (3) connects dimensionless quantities. (ii) Direct check by finite difference: evaluating $\Lambda(\alpha_s)=91.188\,\ee^{-2\pi/(7.6667\alpha_s)}$ at $\alpha_s=0.119$, the exponent is $6.8869$ and $\Lambda=91.188\times\ee^{-6.8869}=0.09310$ GeV, which is an increase of $(0.09310-0.08783)/0.08783=6.0\%$ relative to $0.08783$ GeV at $\alpha_s=0.118$. This agrees with the estimate from the derivative, $5.9\%$ (the difference is a second-order effect). (iii) Independent route: obtaining the magnification factor from $\ln(\mu/\Lambda)$ gives $\ln(91.188/0.08783)=6.945$, and multiplying this by $\delta\alpha_s/\alpha_s=0.001/0.118=0.008475$ gives $0.0589$, in agreement with the result of the derivative formula.

Meaning. The inverse of the coupling constant appearing in the exponent of an exponential function—this single point determines every character of the scales generated by the renormalization group. First, this form is non-analytic around the coupling constant $g=0$ and cannot be Taylor-expanded. Therefore, however high an order we carry perturbation theory to, neither $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}$, nor $T_K$, nor $\Delta_{\rm BCS}$ comes out. Second, as the price of the non-analyticity, a small error in the coupling constant is magnified into a large error in the scale. That $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}$, $T_K$, and $\Delta_{\rm BCS}$ all share the same skeleton means that the effort in particle physics to measure $\alpha_s$ precisely and the effort in condensed matter physics to calculate the electron–phonon coupling or the exchange interaction precisely are driven by exactly the same mathematical necessity. It was no accident that Wilson created the numerical renormalization group for the Kondo problem and lattice gauge theory at about the same time. The frustration that materials scientists feel when designing superconductors, “the last bit of accuracy is out of reach,” comes literally from the same formula as the frustration that accelerator physicists feel when narrowing down $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}$.

E.12 Solutions for Chapter 12: The Weak Interaction

Exercise 12.1: Numerical check of $G_F$ and the range of the weak force

Problem (restated)

Use $G_F = 1.1663788\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$, $m_W=80.377\ \mathrm{GeV}$, $m_Z=91.188\ \mathrm{GeV}$, $\alpha=1/137.036$, and $\hbar c = 197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$.

(1) Find $g_w$ from $G_F/\sqrt2 = g_w^2/(8m_W^2)$, and express $\alpha_w = g_w^2/4\pi$ in the form “$1/N$”.

(2) Find $g_w/e$ (with $e=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}$). Explain why the name “weak interaction” is a misnomer as far as the strength of the coupling is concerned.

(3) Find the range of the weak force, $R_W = \hbar c/(m_Wc^2)$, in fm. What fraction of the proton radius $0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$ is it?

(4) Find the ratio of the weak force to the electromagnetic force at the nucleon separation $r=0.5\ \mathrm{fm}$, $(\alpha_w/\alpha)\ee^{-m_Wr}$.

(5) Show that the same relation $G_F/\sqrt2 = g_z^2/(8m_Z^2)$ holds for the $Z$ boson, using $g_z=g_w/\cos\theta_W$ and $m_Z = m_W/\cos\theta_W$. Check it numerically with $\sin^2\theta_W=0.2312$.

Solution

Strategy. We simply solve the definition of the Fermi constant, $G_F/\sqrt2 = g_w^2/(8m_W^2)$, derived in Section 12.1.3 of this book, for $g_w$, and combine it with Yukawa’s range $R = \hbar/(mc) = 1/m$ (Section 3.1.3 of this book). We compute in natural units ($\hbar=c=1$) and multiply by $\hbar c = 197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$ only when converting to a length.

(1) Solving the defining relation for $g_w^2$ gives

$$ g_w^2 = \frac{8m_W^2\,G_F}{\sqrt2} $$

We substitute step by step. First,

$$ m_W^2 = (80.377)^2 = 6460.462\ \mathrm{GeV^2}, \qquad 8m_W^2 = 51683.70\ \mathrm{GeV^2} $$

Multiplying this by $G_F$ gives

$$ 8m_W^2G_F = 51683.70\times1.1663788\times10^{-5} = 0.6028277 $$

(Since this is $\mathrm{GeV^2}\times\mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$, it is dimensionless. This confirms that the coupling constant is dimensionless.) Dividing by $\sqrt2 = 1.4142136$,

$$ g_w^2 = \frac{0.6028277}{1.4142136} = 0.4262635, \qquad g_w = 0.652889 $$

The quantity corresponding to the fine-structure constant is

$$ \alpha_w = \frac{g_w^2}{4\pi} = \frac{0.4262635}{12.566371} = 0.0339210 = \frac{1}{29.48} $$

That is, $\alpha_w = 1/29.5$.

(2) The electromagnetic coupling is

$$ e = \sqrt{4\pi\alpha} = \sqrt{\frac{12.566371}{137.036}} = \sqrt{0.0916999} = 0.302822 $$

Therefore

$$ \frac{g_w}{e} = \frac{0.652889}{0.302822} = 2.1560, \qquad \frac{\alpha_w}{\alpha} = \frac{g_w^2}{e^2} = \frac{0.4262635}{0.0916999} = 4.6484 $$

The weak coupling constant is $2.16$ times the electromagnetic one, and in terms of coupling strength (the square of the coupling constant) it is $4.65$ times as large. That is, of the two interactions, it is the electromagnetic interaction that is “weak.” The name “weak interaction” was given in the 1930s because of the slowness of $\beta$ decay, and it does not reflect the size of the coupling constant. The cause of the slowness is not the coupling but the shortness of the range, which we see in (3).

(3) Yukawa’s range is

$$ R_W = \frac{\hbar c}{m_Wc^2} = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{80377\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 2.4550\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm} = 2.4550\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{m} $$

The ratio to the proton radius is

$$ \frac{0.84\ \mathrm{fm}}{2.4550\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}} = 342.2 $$

That is, it is $1/342$ of the proton radius.

(4) First we evaluate the exponent.

$$ m_Wr = \frac{r}{R_W} = \frac{0.5}{2.4550\times10^{-3}} = 203.66 $$

Converting to a common logarithm,

$$ \log_{10}\ee^{-203.66} = -\frac{203.66}{\ln10} = -\frac{203.66}{2.302585} = -88.448 $$

Hence $\ee^{-203.66} = 10^{0.552}\times10^{-89} = 3.56\times10^{-89}$. The ratio is

$$ \frac{\alpha_w}{\alpha}\ee^{-m_Wr} = 4.6484\times3.56\times10^{-89} = 1.66\times10^{-88} $$

Although the coupling constant wins by a factor of $4.6$, the exponential factor multiplies the result by $10^{-89}$. Even at the distance at which nucleons touch, the weak force is only $10^{-88}$ times the electromagnetic force.

(5) We first show it as an identity. Substituting $g_z = g_w/\cos\theta_W$ and $m_Z = m_W/\cos\theta_W$, we obtain

$$ \frac{g_z^2}{8m_Z^2} = \frac{g_w^2/\cos^2\theta_W}{8m_W^2/\cos^2\theta_W} = \frac{g_w^2}{8m_W^2} = \frac{G_F}{\sqrt2} $$

That is, $\cos^2\theta_W$ cancels completely between numerator and denominator, so the same $G_F$ comes out whether it is written in terms of the $Z$ or the $W$. This is no accident: as we saw in Section 12.7 of this book, it is a restatement of the fact that $g_z$ and $m_Z$ are defined with the same $\cos\theta_W$, that is, that the $\rho$ parameter equals $1$.

Now the numerical check. From $\sin^2\theta_W = 0.2312$,

$$ \cos\theta_W = \sqrt{1-0.2312} = \sqrt{0.7688} = 0.876812 $$ $$ g_z = \frac{0.652889}{0.876812} = 0.744616, \qquad g_z^2 = 0.554453 $$ $$ m_Z^2 = (91.188)^2 = 8315.25\ \mathrm{GeV^2}, \qquad 8m_Z^2 = 66522.0\ \mathrm{GeV^2} $$ $$ \frac{g_z^2}{8m_Z^2} = \frac{0.554453}{66522.0} = 8.3349\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}} $$

On the other hand,

$$ \frac{G_F}{\sqrt2} = \frac{1.1663788\times10^{-5}}{1.4142136} = 8.2475\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}} $$

The ratio is $8.3349/8.2475 = 1.0106$, that is, a difference of $1.1\ \%$. That something that should hold exactly as an identity is off by $1.1\ \%$ is due to the difference in the definition of $\sin^2\theta_W$. The given value $\sin^2\theta_W = 0.2312$ is an $\overline{\rm MS}$-type value, and the on-shell value, which satisfies $m_Z = m_W/\cos\theta_W$ exactly, is

$$ \sin^2\theta_W^{\rm on\text{-}shell} = 1-\frac{m_W^2}{m_Z^2} = 1-\frac{6460.46}{8315.25} = 0.22306 $$

Indeed, with the $\overline{\rm MS}$ value we get $m_W/\cos\theta_W = 80.377/0.876812 = 91.67\ \mathrm{GeV}$, which is $0.53\ \%$ larger than the measured $91.188\ \mathrm{GeV}$. Its square is $1.1\ \%$ larger.

Verification. Let us recompute $g_w$ of (1) from a completely different relation, $g_w = e/\sin\theta_W$ of Section 12.7 of this book. With $e = 0.302822$ and $\sin\theta_W = \sqrt{0.2312} = 0.480833$, we get $g_w = 0.302822/0.480833 = 0.62978$. This is $3.5\ \%$ smaller than the $0.652889$ of (1). This is not a calculational error: as stated in the caution of Section 12.1.4 of this book, it is because we have not included the running of $\alpha$ ($\hat\alpha(m_Z)=1/127.95$, $\overline{\rm MS}$; see Chapter 10, Section 10.6.4) and the one-loop radiative correction $\Delta r\approx0.036$. A $3\ \%$ agreement in tree-level formulas is as expected, and the order of magnitude and the size relation of $g_w$ ($g_w > e$) do not change. Also, the fact that $8m_W^2G_F$ turned out dimensionless in the course of (1) is consistent with the dimensional counting that $G_F$ carries $\mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$ and $g_w$ is dimensionless.

Meaning. The whole of this problem is the very theme of this chapter: “the weak interaction is not weak, merely short-ranged.” Part (2) concerns the coupling strength, (3) and (4) concern the range, and the number $10^{-88}$ in (4) comes entirely from the exponential factor. The coupling constant wins by a factor of $4.6$, but $\ee^{-r/R_W}$ reduces it by a factor of $10^{-89}$. The same thing happens in condensed matter physics. In a metal the Coulomb interaction becomes $\ee^{-k_{\rm TF}r}/r$ through Thomas–Fermi screening (Section 12.8.5 of this book), and it has almost no effect beyond $1/k_{\rm TF}\sim0.6\ \mathrm{\AA}$. The bare coupling ($e^2$) has not changed at all, yet the exponential screening factor alone turns it into a “weak interaction.” In both cases, what determines the strength is not the coupling constant but the scale. The $1.1\ \%$ discrepancy in (5) is also a practical lesson: in precision tests one must state explicitly which definition of $\sin^2\theta_W$ is used.

Exercise 12.2: The muon lifetime and the Michel spectrum

Problem (restated)

$m_\mu = 105.6584\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_\tau = 1776.86\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $\hbar = 6.582120\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{GeV\,s}$.

(1) Evaluate $\Gamma=G_F^2m_\mu^5/(192\pi^3)$ numerically and find the lifetime in $\mu\mathrm{s}$.

(2) Verify that the Michel spectrum $\dd\Gamma/\dd x = \Gamma\cdot2x^2(3-2x)$ is normalized, and find $\braket{x}$ and the mean electron energy.

(3) Find the probability that the electron energy is at least $90\ \%$ of its maximum value ($x>0.9$).

(4) Using the formula for the spin asymmetry in Section 12.2.6 of this book ($\Gamma^{-1}\dd^2\Gamma/\dd x\,\dd\cos\theta = x^2[(3-2x)+P_\mu\cos\theta(1-2x)]$), find $\braket{\cos\theta}$ for complete polarization $P_\mu=1$.

(5) Find the lifetime of the $\tau$ lepton from $\tau_\tau = B_e(m_\mu/m_\tau)^5\tau_\mu$ without using $G_F$ ($B_e = 0.1782$, $\tau_\mu = 2.19698\ \mu\mathrm{s}$). Compare it with the measured value $290.3\ \mathrm{fs}$.

Solution

Strategy. Part (1) is a substitution into $\Gamma = G_F^2m_\mu^5/(192\pi^3)$, derived in Section 12.2.3 of this book; (2), (3) and (4) are elementary polynomial integrals of the Michel spectrum; and (5) is a calculation that uses only the ratio of the $m^5$ law. In natural units $\Gamma$ has the dimension of $\mathrm{GeV}$, so we divide by $\hbar$ when converting to seconds.

(1) We build up the fifth power of $m_\mu = 0.1056584\ \mathrm{GeV}$ step by step.

$$ m_\mu^2 = 0.011163698,\qquad m_\mu^4 = (0.011163698)^2 = 1.2462814\times10^{-4} $$ $$ m_\mu^5 = 1.2462814\times10^{-4}\times0.1056584 = 1.3168010\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{GeV^5} $$

Also

$$ G_F^2 = (1.1663788\times10^{-5})^2 = 1.3604395\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-4}} $$ $$ 192\pi^3 = 192\times31.006277 = 5953.205 $$

Therefore

$$ \Gamma = \frac{1.3604395\times10^{-10}\times1.3168010\times10^{-5}}{5953.205} = \frac{1.7914281\times10^{-15}}{5953.205} = 3.009183\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

The lifetime is

$$ \tau_\mu = \frac{\hbar}{\Gamma} = \frac{6.582120\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{GeV\,s}}{3.009183\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{GeV}} = 2.18734\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s} = 2.1873\ \mu\mathrm{s} $$

This is $0.44\ \%$ smaller than the measured $2.196981\ \mu\mathrm{s}$. As in Section 12.2.4 of this book, including the phase-space correction due to the electron mass ($-0.019\ \%$) and the QED radiative correction ($-0.420\ \%$) gives $2.19699\ \mu\mathrm{s}$, which agrees to six digits.

(2) We verify the normalization.

$$ \int_0^1 2x^2(3-2x)\,\dd x = \int_0^1\left(6x^2-4x^3\right)\dd x = \left[2x^3-x^4\right]_0^1 = 2-1 = 1 $$

It is indeed $1$. The mean value is

$$ \braket{x} = \int_0^1 x\cdot2x^2(3-2x)\,\dd x = \int_0^1\left(6x^3-4x^4\right)\dd x = \left[\frac{6}{4}x^4-\frac{4}{5}x^5\right]_0^1 = \frac32-\frac45 = \frac{7}{10} = 0.700 $$

Since the electron energy is $E' = xm_\mu/2$,

$$ \braket{E'} = \frac{\braket{x}}{2}m_\mu = 0.35\times105.6584\ \mathrm{MeV} = 36.98\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The endpoint is $E'_{\max} = m_\mu/2 = 52.83\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(3) We use the indefinite integral above as it stands.

$$ P(x>0.9) = \int_{0.9}^{1}\left(6x^2-4x^3\right)\dd x = \left[2x^3-x^4\right]_{0.9}^{1} $$

At the upper limit, $2-1 = 1$. At the lower limit,

$$ 2\times0.729 - 0.6561 = 1.458-0.6561 = 0.8019 $$

Hence

$$ P(x>0.9) = 1 - 0.8019 = 0.1981 = 19.8\ \% $$

An interval of only $10\ \%$ of the width in $x$ contains $20\ \%$ of all electrons. For a uniform distribution it would be $10\ \%$, so the electrons are concentrated near the endpoint at $2$ times the density.

(4) We compute directly from the definition. Write $c\equiv\cos\theta$. The numerator is

$$ \int_0^1\!\dd x\int_{-1}^{1}\!\dd c\;c\,x^2\left[(3-2x)+P_\mu c(1-2x)\right] $$

Since $\int_{-1}^1 c\,\dd c = 0$, the first term vanishes, and since $\int_{-1}^1c^2\dd c = 2/3$, only the second term remains.

$$ = \frac23P_\mu\int_0^1 x^2(1-2x)\,\dd x = \frac23P_\mu\int_0^1\left(x^2-2x^3\right)\dd x = \frac23P_\mu\left[\frac13-\frac12\right] = \frac23P_\mu\times\left(-\frac16\right) = -\frac{P_\mu}{9} $$

In the denominator, the second term vanishes for the same reason, and

$$ \int_0^1\!\dd x\int_{-1}^{1}\!\dd c\;x^2(3-2x) = \int_0^1 2x^2(3-2x)\,\dd x = 1 $$

(This is just the normalization computed in (2).) Therefore

$$ \braket{\cos\theta} = -\frac{P_\mu}{9} $$

For complete polarization $P_\mu=1$, $\braket{\cos\theta} = -1/9 = -0.111$. The negative sign means that the electron tends to be emitted in the opposite direction to the muon spin (for $\mu^-$).

(5) We form the mass ratio.

$$ \frac{m_\mu}{m_\tau} = \frac{105.6584}{1776.86} = 0.05946355 $$

We compute the fifth power step by step.

$$ (0.05946355)^2 = 3.535914\times10^{-3},\qquad (0.05946355)^4 = 1.250268\times10^{-5} $$ $$ (0.05946355)^5 = 1.250268\times10^{-5}\times0.05946355 = 7.43454\times10^{-7} $$

Therefore

$$ \frac{\tau_\tau}{\tau_\mu} = B_e\left(\frac{m_\mu}{m_\tau}\right)^5 = 0.1782\times7.43454\times10^{-7} = 1.324836\times10^{-7} $$ $$ \tau_\tau = 1.324836\times10^{-7}\times2.19698\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s} = 2.9106\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{s} = 291.1\ \mathrm{fs} $$

Relative to the measured $290.3\ \mathrm{fs}$,

$$ \frac{291.1-290.3}{290.3} = 0.26\ \% $$

agreement. What deserves attention is that neither $G_F$ nor $\hbar$ nor $192\pi^3$ enters this calculation. We used only the mass ratio, the branching ratio, and $\tau_\mu$, and it still hits the mark to $0.3\ \%$. This is proof that the $m^5$ law and lepton universality ($g_w$ is the same for the three generations) hold over the wide range of $17^5 = 1.4\times10^6$.

Verification. We check both dimensions and limits. Dimensions: $[G_F^2] = \mathrm{GeV^{-4}}$ and $[m_\mu^5] = \mathrm{GeV^5}$, so $[\Gamma]=\mathrm{GeV}$. Dividing this by $[\hbar]=\mathrm{GeV\,s}$ gives the reciprocal of $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, that is, seconds, so the operation in (1) is correct. Limits: the Michel spectrum of (2) falls to zero as $\propto x^2$ for $x\to0$, and at $x=1$ it takes its maximum value, $2x^2(3-2x)=2$. Also, the $19.8\ \%$ of (3) can be estimated as $2\times0.1 = 0.2$ from the fact that the distribution is nearly constant, at the value $2$, near the endpoint, and this agrees well with the exact value $0.1981$. For (4), putting in $P_\mu = 0$ (unpolarized) gives $\braket{\cos\theta}=0$, which is consistent with the asymmetry originating from parity violation.

Meaning. What (1) shows is that from “one coupling constant and one mass” the lifetime comes out not merely to the order of magnitude but to digits past the decimal point. In particle physics there are not many processes that can be solved this cleanly. The property of (3), that electrons concentrate at the endpoint, is specific to $V-A$, as stated in Section 12.2.5 of this book; for a scalar-type coupling (Michel parameter $\rho=0$) the spectrum would fall to zero at the endpoint. That is, the shape of the spectrum itself serves as a device for measuring the type of the interaction. The $-1/9$ of (4) is the very principle of $\mu$SR (muon spin rotation). A polarized muon precesses in the local magnetic field in the sample and emits a positron in the direction of its spin at the moment of decay. Without this asymmetry, the $\mu$SR technique for measuring the magnetic-field penetration depth of superconductors and the ordering of spin glasses would not exist. The discovery of parity nonconservation in particle physics thus becomes, as it is, the operating principle of a condensed-matter measurement apparatus.

Exercise 12.3: Helicity suppression and the decay constant

Problem (restated)

$m_\pi = 139.570\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_K = 493.677\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_\mu = 105.658\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_e = 0.510999\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(1) Follow the derivation of the pion decay amplitude $\mathcal{M} = \ii(G_F/\sqrt2)V_{ud}f_\pi m_\ell\,\bar u(p_\ell)(1-\gamma^5)v(p_\nu)$ in Section 12.4.1 of this book, and confirm that $\bar u(p_\ell)\slashed{p}_\nu(1-\gamma^5)v(p_\nu)=0$ depends on the neutrino being massless. What happens if $m_\nu\neq0$?

(2) Find the ratio $R_{e/\mu}=\Gamma(\pi\to e\nu)/\Gamma(\pi\to\mu\nu)$ from the formula of Section 12.4.3 of this book, $R_{e/\mu} = (m_e/m_\mu)^2\left[(m_\pi^2-m_e^2)/(m_\pi^2-m_\mu^2)\right]^2$. Show the phase-space factor and the helicity factor separately.

(3) Apply the same formula to the $K$ meson and find $\Gamma(K\to e\nu)/\Gamma(K\to\mu\nu)$. Compare it with the measured value $2.488\times10^{-5}$.

(4) The decay $\tau^-\to\pi^-\nu_\tau$ has a branching ratio as large as $10.8\ \%$ and is not suppressed. Explain why.

(5) The lifetime of $\pi^0\to\gamma\gamma$ is $8.5\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{s}$, which is $9$ orders of magnitude shorter than the $2.6\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{s}$ of $\pi^\pm$. State which interaction is at work in each case, and explain the difference in orders of magnitude qualitatively.

Solution

Strategy. The key is the single line of the Dirac equation $\slashed{p}_\nu v(p_\nu) = -m_\nu v(p_\nu)$. Whether it vanishes determines the structure of the amplitude. Parts (2) and (3) are substitutions into the given ratio formula; the effects of the strong interaction ($f_\pi$, $f_K$), $G_F$, and $V_{ij}$ all cancel in the ratio, so it is determined by the masses alone.

(1) We follow the derivation. Using momentum conservation $p = p_\ell + p_\nu$ to split $\slashed{p} = \slashed{p}_\ell + \slashed{p}_\nu$, the factor in the amplitude becomes

$$ \bar u(p_\ell)\left(\slashed{p}_\ell+\slashed{p}_\nu\right)(1-\gamma^5)v(p_\nu) $$

For the first term, the Dirac equation for the conjugate spinor, $\bar u(p_\ell)\slashed{p}_\ell = m_\ell\,\bar u(p_\ell)$, gives

$$ \bar u(p_\ell)\slashed{p}_\ell(1-\gamma^5)v(p_\nu) = m_\ell\,\bar u(p_\ell)(1-\gamma^5)v(p_\nu) $$

For the second term, since $\gamma^5$ anticommutes with $\gamma^\mu$ ($\gamma^5\slashed{a} = -\slashed{a}\gamma^5$), we pass $\slashed{p}_\nu$ to the right and obtain

$$ \bar u(p_\ell)\slashed{p}_\nu(1-\gamma^5)v(p_\nu) = \bar u(p_\ell)(1+\gamma^5)\slashed{p}_\nu\,v(p_\nu) $$

Here the Dirac equation for the antiparticle spinor is $(\slashed{p}_\nu + m_\nu)v(p_\nu)=0$, that is,

$$ \slashed{p}_\nu v(p_\nu) = -m_\nu\,v(p_\nu) $$

Therefore this term vanishes if and only if $m_\nu=0$. When $m_\nu = 0$, the amplitude consists only of the term proportional to $m_\ell$; this is the helicity suppression.

When $m_\nu\neq0$, the second term survives, and the amplitude becomes

$$ \mathcal{M}\propto \bar u(p_\ell)\left[m_\ell(1-\gamma^5) - m_\nu(1+\gamma^5)\right]v(p_\nu) $$

That is, the amplitude is the sum of a term proportional to $m_\ell$ and a term proportional to $m_\nu$. Because the two have different chiral structures ($(1-\gamma^5)\slashed p_\nu(1-\gamma^5)=0$), they do not interfere even after the spin sum, and only the forms $m_\ell^2+m_\nu^2$ and $m_\ell^2m_\nu^2$ appear in $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2$ (no linear cross term in $m_\ell m_\nu$ arises). In other words, the suppression factor changes from $m_\ell^2$ to $m_\ell^2+m_\nu^2$; the two terms do not cancel each other. The actual decay rate has the form $\Gamma\propto f_P^2\left[(m_\ell^2+m_\nu^2)m_P^2-(m_\ell^2-m_\nu^2)^2\right]\lambda^{1/2}(m_P^2,m_\ell^2,m_\nu^2)/m_P^3$. Physically, a massive neutrino can supply the “wrong helicity” by itself, so the charged lepton no longer has to bear the suppression.

We estimate the size. Using the current upper limit $m_\nu\lesssim0.1\ \mathrm{eV}$, even for the electron channel, where the effect is largest,

$$ \frac{m_\nu}{m_e} = \frac{0.1\ \mathrm{eV}}{5.10999\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{eV}} = 2.0\times10^{-7} $$

and the effect on the decay rate is $10^{-6}$ or less. This is far below the experimental precision ($0.1\ \%$), so we may treat the neutrino as having $m_\nu=0$.

(2) We form the squares of the masses.

$$ m_\pi^2 = (139.570)^2 = 19479.78,\quad m_\mu^2 = (105.658)^2 = 11163.61,\quad m_e^2 = (0.510999)^2 = 0.26112 $$

(All units are $\mathrm{MeV^2}$.) The phase-space factor is

$$ \frac{m_\pi^2-m_e^2}{m_\pi^2-m_\mu^2} = \frac{19479.78-0.26}{19479.78-11163.61} = \frac{19479.52}{8316.17} = 2.34237 $$ $$ \left(\frac{m_\pi^2-m_e^2}{m_\pi^2-m_\mu^2}\right)^2 = (2.34237)^2 = 5.4867 $$

That is, looking at phase space alone, the electron channel is favored by a factor of $5.49$. This is because the lighter lepton emerges with a larger momentum, so the two-body phase space $\abs{\pp}$ is larger.

The helicity factor is

$$ \left(\frac{m_e}{m_\mu}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{0.510999}{105.658}\right)^2 = (4.836337\times10^{-3})^2 = 2.33903\times10^{-5} $$

Multiplying the two,

$$ R_{e/\mu} = 2.33903\times10^{-5}\times5.4867 = 1.2833\times10^{-4} = \frac{1}{7792} $$

The measured value is $1.2327\times10^{-4}$, so this is $4.1\ \%$ larger. This discrepancy is nearly explained by the QED radiative correction ($-3.7\ \%$), and the Standard Model prediction including the correction, $1.2352\times10^{-4}$, agrees with the measured value to $0.2\ \%$.

(3) The structure is exactly the same for the $K$ meson; we simply replace $m_\pi\to m_K$ (the replacements $f_\pi\to f_K$ and $V_{ud}\to V_{us}$ also cancel in the ratio).

$$ m_K^2 = (493.677)^2 = 243716.98\ \mathrm{MeV^2} $$ $$ \frac{m_K^2-m_e^2}{m_K^2-m_\mu^2} = \frac{243716.98-0.26}{243716.98-11163.61} = \frac{243716.72}{232553.37} = 1.048003 $$ $$ \left(1.048003\right)^2 = 1.09831 $$

Since the helicity factor is the same $2.33903\times10^{-5}$ as in (2),

$$ R^{K}_{e/\mu} = 2.33903\times10^{-5}\times1.09831 = 2.5690\times10^{-5} $$

Relative to the measured value $2.488\times10^{-5}$,

$$ \frac{2.5690-2.488}{2.488} = +3.3\ \% $$

is the deviation, which is of the size of the radiative correction, as in the case of the $\pi$. Note that the phase-space factor drops from $5.49$ for the $\pi$ to $1.10$ for the $K$. Because $m_K$ is much larger than $m_\mu$, the presence or absence of $m_\mu$ hardly affects the phase space, and the ratio becomes almost purely the helicity factor $(m_e/m_\mu)^2$ itself.

(4) Helicity suppression operates in the configuration in which a spin-0 particle decays and two fermions fly off back to back. The suppression factor was “the mass of the final-state charged lepton / the available energy.”

In $\tau^-\to\pi^-\nu_\tau$ the roles are interchanged. The decaying particle is the spin-$1/2$ $\tau$, and the pion is in the final state. That is, this is not a “two-body decay of a pseudoscalar meson” but a “two-body decay of a heavy lepton.” Computing with the same matrix element $\bra{0}\bar d\gamma^\mu(1-\gamma^5)u\ket{\pi^-} = \ii f_\pi p^\mu$, the mass that appears in the amplitude is neither $m_\pi$ nor $m_\nu$ but $m_\tau$. Specifically, contracting $p^\mu = p_\tau^\mu - p_\nu^\mu$ with the lepton current leaves $\bar u(p_\nu)\slashed{p}_\tau(1-\gamma^5)u(p_\tau) = m_\tau\bar u(p_\nu)(1-\gamma^5)u(p_\tau)$, while the $\slashed{p}_\nu$ side vanishes because $m_\nu=0$.

Therefore the decay rate has the form $\propto m_\tau^3f_\pi^2(1-m_\pi^2/m_\tau^2)^2$, and the suppression factor $m_\tau^2$ is the available energy $m_\tau$ itself. Because a large mass multiplies, rather than a small mass dividing, there is no suppression at all. In a nutshell, helicity suppression operates in the form $m_\ell/E$: in $\pi\to e\nu$ the mass $m_e$ is extremely small compared with $E=m_\pi/2$, whereas in $\tau\to\pi\nu$ the “lepton mass” is $E$ itself, so the ratio is $1$.

(5) The interactions at work are as follows.

  • $\pi^0\to\gamma\gamma$: the electromagnetic interaction (more precisely, a process of order $\alpha^2$ through the axial anomaly). Since the final state contains two photons, the amplitude is proportional to $e^2$ and the decay rate is proportional to $\alpha^2$.
  • $\pi^\pm\to\mu^\pm\nu$: the weak interaction. The amplitude is proportional to $G_F$ and the decay rate is proportional to $G_F^2$.

The reason $\pi^\pm$ cannot decay electromagnetically is charge conservation. A photon carries no charge, so a charged particle cannot disappear by emitting photons alone. Since $\pi^0$ is neutral, this prohibition is lifted. The available interactions differ—this is the fundamental cause of the difference of orders of magnitude.

We estimate the orders of magnitude numerically. It suffices to compare the dimensionless effective couplings at low energy. On the electromagnetic side, $\alpha = 7.30\times10^{-3}$; on the weak side, the strength of the contact interaction made dimensionless with the $\pi$ scale is

$$ G_Fm_\pi^2 = 1.1663788\times10^{-5}\times0.0194798\ \mathrm{GeV^2}\cdot\mathrm{GeV^{-2}} = 2.272\times10^{-7} $$

The ratio of amplitudes is $\alpha/(G_Fm_\pi^2) = 3.21\times10^{4}$, and the ratio of decay rates is its square,

$$ \left(\frac{\alpha}{G_Fm_\pi^2}\right)^2 \approx 1.0\times10^{9} $$

The actual ratio follows from $\Gamma(\pi^0) = \hbar/8.5\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{s} = 7.74\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and $\Gamma(\pi^\pm) = \hbar/2.6\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{s} = 2.53\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{GeV}$:

$$ \frac{\Gamma(\pi^0)}{\Gamma(\pi^\pm)} = 3.1\times10^{8} $$

The rough estimate $10^9$ and the measured $3\times10^8$ agree within a factor of $3$. The remaining factors include the helicity suppression on the $\pi^\pm$ side, $(m_\mu/m_\pi)^2 = 0.573$, and the phase space, and on the $\pi^0$ side the anomaly coefficient, among others. The point is that the difference of $9$ orders of magnitude comes almost entirely from the square of $G_Fm_\pi^2$, “the smallness of the weak interaction measured on the $\pi$ scale”.

Verification. We check the result of (2) in limiting cases. If $m_e = m_\mu$, then $R_{e/\mu}$ must be exactly $1$. Substituting $m_e\to m_\mu$ into the formula, the helicity factor becomes $1$ and the phase-space factor also becomes $1$, so indeed $R=1$. Conversely, in the limit $m_e\to0$ we have $R\to0$, which agrees with the conclusion of (1) that decay into a massless lepton is impossible. The $K$ value in (3) is $5$ times smaller than the $\pi$ value; this is because the phase-space factor dropped from $5.49$ to $1.10$, which is also confirmed by the fact that the ratio of ratios, $1.2833/2.5690 = 4.995$, agrees with the ratio of the phase-space factors, $5.4867/1.09831 = 4.996$. Also, the fact that $G_Fm_\pi^2$ used in the estimate of (5) is dimensionless is consistent with the dimension $[G_F]=\mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$.

Meaning. The protagonist of this problem is the structure “an exact zero broken by a small mass.” If $m_\nu=0$, the second term is exactly zero; if $m_\ell=0$, the amplitude is exactly zero. And the moment a mass enters, a transition suppressed by the small ratio $m/E$ revives. As stated in Section 12.4.3 of this book, this structure is mathematically identical to the suppression of backscattering in graphene. In ideal graphene, the scattering amplitude $\braket{-\kk|\kk}$ for $\kk\to-\kk$ is exactly zero because of the orthogonality of the pseudospins, and when a gap $\Delta$ opens through an $h$-BN substrate or a perpendicular electric field, it revives as $\abs{\braket{-\kk|\kk}}\propto\Delta/E$. The branching ratio $1.2\times10^{-4}$ of $\pi\to e\nu$ and the high mobility of graphene are both merely the result of computing “the overlap between eigenstates of the chirality operator.” From the side of materials science, this is an instance of the general rule that measuring the residual amount of a process forbidden by a symmetry is the most sensitive way to measure the size of the terms that break the symmetry (mass, gap, strain).

Exercise 12.4: Neutron decay and Sargent’s rule

Problem (restated)

$m_n=939.565\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_p=938.272\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_e=0.510999\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $\lambda=1.2754$, $\abs{V_{ud}}=0.97373$, $f=1.6887$, $\Delta_R=0.039$.

(1) Find the $Q$ value. Also state what would happen if $m_n-m_p$ were smaller than $m_e$.
