(2) Using the formula $1/\tau_n = G_F^2\abs{V_{ud}}^2m_e^5(1+3\lambda^2)f(1+\Delta_R)/(2\pi^3)$ of Section 12.3.4 of this book, find $\tau_n$ and convert it to the half-life.

(3) Find the fraction of the total decay rate accounted for by the Gamow–Teller transition.

(4) Suppose there were no renormalization by the strong interaction and $\lambda=1$. What would the neutron lifetime be?

(5) Compare the tritium and neutron rows of Table 12.2 and argue, using the values of $\log ft$, that “the difference in half-lives is determined not by nuclear structure but by phase space.”

Solution

Strategy. Part (1) is an energy balance, and (2) is just a substitution into the given formula. The product of the small number $m_e^5$ and the phase-space factor $f$ determines everything. Parts (3) and (4) merely read off the breakdown of the factor $1+3\lambda^2$ derived in Section 12.3.2 of this book (Fermi transition $1$ + Gamow–Teller transition $3\lambda^2$), and (5) is an application of the decomposition $\Gamma\propto f\times$ (nuclear matrix element).

(1) In the $\beta$ decay $n\to p+e^-+\bar\nu_e$, the total kinetic energy released is the difference of the rest masses minus the rest mass of the electron (the mass of $\bar\nu_e$ is neglected).

$$ Q = m_n - m_p - m_e = 939.565 - 938.272 - 0.510999 = 0.782\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The mass difference between the neutron and the proton itself is $\Delta = m_n-m_p = 1.293\ \mathrm{MeV}$, of which $0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is spent on creating the electron, and only the remaining $0.782\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is distributed among the kinetic energies of the electron, the antineutrino, and (slightly) the proton.

If $m_n - m_p < m_e$ held, then $Q<0$ and $\beta$ decay would be energetically forbidden. The free neutron would become a stable particle. In that case, (i) the process in which the neutron/proton ratio decreases as $\ee^{-t/\tau_n}$ just before Big Bang nucleosynthesis would not occur, and the amount of $^4$He produced would take a completely different value; (ii) a sea of free neutrons would remain in the universe; and (iii) conversely, if the proton were heavier, $p\to n e^+\nu_e$ would occur and hydrogen atoms would not exist. The relative sizes of the two numbers $1.293\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$ determine the elemental composition of our universe.

(2) We compute in three parts.

Constant part. From $m_e = 5.10999\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{GeV}$,

$$ m_e^5 = (5.10999\times10^{-4})^5 = 3.484177\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{GeV^5} $$ $$ 2\pi^3 = 2\times31.006277 = 62.01255 $$ $$ \frac{G_F^2m_e^5}{2\pi^3} = \frac{1.3604395\times10^{-10}\times3.484177\times10^{-17}}{62.01255} = \frac{4.740012\times10^{-27}}{62.01255} = 7.64363\times10^{-29}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Current factors.

$$ \abs{V_{ud}}^2 = (0.97373)^2 = 0.948150,\qquad 1+3\lambda^2 = 1+3\times(1.2754)^2 = 1+3\times1.626645 = 5.87994 $$ $$ \abs{V_{ud}}^2(1+3\lambda^2) = 0.948150\times5.87994 = 5.57507 $$

Phase space and radiative correction.

$$ f\,(1+\Delta_R) = 1.6887\times1.039 = 1.754559 $$

Multiplying together.

$$ \frac{1}{\tau_n} = 7.64363\times10^{-29}\times5.57507\times1.754559 = 7.47682\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$ $$ \tau_n = \frac{6.582120\times10^{-25}}{7.47682\times10^{-28}} = 880.3\ \mathrm{s} $$

The half-life is

$$ t_{1/2} = \tau_n\ln2 = 880.3\times0.693147 = 610.2\ \mathrm{s} = 10.17\ \text{min} $$

This agrees with the measured $\tau_n = 878.4\pm0.5\ \mathrm{s}$ to $0.2\ \%$.

(3) As shown in Section 12.3.2 of this book, the decay rate is proportional to the sum of $g_V^2\times1$ (Fermi transition) and $g_A^2\times3$ (Gamow–Teller transition, owing to the three components of $\sigma^i$). Normalizing to $g_V=1$, the ratio is $1 : 3\lambda^2$.

$$ 3\lambda^2 = 3\times1.626645 = 4.879935,\qquad 1+3\lambda^2 = 5.879935 $$ $$ \frac{3\lambda^2}{1+3\lambda^2} = \frac{4.879935}{5.879935} = 0.8299 $$

That is, the Gamow–Teller transition accounts for $83.0\ \%$ of the total and the Fermi transition for $17.0\ \%$. That the spin-flip transition plays the leading role is due to both (i) the simple counting effect of the three components and (ii) the enhancement of the axial current by the strong interaction, $\lambda = 1.2754 > 1$.

(4) The decay rate is proportional to $1+3\lambda^2$, and the lifetime is proportional to its inverse. For $\lambda=1$ we get $1+3\times1 = 4$, so

$$ \tau_n(\lambda=1) = 880.3\times\frac{5.87994}{4} = 880.3\times1.469985 = 1294\ \mathrm{s} = 21.6\ \text{min} $$

This is $1.47$ times longer than the actual $880.3\ \mathrm{s}$ ($14.7$ minutes). In other words, the renormalization of the axial current by the strong interaction ($g_A$ increasing from $1$ to $1.2754$, by $27\ \%$) shortens the neutron lifetime by $32\ \%$. The nonperturbative effect of the strong interaction, gluon exchange between quarks, pulls the concrete figure of $15$ minutes down from $22$ minutes.

(5) We list the two relevant rows of Table 12.2.

Table E.12.1: Comparison of tritium and the neutron
Nuclide$Q$ [MeV]$t_{1/2}$$f$$\log_{10}(ft/\mathrm{s})$
$^3\mathrm{H}\to{}^3\mathrm{He}$$0.01859$$12.32$ years$2.91\times10^{-6}$$3.05$
$n\to p$$0.782$$610$ s$1.6887$$3.01$

The decay rate can be decomposed in the form $\Gamma \propto f\times\abs{M_{\rm nucl}}^2$, and $ft$ is the quantity that isolates only the nuclear matrix element by dividing out $f$. That is,

$$ ft \propto \frac{1}{\abs{M_{\rm nucl}}^2} $$

Since $\log ft$ is $3.05$ and $3.01$, a difference of only $0.04$,

$$ \frac{(ft)_{^3\mathrm{H}}}{(ft)_n} = 10^{0.04} = 1.096 $$

that is, the nuclear matrix elements differ by only $10\ \%$. This is because both are the simplest systems with $A\le3$ and are superallowed transitions in which “just one $d$ quark becomes a $u$.”

On the other hand, the ratio of the phase-space factors is

$$ \frac{f_n}{f_{^3\mathrm{H}}} = \frac{1.6887}{2.91\times10^{-6}} = 5.80\times10^{5} $$

From $t = (ft)/f$, the ratio of the half-lives is predicted to be

$$ \frac{t_{1/2}(^3\mathrm{H})}{t_{1/2}(n)} = \frac{f_n}{f_{^3\mathrm{H}}}\times\frac{(ft)_{^3\mathrm{H}}}{(ft)_n} = 5.80\times10^{5}\times1.096 = 6.36\times10^{5} $$

The actual ratio is

$$ \frac{12.32\ \text{yr}}{610\ \mathrm{s}} = \frac{3.888\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{s}}{610\ \mathrm{s}} = 6.37\times10^{5} $$

The difference in half-lives by a factor of $6.4\times10^5$ is completely explained as the product of a $1.10$-fold difference in nuclear structure and a $5.8\times10^5$-fold difference in phase space. The sizes of the contributions become clear when measured in “orders of magnitude.” Of the common logarithm of the half-life ratio, $\log_{10}(6.37\times10^5)=5.80$, phase space accounts for $\log_{10}(5.80\times10^5)=5.76$ and nuclear structure for $\log_{10}1.096=0.04$. That is, of the $5.80$ orders of magnitude, $5.76$ come from phase space, and the share of nuclear structure is only $0.04$ orders of magnitude ($0.7\ \%$ of the total). This is the meaning of “the difference in half-lives is determined not by nuclear structure but by phase space.”

The origin of the phase-space difference is the $Q$ value. The ratio of the $Q$ values is $0.782/0.01859 = 42.1$, and if we apply Sargent’s $Q^5$ rule, valid for $Q\gg m_e$, as it is, we get $42.1^5 = 1.3\times10^8$, which misses the actual $5.8\times10^5$ by a wide margin. This is because the tritium $Q=18.6\ \mathrm{keV}$ is far smaller than $m_e = 511\ \mathrm{keV}$, so the electron lies in the nonrelativistic region and the phase space changes to a different power, $f\propto(W_0-1)^{7/2}$ (the caution in Section 12.3.3 of this book. This power is for the case where the Fermi function $F(Z,W)$ is set to $1$; if the Coulomb correction is included and $F\propto1/\beta$ is used in the low-velocity limit, then $f\propto(W_0-1)^{3}$. For tritium, $\alpha Z/\beta\approx0.06\ll1$, so the $7/2$ approximation suffices). Even so, the conclusion that “the entire difference lies in $f$” does not change.

Verification. We recompute $\tau_n$ of (2) by a completely different route, namely from the ratio to the muon. As in Section 12.3.4 of this book,

$$ \frac{\Gamma_n}{\Gamma_\mu} = 96\,\abs{V_{ud}}^2(1+3\lambda^2)\,f(1+\Delta_R)\left(\frac{m_e}{m_\mu}\right)^5 $$

With $m_e/m_\mu = 4.83632\times10^{-3}$, its fifth power is $2.6459\times10^{-12}$. Hence

$$ \frac{\Gamma_n}{\Gamma_\mu} = 96\times5.57507\times1.754559\times2.6459\times10^{-12} = 2.485\times10^{-9} $$

That is, $\tau_n/\tau_\mu = 4.025\times10^{8}$, and $\tau_n = 4.025\times10^{8}\times2.1873\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{s} = 880\ \mathrm{s}$. This agrees with the $880.3\ \mathrm{s}$ of (2). We also check the dimensions: $[G_F^2m_e^5] = \mathrm{GeV^{-4}}\cdot\mathrm{GeV^5} = \mathrm{GeV}$, and $f$, $\Delta_R$, and $\abs{V_{ud}}^2$ are all dimensionless, so the right-hand side as a whole has the dimension of a decay rate, $\mathrm{GeV}$.

Meaning. The heart of this problem is that “the same $G_F$ and the same physics differ only in the width of the window.” The muon lives $2.2\ \mu\mathrm{s}$, the neutron $878\ \mathrm{s}$, and tritium $12.32$ years. This spread of lifetimes over a factor of about $2\times10^{14}$ comes, almost entirely, not from differences in coupling constants but from $(\text{available energy})^5$. And what is decisive for materials science is the fact that the $Q$ of tritium happens to be only $18.6\ \mathrm{keV}$. If $Q$ were $1\ \mathrm{MeV}$, Sargent’s rule would make the half-life $(18.6/1000)^5 = 2.2\times10^{-9}$ times as long, that is, about 1 second (the $Q^5$ rule holds only for $Q\gg m_e$, so this is merely a guide to the order of magnitude), and handling tritium as a fuel would be impossible in principle. It is thanks to this one $Q$ value that the fusion reactor is something that “might be built.” Similarly, the renormalization of $g_A$ shown in (4) shifts, at the level of $30\ \%$, the values in the half-life tables used to select nuclides for $\beta$ batteries and reduced-activation steels, and the seemingly odd causal chain “the strong interaction determines the speed of the weak interaction” matters in actual materials design.

Exercise 12.5: Unitarity of the CKM matrix and the unitarity triangle

Problem (restated)

Use the values in Table 12.4 and the Wolfenstein parameters $\lambda=0.2250$, $A=0.826$, $\bar\rho=0.159$, $\bar\eta=0.348$.

(1) Check the unitarity of the first row, $\sum_j\abs{V_{uj}}^2$, numerically. How many $\sigma$ is the deviation from $1$ (take the error to be $\pm0.0007$)?

(2) Compute $\abs{V_{cb}}$, $\abs{V_{ub}}$, and $\abs{V_{td}}$ from the Wolfenstein parametrization and compare them with Table 12.4.

(3) Find the three interior angles $\alpha,\beta,\gamma$ of the unitarity triangle from $\bar\rho,\bar\eta$, and verify that they sum to $180^\circ$.

(4) Compute $\sin2\beta$ and compare it with the measured value $0.699\pm0.017$ from $B\to J/\psi K_S$.

(5) Find the Jarlskog invariant $J\simeq A^2\lambda^6\bar\eta$. Also verify that the area of the unnormalized unitarity triangle equals $J/2$ by computing $\abs{V_{cd}V_{cb}}^2\times(\bar\eta/2)$.

Solution

Strategy. For (1), we simply square and add the entries in the first row of Table 12.4. Parts (2) and (5) are substitutions into the Wolfenstein parametrization of Section 12.5.4 of this book. Parts (3) and (4) are elementary geometry of the triangle whose vertices are $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, and $(\bar\rho,\bar\eta)$.

(1) The first row of Table 12.4 reads $\abs{V_{ud}}=0.97373$, $\abs{V_{us}}=0.2243$, and $\abs{V_{ub}}=0.00382$.

$$ \abs{V_{ud}}^2 = (0.97373)^2 = 0.9481501 $$ $$ \abs{V_{us}}^2 = (0.2243)^2 = 0.0503105 $$ $$ \abs{V_{ub}}^2 = (0.00382)^2 = 0.0000146 $$

The sum is

$$ \sum_j\abs{V_{uj}}^2 = 0.9481501+0.0503105+0.0000146 = 0.9984752 $$

The deviation from $1$ is

$$ \Delta = 0.9984752 - 1 = -0.0015248 $$

Dividing by the error $\pm0.0007$ gives

$$ \frac{\abs{\Delta}}{0.0007} = 2.18 $$

That is, it is a $2.2\sigma$ deviation (consistent with the PDG 2022 value $0.9985\pm0.0007$, $2.2\sigma$). This is the unresolved problem known as the Cabibbo angle anomaly. Note that the contribution of $\abs{V_{ub}}^2$ is only $1.5\times10^{-5}$, which is less than $1\ \%$ of the deviation $-1.5\times10^{-3}$. Thus the anomaly is effectively a problem of just two quantities: $\abs{V_{ud}}$ (determined from superallowed $\beta$ decays and neutron decay) and $\abs{V_{us}}$ (determined from $K$ meson decays). Moreover, $\abs{V_{ud}}$ is exactly the quantity we used to compute the neutron lifetime in Exercise 12.4, so the neutron lifetime puzzle and this anomaly are tensions concerning the same physical quantity.

(2) First we construct the basic quantities of the Wolfenstein parametrization.

$$ \lambda^2 = (0.2250)^2 = 0.050625,\qquad \lambda^3 = 0.011390625 $$ $$ A\lambda^2 = 0.826\times0.050625 = 0.0418163,\qquad A\lambda^3 = 0.826\times0.011390625 = 0.00940866 $$

$\abs{V_{cb}}$. In the Wolfenstein parametrization $V_{cb} = A\lambda^2$, so

$$ \abs{V_{cb}} = 0.04182 $$

Compared with the value $0.0408\pm0.0014$ in Table 12.4, the difference is $+0.0010$, that is, $0.7\sigma$.

$\abs{V_{ub}}$. Since $V_{ub} = A\lambda^3(\bar\rho-\ii\bar\eta)$,

$$ \sqrt{\bar\rho^2+\bar\eta^2} = \sqrt{(0.159)^2+(0.348)^2} = \sqrt{0.025281+0.121104} = \sqrt{0.146385} = 0.382603 $$ $$ \abs{V_{ub}} = 0.00940866\times0.382603 = 0.003600 $$

Compared with $0.00382\pm0.00020$ in Table 12.4, this is $-1.1\sigma$. This is sufficient for an approximation that discards terms of order $\lambda^4$ and higher.

$\abs{V_{td}}$. Since $V_{td} = A\lambda^3(1-\bar\rho-\ii\bar\eta)$,

$$ \sqrt{(1-\bar\rho)^2+\bar\eta^2} = \sqrt{(0.841)^2+(0.348)^2} = \sqrt{0.707281+0.121104} = \sqrt{0.828385} = 0.910157 $$ $$ \abs{V_{td}} = 0.00940866\times0.910157 = 0.008563 $$

This agrees with $0.0086\pm0.0002$ in Table 12.4 to within $0.2\sigma$.

All three agree to within about $1\sigma$, confirming that the hierarchical structure of the CKM matrix is captured by the single small parameter $\lambda\simeq0.22$.

(3) The vertices of the normalized unitarity triangle are $(0,0)$, $(1,0)$, and $(\bar\rho,\bar\eta)$. The interior angles can be read off as follows.

$\gamma$ (the angle at the origin). This is the angle subtended at the origin by the vertex $(\bar\rho,\bar\eta)$, so

$$ \tan\gamma = \frac{\bar\eta}{\bar\rho} = \frac{0.348}{0.159} = 2.18868 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \gamma = \arctan(2.18868) = 65.44^\circ $$

$\beta$ (the angle at the point $(1,0)$). The base has length $1$, so the horizontal distance from the right end of the base to the vertex is $1-\bar\rho = 0.841$, and

$$ \tan\beta = \frac{\bar\eta}{1-\bar\rho} = \frac{0.348}{0.841} = 0.413793 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \beta = \arctan(0.413793) = 22.48^\circ $$

$\alpha$ (the angle at the apex). From the sum of the interior angles of a triangle,

$$ \alpha = 180^\circ - \gamma - \beta = 180^\circ - 65.44^\circ - 22.48^\circ = 92.08^\circ $$

The sum is $180.00^\circ$ by definition. This is not a tautology, however. What matters is that $\alpha$, $\beta$, and $\gamma$ are quantities determined independently from completely separate measurements in experiment ($\alpha$ from $B\to\pi\pi,\rho\rho$, $\beta$ from $B\to J/\psi K_S$, and $\gamma$ from the interference in $B\to DK$), and whether the sum of their measured values equals $180^\circ$ is a test of the Standard Model. What we have done here is merely a consistency check: “if we construct three angles from the two numbers $(\bar\rho,\bar\eta)$, their sum is necessarily $180^\circ$.”

(4) From $\beta = 22.48^\circ$ we get $2\beta = 44.96^\circ$.

$$ \sin2\beta = \sin(44.96^\circ) = 0.7066 $$

The difference from the measured value $0.699\pm0.017$ is $0.0076$, that is,

$$ \frac{0.7066-0.699}{0.017} = 0.45\sigma $$

so they agree to within $1\sigma$. Among the direct measurements of $CP$ violation, $\sin2\beta$ is the most precise; it is measured as the time-dependent asymmetry in the rates at which $B$ mesons and anti-$B$ mesons decay to $J/\psi K_S$. It is a nontrivial prediction of the CKM picture that a geometric quantity, “the sine of one angle of a triangle,” appears directly as an asymmetry in the number of events counted at an accelerator.

(5) The Jarlskog invariant.

$$ A^2 = (0.826)^2 = 0.682276,\qquad \lambda^6 = (\lambda^3)^2 = (0.011390625)^2 = 1.297463\times10^{-4} $$ $$ J = A^2\lambda^6\bar\eta = 0.682276\times1.297463\times10^{-4}\times0.348 = 3.081\times10^{-5} $$

This agrees with the experimental value $J = (3.08^{+0.15}_{-0.13})\times10^{-5}$ (PDG 2022).

Relation to the area. We first show the general result. The normalized triangle has a base of length $1$ and a height of $\bar\eta$, so its area is $\bar\eta/2$. The unnormalized triangle is this one enlarged by a factor of $\abs{V_{cd}V_{cb}^*}$, so lengths are multiplied by $\abs{V_{cd}V_{cb}}$ and the area by $\abs{V_{cd}V_{cb}}^2$. That is,

$$ S = \abs{V_{cd}V_{cb}}^2\times\frac{\bar\eta}{2} $$

In the Wolfenstein parametrization $\abs{V_{cd}} = \lambda$ and $\abs{V_{cb}} = A\lambda^2$, so

$$ \abs{V_{cd}V_{cb}}^2 = \left(\lambda\cdot A\lambda^2\right)^2 = A^2\lambda^6 $$ $$ S = A^2\lambda^6\times\frac{\bar\eta}{2} = \frac{A^2\lambda^6\bar\eta}{2} = \frac{J}{2} $$

That is, $S = J/2$ holds identically. We also confirm it numerically.

$$ \abs{V_{cd}V_{cb}} = 0.2250\times0.0418163 = 0.00940866 $$ $$ \abs{V_{cd}V_{cb}}^2 = (0.00940866)^2 = 8.85228\times10^{-5} $$ $$ S = 8.85228\times10^{-5}\times\frac{0.348}{2} = 8.85228\times10^{-5}\times0.174 = 1.5403\times10^{-5} $$

On the other hand, $J/2 = 3.081\times10^{-5}/2 = 1.5403\times10^{-5}$. They agree perfectly.

Verification. We check the angles in (3) against other quantities. $\abs{V_{td}}$ and $\abs{V_{ub}}$ are the lengths of two sides of the triangle (before normalizing by $V_{cd}V_{cb}^*$), and $\sqrt{(1-\bar\rho)^2+\bar\eta^2} = 0.9102$ and $\sqrt{\bar\rho^2+\bar\eta^2} = 0.3826$, computed in (2), are the lengths of the side opposite $\beta$ and the side opposite $\gamma$ in the normalized triangle. Checking the law of sines $\sin\alpha/1 = \sin\beta/0.3826 = \sin\gamma/0.9102$, we find $\sin(22.48^\circ)/0.3826 = 0.38236/0.3826 = 0.99938$ and $\sin(65.44^\circ)/0.9102 = 0.90953/0.9102 = 0.99926$. The common value is $0.9993$ rather than $1$ because the angle opposite the base of length $1$ is $\alpha$; indeed $\sin\alpha = \sin(92.08^\circ) = 0.99933$. The three ratios agree to 4 significant figures, which confirms that (2) and (3) describe the same triangle. Also, the area in (5) is $0.174$ for a triangle with base $1$ and height $\bar\eta=0.348$, and multiplying this by $A^2\lambda^6 = 0.682276\times1.297463\times10^{-4} = 8.8524\times10^{-5}$ gives the same $1.5403\times10^{-5}$.

Meaning. As described in Section 12.5.4 of this book, the unitarity triangle is the “health checkup chart of the Standard Model.” Its three sides and three angles are measured in completely different experiments with different apparatus, and the question is whether they all meet on one and the same triangle. As (5) shows, the area of the triangle is exactly half the magnitude $J$ of $CP$ violation, and the collapse of the triangle (zero area) is equivalent to the conservation of $CP$. And the smallness $J = 3.1\times10^{-5}$—the fact that it is suppressed by $\lambda^6$—is the quantitative basis for the conclusion that the Standard Model alone cannot explain the matter–antimatter asymmetry of the universe (the violation of baryon number symmetry). It falls short of the required asymmetry by about $10$ orders of magnitude. Translated into the language of materials science, this is a refinement problem that asks “can several independent measured quantities be explained simultaneously by a single set of structural parameters?”, and it closely resembles the situation in which a new structure is hiding where the $R$ factor refuses to go down.

Exercise 12.6: Tritium decay and the fuel balance of a fusion reactor

Problem (restated)

Atomic masses $M(^3\mathrm{H})=3.01604928\ \mathrm{u}$, $M(^3\mathrm{He})=3.01602932\ \mathrm{u}$, $1\ \mathrm{u}=931.494\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $N_A=6.022\times10^{23}$, $t_{1/2}=12.32$ years.

(1) Find the $Q$ value in keV. Explain why the electron mass cancels automatically when atomic masses are used.

(2) Find the mean lifetime $\tau$ and the decay rate per year.

(3) Find the specific activity in $\mathrm{Bq/g}$ and $\mathrm{Ci/g}$ ($1\ \mathrm{Ci}=3.7\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{Bq}$).

(4) Taking the mean energy of the $\beta$ ray to be $5.7\ \mathrm{keV}$, find the decay heat in $\mathrm{W/g}$.

(5) Find the mass of tritium consumed per day by a DT reactor with an electrical output of $1\ \mathrm{GW}$ and a thermal efficiency of $40\ \%$ ($Q_{DT}=17.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$).

(6) Let the in-reactor tritium inventory be $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ and the turnover period of the fuel cycle be 1 day. Estimate the extra breeding ratio needed to compensate only for the loss due to decay.

Solution

Strategy. The only entry point of the weak interaction is the $Q$ value in (1); the rest is the exponential decay law and unit conversion. Yet beyond that conversion the fuel balance of a fusion reactor emerges. For the year we use $1\ \text{year} = 3.1557\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}$ (the Julian year).

(1) The difference of the atomic masses is

$$ \Delta M = M(^3\mathrm{H}) - M(^3\mathrm{He}) = 3.01604928 - 3.01602932 = 1.996\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{u} $$ $$ Q = \Delta M\,c^2 = 1.996\times10^{-5}\times931.494\ \mathrm{MeV} = 1.8593\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{MeV} = 18.59\ \mathrm{keV} $$

Why the electron masses cancel. At the level of atomic nuclei, the decay is

$$ {}^3\mathrm{H}\text{(nucleus)} \to {}^3\mathrm{He}\text{(nucleus)} + e^- + \bar\nu_e $$

and the $Q$ value is

$$ Q = M_N(^3\mathrm{H}) - M_N(^3\mathrm{He}) - m_e $$

where $M_N$ is the nuclear mass. However, the masses listed in the table are those of neutral atoms. Neglecting the binding energy,

$$ M(^3\mathrm{H}) = M_N(^3\mathrm{H}) + 1\cdot m_e, \qquad M(^3\mathrm{He}) = M_N(^3\mathrm{He}) + 2\cdot m_e $$

($^3$H has $Z=1$ and so one electron; $^3$He has $Z=2$ and so two electrons.) Substituting these gives

$$ Q = \left[M(^3\mathrm{H})-m_e\right] - \left[M(^3\mathrm{He})-2m_e\right] - m_e = M(^3\mathrm{H}) - M(^3\mathrm{He}) $$

so $m_e$ appears in three places and cancels exactly. This is because counting one extra electron for the daughter nucleus, whose $Z$ has increased by one, corresponds to the one electron created in the decay. In $\beta^-$ decay the atomic mass difference is directly the $Q$ value. (In $\beta^+$ decay one electron of the daughter atom is left over, so $Q = \Delta M - 2m_e$. In electron capture the atomic mass difference is directly $Q$ (less the binding energy of the orbital electron).)

(2) The mean lifetime is

$$ \tau = \frac{t_{1/2}}{\ln2} = \frac{12.32}{0.693147} = 17.774\ \text{yr} $$

The fraction remaining after 1 year is

$$ \ee^{-1/17.774} = \ee^{-0.056262} = 0.945291 $$

Therefore the decay rate per year is

$$ 1 - 0.945291 = 0.05471 = 5.47\ \% $$

That is, even if we do nothing, the tritium decreases by itself by $5.5\ \%$ per year. For the fuel stock of a fusion reactor this is a non-negligible “interest.”

(3) The number of atoms in $1\ \mathrm{g}$ is

$$ N = \frac{N_A}{M} = \frac{6.022\times10^{23}}{3.01605} = 1.9967\times10^{23} $$

Converting the half-life into seconds,

$$ t_{1/2} = 12.32\times3.1557\times10^{7} = 3.8878\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{s} $$

The specific activity (= the decay rate) is

$$ A = \lambda N = \frac{\ln2}{t_{1/2}}N = \frac{0.693147\times1.9967\times10^{23}}{3.8878\times10^{8}} = 3.560\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Bq/g} $$

In curies,

$$ \frac{3.560\times10^{14}}{3.7\times10^{10}} = 9.62\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{Ci/g} $$

That is $9600$ Ci for $1\ \mathrm{g}$. For reference, medical $^{60}$Co sources are in the $10^3$–$10^4$ Ci class, so $1\ \mathrm{g}$ of tritium corresponds to that scale in terms of the amount of radioactivity. However, the $\beta$ ray energy is extremely low (maximum $18.6\ \mathrm{keV}$), the range in air is only about $6\ \mathrm{mm}$, and the rays do not even penetrate the skin, so there is almost no danger from external exposure. The only problem is internal uptake (ingestion or inhalation) (absorption as tritiated water, HTO).

(4) The mean energy carried by the $\beta$ ray is $\bar E_\beta = 5.7\ \mathrm{keV}$ (about $31\ \%$ of $Q$; the rest is carried away by the antineutrino and does not become heat in matter). The heating rate is

$$ P = A\,\bar E_\beta = 3.560\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\times5.7\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{eV}\times1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J/eV} $$ $$ = 3.560\times10^{14}\times9.131\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{J} = 0.325\ \mathrm{W/g} $$

$1\ \mathrm{g}$ of tritium continues to emit $0.33\ \mathrm{W}$. This quantity matters for the thermal design of storage beds and piping, and for assessing the degradation of organic materials (seals, wire insulation) by $\beta$ rays.

(5) The thermal power is

$$ P_{\rm th} = \frac{1\ \mathrm{GW_e}}{0.40} = 2.5\ \mathrm{GW} = 2.5\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{W} $$

The energy per DT reaction is

$$ Q_{DT} = 17.6\ \mathrm{MeV} = 17.6\times10^{6}\times1.602\times10^{-19} = 2.8195\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{J} $$

Therefore the required reaction rate is

$$ \dot N = \frac{2.5\times10^{9}}{2.8195\times10^{-12}} = 8.867\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

Since one tritium atom disappears in each reaction, the mass flow rate is

$$ \dot m_T = \dot N\times\frac{3.016}{N_A} = 8.867\times10^{20}\times\frac{3.016}{6.022\times10^{23}} = 4.441\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{g/s} $$ $$ = 4.441\times10^{-3}\times86400 = 383.7\ \mathrm{g/day} \simeq 140\ \mathrm{kg/year} $$

Considering that the world’s civilian tritium stockpile is only about $20$–$25\ \mathrm{kg}$, the calculation shows that a single reactor would burn through the world’s inventory in 2 months. This is why a reactor must breed its own tritium.

(6) The amount lost to decay in one day from the in-reactor inventory of $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ is

$$ \Delta m = 1000\ \mathrm{g}\times\left(1-\ee^{-\Delta t/\tau}\right), \qquad \frac{\Delta t}{\tau} = \frac{1\ \text{day}}{17.774\times365.25\ \text{days}} = 1.5404\times10^{-4} $$

The exponent is very small, so we may use $1-\ee^{-x}\simeq x$:

$$ \Delta m = 1000\times1.5404\times10^{-4} = 0.154\ \mathrm{g/day} $$

Compared with the daily consumption of $383.7\ \mathrm{g}$,

$$ \frac{0.154}{383.7} = 4.0\times10^{-4} = 0.040\ \% $$

That is, the additional breeding ratio required to compensate for the decay loss alone is only $+0.0004$ in terms of $\mathrm{TBR}$. The actual design requirement is $\mathrm{TBR}\gtrsim1.05$–$1.1$, and the main reasons for the margin are not decay but (i) retention and loss in the recovery and processing steps, (ii) permeation into and retention in structural materials, (iii) neutron leakage and parasitic absorption, and (iv) building up the startup inventory.

The story does not end here, however. The in-reactor inventory of $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ turns over in one day and so is unaffected by decay, but for the out-of-reactor tritium inventory (several kg kept in storage for years as startup and reserve stock), the $5.5\ \%$ per year of (2) applies in full. If $5\ \mathrm{kg}$ is left for one year, $5000\times0.0547 = 274\ \mathrm{g}$ is lost, that is, $0.71$ days’ worth of the reactor’s fuel. Furthermore, in storage materials ($\mathrm{TiT_2}$, $\mathrm{ErT_2}$, etc.) the decay product $^3$He accumulates in the lattice, and, as described in Section 12.8.1 of this book, in a material with $\mathrm{T/M}=1.6$ accelerated release due to helium embrittlement begins after $5.9$ years, when $\mathrm{He/M}\approx0.45$ is reached. The lifetime of the container matters sooner than the loss of the fuel itself.

Verification. We check (3) and (4) by an independent route. Starting from the annual decay rate $5.47\ \%$ of (2), the number of atoms of $1\ \mathrm{g}$ that decay in one year is $1.9967\times10^{23}\times0.0547 = 1.092\times10^{22}$. Dividing this by the number of seconds in a year, $3.1557\times10^{7}$, gives $3.46\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$. This agrees with the $3.560\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{Bq/g}$ of (3) to within $3\ \%$ (the difference is that between the average decay rate over the finite interval of one year and the initial decay rate; since the average is smaller by half of $\lambda\Delta t = 0.0563$, the $2.8\ \%$ difference is as expected). For (5), dividing $140\ \mathrm{kg/year}$ by $1\ \mathrm{GW_e}$: for the annual electric energy of $8.76\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{MWh}$ the fuel is $0.14\ \mathrm{t}$, that is, $63\ \mathrm{MWh_e}$ per $1\ \mathrm{g}$. This is $8$ times that of fission $^{235}$U ($1\ \mathrm{g}$ gives about $24\ \mathrm{MWh_{th}}$, or $8\ \mathrm{MWh_e}$ as electricity), which is reasonable as the ratio $4.1$ of the energy released per nucleon ($3.5\ \mathrm{MeV/nucleon}$ for DT versus $0.85\ \mathrm{MeV/nucleon}$ for fission), multiplied by a factor for the part of the fuel (the deuterium side) that is not counted.

Meaning. This problem is an example in which a single $Q$ value of the weak interaction determines the whole engineering design. $Q = 18.6\ \mathrm{keV}$ gives the half-life of $12.32$ years, which in turn determines the $5.5\ \%$ per year in (2), the specific activity in (3), the decay heat in (4), and the storage-bed lifetime in (6). As we saw in Exercise 12.4 (5), this long half-life comes not from nuclear structure but from the narrowness of the phase space. If $Q$ were $1\ \mathrm{MeV}$, Sargent’s rule would multiply the half-life by $10^{-9}$, and tritium would vanish before we could put it in a container. Conversely, if $Q$ were close to zero, tritium would exist in nature and could have been mined. It is thanks to this one number that nuclear fusion sits in the position of “difficult but not impossible.” And the conclusion shown by (6), that “the real bottleneck is not decay but recovery, permeation, and embrittlement,” makes it clear that materials science is the rate-limiting step in this field.

Exercise 12.7: Nuclide selection for $\beta$ batteries and reduced-activation steels

Problem (restated)

Use the formula $T_{\max}=2T(T+2m_ec^2)/(Mc^2)$ of Section 12.8.2 of this book, with $2m_ec^2=1.022\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(1) For Si ($Mc^2=26162\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $E_d=21\ \mathrm{eV}$), find $T_{\max}$ for $^3$H ($Q=18.6\ \mathrm{keV}$), $^{63}$Ni ($67.0\ \mathrm{keV}$), and $^{147}$Pm ($224.1\ \mathrm{keV}$), and determine whether displacement damage occurs.

(2) What about SiC (C atom: $Mc^2=11178\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $E_d\approx20\ \mathrm{eV}$)? Confirm that lighter atoms are at a disadvantage.

(3) From the specific activity of $^{63}$Ni, $2.08\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{Bq/g}$, and the mean $\beta$ energy of $17.4\ \mathrm{keV}$, find the $\beta$ power, and give the electrical output in $\mathrm{mW/g}$ for a conversion efficiency of $2\ \%$.

(4) Find the integrated energy of that battery ($P\tau$, with $\tau=101.2/\ln2$ years) in $\mathrm{J/g}$, and compare it with a lithium-ion battery ($720\ \mathrm{J/g}$).

(5) Explain quantitatively, using the half-lives in Table 12.9, why Nb is replaced by Ta in reduced-activation steels. Estimate from the half-lives alone the ratio of the residual radioactivity $100$ years after shutdown.

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1) and (2) are substitutions into the given recoil formula and comparisons with the threshold, (3) and (4) are unit conversions, and (5) is the exponential decay law. Physically, this is a situation in which the $Q$ value and half-life fixed by the weak interaction collide directly with engineering criteria: the displacement threshold energy of the material and the waste classification.

(1) We put $T = Q$ (the maximum kinetic energy of the $\beta$ ray) into the formula. Since $T\ll2m_ec^2$, the quantity in parentheses is almost $1.022\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

$^3$H ($T=0.0186\ \mathrm{MeV}$).

$$ T_{\max} = \frac{2\times0.0186\times(0.0186+1.022)}{26162} = \frac{2\times0.0186\times1.0406}{26162} = \frac{0.038711}{26162} = 1.480\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

That is, $T_{\max} = 1.48\ \mathrm{eV}$, which is only one part in $14$ of $E_d = 21\ \mathrm{eV}$. No displacement damage.

$^{63}$Ni ($T=0.0670\ \mathrm{MeV}$).

$$ T_{\max} = \frac{2\times0.0670\times1.0890}{26162} = \frac{0.145926}{26162} = 5.578\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{MeV} = 5.58\ \mathrm{eV} $$

This is $27\ \%$ of $E_d$. No displacement damage.

$^{147}$Pm ($T=0.2241\ \mathrm{MeV}$).

$$ T_{\max} = \frac{2\times0.2241\times1.2461}{26162} = \frac{0.558506}{26162} = 2.135\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{MeV} = 21.35\ \mathrm{eV} $$

This slightly exceeds $E_d = 21\ \mathrm{eV}$. That is, the $\beta$ rays of $^{147}$Pm can knock Si atoms off their lattice sites, although only a very small portion near the endpoint of the spectrum can do so. Displacement damage occurs (just above threshold). In fact, in a $^{147}$Pm battery, the decline in conversion efficiency due to lattice damage is added to the decline in output due to the half-life ($2.62$ years), so it is hard to extend the design lifetime. By contrast, $^{63}$Ni ($t_{1/2}=101$ years) causes no damage and can be used stably on the order of $10$ years. What the $2$-line kinematics determines is the part of this concerning “whether damage sets in or not”; the main cause of the output falling within a few years is the half-life itself.

(2) In the formula the only nuclide-dependent part is the numerator, so if only the target is changed, $T_{\max}$ is proportional to $1/Mc^2$. The ratio of the C atom to the Si atom is

$$ \frac{Mc^2(\mathrm{Si})}{Mc^2(\mathrm{C})} = \frac{26162}{11178} = 2.340 $$

Therefore $T_{\max}$ for the C atom is obtained by multiplying the values in (1) by $2.340$.

Table E.12.2 Maximum recoil energy for different target atoms
Nuclide$Q$ [keV]$T_{\max}$ (Si, $E_d=21\ \mathrm{eV}$)$T_{\max}$ (C, $E_d\approx20\ \mathrm{eV}$)
$^3\mathrm{H}$$18.6$$1.48\ \mathrm{eV}$ (no damage)$3.46\ \mathrm{eV}$ (no damage)
$^{63}\mathrm{Ni}$$67.0$$5.58\ \mathrm{eV}$ (no damage)$13.1\ \mathrm{eV}$ (no damage)
$^{147}\mathrm{Pm}$$224.1$$21.35\ \mathrm{eV}$ (above threshold)$49.96\ \mathrm{eV}$ (damage)

$^{63}$Ni is safe for C as well, with $13.1\ \mathrm{eV} < 20\ \mathrm{eV}$, but $^{147}$Pm reaches $50\ \mathrm{eV}$, $2.5$ times the threshold, which is far more serious than in the case of Si. The lighter the atom, the more easily it recoils and the more easily it is displaced. This is simply the kinematics of a head-on collision (the lighter the target, the larger the velocity it receives), and it comes down to the dependence $T_{\max}\propto1/M$.

This does not mean, however, that SiC is unsuitable for $\beta$ batteries. It is at a disadvantage in that C is displaced, but thanks to its wide gap ($3.3\ \mathrm{eV}$) it has the advantages that (i) the reverse leakage current is small and the conversion efficiency is high, and (ii) the decrease of the minority-carrier lifetime caused by the resulting defects is not as fatal as in Si. The design is decided by the balance between the kinematic disadvantage and the advantage in electronic properties.

(3) The thermal power emitted as $\beta$ rays is

$$ P_\beta = A\,\bar E_\beta = 2.08\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\times17.4\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{eV}\times1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J/eV} $$ $$ = 2.08\times10^{12}\times2.7875\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{J} = 5.798\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{W/g} = 5.80\ \mathrm{mW/g} $$

At a conversion efficiency of $2\ \%$, the electrical power is

$$ P_{\rm el} = 0.02\times5.80 = 0.116\ \mathrm{mW/g} $$

That is, $1\ \mathrm{g}$ of $^{63}$Ni gives $0.12\ \mathrm{mW}$. This is only $10^{-4}$ of the power density of a lithium-ion battery ($\sim1\ \mathrm{W/g}$).

(4) The mean lifetime is

$$ \tau = \frac{101.2}{\ln2} = \frac{101.2}{0.693147} = 146.0\ \text{yr} = 146.0\times3.1557\times10^{7} = 4.607\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s} $$

The cumulative energy is

$$ E_{\rm tot} = P_{\rm el}\,\tau = 1.16\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{W/g}\times4.607\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s} = 5.34\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J/g} $$

The ratio to the lithium-ion battery is

$$ \frac{5.34\times10^{5}}{720} = 742 $$

That is, the cumulative energy is $740$ times larger, and the power is $10^{-4}$ times as large. (If $P_{\rm el}$ is rounded to $1.2\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{W/g}$, we get $5.5\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J/g}$ and $770$ times, the values in the hint in the main text; if it is rounded to one significant figure, $1\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{W/g}$, we get $4.6\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J/g}$ and $640$ times. The result varies by about $2$ parts in ten (20%) depending on the rounding, so it suffices to understand it as “$5\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J/g}$, of the order of $10^{3}$ times.”)

This extreme trade-off determines where $\beta$ batteries are useful: ultralow power consumption (the $\mu\mathrm{W}$ class) over an ultralong period (several decades) in places where replacement is impossible—cardiac pacemakers, backups for deep-space probes, buried sensors, and power sources for MEMS. As long as the average power meets the requirement, they are unmatched by any other battery in capacity. Note also that real systems have moments that require peak power, so a configuration is adopted in which a capacitor is charged slowly by the $\beta$ battery and discharged intermittently.

(5) According to Table 12.9, Nb produces $^{94}$Nb ($t_{1/2}=2.0\times10^{4}$ years) under neutron irradiation, and Ta produces $^{182}$Ta ($t_{1/2}=114$ days). We estimate the surviving fraction $100$ years after shutdown from the half-lives alone.

$^{94}$Nb.

$$ \frac{N(100\ \text{yr})}{N(0)} = 2^{-100/(2.0\times10^{4})} = 2^{-0.005} = 0.99654 $$

Even after $100$ years, $99.65\ \%$ remains. On the human time scale it does not decrease at all.

$^{182}$Ta. Since $100$ years $= 36525$ days, the number of half-lives that elapse is

$$ \frac{36525}{114} = 320.4 $$ $$ \frac{N(100\ \text{yr})}{N(0)} = 2^{-320.4}, \qquad \log_{10}2^{-320.4} = -320.4\times0.30103 = -96.4 $$

That is, $10^{-96}$. It disappears completely. (In reality the number of atoms is finite, so the last atom has decayed away long before $10^{-96}$ is reached: for $1\ \mathrm{kg}$ of Ta, the $10^{24}$ atoms fall below $1$ after $80$ half-lives, about $25$ years, and the last atom has decayed away.)

The ratio of the residual radioactivities is

$$ \frac{A_{^{94}\mathrm{Nb}}(100\ \text{yr})}{A_{^{182}\mathrm{Ta}}(100\ \text{yr})} \sim \frac{0.9965}{10^{-96}} \sim 10^{96} $$

a difference so large that comparing the two is itself meaningless. Merely replacing the element with a heavier one in the same group changes the waste category after $100$ years from “geological disposal” to “shallow land burial or reusable.” This is the design principle of reduced-activation ferritic/martensitic steels (RAFM), and it is the reason why Japan’s F82H (Fe–8Cr–2W–0.2V–0.04Ta) and Europe’s EUROFER97 (Fe–9Cr–1.1W–0.2V–0.12Ta) replace the Mo and Nb of ordinary heat-resistant steels (such as modified 9Cr–1Mo steel) with W and Ta.

Metallurgically, this substitution is a natural one. W is in the same group as Mo (Group 6) and plays the same roles of solid-solution strengthening and precipitation of $\mathrm{M_{23}C_6}$ carbides. Ta is in the same group as Nb (Group 5) and forms MX-type carbonitrides, which refine the grains and are responsible for the creep strength. Simply moving down one row in the same column of the periodic table swaps only the activation properties while almost preserving the mechanical properties. At the same time, impurity control becomes strict: Nb must be $1\ \mathrm{ppm}$ or less, Mo $10\ \mathrm{ppm}$ or less, and Ni $50\ \mathrm{ppm}$ or less. This is because a few ppm that get mixed in from refractories and scrap at the steelmaking stage can change the waste category after $100$ years.

Verification. We compare the result of (1) with the common-sense nonrelativistic limit. In a nonrelativistic head-on elastic collision, the maximum energy that a particle of mass $m$ gives to a stationary target of mass $M$ is $T_{\max} = 4(m/M)T$. Inserting $T = 67\ \mathrm{keV}$ for $^{63}$Ni, $m_ec^2 = 511\ \mathrm{keV}$, and $Mc^2 = 26162\ \mathrm{MeV}$ gives $4\times(0.511/26162)\times67\ \mathrm{keV} = 5.23\ \mathrm{eV}$. This agrees with the relativistic formula’s $5.58\ \mathrm{eV}$ to $7\ \%$ (the difference is the relativistic correction $T/2m_ec^2 = 0.066$). The formula $2T(T+2m_ec^2)/Mc^2$ reduces, for $T\ll m_ec^2$, to $2T\cdot2m_ec^2/Mc^2 = 4(m_e/M)T$, so it is also correct in structure. For (4), we check by another path, the “extracted energy per atom.” The $\beta$ energy that $1$ $^{63}$Ni atom emits during its lifetime is $17.4\ \mathrm{keV}$, and $2\ \%$ of it becomes electricity, so $348\ \mathrm{eV} = 348\times1.602\times10^{-19} = 5.575\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{J}$. The number of atoms in $1\ \mathrm{g}$ is $6.022\times10^{23}/63 = 9.56\times10^{21}$, so $E_{\rm tot} = 9.56\times10^{21}\times5.575\times10^{-17} = 5.33\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J/g}$. This agrees with the $5.34\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{J/g}$ of (4) to $0.3\ \%$ (the residual arises because the given specific activity $2.08\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{Bq/g}$ differs by $0.25\ \%$ from $N/\tau = 9.56\times10^{21}/4.607\times10^{9} = 2.075\times10^{12}\ \mathrm{Bq/g}$).

Meaning. (1)(2) and (5) seem to deal with entirely different matters, but both have the structure that “numbers fixed by the weak interaction (the $Q$ value and the half-life) are compared directly with numbers of the material (the displacement threshold $E_d$ and the $100$ years of the waste criterion).” In the former, the relative size of $T_{\max}$ and $E_d$ decides the lifetime of the battery; in the latter, the relative size of $t_{1/2}$ and $100$ years decides the alloy composition. In both cases the two numbers being compared come from entirely different physics. One is $G_F$ and nuclear structure; the other is the binding energy of the crystal or a societal time scale. The $\Gamma\propto G_F^2Q^5$ that appears in particle physics textbooks turns into two practical documents: the nuclide selection table for $\beta$ batteries and the impurity specification table of a steelworks. This is the clearest example of “why materials scientists should learn particle physics.”

Exercise 12.8: Partial widths of the $Z$ boson, the number of generations, and the weak charge

Problem (restated)

$m_Z = 91.1876\ \mathrm{GeV}$, $\sin^2\theta_W=0.2312$, $\alpha_s(m_Z)=0.118$.

(1) Find the common factor $G_Fm_Z^3/(6\pi\sqrt2)$ in MeV.

(2) Using Table 12.5, find $\Gamma(Z\to\nu\bar\nu)$ (one species) and $\Gamma(Z\to e^+e^-)$.

(3) Multiply the hadronic widths ($u,c$ and $d,s,b$) by the QCD correction $(1+\alpha_s/\pi)$ and find the total width $\Gamma_Z$. Compare it with the measured value $2495.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(4) Find $N_\nu$ from the measured invisible width $499.0\ \mathrm{MeV}$. If there were a fourth neutrino, what would $\Gamma_Z$ be? How many times the measurement error $\pm2.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is the deviation?

(5) Find the weak charge $Q_W$ of $^{133}$Cs ($Z=55$, $N=78$). Also explain why $Q_W\approx-N$.

(6) Find the weak charge of the proton, $Q_W^p = 1-4\sin^2\theta_W$. When $\sin^2\theta_W$ changes by $1\ \%$, $Q_W^p$ changes by how many $\%$?

Solution

Strategy. We sum $\Gamma(Z\to f\bar f) = G_Fm_Z^3N_c^f\left[(c_V^f)^2+(c_A^f)^2\right]/(6\pi\sqrt2)$, derived in Section 12.6.3 of this book, over all channels using the $c_V^2+c_A^2$ of Table 12.5. Parts (5) and (6) are substitutions into the weak-charge formula $Q_W = Z(1-4\sin^2\theta_W)-N$.

(1) We build $m_Z^3$ step by step.

$$ m_Z^2 = (91.1876)^2 = 8315.17\ \mathrm{GeV^2}, \qquad m_Z^3 = 8315.17\times91.1876 = 7.58241\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{GeV^3} $$

The denominator is

$$ 6\pi\sqrt2 = 6\times3.141593\times1.414214 = 26.6573 $$

Therefore

$$ \frac{G_Fm_Z^3}{6\pi\sqrt2} = \frac{1.1663788\times10^{-5}\times7.58241\times10^{5}}{26.6573} = \frac{8.84396}{26.6573} = 0.331765\ \mathrm{GeV} = 331.77\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

This $331.77\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is the common factor of all the partial widths. Below we denote it by $K$.

(2) We use the $c_V^2+c_A^2$ of Table 12.5.

Neutrino (one species). Since $T_3=+1/2$ and $Q=0$, we have $c_V = 1/2 - 0 = 0.5$, $c_A = 0.5$, and $c_V^2+c_A^2 = 0.5$. The color factor is $N_c=1$.

$$ \Gamma(Z\to\nu\bar\nu) = 331.77\times0.5000 = 165.9\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

Charged leptons. Since $T_3=-1/2$ and $Q=-1$,

$$ c_V = -\frac12 - 2\times(-1)\times0.2312 = -0.5+0.4624 = -0.0376, \qquad c_A = -0.5 $$ $$ c_V^2+c_A^2 = 0.001414+0.25 = 0.251414 $$ $$ \Gamma(Z\to e^+e^-) = 331.77\times0.251414 = 83.4\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

This is $0.7\ \%$ smaller than the measured $83.98\pm0.09\ \mathrm{MeV}$. For a tree-level calculation, this is excellent.

(3) For the quarks as well, we use the values of Table 12.5. We multiply by the color factor $N_c=3$.

$$ u,c,t:\quad c_V = \frac12-2\times\frac23\times0.2312 = 0.19173,\quad c_A=0.5,\quad c_V^2+c_A^2 = 0.28676 $$ $$ d,s,b:\quad c_V = -\frac12-2\times\left(-\frac13\right)\times0.2312 = -0.34587,\quad c_A=-0.5,\quad c_V^2+c_A^2 = 0.36962 $$

Multiplying by the color factor gives

$$ N_c(c_V^2+c_A^2)\Big|_{u} = 3\times0.28676 = 0.8603, \qquad N_c(c_V^2+c_A^2)\Big|_{d} = 3\times0.36962 = 1.1089 $$

The quarks lighter than the $Z$ are two species, $u,c$, and three species, $d,s,b$ (the $t$ cannot be produced in the decay because $m_t = 173\ \mathrm{GeV} > m_Z$), so the tree-level hadronic width is

$$ \Gamma_{\rm had}^{\rm tree} = K\times\left(2\times0.8603 + 3\times1.1089\right) = 331.77\times(1.7206+3.3267) = 331.77\times5.0473 = 1674.5\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The QCD correction is

$$ 1+\frac{\alpha_s}{\pi} = 1+\frac{0.118}{3.141593} = 1.03756 $$ $$ \Gamma_{\rm had} = 1674.5\times1.03756 = 1737.4\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

Adding the three charged leptons and the three neutrinos,

$$ \Gamma_Z = 3\times83.4 + 3\times165.9 + 1737.4 = 250.2 + 497.7 + 1737.4 = 2485.3\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The difference from the measured $2495.2\pm2.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is

$$ \frac{2485.3-2495.2}{2495.2} = -0.40\ \% $$

A pencil-and-paper tree-level calculation reproduces the total width of the $Z$ boson to $0.4\ \%$. Converted to a lifetime, $\tau_Z = \hbar/\Gamma_Z = (6.582\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{GeV\,s})/(2.4853\ \mathrm{GeV}) = 2.65\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{s}$.

(4) We divide the invisible width by the Standard Model value per neutrino species, $167.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$ (the tree-level $165.9$ of (2) with higher-order corrections included; it is $1/3$ of the Standard Model prediction $\Gamma_{\rm inv}^{\rm SM}=501.4\ \mathrm{MeV}$).

$$ N_\nu = \frac{499.0}{167.2} = 2.98 $$

There are only three species of neutrinos that are lighter than the $Z$ and couple to the $Z$ in the standard way. This agrees with the official value from the combination of the four LEP experiments, $N_\nu = 2.984\pm0.008$. The shortfall of about $2\sigma$ from $3$ has been discussed for many years; it was found to originate in the treatment of the LEP luminosity (Bhabha scattering), and the value incorporating its 2020 reevaluation is $2.9963\pm0.0074$, consistent with $3$.

If there were a fourth neutrino, the total width would increase by $167.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

$$ \Gamma_Z(N_\nu=4) = 2495.2 + 167.2 = 2662.4\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

Compared with the measurement error $\pm2.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$,

$$ \frac{167.2}{2.3} = 72.7 $$

that is, a deviation of $72\sigma$. Statistically, it is completely excluded. One should savor the strength of this conclusion. It is not that “we searched for a fourth neutrino and did not find it”; rather, “when we measured how fast the $Z$ decays, the number $3$ was written there.” Note also that the sterile neutrinos treated in Chapter 14 of this book can escape this constraint precisely because they do not couple to the $Z$.

(5) We substitute into the weak-charge formula.

$$ 1-4\sin^2\theta_W = 1-4\times0.2312 = 1-0.9248 = 0.0752 $$ $$ Q_W(^{133}\mathrm{Cs}) = 55\times0.0752 - 78 = 4.136 - 78 = -73.86 $$

The Standard Model prediction (including radiative corrections) is $-73.23\pm0.01$ and the measurement is $-72.82\pm0.42$, which agree to $1\ \%$ precision.

Why $Q_W\approx-N$. The proton’s contribution carries the coefficient $(1-4\sin^2\theta_W) = 0.0752$, which is small, $0.075$, rather than $1$. The reason it is small is that $\sin^2\theta_W$ happens to be close to $1/4$. If $\sin^2\theta_W$ were exactly $0.25$, then $1-4\times0.25 = 0$ and the proton would have no weak charge at all. The neutron’s contribution, on the other hand, carries the coefficient $-1$ (the weak charge of the neutron is exactly $-1$). Therefore

$$ Q_W = Z\times0.0752 - N \approx -N $$

In $^{133}$Cs, the contribution of $Z$, $+4.14$, is only $5\ \%$ of the contribution of $N$, $-78$. The neutron, which is electrically neutral, couples $13$ times more strongly than the proton to the weak interaction. The fact that “electric charge” and “weak charge” are entirely different quantities is condensed into this single line.

Let us check at the quark level. The proton is $uud$ and the neutron is $udd$. The vector couplings $c_V$ to the $Z$ are $+0.1917$ for $u$ and $-0.3459$ for $d$, so (in the normalization where the weak charge is multiplied by $2$)

$$ Q_W^p \propto 2c_V^u + c_V^d = 2\times0.19173 - 0.34587 = 0.03760, \qquad Q_W^n \propto c_V^u + 2c_V^d = 0.19173 - 0.69173 = -0.50000 $$

The ratio is $0.03760/(-0.50000) = -0.0752$. That is, $Q_W^p/Q_W^n = -(1-4\sin^2\theta_W)$; indeed, substituting $c_V^u = 1/2-(4/3)\sin^2\theta_W$ and $c_V^d = -1/2+(2/3)\sin^2\theta_W$ yields identically $2c_V^u+c_V^d = 1/2-2\sin^2\theta_W$ and $c_V^u+2c_V^d = -1/2$. The difference is whether the $c_V$ of $u$ and $d$ almost cancel each other or add with the same sign.

(6) The weak charge of the proton is

$$ Q_W^p = 1-4\sin^2\theta_W = 0.0752 $$

A $1\ \%$ change of $\sin^2\theta_W$ means $\Delta(\sin^2\theta_W) = 0.01\times0.2312 = 0.002312$. The change of $Q_W^p$ is

$$ \Delta Q_W^p = -4\times0.002312 = -0.009248 $$

The relative change is

$$ \frac{\abs{\Delta Q_W^p}}{Q_W^p} = \frac{0.009248}{0.0752} = 0.1230 = 12.3\ \% $$

That is, a $1\ \%$ change of $\sin^2\theta_W$ is amplified to $12\ \%$ in the weak charge of the proton. In general, the relative sensitivity of $Q_W^p$ is

$$ \frac{\dd\ln Q_W^p}{\dd\ln\sin^2\theta_W} = \frac{-4\sin^2\theta_W}{1-4\sin^2\theta_W} = \frac{-0.9248}{0.0752} = -12.3 $$

“Measuring a small quantity” turns directly into “having high relative sensitivity.” The Qweak experiment at Jefferson Lab used this amplification to measure the weak charge of the proton directly and obtained $Q_W^p = 0.0719\pm0.0045$ (Standard Model: $0.0708$).

Verification. We check the total width of (3) from another angle. Computing the ratio of the hadronic width to the total width (the hadronic fraction) gives $\Gamma_{\rm had}/\Gamma_Z = 1737.4/2485.3 = 0.699$, and the measured value is $1744.4/2495.2 = 0.699$. They agree. Also, $R_\ell \equiv \Gamma_{\rm had}/\Gamma_{\ell} = 1737.4/83.4 = 20.83$, which agrees with the measured $20.77$ to $0.3\ \%$ (this $R_\ell$ is one of the main measured quantities that determine $\alpha_s(m_Z)$). As for dimensions, $[G_F m_Z^3] = \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}\cdot\mathrm{GeV^3} = \mathrm{GeV}$, and since $c_V^2+c_A^2$ and $N_c$ are dimensionless, the right-hand side correctly has the dimension of a width. The $Q_W$ of (5) is a dimensionless number, as it should be, since it comes from the counting of $Z$ and $N$.

Meaning. What this problem shows is that “from a single coupling structure, $c_V = T_3-2Q\sin^2\theta_W$ and $c_A = T_3$, the lifetime of the $Z$ comes out within $0.4\ \%$, and we can even read off the number of neutrino species.” The $N_\nu=3$ of (4) is a conclusion reached not by searching directly for new particles at an accelerator but by precisely measuring the decay rate of known particles, and it is one of the most brilliant lines of argument in physics: “counting the invisible by subtracting what is visible.” Parts (5) and (6) have an even wider range of application. The “coincidence” that $\sin^2\theta_W$ is close to $1/4$ produces $c_V\approx0$ for the charged leptons and $Q_W^p\approx0$ for the proton, and in both cases amplifies the sensitivity to $\sin^2\theta_W$ by a factor of $10$ or more. This is a general rule of measurement technique. “Measuring the difference of two nearly canceling quantities” gives something small in absolute value but extremely high in relative sensitivity. The same idea appears in every setting of condensed-matter measurements: differential measurements, bridge circuits, lock-in detection, and diffraction experiments that measure weak reflections close to an extinction rule. And the $Z^3$ rule of Section 12.6.4 of this book (the heavier the atom, the more favorable) is precisely a materials choice: “choosing a medium that amplifies the signal.”

Exercise 12.9: “The weak force is not weak” — The crossover point and the breakdown of the effective theory

Problem (restated)

$g_w=0.6529$, $e=0.30282$, $m_W=80.377\ \mathrm{GeV}$, $G_F=1.1663788\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$.

(1) Find the $q$ at which the amplitude ratio $\mathcal{M}_{\rm weak}/\mathcal{M}_{\rm EM} = [g_w^2/(q^2+m_W^2)]/[e^2/q^2]$ equals $1$.

(2) Find, in fm, the $r$ at which $(\alpha_w/\alpha)\ee^{-m_Wr}=1$ in position space.

(3) Find the limiting value of the ratio as $q\to\infty$.

(4) Find the $\sqrt s$ at which the Fermi-theory cross section $\sigma = G_F^2s/\pi$ violates the $s$-wave unitarity bound $\sigma\le4\pi/s$. State the meaning of the fact that this number is larger than $m_W$.

(5) Redo the correspondence table of Table 12.12 yourself, and explain to which part of which equation each of the correspondences “$W$ boson $\leftrightarrow$ phonon,” “$G_F\leftrightarrow$ BCS $-V$,” and “$\sqrt s\sim m_W\leftrightarrow\omega\sim\omega_D$” corresponds. Also state what the breakdown of BCS theory at $\lambda\gtrsim0.5$, which makes Eliashberg theory necessary, and the breakdown of Fermi theory at $\sqrt s\sim700\ \mathrm{GeV}$, which makes electroweak theory necessary, have in common mathematically.

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1)–(3) examine the competition between the propagators $1/(q^2+m_W^2)$ and $1/q^2$, both in momentum space and in position space. In (4) we find the crossing point between the cross section, which keeps growing in proportion to $s$, and the unitarity upper limit, which decreases as $1/s$. Part (5) is a matching of the structure of the formulas. Note that for a spacelike momentum transfer $q^2 < 0$, but the notation of this problem writes $q^2$ for $Q^2 = -q^2 > 0$ (the square of the Euclidean momentum transfer); this is why the denominator of the propagator has the positive sign $q^2+m_W^2$.

(1) Set the ratio equal to $1$.

$$ \frac{g_w^2}{q^2+m_W^2} = \frac{e^2}{q^2} $$

Multiplying both sides by $q^2(q^2+m_W^2)$, we obtain

$$ g_w^2q^2 = e^2\left(q^2+m_W^2\right) \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \left(g_w^2-e^2\right)q^2 = e^2m_W^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q^2 = \frac{e^2m_W^2}{g_w^2-e^2} $$

Inserting the numbers:

$$ e^2 = (0.30282)^2 = 0.0917000, \qquad g_w^2 = (0.6529)^2 = 0.4262784 $$ $$ m_W^2 = (80.377)^2 = 6460.46\ \mathrm{GeV^2} $$ $$ e^2m_W^2 = 0.0917000\times6460.46 = 592.42\ \mathrm{GeV^2} $$ $$ g_w^2-e^2 = 0.4262784-0.0917000 = 0.3345784 $$ $$ q^2 = \frac{592.42}{0.3345784} = 1770.7\ \mathrm{GeV^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad q = 42.08\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

That is, at a momentum transfer of $42\ \mathrm{GeV}$, the magnitudes of the weak and electromagnetic amplitudes become equal. Note that this is well below $m_W = 80.4\ \mathrm{GeV}$. Because the coupling is $4.6$ times stronger, the weak amplitude catches up before the energy reaches the mass of the $W$.

(2) In position space, the ratio of the Yukawa potentials is

$$ \frac{V_{\rm weak}(r)}{V_{\rm EM}(r)} = \frac{\alpha_w\ee^{-m_Wr}/r}{\alpha/r} = \frac{\alpha_w}{\alpha}\ee^{-m_Wr} $$

(the $1/r$ cancels). Setting this equal to $1$ gives

$$ \ee^{-m_Wr} = \frac{\alpha}{\alpha_w} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad m_Wr = \ln\frac{\alpha_w}{\alpha} $$

If we recompute $\alpha_w/\alpha = g_w^2/e^2$ of Exercise 12.1 (2) with the rounded values $g_w=0.6529$ and $e=0.30282$ given in this problem, we get $0.4262784/0.0917000 = 4.6486$ (the difference of $4\times10^{-5}$ from the $4.6484$ of Exercise 12.1 is due to the rounding of the inputs). Therefore

$$ m_Wr = \ln(4.6486) = 1.5366 $$

Multiplying by $R_W = 1/m_W = 2.455\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}$, we obtain

$$ r = 1.5366\times2.455\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm} = 3.772\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm} $$

That is, the crossing distance is only $1.54$ times $R_W$. At shorter distances the weak force is stronger, and at longer distances the electromagnetic force wins. The distance $3.8\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}$ is $1/220$ of the proton radius and $10^{-8}$ times the atomic radius, far smaller than any scale of everyday matter. We feel that “the weak force is weak” because we live far outside this boundary.

(3) As $q\to\infty$, the $m_W^2$ in the denominator becomes negligible, so

$$ \lim_{q\to\infty}\frac{\mathcal{M}_{\rm weak}}{\mathcal{M}_{\rm EM}} = \lim_{q\to\infty}\frac{g_w^2/(q^2+m_W^2)}{e^2/q^2} = \frac{g_w^2}{e^2}\lim_{q\to\infty}\frac{q^2}{q^2+m_W^2} = \frac{g_w^2}{e^2} = \frac{0.4262784}{0.0917000} = 4.649 $$

In the high-energy limit the mass of the $W$ becomes “invisible,” and the weak interaction behaves as a force $4.65$ times stronger than the electromagnetic interaction. Once the mass in the propagator no longer matters, all that remains is the ratio of the bare coupling constants. The $13\ \mathrm{TeV}$ collisions at the LHC lie entirely in this regime, where the name “weak interaction” is completely inappropriate.

(4) In Fermi theory, the cross section of the contact interaction is fixed by dimensional analysis alone. Since $[\sigma] = \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$ and $[G_F^2] = \mathrm{GeV^{-4}}$, the remaining factor must have dimension $\mathrm{GeV^2}$, that is, it must be $s$. Hence $\sigma\simeq G_F^2s/\pi$. On the other hand, the partial-wave amplitude of the $s$ wave ($\ell=0$) has an upper limit from unitarity, $\sigma\le4\pi/s$. The former grows in proportion to $s$, while the latter decreases as $1/s$. They must cross somewhere.

$$ \frac{G_F^2s}{\pi} = \frac{4\pi}{s} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad s^2 = \frac{4\pi^2}{G_F^2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad s = \frac{2\pi}{G_F} $$

Inserting the numbers,

$$ s = \frac{2\times3.141593}{1.1663788\times10^{-5}} = 5.387\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{GeV^2} $$ $$ \sqrt s = \sqrt{5.387\times10^{5}} = 734.0\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

The meaning of this number being larger than $m_W$. The value $\sqrt s = 734\ \mathrm{GeV}$ is $9$ times $m_W = 80.4\ \mathrm{GeV}$. That is, well before Fermi theory reaches its own contradiction (a probability exceeding $1$), the $W$ boson appears as a real particle, and the contact approximation itself is resolved naturally. As the energy is raised, the $q^2$ in the denominator of the propagator begins to matter at $\sqrt s\sim m_W$, and the cross section stops growing in proportion to $s$ and turns to decrease like $\sigma\sim g_w^4/(16\pi s)$. The unitarity crisis does not occur.

This is the way of effective theories. An effective theory tells us by itself when it will break down (the upper limit $\sqrt s\sim734\ \mathrm{GeV}$), but in practice it is handed over to its successor theory at a lower energy. Historically the logic was used in the opposite direction. The argument “there must be something new below $700\ \mathrm{GeV}$” demanded the existence of the $W$ boson, and the same argument (unitarity of $WW$ scattering) demanded a Higgs boson below $1\ \mathrm{TeV}$. Both were right. The violation of unitarity is not a defect of a theory but a device for predicting new particles.

(5) We refill the three columns of Table 12.12 from the viewpoint of which part of each formula corresponds to which.

Table E.12.3: Three examples of “eliminating a heavy boson to obtain a contact interaction” (correspondence of the formulas)
ItemWeak interactionScreening in metalsBCS superconductivity
Exchanged field$W$ bosonPolarization of the electron gas (plasmon)Phonon
Propagator (full form)$\dfrac{1}{q^2-m_W^2}$$\dfrac{4\pi e^2}{q^2+k_{\rm TF}^2}$$\abs{g_\qq}^2\dfrac{2\omega_\qq}{\omega^2-\omega_\qq^2}$
Term dropped$q^2$$q^2$$\omega^2$
Expansion parameter$q^2/m_W^2$$q^2/k_{\rm TF}^2$$\omega^2/\omega_\qq^2$
Low-energy limit (contact constant)$-\dfrac{1}{m_W^2}\ \Rightarrow\ \dfrac{G_F}{\sqrt2}=\dfrac{g_w^2}{8m_W^2}$$\dfrac{4\pi e^2}{k_{\rm TF}^2}=\dfrac{1}{N(E_F)}$$-\dfrac{2\abs{g_\qq}^2}{\omega_\qq}\equiv-V$
Window where the approximation works$\sqrt s\ll m_W$$q\ll k_{\rm TF}$$\abs{\omega}<\omega_D$
Scale of breakdown$\sqrt s\sim m_W$ (formal upper limit $734\ \mathrm{GeV}$)$q\sim k_{\rm TF}$$\omega\sim\omega_D$ (effectively $\lambda\gtrsim0.5$)
Successor theoryElectroweak theory $SU(2)_L\times U(1)_Y$Dynamical screening $\epsilon(\qq,\omega)$ (RPA)Eliashberg theory

“$W$ boson $\leftrightarrow$ phonon.” Both are “mediator bosons with a finite energy scale.” The phonon frequency $\omega_\qq$ enters the denominator of the propagator as $-\omega_\qq^2$ in exactly the same place where the mass $m_W$ of the $W$ enters it as $-m_W^2$. It is also common to both that a pole of the propagator represents a real particle (the $W$ boson / the phonon).

“$G_F\leftrightarrow$ the $-V$ of BCS.” Both are “the constant that remains as a result of dropping the $q^2$ ($\omega^2$) in the denominator.” The replacement $1/(q^2-m_W^2)\to-1/m_W^2$ of Section 12.1.3 of this book and the replacement $2\omega_\qq/(\omega^2-\omega_\qq^2)\to-2/\omega_\qq$ are exactly the same one-line operation. And the consequence “a constant propagator = independent of momentum = a $\delta$ function in position space = a contact interaction” is also common to both. In the same sense that $G_F$ is the strength of Fermi’s four-fermion contact interaction, $-V$ is the strength of the contact attraction in the BCS Hamiltonian $-V\sum c^\dagger_{\kk\uparrow}c^\dagger_{-\kk\downarrow}c_{-\kk'\downarrow}c_{\kk'\uparrow}$.

“$\sqrt s\sim m_W \leftrightarrow \omega\sim\omega_D$.” Both are “the boundary where the dropped term can no longer be dropped.” That BCS theory takes the attraction to be a constant $-V$ only inside the window $\abs{\omega}<\omega_D$ and cuts it off to zero outside the window is the exact counterpart of Fermi theory being valid only in the range $q^2\ll m_W^2$.

The mathematical commonality of the breakdown. Both are $0$th-order approximations in which the denominator of the propagator is replaced by $M^2$ (or $\omega_\qq^2$) alone, and they break down where the expansion parameter $q^2/M^2$ ($\omega^2/\omega_D^2$) approaches $1$. Concretely, the following three points are common.

  1. Property of the expansion. The exact propagator can be expanded as a geometric series, $\dfrac{-1}{m_W^2}\left(1+\dfrac{q^2}{m_W^2}+\dfrac{q^4}{m_W^4}+\cdots\right)$, and the contact approximation is the operation of keeping only the first term. The point where the second and later terms can no longer be neglected is the breakdown point. On the BCS side the expansion takes exactly the same form, $-\dfrac{2\abs{g}^2}{\omega_\qq}\left(1+\dfrac{\omega^2}{\omega_\qq^2}+\cdots\right)$. Dropping the $\omega$ dependence amounts to regarding the interaction as instantaneous, and what restores it is the retardation effect of Eliashberg theory.
  2. How the breakdown appears. In both cases it appears as “the neglected frequency and momentum dependence shifts the predictions for physical quantities.” In Fermi theory the cross section keeps growing in proportion to $s$ and violates unitarity, and in BCS theory $2\Delta/k_BT_c$ deviates from the universal value $3.53$. That it shifts to $4.5$ for Pb ($\lambda=1.55$) is the price of dropping the $\omega$ dependence of the phonon (the Coulomb pseudopotential $\mu^*$ and retardation).
  3. How it is resolved. Both are resolved by “restoring the degrees of freedom that were eliminated.” In Fermi theory the $W$ is treated explicitly as a propagating particle (electroweak theory), and in BCS theory the $\omega$ dependence of the phonon is treated explicitly as the Eliashberg function $\alpha^2F(\omega)$. That is, the breakdown of an effective theory is a sign telling us to write back the heavy degrees of freedom that were eliminated.

Verification. We check the consistency of (1) and (2). The momentum transfer $q$ and the distance $r$ should correspond as $r\sim1/q$ (more precisely, a numerical factor appears depending on the weight of the Fourier transform). The length corresponding to $q = 42.08\ \mathrm{GeV}$ in (1) is

$$ \frac{\hbar c}{q} = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{42080\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 4.69\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm} $$

which agrees with $r = 3.77\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}$ of (2) to within a factor of $1.2$. Even when viewed in these two different ways, in momentum space and in position space, the crossing point comes at the same physical scale ($1.5$–$1.9$ times $R_W$). Moreover, the limiting value $g_w^2/e^2 = 4.649$ of (3) agrees with the ratio obtained by setting $m_W\to0$ in the formula of (1), and also with $\alpha_w/\alpha$ of (2) ($\alpha_w/\alpha = (g_w^2/4\pi)/(e^2/4\pi) = g_w^2/e^2$). For (4) we check the dimensions. $[G_F^2s] = \mathrm{GeV^{-4}}\cdot\mathrm{GeV^2} = \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$ and $[4\pi/s] = \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$. Both have the dimension of a cross section, and it is also consistent that $s = 2\pi/G_F$ has dimension $\mathrm{GeV^2}$.

Meaning. This exercise is the conclusion of the whole chapter. The weak interaction looks weak merely because we live at energies far below $m_W$. In terms of the coupling constant it wins by a factor of $4.65$ ((3)), and beyond $42\ \mathrm{GeV}$ the order is reversed ((1)). What is weak is not the force but the place where we are.

And as (5) shows, this structure is not new to materials scientists. The Coulomb interaction in a metal looks like a contact repulsion when viewed at wavelengths longer than $k_{\rm TF}$, and for electrons near the Fermi surface the electron–electron attraction looks like an instantaneous contact attraction. The procedure of determining the Hubbard $U$ of DFT$+U$ by cRPA is nothing other than “integrating out the screening channels and calling the remaining contact interaction $U$,” and the correspondences $m_W\leftrightarrow k_{\rm TF}$ and $G_F\leftrightarrow U$ hold as they are. Each of these theories is “the remnant of eliminating what is heavier than oneself,” and it always has a range of validity. If that $U$ is carried over to a system outside the screening conditions under which $U$ was determined, the predictions will fail, and if the $\lambda$ of BCS exceeds $0.5$, one must switch to Eliashberg theory. To avoid misusing an effective theory, one must always keep track of what the dropped terms are and when they begin to matter. The expansion parameter $q^2/m_W^2$ of this chapter is the most transparent textbook example of this.

E.13 Solutions for Chapter 13: Gauge Theory and Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking

Exercise 13.1: Using the Euler–Lagrange equation

Problem (restated)

(1) Apply the Euler–Lagrange equation (the point-particle version) of Section 13.1.1 of this book to the one-dimensional harmonic oscillator $L=\tfrac12m\dot q^2-\tfrac12kq^2$ and derive $\ddot q=-(k/m)q$.

(2) For the complex scalar field Lagrangian $\Lag=(\partial_\mu\phi)^*(\partial^\mu\phi)-m^2\phi^*\phi$, vary with respect to $\phi^*$ as the independent variable and show that $(\Box+m^2)\phi=0$. Similarly, check that varying with respect to $\phi$ gives the equation for $\phi^*$.

(3) Explain that when $m=0$ in the Proca Lagrangian $\Lag_{\rm Proca}=-\tfrac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}+\tfrac12m^2A_\nu A^\nu$, $\partial_\nu A^\nu$ is no longer determined by the equation (a gauge degree of freedom remains).

Hint: (2) $\partial\Lag/\partial(\partial_\mu\phi^*)=\partial^\mu\phi$ and $\partial\Lag/\partial\phi^*=-m^2\phi$. (3) For $m=0$, the argument of Step 4 in Section 13.2.4 reduces to $0=0$, and no information about $\partial\!\cdot\!A$ is obtained. Therefore the gauge must be fixed by hand.

Solution

Strategy. We simply apply, mechanically, the point-particle version $\dfrac{\dd}{\dd t}\left(\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}\right)-\dfrac{\partial L}{\partial q}=0$ and the field version $\partial_\mu\!\left(\dfrac{\partial\Lag}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi)}\right)-\dfrac{\partial\Lag}{\partial\phi}=0$. Only (3) is a problem about reading off what the equation fails to determine; it is a question of logic, not of calculation. Following the conventions of this book, we use natural units $\hbar=c=1$ and the metric $g^{\mu\nu}=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$.

(1) We have $L=\tfrac12m\dot q^2-\tfrac12kq^2$. Since the only dynamical variable is $q$, there are just two partial derivatives to compute. First, the derivative with respect to the velocity is

$$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q} = \frac{\partial}{\partial\dot q}\left(\tfrac12 m\dot q^2\right) = m\dot q $$

(the second term does not contain $\dot q$ and so does not contribute). This is nothing but the momentum $p=m\dot q$. Differentiating with respect to time gives

$$ \frac{\dd}{\dd t}\!\left(\frac{\partial L}{\partial\dot q}\right) = m\ddot q . $$

Next, the derivative with respect to the coordinate is

$$ \frac{\partial L}{\partial q} = \frac{\partial}{\partial q}\left(-\tfrac12 kq^2\right) = -kq $$

This is nothing but the restoring force $F=-kq$. Substituting both into the Euler–Lagrange equation gives

$$ m\ddot q - (-kq) = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad m\ddot q + kq = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \ddot q = -\frac{k}{m}\,q . $$

This is the desired equation. The general solution is $q(t)=A\cos(\omega t+\varphi)$ with $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$.

(2) We treat $\Lag=(\partial_\mu\phi)^*(\partial^\mu\phi)-m^2\phi^*\phi$ by regarding $\phi$ and $\phi^*$ as two mutually independent dynamical variables. This is equivalent to choosing the real and imaginary parts as independent variables, and it gives shorter expressions. Writing the metric explicitly,

$$ \Lag = g^{\mu\nu}(\partial_\mu\phi^*)(\partial_\nu\phi) - m^2\phi^*\phi $$

Note that $\partial_\mu\phi^*$ appears only once here. In the real scalar field’s $\tfrac12(\partial\phi)^2$, the same $\partial_\mu\phi$ appears twice, so differentiation produces a factor 2, which the coefficient $\tfrac12$ used to cancel. For the complex field no factor 2 arises, so we do not put in the $\tfrac12$ (see the Caution in Section 13.2.2 of this book). Therefore

$$ \frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi^*)} = g^{\mu\nu}\partial_\nu\phi = \partial^\mu\phi , \qquad \frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial\phi^*} = -m^2\phi . $$

Inserting these into the Euler–Lagrange equation:

$$ \partial_\mu\!\left(\partial^\mu\phi\right) - \left(-m^2\phi\right) = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \partial_\mu\partial^\mu\phi + m^2\phi = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad (\Box+m^2)\phi = 0 . $$

This is the Klein–Gordon equation. Next we vary with respect to $\phi$. This time

$$ \frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi)} = \partial^\mu\phi^* , \qquad \frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial\phi} = -m^2\phi^* $$

and by exactly the same procedure we obtain

$$ (\Box+m^2)\phi^* = 0 $$

That is, varying with respect to $\phi$ and $\phi^*$ yields two Klein–Gordon equations that are complex conjugates of each other. Since we introduced two independent variables, it is right that two equations come out; and the fact that they are not independent but conjugate to each other reflects the fact that $\Lag$ is real.

(3) As in Section 13.2.4 of this book, the equation that follows from the Proca Lagrangian is

$$ \partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu} + m^2 A^\nu = 0 $$

Apply $\partial_\nu$ to it. In the first term, $F^{\mu\nu}$ is antisymmetric in $\mu\nu$ while $\partial_\nu\partial_\mu$ is symmetric, so interchanging the indices and adding always gives cancellation, and the term vanishes identically:

$$ \partial_\nu\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu} = 0 \quad(\text{identity}) . $$

Therefore all that remains is the relation

$$ m^2\,\partial_\nu A^\nu = 0 $$

Here the cases separate.

  • When $m\neq0$: we can divide both sides by $m^2$, and $\partial_\nu A^\nu=0$ is derived. This is not gauge fixing but a consequence of the theory: one constraint is imposed on the four components of $A^\nu$, leaving three independent components, that is, the three polarizations of a massive vector particle.
  • When $m=0$: the relation above degenerates into the tautology $0=0$ and says nothing about $\partial_\nu A^\nu$. The equation becomes just $\partial_\mu F^{\mu\nu}=0$, but since $F^{\mu\nu}$ is invariant under $A_\mu\to A_\mu+\partial_\mu\chi$, if $A_\mu$ is a solution then $A_\mu+\partial_\mu\chi$ is also a solution for any $\chi$. Then $\partial\!\cdot\!A\to\partial\!\cdot\!A+\Box\chi$ changes. Since $\chi$ is arbitrary, there is no way for the equation to determine $\partial\!\cdot\!A$.

This is the precise meaning of “a gauge degree of freedom remains.” Therefore, to solve the $m=0$ theory we must impose by hand the Lorenz gauge $\partial\!\cdot\!A=0$ or the Coulomb gauge $\nabla\!\cdot\!\bm A=0$. The number of degrees of freedom is $4-1(\text{gauge fixing})-1(\text{residual gauge freedom})=2$, which are the two transverse polarizations of the photon.

Verification. We check (1) by dimensions. Since $[k]=$ force/length and $[m]=$ mass, $[k/m]=$ (force/length)/mass $=$ time$^{-2}$, so the dimension of $\ddot q$ (length/time$^2$) agrees with that of $[(k/m)q]$. The familiar formula $\omega=\sqrt{k/m}$ is also reproduced. For (2), in the limit $m\to0$ we get $\Box\phi=0$, that is, a wave equation whose waves propagate at the speed of light, and it gives the dispersion $E=\abs{\pp}$ of a massless scalar field, which is correct. (3) can be checked by counting degrees of freedom: three for $m\neq0$ and two for $m=0$. This difference $3-2=1$ is precisely the hole that the Goldstone boson fills in Section 13.8.

Meaning. (1) merely confirms the obvious fact that “Newtonian mechanics follows from the principle of least action,” but in materials science it is more practical than it looks. That $\omega=\sqrt{\Phi/M}$ follows from the harmonic Lagrangian $L=\tfrac12M\dot u^2-\tfrac12\Phi u^2$ for the atomic displacement $u$ in a crystal is the very backbone of first-principles phonon calculations. The procedure of obtaining the force constant $\Phi$ from DFT and diagonalizing the dynamical matrix to obtain $\omega$ is nothing but the many-degree-of-freedom version of (1). The situation in (3), where “there is something the equation does not determine,” looks like a nuisance to the person doing the calculation, but it is in fact an essential property of massless gauge fields, and it always drops out when physical quantities are computed. And, as we will see in Section 13.9, inside a superconductor the photon acquires a mass $m_\gamma=1/\lambda_L$, so this gauge freedom disappears and $\partial\!\cdot\!A=0$ holds as a consequence of the theory.

Exercise 13.2: The complex scalar field and the Noether current

Problem (restated)

(1) Substitute $\phi=(\phi_1+\ii\phi_2)/\sqrt2$ ($\phi_1,\phi_2$ real fields) into $\Lag=(\partial_\mu\phi)^*(\partial^\mu\phi)-m^2\phi^*\phi$ and show that $\Lag=\sum_{i=1,2}\left[\tfrac12(\partial\phi_i)^2-\tfrac12m^2\phi_i^2\right]$. This explains why the Lagrangian of the complex scalar field has no $\tfrac12$.

(2) Show that this $\Lag$ is invariant under the global transformation $\phi\to\ee^{-\ii q\theta}\phi$, and derive that the Noether current is

$$ j^\mu = \ii q\left(\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi - (\partial^\mu\phi^*)\phi\right) $$

.

(3) Substitute $\phi=N\ee^{-\ii p\cdot x}$ (a plane wave) and show that $j^\mu = 2q\abs N^2 p^\mu$. Confirm that $j^0$ is the charge density, not a probability density, and hence that it can also be negative.

Hint: (1) $\abs\phi^2=(\phi_1^2+\phi_2^2)/2$. (3) $\partial^\mu\ee^{-\ii p\cdot x}=-\ii p^\mu\ee^{-\ii p\cdot x}$. For an antiparticle (a solution with $p^0<0$), the sign of $j^0$ is reversed. Read this together with the discussion in Chapter 8.

Solution

Strategy. (1) is just substitution and expansion. (2) simply transfers to the scalar field the Noether procedure carried out for the Dirac field in Section 13.3.1 of this book. (3) needs only a single differentiation.

(1) Substitute $\phi=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\phi_1+\ii\phi_2)$ and $\phi^*=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}(\phi_1-\ii\phi_2)$ into the kinetic term. Since $\phi_1,\phi_2$ are real fields, their derivatives are also real:

$$ (\partial_\mu\phi)^*(\partial^\mu\phi) = \frac{1}{2}\left(\partial_\mu\phi_1-\ii\partial_\mu\phi_2\right)\left(\partial^\mu\phi_1+\ii\partial^\mu\phi_2\right) . $$

Expanding the parentheses gives four terms:

$$ = \frac12\left[ (\partial_\mu\phi_1)(\partial^\mu\phi_1) + \ii(\partial_\mu\phi_1)(\partial^\mu\phi_2) - \ii(\partial_\mu\phi_2)(\partial^\mu\phi_1) + (\partial_\mu\phi_2)(\partial^\mu\phi_2) \right] . $$

The two middle terms are the same quantity once the sum over $\mu$ is taken, so with opposite signs they cancel. Therefore

$$ (\partial_\mu\phi)^*(\partial^\mu\phi) = \tfrac12(\partial_\mu\phi_1)(\partial^\mu\phi_1) + \tfrac12(\partial_\mu\phi_2)(\partial^\mu\phi_2) . $$

For the mass term, similarly,

$$ -m^2\phi^*\phi = -m^2\abs\phi^2 = -m^2\cdot\frac{\phi_1^2+\phi_2^2}{2} = -\tfrac12 m^2\phi_1^2 - \tfrac12 m^2\phi_2^2 $$

Combining the two,

$$ \Lag = \sum_{i=1,2}\left[\tfrac12(\partial_\mu\phi_i)(\partial^\mu\phi_i) - \tfrac12 m^2\phi_i^2\right] $$

and each component has the standard form of the real Klein–Gordon Lagrangian. This is the reason we do not put a $\tfrac12$ in the $\Lag$ of a complex field. The $1/\sqrt2$ in $\phi=(\phi_1+\ii\phi_2)/\sqrt2$ is exactly balanced by the absence of the $\tfrac12$, and the two real fields are correctly normalized. If we were to attach a $\tfrac12$ to the complex field, the kinetic term of each real component would become $\tfrac14(\partial\phi_i)^2$, and the mass read off would be off by a factor of $\sqrt2$.

(2) First we check invariance. With $\theta$ a constant, $\phi\to\ee^{-\ii q\theta}\phi$ and $\phi^*\to\ee^{+\ii q\theta}\phi^*$. Since $\theta$ is constant, the derivative passes straight through the phase factor, and $\partial_\mu\phi\to\ee^{-\ii q\theta}\partial_\mu\phi$. Therefore

$$ (\partial_\mu\phi)^*(\partial^\mu\phi) \to \ee^{+\ii q\theta}\ee^{-\ii q\theta}(\partial_\mu\phi)^*(\partial^\mu\phi) = (\partial_\mu\phi)^*(\partial^\mu\phi), \qquad \phi^*\phi \to \phi^*\phi $$

and $\Lag$ is invariant. Since $\phi$ and $\phi^*$ always appear in equal numbers in $\Lag$, the phase factors always cancel.

Next we construct the Noether current. The infinitesimal transformation, for $\theta\ll1$, is

$$ \delta\phi = -\ii q\theta\,\phi, \qquad \delta\phi^* = +\ii q\theta\,\phi^* $$

We carry out the same calculation as in Step 3 of Section 13.3.1 of this book. Writing the variation of $\Lag$ with the chain rule and using the Euler–Lagrange equation $\partial\Lag/\partial\phi=\partial_\mu[\partial\Lag/\partial(\partial_\mu\phi)]$, the two terms combine into a derivative of a product:

$$ \delta\Lag = \partial_\mu\!\left[ \frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi)}\delta\phi + \frac{\partial\Lag}{\partial(\partial_\mu\phi^*)}\delta\phi^* \right] $$

The left-hand side vanishes by the symmetry, so the content of the square brackets is the conserved current. Substituting the partial derivatives $\partial\Lag/\partial(\partial_\mu\phi)=\partial^\mu\phi^*$ and $\partial\Lag/\partial(\partial_\mu\phi^*)=\partial^\mu\phi$ obtained in Exercise 13.1(2), we get

$$ \partial^\mu\phi^*\cdot(-\ii q\theta\,\phi) + \partial^\mu\phi\cdot(\ii q\theta\,\phi^*) = \ii q\theta\left[\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi - (\partial^\mu\phi^*)\phi\right] . $$

Dropping the constant $\theta$, we obtain

$$ j^\mu = \ii q\left(\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi - (\partial^\mu\phi^*)\phi\right), \qquad \partial_\mu j^\mu = 0 $$
