This is the desired current. Let us also check that $j^\mu$ is real. We have $(j^\mu)^*=-\ii q(\phi\partial^\mu\phi^*-(\partial^\mu\phi)\phi^*)=\ii q(\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi-(\partial^\mu\phi^*)\phi)=j^\mu$, so it is indeed real.

(3) Substitute the plane wave $\phi=N\ee^{-\ii p\cdot x}$ ($p\cdot x=p^\mu x_\mu=Et-\pp\cdot\xx$). From the hint, $\partial^\mu\ee^{-\ii p\cdot x}=-\ii p^\mu\ee^{-\ii p\cdot x}$, so

$$ \partial^\mu\phi = -\ii p^\mu N\ee^{-\ii p\cdot x}, \qquad \partial^\mu\phi^* = +\ii p^\mu N^*\ee^{+\ii p\cdot x} . $$

Hence the two terms are, respectively,

$$ \phi^*\partial^\mu\phi = N^*\ee^{\ii p\cdot x}\cdot(-\ii p^\mu N\ee^{-\ii p\cdot x}) = -\ii p^\mu\abs N^2, $$ $$ (\partial^\mu\phi^*)\phi = \ii p^\mu N^*\ee^{\ii p\cdot x}\cdot N\ee^{-\ii p\cdot x} = +\ii p^\mu\abs N^2 $$

and the phase factors cancel out cleanly. The difference is $-2\ii p^\mu\abs N^2$, so

$$ j^\mu = \ii q\cdot\left(-2\ii p^\mu\abs N^2\right) = 2q\abs N^2 p^\mu . $$

In particular, the time component is $j^0=2q\abs N^2 E$. Here $q$ is the electric charge, so for a particle with charge of the opposite sign the sign of $j^0$ is reversed. Moreover, as we saw in Section 9.1 of Chapter 9, the Klein–Gordon equation has solutions with $p^0=-E<0$, which are interpreted as antiparticles. For those solutions the sign of $j^0$ is reversed. Therefore $j^0$ cannot be positive definite and cannot be interpreted as a probability density. $j^0$ is a charge density, and it is allowed to be negative. This is the correct resolution of the old difficulty of the “negative probability density of the Klein–Gordon equation.”

Verification. We check the dimensions. In natural units, $[\Lag]=$ mass$^4$ gives $[\phi]=$ mass$^1$, and hence $[j^\mu]=[q][\phi]^2[p]=$ mass$^3$ ($q$ is dimensionless). On the other hand, $j^0$ is a charge density and so has the dimension “charge/volume,” that is, length$^{-3}=$ mass$^3$, which agrees. Looking at the nonrelativistic limit, as $E\to m$ we get $j^0\to2qm\abs N^2$. With the commonly used normalization $\abs N^2=1/2E$ we get $j^0=q$, which has the natural interpretation “charge $q$ per particle.” This is why the factor $2E$ appears in the relativistic normalization.

Meaning. This is the scalar-field version of Noether’s theorem, which says that charge conservation follows from a single global $\mathrm{U}(1)$ symmetry. What deserves attention is that “being complex” as seen in (1), “having a $\mathrm{U}(1)$ symmetry” as seen in (2), and “carrying charge” are three ways of stating one and the same fact. A real field has $\phi=\phi^*$, so $j^\mu=0$; that is, it is a neutral particle. This is why $\pi^0$ is described by a real field and $\pi^\pm$ by a complex field. This structure appears just as it is in materials science. The order parameter $\Psi$ of a superconductor is a complex number because the Cooper pair carries charge $e^*=2e$ (Section 13.9.1 of this book), and the fact that the gradient of the phase $\vartheta$ of $\Psi$ gives the supercurrent $\bm j_s$ is precisely the nonrelativistic version of the $j^\mu\propto\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi-\text{c.c.}$ derived here. The key point common to both is that what carries the charge is not the amplitude but the phase gradient.

Exercise 13.3: The covariant derivative and local gauge invariance

Problem (restated)

(1) For $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+\ii qA_\mu$, $\psi\to\ee^{\ii\theta(x)}\psi$, and $A_\mu\to A_\mu-\tfrac1q\partial_\mu\theta$, verify that $D_\mu\psi\to\ee^{\ii\theta(x)}D_\mu\psi$ (reproducing Step 4 of Section 13.3.2).

(2) Write down the term that remains when the mass term $\tfrac12m^2A_\mu A^\mu$ is gauge-transformed, and show that it does not vanish identically.

(3) Conversely, show that $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ is gauge-invariant. Furthermore, argue from the inhomogeneity of the transformation law of $A_\mu$ why one cannot construct a “cleverer” gauge-invariant mass term containing $A_\mu A^\mu$.

Hint: (2) The remaining terms are $-\tfrac{m^2}{q}A^\mu\partial_\mu\theta+\tfrac{m^2}{2q^2}(\partial\theta)^2$. (3) $F_{\mu\nu}$ is invariant because $\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\theta=\partial_\nu\partial_\mu\theta$. The very fact that $\partial_\mu\theta$ is added to $A_\mu$ prevents the existence of an invariant containing two $A$'s. However, when $\phi$ has a vacuum expectation value, $\abs{D_\mu\phi}^2$ becomes an effective mass term. This is the loophole of the Higgs mechanism.

Solution

Strategy. Each part is just a matter of substituting the transformation law and expanding, but the second half of (3) is the negative claim “why such a term cannot be built,” so we must identify which property is the obstruction and argue from it. The key is that the transformation law of $A_\mu$ is inhomogeneous (a term $-\tfrac1q\partial_\mu\theta$ that is not proportional to $A_\mu$ is added).

(1) Write the covariant derivative after the transformation as $D'_\mu=\partial_\mu+\ii qA'_\mu$. Inserting $A'_\mu=A_\mu-\tfrac1q\partial_\mu\theta$ gives

$$ D'_\mu = \partial_\mu + \ii qA_\mu - \ii q\cdot\frac1q\partial_\mu\theta = \partial_\mu + \ii qA_\mu - \ii(\partial_\mu\theta) $$

We apply this to the transformed field $\psi'=\ee^{\ii\theta(x)}\psi$. By the product rule, the first term gives

$$ \partial_\mu\!\left(\ee^{\ii\theta}\psi\right) = \ee^{\ii\theta}\partial_\mu\psi + \ii(\partial_\mu\theta)\ee^{\ii\theta}\psi $$

The remaining two terms are mere multiplications, so

$$ D'_\mu\psi' = \ee^{\ii\theta}\partial_\mu\psi + \ii(\partial_\mu\theta)\ee^{\ii\theta}\psi + \ii qA_\mu\ee^{\ii\theta}\psi - \ii(\partial_\mu\theta)\ee^{\ii\theta}\psi . $$

The second and fourth terms cancel exactly. What remains is

$$ D'_\mu\psi' = \ee^{\ii\theta}\left(\partial_\mu\psi + \ii qA_\mu\psi\right) = \ee^{\ii\theta}\,D_\mu\psi $$

That is, $D_\mu\psi$ transforms in exactly the same way as $\psi$ itself. This is the meaning of “covariant.” Thanks to this property, $\bar\psi\gamma^\mu D_\mu\psi\to\bar\psi\ee^{-\ii\theta}\ee^{\ii\theta}\gamma^\mu D_\mu\psi=\bar\psi\gamma^\mu D_\mu\psi$ is guaranteed, and $\Lag=\bar\psi(\ii\gamma^\mu D_\mu-m)\psi$ becomes locally $\mathrm{U}(1)$-invariant.

(2) Substitute $A_\mu\to A_\mu-\tfrac1q\partial_\mu\theta$ into the mass term:

$$ \tfrac12 m^2 A_\mu A^\mu \;\longrightarrow\; \tfrac12 m^2\left(A_\mu-\tfrac1q\partial_\mu\theta\right)\left(A^\mu-\tfrac1q\partial^\mu\theta\right) . $$

Expanding the parentheses produces two cross terms, but they are identical, so together they give a factor of 2:

$$ = \tfrac12 m^2 A_\mu A^\mu - \tfrac12 m^2\cdot\frac{2}{q}A^\mu\partial_\mu\theta + \tfrac12 m^2\cdot\frac{1}{q^2}(\partial_\mu\theta)(\partial^\mu\theta) $$ $$ = \tfrac12 m^2 A_\mu A^\mu \;\underbrace{-\;\frac{m^2}{q}A^\mu\partial_\mu\theta + \frac{m^2}{2q^2}(\partial_\mu\theta)(\partial^\mu\theta)}_{\text{remaining terms}} . $$

This agrees with the form in the hint. Let us show that this does not vanish identically. We argue by contradiction. Suppose the remaining terms vanish for every $\theta(x)$. Then, in particular, taking $\theta$ small, $\theta\to\epsilon\theta$ ($\epsilon\ll1$), the first-order and second-order terms in $\epsilon$ would each have to vanish independently. The first-order term is $-\dfrac{m^2}{q}A^\mu\partial_\mu\theta$. If $m\neq0$, it cannot vanish for all $\theta(x)$ and all field configurations $A^\mu(x)$ (for example, if we choose a constant gradient $\theta=k\cdot x$, there are plenty of configurations with $A^\mu k_\mu\neq0$). This is a contradiction. Note that if we integrate over spacetime to form the action and then integrate by parts, we can rewrite $-\frac{m^2}{q}\int A^\mu\partial_\mu\theta\,\dd^4x=+\frac{m^2}{q}\int(\partial_\mu A^\mu)\theta\,\dd^4x$, but this too does not vanish for configurations with $\partial\!\cdot\!A\neq0$. In the end, a mass term cannot be written for a gauge field.

(3) First we show the invariance of $F_{\mu\nu}$. Substituting the transformation law into the definition gives

$$ F'_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu\!\left(A_\nu-\tfrac1q\partial_\nu\theta\right) - \partial_\nu\!\left(A_\mu-\tfrac1q\partial_\mu\theta\right) = F_{\mu\nu} - \frac1q\left(\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\theta - \partial_\nu\partial_\mu\theta\right) . $$

If $\theta(x)$ is a smooth function, the partial derivatives commute, so the expression in parentheses is zero and $F'_{\mu\nu}=F_{\mu\nu}$. Since it is invariant as a tensor, its scalar contraction $F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ is of course invariant too. Hence $-\tfrac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ may be added to $\Lag$.

Next we discuss why no “cleverer mass term” can be built. The transformation law of $A_\mu$

$$ A_\mu \to A_\mu - \frac1q\partial_\mu\theta $$

is inhomogeneous in the sense that a term not proportional to $A_\mu$ is added. This is decisively different from an ordinary field (for example, $\psi\to\ee^{\ii\theta}\psi$), which transforms homogeneously. For a homogeneous transformation, one can build an invariant by combining fields so that the phases cancel (as $\bar\psi\psi$ does). With an inhomogeneous one, however, no matter how many $A$’s we combine, there is nothing to cancel the added $\partial\theta$. Concretely, consider a general term containing two $A$’s, $C^{\mu\nu}A_\mu A_\nu$ (where $C^{\mu\nu}$ is a constant tensor containing no fields). Under the transformation it necessarily leaves the remainder

$$ -\frac{2}{q}C^{\mu\nu}A_\mu\partial_\nu\theta + \frac{1}{q^2}C^{\mu\nu}(\partial_\mu\theta)(\partial_\nu\theta) $$

which does not vanish unless $C^{\mu\nu}=0$. One might also try combining $A$ acted on by derivatives, but among combinations containing derivatives, the only gauge-invariant one is $F_{\mu\nu}$ (and its covariant derivatives); since $F_{\mu\nu}$ always contains one derivative, a term built from $F$ has the wrong mass dimension even if it is quadratic in $A$, and so is not a mass term ($F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}$ is a kinetic term). In other words, the obstruction is not technical but structural: the inhomogeneity of the transformation law.

There is, however, exactly one way out. We only have to make $C^{\mu\nu}$ not a constant tensor but a field. Concretely, if we introduce a scalar field $\phi$ and write $\abs{D_\mu\phi}^2$, this is gauge-invariant as a whole, and moreover, when expanded it contains a term $q^2\abs\phi^2A_\mu A^\mu$. If $\phi$ has a vacuum expectation value $\braket{\abs\phi}=v/\sqrt2$, this term becomes $\tfrac12q^2v^2A_\mu A^\mu$, which is effectively a mass term. The mass is $m_B=qv$. A mass appears while gauge invariance is preserved because the “coefficient” is originally a field, whose vacuum value happens to be nonzero. This is the loophole that is the Higgs mechanism, and it is none other than the content of Section 13.8.1 of this book.

Verification. Let us check the dimensions of the remaining terms in (2). In natural units, $[A_\mu]=$ mass$^1$, $[\theta]=0$ (the phase is dimensionless), $[\partial_\mu]=$ mass$^1$, and $[q]=0$. Hence $[m^2A^\mu\partial_\mu\theta]=2+1+1=4$ and $[m^2(\partial\theta)^2/q^2]=2+1+1=4$, which agrees with the dimension 4 of $\Lag$. If a term with the wrong dimension had appeared, it would signal a calculational error. Also, the conclusion of (1) gives $D_\mu\to\partial_\mu$ as $q\to0$ (switching off the coupling to the gauge field), but then the transformation law of $A_\mu$, $-\tfrac1q\partial_\mu\theta$, diverges. This means that “at zero coupling constant the local gauge transformation itself cannot be defined,” which is the correct statement that a field not coupled to a gauge field has no local phase degree of freedom.

Meaning. This problem confirms, by the shortest possible calculation, the central proposition of this chapter that “gauge invariance forbids mass.” This prohibition is welcome in QED (the photon is indeed massless) but a nuisance in the weak interaction (the $W$ and $Z$ weigh as much as $80$–$91\ \mathrm{GeV}$). The resolution of that difficulty is the Higgs mechanism. From the materials-science side, the loophole in (3) can be observed as a very concrete phenomenon. Inside a superconductor, the condensation of Cooper pairs $\braket\Psi\neq0$ plays the role of the “vacuum expectation value of $\phi$,” and the kinetic term $\frac{1}{2m^*}\abs{(-\ii\hbar\nabla-e^*\bm A)\Psi}^2$ of the Ginzburg–Landau free energy, when expanded, yields a term $\frac{e^{*2}\abs{\Psi_\infty}^2}{2m^*}\bm A^2$. This gives the photon a mass $m_\gamma c^2=\hbar c/\lambda_L$ ($5.06\ \mathrm{eV}$ for Nb and Pb; we check the number in Exercise 13.7), and is observed directly as the Meissner effect. The abstract proposition “a gauge-invariant mass term cannot be written, but it can be built if there is a condensate” becomes a fact one can verify by hand: when a magnet is brought close to a superconductor, the magnetic field does not penetrate.

Exercise 13.4: The Yang–Mills field strength

Problem (restated)

(1) For $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ ($f^{abc}=\varepsilon^{abc}$), write out $F^a_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A^a_\nu-\partial_\nu A^a_\mu-gf^{abc}A^b_\mu A^c_\nu$ of Section 13.4.2 in components, and verify that $F^1_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu A^1_\nu-\partial_\nu A^1_\mu-g(A^2_\mu A^3_\nu-A^3_\mu A^2_\nu)$.

(2) Verify that in the Abelian limit ($f^{abc}\to0$) this expression reduces to Maxwell’s $F_{\mu\nu}$, and state why the photon has no self-coupling.

(3) Find the dependence on $g$ of the coupling constants of the cubic and quartic terms in the expansion of $-\tfrac14F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\mu\nu}$, and state which order in $\alpha_s=g_s^2/4\pi$ each contributes at.

Hint: (2) $\mathrm{U}(1)$ has a single generator, so $[T,T]=0$, and hence the structure constants vanish. “The photon carries no charge” and “the photon does not couple to itself” are one and the same fact. (3) The cubic term is $g$ and the quartic term is $g^2$. Both contribute at first order in $\alpha_s$ in the amplitude (for a process with two external gluon lines, $g^2\propto\alpha_s$).

Solution

Strategy. (1) is just writing out the index sums. (2) uses the algebraic fact that in a group with only one generator the commutator is necessarily zero. (3) splits $F^a_{\mu\nu}$ into a “derivative part” and a “nonlinear part,” expands the square, and classifies the terms by the number of $A$’s.

(1) For $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ there are three generators ($a=1,2,3$), and the structure constant is the totally antisymmetric $\varepsilon^{abc}$ ($\varepsilon^{123}=+1$). Setting $a=1$, the nonlinear term is

$$ -g\,\varepsilon^{1bc}A^b_\mu A^c_\nu $$

with the sum taken over $b,c$. $\varepsilon^{1bc}$ is nonzero only for the two choices $(b,c)=(2,3)$ and $(3,2)$, with $\varepsilon^{123}=+1$ and $\varepsilon^{132}=-1$, respectively. Hence

$$ -g\,\varepsilon^{1bc}A^b_\mu A^c_\nu = -g\left(\varepsilon^{123}A^2_\mu A^3_\nu + \varepsilon^{132}A^3_\mu A^2_\nu\right) = -g\left(A^2_\mu A^3_\nu - A^3_\mu A^2_\nu\right) . $$

Therefore

$$ F^1_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A^1_\nu - \partial_\nu A^1_\mu - g\left(A^2_\mu A^3_\nu - A^3_\mu A^2_\nu\right) $$

The others take the same form under the cyclic permutation of the indices $1\to2\to3\to1$:

$$ F^2_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A^2_\nu - \partial_\nu A^2_\mu - g\left(A^3_\mu A^1_\nu - A^1_\mu A^3_\nu\right), $$ $$ F^3_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A^3_\nu - \partial_\nu A^3_\mu - g\left(A^1_\mu A^2_\nu - A^2_\mu A^1_\nu\right) $$

We can see that the nonlinear term has the form of a three-dimensional vector product $\bm A_\mu\times\bm A_\nu$ (the adjoint representation of $\mathrm{SU}(2)$ is a three-dimensional vector). That is, we can write compactly $\bm F_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu\bm A_\nu-\partial_\nu\bm A_\mu-g\,\bm A_\mu\times\bm A_\nu$. Products of identical indices (for example, $A^1_\mu A^1_\nu$) do not appear because $\varepsilon^{abc}$ is antisymmetric.

(2) In $\mathrm{U}(1)$ there is only one generator. Writing it as $T$, the commutator is $[T,T]=TT-TT=0$, identically zero. In general $[T^a,T^b]=\ii f^{abc}T^c$, so this means $f^{abc}=0$. The nonlinear term therefore disappears, and we obtain

$$ F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu $$

the Maxwell field strength. Written in components, $F^{0i}=-E^i$ and $F^{ij}=-\varepsilon^{ijk}B^k$, which is the familiar electromagnetic field tensor.

The reason the photon has no self-coupling is given by this very calculation. A gauge field couples to itself because terms with three and four $A$’s arise when the nonlinear term $-gf^{abc}A^b_\mu A^c_\nu$ is substituted into $-\tfrac14FF$. If $f^{abc}=0$, no such terms exist in the first place. To put it more physically, as we saw in Step 3 of Section 13.4.1 of this book, in the non-Abelian case the gauge field is rotated under the adjoint representation, $\mathbb{A}'_\mu=U\mathbb{A}_\mu U^{-1}+\cdots$; that is, the gauge field itself carries the charge of the group. Gluons carry color charge, so they couple to one another. The photon, on the other hand, carries no charge because the adjoint representation of $\mathrm{U}(1)$ is trivial (one-dimensional, undergoing no rotation), and hence it couples neither to itself nor to other photons. “The photon is electrically neutral” and “the photon has no self-coupling” are two ways of stating one and the same fact.

(3) Split $F^a_{\mu\nu}$ into the part containing only derivatives and the part quadratic in $A$ (we write the derivative part as $K^a_{\mu\nu}$; because it would be confusable with the structure constant $f^{abc}$, we avoid the letter $f$):

$$ F^a_{\mu\nu} = \underbrace{\partial_\mu A^a_\nu-\partial_\nu A^a_\mu}_{\displaystyle K^a_{\mu\nu}} \;-\; \underbrace{g f^{abc}A^b_\mu A^c_\nu}_{\displaystyle G^a_{\mu\nu}} . $$

Then

$$ -\tfrac14 F^a_{\mu\nu}F^{a\mu\nu} = -\tfrac14\left(K^a-G^a\right)_{\mu\nu}\left(K^a-G^a\right)^{\mu\nu} = -\tfrac14 K^aK^a + \tfrac12 K^aG^a - \tfrac14 G^aG^a $$

and, restoring the definition of $G^a$,

  • Terms with two $A$’s: $-\tfrac14 K^a_{\mu\nu}K^{a\mu\nu}$. It contains no coupling constant. It is the kinetic term of the free field and gives the propagator.
  • Terms with three $A$’s: $\tfrac12 K^aG^a = +\dfrac{g}{2}f^{abc}\,K^{a\mu\nu}A^b_\mu A^c_\nu$. The coupling constant is of first order in $g$. Since it contains one derivative, momenta appear in the vertex factor (Step 3 of Section 13.5.1 of this book).
  • Terms with four $A$’s: $-\tfrac14 G^aG^a = -\dfrac{g^2}{4}f^{abc}f^{ade}A^b_\mu A^c_\nu A^{d\mu}A^{e\nu}$. The coupling constant is of first order in $g^2$, that is, of second order in $g$. It contains no derivatives.

Let us look at the relation to $\alpha_s=g_s^2/4\pi$. Counting the scattering amplitude $\mathcal M$ in powers of $g_s$, the lowest-order diagrams for, say, $gg\to gg$ are of two kinds: diagrams that use two three-gluon vertices ($g_s\times g_s=g_s^2$) and diagrams that use one four-gluon vertex ($g_s^2$). Both give $\mathcal M\propto g_s^2\propto\alpha_s$ and contribute at the same order. The cross section is $\abs{\mathcal M}^2$, hence of order $\alpha_s^2$. It is because the two are of the same order in this way that gauge invariance (transversality) is destroyed unless both the three-point and four-point couplings are included at the same time.

Verification. We check the dimensions. In natural units $[A_\mu]=1$ (mass dimension), $[\partial_\mu]=1$, and $[g]=0$. Then the cubic term has $[g]+[\partial]+[A]^3=0+1+3=4$ and the quartic term has $[g^2]+[A]^4=0+4=4$, and both satisfy $[\Lag]=4$. The dimensionlessness of the coupling constant is confirmed at the same time, and this is part of the reason why Yang–Mills theory is renormalizable. Also, setting $g\to0$ in (1) decomposes it into three Maxwell fields, consistent with the result of (2).

Meaning. The nonlinear term $-gf^{abc}A^bA^c$ looks like a mere addition to $F^a_{\mu\nu}$, but it determines most of the properties of QCD. The number $11$ in the $\beta$ function (Section 13.4.2 of this book) is the contribution of gluon loops from this term; because it outweighs the quark contribution, whose sign is $-\tfrac23n_f$, we get $\beta<0$, and asymptotic freedom arises. That the coupling becomes strong at low energies, that the color lines of force are bundled into a tube, and that confinement occurs are also due to the same term. From the viewpoint of materials science, the nonlinear term in (1) is a nonlinearity of the “the field quantity becomes its own source” type, and is a mathematical relative of systems in which the order parameter itself generates the field, such as the exchange interaction of a ferromagnet or the Frank elasticity of a liquid crystal. What is decisively different, however, is that the Yang–Mills nonlinearity is not a phenomenological approximation but is determined uniquely by the requirement of the symmetry of local gauge invariance. There is only a single coupling constant $g$, and even the relative sizes of the three-point and four-point couplings cannot be chosen freely.

Exercise 13.5: Counting Goldstone modes

Problem (restated)

(1) In the $\mathrm{O}(N)$-symmetric model of $N$ real scalar fields, $V=-\tfrac12\mu^2\bm\phi^2+\tfrac\lambda4(\bm\phi^2)^2$, choose $\braket{\bm\phi}=(0,\dots,0,v)$. Find the residual symmetry $H$ and show that the number of Goldstone bosons is $N-1$.

(2) Verify that $N=2$ agrees with the complex scalar model of Section 13.7.2.

(3) Verify that in the Standard Model breaking $\mathrm{SU}(2)_L\times\mathrm{U}(1)_Y\to\mathrm{U}(1)_{\rm em}$ three Goldstone bosons appear and that they become the longitudinal polarizations of $W^+,W^-,Z^0$, by counting degrees of freedom (starting from the 4 degrees of freedom of the Higgs doublet and the $4\times2=8$ degrees of freedom of the four gauge fields).

Hint: (1) $H=\mathrm{O}(N-1)$. Since $\dim\mathrm{O}(N)=N(N-1)/2$, we have $N(N-1)/2-(N-1)(N-2)/2=N-1$. (3) Before breaking: $4+8=12$. After breaking: Higgs boson 1 $+$ three massive vectors $\times3$ $+$ photon $\times2$ $=1+9+2=12$.

Solution

Strategy. There are two routes: use the counting formula of Goldstone’s theorem, $N_{\rm NG}=\dim G-\dim H$, or actually expand the potential and count the zero eigenvalues of the mass matrix. Carrying out both and seeing that they agree is the surest way. Part (3) is a problem of confirming that the group-theoretic counting and the counting of degrees of freedom give the same answer.

(1) First we determine the vacuum. Let $\bm\phi^2\equiv\bm\phi\cdot\bm\phi=\sum_{i=1}^N\phi_i^2\equiv s$. Then $V=-\tfrac12\mu^2s+\tfrac\lambda4s^2$, and

$$ \frac{\dd V}{\dd s} = -\tfrac12\mu^2 + \tfrac\lambda2 s = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad s_{\rm min} = \frac{\mu^2}{\lambda}, \qquad v = \frac{\mu}{\sqrt\lambda} $$

(the same as $v=\mu/\sqrt\lambda$ in Section 13.7.2 of this book). The minimum is attained at every point on the sphere $S^{N-1}$ of dimension $N-1$ satisfying $\bm\phi^2=v^2$, and of these we choose $\braket{\bm\phi}=(0,\dots,0,v)$.

Residual symmetry. We look for those transformations in $G=\mathrm{O}(N)$ that leave this vector unchanged. Since only the $N$th component is nonzero, every rotation that fixes the $N$th axis and rotates the remaining $N-1$ axes preserves the vacuum. That is,

$$ H = \mathrm{O}(N-1) . $$

Conversely, rotations that move the $N$th axis (rotations mixing the $N$th axis with the $i$th axis, $i=1,\dots,N-1$) move the vacuum to a different point and are therefore broken. There are $N-1$ such broken rotations.

Counting. The generators of $\mathrm{O}(N)$ are the antisymmetric $N\times N$ matrices, so $\dim\mathrm{O}(N)=N(N-1)/2$, and $\mathrm{O}(N-1)$ has $(N-1)(N-2)/2$. Hence

$$ N_{\rm NG} = \frac{N(N-1)}{2} - \frac{(N-1)(N-2)}{2} = \frac{(N-1)\left[N-(N-2)\right]}{2} = \frac{(N-1)\cdot 2}{2} = N-1 . $$

Direct check with the mass matrix. Expand $\bm\phi=(\pi_1,\dots,\pi_{N-1},\,v+\eta)$. Then $\bm\phi^2=\bm\pi^2+(v+\eta)^2$. Using $\mu^2=\lambda v^2$ and completing the square in $V$, we obtain

$$ V = -\tfrac12\lambda v^2\,\bm\phi^2 + \tfrac\lambda4\left(\bm\phi^2\right)^2 = \frac\lambda4\left(\bm\phi^2-v^2\right)^2 - \frac{\lambda v^4}{4} $$

Here

$$ \bm\phi^2 - v^2 = \bm\pi^2 + (v+\eta)^2 - v^2 = \bm\pi^2 + 2v\eta + \eta^2 $$

so that

$$ V = \frac\lambda4\left(2v\eta + \eta^2 + \bm\pi^2\right)^2 - \text{constant} = \lambda v^2\eta^2 + \lambda v\,\eta\left(\eta^2+\bm\pi^2\right) + \frac\lambda4\left(\eta^2+\bm\pi^2\right)^2 - \text{constant} . $$

Looking only at the quadratic terms, there is nothing but $\lambda v^2\eta^2$. No quadratic term in $\bm\pi$ appears anywhere ($\bm\pi^2$ appears only in the forms $\eta\bm\pi^2$ or $(\bm\pi^2)^2$ at the lowest). Together with the fact that the kinetic term takes the standard form $\tfrac12(\partial\eta)^2+\tfrac12(\partial\bm\pi)^2$, comparing with $\tfrac12m^2(\text{field})^2$ we obtain

$$ m_\eta^2 = 2\lambda v^2 = 2\mu^2, \qquad m_{\pi_i}^2 = 0 \quad (i=1,\dots,N-1) $$

There are $N-1$ massless fields, in agreement with the group-theoretic counting.

(2) Set $N=2$. For $\bm\phi=(\phi_1,\phi_2)$,

$$ V = -\tfrac12\mu^2\left(\phi_1^2+\phi_2^2\right) + \frac\lambda4\left(\phi_1^2+\phi_2^2\right)^2 . $$

On the other hand, the complex scalar model of Section 13.7.2 of this book has $V=-\mu^2\abs\phi^2+\lambda\abs\phi^4$, and with $\phi=(\phi_1+\ii\phi_2)/\sqrt2$ we have $\abs\phi^2=(\phi_1^2+\phi_2^2)/2$, so that

$$ V = -\mu^2\cdot\frac{\phi_1^2+\phi_2^2}{2} + \lambda\cdot\frac{\left(\phi_1^2+\phi_2^2\right)^2}{4} = -\tfrac12\mu^2\left(\phi_1^2+\phi_2^2\right) + \frac\lambda4\left(\phi_1^2+\phi_2^2\right)^2 . $$

The expressions are exactly the same. As for the symmetry, the rotation group $\mathrm{SO}(2)$ (rotations of the plane) and $\mathrm{U}(1)$ (phase rotations of a complex number) are isomorphic, $\mathrm{SO}(2)\cong\mathrm{U}(1)$, with $\dim=1$ ($\mathrm{O}(2)=\mathrm{SO}(2)\rtimes\mathbb{Z}_2$, which includes reflections, is not isomorphic to $\mathrm{U}(1)$). For $G=\mathrm{O}(2)$, the stabilizer subgroup of $(0,v)$ is $H=\mathrm{O}(1)=\{\pm1\}$ (the reflection $\phi_1\to-\phi_1$), which is a discrete group, so $\dim H=0$. Hence $N_{\rm NG}=1-0=1$, which also agrees with the formula $N-1=2-1=1$ of (1). The masses, too, $m_\eta^2=2\lambda v^2$ and $m_\xi^2=0$, agree with the results of Section 13.7.2. The “one direction along the valley” of the Mexican hat is the Goldstone mode $\xi$, which in the language of $\mathrm{O}(2)$ corresponds to “the only rotation generator being broken.”

(3) First we count group-theoretically. The generators of $G=\mathrm{SU}(2)_L\times\mathrm{U}(1)_Y$ number $3+1=4$, and what remains after the breaking is the electromagnetic $H=\mathrm{U}(1)_{\rm em}$, with one generator. Therefore

$$ N_{\rm NG} = \dim G - \dim H = 4 - 1 = 3 . $$

Next we count by degrees of freedom. Before breaking, we have

  • Higgs doublet $\Phi=(\phi^+,\phi^0)^T$: two complex components $=$ 4 real degrees of freedom.
  • The four gauge fields $W^1,W^2,W^3,B$: each is massless and so has two transverse polarizations, for a total of $4\times2=$ 8.

The total is $4+8=12$. After the breaking we have

  • Higgs boson $h$: one real scalar $=$ 1.
  • $W^+,W^-,Z^0$: these are massive vector particles, so each has three polarizations $\lambda=0,\pm1$, for a total of $3\times3=$ 9.
  • Photon $\gamma$: it remains massless, so it has two transverse polarizations, for a total of 2.

The total is $1+9+2=12$. The total number is the same before and after. Following how the itemized count changes, one of the four degrees of freedom of the Higgs doublet becomes the physical Higgs boson $h$, and the remaining three are Goldstone bosons. On the gauge-field side, meanwhile, each of the three fields $W^+,W^-,Z^0$ newly acquires one longitudinal polarization ($\lambda=0$), so the count increases by $3$ degrees of freedom. Since the gain and the loss balance exactly, we obtain the correspondence

$$ \underbrace{3}_{\text{Goldstone bosons}} \;\longrightarrow\; \underbrace{3}_{W^+_L,\;W^-_L,\;Z^0_L} $$

That is, the three Goldstone bosons are “eaten” by $W^+,W^-,Z^0$ and become their longitudinal polarizations. The photon remains massless because the vacuum $\braket\Phi=\tfrac1{\sqrt2}(0,v)^T$ is electrically neutral and does not break $\mathrm{U}(1)_{\rm em}$; consequently there is no leftover Goldstone boson to give to the photon. The fact that the counting closes exactly, $12=12$, guarantees the consistency of this picture.

Verification. Putting $N=3$ into the general formula of (1) gives $N_{\rm NG}=2$, which agrees with the $\mathrm{O}(3)$ model example in Section 13.7.3 of this book ($G=\mathrm{O}(3)$, $\dim=3$; $H=\mathrm{O}(2)$, $\dim=1$; $3-1=2$). Likewise, $N=4$ gives $N_{\rm NG}=3$, which is the case in which $\mathrm{O}(4)$ breaks to $\mathrm{O}(3)$, and the number of Goldstone bosons agrees with the electroweak case of (3) ($\mathrm{SO}(4)$ is locally isomorphic to $\mathrm{SU}(2)\times\mathrm{SU}(2)$, and $\mathrm{SO}(3)$ is locally isomorphic to $\mathrm{SU}(2)$; strictly speaking they differ only by a $\mathbb{Z}_2$ quotient). Indeed, the four real components of the Higgs doublet can be regarded as an $\mathrm{O}(4)$ vector, so this is no coincidence. Furthermore, putting the values $\lambda=0.12940$ and $v=246.2\ \mathrm{GeV}$ from Exercise 13.6(2) into the mass formula $m_\eta^2=2\lambda v^2$ derived in (1) gives $m_\eta=\sqrt{2\times0.12940}\times246.2=125.25\ \mathrm{GeV}$, which returns exactly to the observed Higgs mass. If we instead use $0.129$, which is $\lambda$ rounded to three significant figures, we obtain $125.05\ \mathrm{GeV}$, which is off by $0.2\ \mathrm{GeV}$. Since $\lambda$ was originally computed backward from $m_H$, the unrounded value must be used in a check that works backward to return to the starting value.

Meaning. The fact that the number of Goldstone bosons is determined by “the number of broken generators” is used routinely more in materials science than in particle physics. The statement that a crystal breaks the continuous translation symmetry of the liquid in all three directions and therefore has three acoustic phonons (one longitudinal and two transverse) is precisely this counting. The acoustic sum rule, which requires the acoustic modes at the $\Gamma$ point to have $\omega=0$ in a first-principles phonon calculation, is also nothing other than the lattice version of Goldstone’s theorem. However, as the warning in Section 13.7.3 of this book says, in systems without Lorentz invariance the counting changes. In a ferromagnet, the number of broken generators in $\mathrm{SO}(3)\to\mathrm{SO}(2)$ is two, but because $\braket{S^z}\neq0$ the two form a conjugate pair, and only one magnon appears (with dispersion $\omega\propto q^2$). In an antiferromagnet, on the other hand, there are two (with $\omega\propto q$). Someone who measures this difference with inelastic neutron scattering is in fact measuring the nonrelativistic version of Goldstone’s theorem.

Exercise 13.6: The Abelian Higgs model and Standard Model numbers

Problem (restated)

(1) Following the calculation of Section 13.8.1, show from the cubic term $q^2v\,\eta B_\mu B^\mu$ of $\Lag$ that the coupling of the Higgs boson to the gauge field can be written $g_{\eta BB}=2m_B^2/v$.

(2) From $m_H=125.25\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and $v=246.2\ \mathrm{GeV}$, find the Higgs self-coupling $\lambda$ and the potential parameter $\mu$.

(3) Compute the Yukawa coupling $y_t$ of Table 13.3 from $m_t=172.7\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and verify that it is close to $1$. Also find its ratio to the electron’s $y_e$.

Hint: (2) $\lambda=m_H^2/2v^2 = 125.25^2/(2\times246.2^2)=0.129$, $\mu=m_H/\sqrt2=88.6\ \mathrm{GeV}$. (3) $y_t=\sqrt2\times172.7/246.2=0.992$, $y_e=2.94\times10^{-6}$. The ratio is $3.4\times10^5$. This six-orders-of-magnitude hierarchy is the “flavor puzzle.”

Solution

Strategy. For (1) we apply the rule for reading off a Feynman rule from the Lagrangian (Section 13.5.1, Step 1 of this book: “remove the fields from the interaction term, multiply by $\ii$, and multiply by the number of permutations of identical fields”). (2) and (3) are numerical calculations, and all of them were checked with python3.

(1) First we confirm where the cubic term in question comes from. In the unitary gauge the phase of the Higgs field is absorbed by a gauge transformation, so we can write $\phi=\dfrac{v+\eta(x)}{\sqrt2}$ ($\eta$ is a real field), and using the covariant derivative $D_\mu=\partial_\mu+\ii qB_\mu$ we have

$$ \abs{D_\mu\phi}^2 = \left(\partial_\mu\phi^*-\ii qB_\mu\phi^*\right)\left(\partial^\mu\phi+\ii qB^\mu\phi\right) = \tfrac12(\partial_\mu\eta)(\partial^\mu\eta) + q^2\abs\phi^2\,B_\mu B^\mu $$

(since $\phi$ is real, $\phi^*\partial^\mu\phi-(\partial^\mu\phi^*)\phi=0$, and the cross term linear in $B_\mu$ drops out). Substituting $\abs\phi^2=(v+\eta)^2/2$ into this, as in Step 6 of Section 13.8.1 of this book, the quadratic term in $B$ of $\Lag$ is

$$ \frac{q^2(v+\eta)^2}{2}B_\mu B^\mu = \underbrace{\frac{q^2v^2}{2}B_\mu B^\mu}_{\text{mass term}} + \underbrace{q^2v\,\eta\,B_\mu B^\mu}_{\text{cubic term}} + \underbrace{\frac{q^2}{2}\eta^2 B_\mu B^\mu}_{\text{quartic term}} $$

Comparing the first term with the standard Proca form $\tfrac12m_B^2B_\mu B^\mu$, we obtained $m_B=qv$, so conversely

$$ q^2 = \frac{m_B^2}{v^2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad q^2 v = \frac{m_B^2}{v} $$

Therefore the cubic term can be written as

$$ \Lag_{\rm int} = \frac{m_B^2}{v}\,\eta\,B_\mu B^\mu $$

From this we read off the vertex factor. Remove the fields $\eta$, $B_\mu$, $B_\nu$, multiply by $\ii$, and since there are two identical fields $B$, add the two ways of permuting them (symmetry factor $2!=2$); this gives

$$ \ii\cdot\frac{m_B^2}{v}\cdot 2\,g^{\mu\nu} = \ii\,\frac{2m_B^2}{v}\,g^{\mu\nu} $$

That is, the coupling constant is

$$ g_{\eta BB} = \frac{2m_B^2}{v} $$

Put another way, the mass term has the form not of $\tfrac12m_B^2B^2$ but of

$$ \frac12 m_B^2\left(1+\frac{\eta}{v}\right)^2 B_\mu B^\mu $$

In other words, the fluctuation $\eta$ of the Higgs field shakes the very mass of the gauge particle. This is why the coupling strength is proportional to $m_B^2$. In the fermion case (Section 13.8.4 of this book), $\bar\psi$ and $\psi$ are different fields, so no symmetry factor appears, and $g_{\eta ff}=m_f/v$ is proportional to the first power of the mass. The difference between the square for bosons and the first power for fermions comes from the fact that the mass terms have coefficients $m^2$ and $m$, respectively, multiplying the square of the field.

(2) The Higgs boson mass is $m_\eta=\sqrt{2\lambda}\,v$ from Section 13.8.1 of this book. Solving this for $\lambda$ gives

$$ \lambda = \frac{m_H^2}{2v^2} . $$

Now we insert numbers. With $m_H=125.25\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and $v=246.2\ \mathrm{GeV}$,

$$ m_H^2 = 125.25^2 = 1.5688\times10^4\ \mathrm{GeV^2}, \qquad 2v^2 = 2\times246.2^2 = 2\times6.0614\times10^4 = 1.2123\times10^5\ \mathrm{GeV^2} $$ $$ \lambda = \frac{1.5688\times10^4}{1.2123\times10^5} = 0.12940 . $$

Next is $\mu$. From $m_\eta=\sqrt{2\lambda}\,v=\sqrt2\,\mu$ in Section 13.8.1 of this book,

$$ \mu = \frac{m_H}{\sqrt2} = \frac{125.25}{1.41421} = 88.565\ \mathrm{GeV} . $$

To summarize, $\lambda=0.129$ and $\mu=88.6\ \mathrm{GeV}$, which agree with the values in the hint. That $\lambda$ is considerably smaller than $1$ means that the Higgs sector is weakly coupled (perturbation theory can be used). On the other hand, since $\lambda$ is not too close to zero, the valley of the Mexican hat is reasonably deep.

(3) The Yukawa coupling is obtained by solving $m_f=y_fv/\sqrt2$ of Section 13.8.4 of this book in reverse: $y_f=\sqrt2\,m_f/v$. Since the top quark has $m_t=172.7\ \mathrm{GeV}$,

$$ y_t = \frac{\sqrt2\times172.7}{246.2} = \frac{244.23}{246.2} = 0.9920 . $$

It is indeed extremely close to $1$. It is too close to be a coincidence, so it is suspected that there is some meaning behind it (the discussion in Section 13.8.4 of this book). For the electron, $m_e=0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}=0.511\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GeV}$, so

$$ y_e = \frac{\sqrt2\times0.511\times10^{-3}}{246.2} = \frac{7.2266\times10^{-4}}{246.2} = 2.935\times10^{-6} . $$

Taking the ratio, $\sqrt2/v$ is common to both, so it is simply the mass ratio:

$$ \frac{y_t}{y_e} = \frac{m_t}{m_e} = \frac{172.7}{0.511\times10^{-3}} = 3.380\times10^{5} . $$

That is, a factor of about $3.4\times10^5$, a gap of five and a half orders of magnitude. Looking at all of Table 13.3, the values are scattered over six orders of magnitude, from $y_e\sim10^{-6}$ to $y_t\sim1$, and the Standard Model explains none of this. They are all free parameters determined from experiment. This is the problem known as the “flavor puzzle.”

Verification. Substitute the values of (2) back into the original formulas. $m_\eta=\sqrt{2\lambda}\,v=\sqrt{2\times0.129404}\times246.2=125.25\ \mathrm{GeV}$ returns to $m_H$. Also $v=\mu/\sqrt\lambda=88.565/\sqrt{0.129404}=246.2\ \mathrm{GeV}$ returns to $v$. $\mu^2=\lambda v^2$ also agrees: $88.565^2=7843.8$ and $0.129404\times246.2^2=7843.8$. (3) is confirmed by the agreement of $y_t/\sqrt2=m_t/v=172.7/246.2=0.70146$ with $0.9920/\sqrt2=0.70146$. We also look at the dimensions of (1). $[g_{\eta BB}]=[m_B^2/v]=2-1=1$, that is, mass dimension 1. Since $\eta B_\mu B^\mu$ has dimension 3, the coefficient must have dimension 1 for $[\Lag]=4$. This is correct.

Meaning. The $g_{\eta BB}=2m_B^2/v$ of (1) and the $g_{\eta ff}=m_f/v$ of (3) are the most characteristic predictions of the Higgs boson. Since the Higgs boson “couples in proportion to mass,” heavier particles couple more strongly; at the LHC, $H\to b\bar b$ (branching ratio 58%), $H\to WW$, and $H\to ZZ$ appear first, and decays to light particles are extremely rare. This is why evidence for $H\to\mu\mu$ (CMS, $3.0\sigma$) was obtained only in 2020 (it has not yet reached an observation at $5\sigma$). When the measured coupling constants are plotted against mass, they lie on two straight lines, $\sqrt{g}\propto m$ for $W,Z$ and $g\propto m$ for fermions, over more than three orders of magnitude, from $0.1\ \mathrm{GeV}$ to $170\ \mathrm{GeV}$. From the materials-science side, the picture in (1) that “fluctuations of the Higgs field shake the mass of the gauge particle” is precisely the mechanism by which the Higgs (amplitude) mode of a superconductor couples to the electromagnetic field. As we saw in Section 13.9.4 of this book, the amplitude mode has only a quadratic coupling $\eta B_\mu B^\mu$, so it is invisible in linear optical absorption and is caught for the first time by nonlinear spectroscopy such as THz third-harmonic generation. The vertex structure of one $\eta$ and two $B$ directly determines the experimental method of “exciting the Higgs mode with two incident photons.”

Exercise 13.7: Obtaining the photon mass from the London penetration depth

Problem (restated)

Use $\hbar c = 197.327\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$.

(1) For Nb with $\lambda_L=39\ \mathrm{nm}$ and for YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_7$ with in-plane ($ab$-plane) $\lambda_L\approx150\ \mathrm{nm}$, find $m_\gamma c^2=\hbar c/\lambda_L$.

(2) Suppose that $m_\gamma c^2 = 1\ \mathrm{meV}$. What would $\lambda_L$ be? Compare this value with the penetration depths of actual superconductors and confirm that “the photon mass is not on the meV scale.”

(3) Taking the conduction-electron density of Pb to be $n=1.32\times10^{29}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ (valence 4, atomic density $3.30\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$), compute $\omega_p$ and $\lambda_L=c/\omega_p$, and compare with the measured $\lambda_L=39\ \mathrm{nm}$. Discuss why a difference arises.

Hint: (1) Nb: $5.06\ \mathrm{eV}$, YBCO: $1.32\ \mathrm{eV}$. (2) $\lambda_L=197.327\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}/10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}=1.97\times10^5\ \mathrm{nm}=0.2\ \mathrm{mm}$. This is four orders of magnitude larger than the actual penetration depth and is unrealistic. (3) $\omega_p=2.05\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\hbar\omega_p=13.5\ \mathrm{eV}$, $\lambda_L=14.6\ \mathrm{nm}$. This is 2.7 times smaller than the measured value. The reasons are (i) the band effective mass differs from $m_e$, and (ii) Pb is a Pippard (nonlocal) superconductor with $\xi_0\gg\lambda_L$, for which the effective penetration depth is longer than the London value.

Solution

Strategy. We simply turn $m_\gamma c^2=\hbar c/\lambda_L$, derived in Section 13.9.2 of this book (a consequence of the London equation and the static Proca equation having the same form), into numbers. Only (3) is a problem in which we estimate $\lambda_L$ from the superfluid density on a first-principles basis and compare it with the measurement. All numerical values were computed with python3.

(1) We need only divide $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}$ by $\lambda_L$ (in nm). For Nb ($\lambda_L=39\ \mathrm{nm}$),

$$ m_\gamma c^2 = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{39\ \mathrm{nm}} = 5.0597\ \mathrm{eV} \simeq 5.06\ \mathrm{eV} . $$

For YBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_7$ in the $ab$ plane ($\lambda_L\approx150\ \mathrm{nm}$),

$$ m_\gamma c^2 = \frac{197.327}{150} = 1.3155\ \mathrm{eV} \simeq 1.32\ \mathrm{eV} . $$

This agrees with the values in the hint. The longer the penetration depth of a material, the lighter the photon. The smaller the superfluid density, the closer to “vacuum,” and in a system with small $n_s$ such as a cuprate the photon mass is also small. For reference, for Al ($16\ \mathrm{nm}$) in Table 13.5 it is $12.3\ \mathrm{eV}$, and for Sn ($34\ \mathrm{nm}$) it is $5.80\ \mathrm{eV}$.

(2) Solve the same formula in reverse. With $m_\gamma c^2=1\ \mathrm{meV}=10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}$,

$$ \lambda_L = \frac{\hbar c}{m_\gamma c^2} = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}} = 1.97327\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{nm} = 197\ \mathrm{\mu m} \simeq 0.2\ \mathrm{mm} . $$

The penetration depths of real superconductors lie in the range $16$–$150\ \mathrm{nm}$, so $0.2\ \mathrm{mm}$ is larger by a factor of about $10^3$–$10^4$, that is, by three to four orders of magnitude. $0.2\ \mathrm{mm}$ is a thickness visible to the naked eye, and if a magnetic field penetrated that deeply, it could not be called the “Meissner effect.” Therefore the photon mass in a superconductor cannot be on the meV scale.

This confirmation has practical significance. The superconducting gap $2\Delta$ is on the meV scale ($2.7\ \mathrm{meV}$ in Pb), so one is easily led to think, “the energy scale of superconductivity is meV, so the photon mass must also be meV.” However, as the warning in Section 13.9.2 of this book says, what determines the photon mass is not the gap but the superfluid density, and through the relation $m_\gamma c^2=\hbar\omega_{p,s}$ it is directly tied to the plasma energy of the metal (on the eV scale). The gap and the penetration depth, though properties of the same superconductor, are separate scales four orders of magnitude apart.

(3) The definition of the superfluid plasma frequency,

$$ \omega_p = \sqrt{\frac{ne^2}{\varepsilon_0 m_e}} $$

is evaluated with $n=1.32\times10^{29}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$, $e=1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C}$, $\varepsilon_0=8.854\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{F/m}$, and $m_e=9.109\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{kg}$. Computing the numerator and denominator separately,

$$ ne^2 = 1.32\times10^{29}\times\left(1.602\times10^{-19}\right)^2 = 1.32\times10^{29}\times2.5664\times10^{-38} = 3.3877\times10^{-9}, $$ $$ \varepsilon_0 m_e = 8.854\times10^{-12}\times9.109\times10^{-31} = 8.0651\times10^{-42} $$

The ratio is $4.2004\times10^{32}\ \mathrm{s^{-2}}$, and taking its square root,

$$ \omega_p = 2.0496\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} \simeq 2.05\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} . $$

Converting to energy,

$$ \hbar\omega_p = 1.0546\times10^{-34}\times2.0496\times10^{16} = 2.1615\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J} = \frac{2.1615\times10^{-18}}{1.602\times10^{-19}}\ \mathrm{eV} = 13.49\ \mathrm{eV} . $$

The penetration depth is $\lambda_L=c/\omega_p$, so

$$ \lambda_L = \frac{2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}}{2.0496\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}} = 1.4627\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m} = 14.63\ \mathrm{nm} . $$

Comparing with the measured value $39\ \mathrm{nm}$,

$$ \frac{39}{14.63} = 2.67 $$

times, the computed value is smaller (= the photon mass is overestimated). Since $\lambda_L\propto\sqrt{m^*/n_s}$, this factor of $2.67$ corresponds to a discrepancy of $2.67^2=7.1$ times in $m^*/n_s$. There are two candidate causes, but the main one is (ii).

  • (i) Band effective mass. The calculation above treats the conduction electrons as free electrons (mass $m_e$). Since $\lambda_L\propto\sqrt{m^*/n_s}$, the penetration depth becomes longer if $m^*$ is large and $n_s$ is small. However, as the verification below shows, the free-electron-model value $\hbar\omega_p=13.5\ \mathrm{eV}$ agrees well with the measured plasmon of Pb (about $13\ \mathrm{eV}$), and the Drude weight $n/m^*$ itself hardly deviates from the free-electron value. Therefore this effect is not the main cause.
  • (ii) Pippard nonlocality. The London equation is a local relation in which $\bm j_s(\bm r)$ is determined only by $\bm A(\bm r)$ at the same point, but this is correct only when the size of the Cooper pair (the BCS coherence length $\xi_0$) is shorter than $\lambda_L$. For Pb, $\xi_0\approx83\ \mathrm{nm}$ against a London value $\lambda_L\approx15\ \mathrm{nm}$, so it lies in the extreme Pippard (nonlocal) regime with $\xi_0\gg\lambda_L$. In this case the response is averaged over a range $\xi_0$, so the current is reduced and the effective penetration depth becomes longer. Using Pippard’s estimate $\lambda_{\rm eff}\sim(\lambda_L^2\xi_0)^{1/3}$ gives $(14.63^2\times83)^{1/3}=26.1\ \mathrm{nm}$, which is $1.8$ times the London value and comes considerably closer to the measured $39\ \mathrm{nm}$. The remaining factor of about $1.5$ falls within the range of the numerical coefficient of the Pippard formula and corrections due to impurity scattering. The measured $39\ \mathrm{nm}$ is not the London value but the effective penetration depth $\lambda_{\rm eff}$.

Conversely, Pb, a type-I superconductor with $\kappa\approx0.4$, is precisely a material in which this nonlocality matters.

Verification. The two answers of (3) are not independent of each other, so we can check their consistency. Putting $\lambda_L=14.63\ \mathrm{nm}$ into $m_\gamma c^2=\hbar c/\lambda_L=\hbar\omega_{p,s}$ of Section 13.9.2 of this book gives

$$ \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}}{14.63\ \mathrm{nm}} = 13.49\ \mathrm{eV} $$

which agrees exactly with the $\hbar\omega_p=13.49\ \mathrm{eV}$ found above. This is natural, since combining $\lambda_L=c/\omega_p$ with $m_\gamma c^2=\hbar c/\lambda_L$ gives $m_\gamma c^2=\hbar\omega_p$, but it confirms that there is no error in the unit conversion. Also, checking (1) in SI units, $m_\gamma=\hbar/(\lambda_Lc)=1.055\times10^{-34}/(3.9\times10^{-8}\times2.998\times10^8)=9.02\times10^{-36}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $m_\gamma c^2=9.02\times10^{-36}\times(2.998\times10^8)^2=8.11\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}=5.06\ \mathrm{eV}$, which agree. Furthermore, as an order-of-magnitude check, the measured plasmon of Pb (EELS) is about $13\ \mathrm{eV}$, and the $13.5\ \mathrm{eV}$ found above agrees well. That is, the free-electron model predicts the normal-state plasma frequency well, but misses $\lambda_L$, which involves the superfluid density, by the amount of the nonlocality.

Meaning. The claim of this chapter that “measuring the penetration depth is measuring the photon mass in a superconductor” has now become a concrete number. The $5.06\ \mathrm{eV}$ of Nb is only $10^{-5}$ of the electron rest mass, but compared with the zero mass the photon originally has, it is infinitely heavy. It differs by ten orders of magnitude from the $80.377\ \mathrm{GeV}$ of the $W$ boson, but the equation is the same Proca equation. The discussion of (3) is even more practical. This problem shows that when one tries to predict the penetration depth from the superfluid density in a first-principles calculation, the free-electron approximation is off by a factor of two to three. To get it right, one must use the Drude weight (plasma-frequency tensor) obtained from the band structure, and in addition judge the nonlocal correction by looking at the relative sizes of $\xi_0$ and $\lambda_L$. In the language of particle physics, this says that “if vacuum polarization is nonlocal, the estimate of the gauge-field mass is shifted,” and the same caution is needed in condensed matter and in particle physics alike.

Exercise 13.8: A dictionary between Ginzburg–Landau theory and the Higgs mechanism

Problem (restated)

(1) Substitute $\Psi=\Psi_\infty(1+f)$ into the GL equation $a\Psi+b\abs\Psi^2\Psi-\frac{\hbar^2}{2m^*}\nabla^2\Psi=0$, linearize in $f$, and show that the decay length of $f$ is $\xi_{\rm GL}/\sqrt2$ (where $\xi_{\rm GL}\equiv\hbar/\sqrt{2m^*\abs a}$).

(2) Using the fact that this decay length corresponds to $1/m_\eta$ in the Abelian Higgs model, derive $\kappa=\lambda_L/\xi_{\rm GL}=m_\eta/(\sqrt2\,m_B)$. Verify that the boundary between type I and type II, $\kappa=1/\sqrt2$, corresponds to $m_\eta=m_B$.

(3) Regard the Standard Model as a “superconductor,” set $m_\eta\to m_H=125.25\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and $m_B\to m_Z=91.188\ \mathrm{GeV}$, find $\kappa$, and decide whether it is type I or type II.

(4) Find numerically the depth of the potential at the bottom of the Mexican hat, $V_{\min}=-\lambda v^4/4$, and compare it with the observed dark-energy density of the universe, $\rho_\Lambda\approx(2.3\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{GeV})^4=2.8\times10^{-47}\ \mathrm{GeV^4}$.

Hint: (1) Using $a=-b\abs{\Psi_\infty}^2$, we get $\nabla^2f=(4m^*\abs a/\hbar^2)f$. (3) $\kappa=125.25/(\sqrt2\times91.188)=0.971>1/\sqrt2=0.707$, so it is type II. (4) $\abs{V_{\min}}=0.129\times246.2^4/4=1.2\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{GeV^4}$. The ratio to $\rho_\Lambda$ is $4\times10^{54}$, that is, a discrepancy of 55 orders of magnitude. This is the cosmological constant problem. It means that the energy of the electroweak vacuum is (for some reason) almost exactly canceled.

Solution

Strategy. (1) is the standard procedure of linearizing around the equilibrium solution. (2) uses the dictionary of Table 13.4 as it stands. (3) and (4) are numerical, and were computed with python3. (4) is the most dispiriting number in this book, but one should count the orders of magnitude honestly.

(1) In a uniform system without a magnetic field, the equilibrium solution $\Psi_\infty$ is obtained by dropping the spatial-derivative term of the GL equation:

$$ a\Psi_\infty + b\abs{\Psi_\infty}^2\Psi_\infty = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \abs{\Psi_\infty}^2 = -\frac ab = \frac{\abs a}{b} $$

(since $T<T_c$, we have $a<0$, and hence $a=-\abs a$). Into this we substitute $\Psi=\Psi_\infty(1+f)$ ($f$ is a small real fluctuation). Since $\abs\Psi^2=\abs{\Psi_\infty}^2(1+f)^2$ and $\nabla^2\Psi=\Psi_\infty\nabla^2f$, we have

$$ a\Psi_\infty(1+f) + b\abs{\Psi_\infty}^2\Psi_\infty(1+f)^3 - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m^*}\Psi_\infty\nabla^2f = 0 . $$

Dividing both sides by $\Psi_\infty\neq0$ gives

$$ a(1+f) + b\abs{\Psi_\infty}^2(1+f)^3 - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m^*}\nabla^2f = 0 . $$

Now we use $b\abs{\Psi_\infty}^2=-a=\abs a$, which turns the first two terms into

$$ -\abs a(1+f) + \abs a(1+f)^3 - \frac{\hbar^2}{2m^*}\nabla^2f = 0 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \abs a\left[(1+f)^3-(1+f)\right] = \frac{\hbar^2}{2m^*}\nabla^2f . $$

We keep terms only to first order in $f$. Since $(1+f)^3\simeq1+3f$ and $(1+f)=1+f$, the bracket is $(1+3f)-(1+f)=2f$. Therefore

$$ 2\abs a\,f = \frac{\hbar^2}{2m^*}\nabla^2f \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \nabla^2 f = \frac{4m^*\abs a}{\hbar^2}\,f $$

and the equation in the hint follows. In the one-dimensional problem with the surface at $x=0$ and the interior at $x>0$, the solution is $f\propto\ee^{-x/\ell}$, and substitution gives $1/\ell^2=4m^*\abs a/\hbar^2$, that is,

$$ \ell = \frac{\hbar}{\sqrt{4m^*\abs a}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\cdot\frac{\hbar}{\sqrt{2m^*\abs a}} = \frac{\xi_{\rm GL}}{\sqrt2} . $$

Fluctuations of the amplitude of the order parameter decay over the length $\xi_{\rm GL}/\sqrt2$. The factor $\sqrt2$ appears because the linearization produces the coefficient 2 in $(1+f)^3-(1+f)\to2f$. The very definition of $\xi_{\rm GL}$ contains no coefficient 2, so the two lengths differ by a factor $\sqrt2$.

(2) On the Abelian Higgs model side, what corresponds to this is the spatial decay of the Higgs field $\eta$. The static Yukawa-type solution for a field of mass $m_\eta$ decays as $\ee^{-m_\eta r}$, so the decay length is $1/m_\eta$. Equating it with the result of (1), we obtain

$$ \frac{1}{m_\eta} = \frac{\xi_{\rm GL}}{\sqrt2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \xi_{\rm GL} = \frac{\sqrt2}{m_\eta} . $$

This is the “coherence length $\leftrightarrow\sqrt2/m_\eta$” of Table 13.4. On the other hand, for the magnetic field (the gauge field), as we saw in Section 13.9.2 of this book, $\lambda_L=1/m_B$. Hence the GL parameter can be written as

$$ \kappa \equiv \frac{\lambda_L}{\xi_{\rm GL}} = \frac{1/m_B}{\sqrt2/m_\eta} = \frac{1}{m_B}\cdot\frac{m_\eta}{\sqrt2} = \frac{m_\eta}{\sqrt2\,m_B} $$

We examine the boundary.

$$ \kappa = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \frac{m_\eta}{\sqrt2\,m_B} = \frac{1}{\sqrt2} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad m_\eta = m_B . $$

That is, the type-I / type-II boundary is the point where the masses of the Higgs boson and the gauge boson are exactly equal. And

  • $m_\eta < m_B$ (the Higgs is light = the coherence length is long) $\Rightarrow\kappa<1/\sqrt2\Rightarrow$ type I. Vortices attract each other.
  • $m_\eta > m_B$ (the Higgs is heavy = the coherence length is short) $\Rightarrow\kappa>1/\sqrt2\Rightarrow$ type II. Vortices repel each other and form an Abrikosov lattice.

Physically, this can be read as follows. In the core of a vortex the order parameter is destroyed, and the condensation energy for that region is lost (the core radius is $\xi_{\rm GL}$). On the other hand, the magnetic field penetrates, which gains magnetic energy (the spread of the field is $\lambda_L$). The ratio $\kappa$ of the two decides which wins. In field theory the point $m_\eta=m_B$ is called the Bogomolny point, where the force between vortices vanishes exactly. This is because scalar exchange (attraction) and vector exchange (repulsion) balance, even including the Yukawa-type decay lengths.

(3) We substitute the Standard Model values. With $m_\eta\to m_H=125.25\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and $m_B\to m_Z=91.188\ \mathrm{GeV}$,

$$ \kappa = \frac{m_H}{\sqrt2\,m_Z} = \frac{125.25}{1.41421\times91.188} = \frac{125.25}{128.96} = 0.9712 . $$

Since the value at the boundary is $1/\sqrt2=0.7071$,

$$ \kappa = 0.971 \;>\; 0.707 $$

that is, it is type II. The electroweak vacuum of our universe lies on the same side as Nb ($\kappa\approx1$) and Nb$_3$Sn. Incidentally, if we take the $W$ ($m_W=80.377\ \mathrm{GeV}$) rather than the $Z$ as the gauge boson, then $\kappa=125.25/(\sqrt2\times80.377)=1.102$, which is again type II. The conclusion does not change whichever we use. Since $m_H$ and $m_Z$ happen to be close in value, $\kappa$ lies very near $1$, that is, not so far from the Bogomolny point.

(4) The depth of the bottom of the Mexican hat is the constant term that appeared when completing the square in Step 4 of Section 13.7.2 of this book. Since $V=\lambda(s-v^2/2)^2-\lambda v^4/4$ (with $s=\abs\phi^2$),

$$ V_{\min} = -\frac{\lambda v^4}{4} . $$

We insert numbers. Here $\lambda=0.12940$ (Exercise 13.6(2)) and $v=246.2\ \mathrm{GeV}$. First,

$$ v^4 = 246.2^4 = \left(246.2^2\right)^2 = \left(6.0614\times10^4\right)^2 = 3.6741\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{GeV^4} $$

so

$$ \abs{V_{\min}} = \frac{0.12940\times3.6741\times10^{9}}{4} = \frac{4.7546\times10^{8}}{4} = 1.1886\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{GeV^4} . $$

That is, about $1.2\times10^8\ \mathrm{GeV^4}$. Converted to an energy scale, $\abs{V_{\min}}^{1/4}=104.4\ \mathrm{GeV}$, which is the electroweak scale itself. Compared with the dark energy density,

$$ \frac{\abs{V_{\min}}}{\rho_\Lambda} = \frac{1.1886\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{GeV^4}}{2.8\times10^{-47}\ \mathrm{GeV^4}} = 4.25\times10^{54} . $$

This is a factor of about $10^{55}$, that is, a discrepancy of 55 orders of magnitude. Compared on the energy scale, it is $104.4\ \mathrm{GeV}$ versus $2.3\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{GeV}$, a ratio of $4.5\times10^{13}$ (consistent with $(4.25\times10^{54})^{1/4}$).

The meaning of this is serious. In general relativity the energy density of the vacuum acts directly on gravity as a cosmological constant. The bottom of the Higgs potential takes the huge negative value $-1.2\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{GeV^4}$, whereas the observed vacuum energy is the extremely small positive value $+2.8\times10^{-47}\ \mathrm{GeV^4}$. Therefore some other contribution must be canceling the Higgs vacuum energy to a precision of $55$ digits. Moreover, this is not a matter of the Higgs alone: the QCD condensate ($\sim(0.2\ \mathrm{GeV})^4$) and the zero-point energies of all fields contribute in the same way. Why their sum comes out almost exactly zero, nobody knows. This is the cosmological constant problem.

Verification. We check (4) with a different expression. Using $v^2=\mu^2/\lambda$, we can write $\abs{V_{\min}}=\lambda v^4/4=\lambda(\mu^2/\lambda)^2/4=\mu^4/(4\lambda)$. Inserting $\mu=88.565\ \mathrm{GeV}$ from Exercise 13.6(2), we get $\mu^4=6.1525\times10^7$ and $4\lambda=0.51762$, so $\mu^4/(4\lambda)=1.1886\times10^8\ \mathrm{GeV^4}$, which agrees with the above. Since the same value came out by two independent routes, the calculation is correct. (3) can be checked in limits. For $m_\eta\to0$ (the Higgs infinitely light = the coherence length infinitely long), $\kappa\to0$ and the superconductor is perfectly type I; for $m_B\to0$ (the gauge field massless = the penetration depth infinite), $\kappa\to\infty$ and it is extremely type II; both agree with intuition. For (1), in the limit $\abs a\to0$ ($T\to T_c$) the decay length diverges. This is in accord with the common knowledge of critical phenomena that the coherence length diverges at the transition point.

Meaning. (1)–(3) show that $\kappa$, the index used in the materials design of superconductors, is none other than the “mass ratio of the Higgs boson to the gauge boson.” Nb$_3$Sn and NbTi are used for superconducting magnets because, with $\kappa\gg1/\sqrt2$, magnetic flux can enter as Abrikosov vortices and superconductivity is not destroyed even in high fields. Applying the same discriminant to the universe, our vacuum turns out to be a type-II superconductor with $\kappa=0.971$. If $m_H$ had been a little lighter, with $m_H<m_Z$, the universe would have been a type-I “superconductor,” and the behavior of electroweak strings (cosmic strings) would also have been different. (4) is the enormous mismatch that appears when the same dictionary is applied to the vacuum energy. In a superconductor the condensation energy density (of order $\sim10^3\ \mathrm{J/m^3}$ for Pb) is a real, measurable quantity, observed as the jump in the specific heat. In the universe, however, the same condensation energy should act on gravity but does not. The contrast between materials science, which has ways to measure the condensation energy, and cosmology, in which that value is off by 55 orders of magnitude, is the theme of this problem.

E.14 Solutions for Chapter 14: Neutrino Oscillations and Majorana Particles

Exercise 14.1: The two-flavor oscillation probability once more

Problem (restated)

Without retracing the derivation in the main text, carry out the calculation yourself to the end.

(1) Starting from $\ket{\nu_e}=\cos\theta\ket{\nu_1}+\sin\theta\ket{\nu_2}$, find $\braket{\nu_e|\nu(t)}$ at time $t$.

(2) Compute $P(\nu_e\to\nu_e)=\abs{\braket{\nu_e|\nu(t)}}^2$ and show that it equals $1-\sin^22\theta\sin^2(\phi/2)$ (with $\phi=(E_2-E_1)t$).

(3) Verify that $P(\nu_e\to\nu_e)+P(\nu_e\to\nu_\mu)=1$.

(4) For $\theta=45^\circ$ (maximal mixing), express in terms of $\Delta m^2$ and $E$ the smallest $L$ at which $P(\nu_e\to\nu_\mu)$ reaches $1$.

Solution

Strategy. The only tools we use are the two-flavor mixing of Section 14.2.2 of Chapter 14 of this book, $\ket{\nu_e}=\cos\theta\ket{\nu_1}+\sin\theta\ket{\nu_2}$ and $\ket{\nu_\mu}=-\sin\theta\ket{\nu_1}+\cos\theta\ket{\nu_2}$, and the fact that the mass eigenstates rotate with the phase $\ee^{-\ii E_it}$. In the main text we projected onto the $\nu_\mu$ component; here we project onto the $\nu_e$ component. Only the target of the projection differs and the procedure is identical, and at the end we check that the two are connected through the sum of probabilities. Note that $\ket{\nu_1},\ket{\nu_2}$ are eigenstates of the free Hamiltonian, so they form an orthonormal set $\braket{\nu_i|\nu_j}=\delta_{ij}$, and since the mixing matrix is a real orthogonal matrix, $\ket{\nu_e},\ket{\nu_\mu}$ also form an orthonormal set.

(1) The initial condition is $\ket{\nu(0)}=\ket{\nu_e}$. We time-evolve it while keeping it expanded in the mass eigenstates. The expansion coefficients are numbers and are not subject to time evolution; only the phases of the basis kets move:

$$ \ket{\nu(t)} = \cos\theta\,\ee^{-\ii E_1t}\ket{\nu_1} + \sin\theta\,\ee^{-\ii E_2t}\ket{\nu_2} $$

Here $E_i=\sqrt{\bm p^2+m_i^2}$. Next we multiply from the left by $\bra{\nu_e}=\cos\theta\bra{\nu_1}+\sin\theta\bra{\nu_2}$. Since the mixing angle $\theta$ is real, taking the complex conjugate when forming the bra does not change the coefficients. Using $\braket{\nu_1|\nu_1}=\braket{\nu_2|\nu_2}=1$ and $\braket{\nu_1|\nu_2}=\braket{\nu_2|\nu_1}=0$, the cross terms drop out and we obtain

$$ \braket{\nu_e|\nu(t)} = \cos^2\theta\,\ee^{-\ii E_1t} + \sin^2\theta\,\ee^{-\ii E_2t} $$

At $t=0$ this becomes $\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta=1$, confirming that the normalization is preserved. Also, if $E_1=E_2$ (degenerate masses), this amplitude is itself a phase factor of absolute value $1$, and nothing happens.

(2) We factor out the common factor $\ee^{-\ii E_1t}$. Taking the absolute value, this factor becomes $1$ and drops out, so with $\phi\equiv(E_2-E_1)t$ we have

$$ \braket{\nu_e|\nu(t)} = \ee^{-\ii E_1t}\left(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta\,\ee^{-\ii\phi}\right) $$ $$ P(\nu_e\to\nu_e) = \abs{\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta\,\ee^{-\ii\phi}}^2 $$

The squared absolute value of a complex number $a+b\ee^{-\ii\phi}$ (with $a,b$ real), separating real and imaginary parts, is

$$ (a+b\cos\phi)^2+(b\sin\phi)^2 = a^2+2ab\cos\phi+b^2\cos^2\phi+b^2\sin^2\phi = a^2+b^2+2ab\cos\phi $$

Substituting $a=\cos^2\theta$ and $b=\sin^2\theta$ gives

$$ P(\nu_e\to\nu_e) = \cos^4\theta+\sin^4\theta+2\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta\,\cos\phi $$

Here we prepare two identities. First,

$$ \cos^4\theta+\sin^4\theta =\left(\cos^2\theta+\sin^2\theta\right)^2-2\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta =1-2\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta $$

Second, from $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$ we have $\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta=\tfrac14\sin^22\theta$, and hence $2\cos^2\theta\sin^2\theta=\tfrac12\sin^22\theta$. Substituting these,

$$ P(\nu_e\to\nu_e) = 1-\frac12\sin^22\theta+\frac12\sin^22\theta\cos\phi = 1-\frac12\sin^22\theta\left(1-\cos\phi\right) $$

Finally, using the half-angle formula $1-\cos\phi=2\sin^2(\phi/2)$, we obtain

$$ P(\nu_e\to\nu_e) = 1-\sin^22\theta\,\sin^2\frac{\phi}{2} $$

Inserting the ultrarelativistic expansion $E_i\simeq p+m_i^2/2p$ and $t\simeq L$ gives $\phi/2=\Delta m^2L/4E$, which agrees with the survival-probability formula in the main text.

(3) For the transition probability, we simply take $\ket{\nu_\mu}$ as the target of the projection, with the same procedure. Since $\braket{\nu_\mu|\nu_1}=-\sin\theta$ and $\braket{\nu_\mu|\nu_2}=\cos\theta$,

$$ \braket{\nu_\mu|\nu(t)} = -\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\ee^{-\ii E_1t}+\cos\theta\sin\theta\,\ee^{-\ii E_2t} =\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\ee^{-\ii E_1t}\left(\ee^{-\ii\phi}-1\right) $$ $$ \abs{\ee^{-\ii\phi}-1}^2=(\cos\phi-1)^2+\sin^2\phi=2-2\cos\phi=4\sin^2\frac{\phi}{2} $$ $$ P(\nu_e\to\nu_\mu)=\frac14\sin^22\theta\times4\sin^2\frac{\phi}{2}=\sin^22\theta\,\sin^2\frac{\phi}{2} $$

Therefore the sum is

$$ P(\nu_e\to\nu_e)+P(\nu_e\to\nu_\mu) =\left(1-\sin^22\theta\sin^2\frac{\phi}{2}\right)+\sin^22\theta\sin^2\frac{\phi}{2}=1 $$

This is no accident. Since $\{\ket{\nu_e},\ket{\nu_\mu}\}$ is a complete set, $\ket{\nu_e}\bra{\nu_e}+\ket{\nu_\mu}\bra{\nu_\mu}=\mathbb 1$, and

$$ \sum_{\beta=e,\mu}\abs{\braket{\nu_\beta|\nu(t)}}^2 = \braket{\nu(t)|\nu(t)}=1 $$

follows automatically from the unitarity of the time evolution. That is, the probabilities summing to $1$ is a direct consequence of the mixing matrix being unitary. The same argument gives $\sum_\beta P_{\alpha\beta}=1$ for three flavors as well.

(4) For $\theta=45^\circ$ we have $2\theta=90^\circ$, so $\sin^22\theta=1$, and the transition probability is

$$ P(\nu_e\to\nu_\mu)=\sin^2\left(\frac{\Delta m^2L}{4E}\right) $$

This reaches $1$ when $\sin^2(\cdots)=1$, that is, when the phase is an odd multiple of $\pi/2$, and the smallest distance is given by

$$ \frac{\Delta m^2L}{4E}=\frac{\pi}{2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L=\frac{2\pi E}{\Delta m^2} $$

Compared with the oscillation length $L_\mathrm{osc}=4\pi E/\Delta m^2$ of Chapter 14 of this book, this is exactly $L_\mathrm{osc}/2$, that is, the position of the first oscillation maximum. In practical units, from $1.267\,\Delta m^2L/E=\pi/2$,

$$ L[\mathrm{km}]=\frac{\pi}{2\times1.267}\frac{E[\mathrm{GeV}]}{\Delta m^2[\mathrm{eV^2}]} =1.24\,\frac{E[\mathrm{GeV}]}{\Delta m^2[\mathrm{eV^2}]} $$

Substituting $E\approx0.6\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and $\abs{\Delta m_{32}^2}=2.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV^2}$ gives $L=1.24\times0.6/(2.5\times10^{-3})=298\ \mathrm{km}$. The actual baseline of T2K is $295\ \mathrm{km}$ from J-PARC to Super-Kamiokande, a distance that was fixed beforehand by geography. Therefore what T2K designed was not $L$ but $E$: by pointing the beam $2.5^\circ$ off the beam axis (the off-axis method), the flux peak is narrowed to $E\simeq0.6\ \mathrm{GeV}$, so that $295\ \mathrm{km}$ falls at the first oscillation maximum. In any case, the binding condition is the combination $L/E$, and this formula supplies it.

Verification. We check three limits. First, for $\theta\to0$, $\sin^22\theta\to0$, so $P(\nu_e\to\nu_e)\to1$ and $P(\nu_e\to\nu_\mu)\to0$. Without mixing, the flavor does not change. Second, for $\Delta m^2\to0$ (degenerate masses), $\phi\to0$, so $\sin^2(\phi/2)\to0$, and again $P(\nu_e\to\nu_e)\to1$. The two conditions read off in Step 3 of the main text, that oscillations do not occur if either condition is missing, survive in the final formula as well. Third, the dimensions. In natural units $\hbar=c=1$, $[\Delta m^2]=\mathrm{eV^2}$, $[L]=\mathrm{eV^{-1}}$, $[E]=\mathrm{eV}$, so $\Delta m^2L/4E$ is $\mathrm{eV^2}\cdot\mathrm{eV^{-1}}\cdot\mathrm{eV^{-1}}$, which is dimensionless and is correctly a phase.

Meaning. The final formula separates completely into the product of $\sin^22\theta$ (the depth) and $\sin^2(\Delta m^2L/4E)$ (the period), so an experiment can read off the mixing angle from the former and the mass-squared difference from the latter, independently. And the mathematics treated here is precisely that of coherent Rabi oscillations of a two-level system. The structure in which the eigenvalue difference $E_2-E_1$ determines the angular frequency of the oscillation and the basis misalignment $\theta$ determines its amplitude is identical to Rabi oscillations in NMR and ESR, charge oscillations in a double quantum dot, and quantum beats seen in ultrafast spectroscopy. For a materials scientist, neutrino oscillation can be read as “a familiar two-level problem, solved with an energy difference smaller by orders of magnitude, $10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV^2}$, and a propagation distance longer by orders of magnitude, $10^2$–$10^4\ \mathrm{km}$.” Oscillations are observable because in the phase $\Delta m^2L/4E$ the “extremely small $\Delta m^2$” and the “extremely large $L$” cancel in the product, giving a phase of $O(1)$.

Exercise 14.2: Deriving $1.27$ yourself, and designing an experiment

Problem (restated)

(1) Starting from $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$, derive, without looking at the main text, the conversion factor for $\Delta m^2$ measured in $\mathrm{eV^2}$, $L$ in $\mathrm{km}$, and $E$ in $\mathrm{GeV}$.

(2) Show that the same coefficient can also be used when $L$ is in m and $E$ is in MeV.

(3) Find the oscillation length $L_\mathrm{osc}$ for reactor $\bar\nu_e$ with $\Delta m_{21}^2=7.53\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV^2}$ and $E=3.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(4) JUNO was placed at $L=52.5\ \mathrm{km}$ in order to measure $\Delta m_{21}^2$ and the mass ordering simultaneously. What is the phase at $E=3.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$, in rad? Is it an oscillation maximum or minimum?

Solution

Strategy. The only tool is dimensional analysis. From the single requirement that the phase be dimensionless, the way $\hbar$ and $c$ enter is uniquely fixed. We then translate $\hbar c$ into “experimentalist’s units.” The numerical values were recomputed within this solution using python3 as a calculator.

(1) In natural units the phase is $\Delta m^2L/4E$. We remove $\hbar=c=1$ and restore the dimensions. Since $\Delta m^2$ is a mass squared, to convert it to energy we multiply by $c^4$ and write $\Delta m^2c^4$ ($mc^2$ is an energy, and its square is $m^2c^4$). Then

$$ \frac{\Delta m^2c^4\,L}{4E} \quad\longrightarrow\quad \frac{[\mathrm{eV^2}]\cdot[\mathrm{m}]}{[\mathrm{eV}]}=[\mathrm{eV\cdot m}] $$

leaves a surplus dimension. The only constant that can cancel it is $\hbar c$ (the dimension of $\hbar c$ is energy $\times$ length). Therefore the restored form is uniquely

$$ \frac{\Delta m^2L}{4E}\Big|_{\hbar=c=1} \ \longrightarrow\ \frac{\Delta m^2c^4\,L}{4\,\hbar c\,E} $$

Next we write $\hbar c$ in eV m. Since $1\ \mathrm{MeV}=10^6\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $1\ \mathrm{fm}=10^{-15}\ \mathrm{m}$,

$$ \hbar c = 197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm} = 197.327\times10^{6}\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{eV\,m} = 1.97327\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{eV\,m} $$

Let the numerical values in experimentalist’s units be $\widetilde{\Delta m^2}$ (in units of $\mathrm{eV^2}$), $\widetilde L$ (in km, $L=10^3\widetilde L\ \mathrm{m}$), and $\widetilde E$ (in GeV, $E=10^9\widetilde E\ \mathrm{eV}$). Then

$$ \frac{\Delta m^2c^4L}{4\hbar cE} =\frac{\widetilde{\Delta m^2}\ \mathrm{eV^2}\times10^3\widetilde L\ \mathrm{m}} {4\times1.97327\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{eV\,m}\times10^9\widetilde E\ \mathrm{eV}} $$

The units cancel completely, as $\mathrm{eV^2\cdot m}/(\mathrm{eV\,m\cdot eV})$. Keeping only the numerical coefficient,

$$ \frac{10^3}{4\times1.97327\times10^{-7}\times10^{9}} =\frac{10^3}{4\times197.327} =\frac{10^3}{789.308} =1.26693 $$

that is,

$$ \frac{\Delta m^2L}{4E}=1.2669\,\frac{\Delta m^2[\mathrm{eV^2}]\ L[\mathrm{km}]}{E[\mathrm{GeV}]} $$

The number $1.27$ is merely the natural constant $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$ translated into the human-convenience units $\mathrm{km}$, $\mathrm{GeV}$, and $\mathrm{eV^2}$, and it contains no physical content.

(2) In the same formula we rewrite $L=\widetilde L\ \mathrm{m}$ (in units of m) and $E=10^6\widetilde E\ \mathrm{eV}$ (in units of MeV).

$$ \frac{\widetilde{\Delta m^2}\ \mathrm{eV^2}\times\widetilde L\ \mathrm{m}} {4\times1.97327\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{eV\,m}\times10^{6}\widetilde E\ \mathrm{eV}} =\frac{1}{4\times1.97327\times10^{-1}}\frac{\widetilde{\Delta m^2}\widetilde L}{\widetilde E} =\frac{1}{0.789308}\frac{\widetilde{\Delta m^2}\widetilde L}{\widetilde E} $$

The coefficient is $1/0.789308=1.26693$, exactly the same as in (1). The reason is clear: in $\mathrm{km}\to\mathrm{m}$ the numerator is multiplied by $10^{-3}$, and in $\mathrm{GeV}\to\mathrm{MeV}$ the denominator is multiplied by $10^{-3}$ as well, so they cancel in the ratio. In general, if the units of $L$ and $E$ are changed by the same factor, the coefficient is unchanged. Reactor experiments have $L\sim10^3\ \mathrm{m}$ and $E\sim$ a few MeV, so this way of reading it gives numbers that are easier to handle.

(3) The oscillation length is the distance over which the phase advances by $\pi$ (the period of $\sin^2$ is $\pi$).

$$ 1.26693\,\frac{\widetilde{\Delta m^2}\widetilde L_\mathrm{osc}}{\widetilde E}=\pi \quad\Longrightarrow\quad L_\mathrm{osc}[\mathrm{km}]=\frac{\pi}{1.26693}\frac{E[\mathrm{GeV}]}{\Delta m^2[\mathrm{eV^2}]} =2.4797\,\frac{E[\mathrm{GeV}]}{\Delta m^2[\mathrm{eV^2}]} $$

We substitute $E=3.6\ \mathrm{MeV}=3.6\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and $\Delta m_{21}^2=7.53\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV^2}$.

$$ \frac{E}{\Delta m^2}=\frac{3.6\times10^{-3}}{7.53\times10^{-5}}=47.809 $$ $$ L_\mathrm{osc}=2.4797\times47.809=118.55\ \mathrm{km} $$

That is, $L_\mathrm{osc}\simeq119\ \mathrm{km}$, and the first oscillation maximum lies at half of this, $59.3\ \mathrm{km}$. This agrees with the $118.6\ \mathrm{km}$ in the hint in the main text (obtained using the coefficient $2.48$).

(4) The phase for JUNO is

$$ \Phi = 1.26693\times\frac{7.53\times10^{-5}\times52.5}{3.6\times10^{-3}} $$

Computing the numerator first, $7.53\times10^{-5}\times52.5=3.95325\times10^{-3}$; dividing this by $3.6\times10^{-3}$ gives $1.09813$; and finally multiplying by $1.26693$,

$$ \Phi = 1.3913\ \mathrm{rad} $$

Dividing by $\pi$ gives $\Phi/\pi=0.4428$, so $\Phi\approx0.44\pi$, that is, it lies just short of the first oscillation maximum $\pi/2=1.5708\ \mathrm{rad}$. The oscillation factor and the survival probability are

$$ \sin^2\Phi = \sin^2(1.3913)=0.9681 $$ $$ P(\bar\nu_e\to\bar\nu_e)=1-\sin^22\theta_{12}\sin^2\Phi =1-0.851\times0.9681=0.176 $$

(We used $\sin^22\theta_{12}=4\sin^2\theta_{12}\cos^2\theta_{12}=4\times0.307\times0.693=0.851$ from $\sin^2\theta_{12}=0.307$ in Table 14.5.) Since $\sin^2\Phi$ is $0.968$, close to the maximum value, this is almost exactly at the minimum of the survival probability (the oscillation maximum). Relative to $L_\mathrm{osc}/2=59.3\ \mathrm{km}$, $52.5\ \mathrm{km}$ is $0.89$ times as large, and since the crest of $\sin^2$ is flat near the top, the sensitivity hardly drops even if one is somewhat off.

There are two reasons JUNO was placed here. First, it can capture the large-amplitude oscillation due to $\Delta m_{21}^2$ at its deepest point. Second, the fine ripples due to $\Delta m_{31}^2$ (whose phase is faster by a factor $\abs{\Delta m_{31}^2}/\Delta m_{21}^2=32.5$) are superimposed there, and the positions of these ripples shift in opposite directions for NO and IO, so the mass ordering can be read off from the fine structure of the energy spectrum. This requires an extremely good energy resolution of $3\%/\sqrt{E[\mathrm{MeV}]}$.

Verification. We check the coefficient by an independent route. Translating $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$ into a length in $\mathrm{eV^{-1}}$, $1\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}}=1.97327\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{m}$, so $1\ \mathrm{km}=10^3/(1.97327\times10^{-7})\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}}=5.0677\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}}$, and $1\ \mathrm{GeV}=10^9\ \mathrm{eV}$. Therefore, inserting $\Delta m^2=1\ \mathrm{eV^2}$, $L=1\ \mathrm{km}$, and $E=1\ \mathrm{GeV}$ into $\Delta m^2L/4E$ gives $1\times5.0677\times10^9/(4\times10^9)=1.2669$, which agrees with the value in (1). Checking the answer to (3) by another route, the first maximum is $L_\mathrm{osc}/2=1.24\times47.809=59.28\ \mathrm{km}$, and the fact that the effective distance of KamLAND, $\sim180\ \mathrm{km}$, is about three times that is consistent with the statement in the main text.

Meaning. The core of this exercise is the recognition that “$1.27$ is not a physical constant but a unit conversion.” The same structure appears frequently in condensed matter physics as well. For example, $\hbar\omega[\mathrm{meV}]=4.136\,\nu[\mathrm{THz}]$, $\lambda[\mathrm{nm}]=1239.8/E[\mathrm{eV}]$, or $E[\mathrm{meV}]=81.81/\lambda[\AA]^2$ used in inelastic neutron scattering are all just numbers that translate $\hbar$ and $c$ (or the neutron mass) into laboratory units. Once you have derived it yourself, you no longer need to memorize the coefficient, and you can immediately judge how the coefficient moves when the units are changed. And as (4) shows, the baseline of an experiment is determined by working backward from the “phase one wants to build.” Once the $\Delta m^2$ to be measured is fixed, $L/E$ is fixed, and from it the geographic arrangement of the accelerator and detector is fixed. This is exactly the same design philosophy as in condensed matter measurements, where the spectrometer resolution and the incident energy are designed from the energy scale one wants to measure.

Exercise 14.3: The up–down asymmetry of atmospheric neutrinos

Problem (restated)

Take $\Delta m_{31}^2=2.45\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV^2}$, $\sin^22\theta_{23}=1$ (approximating maximal mixing), and the Earth’s radius $R_\oplus=6371\ \mathrm{km}$.

(1) For the zenith angle $\theta_z$ ($\cos\theta_z=1$ means from directly overhead, $-1$ from directly below), verify from geometry that the flight distance is approximately given by $L(\theta_z)\simeq\sqrt{(R_\oplus+h)^2-(R_\oplus\sin\theta_z)^2}-R_\oplus\cos\theta_z$ (where $h=15\ \mathrm{km}$ is the production altitude).

(2) For $E=1\ \mathrm{GeV}$, find $P(\nu_\mu\to\nu_\mu)$ for neutrinos from directly overhead ($\cos\theta_z=1$) and from directly below ($\cos\theta_z=-1$).

(3) Find the up–down ratio $U/D\equiv P_\mathrm{up}/P_\mathrm{down}$, and explain the “deficit of upward-going $\nu_\mu$” observed by Super-Kamiokande.

(4) Carry out the same calculation for $\nu_e$ using $\sin^22\theta_{13}=0.086$. Why is the up–down asymmetry of $\nu_e$ almost invisible?

Solution

Strategy. Part (1) is pure plane geometry (the law of cosines). Parts (2)–(4) simply insert the $L$ of (1) into the practical form $P=\sin^22\theta\sin^2(1.267\Delta m^2L/E)$ of Chapter 14 of this book, but we must note that on the long-distance side the phase becomes so large that averaging occurs. All numerical values were computed with python3. Following the terminology of Section 14.3.1 of this book, “down-going events” are the short-distance ones born in the atmosphere directly above the detector and coming down, and “up-going events” are the long-distance ones born on the far side of the Earth and thrusting up through the Earth.

(1) Let the center of the Earth be $O$, the position of the detector $D$, and the production point of the neutrino $S$. Since the detector may be regarded as being on the surface, $\abs{OD}=R_\oplus$, and since the production point is in the atmosphere at altitude $h$, $\abs{OS}=R_\oplus+h$. The flight distance we want is $L=\abs{SD}$.

The zenith angle $\theta_z$ is the angle, measured at the detector, between “straight up (the direction from $O$ to $D$, that is, the outward radial direction)” and “the direction in which $S$ is seen from $D$.” On the other hand, the interior angle $\angle ODS$ at vertex $D$ of triangle $ODS$ is the angle between “the direction in which $O$ is seen from $D$” and “the direction in which $S$ is seen from $D$.” The former is exactly opposite to straight up, so the two angles are supplementary, and

$$ \angle ODS = \pi-\theta_z $$

Sides $\abs{OD}=R_\oplus$ and $\abs{DS}=L$ enclose this interior angle, and the opposite side is $\abs{OS}=R_\oplus+h$, so by the law of cosines

$$ (R_\oplus+h)^2 = R_\oplus^2 + L^2 - 2R_\oplus L\cos\left(\pi-\theta_z\right) = R_\oplus^2+L^2+2R_\oplus L\cos\theta_z $$

Here we used $\cos(\pi-\theta_z)=-\cos\theta_z$. That the angle has been taken correctly can be checked in extreme cases. For $\theta_z=0$, coming down from directly overhead, $\angle ODS=\pi$, and $O,D,S$ lie on a straight line in this order. The equation above then becomes $(R_\oplus+h)^2=(R_\oplus+L)^2$, which gives $L=h$, indeed describing the situation “born $15\ \mathrm{km}$ overhead and falling straight down.” Conversely, for $\theta_z=\pi$ (from directly below), $\angle ODS=0$, with $O$ lying between $D$ and $S$, and $L=2R_\oplus+h$. Now let us solve the equation above for $L$.
