$$ L^2 + 2R_\oplus\cos\theta_z\,L + \left[R_\oplus^2-(R_\oplus+h)^2\right]=0 $$ $$ L = -R_\oplus\cos\theta_z \pm\sqrt{R_\oplus^2\cos^2\theta_z-R_\oplus^2+(R_\oplus+h)^2} $$

The content of the square root can be rewritten as $(R_\oplus+h)^2-R_\oplus^2(1-\cos^2\theta_z)=(R_\oplus+h)^2-R_\oplus^2\sin^2\theta_z$. Since we must have $L>0$, we take the $+$ sign. Therefore

$$ L(\theta_z)=\sqrt{(R_\oplus+h)^2-\left(R_\oplus\sin\theta_z\right)^2}-R_\oplus\cos\theta_z $$

is obtained, in agreement with the formula in the problem. We check two limits. For $\cos\theta_z=1$ ($\sin\theta_z=0$), $L=(R_\oplus+h)-R_\oplus=h=15\ \mathrm{km}$, and for $\cos\theta_z=-1$, $L=(R_\oplus+h)+R_\oplus=2R_\oplus+h=2\times6371+15=12\,757\ \mathrm{km}$. In the horizontal direction ($\cos\theta_z=0$), $L=\sqrt{(R_\oplus+h)^2-R_\oplus^2}=\sqrt{2R_\oplus h+h^2}=437\ \mathrm{km}$. The meaning of this formula is that even while sitting at the same detector, the flight distance swings from $15\ \mathrm{km}$ to $12\,757\ \mathrm{km}$, a factor of $850$.

(2) The phase is $\Phi=1.26693\,\Delta m^2[\mathrm{eV^2}]L[\mathrm{km}]/E[\mathrm{GeV}]$.

Downward events ($\cos\theta_z=+1$, $L=15\ \mathrm{km}$).

$$ \Phi_\mathrm{down}=1.26693\times2.45\times10^{-3}\times\frac{15}{1}=0.046560\ \mathrm{rad} $$ $$ \sin^2\Phi_\mathrm{down}=\sin^2(0.046560)=2.1662\times10^{-3} $$ $$ P_\mathrm{down}(\nu_\mu\to\nu_\mu)=1-1\times2.1662\times10^{-3}=0.99783 $$

Since the phase is only $0.047\ \mathrm{rad}$, there is almost no oscillation. This is because $15\ \mathrm{km}$ is a mere $1.5\%$ of the oscillation length $L_\mathrm{osc}=2.4797\times1/(2.45\times10^{-3})=1012\ \mathrm{km}$.

Upward events ($\cos\theta_z=-1$, $L=12\,757\ \mathrm{km}$).

$$ \Phi_\mathrm{up}=1.26693\times2.45\times10^{-3}\times12\,757=39.598\ \mathrm{rad} $$

This is $12.60$ times $\pi$. Substituting formally gives $\sin^2(39.598)=0.8964$, but this number is meaningless. The reason is that $\Phi$ depends on both $L$ and $E$, and in an actual measurement

  • $L$ is smeared by the angular resolution in the zenith angle ($20^\circ$–$30^\circ$ for events at the $1\ \mathrm{GeV}$ level),
  • $E$ is smeared by the energy resolution and, to begin with, by the fact that atmospheric neutrinos have a continuous power-law spectrum,

so the phase fluctuates by more than $\pi$. Averaging $\sin^2$ over a uniform phase distribution gives $\braket{\sin^2\Phi}=1/2$, so

$$ P_\mathrm{up}(\nu_\mu\to\nu_\mu)=1-\frac12\sin^22\theta_{23}=1-\frac12=0.50 $$

That is, the $\nu_\mu$ that have come up through the Earth are reduced by half.

(3) The up/down ratio is

$$ \frac{U}{D}=\frac{P_\mathrm{up}}{P_\mathrm{down}}=\frac{0.50}{0.99783}=0.5011\simeq0.50 $$

Let us sort out why this value $0.5$ was decisive. The prediction of the absolute atmospheric neutrino flux carries an uncertainty of about $20\%$, which comes from the cosmic-ray spectrum and the hadron production model. Therefore, if the only fact were that “$\nu_\mu$ are short by 30%,” an escape route would remain: an error in the theoretical calculation. However, since the Earth is spherically symmetric and cosmic rays are isotropic, the production rates of $\nu_\mu$ coming from above and $\nu_\mu$ coming from below are equal. Taking the ratio $U/D$ cancels both the absolute flux and the uncertainty of the production model completely, and since the detector and the energy range are the same, the experimental systematic errors are also common. The only remaining difference is the flight distance, and there the $L$ dependence was clearly visible. In 1998, Super-Kamiokande showed this, making it impossible to explain the disappearance of $\nu_\mu$ by anything other than oscillation. Moreover, there was no increase in $\nu_e$ corresponding to the vanished $\nu_\mu$; the destination was $\nu_\tau$.

(4) The survival probability of $\nu_e$ also takes the same form in the two-generation approximation with respect to $\Delta m_{31}^2$, with only the depth of the mixing replaced by $\sin^22\theta_{13}=0.086$.

$$ P_\mathrm{down}(\nu_e\to\nu_e)=1-0.086\times\sin^2(0.046560)=1-0.086\times2.1662\times10^{-3}=0.99981 $$ $$ P_\mathrm{up}(\nu_e\to\nu_e)=1-\frac{0.086}{2}=1-0.043=0.957 $$ $$ \frac{U}{D}=\frac{0.957}{0.99981}=0.9572 $$

That is, the deficit of upward $\nu_e$ is $1-0.9572=0.043$, only $4.3\%$, more than an order of magnitude smaller than the $50\%$ for $\nu_\mu$. The reason is simple: the depth of the oscillation is determined directly by $\sin^22\theta$. Since $\theta_{23}\approx48^\circ$ is nearly maximal mixing, $\sin^22\theta_{23}\approx1$, whereas $\theta_{13}=8.53^\circ$ is small and gives only $\sin^22\theta_{13}=0.086$. The smallness of the mixing angle translates directly into the smallness of the asymmetry.

Experimentally, a $4\%$ deficit is buried in the $20\%$ flux uncertainty of atmospheric neutrinos. It was in 2012 that $\theta_{13}$ was first measured significantly, by the reactor experiments (Daya Bay, RENO, Double Chooz). There, taking the ratio of the near and far detectors eliminated the flux uncertainty, and the shallow oscillation of $0.086$ was finally captured. At the time of the discovery the precision of $\sin^22\theta_{13}$ was about $1$–$2$ parts in ten, but with subsequent accumulation of statistics Daya Bay has reached a few $\%$, and $\theta_{13}$ is now the most precisely measured of the three mixing angles. What mattered here, too, was that what was measured was not the absolute flux but the near/far ratio.

Verification. First, we check the limiting values of the formula for $L$ independently ($h$, $\sqrt{2R_\oplus h}$, $2R_\oplus+h$). Second, we re-examine the phase $\Phi_\mathrm{up}=39.6\ \mathrm{rad}$ in terms of the oscillation length. Since $L_\mathrm{osc}=2.4797\times E/\Delta m^2=1012\ \mathrm{km}$, we have $12\,757/1012=12.6$ periods, which agrees with $\Phi_\mathrm{up}/\pi=12.60$. Third, we check where the vanished $\nu_\mu$ went. In the two-generation approximation $P(\nu_\mu\to\nu_\tau)=\sin^22\theta_{23}\sin^2\Phi$, which averages to $0.50$ for upward events. Since $P_\mathrm{up}(\nu_\mu\to\nu_\mu)+P_\mathrm{up}(\nu_\mu\to\nu_\tau)=0.50+0.50=1$, probability is conserved.

Meaning. What this exercise teaches is a general rule of experimental physics: measurements of absolute values depend on the model; measurements of ratios do not. In atmospheric neutrinos the zenith-angle ratio played this role, and in reactor experiments the near/far detector ratio did. The very same structure exists in materials measurements. Absolute values of reflectivity or scattering intensity are contaminated by the calibration of the incident intensity, the sample shape, and the instrument function, and are hard to trust; but the polarization ratio of the same sample, the rate of change with temperature, and the ratio to a reference sample are orders of magnitude more reliable because the common systematic errors cancel. That the discovery of neutrino oscillation was achieved by a “measurement of ratios” is worth remembering as a textbook case of measurement design.

Exercise 14.4: Looking for the MSW resonance in the Earth as well

Problem (restated)

(1) Find the electron density $n_e$ of the Earth’s mantle ($\rho\approx4.5\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$, $Y_e=0.5$).

(2) Find the matter potential there, $V_\mathrm{CC}=\sqrt2G_Fn_e$, in eV.

(3) Find the MSW resonance energy for $\Delta m_{31}^2=2.45\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV^2}$ and $\theta_{13}=8.53^\circ$.

(4) What does this result mean for NOvA ($L=810\ \mathrm{km}$, $E=2\ \mathrm{GeV}$) and DUNE ($L=1300\ \mathrm{km}$, $E=2.5\ \mathrm{GeV}$)? Also explain why using the fact that the matter effect changes sign between $\nu$ and $\bar\nu$ makes it possible to determine the mass ordering.

Solution

Strategy. The tools we use are the matter potential $V_\mathrm{CC}=\sqrt2G_Fn_e$ of Section 14.3.4 of this book, the MSW resonance condition $(\Delta m^2/2E)\cos2\theta=\sqrt2G_Fn_e$, and the formula for the effective mixing angle in matter. To bridge natural units and cgs units we use $\hbar c=1.97327\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{GeV\,cm}$. All numerical values were computed with python3.

(1) The electron number density is obtained by multiplying the mass density by Avogadro’s number and by the “number of electrons per nucleon” $Y_e$. Here $Y_e=Z/A$ is the ratio of the electron number to the nucleon number, and the main constituents of the mantle (O, Si, Mg, Fe) all have $Z/A\simeq0.5$.

$$ n_e = \rho\,N_A\,Y_e = 4.5\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\times6.022\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{mol^{-1}}\times0.5 $$ $$ = 1.355\times10^{24}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} $$

For reference, this is smaller by a factor of $44$ than the value $n_e\approx6.0\times10^{25}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ at the center of the Sun ($\rho\approx150\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$, $Y_e\approx0.67$). On the other hand, note that it is of the same order as the total electron density of solids ($2\times10^{24}$ for Fe and $8\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ for $\mathrm{SiO_2}$). What neutrinos feel is not the conduction electrons (Cu: $8.5\times10^{22}$, Al: $1.8\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$) but all the electrons, including the bound ones, and as a material this is a perfectly ordinary density.

(2) Since we calculate in natural units, we first translate $\mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ into $\mathrm{GeV^3}$. From $\hbar c=1.97327\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{GeV\,cm}$ we have $1\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}=1.97327\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and therefore

$$ 1\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} = \left(1.97327\times10^{-14}\right)^3\ \mathrm{GeV^3} = 7.6835\times10^{-42}\ \mathrm{GeV^3} $$

Inserting $G_F=1.1664\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$ and collecting the coefficients, we get

$$ \sqrt2\,G_F\times7.6835\times10^{-42} =1.41421\times1.1664\times10^{-5}\times7.6835\times10^{-42} =1.2674\times10^{-46} $$

That is, $V_\mathrm{CC}=1.267\times10^{-46}\,n_e[\mathrm{cm^{-3}}]\ \mathrm{GeV}$ (this $1.267$ is completely unrelated to the $1.267$ of Exercise 14.2; it is merely a coincidence). Substituting the mantle value, we obtain

$$ V_\mathrm{CC} = 1.2674\times10^{-46}\times1.355\times10^{24}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 1.717\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$ $$ = 1.717\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{eV} = 0.172\ \mathrm{peV} $$

A value of $0.17\ \mathrm{peV}$ is unimaginably small as an energy scale for matter (it is $10^{-11}$ times the room-temperature $k_BT=25\ \mathrm{meV}$). But what it is compared with is just as small, so it matters.

(3) We solve the resonance condition for $E$.

$$ \frac{\Delta m_{31}^2}{2E_\mathrm{res}}\cos2\theta_{13}=V_\mathrm{CC} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad E_\mathrm{res}=\frac{\Delta m_{31}^2\cos2\theta_{13}}{2V_\mathrm{CC}} $$

From $\theta_{13}=8.53^\circ$ we have $2\theta_{13}=17.06^\circ$ and $\cos(17.06^\circ)=0.95600$. The numerator is

$$ 2.45\times10^{-3}\times0.95600 = 2.3422\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV^2} $$

and the denominator is $2\times1.717\times10^{-13}=3.434\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{eV}$. Therefore

$$ E_\mathrm{res} = \frac{2.3422\times10^{-3}}{3.434\times10^{-13}}\ \mathrm{eV} = 6.82\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{eV} = 6.8\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

This agrees with the value $6.8\ \mathrm{GeV}$ in the hint in the main text. Note that if one rounds midway to $V=1.71\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{eV}$, one obtains $6.9\ \mathrm{GeV}$. Computing without rounding from $n_e=1.355\times10^{24}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ gives $V=1.717\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $E_\mathrm{res}=6.82\ \mathrm{GeV}$, so to two significant figures $E_\mathrm{res}\simeq6.8\ \mathrm{GeV}$. In any case the conclusion “a few GeV” does not change.

(4) The beam energies of NOvA and DUNE are $E=2$–$2.5\ \mathrm{GeV}$, which is $0.3$–$0.4$ times the resonance energy $6.8\ \mathrm{GeV}$. They are not right on the resonance, but they are not so far from it that the matter effect can be neglected. To see this quantitatively, we need only substitute into the effective mixing angle in matter from Section 14.3.4 of this book,

$$ \sin^22\theta_m =\frac{\sin^22\theta_{13}} {\left(\cos2\theta_{13}-\dfrac{2EV_\mathrm{CC}}{\Delta m_{31}^2}\right)^2+\sin^22\theta_{13}} $$

Computing the dimensionless parameter $x\equiv2EV_\mathrm{CC}/\Delta m_{31}^2$, we obtain

$$ x_\mathrm{NOvA} = \frac{2\times2\times10^{9}\times1.717\times10^{-13}}{2.45\times10^{-3}}=0.280, \qquad x_\mathrm{DUNE} = \frac{2\times2.5\times10^{9}\times1.717\times10^{-13}}{2.45\times10^{-3}}=0.350 $$

(We have used $E$ in eV, $V$ in eV, and $\Delta m^2$ in $\mathrm{eV^2}$ throughout.) The vacuum value is $\sin^22\theta_{13}=\sin^2(17.06^\circ)=0.0861$ (the PDG 2022 value in Table 14.5; the $0.086$ given in Exercise 14.3 is this rounded to two digits). For the normal hierarchy ($\Delta m_{31}^2>0$, neutrinos) the parenthesis in the denominator becomes $0.9560-x$, and

$$ \sin^22\theta_m^\mathrm{NOvA}=\frac{0.0861}{(0.9560-0.280)^2+0.0861}=0.158 \quad(\text{vs. vacuum: }1.84\text{ times}) $$ $$ \sin^22\theta_m^\mathrm{DUNE}=\frac{0.0861}{(0.9560-0.350)^2+0.0861}=0.190 \quad(\text{vs. vacuum: }2.21\text{ times}) $$

For antineutrinos, $V_\mathrm{CC}\to-V_\mathrm{CC}$, that is, $x\to-x$, so the parenthesis in the denominator becomes $0.9560+x$, and

$$ \sin^22\bar\theta_m^\mathrm{NOvA}=\frac{0.0861}{(0.9560+0.280)^2+0.0861}=0.0533 \quad(\text{vs. vacuum: }0.62\text{ times}) $$ $$ \sin^22\bar\theta_m^\mathrm{DUNE}=\frac{0.0861}{(0.9560+0.350)^2+0.0861}=0.0480 \quad(\text{vs. vacuum: }0.56\text{ times}) $$

That is, for NO the mixing-angle factor of $\nu_\mu\to\nu_e$ is enhanced by a factor of $1.8$–$2.2$, and for $\bar\nu_\mu\to\bar\nu_e$ it is suppressed to about $0.6$ times. However, in matter the effective $\Delta m^2$ also changes by a factor of $\sqrt{(\cos2\theta_{13}-x)^2+\sin^22\theta_{13}}$, so the change in the appearance probability itself for an experiment placed at the first vacuum oscillation maximum is about $1.5$ times for NOvA and $1.7$ times for DUNE (and $0.5$ times and $0.4$ times, respectively, for $\bar\nu$). For IO ($\Delta m_{31}^2<0$) the roles of the sign of $x$ are interchanged, so enhancement and suppression are completely reversed. Therefore the sign of the asymmetry between the appearance probabilities of $\nu$ and $\bar\nu$,

$$ \mathcal A \equiv \frac{P(\nu_\mu\to\nu_e)-P(\bar\nu_\mu\to\bar\nu_e)}{P(\nu_\mu\to\nu_e)+P(\bar\nu_\mu\to\bar\nu_e)} $$

tells us the mass ordering directly. The longer the baseline, the more matter is traversed and the larger the effect, so DUNE at $1300\ \mathrm{km}$ has stronger discriminating power than NOvA at $810\ \mathrm{km}$.

There is, however, a pitfall here. The asymmetry due to the CP phase $\delta$ also appears in the same observable, and it can move in the same direction, so the matter effect and CP violation are degenerate. From “$\nu$ increased and $\bar\nu$ decreased” alone, one cannot tell whether it is NO or $\delta$ near $270^\circ$. There are two ways to separate them. First, the matter effect grows with $L$ (the amount of matter traversed), whereas the CP effect is a function of $L/E$, so they can be separated by combining experiments with different baselines. The joint analysis of T2K ($295\ \mathrm{km}$, small matter effect) and NOvA ($810\ \mathrm{km}$, medium matter effect) is exactly this. Second, if one looks out to the second oscillation maximum, as DUNE does, the $\delta$ dependence enters with a different phase from that at the first maximum, so independent information is obtained. JUNO (Exercise 14.2) determines the mass ordering by a purely geometric method independent of matter effects, and thus provides a third, independent verification.

Verification. First, we check the validity of the coefficient by comparison with the Sun. Against the value at the center of the Sun in the main text, $V^\odot=7.6\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{eV}$, the density ratio is $n_e^\odot/n_e^\mathrm{mantle}=6.0\times10^{25}/1.355\times10^{24}=44.3$. We get $1.717\times10^{-13}\times44.3=7.61\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{eV}$, which agrees with the value in the main text. The structure that the potential is proportional to $n_e$ is working correctly. Second, we check the dimensions. $[\Delta m^2/2E]=\mathrm{eV^2}/\mathrm{eV}=\mathrm{eV}$ and $[V]=\mathrm{eV}$, so both sides of the resonance condition have the dimension of energy. Third, we check the nature of the resonance. When $x=\cos2\theta_{13}=0.9560$ (that is, $E=E_\mathrm{res}$), the first term of the denominator vanishes and $\sin^22\theta_m=1$, that is, maximal mixing. The heart of the MSW effect is that even if $\theta_{13}$ is as small as $8.53^\circ$, it can become $45^\circ$ in matter.

Meaning. As Table 14.4 in Section 14.3.4 of this book shows, the mathematics of the MSW effect is precisely a $2\times2$ avoided crossing. The diagonal elements move with an external parameter (here the electron density; in condensed matter, the wave number, composition, or magnetic field), and a constant off-diagonal coupling $B$ makes the levels repel at the crossing point. The minimum of the gap is $2\abs{B}$, and the mixing there is $50:50$. This is exactly the same equation as the band-gap formation in the $\bm k\cdot\bm p$ two-band model, the band inversion due to spin–orbit coupling, and Rabi resonance in NMR. Furthermore, the criterion that if the density changes slowly the state stays in the same matter eigenstate (adiabatic), and if it changes quickly the state jumps over (nonadiabatic), can also be written in common form by the Landau–Zener formula $P_\mathrm{LZ}=\exp(-\pi\gamma/2)$. The $\gamma$ used in analyzing Bloch oscillations in superlattices, charge transfer in quantum dots, and quantum tunneling in single-molecule magnets has the same functional form as the $\gamma$ of solar neutrinos. This is not an analogy: we are simply solving the same two-level problem with different parameters.

Exercise 14.5: Numbers for the seesaw mechanism

Problem (restated)

(1) Find the eigenvalues of the $2\times2$ mass matrix $\mathcal M=\begin{pmatrix}0&m_D\\ m_D&M_R\end{pmatrix}$ exactly, and verify that the expansion for $M_R\gg m_D$ gives the results of the main text, $m_\nu\simeq m_D^2/M_R$ and $m_N\simeq M_R$.

(2) Show from the determinant that $m_\nu M_R=m_D^2$ holds exactly, without any expansion.

(3) Assume $m_\nu=0.05\ \mathrm{eV}$, and find $M_R$ when $m_D$ is taken to be the bottom quark mass $4.18\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and the charm mass $1.27\ \mathrm{GeV}$, respectively.

(4) Conversely, if $M_R=1\ \mathrm{TeV}$ (within reach of the LHC), what is $m_D$? What is the Yukawa coupling $y_\nu=\sqrt2m_D/v$ ($v=246\ \mathrm{GeV}$) then? Comment by comparing it with the electron Yukawa coupling $y_e=2.9\times10^{-6}$.

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1) and (2) need only linear algebra, namely the diagonalization of a $2\times2$ symmetric matrix. For parts (3) and (4), we put numbers into the seesaw formula of Section 14.6.4 of this book. If we carry out the conversion between eV and GeV ($1\ \mathrm{GeV}=10^9\ \mathrm{eV}$) carefully just once, the rest is calculator work. The numbers were checked with python3.

(1) We write down the characteristic equation.

$$ \det(\mathcal M-\lambda\mathbb 1) =\det\begin{pmatrix}-\lambda&m_D\\ m_D&M_R-\lambda\end{pmatrix} =-\lambda(M_R-\lambda)-m_D^2 =\lambda^2-M_R\lambda-m_D^2=0 $$

By the quadratic formula, the exact eigenvalues are

$$ \lambda_\pm = \frac{M_R\pm\sqrt{M_R^2+4m_D^2}}{2} $$

The discriminant $M_R^2+4m_D^2$ is always positive, so both eigenvalues are real (as they must be for a real symmetric matrix), and they have opposite signs, $\lambda_+>0>\lambda_-$. Next we expand with $\epsilon\equiv m_D/M_R\ll1$.

$$ \sqrt{M_R^2+4m_D^2}=M_R\sqrt{1+4\epsilon^2} =M_R\left(1+2\epsilon^2-2\epsilon^4+O(\epsilon^6)\right) $$

Here we substituted $u=4\epsilon^2$ into $\sqrt{1+u}=1+u/2-u^2/8+\cdots$. Therefore

$$ \lambda_+ = \frac{M_R+M_R(1+2\epsilon^2-\cdots)}{2} = M_R\left(1+\epsilon^2+O(\epsilon^4)\right) = M_R + \frac{m_D^2}{M_R}+\cdots \simeq M_R $$ $$ \lambda_- = \frac{M_R-M_R(1+2\epsilon^2-\cdots)}{2} = -M_R\epsilon^2+O(M_R\epsilon^4) = -\frac{m_D^2}{M_R}+\cdots $$

The sign of $\lambda_-$ is negative, but the sign of the mass term can be absorbed by redefining the phase of the Majorana field as $\nu\to\ii\nu$, so the physical mass is the absolute value:

$$ m_\nu \simeq \frac{m_D^2}{M_R},\qquad m_N\simeq M_R $$

This reproduces the result in the main text. Checking numerically with $M_R=1\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and $m_D=10^{-4}\ \mathrm{GeV}$, the exact solution is $\lambda_+=1.00000001$, $\lambda_-=-9.99999994\times10^{-9}$, and the approximate formulas give $1.00000001$ and $-1.0\times10^{-8}$; they agree to the accuracy $O(\epsilon^4)=10^{-16}$.

(2) The determinant equals the product of the eigenvalues (an invariant that does not depend on the choice of basis). On the other hand, computing directly from the matrix elements gives

$$ \det\mathcal M = 0\times M_R - m_D\times m_D = -m_D^2 $$

Therefore, without using any expansion,

$$ \lambda_+\lambda_- = -m_D^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \abs{\lambda_+}\abs{\lambda_-} = m_D^2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad m_\nu\,m_N = m_D^2 $$

holds exactly. As a double check, we can also confirm this directly from the quadratic formula.

$$ \lambda_+\lambda_- =\frac{M_R+\sqrt{M_R^2+4m_D^2}}{2}\cdot\frac{M_R-\sqrt{M_R^2+4m_D^2}}{2} =\frac{M_R^2-\left(M_R^2+4m_D^2\right)}{4} =-m_D^2 $$

This is the origin of the name “seesaw.” With the fulcrum ($m_D$) held fixed, if one side is lifted, the other side must go down. The fact that the $(1,1)$ entry is zero, that is, that we have dropped the left-handed Majorana mass $m_L$, is what guarantees the conservation of this product.

(3) We have $m_\nu=0.05\ \mathrm{eV}=5\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{GeV}$ (since $0.05/10^9=5\times10^{-11}$). We write the relation of (2) as $M_R=m_D^2/m_\nu$ and substitute.

Bottom quark, $m_D=4.18\ \mathrm{GeV}$.

$$ M_R = \frac{(4.18)^2}{5\times10^{-11}} = \frac{17.472}{5\times10^{-11}} = 3.49\times10^{11}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Charm quark, $m_D=1.27\ \mathrm{GeV}$.

$$ M_R = \frac{(1.27)^2}{5\times10^{-11}} = \frac{1.6129}{5\times10^{-11}} = 3.23\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Placing these next to the values in Table 14.8 of the main text, $6.3\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{GeV}$ for the $\tau$ ($1.777\ \mathrm{GeV}$) and $6.0\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{GeV}$ for the top ($173\ \mathrm{GeV}$), we see clearly that changing $m_D$ by two orders of magnitude changes $M_R$ by four orders of magnitude ($M_R\propto m_D^2$). In any case, we obtain scales of $10^{10}$–$10^{15}\ \mathrm{GeV}$, which accelerators can never reach.

(4) We solve in the opposite direction. With $M_R=1\ \mathrm{TeV}=10^3\ \mathrm{GeV}$,

$$ m_D = \sqrt{m_\nu M_R} = \sqrt{5\times10^{-11}\times10^{3}} = \sqrt{5\times10^{-8}} = 2.236\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 224\ \mathrm{keV} $$

The Yukawa coupling is

$$ y_\nu = \frac{\sqrt2\,m_D}{v} = \frac{1.41421\times2.236\times10^{-4}}{246} = \frac{3.1623\times10^{-4}}{246} = 1.286\times10^{-6} $$

We compare this with the electron’s Yukawa coupling. From $m_e=0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}=5.11\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{GeV}$,

$$ y_e = \frac{1.41421\times5.11\times10^{-4}}{246}=2.94\times10^{-6} $$

which agrees with the given value $2.9\times10^{-6}$. Taking the ratio,

$$ \frac{y_\nu}{y_e}=\frac{1.286\times10^{-6}}{2.94\times10^{-6}}=0.44 $$

that is, $y_\nu$ is $0.44$ times the electron’s Yukawa coupling, roughly half.

Commentary. The seesaw mechanism is often criticized for “introducing an unverifiable scale of $10^{15}\ \mathrm{GeV}$.” The calculation in (4), however, puts that criticism in perspective. Even if we place $M_R$ at $1\ \mathrm{TeV}$, within reach of the LHC, the required Yukawa coupling is only $1.3\times10^{-6}$. This is of the same order as the electron’s Yukawa coupling, which the Standard Model actually employs. In other words, the “fine-tuning” demanded by a TeV-scale seesaw is no worse than the existing puzzle of why the electron mass is $0.511\ \mathrm{MeV}$. This is the basis of the claims of low-scale seesaw models (and of variants such as the inverse seesaw and the linear seesaw). And if $M_R\sim\mathrm{TeV}$, there is a possibility of producing the heavy Majorana neutrino $N$ directly at an accelerator. This is why searches continue at the LHC for same-sign dileptons $+$ two jets ($pp\to\ell^\pm\ell^\pm jj$, a decisive signal that violates lepton number by two units).

Verification. First, we check the consistency of (3) and (4). Putting the $m_D=2.236\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{GeV}$ obtained in (4) back into the formula of (3), we get $M_R=(2.236\times10^{-4})^2/(5\times10^{-11})=(5.0\times10^{-8})/(5\times10^{-11})=1.0\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{GeV}$, which returns to the starting point of $1\ \mathrm{TeV}$. Second, we check using the mixing angle. By Step 5 of Section 14.6.4 of this book, the fraction in which the heavy state mixes into the light state is $\theta^2\simeq(m_D/M_R)^2=m_\nu/M_R$. For $M_R=6\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{GeV}$ (the top case), $\theta^2=(5\times10^{-11})/(6\times10^{14})=8\times10^{-26}$, which agrees with the $\sim10^{-25}$ in the main text. On the other hand, for $M_R=1\ \mathrm{TeV}$, $\theta^2=5\times10^{-11}/10^3=5\times10^{-14}$; this is still extremely small, but it is $12$ orders of magnitude larger than $10^{-26}$. Third, the dimensions. $m_D^2/M_R$ is $[\mathrm{GeV^2}]/[\mathrm{GeV}]=[\mathrm{GeV}]$, which is correctly a mass.

Meaning. The essence of the seesaw mechanism is the conservation of the product $m_\nu m_N=m_D^2$, which is a direct consequence of the fact that the determinant is a basis invariant. The same structure appears repeatedly in condensed matter physics. In a $2\times2$ two-band model, if we hold the hybridization $b$ fixed and push one level up, the other level must be pushed down (level repulsion, and the product of the eigenvalues is fixed to $\det$). The fact that a deep bound state becomes shallower the closer an impurity level approaches the conduction band is the same arithmetic. And the very idea that “the small observed quantity ($m_\nu$) is the shadow of an unseen large quantity ($M_R$)” is the idea of an effective model. When high-energy degrees of freedom are integrated out, operators suppressed by $1/M_R$ remain at low energy—this is logically the same operation as the pseudopotential method, which eliminates core levels to build an effective Hamiltonian for the valence band, or as the renormalization that eliminates high-energy phonons to obtain low-frequency effective force constants.

Exercise 14.6: The effective Majorana mass $m_{\beta\beta}$ and the mass ordering

Problem (restated)

Use $s_{12}^2=0.307$, $c_{12}^2=0.693$, $c_{13}^2=0.978$, $s_{13}^2=0.0220$, $\Delta m_{21}^2=7.53\times10^{-5}$, $\abs{\Delta m_{31}^2}=2.45\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV^2}$.

(1) For the normal hierarchy with the lightest mass $m_1=0$, find the maximum and minimum values of $m_{\beta\beta}$.

(2) Find them similarly for the inverted hierarchy with $m_3=0$.

(3) For the degenerate hierarchy ($m_1\simeq m_2\simeq m_3\equiv m_0\gg0.05\ \mathrm{eV}$), express the allowed range of $m_{\beta\beta}$ in terms of $m_0$.

(4) Show that in the normal hierarchy there exists a value of $m_1$ for which $m_{\beta\beta}$ becomes exactly zero (that is, cancels completely), and find that value. What does this mean for experiments?

Solution

Strategy. The starting points are the definition $m_{\beta\beta}=\abs{\sum_iU_{ei}^2m_i}$ of Section 14.4.3 of this book and the first row of the PMNS matrix in Section 14.5.1, $U_{e1}=c_{12}c_{13}$, $U_{e2}=s_{12}c_{13}$, $U_{e3}=s_{13}\ee^{-\ii\delta}$. Including the Majorana phases $\alpha_{21},\alpha_{31}$, we have

$$ m_{\beta\beta}=\left|c_{12}^2c_{13}^2m_1 +s_{12}^2c_{13}^2m_2\,\ee^{\ii\alpha_{21}} +s_{13}^2m_3\,\ee^{\ii(\alpha_{31}-2\delta)}\right| $$

Since the phases are unknown, this is the length of the sum of three vectors of lengths $A_1,A_2,A_3$ pointing in arbitrary directions. As an elementary fact in the complex plane, its maximum is $A_1+A_2+A_3$, attained when the three are aligned in the same direction, and its minimum is $0$ if the longest one is at most the sum of the other two (so that the triangle inequality closes), and otherwise “longest $-$ sum of the other two.” That is, with $A_\mathrm{max}=\max_iA_i$,

$$ m_{\beta\beta}^\mathrm{min}=\max\left(0,\ 2A_\mathrm{max}-\sum_iA_i\right) $$

Below we write $A_1\equiv c_{12}^2c_{13}^2m_1$, $A_2\equiv s_{12}^2c_{13}^2m_2$, $A_3\equiv s_{13}^2m_3$. All numerical values were computed with python3.

(1) For the normal hierarchy with $m_1=0$, the mass-squared differences give

$$ m_2=\sqrt{\Delta m_{21}^2}=\sqrt{7.53\times10^{-5}}=8.678\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}=8.678\ \mathrm{meV} $$ $$ m_3=\sqrt{\abs{\Delta m_{31}^2}}=\sqrt{2.45\times10^{-3}}=4.950\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{eV}=49.50\ \mathrm{meV} $$

The lengths of the three vectors are

$$ A_1=c_{12}^2c_{13}^2\times0=0 $$ $$ A_2=0.307\times0.978\times8.678=2.605\ \mathrm{meV} $$ $$ A_3=0.0220\times49.50=1.089\ \mathrm{meV} $$

Since $A_1=0$, this is effectively the sum of two vectors. If they point in the same direction we get the sum, and if in opposite directions the difference, so

$$ m_{\beta\beta}^\mathrm{max}=2.605+1.089=3.69\ \mathrm{meV} $$ $$ m_{\beta\beta}^\mathrm{min}=\abs{2.605-1.089}=1.52\ \mathrm{meV} $$

That is, $m_{\beta\beta}^\mathrm{NO}(m_1=0)\in[1.5,\ 3.7]\ \mathrm{meV}$. This agrees with the values in the main text.

(2) For the inverted hierarchy with $m_3=0$, $\nu_3$ is the lightest, so

$$ m_1=\sqrt{\abs{\Delta m_{31}^2}}=\sqrt{2.45\times10^{-3}}=49.50\ \mathrm{meV} $$ $$ m_2=\sqrt{\abs{\Delta m_{31}^2}+\Delta m_{21}^2}=\sqrt{2.45\times10^{-3}+7.53\times10^{-5}} =\sqrt{2.5253\times10^{-3}}=50.25\ \mathrm{meV} $$

(In the example in the main text, from the inverted-hierarchy values in Table 14.5, $m_2=\sqrt{\abs{\Delta m_{32}^2}}=\sqrt{2.536\times10^{-3}}=50.4\ \mathrm{meV}$ and $m_1=49.6\ \mathrm{meV}$ are used. Since $\abs{\Delta m_{32}^2}=\abs{\Delta m_{31}^2}+\Delta m_{21}^2$, the approach is the same, but because the $\abs{\Delta m_{31}^2}=2.45\times10^{-3}$ of this problem is a rounded input, $m_1,m_2$ come out about $0.1\ \mathrm{meV}$ smaller.) The lengths of the three vectors are

$$ A_1=0.693\times0.978\times49.50=33.55\ \mathrm{meV} $$ $$ A_2=0.307\times0.978\times50.25=15.09\ \mathrm{meV} $$ $$ A_3=0.0220\times0=0 $$

$A_1$ is the largest and $A_1>A_2+A_3=15.09$, so cancellation cannot occur.

$$ m_{\beta\beta}^\mathrm{max}=33.55+15.09=48.64\ \mathrm{meV} $$ $$ m_{\beta\beta}^\mathrm{min}=33.55-15.09=18.46\ \mathrm{meV} $$

That is, $m_{\beta\beta}^\mathrm{IO}(m_3=0)\in[18.5,\ 48.6]\ \mathrm{meV}$. The main text, using the $m_1,m_2$ from the note above, gives $[\,33.6-15.1,\ 33.6+15.1\,]=[18.5,\ 48.7]\ \mathrm{meV}$. The difference of $0.1\ \mathrm{meV}$ in the upper limit is already buried in the experimental uncertainty of $\abs{\Delta m_{31}^2}$ itself (about $1\%$, which is $0.5\%$ when converted to $m$, that is, $\pm0.25\ \mathrm{meV}$). The fact that the lower end of this interval is away from zero determines the entire experimental strategy. In the inverted hierarchy, $m_{\beta\beta}$ is always at least $18.5\ \mathrm{meV}$, so if the sensitivity is lowered to that level, IO can be settled one way or the other.

(3) For the degenerate hierarchy $m_1\simeq m_2\simeq m_3=m_0$, the mass can be factored out as a common factor.

$$ m_{\beta\beta}=m_0\left|c_{12}^2c_{13}^2 +s_{12}^2c_{13}^2\ee^{\ii\alpha_{21}} +s_{13}^2\ee^{\ii(\alpha_{31}-2\delta)}\right| $$

The maximum occurs when the three terms are aligned in the same direction:

$$ m_{\beta\beta}^\mathrm{max}=m_0\left(c_{12}^2c_{13}^2+s_{12}^2c_{13}^2+s_{13}^2\right) =m_0\left[c_{13}^2\left(c_{12}^2+s_{12}^2\right)+s_{13}^2\right] =m_0\left(c_{13}^2+s_{13}^2\right)=m_0 $$

That is, it is exactly $m_0$ (we used $c_{12}^2+s_{12}^2=1$ and $c_{13}^2+s_{13}^2=1$; with the given numbers as well, $0.978+0.0220=1.000$). This is the natural result that, when all the phases are aligned, the sum of $\abs{U_{ei}}^2$ equals $1$ by unitarity.

For the minimum, we compare the largest term, $A_1=c_{12}^2c_{13}^2m_0=0.693\times0.978\,m_0=0.6778\,m_0$, with the sum of the other two terms, $A_2+A_3=(0.307\times0.978+0.0220)m_0=(0.3002+0.0220)m_0=0.3222\,m_0$. Since $A_1>A_2+A_3$, complete cancellation is impossible, and

$$ m_{\beta\beta}^\mathrm{min}=m_0\abs{c_{12}^2c_{13}^2-s_{12}^2c_{13}^2-s_{13}^2} =m_0\abs{c_{13}^2\cos2\theta_{12}-s_{13}^2} $$ $$ =m_0\abs{0.978\times(0.693-0.307)-0.0220} =m_0\abs{0.3775-0.0220}=0.356\,m_0 $$

Therefore $m_{\beta\beta}\in[0.356\,m_0,\ m_0]$. The reason the minimum does not reach zero is that $\cos2\theta_{12}=0.386$ is sufficiently large, that is, that $\theta_{12}=33.6^\circ$ is far from maximal mixing, $45^\circ$. In general, the condition for cancellation to be possible is “the longest vector $\le$ the sum of the other two,” that is,

$$ c_{12}^2c_{13}^2\ \le\ s_{12}^2c_{13}^2+s_{13}^2 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \cos2\theta_{12}\ \le\ \frac{s_{13}^2}{c_{13}^2}=\frac{0.0220}{0.978}=0.0225 $$

This means $\theta_{12}\ge44.36^\circ$. The measured $33.6^\circ$ is as much as $11^\circ$ away from this, so the condition is badly violated. Conversely, if $\theta_{12}$ were within $0.64^\circ$ of $45^\circ$, then $A_1$ and $A_2$ would have nearly equal lengths, a triangle with $A_3$ as the third side would close, and the minimum would drop all the way to $0$ (for $\theta_{12}=45^\circ$ exactly, $A_1=A_2=0.489\,m_0$ and $A_3=0.0220\,m_0$, and indeed $A_2+A_3>A_1$). The fact that the solar mixing angle is sufficiently far from maximal mixing forbids complete cancellation in the degenerate hierarchy. It is fortunate that the measured value is as much as $11^\circ$ away from the boundary at $44.36^\circ$, and this lower limit of $0.356\,m_0$ will not be overturned even as the measurement precision of the mixing angle improves. The experimental fact that $\theta_{12}$ is not near $45^\circ$ directly guarantees the sensitivity of $0\nu\beta\beta$ to the degenerate hierarchy.

Note also that the degenerate hierarchy collides head-on with cosmology. If $m_0\gg0.05\ \mathrm{eV}$, the mass sum is $\Sigma=3m_0\gg0.15\ \mathrm{eV}$, which already exceeds the Planck+BAO upper limit $\Sigma<0.12\ \mathrm{eV}$. As long as we trust $\Lambda$CDM, the degenerate hierarchy is almost excluded.

(4) We follow what happens as $m_1$ is increased from $0$ in the normal hierarchy. Since $m_2=\sqrt{m_1^2+\Delta m_{21}^2}$ and $m_3=\sqrt{m_1^2+\abs{\Delta m_{31}^2}}$, the lengths of all three vectors are functions of $m_1$.

$$ A_1(m_1)=0.6778\,m_1,\qquad A_2(m_1)=0.3002\sqrt{m_1^2+7.53\times10^{-5}},\qquad A_3(m_1)=0.0220\sqrt{m_1^2+2.45\times10^{-3}} $$

$m_{\beta\beta}=0$ is possible when the three vectors can close into a triangle, that is, when the longest one is at most the sum of the other two.

At $m_1=0$. $A_1=0$, $A_2=2.605$, $A_3=1.089\ \mathrm{meV}$. The largest is $A_2$, and $A_1+A_3=1.089<2.605$, so the triangle does not close. Cancellation is impossible, and the minimum is $1.52\ \mathrm{meV}$ (this is the result of (1)).

As $m_1$ is increased. $A_1$ grows linearly in proportion to $m_1$, but $A_2$, being $\sqrt{m_1^2+\Delta m_{21}^2}$, hardly grows while $m_1$ is small, and $A_3$ stays at $A_3\simeq1.09\ \mathrm{meV}$ because $m_3\simeq49.5\ \mathrm{meV}$ is almost constant. Therefore $A_1$ eventually catches up. Solving $A_2=A_1+A_3$ gives the boundary

$$ m_1^\mathrm{low}=2.38\ \mathrm{meV} $$

(At this point $A_1=1.611$, $A_2=2.701$, $A_3=1.090\ \mathrm{meV}$, and indeed $A_2=A_1+A_3$ holds.)

As it is increased further. This time $A_1$ grows too large, so that $A_1>A_2+A_3$, and the triangle again fails to close. Solving $A_1=A_2+A_3$ gives the boundary

$$ m_1^\mathrm{high}=6.40\ \mathrm{meV} $$

(At this point $A_1=4.335$, $A_2=3.237$, $A_3=1.098\ \mathrm{meV}$.)

Therefore complete cancellation can occur only within the narrow window

$$ 2.38\ \mathrm{meV}\ \lesssim\ m_1\ \lesssim\ 6.40\ \mathrm{meV} $$

(this is consistent with “about $2$–$7\ \mathrm{meV}$” in the hint in the main text; the exact boundaries are the two values above). Inside this window, if the Majorana phases take particular values, $m_{\beta\beta}$ becomes exactly zero. Near the center of the window, at $m_1=5\ \mathrm{meV}$, the allowed range is $m_{\beta\beta}\in[0,\ 7.49]\ \mathrm{meV}$, and outside the window, at $m_1=10\ \mathrm{meV}$, it is $[1.69,\ 11.86]\ \mathrm{meV}$.

The implication for experiments is serious. Even if neutrinos are Majorana particles, $0\nu\beta\beta$ may not be observed at all. If, in the normal hierarchy, the lightest mass happens to fall in the window of a few meV and the Majorana phases happen to take the canceling values, the half-life becomes infinite. Therefore “not finding $0\nu\beta\beta$” does not rule out the Majorana nature. Conversely, “finding it” implies the existence of $\Delta L=2$, and by the Schechter–Valle theorem it proves that the neutrino is a Majorana particle. The logic of this field is asymmetric—a discovery is decisive, but a non-discovery is not.

Verification. First, we confirmed that the maximum in (3) is exactly $m_0$ by unitarity. This serves as an independent check ($\abs{U_{e1}}^2+\abs{U_{e2}}^2+\abs{U_{e3}}^2=1$). Second, the continuity between (1) and (4). Putting $m_1=0$ into the $A_i(m_1)$ of (4) gives $A_2=0.3002\times8.678=2.605$ and $A_3=0.0220\times49.50=1.089\ \mathrm{meV}$, which agree with the values in (1). Third, we compare the lower limit of IO in (2) with current experiments. The KamLAND-Zen upper limit is $m_{\beta\beta}<28$–$122\ \mathrm{meV}$ (the range arising from the uncertainty of the nuclear matrix elements), and the best value, $28\ \mathrm{meV}$, comes within a factor of $1.5$ of the IO lower limit of $18.5\ \mathrm{meV}$. Considering that the sensitivity improves only as $m_{\beta\beta}\propto(b\Delta E/Mt)^{1/4}$, an improvement by a factor of $1.5$ requires increasing $M t/(b\Delta E)$ by a factor of $5$.

Meaning. The single fact that $m_{\beta\beta}$ is weighted by $U_{ei}^2$ (the square without absolute value) rather than by $\abs{U_{ei}}^2$ causes all of this. Since $m_\beta^2=\sum_i\abs{U_{ei}}^2m_i^2$ (the $\beta$-decay endpoint) is a sum of non-negative quantities, cancellation cannot occur in principle, whereas $m_{\beta\beta}$ is a sum of complex numbers and so interferes. This is the difference between an “incoherent sum” and a “coherent sum.” There are also situations in condensed matter physics in which the same distinction is decisive. Extinction rules arise in X-ray and neutron diffraction because the structure factor $F=\sum_jf_j\ee^{\ii\bm Q\cdot\bm r_j}$ is a sum of amplitudes, whereas the intensity sum rule of inelastic scattering is a sum of $\abs{\cdot}^2$ and so does not vanish. Or again, there are configurations in which the amplitudes of multiple-scattering paths cancel and the EXAFS oscillation disappears, while the total absorption cross section never becomes negative. The reason that the non-observation of $0\nu\beta\beta$ does not rule out the Majorana nature is exactly the same logic as the fact that, even when an extinction rule appears in diffraction, it does not mean the atoms are absent from that place.

Exercise 14.7: The Kitaev chain and nanowires

Problem (restated)

(1) From the definition of the Majorana decomposition, $\gamma_{2j-1}=c_j+c_j^\dagger$ and $\gamma_{2j}=-\ii(c_j-c_j^\dagger)$, verify directly that $\gamma_a^\dagger=\gamma_a$, $\gamma_a^2=1$, and $\{\gamma_a,\gamma_b\}=2\delta_{ab}$ (use $\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}$ and $\{c_i,c_j\}=0$).

(2) Verify from the Majorana representation of the Kitaev chain in Chapter 14 of this book that at the sweet spot $\mu=0$, $t=\Delta$ the Hamiltonian becomes $\Ham=\ii t\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}$.

(3) From the dispersion relation $E(k)=\pm\sqrt{(2t\cos k+\mu)^2+4\Delta^2\sin^2k}$ of Chapter 14 of this book, find the $(\mu,k)$ at which the gap closes, and show that the condition for the topological phase is $\abs{\mu}<2t$. Also verify that at $\mu=0$, $t=\Delta$ the band becomes perfectly flat.

(4) Define the fermion “across sites” $d_j\equiv(\gamma_{2j}+\ii\gamma_{2j+1})/2$, and show that the Hamiltonian at the sweet spot can be written $\Ham=2t\sum_j(d_j^\dagger d_j-1/2)$. What are the ground-state energy and the degeneracy?

(5) Suppose an InSb nanowire ($g^*=51$) is brought into proximity with Nb ($\Delta=1.4\ \mathrm{meV}$; literature values range over $1.4$–$1.55\ \mathrm{meV}$, and $2\Delta=3.05\ \mathrm{meV}$ in the exercise of Chapter 1 corresponds to $\Delta\simeq1.5\ \mathrm{meV}$). What magnetic field is needed to enter the topological phase? Compare with the case of Al ($\Delta=0.20\ \mathrm{meV}$) and discuss why Al is used in actual experiments.

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1)–(4) are completed by algebra alone. The tools are the canonical anticommutation relations $\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}$, $\{c_i,c_j\}=\{c_i^\dagger,c_j^\dagger\}=0$ (hence $c_i^2=(c_i^\dagger)^2=0$), and the Majorana representation of the Kitaev chain derived in Section 14.8.2 of this book. Part (5) is a numerical calculation that merely inserts $V_Z=g^*\mu_BB/2$ into the topological condition $V_Z>\sqrt{\Delta^2+\mu^2}$ of Section 14.8.3 of this book; we checked it with python3.

(1) Self-adjointness. Since $c_j$ and $c_j^\dagger$ are Hermitian conjugates of each other,

$$ \gamma_{2j-1}^\dagger = \left(c_j+c_j^\dagger\right)^\dagger = c_j^\dagger+c_j=\gamma_{2j-1} $$ $$ \gamma_{2j}^\dagger = \left[-\ii\left(c_j-c_j^\dagger\right)\right]^\dagger = +\ii\left(c_j^\dagger-c_j\right) = -\ii\left(c_j-c_j^\dagger\right)=\gamma_{2j} $$

The factor $-\ii$ in the definition of $\gamma_{2j}$ is there precisely to make it self-adjoint ($c-c^\dagger$ is anti-Hermitian, so multiplying by $\ii$ makes it Hermitian).

The square is $1$. We use $c_j^2=(c_j^\dagger)^2=0$ and $\{c_j,c_j^\dagger\}=c_jc_j^\dagger+c_j^\dagger c_j=1$.

$$ \gamma_{2j-1}^2=\left(c_j+c_j^\dagger\right)^2 =\underbrace{c_j^2}_{0}+c_jc_j^\dagger+c_j^\dagger c_j+\underbrace{(c_j^\dagger)^2}_{0} =\left\{c_j,c_j^\dagger\right\}=1 $$ $$ \gamma_{2j}^2=-\left(c_j-c_j^\dagger\right)^2 =-\left(\underbrace{c_j^2}_{0}-c_jc_j^\dagger-c_j^\dagger c_j+\underbrace{(c_j^\dagger)^2}_{0}\right) =+\left\{c_j,c_j^\dagger\right\}=1 $$

Anticommutation of the two on the same site.

$$ \left\{\gamma_{2j-1},\gamma_{2j}\right\} =-\ii\left[\left(c_j+c_j^\dagger\right)\left(c_j-c_j^\dagger\right) +\left(c_j-c_j^\dagger\right)\left(c_j+c_j^\dagger\right)\right] $$

We expand the products inside the brackets, dropping $c_j^2=(c_j^\dagger)^2=0$:

$$ \left(c_j+c_j^\dagger\right)\left(c_j-c_j^\dagger\right)=-c_jc_j^\dagger+c_j^\dagger c_j $$ $$ \left(c_j-c_j^\dagger\right)\left(c_j+c_j^\dagger\right)=+c_jc_j^\dagger-c_j^\dagger c_j $$

These two have opposite signs and add up to zero. Hence $\{\gamma_{2j-1},\gamma_{2j}\}=0$.

Different sites. For $i\neq j$, $c_i,c_i^\dagger$ anticommute with all of $c_j,c_j^\dagger$. Since $\gamma_a$ (coming from site $i$) and $\gamma_b$ (coming from site $j$) are each a linear combination of $c$ and $c^\dagger$, they anticommute term by term, and $\{\gamma_a,\gamma_b\}=0$.

Summarizing, $\{\gamma_a,\gamma_b\}=2\delta_{ab}$ for all $a,b$. This is nothing other than a Clifford algebra with $2N$ generators. It has the same form as $\{\gamma^\mu,\gamma^\nu\}=2g^{\mu\nu}$ for the $\gamma$ matrices, and here lies the justification for saying that the Majorana condition $\psi^c=\psi$ on the particle-physics side and $\gamma=\gamma^\dagger$ on the condensed-matter side are “the same at the level of the algebra.” From the inverse transformation $c_j=(\gamma_{2j-1}+\ii\gamma_{2j})/2$, $c_j^\dagger=(\gamma_{2j-1}-\ii\gamma_{2j})/2$, one can likewise verify that $\{c_i,c_j^\dagger\}=\delta_{ij}$ is recovered, so the transformation is invertible.

(2) First we reproduce the rewriting of Section 14.8.2 of this book. Substitute $c_j=(\gamma_{2j-1}+\ii\gamma_{2j})/2$ and $c_j^\dagger=(\gamma_{2j-1}-\ii\gamma_{2j})/2$.

Number operator.

$$ c_j^\dagger c_j=\frac14\left(\gamma_{2j-1}-\ii\gamma_{2j}\right)\left(\gamma_{2j-1}+\ii\gamma_{2j}\right) =\frac14\left(\gamma_{2j-1}^2+\gamma_{2j}^2+\ii\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j}-\ii\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j-1}\right) $$

From $\gamma^2=1$ and $\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j-1}=-\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j}$,

$$ c_j^\dagger c_j=\frac14\left(2+2\ii\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j}\right) =\frac12+\frac{\ii}{2}\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad c_j^\dagger c_j-\frac12=\frac{\ii}{2}\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j} $$

Hopping term. Expanding $c_j^\dagger c_{j+1}+c_{j+1}^\dagger c_j$ by the same procedure, the terms in $\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j+1}$ and $\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+2}$ cancel between the Hermitian conjugates (h.c.), leaving

$$ -t\left(c_j^\dagger c_{j+1}+c_{j+1}^\dagger c_j\right) =-\frac{\ii t}{2}\left(\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j+2}-\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}\right) $$

Pairing term. Similarly,

$$ \Delta\,c_jc_{j+1}+\Delta\,c_{j+1}^\dagger c_j^\dagger =\frac{\ii\Delta}{2}\left(\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j+2}+\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}\right) $$

Adding the two, the coefficient of $\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j+2}$ (which connects the left Majorana of site $j$ with the right Majorana of site $j+1$) is $\ii(\Delta-t)/2$, and the coefficient of $\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}$ (the adjacent inner pair) is $\ii(\Delta+t)/2$. Therefore

$$ \Ham = -\frac{\ii\mu}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j} +\frac{\ii}{2}\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\left[(\Delta-t)\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j+2}+(\Delta+t)\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}\right] $$

Now we set the sweet spot $\mu=0$, $t=\Delta$. The first term vanishes outright because $\mu=0$. In the second term, the coefficient of $\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j+2}$ vanishes because $\Delta-t=0$. Only the $\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}$ term remains, and its coefficient is $\ii(\Delta+t)/2=\ii(2t)/2=\ii t$. Hence

$$ \Ham = \ii t\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1} $$

is obtained. Since the sum runs over $j=1,\dots,N-1$, only $2N-2$ Majorana operators, $\gamma_2,\gamma_3,\dots,\gamma_{2N-1}$, appear. $\gamma_1$ (left end) and $\gamma_{2N}$ (right end) never appear in the Hamiltonian. These two therefore commute with $\Ham$, and the nonlocal fermion $f=(\gamma_1+\ii\gamma_{2N})/2$ built from them has exactly zero energy.

(3) The quantity under the square root of the dispersion relation is the sum of two nonnegative terms.

$$ E(k)=\pm\sqrt{\left(2t\cos k+\mu\right)^2+4\Delta^2\sin^2k} $$

For $E=0$, both terms must vanish at the same time. If $\Delta\neq0$, the second term vanishes only for $\sin k=0$, that is, only when $k=0$ or $k=\pi$ (within the Brillouin zone $-\pi<k\le\pi$). Substituting these values gives

$$ k=0:\quad 2t+\mu=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \mu=-2t $$ $$ k=\pi:\quad -2t+\mu=0\ \Longrightarrow\ \mu=+2t $$

That is, the gap closes only on the two lines $\abs{\mu}=2t$.

These two lines divide the $\mu$ axis into three regions. To decide which one is topologically nontrivial, it suffices to look at the sign of the product of the normal-state energies at $k=0$ and $k=\pi$, $\xi_0=-2t-\mu$ and $\xi_\pi=2t-\mu$.

$$ \xi_0\,\xi_\pi = (-2t-\mu)(2t-\mu) = -(2t+\mu)(2t-\mu) = -(4t^2-\mu^2) = \mu^2-4t^2 $$

Therefore

$$ \mathrm{sgn}\left(\xi_0\xi_\pi\right)<0 \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \mu^2<4t^2 \ \Longleftrightarrow\ \abs{\mu}<2t $$

The meaning is clear: when $\abs{\mu}<2t$, $\xi_0$ and $\xi_\pi$ have opposite signs, that is, the normal-state band crosses the Fermi level (the band is partially occupied). Even after the superconducting gap opens, the “orientation” of the Bogoliubov wave function at $k=0$ and at $k=\pi$ is reversed, and this twist appears as zero modes at the ends. For $\abs{\mu}>2t$ the band is either empty or full, and nothing happens (the trivial phase).

Check of the flat band. Substituting $\mu=0$, $t=\Delta$ gives

$$ E(k)=\pm\sqrt{\left(2t\cos k\right)^2+4t^2\sin^2k} =\pm\sqrt{4t^2\left(\cos^2k+\sin^2k\right)} =\pm2t $$

which does not depend on $k$ at all. These are two perfectly flat bands. Flatness means that the group velocity $\partial E/\partial k$ is zero, so excitations do not propagate at all. Conversely, the coherence length is $\xi=0$, that is, the zero modes at the ends are localized exactly on the single end site. Indeed, as we saw in (2), at the sweet spot $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_{2N}$ are completely isolated and do not even have an exponential tail. Away from the sweet spot (while keeping $\abs{\mu}<2t$), the bands acquire dispersion, the coherence length grows to $\xi\sim\hbar v_F/\Delta$, and the end levels split by an amount of order $\ee^{-L/\xi}$.

(4) We use $d_j=(\gamma_{2j}+\ii\gamma_{2j+1})/2$ and its conjugate $d_j^\dagger=(\gamma_{2j}-\ii\gamma_{2j+1})/2$. First we confirm that this is indeed a fermion.

$$ d_j^\dagger d_j=\frac14\left(\gamma_{2j}-\ii\gamma_{2j+1}\right)\left(\gamma_{2j}+\ii\gamma_{2j+1}\right) =\frac14\left(2+2\ii\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}\right) =\frac12+\frac{\ii}{2}\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1} $$ $$ d_jd_j^\dagger=\frac14\left(\gamma_{2j}+\ii\gamma_{2j+1}\right)\left(\gamma_{2j}-\ii\gamma_{2j+1}\right) =\frac12-\frac{\ii}{2}\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1} $$

Adding them gives $\{d_j,d_j^\dagger\}=1$, so it is indeed a fermion. Solving the first equation above for $\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}$ gives

$$ \ii\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}=2d_j^\dagger d_j-1 $$

(equivalent to the hint in the problem, $\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1}=-\ii(2d_j^\dagger d_j-1)$). Substituting this into the result of (2),

$$ \Ham=\ii t\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\gamma_{2j}\gamma_{2j+1} = t\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\left(2d_j^\dagger d_j-1\right) = 2t\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\left(d_j^\dagger d_j-\frac12\right) $$

is obtained. This describes $N-1$ noninteracting quasiparticle levels, each with excitation energy $2t$ (consistent with the bulk gap $E=\pm2t$ found in (3)).

Ground-state energy. Since $t>0$, the lowest energy is attained when all the $d_j$ are empty. Substituting $d_j^\dagger d_j=0$,

$$ E_0 = 2t\sum_{j=1}^{N-1}\left(0-\frac12\right) = -t\,(N-1) $$

Degeneracy. This is the key point. From $2N$ Majorana operators one can build $N$ complex fermions. Now $d_1,\dots,d_{N-1}$ use up the $2N-2$ operators $\gamma_2,\gamma_3,\dots,\gamma_{2N-1}$, but $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_{2N}$ are left over. The $f=(\gamma_1+\ii\gamma_{2N})/2$ built from these two is the $N$th fermion, and since it does not appear in $\Ham$, its occupation number $n_f=0,1$ does not change the energy. Therefore

$$ \text{ground-state degeneracy} = 2 $$

The two states differ in fermion parity $(-1)^{\hat N}$, and since $f$ is an operator spanning the two places at the left and right ends of the chain, separated by $N$ sites, local perturbations do not mix them. To mix them, one must touch both $\gamma_1$ and $\gamma_{2N}$ at the same time, and the amplitude of such an operator is exponentially small in the chain length, as $\ee^{-L/\xi}$. This is the substance of topological protection, and it is the meaning of the statement that the information is stored not “in one place” but in “the correlation between two places.”

(5) The topological condition of Section 14.8.3 of this book is $V_Z>\sqrt{\Delta^2+\mu^2}$. At the optimal condition $\mu=0$ (the chemical potential is tuned to the band bottom) this becomes $V_Z>\Delta$, and substituting $V_Z=g^*\mu_BB/2$ gives

$$ B_c=\frac{2\Delta}{g^*\mu_B} $$

Here $\mu_B=5.788\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{meV/T}$ and $g^*=51$ (InSb). The denominator, $51\times5.788\times10^{-2}=2.952\ \mathrm{meV/T}$, is common to both cases, so

Nb ($\Delta=1.4\ \mathrm{meV}$).

$$ B_c=\frac{2\times1.4}{2.952}=\frac{2.8}{2.952}=0.95\ \mathrm{T} $$

Al ($\Delta=0.20\ \mathrm{meV}$).

$$ B_c=\frac{2\times0.20}{2.952}=\frac{0.40}{2.952}=0.14\ \mathrm{T} $$

Nb requires a magnetic field $7$ times larger.

The motivation for using Nb is clear. The upper limit of the topological gap (the gap that protects the zero modes) is bounded by the induced gap $\Delta$, so if $\Delta$ is $7$ times larger, then in principle the zero modes should survive up to $7$ times higher temperatures and against $7$ times stronger disorder. The thermal energy at the measurement temperature of $20\ \mathrm{mK}$ is $k_BT=1.72\ \mu\mathrm{eV}$, so even for the $0.20\ \mathrm{meV}$ of Al there is a margin of a factor of $116$, but the actual topological gap is much smaller than $\Delta$ (of order $E_\mathrm{gap}\sim\alpha_Rk_F$), so the larger the margin, the better.

Nevertheless, there are two reasons why Al is used in actual experiments.

  • (i) The required magnetic field is too large. The usable field has an upper limit: beyond the parallel critical field of the superconducting thin film itself (about $2$–$3\ \mathrm{T}$), the proximity effect itself disappears. In addition, a strong field causes orbital effects and subband mixing in the semiconductor, and the effective value of $g^*$ also drops. For Al the window is wide, $0.14\ \mathrm{T}\lesssim B\lesssim2\ \mathrm{T}$, but for Nb the lower limit is pushed up to $0.95\ \mathrm{T}$ and the window becomes extremely narrow.
  • (ii) The quality of the interface is decisive. Al can be grown epitaxially in situ on InAs or InSb in ultrahigh vacuum. The lattice matching is good, and an atomically sharp interface with neither an oxide layer nor a disordered layer in between can be made, so a “hard gap,” in which the density of states inside the gap is truly zero, is obtained. Nb has a high melting point and is highly reactive, so it readily reacts with III–V semiconductors and forms a disordered layer at the interface, and what one obtains is a “soft gap” full of subgap states. And subgap states are precisely the breeding ground of the false positives (Andreev bound states created by disorder) discussed in Section 14.8.5 of this book.

That is, “interface quality” was given priority over “gap size.” This is a typical example of materials selection, a judgment that appears again and again in condensed-matter experiments: the material with the better numbers loses out on ease of fabrication, interface, and stability, and is not adopted. Incidentally, InSb is preferred to InAs because $g^*=51$ is $3.4$ times larger than $15$, so that $B_c$ for the same $\Delta$ stays low, $0.14\ \mathrm{T}$ versus $0.46\ \mathrm{T}$, and because the Rashba constant $\alpha_R\approx0.2$–$0.3\ \mathrm{eV\,\AA}$ is among the largest of any semiconductor, so that a topological gap $\sim\alpha_Rk_F$ can be obtained.

Verification. First, counting the degrees of freedom. A chain of $N$ sites has $2N$ Majorana operators, and in (4) we divided them into $N-1$ operators $d_j$ ($2N-2$ Majorana operators) and $1$ operator $f$ ($2$ Majorana operators). The total is $N$ fermions, which agrees with the starting point $c_1,\dots,c_N$. No degrees of freedom were gained or lost along the way. Second, the consistency of the energies. The quasiparticle excitation energy $2t$ in (4) agrees with the band $E=\pm2t$ at the sweet spot in (3) (gap $4t$, excitation energy $2t$). Third, we look at the trivial-phase limit. For $t=\Delta=0$, $\mu\neq0$, only the first term of (2) remains, and $\Ham=-(\ii\mu/2)\sum_j\gamma_{2j-1}\gamma_{2j}=-\mu\sum_j(c_j^\dagger c_j-1/2)$. This is exactly the $\mu$ term of the original Kitaev Hamiltonian, which shows that the rewriting is correct. In this case all $2N$ Majorana operators appear in the Hamiltonian, and nothing is left at the ends. Fourth, we back-calculate the numbers of (5). For $B_c=0.14\ \mathrm{T}$, $V_Z=51\times5.788\times10^{-2}\times0.14/2=0.207\ \mathrm{meV}$, which indeed slightly exceeds $\Delta=0.20\ \mathrm{meV}$.

Meaning. The calculation carried out in this exercise is, formally, a vacuous operation that merely “splits a complex number into its real and imaginary parts.” The content arises at a single point: which pairs the Hamiltonian connects. In the trivial phase, $\gamma_{2j-1}$ and $\gamma_{2j}$ on the same site pair up; in the topological phase, $\gamma_{2j}$ and $\gamma_{2j+1}$ on adjacent sites pair up. The total number of Majorana operators is the same, $2N$, and the only difference is the “way they are connected.” And to change the way they are connected, the bulk gap must close somewhere—this is the meaning of the topological phase transition.

The contrast with the Majorana neutrino on the particle-physics side also becomes clear. What they have in common is the self-adjointness condition, the broken $U(1)$ charge (lepton number, and the electric charge absorbed by the superconducting condensate), half the degrees of freedom of a complex fermion, and the Clifford algebra. The difference is that the neutrino is a massive solution of the Lorentz-invariant Dirac equation, whereas the zero mode is an $E=0$ solution of the BdG equation, rides on a lattice, and possesses topological protection and non-Abelian statistics. The same algebra rides on a different kinematics. And the practical benefit for materials scientists is this: once you have understood the meaning of $\psi^c=\psi$ together with the violation of lepton number, you can read in one line what $\gamma=\gamma^\dagger$ in a paper on topological superconductors is claiming.

E.15 Solutions for Chapter 15: Beyond the Standard Model

Exercise 15.1: Higgs Yukawa couplings and decay widths

Problem (restated)

The vacuum expectation value is $v=(\sqrt2G_F)^{-1/2}$, and the Yukawa coupling is given by $y_f=\sqrt2m_f/v$. The decay width into a fermion pair is

$$ \Gamma(H\to f\bar f) = \frac{N_c\,m_H\,y_f^2}{16\pi}\left(1-\frac{4m_f^2}{m_H^2}\right)^{3/2} $$

($N_c$ is the number of colors: 3 for quarks and 1 for leptons). Let $m_H=125.25$ GeV and $\Gamma_H=4.07$ MeV.

(1) Find $v$ from $G_F=1.1664\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$.

(2) Find the Yukawa couplings $y_f$ for $m_t=172.69$, $\overline m_b(\overline m_b)=4.18$, $m_\tau=1.77686$, $m_e=5.11\times10^{-4}$ (all in GeV). What is $y_t/y_e$?

(3) Compute $\Gamma(H\to\tau^+\tau^-)$ and compare it with the value obtained from the branching ratio $6.27\ \%$ in Table 15.2.

(4) What happens if you compute $\Gamma(H\to b\bar b)$ using the $\overline{\rm MS}$ mass $\overline m_b(\overline m_b)=4.18$ GeV as it stands for $m_b$? What happens if you use the running mass at the $m_H$ scale, $\overline{m}_b(m_H)=2.79$ GeV? Furthermore, compare the result multiplied by the QCD correction factor $1+5.67\alpha_s/\pi$ ($\alpha_s(m_H)=0.113$) with the measured branching ratio.

Solution

Strategy. The only tools we use are $v=(\sqrt2G_F)^{-1/2}$ and $y_f=\sqrt2m_f/v$ from Chapter 15 of this book, together with the two-body decay-width formula given in the problem. The calculation itself amounts to substitution, but in (4) the answer moves by more than a factor of 2 depending on the scale at which the mass we insert is defined. This is the theme of this problem.

(1) First we form $\sqrt2\,G_F$.

$$ \sqrt2\,G_F = 1.414214\times1.1664\times10^{-5} = 1.649539\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}} $$

$v^2$ is its inverse.

$$ v^2 = \frac{1}{1.649539\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}} = 6.06230\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{GeV^2} $$

Taking the square root,

$$ v = \sqrt{6.06230\times10^{4}} = 246.22\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

This agrees with the value given by the derivation in Chapter 15 of this book ($g_w$ drops out of $G_F/\sqrt2=g_w^2/8m_W^2$ and $m_W=g_wv/2$). Note also that $G_F$ is a quantity fixed by the lifetime of the $\mu$ particle alone, so the electroweak symmetry-breaking scale of $246$ GeV reduces to a measurement of $\mu$ decay.

(2) It is convenient to form first the conversion factor common to all $y_f=\sqrt2m_f/v$.

$$ \frac{\sqrt2}{v} = \frac{1.414214}{246.22\ \mathrm{GeV}} = 5.74374\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-1}} $$

All that remains is to multiply by the masses.

$$ y_t = 172.69\times5.74374\times10^{-3} = 0.9919 $$ $$ y_b\big|_{\overline m_b(\overline m_b)} = 4.18\times5.74374\times10^{-3} = 2.4009\times10^{-2} $$ $$ y_\tau = 1.77686\times5.74374\times10^{-3} = 1.02059\times10^{-2} $$ $$ y_e = 5.11\times10^{-4}\times5.74374\times10^{-3} = 2.9351\times10^{-6} $$

Taking the ratio, $v$ cancels completely and we are left with the mass ratio itself.

$$ \frac{y_t}{y_e} = \frac{m_t}{m_e} = \frac{172.69}{5.11\times10^{-4}} = 3.379\times10^{5} $$

That is, $3.4\times10^5$, five and a half orders of magnitude. That the top Yukawa coupling is almost exactly $1$ ($y_t=0.99$) is a striking fact for a coincidence, and it is often said that “only the top has a natural value.” On the other hand, the electron’s $2.9\times10^{-6}$ has no explanation anywhere in the Standard Model.

(3) Since the $\tau$ is a lepton, $N_c=1$. First we evaluate the phase-space factor. With $m_\tau^2=(1.77686)^2=3.15723\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ and $m_H^2=(125.25)^2=1.568756\times10^4\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$,

$$ \frac{4m_\tau^2}{m_H^2} = \frac{4\times3.15723}{1.568756\times10^{4}} = \frac{12.6289}{1.568756\times10^{4}} = 8.0503\times10^{-4} $$ $$ \left(1-8.0503\times10^{-4}\right)^{3/2} = 0.99879 $$

Since the $\tau$ is light compared with $m_H/2=62.6$ GeV, the phase-space suppression is only $0.12\ \%$. Next, using $y_\tau^2=(1.02059\times10^{-2})^2=1.04160\times10^{-4}$ and $16\pi=50.2655$,

$$ \Gamma(H\to\tau^+\tau^-) = \frac{1\times125.25\times1.04160\times10^{-4}}{50.2655}\times0.99879 = \frac{1.30460\times10^{-2}}{50.2655}\times0.99879 $$ $$ = 2.5954\times10^{-4}\times0.99879 = 2.5923\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 0.2592\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

On the other hand, the partial width obtained from the measured branching ratio is

$$ \Gamma_{\rm exp} = B\times\Gamma_H = 0.0627\times4.07\ \mathrm{MeV} = 0.2552\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The ratio is $0.2592/0.2552=1.016$, that is, agreement to $1.6\ \%$. Merely substituting measured values into the tree-level formula gives agreement at the percent level.

(4) First we insert the $\overline{\rm MS}$ mass $\overline m_b(\overline m_b)=4.18$ GeV as it stands. With $N_c=3$ and $y_b^2=(2.4009\times10^{-2})^2=5.76428\times10^{-4}$, the phase-space factor is

$$ \frac{4m_b^2}{m_H^2} = \frac{4\times17.4724}{1.568756\times10^{4}} = 4.4551\times10^{-3}, \qquad \left(1-4.4551\times10^{-3}\right)^{3/2} = 0.99333 $$

Therefore

$$ \Gamma(H\to b\bar b)\big|_{\overline m_b(\overline m_b)} = \frac{3\times125.25\times5.76428\times10^{-4}}{50.2655}\times0.99333 = \frac{0.216588}{50.2655}\times0.99333 $$ $$ = 4.3088\times10^{-3}\times0.99333 = 4.280\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 4.280\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

This exceeds the total decay width $\Gamma_H=4.07$ MeV. Since a single channel exceeds the whole, the branching ratio becomes $4.280/4.07=1.05>1$, an obvious contradiction (dropping the phase-space factor to get $4.309$ MeV makes it even worse). It is not that something is wrong somewhere in the calculation; rather, the definition of the mass we inserted is wrong.

Next we use $\overline{m}_b(m_H)=2.79$ GeV, the $\overline{\rm MS}$ mass run up to the $m_H$ scale.

$$ y_b = 2.79\times5.74374\times10^{-3} = 1.60251\times10^{-2}, \qquad y_b^2 = 2.56804\times10^{-4} $$ $$ \frac{4m_b^2}{m_H^2} = \frac{4\times7.7841}{1.568756\times10^{4}} = 1.98478\times10^{-3}, \qquad \left(1-1.98478\times10^{-3}\right)^{3/2} = 0.99702 $$ $$ \Gamma\big|_{\overline{m}_b} = \frac{3\times125.25\times2.56804\times10^{-4}}{50.2655}\times0.99702 = 1.9197\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GeV}\times0.99702 $$ $$ = 1.9140\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 1.914\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The mass fell as $4.18\to2.79$, that is, by a factor of $1.50$, so because $y_b^2\propto m_b^2$ the width dropped by a factor of $2.24$. Finally we multiply by the QCD correction factor.

$$ 1+\frac{5.67\,\alpha_s}{\pi} = 1+\frac{5.67\times0.113}{3.14159} = 1+0.20394 = 1.2039 $$ $$ \Gamma\big|_{\overline{m}_b+{\rm QCD}} = 1.914\times1.2039 = 2.304\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The value obtained from the measured branching ratio $58.2\ \%$ is

$$ \Gamma_{\rm exp} = 0.582\times4.07 = 2.369\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

and the residual is $2.7\ \%$ (this agrees with the $2.37$ MeV in Table 15.2). Including higher-order QCD corrections and electroweak corrections, this difference is almost closed.

Verification. We check the dimensions. $y_f$ is dimensionless, $m_H$ is in GeV, and the phase-space factor is also dimensionless, so $\Gamma$ has the dimension of GeV. Correct. The limits can also be checked. As $m_f\to m_H/2$, $(1-4m_f^2/m_H^2)^{3/2}\to0$, so the width closes exactly at the threshold. Also, dividing the result of (3) by the total width,

$$ \frac{\Gamma(\tau\tau)}{\Gamma_H} = \frac{2.5923\times10^{-4}}{4.07\times10^{-3}} = 6.37\ \% $$

which agrees with the predicted value $6.27\ \%$ in Table 15.2 to within $0.1$ percentage points. This is an independent cross-check.

Meaning. What (3) shows is that the Higgs-mechanism prediction $y_f=\sqrt2m_f/v$ has been verified at the level of a few $\%$ for the $\tau$, a third-generation lepton. And what (4) shows is the lesson of Chapter 11 of this book: a quark mass has no meaning as a number unless one specifies “the scale at which it was measured.” The same phrase “the mass of the $b$ quark” is $4.18$ GeV for the $\overline{\rm MS}$ mass $\overline m_b(\overline m_b)$ and $2.79$ GeV for $\overline m_b(m_H)$ run up to the $m_H$ scale, a difference of a factor of $1.5$, and for the decay width, which depends on the square, a difference of a factor of $2.2$. It is rather fortunate that the error exposes itself so blatantly, with the branching ratio exceeding 1 if one of the two (the former) is inserted.

The counterpart in materials science is the fact that effective masses and band gaps depend on “the approximation, temperature, and volume at which they are defined.” If one mixes the LDA gap, the $GW$ gap, and the optical gap, discrepancies of a factor of 2 arise in the same way. Stating the method and the scale together when quoting a computed value is not a matter of etiquette but a physical necessity.

Exercise 15.2: Quantifying the hierarchy problem and the scale that “naturalness” demands

Problem (restated)

The correction to the Higgs mass squared from the top-quark loop is $\delta m_H^2=-(3y_t^2/8\pi^2)\Lambda^2$ in Chapter 15 of this book. Define the degree of fine-tuning as $\Delta\equiv\abs{\delta m_H^2}/m_H^2$.

(1) Find the coefficient $3y_t^2/8\pi^2$ numerically ($y_t=0.992$).

(2) Find $\Delta$ for each of $\Lambda=10$ TeV, $2\times10^{16}$ GeV, and $M_{\rm Pl}=1.22\times10^{19}$ GeV.

(3) If we require $\Delta<10$ (that is, no fine-tuning of $10\ \%$ or finer), what is the upper limit on $\Lambda$?

(4) Compare the result of (3) with the experimental lower limits in Table 15.4, and discuss the present status of the criterion of “naturalness.” Also, explain in terms of chiral symmetry why the correction to the electron mass, $\delta m_e/m_e=(3\alpha/4\pi)\ln(\Lambda^2/m_e^2)$, amounts to only $18\ \%$ even for $\Lambda=M_{\rm Pl}$.

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1)–(3) merely put numbers into the quadratic-divergence formula of Chapter 15 and solve a linear equation. The key points are that, because of the power dependence $\delta m_H^2\propto\Lambda^2$, $\Delta$ runs wild as the square of $\Lambda$, and conversely that imposing an upper limit on $\Delta$ fixes $\Lambda$ uniquely. Part (4) uses 't Hooft’s argument of technical naturalness.

(1) From $y_t=0.992$ we have $y_t^2=0.98406$, and $8\pi^2=78.9568$.

$$ \frac{3y_t^2}{8\pi^2} = \frac{3\times0.98406}{78.9568} = \frac{2.95219}{78.9568} = 0.03739 $$

That is, $0.0374$. That the coefficient is small, about $0.04$ rather than $1$, does not change the conclusions below at all, because $\Lambda^2$ varies by more than $30$ orders of magnitude.

(2) The reference observable is $m_H^2=(125.25)^2=1.56876\times10^4\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$.

For $\Lambda=10\ \mathrm{TeV}=10^4$ GeV, $\Lambda^2=10^{8}\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$, so

$$ \abs{\delta m_H^2} = 0.03739\times10^{8} = 3.739\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{GeV^2}, \qquad \Delta = \frac{3.739\times10^{6}}{1.56876\times10^{4}} = 238 $$

For $\Lambda=2\times10^{16}$ GeV (the grand-unification scale), $\Lambda^2=4\times10^{32}\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ and

$$ \abs{\delta m_H^2} = 0.03739\times4\times10^{32} = 1.4956\times10^{31}\ \mathrm{GeV^2}, \qquad \Delta = \frac{1.4956\times10^{31}}{1.56876\times10^{4}} = 9.53\times10^{26} $$

For $\Lambda=M_{\rm Pl}=1.22\times10^{19}$ GeV, $\Lambda^2=1.4884\times10^{38}\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$ and

$$ \abs{\delta m_H^2} = 0.03739\times1.4884\times10^{38} = 5.565\times10^{36}\ \mathrm{GeV^2}, \qquad \Delta = \frac{5.565\times10^{36}}{1.56876\times10^{4}} = 3.55\times10^{32} $$

The bare mass squared and the quantum correction are both of order $10^{36}\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$, yet their difference must settle at $1.6\times10^4\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$. This is a tuning in which the two agree to 32 digits and differ at the 33rd digit.

(3) We solve $\Delta=0.03739\,\Lambda^2/m_H^2<10$ for $\Lambda$.

$$ \Lambda^2 < \frac{10\,m_H^2}{0.03739} = \frac{10\times1.56876\times10^{4}}{0.03739} = \frac{1.56876\times10^{5}}{0.03739} = 4.196\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{GeV^2} $$ $$ \Lambda < \sqrt{4.196\times10^{6}} = 2.048\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{GeV} \approx 2.0\ \mathrm{TeV} $$

That is, from the mere requirement that “we do not want fine-tuning of $10\ \%$ or worse,” we obtain the quantitative prediction that new physics must lie below $2$ TeV. This is the reason why, since the 1980s, supersymmetry was expected at the TeV scale. Note also that even if we relax the requirement to $\Delta<100$ (allowing $1\ \%$ fine-tuning), we only get $\Lambda<6.5$ TeV. Since $\Lambda$ grows only as $\sqrt{\Delta}$, relaxing the requirement by one order of magnitude only raises the allowed scale by a factor of $\sqrt{10}=3.2$.

(4) The experimental lower limits in Table 15.4 are $\sim2.3$ TeV for the gluino, $\sim1.3$ TeV for the stop, $\sim1.9$ TeV for first- and second-generation squarks, and $\sim0.7$ TeV for the chargino. Compared with the $2.0$ TeV of (3), the gluino and squarks have already crossed that line, and the stop is also stuck at the same order of magnitude. Comparing with the “naturalness requirement” column of the same table (gluino $\lesssim1.5$ TeV, stop $\lesssim0.5$ TeV), we must say that naturalness in its most naive form has already been ruled out by experiment. In addition, producing $m_H=125$ GeV in the MSSM requires a heavy stop of $3$–$10$ TeV, which itself brings back fine-tuning at the $1\ \%$ level (the little hierarchy problem). “Naturalness” was a useful guide with predictive power, but its prediction did not come true. Stating this fact without obscuring it is this chapter’s attitude.

For the electron the story is entirely different. With $\alpha=1/137.036$,

$$ \ln\frac{\Lambda^2}{m_e^2} = 2\ln\frac{1.22\times10^{19}}{5.11\times10^{-4}} = 2\ln\left(2.388\times10^{22}\right) = 2\times51.53 = 103.1 $$ $$ \frac{\delta m_e}{m_e} = \frac{3\alpha}{4\pi}\times103.1 = \frac{3\times7.2974\times10^{-3}}{12.566}\times103.1 = 1.742\times10^{-3}\times103.1 = 0.180 $$

That is, $18\ \%$. Even when $\Lambda$ is as enormous as $M_{\rm Pl}$, the correction is only this large. There are two reasons, which are essentially the same. First, the correction grows only with the logarithm of $\Lambda$. Second, the correction is proportional to $m_e$ itself (multiplicative renormalization).

What guarantees this is chiral symmetry. In the limit $m_e\to0$, the Lagrangian becomes invariant under the transformations that rotate left-handed and right-handed fields independently,

$$ \psi_L \to \ee^{\ii\theta_L}\psi_L,\qquad \psi_R \to \ee^{\ii\theta_R}\psi_R $$

(only the mass term $-m_e\bar\psi\psi=-m_e(\bar\psi_L\psi_R+\bar\psi_R\psi_L)$ breaks this symmetry). Since the point at which the symmetry is restored is preserved by quantum corrections, a theory starting from $m_e=0$ cannot generate $m_e\ne0$ no matter to how high a loop order we go. Therefore $\delta m_e$ necessarily contains a factor of $m_e$, and the only remaining $\Lambda$ dependence is the logarithm needed to make it dimensionless. This is the content of 't Hooft’s technical naturalness: “if setting a parameter to zero increases the symmetry, then the smallness of that parameter is natural.”

For a scalar there is no corresponding symmetry. Even if $m_H\to0$, the symmetry of the Higgs-field Lagrangian does not increase (both the gauge symmetry and the global symmetry hold independently of $m_H$). With nothing to protect it, the correction is lifted up to the largest dimensionful quantity, namely the square of the cutoff $\Lambda$. Supersymmetry can be understood as a device that, by giving a scalar a fermionic partner, transplants to the scalar the protection afforded to fermions by chiral symmetry.

Verification. We confirm the dimensions. $\delta m_H^2$ is in $\mathrm{GeV^2}$ and $m_H^2$ is also in $\mathrm{GeV^2}$, so $\Delta$ is dimensionless. Good. We can also check by scaling. Since $\Delta\propto\Lambda^2$, if $\Lambda$ increases by a factor of $1.22\times10^{15}$ from $10^4$ GeV to $1.22\times10^{19}$ GeV, then $\Delta$ should increase by a factor of $(1.22\times10^{15})^2=1.488\times10^{30}$, giving

$$ 238\times1.488\times10^{30} = 3.54\times10^{32} $$

which agrees with the $3.55\times10^{32}$ found directly in (2). The back-calculation of (3) can also be checked. Putting $\Lambda=2.048$ TeV into the formula of (2) gives $\Delta=0.03739\times4.194\times10^{6}/1.56876\times10^{4}=9.997$, which is $10$ as required.

Meaning. The hierarchy problem is not an aesthetic complaint that “it feels bad”; it is a problem that can be written as a number. And precisely because it can be written as a number, it can be cornered by experiment. The fact that the LHC found nothing below $2$ TeV means that fine-tuning of $\Delta\gtrsim10$ is real. The responses to this fall into three: (i) wait for somewhat heavier new physics, (ii) abandon the criterion of naturalness itself (the anthropic principle, the multiverse), and (iii) look for a different framework in which the quadratic divergence does not appear in the first place; the matter has not been settled.

In the language of condensed matter physics, this is exactly isomorphic to the situation in which the quadratic coefficient $a(T-T_c)$ of the Ginzburg–Landau free energy, not being protected by symmetry, is fixed at the microscopic scale (of order electronvolts), while the observed $T_c$ is of order millielectronvolts to at most a few tens of millielectronvolts. The reason it is extremely difficult to predict $T_c$ to within a few $\%$ by first-principles calculations is that a small quantity must be obtained as the difference of large quantities, which is the same structure as the fine-tuning of the Higgs mass.

Exercise 15.3: Finding the crossing point of the running couplings yourself

Problem (restated)

Use the one-loop renormalization group equation ($\alpha_i^{-1}(\mu)=\alpha_i^{-1}(m_Z)-(b_i/2\pi)\ln(\mu/m_Z)$ in Chapter 15 of this book) and the starting values at $m_Z$, $\alpha_1^{-1}=59.02$, $\alpha_2^{-1}=29.58$, $\alpha_3^{-1}=8.48$. Let $t\equiv\ln(\mu/m_Z)$.

(1) Using the Standard Model coefficients $(b_1,b_2,b_3)=(41/10,\,-19/6,\,-7)$, find the scales of the crossing points of $\alpha_1=\alpha_3$ and of $\alpha_2=\alpha_3$.

(2) Using the MSSM coefficients $(b_1,b_2,b_3)=(33/5,\,1,\,-3)$ (for simplicity, place the superpartner thresholds at $m_Z$), find the crossing point $M_X$ of $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$ and the value of $\alpha_G^{-1}$ there.

(3) Substitute the $t$ found in (2) into the expression for $\alpha_3^{-1}$, and check whether the three curves really meet at a single point (state the degree of agreement in $\%$).

(4) At the grand unification point, $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$. Using the normalization $\alpha_1=(5/3)\alpha_Y$, show that $\sin^2\theta_W=3/8$ in this case. Where does the difference from the measured value $0.2312$ come from?

Solution

Strategy. The one-loop renormalization group equation makes $\alpha_i^{-1}$ a linear function of $t=\ln(\mu/m_Z)$. So what we have to do is a junior high school problem: find the crossing points of three straight lines. The physics enters only through which $b_i$ we use (that is, which particles run). We use $m_Z=91.19$ GeV.

(1) Divide the Standard Model coefficients by $2\pi=6.28319$ to make the slopes of the lines. We have $b_1=41/10=4.100$, $b_2=-19/6=-3.16667$, $b_3=-7$. Watch the signs (the expression for $\alpha_i^{-1}$ is multiplied by $-b_i/2\pi$, so if $b_i<0$, then $\alpha_i^{-1}$ increases).

$$ \alpha_1^{-1}(t) = 59.02 - \frac{4.100}{6.28319}\,t = 59.02 - 0.65254\,t $$ $$ \alpha_2^{-1}(t) = 29.58 + \frac{3.16667}{6.28319}\,t = 29.58 + 0.50399\,t $$ $$ \alpha_3^{-1}(t) = 8.48 + \frac{7.000}{6.28319}\,t = 8.48 + 1.11409\,t $$

$\alpha_1=\alpha_3$ is the same as $\alpha_1^{-1}=\alpha_3^{-1}$.

$$ 59.02 - 0.65254\,t = 8.48 + 1.11409\,t \;\Longrightarrow\; 50.54 = 1.76663\,t \;\Longrightarrow\; t = 28.608 $$ $$ \mu = m_Z\,\ee^{28.608} = 91.19\times2.657\times10^{12} = 2.42\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

For $\alpha_2=\alpha_3$,

$$ 29.58 + 0.50399\,t = 8.48 + 1.11409\,t \;\Longrightarrow\; 21.10 = 0.61009\,t \;\Longrightarrow\; t = 34.585 $$ $$ \mu = 91.19\times\ee^{34.585} = 9.55\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

For reference, the remaining one, $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$, gives $t=25.456$ from $29.44=1.15653\,t$, so $\mu=1.04\times10^{13}$ GeV. The three crossing points are scattered at $1.0\times10^{13}$, $2.4\times10^{14}$, and $9.6\times10^{16}$ GeV, and the shaded triangle in Figure 15.3 does not close. With the particle content of the Standard Model, the three lines do not meet at a single point. Moreover, the discrepancy is nearly 4 orders of magnitude in $\mu$ and several units in the value of $\alpha^{-1}$, which cannot possibly be explained by the experimental errors of the starting values (an error of $\pm0.001$ in $\alpha_s$ corresponds to $\pm0.07$ in $\alpha_3^{-1}$).

(2) The MSSM coefficients are $b_1=33/5=6.600$, $b_2=1$, $b_3=-3$. What is essential is that the sign of $b_2$ changes ($SU(2)_L$ is no longer asymptotically free) and that $b_3$ weakens from $-7$ to $-3$.

$$ \alpha_1^{-1}(t) = 59.02 - \frac{6.600}{6.28319}\,t = 59.02 - 1.05042\,t $$ $$ \alpha_2^{-1}(t) = 29.58 - \frac{1.000}{6.28319}\,t = 29.58 - 0.159155\,t $$ $$ \alpha_3^{-1}(t) = 8.48 + \frac{3.000}{6.28319}\,t = 8.48 + 0.477465\,t $$

From $\alpha_1^{-1}=\alpha_2^{-1}$,

$$ 59.02 - 1.05042\,t = 29.58 - 0.159155\,t \;\Longrightarrow\; 29.44 = 0.891268\,t \;\Longrightarrow\; t = 33.032 $$ $$ M_X = 91.19\times\ee^{33.032} = 91.19\times2.215\times10^{14} = 2.02\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

The coupling constant there follows from the expression for $\alpha_2^{-1}$:

$$ \alpha_G^{-1} = 29.58 - 0.159155\times33.032 = 29.58 - 5.257 = 24.32 $$

That is, $\alpha_G=1/24.32=0.0411$. Checking with the expression for $\alpha_1^{-1}$ gives the same value, $59.02-1.05042\times33.032=59.02-34.697=24.32$ (as it must, since this is the crossing point).

(3) Insert the same $t=33.032$ into the expression for $\alpha_3^{-1}$, which we have not used at all in the calculation. This is the point of the problem: since $\alpha_3$ did not appear in the equation that fixes the crossing point, this is a test of a prediction.

$$ \alpha_3^{-1}(33.032) = 8.48 + 0.477465\times33.032 = 8.48 + 15.771 = 24.25 $$

The three values are $\alpha_1^{-1}=24.32$, $\alpha_2^{-1}=24.32$, $\alpha_3^{-1}=24.25$. The spread is

$$ \frac{24.32-24.25}{24.30} = \frac{0.07}{24.30} = 2.9\times10^{-3} = 0.29\ \% $$

that is, they agree to within $0.3\ \%$. Recall that in the Standard Model the corresponding quantity was off by somewhat more than 10% (at $t=25.456$, where $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$ on the lines of (1), $\alpha_{1,2}^{-1}=42.41$ while $\alpha_3^{-1}=36.84$, that is, $14\ \%$); this is a dramatic improvement. Three independent numbers measured at $m_Z$ ($\alpha_{\rm em}$, $\sin^2\theta_W$, $\alpha_s$) are extrapolated over 14 orders of magnitude and gather at a single point to within $0.3\ \%$, so it is hard to dismiss this as a coincidence. This is what has been called the “circumstantial evidence” for supersymmetry.
