In fairness, however, we should add that this calculation is a one-loop calculation with all superpartner thresholds placed at $m_Z$. If we include the actual thresholds (around $1$ TeV), two-loop effects, and corrections from higher-dimensional operators near the unification scale, the degree of agreement loosens to a few $\%$. Even so, the difference from the Standard Model is obvious.

(4) The Weinberg angle is defined by $\tan\theta_W=g'/g$, that is,

$$ \sin^2\theta_W = \frac{g'^2}{g^2+g'^2} = \frac{\alpha_Y}{\alpha_2+\alpha_Y} $$

(with $\alpha_Y=g'^2/4\pi$, $\alpha_2=g^2/4\pi$). At the grand unification point the couplings merge into the single coupling $\alpha_G$ of $SU(5)$, so $\alpha_2=\alpha_G$, and from the $SU(5)$ normalization $\alpha_1=(5/3)\alpha_Y=\alpha_G$ we get

$$ \alpha_Y = \frac35\,\alpha_G $$

Substituting, $\alpha_G$ cancels out.

$$ \sin^2\theta_W\big|_{M_X} = \frac{(3/5)\alpha_G}{\alpha_G+(3/5)\alpha_G} = \frac{3/5}{1+3/5} = \frac{3/5}{8/5} = \frac38 = 0.375 $$

This is a rational number fixed by group theory alone. The difference from the measured value $\sin^2\theta_W(m_Z)=0.2312$ is precisely the quantum correction accumulated while running down from $M_X$ to $m_Z$. Indeed, $\alpha_Y$ and $\alpha_2$ have different $b_i$, so they run at different speeds and their ratio changes. That the value at $m_Z$ is the awkward number $0.2312$ is the result of a $14$-orders-of-magnitude extrapolation.

The correct way to read this is in the reverse direction. Starting from the “clean number” $3/8$ at the unification point and running down to $m_Z$ with the renormalization group equation, one obtains $0.2312$. The starting values $\alpha_1^{-1}=59.02$, $\alpha_2^{-1}=29.58$ in (2) and (3) of this problem were constructed from $\hat\alpha_{\rm em}^{-1}(m_Z)=127.95$ ($\overline{\rm MS}$; see Chapter 10, Section 10.6.4) and $\sin^2\theta_W=0.23122$. Hence the very existence of the $\alpha_1=\alpha_2$ crossing point in (2) is the same statement as the claim that “running $0.2312$ up to $M_X$ gives $3/8$.” That an awkward measured number turns into a rational number far away is an example of the predictive power of the renormalization group.

Verification. Look at the dimensions. $t=\ln(\mu/m_Z)$ is dimensionless, $b_i/2\pi$ is dimensionless, and $\alpha_i^{-1}$ is dimensionless, so everything is consistent. The signs can also be checked. $b_3=-7<0$ means asymptotic freedom ($\alpha_3$ decreases as $\mu$ increases, that is, $\alpha_3^{-1}$ increases), and indeed $\alpha_3^{-1}$ increases from $8.48$ to $24.25$. $b_1>0$ means QED-like screening ($\alpha_1$ increases as $\mu$ increases), and $\alpha_1^{-1}$ decreases from $59.02$ to $24.32$. Both agree with the picture of Chapter 11.

As one more check, let us verify the $3/8$ of (4) numerically as well. If $\alpha_G^{-1}=24.32$, then $\alpha_2^{-1}=24.32$ and $\alpha_Y^{-1}=(5/3)\times24.32=40.53$, so

$$ \sin^2\theta_W = \frac{\alpha_Y}{\alpha_2+\alpha_Y} = \frac{1/40.53}{1/24.32+1/40.53} = \frac{0.024673}{0.041118+0.024673} = 0.3750 $$

which is exactly $3/8$.

Meaning. This exercise is just a calculation of “drawing three straight lines,” but a great deal can be read from it. First, minimal $SU(5)$ can be ruled out from this single point alone. It is rare for the refutation of a theory to take a form so simple that it can be carried out with paper and a calculator. Second, the convergence in the MSSM is a nontrivial relation among three measured numbers, and it remains an “interesting numerical fact” regardless of whether the hypothesis is right. Third, $\sin^2\theta_W=3/8$ expresses most concisely the idea of unification: the strengths of three forces that seem unrelated at low energies can be reduced to a single number at high energies.

What the running of the renormalization group does physically is the same as screening by a medium, as Chapter 15 of this book describes. The same mechanism by which a bare charge in a dielectric is screened by polarization, so that the effective interaction strength changes with distance (= energy scale), operates here as vacuum polarization. The everyday quantity corresponding to this on the materials science side is the $q$ dependence of the static dielectric function $\varepsilon(q)$, and the fact that the effective interaction looks completely different inside and outside the Thomas–Fermi screening length is also a kind of “running” of the same sort.

Exercise 15.4: Proton decay lifetime and Super-Kamiokande

Problem (restated)

The proton decay width is estimated by the formula $\Gamma\sim\alpha_G^2m_p^5/M_X^4$ of Chapter 15 of this book. Let $m_p=0.9383$ GeV, $\hbar=6.582\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{GeV\,s}$, and 1 year $=3.156\times10^7$ s.

(1) Find $\tau_p$ in years for $M_X=10^{15}$ GeV and $\alpha_G=1/40$.

(2) From the lower limit $\tau_p>1.6\times10^{34}$ years of the 2017 Super-Kamiokande analysis, find the lower limit on $M_X$. What does one obtain with $2.4\times10^{34}$ years from the 2020 analysis?

(3) The effective volume of Super-Kamiokande is $22.5$ kton of ultrapure water. One water molecule contains 10 protons (8 from $^{16}$O and 2 from H). Find the total number of target protons.

(4) Take a detection efficiency $\varepsilon=0.4$ and zero background. If 0 events are observed in 20 years, the $90\ \%$ confidence upper limit is 2.3 events. Find the resulting lower limit on $\tau_p$ and check whether it is consistent with the value in (2). Also state how many events would have been observed if it had been $\tau_p=10^{33}$ years.

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1) and (2) need only the width formula from dimensional analysis in Chapter 15 of this book and the scaling $\tau\propto M_X^4$. Parts (3) and (4) follow how the sensitivity of a particle-physics experiment is built up, and all we use is Avogadro’s number and the one-line relation “exposure $=$ number of targets $\times$ time.” The only point to watch is that we use $\hbar$ to convert $\Gamma$ [GeV] in natural units into seconds.

(1) First compute $m_p^5$.

$$ m_p^5 = (0.9383)^5 = 0.7273\ \mathrm{GeV^5} $$

Since $\alpha_G=1/40$, $\alpha_G^2=1/1600=6.250\times10^{-4}$, and $M_X^4=(10^{15})^4=10^{60}\ \mathrm{GeV^4}$.

$$ \Gamma = \frac{\alpha_G^2\,m_p^5}{M_X^4} = \frac{6.250\times10^{-4}\times0.7273}{10^{60}} = \frac{4.546\times10^{-4}}{10^{60}} = 4.546\times10^{-64}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

The lifetime is $\tau=\hbar/\Gamma$ (since $\Gamma$ is measured in dimensions of energy, multiplying by $\hbar$ [$\mathrm{GeV\,s}$] gives seconds).

$$ \tau_p = \frac{6.582\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{GeV\,s}}{4.546\times10^{-64}\ \mathrm{GeV}} = 1.448\times10^{39}\ \mathrm{s} $$ $$ \tau_p = \frac{1.448\times10^{39}}{3.156\times10^{7}} = 4.59\times10^{31}\ \text{yr} $$

This was the expectation around 1980. It is a staggering $3\times10^{21}$ times the age of the universe, $1.4\times10^{10}$ years, but if we gather $10^{33}$ protons, then $10^{33}/4.6\times10^{31}\approx22$ of them decay per year. A long lifetime can be bought with the number of targets. This is the idea behind the large water-tank experiments.

(2) The only dependence of the formula on $M_X$ is $\tau_p\propto M_X^4$ (with $\alpha_G$ and $m_p$ held fixed). Therefore

$$ \frac{M_X^{\rm min}}{10^{15}\ \mathrm{GeV}} = \left(\frac{\tau_p^{\rm min}}{4.59\times10^{31}\ \text{yr}}\right)^{1/4} = \left(\frac{1.6\times10^{34}}{4.59\times10^{31}}\right)^{1/4} = (348.7)^{1/4} $$

The $4$th root is obtained by taking the square root twice: $348.7^{1/2}=18.67$, $18.67^{1/2}=4.321$. Thus

$$ M_X > 4.32\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{GeV} \approx 4.3\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

What matters here is the bluntness of the fourth root. Even if the lower limit on the lifetime rises by a factor of $348$, the lower limit on $M_X$ rises only by a factor of $4.3$. Conversely, to raise $M_X$ by one more order of magnitude, the lifetime sensitivity must be extended by 4 orders of magnitude. This is why proton decay searches are experiments in which “sensitivity is hard to improve.”

Using $2.4\times10^{34}$ years from the 2020 analysis, the same calculation gives

$$ \frac{M_X^{\rm min}}{10^{15}\ \mathrm{GeV}} = \left(\frac{2.4\times10^{34}}{4.59\times10^{31}}\right)^{1/4} = (522.9)^{1/4} = 4.78, \qquad M_X > 4.8\times10^{15}\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Even though the lower limit on the lifetime increases by a factor of $1.5$, the lower limit on $M_X$ increases only by a factor of $1.5^{1/4}=1.11$, that is, by only 10%. The bluntness of the fourth root appears here as well.

On the other hand, as Section 15.2.3 of Chapter 15 showed, the unification scale of minimal $SU(5)$ is only $2.4\times10^{14}$ GeV at the $\alpha_1=\alpha_3$ crossing point. The lower limit $4.3\times10^{15}$ GeV exceeds this by more than one order of magnitude. Minimal $SU(5)$ is independently ruled out by two facts: the non-convergence of the coupling constants and the non-observation of proton decay.

(3) The effective volume is $22.5$ kton $=2.25\times10^{7}$ kg $=2.25\times10^{10}$ g. The formula weight of water, $\mathrm{H_2O}$, is $2\times1.008+15.999=18.015$, so the amount of substance is

$$ n = \frac{2.25\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{g}}{18.015\ \mathrm{g/mol}} = 1.249\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{mol} $$

Multiplying by Avogadro’s number gives the number of molecules:

$$ N_{\rm mol} = 1.249\times10^{9}\times6.022\times10^{23} = 7.521\times10^{32}\ \text{molecules} $$

Per $\mathrm{H_2O}$ molecule there are 8 protons in oxygen and one each in the two hydrogens, for a total of 10 protons. Therefore

$$ N_p = 7.521\times10^{32}\times10 = 7.52\times10^{33}\ \text{protons} $$

As an order-of-magnitude rule to remember, “a kiloton of water contains $3\times10^{32}$ protons,” so $22.5$ kton contains $7.5\times10^{33}$. Strictly speaking, bound protons (the 8 in the oxygen nucleus) and free protons (the 2 in hydrogen) have different detection efficiencies because of nuclear effects, so the actual analysis treats them separately. Here we count them uniformly, as the problem instructs.

(4) The exposure (number of targets $\times$ observation time) is

$$ N_pT = 7.521\times10^{33}\times20\ \text{yr} = 1.504\times10^{35}\ \text{proton}\cdot\text{yr} $$

When there are $N_p$ particles of lifetime $\tau_p$, the number that decay in a time $T$ ($\ll\tau_p$) is $N_pT/\tau_p$, and of these the fraction $\varepsilon$ can be detected. The expected number of observed events is

$$ \mu = \frac{\varepsilon\,N_p T}{\tau_p} $$

With zero background and 0 events, the $90\ \%$ confidence-level upper limit is $\mu<2.3$ (solving $\ee^{-\mu}=0.10$ for the Poisson distribution gives $\mu=2.303$), so solving for $\tau_p$,

$$ \tau_p > \frac{\varepsilon\,N_p T}{2.3} = \frac{0.4\times1.504\times10^{35}}{2.3} = \frac{6.017\times10^{34}}{2.3} = 2.6\times10^{34}\ \text{yr} $$

This is of the same order as the published value $1.6\times10^{34}$ years used in problem (2), and is consistent with it. The actual lower limit is somewhat weaker (smaller) than this naive estimate because the detection efficiency for bound protons is lower than for free protons, because a small number of atmospheric neutrino events remain as background, and because the period usable for the analysis is shorter than the total running period, among other reasons. Agreement in order of magnitude is enough.

If $\tau_p=10^{33}$ years, the expected number of events would be

$$ \mu = \frac{0.4\times1.504\times10^{35}}{10^{33}} = 60.2\ \text{events} $$

Sixty events in a zero-background experiment cannot be missed. The final state of $p\to e^+\pi^0$ consists of $e^+$ and the two photons from $\pi^0\to2\gamma$, and has the striking features that the total energy equals $m_p=938$ MeV and the total momentum is nearly zero. The probability that background atmospheric neutrino events satisfy this condition by chance is extremely low. Therefore the result “nothing was found” is not a lack of sensitivity but a genuine negation.

Verification. Look at the dimensions. $\alpha_G$ is dimensionless, and $m_p^5/M_X^4$ has dimensions $\mathrm{GeV^5/GeV^4}=\mathrm{GeV}$, which matches the dimension of $\Gamma$. This is correct. Dividing by $\hbar$ [$\mathrm{GeV\,s}$] to get seconds is also consistent.

We also check by scaling. Putting $M_X=4.32\times10^{15}$ GeV from (2) back into the formula of (1),

$$ \tau_p = 4.59\times10^{31}\times(4.321)^4 = 4.59\times10^{31}\times348.7 = 1.6\times10^{34}\ \text{yr} $$

which exactly reproduces the lower limit we started from. The two results of (4) are also consistent with each other. For $\tau_p=2.6\times10^{34}$ years, $\mu=0.4\times1.504\times10^{35}/2.6\times10^{34}=2.3$, which is indeed the $90\ \%$ upper limit.

Meaning. What this exercise depicts is an experiment completely covering and refuting the region that theory most expected, the clearest event in particle physics in the second half of the twentieth century. Against the prediction $\tau_p\sim10^{31\text{--}32}$ years, experiment pushed through to $10^{34}$ years. Moreover, there is no escape route of “the sensitivity is still insufficient.” As (4) shows, tens of events should have appeared if the predicted region were correct.

However, grand unification itself is not dead. In supersymmetric $SU(5)$ and $SO(10)$, $M_X\sim2\times10^{16}$ GeV, and putting this into the formula of (1) gives $\tau_p\sim4.59\times10^{31}\times(20)^4=7\times10^{36}$ years. However, the formula of (1) assumes $\alpha_G=1/40$; if we use the MSSM unified coupling $\alpha_G\simeq1/24$ found in Exercise 15.3, then from $\tau\propto\alpha_G^{-2}$ the lifetime is multiplied by $(24.3/40)^2=0.37$, that is, $\tau_p\sim3\times10^{36}$ years. In any case, the $e^+\pi^0$ mode comfortably exceeds the present lower limit. Note, however, that in supersymmetric GUTs the dimension-5 operator makes $p\to K^+\bar\nu$ the dominant mode, and this is already in tension with the Super-K lower limit ($\tau/B>5.9\times10^{33}$ years). The next-generation Hyper-Kamiokande (effective mass $188$ kton) and DUNE (liquid argon, $40$ kton) approach $10^{35}$ years. Proton decay is still a living experimental problem.

The connection to materials science actually lies in the single line of (3). To realize the number of targets $7.5\times10^{33}$, one must keep $22.5$ kton of water, moreover with radioactive impurities such as $^{222}$Rn removed to the utmost limit. What determines the performance of the detector is not the measuring instrument but the purity of the target material itself. The same picture appears in the dark matter detectors of Section 15.6 ($^{238}\mathrm{U}<8\times10^{-14}$ g/g). The sensitivity of a particle-physics experiment is often limited by the purity of materials.

Exercise 15.5: Getting a feel for the baryon asymmetry

Problem (restated)

Let $\eta=n_B/n_\gamma=6.1\times10^{-10}$, the CMB photon number density $n_\gamma=411\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, $m_p=1.673\times10^{-24}$ g, and the critical density $\rho_c=8.54\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$.

(1) Find the present average baryon number density $n_B$ of the universe.

(2) Convert it to a baryon mass density, find $\Omega_b=\rho_b/\rho_c$, and compare it with the value in Table 15.5.

(3) Find the average spacing between protons, $n_B^{-1/3}$. State it by comparison with a familiar length.

(4) Suppose the early universe had $N+\Delta N$ quarks and $N$ antiquarks, and find $\Delta N/N$. Also state what the present $n_B/n_\gamma$ would be if $\Delta N=0$ (it becomes $\sim10^{-18}$ through the freeze-out of annihilation), and say by how many orders of magnitude it differs from the observed value.

Solution

Strategy. All we use is the definition $\eta\equiv n_B/n_\gamma$ from Chapter 15 of this book and the post-annihilation bookkeeping $\eta\approx\Delta N/2N$. The calculation comes down to multiplications and a cube root, but the point of this problem is to get a feel for the size of the numbers that come out.

(1) This is just the definition.

$$ n_B = \eta\,n_\gamma = 6.1\times10^{-10}\times411\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} = 2.507\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} $$

Since $1\ \mathrm{m^3}=10^6\ \mathrm{cm^3}$, this is $0.251$ per $\mathrm{m^3}$. Averaged over the whole universe, there are only $0.25$ protons in $1$ cubic meter.

The given value $n_\gamma=411\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ can also be checked independently from blackbody radiation at $T_0=2.7255$ K. From the integral over the Bose distribution, the photon number density is

$$ n_\gamma = \frac{2\zeta(3)}{\pi^2}\left(\frac{k_BT_0}{\hbar c}\right)^3 $$

(with $\zeta(3)=1.20206$). Since $k_BT_0=2.349\times10^{-4}$ eV and $\hbar c=1.9733\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV\,cm}$, we have $k_BT_0/\hbar c=11.90\ \mathrm{cm^{-1}}$, and its cube is $1.686\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$. The coefficient is $2\times1.20206/9.8696=0.2436$, so

$$ n_\gamma = 0.2436\times1.686\times10^{3} = 411\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} $$

which reproduces the given value. Note that $n_\gamma$ is fixed by the temperature alone (no cosmological parameters are used at all). Precisely because the denominator of $\eta$ is known with confidence, a measurement of $\eta$ is directly a measurement of $n_B$.

(2) Baryons are almost entirely protons and neutrons, and both masses can be approximated by $m_p$ (the correction due to the mixture of hydrogen and helium is a few $\%$).

$$ \rho_b = n_B\,m_p = 2.507\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\times1.673\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{g} = 4.194\times10^{-31}\ \mathrm{g/cm^3} $$

Convert to SI. Since $1\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}=10^3\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$,

$$ \rho_b = 4.194\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} $$ $$ \Omega_b = \frac{\rho_b}{\rho_c} = \frac{4.194\times10^{-28}}{8.54\times10^{-27}} = 0.0491 $$

This agrees to $0.4\ \%$ with the Planck 2018 value $\Omega_b=0.0493$ in Table 15.5. What is remarkable is that the two come from entirely different measurements. $\eta=6.1\times10^{-10}$ comes from Big Bang nucleosynthesis (the abundance ratios of D, $^4$He, and $^7$Li) and from the ratio of the acoustic peaks of the CMB, while $\rho_c$ is obtained independently from the Hubble constant. The nuclear reactions of the early universe, the acoustic oscillations of photons $38$ ten-thousand years (380,000 years) later, and the present expansion rate all point to the same number.

(3) The mean spacing is the number density to the power $-1/3$.

$$ n_B^{-1/3} = \left(2.507\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\right)^{-1/3} $$

Let us make the exponent easier to handle. Writing $2.507\times10^{-7}=250.7\times10^{-9}$, we have $(10^{-9})^{-1/3}=10^{3}$ and $(250.7)^{-1/3}=1/6.305=0.1586$, so

$$ n_B^{-1/3} = 0.1586\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{cm} = 158.6\ \mathrm{cm} = 1.59\ \mathrm{m} $$

That is, there is on average one proton in a cube $1.6$ m on a side. Just picture a cube about as tall as a person. Our sense that we live in a “world made of matter” is merely a local circumstance, caught in a density fluctuation exceeding a factor of $10^{5}$, namely a galaxy. The cosmic average is far more dilute than any ultrahigh vacuum that can be made in a laboratory (even an ultrahigh vacuum of $10^{-10}$ Pa has a molecular number density of about $2\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, which is $10^{11}$ times the cosmic average).

(4) Suppose that in the early universe there were $N+\Delta N$ quarks and $N$ antiquarks. As the temperature falls, all $N$ pairs annihilate and produce photons. Each pair yields two photons, so there are $2N$ photons and $\Delta N$ surviving baryons (we drop here the factor of 3 coming from three quarks making one baryon. Including this factor gives $\Delta N/N\approx6\eta=3.7\times10^{-9}$ in Section 15.3.1 of the main text, but both are of the order of “a few parts in a billion”). Therefore

$$ \eta \approx \frac{\Delta N}{2N} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{\Delta N}{N} \approx 2\eta = 2\times6.1\times10^{-10} = 1.22\times10^{-9} $$

That is, it was a tiny difference, of the kind in which for every $10^{9}$ antiquarks there were $10^{9}+1$ quarks. The atoms that make up our bodies now are nothing other than the “survivors of $1$ part in $10$ hundred million (one billion).”

What would happen if $\Delta N=0$? If the situation were perfectly symmetric, quarks and antiquarks would keep disappearing by pair annihilation, but as the density drops with the expansion of the universe, the annihilation rate $\Gamma=n\langle\sigma v\rangle$ falls below the Hubble rate $H$, and the reaction freezes out there (the freeze-out condition in Chapter 15 of this book). What remains is the symmetric relic abundance, with $n_B/n_\gamma\sim10^{-18}$. The ratio of the observed value $6.1\times10^{-10}$ to this is

$$ \frac{6.1\times10^{-10}}{10^{-18}} = 6\times10^{8} $$

that is, 8 orders of magnitude. These 8 orders of magnitude are not something that can be settled by simply putting an asymmetry in as an initial condition (if there was inflation, an asymmetry put in as an initial condition would be diluted away). The asymmetry must be produced by a physical process. This is the logic that demands the three Sakharov conditions (baryon number violation, $C$ and $CP$ violation, and departure from thermal equilibrium).

Verification. We derive $\rho_b$ by an independent route and compare. As an energy density,

$$ \rho_b c^2 = n_B\,m_pc^2 = 2.507\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}\times0.9383\ \mathrm{GeV} = 2.352\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{GeV/cm^3} = 0.235\ \mathrm{GeV/m^3} $$

The baryon entry of Table 15.5 is $0.24\ \mathrm{GeV/m^3}$, which agrees. Also, the spacing in (3) and the density in (1) are consistent with each other: $(1.586\ \mathrm{m})^3=3.99\ \mathrm{m^3}$, and $0.251\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}\times3.99\ \mathrm{m^3}=1.00$ particle. Good.

Meaning. The number $\eta=6\times10^{-10}$ is an order form addressed to particle physics from cosmological observation. The Standard Model cannot fill this order. As calculated in Chapter 15 of this book, the asymmetry that Kobayashi–Maskawa $CP$ violation can produce stops at the dimensionless quantity $d_{CP}\sim10^{-20}$ (at $T\sim100$ GeV), obtained by multiplying the Jarlskog invariant $J=3.08\times10^{-5}$ by all the mass-squared differences between generations, and it is short by ten orders of magnitude of the required $\eta\sim10^{-10}$. Moreover, for $m_H=125$ GeV the electroweak phase transition is not first order but a crossover, so the third condition (departure from thermal equilibrium) cannot be met. Note also that the $10^{-18}$ treated in (4) is “the amount left over by the freeze-out of annihilation when there is no asymmetry at all,” and is a different number from the amount produced by $CP$ violation. The moment $m_H$ was measured, one scenario, electroweak baryogenesis, disappeared.

The leading alternative is leptogenesis, in which the out-of-equilibrium decay of the right-handed Majorana neutrinos of Chapter 14 of this book first creates a lepton number asymmetry, and sphaleron processes then convert it into baryon number. The lightness of neutrinos and the survival of matter in the universe come down to one and the same scale, $M_R\sim10^{14\text{--}15}$ GeV—this is the appeal of the scenario.

Incidentally, the figure in (3), “one proton in a cube $1.6$ m on a side,” is also useful for calibrating one’s sense in materials science. The atomic number density in a solid is $\sim5\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, which is $2\times10^{29}$ times the cosmic average. The objects that we call “matter” and work with are, seen from the universe as a whole, nothing other than an abnormally concentrated, exceptional state.

Exercise 15.6: Finding the amount of dark matter from a rotation curve

Problem (restated)

Use the rotation-curve formula $v(r)=\sqrt{GM(r)/r}$ of Chapter 15 of this book. Let $1\ \mathrm{kpc}=3.086\times10^{19}$ m, $G=6.674\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{m^3kg^{-1}s^{-2}}$, $M_\odot=1.989\times10^{30}$ kg, and $1\ \mathrm{kg}=5.610\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{GeV}/c^2$. Suppose the rotation speed of the Milky Way is flat at $v=220$ km/s from $r=8$ kpc to $50$ kpc.

(1) Find the total mass $M(<8\ \mathrm{kpc})$ inside $r=8$ kpc (the position of the Sun) in units of $M_\odot$.

(2) Find $M(<50\ \mathrm{kpc})$. The total amount of luminous matter is about $6\times10^{10}M_\odot$. How many times larger than the luminous matter is the dark matter?

(3) If $v$ is constant, $\rho(r)=v^2/(4\pi Gr^2)$. Find $\rho$ at $r=8$ kpc in units of $\mathrm{GeV/cm^3}$. Compare it with the $0.3$–$0.4\ \mathrm{GeV/cm^3}$ that direct-search experiments use as the standard value, and state why a difference appears.

(4) Take the local density to be $0.4\ \mathrm{GeV/cm^3}$, $M_\chi=100$ GeV, and the relative velocity $220$ km/s. How many WIMPs pass through a palm-sized ($100\ \mathrm{cm^2}$) surface per second? Why are they nevertheless not detected?

Solution

Strategy. All we use is $M(r)=v^2r/G$, obtained by solving $v=\sqrt{GM(r)/r}$ of Chapter 15 of this book for the mass, and $\rho(r)=v^2/4\pi Gr^2$, obtained from it by differentiation. The real substance of this problem is carrying out the unit conversions (from kpc to m, and from kg to GeV) carefully.

(1) First, put everything in SI units.

$$ r = 8\ \mathrm{kpc} = 8\times3.086\times10^{19}\ \mathrm{m} = 2.4688\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{m} $$ $$ v = 220\ \mathrm{km/s} = 2.20\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{m/s}, \qquad v^2 = 4.84\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2} $$

Substitute into $M(r)=v^2r/G$.

$$ M(<8\ \mathrm{kpc}) = \frac{4.84\times10^{10}\times2.4688\times10^{20}}{6.674\times10^{-11}} = \frac{1.1949\times10^{31}}{6.674\times10^{-11}} = 1.790\times10^{41}\ \mathrm{kg} $$

Measured in solar masses,

$$ M(<8\ \mathrm{kpc}) = \frac{1.790\times10^{41}}{1.989\times10^{30}} = 9.00\times10^{10}\,M_\odot $$

That is, $9.0\times10^{10}$ solar masses.

(2) If $v$ is constant, then $M(r)=v^2r/G\propto r$. Therefore, extending the radius $8\to50$ kpc multiplies the mass by $50/8=6.25$.

$$ M(<50\ \mathrm{kpc}) = 9.00\times10^{10}\times6.25 = 5.63\times10^{11}\,M_\odot $$

Compared with the luminous matter, $6\times10^{10}M_\odot$, the total mass is

$$ \frac{5.63\times10^{11}}{6\times10^{10}} = 9.4\ \text{times} $$

as large. If we take only the dark component, after subtracting the luminous component,

$$ \frac{5.63\times10^{11}-6\times10^{10}}{6\times10^{10}} = \frac{5.03\times10^{11}}{6\times10^{10}} = 8.4\ \text{times} $$

In either case, the conclusion that the non-luminous (dark) mass is 8–9 times the luminous mass does not change. The “9 times” in the explanatory text of Figure 15.5 is the former way of counting.

(3) Substitute $r=2.4688\times10^{20}$ m into $\rho(r)=v^2/(4\pi Gr^2)$. We have $r^2=6.0950\times10^{40}\ \mathrm{m^2}$ and $4\pi G=4\pi\times6.674\times10^{-11}=8.3865\times10^{-10}$.

$$ \rho = \frac{4.84\times10^{10}}{8.3865\times10^{-10}\times6.0950\times10^{40}} = \frac{4.84\times10^{10}}{5.1117\times10^{31}} = 9.468\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} $$

Convert to natural units. Since $1\ \mathrm{kg}=5.610\times10^{26}\ \mathrm{GeV}/c^2$,

$$ \rho = 9.468\times10^{-22}\times5.610\times10^{26} = 5.312\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{GeV/m^3} $$ $$ = \frac{5.312\times10^{5}}{10^{6}}\ \mathrm{GeV/cm^3} = 0.531\ \mathrm{GeV/cm^3} $$

This comes out $30$–$80\ \%$ larger than the $0.3$–$0.4\ \mathrm{GeV/cm^3}$ used by direct-detection experiments. The reason is that what we used here is the simplification of an isothermal sphere with $\rho\propto r^{-2}$. This model assumes that the entire mass of the galaxy is carried by the dark matter halo. In reality, the stars and gas of the disk, and the central bulge, contribute substantially to the rotation speed at the position of the Sun (the blue dashed line and the green curve in Figure 15.5). If we decompose $v^2=v_{\rm disk}^2+v_{\rm gas}^2+v_{\rm halo}^2$, the contribution of the halo alone, $v_{\rm halo}$, is smaller than $220$ km/s, and since $\rho\propto v_{\rm halo}^2$, the local density is smaller as well. In addition, the fact that a real halo is shallower than $r^{-2}$ near the center (the NFW profile, for example) also matters.

(4) The number density is the mass density divided by the mass per particle.

$$ n_\chi = \frac{0.4\ \mathrm{GeV/cm^3}}{100\ \mathrm{GeV}} = 4\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} $$

The flux (the number passing per unit area per unit time) is $n_\chi v$. Since $v=220\ \mathrm{km/s}=2.2\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{cm/s}$,

$$ \Phi = n_\chi v = 4\times10^{-3}\times2.2\times10^{7} = 8.8\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}s^{-1}} $$

The number passing through a palm-sized $100\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ is

$$ 8.8\times10^{4}\times100 = 8.8\times10^{6}\ \text{per second} $$

That is, $880$ ten-thousands (8.8 million) per second. Right now, that many dark matter particles are passing through the palm of your hand as you read this sentence (if the hypothesis is correct).

The one and only reason they are still not detected is the small cross section. The current upper limit is $\sigma_p\lesssim10^{-47}\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ per nucleon, only $10^{-23}$ times the nuclear reaction cross section of a nucleon, $\sim10^{-24}\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ (a barn) (the latest value quoted in Chapter 15 of this book is the LZ value of $2.2\times10^{-48}\ \mathrm{cm^2}$ ($m_\chi=40$ GeV, 2024), and the estimate below would become $4.5$ times more stringent). Let us estimate the mean free path. With the Earth’s mean density $5.5\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$ and mean mass number $\bar A\approx30$, the number density of nuclei is

$$ n_N = \frac{5.5}{30\times1.66\times10^{-24}} = 1.1\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}} $$

In spin-independent scattering, the coherent enhancement $\sigma_N=\sigma_p A^2(\mu_N/\mu_p)^2$ takes effect. With $M_\chi=100$ GeV and $m_N=30\times0.9315=28$ GeV, the reduced mass is $\mu_N=21.8$ GeV and $\mu_p=0.930$ GeV, so $(\mu_N/\mu_p)^2=550$ and $A^2=900$.

$$ \sigma_N = 10^{-47}\times900\times550 = 5.0\times10^{-42}\ \mathrm{cm^2} $$ $$ \lambda = \frac{1}{n_N\sigma_N} = \frac{1}{1.1\times10^{23}\times5.0\times10^{-42}} = 1.8\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{cm} = 1.8\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{m} \approx 1.9\ \text{light-years} $$

This is $1.4\times10^{9}$ times the Earth’s diameter, $1.27\times10^{7}$ m. The Earth is almost perfectly transparent to dark matter, and the probability that a single WIMP scatters while passing through the Earth is only about $10^{-9}$. That is why detectors can only make up for this with a large target mass, a long exposure time, and thorough background rejection.

Verification. We check the dimensions. $v^2r/G$ is $(\mathrm{m^2/s^2})(\mathrm{m})/(\mathrm{m^3kg^{-1}s^{-2}})=\mathrm{kg}$, a mass. $v^2/(4\pi Gr^2)$ is $(\mathrm{m^2/s^2})/(\mathrm{m^3kg^{-1}s^{-2}}\cdot\mathrm{m^2})=\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, a density. Both are correct.

We also check the consistency of (1) and (3). Integrating $\rho=v^2/(4\pi Gr^2)$ over spherical shells,

$$ M(r) = \int_0^r 4\pi r'^2\,\frac{v^2}{4\pi Gr'^2}\,\dd r' = \frac{v^2 r}{G} $$

which indeed returns the formula used in (1). Furthermore, comparing the result of (3) with the cosmic average, the mean density of dark matter in Table 15.5 is $1.3\ \mathrm{GeV/m^3}$, so

$$ \frac{0.531\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{GeV/m^3}}{1.3\ \mathrm{GeV/m^3}} = 4\times10^{5} $$

that is, the dark matter density near the Sun is $40$ ten-thousand times (400,000 times) the cosmic average. The structure called a galaxy has gathered matter by that much, which is reasonable as an order of magnitude.

Meaning. The rotation curve is the oldest and simplest of the four independent lines of evidence for dark matter (rotation curves, gravitational lensing, the Bullet Cluster, and the CMB). All that is needed is Newtonian mechanics and the Doppler effect; neither general relativity nor cosmology is required. The ratio “$8$–$9$” in (2) is of the same order as the cosmic-wide ratio $\Omega_{\rm DM}/\Omega_b=0.264/0.0493=5.4$, and entirely different observations point to the same conclusion.

The contrast between the $8.8\times10^{6}$ per second in (4) and the mean free path of $1.9$ light-years summarizes the difficulty of dark matter searches. The flux is enormous, yet the particles do not interact. So the only ways to raise the sensitivity are to increase the target mass, to lower the threshold, or to reduce the background. And all of these are materials issues. How large a crystal can be grown (Section 15.6.4), how small a heat capacity can be made at how low a temperature ($\Delta E=\sqrt{k_BT^2C}$), and how much $^{238}$U can be removed ($<8\times10^{-14}$ g/g). It is at precisely this one point that the frontier of particle physics meets the frontier of materials science.

Exercise 15.7: Choosing the target nucleus — recoil energy and coherence

Problem (restated)

Use the recoil-energy formula $E_R^{\max}=2\mu^2v^2/m_N$ ($\mu=M_\chi m_N/(M_\chi+m_N)$) of Chapter 15 of this book. Let $v=220$ km/s ($v^2=5.386\times10^{-7}c^2$) and the nuclear mass $m_N=A\times0.9315$ GeV.

(1) Regarding this formula as a function of $m_N$, find the $m_N$ that gives the maximum. State the result in words.

(2) For $M_\chi=5$ GeV, find $E_R^{\max}$ in keV for Si ($A=28.1$), Ge ($A=72.6$), and Xe ($A=131.3$).

(3) From the result of (1), find the optimal target mass number $A$ for $M_\chi=5$ GeV. Which elements qualify?

(4) In spin-independent scattering, $\sigma_N\propto A^2\mu_N^2$. Explain, using (2), (3), and Table 15.8, why Si and superfluid $^4$He are used in searches for $M_\chi\lesssim10$ GeV even though heavy nuclei are advantageous in cross section.

Solution

Strategy. Part (1) requires only a single-variable derivative. Because the reduced mass $\mu$ contains $m_N$, the trick is to first expand $\mu$ and rewrite the expression in terms of $m_N$ alone, and then differentiate. Parts (2) and (3) are substitutions. Part (4) is an argument that sets two competing requirements, kinematics ($E_R$) and the cross section ($A^2$), against a third condition, the detector threshold.

(1) Substitute $\mu=M_\chi m_N/(M_\chi+m_N)$ and write the expression as a function of $m_N$.

$$ E_R^{\max}(m_N) = \frac{2\mu^2v^2}{m_N} = \frac{2v^2}{m_N}\cdot\frac{M_\chi^2m_N^2}{(M_\chi+m_N)^2} = 2M_\chi^2v^2\,\frac{m_N}{(M_\chi+m_N)^2} $$

Differentiate with respect to $m_N$. By the quotient rule,

$$ \frac{\dd}{\dd m_N}\frac{m_N}{(M_\chi+m_N)^2} = \frac{(M_\chi+m_N)^2 - m_N\cdot2(M_\chi+m_N)}{(M_\chi+m_N)^4} = \frac{(M_\chi+m_N)-2m_N}{(M_\chi+m_N)^3} = \frac{M_\chi-m_N}{(M_\chi+m_N)^3} $$

Therefore

$$ \frac{\dd E_R^{\max}}{\dd m_N} = 2M_\chi^2v^2\,\frac{M_\chi-m_N}{(M_\chi+m_N)^3} $$

Since the denominator is positive, the sign of the derivative is determined by the sign of $M_\chi-m_N$. It is positive for $m_N<M_\chi$ and negative for $m_N>M_\chi$. Hence

$$ m_N = M_\chi \quad\text{maximal at} $$

The value there is

$$ E_R^{\max}\big|_{m_N=M_\chi} = 2M_\chi^2v^2\,\frac{M_\chi}{(2M_\chi)^2} = \frac{M_\chi v^2}{2} $$

In words, the energy transfer is maximal when the WIMP mass equals the target-nucleus mass. This is a general property of elastic scattering, the same as the fact that in billiards a head-on hit on a ball of equal mass passes on the momentum completely (and it is for exactly the same reason that light elements such as water and graphite are used as neutron moderators). The two limits stated in Step 3 of Chapter 15 of this book balance at $m_N=M_\chi$: for $M_\chi\gg m_N$, $E_R^{\max}\to2m_Nv^2$ (a light target flies off briskly with speed $2v$, but because its mass is small it cannot carry much energy), and for $M_\chi\ll m_N$, $E_R^{\max}\to2M_\chi^2v^2/m_N$ (a light projectile cannot move a heavy target).

(2) Take $M_\chi=5$ GeV and $v^2=5.386\times10^{-7}$ (in units with $c=1$). We construct the nuclear mass and the reduced mass in turn.

Si ($A=28.1$):

$$ m_N = 28.1\times0.9315 = 26.175\ \mathrm{GeV}, \qquad \mu = \frac{5\times26.175}{5+26.175} = \frac{130.88}{31.175} = 4.1981\ \mathrm{GeV} $$ $$ E_R^{\max} = \frac{2\times(4.1981)^2\times5.386\times10^{-7}}{26.175} = \frac{2\times17.624\times5.386\times10^{-7}}{26.175} = \frac{1.8985\times10^{-5}}{26.175} $$ $$ = 7.253\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 0.725\ \mathrm{keV} $$

Ge ($A=72.6$):

$$ m_N = 72.6\times0.9315 = 67.627\ \mathrm{GeV}, \qquad \mu = \frac{5\times67.627}{72.627} = 4.6558\ \mathrm{GeV} $$ $$ E_R^{\max} = \frac{2\times21.676\times5.386\times10^{-7}}{67.627} = 3.453\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 0.345\ \mathrm{keV} $$

Xe ($A=131.3$):

$$ m_N = 131.3\times0.9315 = 122.31\ \mathrm{GeV}, \qquad \mu = \frac{5\times122.31}{127.31} = 4.8036\ \mathrm{GeV} $$ $$ E_R^{\max} = \frac{2\times23.075\times5.386\times10^{-7}}{122.31} = 2.032\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 0.203\ \mathrm{keV} $$

Si gives a recoil energy $0.725/0.203=3.6$ times that of Xe. Note that $\mu$ itself hardly changes: $4.20$, $4.66$, $4.80$ (since the nuclei are much heavier than $M_\chi=5$ GeV, it saturates at $\mu\to M_\chi=5$ GeV). What makes the difference is $m_N$ in the denominator.

(3) By (1), the optimal condition is $m_N=M_\chi=5$ GeV, so

$$ A_{\rm opt} = \frac{5\ \mathrm{GeV}}{0.9315\ \mathrm{GeV}} = 5.4 $$

The nuclei that match are helium ($A=4$) and lithium ($A=7$). The recoil energy in that case is

$$ E_R^{\max} = \frac{M_\chi v^2}{2} = \frac{5\times5.386\times10^{-7}}{2} = 1.347\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 1.35\ \mathrm{keV} $$

Comparing the results of (2) with this maximum, Si extracts only $0.725/1.347=54\ \%$, Ge $26\ \%$, and Xe $15\ \%$. It is indeed for this reason that superfluid $^4$He in HeRALD (at the proposal stage), $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ sapphire and $\mathrm{CaWO_4}$ containing light O (CRESST-III), and Si in SuperCDMS, SENSEI, and DAMIC-M are used in searches for light dark matter (CROSS, which uses $\mathrm{Li_2MoO_4}$ bolometers, is a search for the $0\nu\beta\beta$ decay of $^{100}$Mo and not a dark-matter search).

(4) The two requirements collide head-on. The cross section is

$$ \sigma_N = \sigma_p\,A^2\,\frac{\mu_N^2}{\mu_p^2}\,F^2(q) $$

where $A^2$ is $17240$ for Xe against $789$ for Si, a factor of $21.8$. Also $\mu_N^2$ is larger for Xe by a factor $(4.804/4.198)^2=1.31$. Together, Xe has a cross section $28.6$ times that of Si. Naively, Xe wins by a landslide.

However, the detector has a threshold. The nuclear-recoil threshold of a liquid-Xe dual-phase TPC is $\sim1\ \mathrm{keV_{nr}}$, and the maximum recoil energy $0.203$ keV for $M_\chi=5$ GeV found in (2) lies far below it. Moreover, $0.203$ keV is the “maximum”: the actual recoil-energy distribution spreads almost uniformly from $0$ to $E_R^{\max}$, and only the tail of the velocity distribution can exceed the threshold. Events below the threshold are not counted at all, no matter how large the cross section is. Multiply a cross section $28.6$ times larger by $0$ and you still get $0$.

A light target is favored twice over. First, the same WIMP gives a larger recoil (Si gives $3.6$ times that of Xe). Second, the readout technologies available for light targets have lower thresholds. As Table 15.8 and Figure 15.6 of Chapter 15 of this book show, the $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$/$\mathrm{CaWO_4}$ bolometers of CRESST-III have a threshold of $30$ eV, and Si Skipper CCDs (SENSEI, DAMIC-M) can count ionization with the resolution of a single electron-hole pair (in Si, one pair requires $3.7$ eV on average, and the threshold is the band gap of $1.1$–$1.2$ eV). Even if we lose a factor of $20$ in $A^2$, lowering the threshold from $1$ keV to $30$ eV, or to the eV level, returns a gain in sensitivity of orders of magnitude.

To summarize, the answer changes with the mass range. At $M_\chi\sim100$ GeV, Xe is best (in Table 15.8, too, $E_R^{\max}=26.7$ keV is sufficiently large compared with the threshold, and the gain in $A^2$ counts in full). At $M_\chi\lesssim10$ GeV, kinematics dominates, and Si, $^4$He, and oxides containing O win. CRESST-III uses $\mathrm{CaWO_4}$ because the heavy W (high $A^2$) and the light O (kinematic sensitivity to light WIMPs) can coexist in a single crystal. The choice of target material is, in itself, the choice of the dark-matter mass range to be searched.

Verification. Check the dimensions. $\mu^2v^2/m_N$ is $\mathrm{GeV^2}\cdot(\text{dimensionless})/\mathrm{GeV}=\mathrm{GeV}$, an energy. This is correct (since $v$ is measured in units with $c=1$, $v^2$ is dimensionless).

We also check the limit. For $M_\chi\ll m_N$, $\mu\to M_\chi$ and $E_R^{\max}\to2M_\chi^2v^2/m_N$. Applied to Xe, this gives

$$ \frac{2\times25\times5.386\times10^{-7}}{122.31} = 2.202\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 0.220\ \mathrm{keV} $$

This agrees with the exact $0.203$ keV to within $8\ \%$ (since $M_\chi/m_N=0.041$, a deviation of this size is reasonable). We can also confirm that Table 15.8 is reproduced by the same formula: Si at $M_\chi=1$ GeV gives $38.2$ eV and Xe at $M_\chi=100$ GeV gives $26.7$ keV, in agreement with the values in the table.

Meaning. The conclusion of this exercise is that the design of a particle-physics experiment becomes, as it stands, a problem of materials selection. Once the mass of the particle to be searched for is fixed, the optimal mass number of the target nucleus is fixed ($A\approx M_\chi/0.93$ GeV). But whether a large, high-purity, low-radioactivity crystal or liquid can be made from that element is an entirely different problem. Xe has effective self-shielding and allows two-channel discrimination, but is rare and expensive; Ge can be grown as ultra-high-purity single crystals, but the cosmogenic nuclide $^{68}$Ge becomes a problem; $\mathrm{CaWO_4}$ covers a wide range kinematically, but radiopurity in crystal growth is difficult; and so on.

From the standpoint of someone who works with phonons, “how far the threshold can be lowered” in (4) is fundamentally a problem of specific heat and the Debye temperature. Combining $\Delta E=\sqrt{k_BT^2C}$ of Chapter 15 of this book with the Debye model $C\propto(T/\Theta_D)^3$ gives $\Delta E\propto T^{5/2}\Theta_D^{-3/2}$, so a hard material with a high Debye temperature is favored. This is half of the reason why $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ ($\Theta_D\approx1040$ K) is used in CRESST. The requirement of a hard oxide built from light elements comes out of kinematics and thermodynamics at the same time.

Exercise 15.8: The cosmological constant problem — deriving the 120 orders of magnitude yourself

Problem (restated)

Let $H_0=67.4\ \mathrm{km\,s^{-1}Mpc^{-1}}$, $1\ \mathrm{Mpc}=3.086\times10^{22}$ m, $G=6.674\times10^{-11}$, $\Omega_\Lambda=0.685$, $\hbar c=1.973\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{GeV\,m}$, and $1\ \mathrm{GeV}=1.602\times10^{-10}$ J.

(1) Find $\rho_c=3H_0^2/8\pi G$ in units of $\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, and then find $\rho_\Lambda$.

(2) Express $\rho_\Lambda c^2$ in $\mathrm{J/m^3}$, and further convert it to units of $\mathrm{GeV^4}$ ($1\ \mathrm{GeV^4}=2.086\times10^{37}\ \mathrm{J/m^3}$).

(3) Find $\rho_\Lambda^{1/4}$ in meV. Compare it with $k_BT_0$ corresponding to the temperature of the CMB ($T_0=2.7255$ K).

(4) For the naive field-theory prediction $\rho_{\rm vac}\sim\Lambda^4$, find $\rho_{\rm vac}/\rho_\Lambda$ for $\Lambda=M_{\rm Pl}=1.22\times10^{19}$ GeV and for $\Lambda=\Lambda_{\rm QCD}=0.2$ GeV. Also restate $\rho_\Lambda c^2$ as “the rest energy of how many protons per cubic meter.”

Solution

Strategy. All we have to do is unit conversion. Yet the whole point of this problem lies in the passage from SI ($\mathrm{kg/m^3}$) to natural units ($\mathrm{GeV^4}$). The energy density becomes $[\mathrm{GeV^4}]$ in natural units because the energy $[\mathrm{GeV}]$ is divided by a volume $[\mathrm{GeV^{-3}}]$ (since a length is $\hbar c/E$). Finally, we take the fourth root and reinterpret $\rho_\Lambda$ as an “energy scale.”

(1) First convert $H_0$ to SI. Divide $67.4\ \mathrm{km/s}=6.74\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m/s}$ by $1\ \mathrm{Mpc}=3.086\times10^{22}$ m.

$$ H_0 = \frac{6.74\times10^{4}\ \mathrm{m/s}}{3.086\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{m}} = 2.184\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

(Its inverse is $4.58\times10^{17}$ s $=1.45\times10^{10}$ years, which is the order of magnitude of the age of the universe.) The critical density is

$$ \rho_c = \frac{3H_0^2}{8\pi G} = \frac{3\times(2.184\times10^{-18})^2}{8\pi\times6.674\times10^{-11}} = \frac{3\times4.770\times10^{-36}}{1.6774\times10^{-9}} $$ $$ = \frac{1.4310\times10^{-35}}{1.6774\times10^{-9}} = 8.53\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} $$

This is the famous number of $5$ hydrogen atoms per $\mathrm{m^3}$ ($8.53\times10^{-27}/1.673\times10^{-27}=5.10$ atoms). It differs only in the last digit from the $\rho_c=8.54\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3}$ given in Exercise 15.5, but this is a difference of rounding ($1.4310/1.6774=0.8531$), and the two numbers agree to within $0.1\ \%$. The part due to dark energy is

$$ \rho_\Lambda = \Omega_\Lambda\,\rho_c = 0.685\times8.53\times10^{-27} = 5.84\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg/m^3} $$

(2) From $c=2.998\times10^{8}$ m/s, $c^2=8.988\times10^{16}\ \mathrm{m^2/s^2}$.

$$ \rho_\Lambda c^2 = 5.84\times10^{-27}\times8.988\times10^{16} = 5.25\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J/m^3} $$

Divide by the given conversion $1\ \mathrm{GeV^4}=2.086\times10^{37}\ \mathrm{J/m^3}$.

$$ \rho_\Lambda = \frac{5.25\times10^{-10}}{2.086\times10^{37}} = 2.52\times10^{-47}\ \mathrm{GeV^4} $$

Let us also check the conversion factor itself. Packing an energy of $1$ GeV into a cube whose side is the Compton wavelength corresponding to 1 GeV gives

$$ \left(\frac{\hbar c}{1\ \mathrm{GeV}}\right)^3 = (1.973\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{m})^3 = 7.68\times10^{-48}\ \mathrm{m^3} $$ $$ 1\ \mathrm{GeV^4} = \frac{1.602\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J}}{7.68\times10^{-48}\ \mathrm{m^3}} = 2.086\times10^{37}\ \mathrm{J/m^3} $$

It indeed reproduces the given value.

(3) The fourth root is found by taking the square root twice. The trick for hand calculation is to shift the digits of the mantissa so that the exponent of $10$ is always even. For the first root, shift $-47$ to $-48$.

$$ \left(2.52\times10^{-47}\right)^{1/2} = \left(25.2\times10^{-48}\right)^{1/2} = \sqrt{25.2}\times10^{-24} = 5.020\times10^{-24} $$

For the second root, $-24$ can be halved as it is, but it is easier to preserve significant figures by shifting to $-26$ and using $\sqrt{502.0}=22.41$ than by using $\sqrt{5.020}=2.240$.

$$ \left(5.020\times10^{-24}\right)^{1/2} = \left(502.0\times10^{-26}\right)^{1/2} = \sqrt{502.0}\times10^{-13} = 22.41\times10^{-13} $$

Therefore

$$ \rho_\Lambda^{1/4} = 2.241\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{GeV} = 2.24\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV} = 2.24\ \mathrm{meV} $$

This is a millielectronvolt. The energy corresponding to the CMB temperature is

$$ k_BT_0 = 8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/K}\times2.7255\ \mathrm{K} = 2.349\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{eV} = 0.235\ \mathrm{meV} $$

so

$$ \frac{\rho_\Lambda^{1/4}}{k_BT_0} = \frac{2.24}{0.235} = 9.5 $$

That is, about a factor of $10$. Whether the closeness of the two has a deep meaning is not known (the mainstream view is that it is a coincidence). What matters is that $2.24$ meV is unlike any other scale in particle physics. It is $10^{14}$ times smaller than the electroweak scale of $246$ GeV, $10^{11}$ times smaller than the QCD scale of $0.2$ GeV, and $2\times10^{8}$ times smaller than the electron mass; even the neutrino mass ($\sim50$ meV) is 20 times larger than this. Converting to a wavelength, $hc/E=1240\ \mathrm{eV\,nm}/2.24\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}=5.5\times10^{5}$ nm $=0.55$ mm, which corresponds to a photon in the far-infrared and terahertz region.

(4) Taking the cutoff at the Planck mass gives

$$ M_{\rm Pl}^4 = (1.22\times10^{19})^4 = 2.215\times10^{76}\ \mathrm{GeV^4} $$ $$ \frac{\rho_{\rm vac}}{\rho_\Lambda} = \frac{2.215\times10^{76}}{2.52\times10^{-47}} = 8.8\times10^{122} $$

That is, an overestimate by $123$ orders of magnitude (even including the factor $1/16\pi^2$ lowers this by only $10^{2.2}$, giving $121$ orders of magnitude). Lowering the cutoff to the QCD scale gives

$$ \Lambda_{\rm QCD}^4 = (0.2)^4 = 1.6\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GeV^4} $$ $$ \frac{\rho_{\rm vac}}{\rho_\Lambda} = \frac{1.6\times10^{-3}}{2.52\times10^{-47}} = 6.35\times10^{43} $$

This is $44$ orders of magnitude, in agreement with the $6.3\times10^{43}$ of Table 15.6. The QCD scale is “the lowest scale known to exist beyond doubt” (the chiral condensate $\braket{\bar qq}\ne0$ and the gluon condensate are both real), so this is close to an inescapable lower bound. As Table 15.6 shows, wherever we cut off, we are not saved.

Now the conversion to protons. Converting $\rho_\Lambda c^2=5.25\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J/m^3}$ to GeV gives

$$ \frac{5.25\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J/m^3}}{1.602\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{J/GeV}} = 3.28\ \mathrm{GeV/m^3} $$

Dividing by the proton rest energy $m_pc^2=0.938$ GeV gives

$$ \frac{3.28}{0.938} = 3.5\ \text{protons} $$

That is, $3.5$ protons’ worth per $1\ \mathrm{m^3}$. This is the density of the component that accounts for $68.5\ \%$ of the energy of the universe and accelerates its expansion: only this much.

Verification. Compare with Table 15.5. The dark-energy entry of the table is $3.3\ \mathrm{GeV/m^3}$, which agrees with the $3.28\ \mathrm{GeV/m^3}$ found above. This is an independent check.

Check the dimensions too. $3H_0^2/8\pi G$ is $\mathrm{s^{-2}}/(\mathrm{m^3kg^{-1}s^{-2}})=\mathrm{kg/m^3}$, a density. This is correct. The order of magnitude of the fourth root can also be checked by a rough estimate. Dividing the exponent $-47$ of $\rho_\Lambda=2.52\times10^{-47}\ \mathrm{GeV^4}$ by 4 gives $-11.75$, so $\rho_\Lambda^{1/4}\sim10^{-11.75}=1.8\times10^{-12}$ GeV, which agrees in order of magnitude with the $2.24\times10^{-12}$ GeV obtained.

One more check: the relation between the two ratios in (4) is also consistent. $M_{\rm Pl}/\Lambda_{\rm QCD}=1.22\times10^{19}/0.2=6.1\times10^{19}$, and its fourth power is $1.385\times10^{79}$. Multiplying this by $6.35\times10^{43}$ gives $8.8\times10^{122}$, in agreement with the Planck case.

Meaning. The number $10^{122}$ is the worst disagreement between theory and experiment known in physics. Even the $10^{32}$ of the hierarchy problem looks cute by comparison. Moreover, unlike the hierarchy problem, it cannot be solved by a known symmetry such as supersymmetry. If supersymmetry were exact, the zero-point energies of bosons and fermions would cancel exactly to zero, but supersymmetry is broken, and even if we cut off at the breaking scale ($>1$ TeV), a factor $(1\ \mathrm{TeV})^4/\rho_\Lambda=4\times10^{58}$ remains.

The asymmetry pointed out in Chapter 15 of this book is decisive here. In condensed matter physics, zero-point energy is observed as a real effect. The Casimir force ($13\ \mathrm{N/m^2}$ at $d=100$ nm, which actually matters in the design of MEMS), the van der Waals force, and the zero-point energy of lattice vibrations $\sum_{\qq s}\hbar\omega_{\qq s}/2$ (a quantity handled routinely in first-principles phonon calculations) are all real. What they have in common, however, is that what is measured is always a “difference.” It is the change when a plate is moved, the change when an isotope is substituted, the change when the volume is varied (the Grüneisen parameter). The absolute value never appears in an observable.

For those who do phonon calculations, this is everyday business. The absolute value of the zero-point vibrational energy is absorbed into the origin of the ground-state energy, and only the volume dependence $\partial(\sum\hbar\omega/2)/\partial V$ (which enters the discussion of negative thermal expansion) and isotope differences are meaningful. The very fact that we can have the convenient escape route “the origin of energy is arbitrary” is due to nothing other than the fact that we can ignore gravity. Only gravity couples to the absolute value of energy. The moment gravity is included, the constant term we usually discard becomes an observable. The essence of the cosmological constant problem is exhausted by this one line.

E.16 Solutions for Chapter 16: Where Particle Physics Meets Materials Science

Exercise 16.1: Energy partition in the D$^3$He reaction

Problem (restated)

Consider $\mathrm{D}+{}^{3}\mathrm{He}\to{}^{4}\mathrm{He}+p$. The nuclear masses are $m_d=1875.6127$, $m_{{}^3\mathrm{He}}=2808.3915$, $m_\alpha=3727.3794$, and $m_p=938.2721\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(1) Find the $Q$ value.

(2) Using the exact relativistic solution of the same form as the exact relativistic solution in Chapter 16 of this book (the expression of the form $T_n = Q(Q+2m_\alpha)/2W$), find the kinetic energies of the $p$ and the $\alpha$.

(3) Compare them with the nonrelativistic approximation in which the mass numbers are taken in the ratio $4:1$, and find the relative error.

(4) This reaction is called “aneutronic,” yet neutrons do appear from an actual D$^3$He plasma. Where do they come from? Explain, referring to Table 16.2.

Solution

Strategy. We simply carry over, word for word, the procedure applied to the DT reaction in Section 16.1.1 of this book to D$^3$He. The only tool is the four-momentum conservation of Chapter 4; no nuclear structure is needed at all. We regard the initial state as a two-particle system at rest and recast the problem as the two-body decay of a “particle” whose invariant mass is $W$.

(1) The $Q$ value is the difference between the rest masses of the initial and final states. The sum for the initial state is

$$ M_i = m_d + m_{{}^3\mathrm{He}} = 1875.6127 + 2808.3915 = 4684.0042\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

and the sum for the final state is

$$ M_f = m_\alpha + m_p = 3727.3794 + 938.2721 = 4665.6515\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

Therefore

$$ Q = M_i - M_f = 4684.0042 - 4665.6515 = 18.3527\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

This is slightly larger than the DT value $Q=17.5888\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Per nucleon it is $18.3527/5 = 3.67\ \mathrm{MeV}$, which also exceeds the DT value of $3.52\ \mathrm{MeV}$. In terms of energy alone, D$^3$He is actually the more “appetizing” fuel. As we will see in the next exercise, Exercise 16.2, the problem is whether one can get there at all.

(2) Starting from D and ${}^3$He at rest, the invariant mass of the system is $W=\sqrt{s}=M_i = 4684.0042\ \mathrm{MeV}$. The final state consists of the two bodies $\alpha$ and $p$, and in the center-of-mass frame $\bm{p}_\alpha=-\bm{p}_p$. We may use the derivation of Section 16.1.1 of this book as it stands. There, for the neutron side, we obtained

$$ T_n = \frac{Q\,(Q+2m_\alpha)}{2W} $$

Looking back at how this expression was built, the structure was this: “when $T_X = E_X - m_X$ is computed, only the mass of the partner particle $Y$ remains, paired with $Q$, and the mass of $X$ itself disappears completely.” That is, the mass of the partner appears in the kinetic energy of the particle of interest. Hence in the present case, the partner of the $\alpha$ is the $p$ and the partner of the $p$ is the $\alpha$, so

$$ T_p = \frac{Q\,(Q+2m_\alpha)}{2W}, \qquad T_\alpha = \frac{Q\,(Q+2m_p)}{2W} $$

Now we insert the numbers. First, the denominator is $2W = 9368.0084\ \mathrm{MeV}$. For the proton,

$$ T_p = \frac{18.3527\times(18.3527 + 2\times3727.3794)}{9368.0084} = \frac{18.3527\times7473.1115}{9368.0084} = \frac{1.371518\times10^{5}}{9368.0084} = 14.6404\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

For the $\alpha$ particle,

$$ T_\alpha = \frac{18.3527\times(18.3527 + 2\times938.2721)}{9368.0084} = \frac{18.3527\times1894.8969}{9368.0084} = \frac{3.477647\times10^{4}}{9368.0084} = 3.7123\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

As a check, we also derive it from the original two-body decay formula. Since $W^2 = 2.193990\times10^{7}$, $m_p^2 = 8.80355\times10^{5}$, and $m_\alpha^2=1.389336\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{MeV^2}$,

$$ E_p = \frac{W^2 + m_p^2 - m_\alpha^2}{2W} = \frac{2.193990\times10^{7} + 0.0880355\times10^{7} - 1.389336\times10^{7}}{9368.0084} = 952.9125\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ $$ T_p = E_p - m_p = 952.9125 - 938.2721 = 14.6404\ \mathrm{MeV}\quad\checkmark $$

The two agree exactly. Note also that the common center-of-mass momentum is $p^*=\sqrt{E_p^2-m_p^2}=166.40\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(3) In the nonrelativistic approximation the momenta are equal and opposite ($p_\alpha=p_p$) and $T=p^2/2m$, so $T_\alpha/T_p = m_p/m_\alpha$. Substituting the mass-number ratio $1:4$ for this gives $T_p:T_\alpha = 4:1$, that is,

$$ T_p^{\rm approx} = \tfrac45 Q = \tfrac45\times18.3527 = 14.6822\ \mathrm{MeV}, \qquad T_\alpha^{\rm approx} = \tfrac15 Q = 3.6705\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The relative errors are

$$ \frac{T_p^{\rm approx}-T_p}{T_p} = \frac{14.6822-14.6404}{14.6404} = +2.85\times10^{-3} = +0.28\% $$ $$ \frac{T_\alpha^{\rm approx}-T_\alpha}{T_\alpha} = \frac{3.6705-3.7123}{3.7123} = -1.12\times10^{-2} = -1.12\% $$

On the proton side the error is $0.3\%$, but on the $\alpha$ side it reaches $1.1\%$. This is not surprising. The absolute deviation in energy is the same $0.042\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for both (the sum of the partition is fixed at $Q$, so what one gains the other loses), and dividing it by the smaller one, $T_\alpha=3.71\ \mathrm{MeV}$, makes the relative error about four times larger. To separate the contributions to the error, we also work out the nonrelativistic approximation using the actual nuclear masses instead of the mass numbers:

$$ T_p = Q\,\frac{m_\alpha}{m_\alpha+m_p} = 18.3527\times0.798897 = 14.6619\ \mathrm{MeV}, \qquad T_\alpha = 3.6908\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

and the errors become $+0.15\%$ and $-0.58\%$, respectively. That is, about half of the total error comes from “substituting mass numbers” and the other half from “treating the problem nonrelativistically.” This is exactly the same structure as in the DT case.

(4) Looking at Table 16.2, the “neutron” column in the D$^3$He row reads “none at first order.” The phrase “at first order” is the crux. A D$^3$He plasma by definition always contains deuterium, so D–D collisions inevitably occur. From the two DD rows of Table 16.2,

$$ \mathrm{D}+\mathrm{D}\to{}^{3}\mathrm{He}+n\quad(Q=3.269\ \mathrm{MeV},\ n\ \text{is}\ 2.45\ \mathrm{MeV}) $$ $$ \mathrm{D}+\mathrm{D}\to\mathrm{T}+p\quad(Q=4.033\ \mathrm{MeV}) $$

these two branches occur at roughly $50{:}50$. The former directly emits a $2.45\ \mathrm{MeV}$ neutron. Furthermore, if the T produced by the latter reacts with D in the fuel, then

$$ \mathrm{D}+\mathrm{T}\to{}^{4}\mathrm{He}+n\quad(n\ \text{is}\ 14.03\ \mathrm{MeV}) $$

and even the $14\ \mathrm{MeV}$ neutrons, the most troublesome from the standpoint of irradiation damage to the first wall, are emitted. Moreover, since the DT reactivity is far larger than any other, as Table 16.2 shows, even a small amount of T makes a non-negligible contribution to the neutrons.

Let us estimate the amounts. Let $n_D=n_{{}^3\mathrm{He}}=n/2$. Avoiding double counting of identical particles, the DD reaction rate is $\frac12 n_D^2\braket{\sigma v}_{DD}$, and the D$^3$He reaction rate is $n_Dn_{{}^3\mathrm{He}}\braket{\sigma v}_{D^3\mathrm{He}}$. Using the values in Table 16.2, the ratio of the neutron-emitting DD branch to the D$^3$He reaction rate is

$$ \frac{\frac12\cdot\frac12\braket{\sigma v}_{DD}}{\braket{\sigma v}_{D^3\mathrm{He}}} = \begin{cases} \dfrac{0.25\times1.2\times10^{-24}}{2.6\times10^{-25}} = 1.15 & (T=10\ \mathrm{keV})\\[2mm] \dfrac{0.25\times5.2\times10^{-24}}{7.0\times10^{-24}} = 0.19 & (T=20\ \mathrm{keV}) \end{cases} $$

We denote the ratio obtained here by $r$ ($r=1.15$ at $T=10\ \mathrm{keV}$ and $r=0.19$ at $T=20\ \mathrm{keV}$). Since the branching ratio is $50{:}50$, the reaction rate of the branch that produces T is also $r$, and taking one D$^3$He reaction as the reference, the power output and the neutron energy are counted as

$$ P_{\rm tot} = 18.35 + r\,(3.269+4.033)\ \mathrm{MeV}, \qquad P_n = r\times2.45\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

Hence the fraction of the total power carried by neutrons is

$$ \frac{P_n}{P_{\rm tot}} = \begin{cases} \dfrac{1.15\times2.45}{18.35+1.15\times7.302} = \dfrac{2.818}{26.75} = 0.105 & (T=10\ \mathrm{keV})\\[2mm] \dfrac{0.19\times2.45}{18.35+0.19\times7.302} = \dfrac{0.466}{19.74} = 0.024 & (T=20\ \mathrm{keV}) \end{cases} $$

That is, even at $T=20\ \mathrm{keV}$ about $2\%$, and at $T=10\ \mathrm{keV}$ about $10\%$, leaves as neutrons. The higher the operating temperature, the more DD is disfavored relatively (the rise of $\braket{\sigma v}_{D^3\mathrm{He}}$ is steeper than that of DD), and this is one of the reasons why D$^3$He reactors aim at high temperatures. Note that the DT reactions caused by the by-product T are not counted here; their contribution depends on whether the T can be exhausted before it burns up, and in the worst case $14\ \mathrm{MeV}$ neutrons are added. “Aneutronic” is not an absolute property; it is merely a relative expression meaning that the neutron fraction is smaller by orders of magnitude than the $80\%$ of DT.

Verification. We check whether energy conservation closes. $T_p + T_\alpha = 14.6404+3.7123 = 18.3527\ \mathrm{MeV} = Q$ ✓. Momentum conservation can be confirmed as follows: from the $\alpha$ side we independently obtain $E_\alpha=(W^2+m_\alpha^2-m_p^2)/2W = 3731.0917\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $p^*=\sqrt{E_\alpha^2-m_\alpha^2}=166.40\ \mathrm{MeV}$, which agrees with the $166.40\ \mathrm{MeV}$ from the proton side ✓. The dimensions are also correct: $Q(Q+2m_\alpha)/2W$ is [energy$^2$]/[energy] = [energy] ✓. Furthermore, taking the limit $Q\ll m$ gives $T_p\to Qm_\alpha/(m_\alpha+m_p)$, which reduces to the nonrelativistic formula with actual masses obtained in (3) ✓.

Meaning. The reason this partition is a matter for materials science is that the products of D$^3$He are both charged particles. The $p$ ($+e$) and the $\alpha$ ($+2e$) are both confined by the magnetic field and remain in the plasma, so they do not strike the wall. In principle even direct energy conversion (converting the kinetic energy of charged particles directly into electric power with an electrostatic field) is possible, and since no thermal cycle is involved the efficiency is also higher. This is exactly the opposite of DT, where $80\%$ is driven into the wall as electrically neutral neutrons. That is why D$^3$He looks like a dream fuel to materials people. However, as we saw in (4), parasitic DD reactions produce neutrons, and as we will see in Exercise 16.2, ignition itself is harder by orders of magnitude. One and the same tool, four-momentum conservation, teaches us on the one hand “why nuclear fusion is a materials problem” and on the other “why that loophole is closed.”

Exercise 16.2: Comparing fuels with the Gamow factor

Problem (restated)

Use the Gamow energy formula $E_G = 2m_rc^2(\pi\alpha Z_1Z_2)^2$ of Chapter 16 of this book, and $P=\exp(-\sqrt{E_G/E})$.

(1) Find $E_G$ for the DD reaction ($Z_1Z_2=1$, $m_r = m_d/2 = 937.81\ \mathrm{MeV}$).

(2) Find $E_G$ for the D$^3$He reaction ($Z_1Z_2=2$, $m_r = 1124.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$), and state how many times larger it is than the $1.182\ \mathrm{MeV}$ of DT.

(3) Compute the transmission probability $P$ at $E = 100\ \mathrm{keV}$ for DT and for D$^3$He, and find their ratio.

(4) Compare the result of (3) with the ratio of $\braket{\sigma v}$ in Table 16.2, and if there is a difference, state its cause.

Solution

Strategy. $E_G$ is a purely kinematic (more precisely, Coulombic) quantity determined only by the reduced mass and the product of the charges. On the other hand, $\braket{\sigma v}$ involves two additional ingredients: nuclear structure (the $S$ factor) and the Maxwell average. The point of this problem is to separate these two layers deliberately. As a common constant we use $\pi\alpha = \pi/137.036 = 0.02292531$.

(1) In the DD reaction both particles are deuterons, so $Z_1Z_2 = 1\times1 = 1$, and the reduced mass is $m_r = m_dm_d/(m_d+m_d)=m_d/2 = 1875.6127/2 = 937.806\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Therefore

$$ E_G^{\rm DD} = 2\times937.806\ \mathrm{MeV}\times(0.02292531\times1)^2 = 1875.61\times5.25570\times10^{-4} $$ $$ = 0.98577\ \mathrm{MeV} \simeq 0.986\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

This is smaller than the DT value of $1.182\ \mathrm{MeV}$. The charges are the same ($Z_1Z_2=1$), and the difference is due only to the reduced mass becoming lighter, $1124.65\to937.81\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Indeed, $0.98577/1.18216 = 0.8339 = 937.81/1124.65$ ✓. This is the effect of the de Broglie wavelength: the lighter the fuel, the more easily it tunnels through the barrier.

(2) In D$^3$He, $Z_1=1$ (D) and $Z_2=2$ ($^3$He), so $Z_1Z_2=2$, and the reduced mass is $m_r = 1875.6127\times2808.3915/4684.0042 = 1124.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$ (by coincidence nearly the same as the DT value of $1124.65\ \mathrm{MeV}$, because the combination is the same: D and a partner of mass number 3).

$$ E_G^{\mathrm{D}^3\mathrm{He}} = 2\times1124.6\times(0.02292531\times2)^2 = 2249.2\times(0.04585062)^2 = 2249.2\times2.10228\times10^{-3} $$ $$ = 4.7284\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The ratio to DT is

$$ \frac{E_G^{\mathrm{D}^3\mathrm{He}}}{E_G^{\rm DT}} = \frac{4.7284}{1.18216} = 4.000 $$

It is exactly $4$ times as large. The reason is clear from the structure of the formula: in $E_G\propto m_r(Z_1Z_2)^2$ the value of $m_r$ is almost equal, and $(Z_1Z_2)^2$ goes from $1\to4$, nothing more.

(3) We substitute $E=100\ \mathrm{keV}=0.100\ \mathrm{MeV}$. For DT,

$$ 2\pi\eta = \sqrt{\frac{E_G}{E}} = \sqrt{\frac{1.18216}{0.100}} = \sqrt{11.8216} = 3.4383 $$ $$ P_{\rm DT} = \ee^{-3.4383} = 3.212\times10^{-2} $$

For D$^3$He,

$$ 2\pi\eta = \sqrt{\frac{4.7284}{0.100}} = \sqrt{47.284} = 6.8764 $$ $$ P_{\mathrm{D}^3\mathrm{He}} = \ee^{-6.8764} = 1.032\times10^{-3} $$

The ratio is

$$ \frac{P_{\rm DT}}{P_{\mathrm{D}^3\mathrm{He}}} = \ee^{-3.4383+6.8764} = \ee^{3.4381} = 31.1 $$

Just because $E_G$ is $4$ times larger (the quantity in the exponent is only $\sqrt{4}=2$ times larger), the transmission probability differs by a factor of $31$. This is an example that shows well how fearsome the exponential function is. For reference, for DD we have $2\pi\eta=\sqrt{9.8577}=3.1397$ and $P=4.33\times10^{-2}$, so it passes through even more easily than DT.

(4) Looking at $\braket{\sigma v}$ in Table 16.2, at $T=10\ \mathrm{keV}$ DT is $1.1\times10^{-22}$ and D$^3$He is $2.6\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{m^3/s}$, so the ratio is

$$ \frac{1.1\times10^{-22}}{2.6\times10^{-25}} = 423 $$

This differs by more than an order of magnitude from the factor of $31$ obtained in (3). There are two causes.

Cause 1: The Maxwell average is not a comparison at “one common energy.” The reactivity is the integral

$$ \braket{\sigma v} = \sqrt{\frac{8}{\pi m_r}}\;\frac{1}{(k_BT)^{3/2}}\int_0^\infty S(E)\, \ee^{-E/k_BT-\sqrt{E_G/E}}\,\dd E $$

whose integrand has a sharp peak at the Gamow peak of Figure 16.1(b) of this book,

$$ E_0 = \left(\frac{E_G\,(k_BT)^2}{4}\right)^{1/3} $$

At $T=10\ \mathrm{keV}$, $E_0 = 30.9\ \mathrm{keV}$ for DT, whereas $E_0 = 49.1\ \mathrm{keV}$ for D$^3$He, so in the first place the representative energy at which the reaction occurs is different. Comparing at the single point of $100\ \mathrm{keV}$ is, for both, a condition far removed from a real plasma. If we assume $S$ to be constant and carry out the integral above numerically, the ratio at $T=10\ \mathrm{keV}$ becomes $187$. The step from $31$ to this value is explained purely by the Gamow factor and the Maxwell distribution.

Cause 2: The remaining factor $423/187 \simeq 2.3$ is the $S$ factor, that is, nuclear structure. As stated in the Caution in Section 16.1.2 of this book, the $J^\pi=3/2^+$ resonance of $^5$He sits right at $64\ \mathrm{keV}$ in the center-of-mass frame for DT. For this reason the $S(E)$ of DT rises substantially in the region $10\text{–}60\ \mathrm{keV}$. D$^3$He, on the other hand, has no resonance at this position, and the cross-section peak lies at $250\ \mathrm{keV}$, far from the plasma temperature. Indeed, evaluating $S=\sigma E\exp(\sqrt{E_G/E})$ from the peak value of the cross section gives $23.5$ for DT and $17.4\ \mathrm{b\,MeV}$ for D$^3$He. In addition, the $S$ of D$^3$He drops to about $7\ \mathrm{MeV\,b}$ at the Gamow peak ($49\ \mathrm{keV}$), far from the $250\ \mathrm{keV}$ resonance, so the ratio of $S$ opens up to a factor of 2–3 on the low-temperature side.

The situation is the same at $T=20\ \mathrm{keV}$. Reading from the Bosch–Hale parametrization, DT is $4.2\times10^{-22}$ and D$^3$He is $3.5\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{m^3/s}$, so the ratio is about $120$. Since the Gamow-only calculation gives $61$, the remaining factor of about 2 is again the advantage in the $S$ factor due to the $^5$He resonance. In fact, at $T=20\ \mathrm{keV}$ the Gamow peak is at $E_0=49\ \mathrm{keV}$, still short of the resonance ($64\ \mathrm{keV}$), and the width of the window, $\Delta\simeq(4/\sqrt3)\sqrt{E_0k_BT}\simeq72\ \mathrm{keV}$, entirely includes the resonance, so the benefit DT receives from the resonance does not diminish even at this temperature. The boundary between “the part that the Gamow factor can explain” and “the part it cannot” is itself the fingerprint of nuclear structure.

Verification. We check the dimensions. In $E_G = 2m_rc^2(\pi\alpha Z_1Z_2)^2$, $\alpha$ is dimensionless, so $E_G$ has the dimension of energy ✓. $\sqrt{E_G/E}$ is dimensionless and may be placed in the exponent ✓. As a comparison with a known value, Section 16.1.2 of this book obtained, for DT, $2\pi\eta=4.298$ and $P=1.36\times10^{-2}$ with $E_G=1.1822\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $E=64\ \mathrm{keV}$. Putting $E=100\ \mathrm{keV}$ into the same formula should make the exponent smaller and $P$ larger, and indeed $3.21\times10^{-2} > 1.36\times10^{-2}$ ✓. Also, for $p^{11}$B this book gives $E_G=22.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and $2\times859.6\times(5\times0.02292531)^2 = 1719.2\times0.0131393 = 22.59\ \mathrm{MeV}$ agrees ✓.

Meaning. The conclusion of this exercise is cruel for materials science. The content of the exponent, $E_G\propto(Z_1Z_2)^2$, is the strength of the Coulomb interaction itself, and no engineering ingenuity can change it. The idea that “if we use a fuel that does not emit neutrons, the problem of irradiation damage to the first wall disappears” runs head-on into the wall that $E_G$ becomes $4$ times larger (D$^3$He) or $19$ times larger ($p^{11}$B). Moreover, fuels with large $Z$ also increase the bremsstrahlung loss $P_{\rm br}\propto Z_{\rm eff}\,n_e^2\sqrt{T_e}$ (the definition $Z_{\rm eff}=\sum_in_iZ_i^2/n_e$ already contains $Z^2$). In the end we have no choice but to live with $14\ \mathrm{MeV}$ neutrons, and that is precisely why the development of reduced-activation ferritic steel, tungsten, and SiC/SiC composites is necessary. The necessity of materials development is derived from a single exponent written only in terms of the fine-structure constant and the atomic numbers.

Exercise 16.3: Irradiation damage in tungsten

Problem (restated)

A $14.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$ neutron is incident on W ($A=184$, $E_d=90\ \mathrm{eV}$).

(1) Find $\Lambda = 4mM/(m+M)^2$ and the maximum PKA energy $T_{\max}$.

(2) Taking the mean PKA energy to be $T_{\max}/2$ and the Lindhard factor to be $\xi=0.75$, find the damage energy $T_{\rm dam}$, and compute the number of defects $N_d$ with the NRT model ($\xi=0.75$ is the value $0.71$, obtained by inserting $Z=74$, $A=184$, $T=0.152\ \mathrm{MeV}$ into the Lindhard formula of Section 16.2.2, rounded. In heavy W the contribution of electronic stopping power is small, so $\xi$ is larger than for Fe. The exercise in Chapter 1 roughly takes $0.6$, but the present value is more accurate).

(3) Taking the total reaction cross section of W at $14\ \mathrm{MeV}$ to be $5.4\ \mathrm{b}$, find the displacement cross section $\sigma_{\rm dpa}$.

(4) Find the dpa for one year of operation at a wall loading of $1\ \mathrm{MW/m^2}$ ($\phi=4.43\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}s^{-1}}$), and compare it with the Fe values of Section 16.2 ($7.7\ \mathrm{dpa}$ from an estimate by the same procedure, and $10\ \mathrm{dpa}$ from the design conversion rule).

Solution

Strategy. We repeat for W, in the same order, the four steps that Section 16.2 of this book took for Fe (kinematics $\to$ Lindhard $\to$ NRT $\to$ product with the flux). The point is to follow the structure: at every step W is more favorable than Fe, and the product of these factors gives the final difference.

(1) Take the mass number of the neutron to be $m=1$ and that of W to be $M=184$. Then

$$ \Lambda_{\rm W} = \frac{4mM}{(m+M)^2} = \frac{4\times1\times184}{(1+184)^2} = \frac{736}{185^2} = \frac{736}{34225} = 2.1505\times10^{-2} $$

Therefore the maximum PKA energy is

$$ T_{\max} = \Lambda_{\rm W}\,E_n = 2.1505\times10^{-2}\times14.1\ \mathrm{MeV} = 0.30322\ \mathrm{MeV} \simeq 0.303\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

This agrees with the value $0.303\ \mathrm{MeV}$ in Table 16.3. Compared with Fe, for which $\Lambda=4\times56/57^2 = 0.06894$ and $T_{\max}=0.972\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $\Lambda$ is smaller by a factor of $3.2$. Since $\Lambda\simeq 4m/M$ for $M\gg m$, the ratio of mass numbers, $184/56=3.29$, appears directly.

(2) For isotropic scattering in the center-of-mass frame, $\braket{\sin^2(\theta_{\rm CM}/2)}=1/2$, so the average PKA energy is

$$ \braket{T} = \frac{T_{\max}}{2} = \frac{0.30322}{2} = 0.15161\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

Of this, only the fraction given by the Lindhard factor $\xi$ goes into collisions with atomic nuclei (that is, into defect production); the rest is lost to electronic excitation. Using $\xi=0.75$ as given, we obtain

$$ T_{\rm dam} = \xi\braket{T} = 0.75\times0.15161 = 0.11371\ \mathrm{MeV} = 1.1371\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{eV} $$

The NRT model gives $N_d = 0.8\,T_{\rm dam}/(2E_d)$, so inserting $E_d=90\ \mathrm{eV}$,

$$ N_d = \frac{0.8\times1.1371\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{eV}}{2\times90\ \mathrm{eV}} = \frac{9.0968\times10^{4}}{180} = 505.4 \simeq 5.1\times10^{2} $$

That is, each time a neutron strikes one W atom, about $500$ Frenkel pairs are produced. Compared with the $2.2\times10^{3}$ obtained for Fe by the same procedure in Section 16.2.3 of this book (average PKA $\braket{T}=0.49\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $\xi=0.45$), this is about $1/4.4$. (Compared with the $3.5\times10^{3}$ for a $1\ \mathrm{MeV}$ PKA in Section 16.2.2 it is $1/7$, but that is a comparison in which the PKA energies are not matched.)

Here we check where the value $\xi=0.75$ stands, rather than swallowing it as given. The Lindhard formula of Section 16.2.2 of this book is

$$ \xi = \frac{1}{1+k\,g(\varepsilon)},\qquad \varepsilon = \frac{T}{E_L},\qquad g(\varepsilon) = 3.4008\,\varepsilon^{1/6} + 0.40244\,\varepsilon^{3/4} + \varepsilon $$

and for self-recoil we had $E_L = 86.9\,Z^{7/3}\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $k = 0.1337\,Z^{2/3}A^{-1/2}$. For W ($Z=74$, $A=184$),

$$ E_L = 86.9\times74^{7/3} = 86.9\times2.299\times10^{4} = 2.00\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV}, \qquad k = \frac{0.1337\times74^{2/3}}{\sqrt{184}} = \frac{0.1337\times17.63}{13.56} = 0.1737 $$

(compared with $E_L=1.74\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $k=0.157$ for Fe, $E_L$ is larger by a factor of $11.5$). For $\braket{T}=0.1516\ \mathrm{MeV}$ we have $\varepsilon = 1.516\times10^{5}/2.00\times10^{6} = 0.0758$, so

$$ g(0.0758) = 3.4008\times0.6505 + 0.40244\times0.1445 + 0.0758 = 2.346, \qquad \xi = \frac{1}{1+0.1737\times2.346} = 0.710 $$

which agrees well with the given $0.75$ (a $5\%$ difference). Putting the same $\braket{T}$ into Fe gives $\varepsilon = 1.516\times10^{5}/1.74\times10^{5} = 0.87$ and only $\xi=0.58$. Moreover, in the Fe calculation of Section 16.2.3 of this book, $\braket{T}=0.49\ \mathrm{MeV}$ ($\varepsilon=2.82$), so $\xi=0.45$. In other words, $\xi$ is large for W for a double reason. (i) Because W is heavy, $\braket{T}$ itself is smaller, at $1/3.2$. (ii) Because $Z$ is large, $E_L$ is $11.5$ times larger, so $\varepsilon$ is small even for the same $T$. Both act to lower $\varepsilon$, and as $\varepsilon\to0$ we have $g\to0$ and $\xi\to1$ (everything goes into nuclear collisions). In a heavy element, a large fraction of the energy is lost in nuclear collisions before it can be handed to the electron system. Note, however, that this is an unfavorable factor for W (it is counted in (4)).

(3) The displacement cross section is the reaction cross section multiplied by the “number of defects per nuclear reaction”:

$$ \sigma_{\rm dpa} \simeq \sigma_{\rm tot}\times N_d = 5.4\ \mathrm{b}\times505.4 = 2.729\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{b} \simeq 2.7\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{b} $$

Converting to SI, since $1\ \mathrm{b}=10^{-24}\ \mathrm{cm^2}$,

$$ \sigma_{\rm dpa} = 2.729\times10^{3}\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{cm^2} = 2.729\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{cm^2} $$

While nuclear reaction cross sections are a few barns, the displacement cross section reaches the $\mathrm{kb}$ level for no other reason than that a single collision produces $N_d\sim10^{2\text{–}3}$ defects.

(4) The dpa per unit time is the product of the flux and the cross section:

$$ \frac{\dd(\mathrm{dpa})}{\dd t} = \sigma_{\rm dpa}\,\phi = 2.729\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{cm^2}\times4.43\times10^{13}\ \mathrm{cm^{-2}s^{-1}} = 1.209\times10^{-7}\ \mathrm{dpa/s} $$

Taking one year of full-power operation to be $3.156\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{s}$,

$$ \mathrm{dpa}(1\ \mathrm{yr}) = 1.209\times10^{-7}\times3.156\times10^{7} = 3.82\ \mathrm{dpa} $$

That is, $1\ \mathrm{MW\,yr/m^2}$ gives about $3.8\ \mathrm{dpa}$. This is about half of the $7.7\ \mathrm{dpa}$ obtained for Fe by the same procedure in Section 16.2.3 of this book, and about $1/3$ of the conversion rule $1\ \mathrm{MW\,yr/m^2}\simeq10\ \mathrm{dpa}$ (steel) used in design.

Decomposing, factor by factor, the reason why W is “less easily damaged” than Fe by more than a factor of $2$, we obtain the following.

  • Kinematics: $\Lambda$ is $1/3.2$ (the recoil is small because W is heavy)
  • Coupling strength: $E_d$ is $90/40=2.25$ times larger (it takes $2.25$ times the energy to knock an atom out)
  • Electronic stopping: $\xi$ is $0.75$ versus $0.45$, a factor of $1.67$ (this acts unfavorably for W)
  • Nuclear reaction cross section: $5.4/2.5 = 2.16$ times (this too is unfavorable for W)

Taking the product, $\frac{1}{3.2}\times\frac{1}{2.25}\times1.67\times2.16 = 0.50$, and $7.7\times0.50=3.8\ \mathrm{dpa}$ ✓. The accounting is that the advantage of the first two factors outweighs the disadvantage of the latter two by just about a factor of two.

Verification. Compare with the rightmost column $T_{\max}/2E_d$ of Table 16.3. For W, $0.30322\times10^{6}/(2\times90)=1.68\times10^{3}$, which agrees with the table’s $1.7\times10^{3}$ ✓. For Fe, $0.972\times10^{6}/80 = 1.22\times10^{4}$, which agrees with the table’s $1.2\times10^{4}$ ✓. The ratio is $7.2$, which is also consistent with the statement in this book that “$T_{\max}/2E_d$ is $1/7$ of that of Fe” ✓. The dimensions also work: $[\mathrm{cm^2}]\times[\mathrm{cm^{-2}s^{-1}}] = [\mathrm{s^{-1}}]$, and since dpa is dimensionless, $\mathrm{dpa/s}$ is correct ✓.

Meaning. The number $3.8\ \mathrm{dpa/(MW\,yr\,m^{-2})}$ in this problem is the product of four quantities of entirely different origins: the kinematics of elastic scattering from Chapter 4 ($\Lambda$), Lindhard’s stopping-power theory ($\xi$), an empirical coefficient based on MD calculations (the $0.8$ of NRT), and nuclear data ($\sigma_{\rm tot}$). From the standpoint of particle physics only the first is “our own territory,” yet that one factor fixes the order of magnitude. The reasons usually given first for choosing tungsten as a plasma-facing material are its low sputtering yield and high melting point, but the fact that “being heavy” itself reduces the damage kinematically is just as fundamental. Note also that, as the caution in Section 16.2.2 of this book says, the NRT-dpa obtained here is not the number of defects that actually remain; once the arc-dpa correction is applied it drops to a little over $1$ in 10 for W (about $3$ in 10 even for Fe). The dpa is less a physical quantity than a common currency for comparing irradiation doses, and one must not forget this and swallow the numbers in papers uncritically.

Exercise 16.4: Using the Lawson criterion yourself

Problem (restated)

Suppose $\braket{\sigma v}=1.1\times10^{-24}T^2\ \mathrm{m^3/s}$ ($T$ in $\mathrm{keV}$) and $E_\alpha=3.52\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(1) Evaluate the ignition condition $n\tau_E \ge 12T/(\braket{\sigma v}E_\alpha)$ at $T=15\ \mathrm{keV}$.
