(2) Find the required $\tau_E$ for the typical tokamak value $n=1.0\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$.

(3) In inertial fusion, $n=1.0\times10^{31}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ ($1000$ times the solid density). Find the required $\tau$, compute the distance light travels in that time, and compare it with the size of the pellet.

(4) Explain, in terms of the equations, why the triple product $nT\tau_E$ becomes a constant independent of temperature.

Solution

Strategy. We simply turn the derivation of Section 16.1.4 of this book into numbers. Only the system of units needs care. If $T$ and $E_\alpha$ are expressed in the same energy unit ($\mathrm{keV}$), then since $\braket{\sigma v}$ is in $\mathrm{m^3/s}$, $n\tau_E$ comes out in $\mathrm{m^{-3}\,s}$.

(1) First we evaluate the reactivity. Since $T=15\ \mathrm{keV}$,

$$ \braket{\sigma v} = 1.1\times10^{-24}\times(15)^2 = 1.1\times10^{-24}\times225 = 2.475\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{m^3/s} $$

We also convert $E_\alpha = 3.52\ \mathrm{MeV} = 3520\ \mathrm{keV}$. The ignition condition is

$$ n\tau_E \;\ge\; \frac{12\,T}{\braket{\sigma v}\,E_\alpha} = \frac{12\times15\ \mathrm{keV}}{2.475\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{m^3/s}\times3520\ \mathrm{keV}} = \frac{180}{8.712\times10^{-19}}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}\,s} $$ $$ = 2.066\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}\,s} $$

Incidentally, the triple product is

$$ nT\tau_E \ge 2.066\times10^{20}\times15 = 3.10\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{keV\,s\,m^{-3}} $$

which agrees exactly with the $3.10\times10^{21}$ obtained in Section 16.1.4 of this book.

(2) We just substitute $n=1.0\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$:

$$ \tau_E \ge \frac{2.066\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}\,s}}{1.0\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}} = 2.07\ \mathrm{s} $$

That is, if the plasma can be kept warm so that the injected heat takes about $2$ seconds to escape completely, it ignites by itself. The $\tau_E$ of JET is $\sim1\ \mathrm{s}$, and the ITER design value is $\sim3.7\ \mathrm{s}$. This one line shows why ITER is said to be “a device within reach of ignition.” Note also that $\tau_E$ becomes longer the larger the device is (the larger the volume/surface-area ratio). The reason a fusion reactor must be huge is, in the end, also this $2$ seconds.

(3) Raising the density by $11$ orders of magnitude lowers the required time by $11$ orders of magnitude:

$$ \tau \ge \frac{2.066\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}\,s}}{1.0\times10^{31}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}} = 2.066\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{s} = 20.7\ \mathrm{ps} $$

The distance light travels in this time is

$$ c\tau = 2.998\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}\times2.066\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{s} = 6.19\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{m} = 6.2\ \mathrm{mm} $$

The radius of the compressed pellet is $\sim30\ \mu\mathrm{m}$, so during the confinement time light travels a distance as much as $200$ times the pellet radius. In other words, the plasma must be held for a time much longer than “the time light takes to cross the pellet.”

Then what holds it? A device that confines it from outside cannot act in time (no machine operates in $20\ \mathrm{ps}$). Only inertia holds it. The hot plasma expands at its own sound speed and disperses, so the effective confinement time is determined by “radius/sound speed.” The ion sound speed of a DT plasma, with the ion mass $m_i\simeq2.5\,u = 4.15\times10^{-27}\ \mathrm{kg}$ and $T=15\ \mathrm{keV}=2.403\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{J}$, is

$$ c_s \sim \sqrt{\frac{2k_BT}{m_i}} = \sqrt{\frac{2\times2.403\times10^{-15}}{4.15\times10^{-27}}} = 1.08\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s} $$ $$ \tau_{\rm inertial} \sim \frac{R}{c_s} = \frac{30\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{m}}{1.08\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{m/s}} = 2.8\times10^{-11}\ \mathrm{s} = 28\ \mathrm{ps} $$

This is nearly the same as the required value, $20.7\ \mathrm{ps}$. The design value of $30\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ for the pellet radius in inertial fusion is determined almost entirely by the Lawson criterion and the sound speed. That the two agree is no accident; the device is designed so that they do.

(4) The triple-product condition was

$$ n\,T\,\tau_E \;\ge\; \frac{12\,T^2}{\braket{\sigma v}\,E_\alpha} $$

Substituting $\braket{\sigma v} = CT^2$ ($C=1.1\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}\,keV^{-2}}$) here gives

$$ n\,T\,\tau_E \;\ge\; \frac{12\,T^2}{C\,T^2\,E_\alpha} = \frac{12}{C\,E_\alpha} $$

and $T$ disappears completely from the right-hand side. The numerical value is

$$ \frac{12}{1.1\times10^{-24}\times3520} = \frac{12}{3.872\times10^{-21}} = 3.10\times10^{21}\ \mathrm{keV\,s\,m^{-3}} $$

Restating physically why the cancellation occurs: the loss power $P_{\rm loss}=3nT/\tau_E$ increases in proportion to $T$ to the first power. The heating power $P_\alpha = (n^2/4)\braket{\sigma v}E_\alpha$, on the other hand, increases as the second power of $T$ through $\braket{\sigma v}\propto T^2$. On balance, raising the temperature favors heating by one power. That advantage exactly balances the upgrade of the left-hand side of the condition from $n\tau_E$ to $nT\tau_E$. Hence in the range $8\text{–}25\ \mathrm{keV}$ the requirement is the same $3.1\times10^{21}$ whatever temperature one operates at.

This holds, however, only in the range where $\braket{\sigma v}\propto T^2$ is valid. For $T\gtrsim25\ \mathrm{keV}$ the growth of the DT reactivity slows (because one passes the $64\ \mathrm{keV}$ resonance), and bremsstrahlung loss $\propto\sqrt{T}$ also comes into play, so the triple-product requirement turns upward again. This is why the actual optimal operating temperature lies around $T\simeq14\text{–}15\ \mathrm{keV}$, and it is no accident that (1) has you choose $T=15\ \mathrm{keV}$.

Verification. Follow the units. $[12T/(\braket{\sigma v}E_\alpha)] = \mathrm{keV}/(\mathrm{m^3\,s^{-1}}\cdot\mathrm{keV}) = \mathrm{m^{-3}\,s}$ ✓, which matches the dimensions of $n\tau_E$. Redoing the calculation at $T=10\ \mathrm{keV}$, $\braket{\sigma v}=1.1\times10^{-22}$ and $n\tau_E\ge 12\times10/(1.1\times10^{-22}\times3520)=3.10\times10^{20}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}s}$, which agrees with the $3.1\times10^{20}$ of Step 5 in Section 16.1.4 of this book ✓. Moreover, the triple product is $3.10\times10^{21}$, the same value as in (1), so the claim of (4) is confirmed numerically as well ✓. Checking against Table 16.2: at $T=10$, $CT^2 = 1.1\times10^{-22}$ (table value $1.1\times10^{-22}$ ✓), and at $T=20$, $4.4\times10^{-22}$ (table value $4.2\times10^{-22}$, within $5\%$ ✓).

Meaning. At first sight the Lawson criterion looks like a purely plasma-physics formula. But the $E_\alpha=3.52\ \mathrm{MeV}$ sitting on its right-hand side is nothing more than the result of four-momentum conservation dividing the $Q$ value in the ratio $1:4$, as we saw in Exercise 16.1. Had the $\alpha$ received $80\%$, the right-hand side would be $1/4$ as large, the triple-product requirement would drop to $7.8\times10^{20}$, and by this calculation JET would have ignited as early as 1997. One quarter of the reason why fusion has been difficult for half a century lies in the nuclear mass ratio $m_\alpha/m_n\simeq4$. And this same division also drives a $14\ \mathrm{MeV}$ neutron into the wall (Exercise 16.3). The difficulty of ignition and the difficulty of materials are the two faces of one and the same piece of kinematics.

Exercise 16.5: Size and energy of a muonic atom

Problem (restated)

Use $m_\mu/m_e = 206.768$, $m_d/m_e = 3670.483$, $m_t/m_e = 5496.92$, $a_0 = 52917.7\ \mathrm{fm}$, and $\mathrm{Ry}=13.606\ \mathrm{eV}$.

(1) Find the reduced masses (in units of $m_e$) of $d\mu$ and $t\mu$.

(2) Find the Bohr radius and the ground-state energy of each.

(3) Find the energy released in the reaction $d\mu + t \to t\mu + d$. Explain why the sign of this quantity is favorable for muon-catalyzed fusion.

(4) Find the number of cycles in the cycle-number formula of Chapter 16 of this book for $\omega_s = 0.0045$ and $\lambda_c\tau_\mu = 264$, and also find the upper limit in the limit $\lambda_c\to\infty$.

Solution

Strategy. We only need to put the reduced masses correctly into the two-body Coulomb bound-system formulas of Chapter 7, $a = a_0(m_e/m_r)$ and $E_1 = -\mathrm{Ry}\,(m_r/m_e)$. The crux of this problem is that the crude rule of thumb “$1/207$” cannot produce the $48\ \mathrm{eV}$ of (3).

(1) The reduced mass is $m_r = m_1m_2/(m_1+m_2)$. For the $d\mu$ system,

$$ \frac{m_r^{d\mu}}{m_e} = \frac{206.768\times3670.483}{206.768+3670.483} = \frac{7.589384\times10^{5}}{3877.251} = 195.741 $$

For the $t\mu$ system,

$$ \frac{m_r^{t\mu}}{m_e} = \frac{206.768\times5496.92}{206.768+5496.92} = \frac{1.136587\times10^{6}}{5703.688} = 199.272 $$

Both are smaller than $m_\mu/m_e = 206.768$. If the nucleus were infinitely heavy we would have $m_r\to m_\mu$, but in reality a correction of $m_\mu/m_d = 1/17.75$ enters for the deuteron and $1/26.6$ for the triton. Because the triton is heavier, the reduced mass is closer to the muon mass. This small $1.8\%$ difference between $195.74$ and $199.27$ is the key to everything that follows.

(2) The Bohr radius is inversely proportional to the reduced mass: $a = a_0\,(m_e/m_r)$.

$$ a_{d\mu} = \frac{52917.7\ \mathrm{fm}}{195.741} = 270.34\ \mathrm{fm} \simeq 270.3\ \mathrm{fm} $$ $$ a_{t\mu} = \frac{52917.7\ \mathrm{fm}}{199.272} = 265.55\ \mathrm{fm} \simeq 265.6\ \mathrm{fm} $$

The ground-state energy is proportional to the reduced mass: $E_1 = -\mathrm{Ry}\,(m_r/m_e)$.

$$ E_1^{d\mu} = -13.606\ \mathrm{eV}\times195.741 = -2663.26\ \mathrm{eV} = -2.663\ \mathrm{keV} $$ $$ E_1^{t\mu} = -13.606\ \mathrm{eV}\times199.272 = -2711.30\ \mathrm{eV} = -2.711\ \mathrm{keV} $$

For comparison, the naive value with an infinitely heavy nucleus is $a_\mu = 52917.7/206.768 = 255.9\ \mathrm{fm}$, which is smaller than the actual $a_{d\mu}=270.3\ \mathrm{fm}$ by $14.4\ \mathrm{fm}$, or $5.3\%$. The rule of thumb “a muonic atom is $1/207$ the size of a hydrogen atom” is in reality $1/196$ ($d\mu$) or $1/199$ ($t\mu$).

(3) The $Q$ value of the exchange reaction $d\mu + t \to t\mu + d$ is precisely the difference of the binding energies. The binding energy of the initial state is $2663.26\ \mathrm{eV}$ for $d\mu$, and that of the final state is $2711.30\ \mathrm{eV}$ for $t\mu$, so by moving to the more deeply bound side,

$$ \Delta E = \abs{E_1^{t\mu}} - \abs{E_1^{d\mu}} = 2711.30 - 2663.26 = 48.04\ \mathrm{eV} $$

is released. That is, this is an exothermic reaction ($Q=+48\ \mathrm{eV}$).

There are two reasons why this sign is favorable for muon-catalyzed fusion.

  • It proceeds spontaneously. Because the reaction is exothermic, there is no reaction threshold, and it happens at every collision. At room temperature ($k_BT\sim0.025\ \mathrm{eV}$) or at liquid-hydrogen temperature, $48\ \mathrm{eV}$ is $2000$ times the thermal energy, and the reverse reaction $t\mu + d \to d\mu + t$ is completely forbidden, with a Boltzmann factor $\exp(-48/0.025)=\ee^{-1900}$. In other words, it proceeds in only one direction.
  • It makes the necessary intermediate for us. What we want to fuse is the $dt\mu$ molecule. For that we need $t\mu$. However, when a muon is stopped in a D/T mixture, both $d\mu$ and $t\mu$ form indiscriminately. Without this transfer reaction, the $d\mu$ that formed would only make $dd\mu$ and undergo DD fusion, and half of the opportunities for the $17.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$ DT fusion would be lost. The $48\ \mathrm{eV}$ drop sweeps all the muons over to the triton side.

Note that the origin of this $48\ \mathrm{eV}$ is, in the end, only the nuclear-mass fact that “the triton is $1.5$ times heavier than the deuteron.” The isotope effect determines the direction of the catalytic cycle.

(4) The formula for the number of cycles in Section 16.9.2 of this book is

$$ N_c = \frac{1}{\;\omega_s + (\lambda_c\tau_\mu)^{-1}\;} $$

The first term of the denominator represents the loss due to sticking, and the second term the loss due to the muon lifetime. Inserting $\omega_s=0.0045$ and $\lambda_c\tau_\mu=264$ gives

$$ (\lambda_c\tau_\mu)^{-1} = \frac{1}{264} = 3.788\times10^{-3} $$ $$ N_c = \frac{1}{4.500\times10^{-3} + 3.788\times10^{-3}} = \frac{1}{8.288\times10^{-3}} = 120.7 \simeq 121 $$

The breakdown of the losses is $4.500/8.288 = 54\%$ for sticking and $46\%$ for decay. The two are now nearly balanced.

In the limit $\lambda_c\to\infty$ (the ideal limit in which the cycle can be run infinitely fast), the second term vanishes and

$$ N_c^{\max} = \frac{1}{\omega_s} = \frac{1}{0.0045} = 222.2 \simeq 222 $$

This is the upper limit in principle. Against the $N_c\gtrsim300\text{–}500$ needed for break-even, no amount of engineering can take us beyond $222$. In terms of energy, the upper limit is $222\times17.6\ \mathrm{MeV} = 3.9\ \mathrm{GeV}$, which is just balanced against the production cost of one muon, $3\text{–}5\ \mathrm{GeV}$. It is an extremely cruel number: it seems within reach if one tries hard, yet is never reached.

Verification. We check with dimensions and limits. $m_r$ has the dimension of mass, and in the limit $m_1\gg m_2$ it converges to $m_r\to m_2$ (the lighter one). Indeed, taking $m_d\to\infty$ gives $m_r\to m_\mu = 206.768\,m_e$, and $a\to255.9\ \mathrm{fm}$ ✓. Also, $a\cdot\abs{E_1}$ should equal $a_0\mathrm{Ry}$ (the reduced mass cancels): $270.34\times2663.26 = 7.200\times10^{5}$, $52917.7\times13.606 = 7.200\times10^{5}$ ✓. For $t\mu$ as well, $265.55\times2711.30 = 7.200\times10^{5}$ ✓. This reflects the fact that, from $\abs{E_1}=\frac12\alpha^2m_rc^2$ and $a=\hbar/(m_rc\alpha)$, the product $a\abs{E_1}=\frac12\alpha\hbar c$ is independent of the reduced mass. Numerically, since $\hbar c = 197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm} = 1.97327\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{eV\,fm}$, we have $\frac12\times1.97327\times10^{8}/137.036 = 7.200\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{eV\,fm}$ ✓. As for (4), for $\omega_s\to0$ we get $N_c\to\lambda_c\tau_\mu = 264$ (determined by the lifetime alone), and for $\lambda_c\tau_\mu\to\infty$ we get $N_c\to222$; both limits make sense ✓.

Meaning. This problem shows numerically the moment at which materials engineering runs into a wall set by the laws of physics. As we saw in (1)–(3), the size, the energy, and the isotope difference of a muonic atom are all determined by a single quantity, the reduced mass. Neither crystal structure nor temperature nor density enters. The upper limit $1/\omega_s$ in (4) is similar: $\omega_s$ is a purely quantum-mechanical quantity, the overlap integral between the $dt\mu$ wave function immediately after fusion and the $(\alpha\mu)$ bound state. All that engineering can move is $\lambda_c$ (optimization of density, temperature, and D/T ratio), and that touches only the second term of the denominator. However far we drive the second term to zero, as long as the first term is $0.0045$ we cannot exceed $222$. On the other hand, this same physics has another use. The fusion of $dt\mu$ occurs in $10^{-12}\ \mathrm{s}$ and emits a $14\ \mathrm{MeV}$ neutron. It cannot serve as an energy source, but it is quite viable as a compact, subcritical source of $14\ \mathrm{MeV}$ neutrons, and it could provide just the kind of venue for materials irradiation tests that we calculated in Exercise 16.3. It is a typical example of a failed technology becoming a tool in another field.

Exercise 16.6: Mastering the neutron conversion formulas

Problem (restated)

Use $E[\mathrm{meV}]=81.804/\lambda^2[\mathrm{Å}^2]$ and $v[\mathrm{m/s}]=3956/\lambda[\mathrm{Å}]$.

(1) Find $E$ and $v$ for a cold neutron with $\lambda = 5.0\ \mathrm{Å}$ and an epithermal neutron with $\lambda = 0.50\ \mathrm{Å}$.

(2) In a time-of-flight (TOF) spectrometer with flight distance $L=20\ \mathrm{m}$, find the time of flight of a neutron with $\lambda=2.0\ \mathrm{Å}$.

(3) For a pulse width of $70\ \mu\mathrm{s}$, find the wavelength resolution $\Delta\lambda/\lambda$ under the conditions of (2). $\Delta d/d$ is of the same order.

(4) What should be done with $L$ to improve the resolution by a factor of $10$? What is the price?

Solution

Strategy. Both of the two given conversion formulas were built in Section 16.6.2 of this book from $\hbar c = 1973.27\ \mathrm{eV\,Å}$ and $m_nc^2 = 939.565\ \mathrm{MeV}$. They use only the nonrelativistic free-particle relations $E=p^2/2m_n$ and $p=h/\lambda$. The resolution of the TOF method follows simply by reading the uncertainty in the time of flight directly as an uncertainty in the wavelength.

(1) Cold neutron, $\lambda=5.0\ \mathrm{Å}$:

$$ E = \frac{81.804}{(5.0)^2} = \frac{81.804}{25} = 3.272\ \mathrm{meV}, \qquad v = \frac{3956}{5.0} = 791.2\ \mathrm{m/s} $$

Epithermal neutron, $\lambda=0.50\ \mathrm{Å}$:

$$ E = \frac{81.804}{(0.50)^2} = \frac{81.804}{0.25} = 327.2\ \mathrm{meV}, \qquad v = \frac{3956}{0.50} = 7912\ \mathrm{m/s} $$

When the wavelength differs by a factor of $10$, the energy differs by a factor of $100$ and the velocity by a factor of $10$. In terms of $k_BT$, $3.27\ \mathrm{meV}$ corresponds to $38\ \mathrm{K}$ (the temperature range of a liquid-hydrogen moderator), and $327\ \mathrm{meV}$ to $3800\ \mathrm{K}$. The former is the regime for measuring molecular rotational motion and spin waves, and the latter the regime for measuring vibrations of chemical bonds (the $\mathrm{OH}$ stretch is about $450\ \mathrm{meV}$). For simple metals (Al has $2d_{111}=4.7\ \mathrm{Å}$, and Fe has $2d_{110}=4.1\ \mathrm{Å}$), $\lambda=5\ \mathrm{Å}$ exceeds $2d_{\max}$, so no Bragg reflection occurs and the neutrons are transmitted (the Bragg cutoff; the condition is $\lambda > 2d_{\max}$. For Si, $2d_{111}=6.3\ \mathrm{Å}$, so even $5\ \mathrm{Å}$ still diffracts). This long-wavelength side is used mainly for small-angle scattering and inelastic scattering.

(2) The velocity for $\lambda=2.0\ \mathrm{Å}$ is

$$ v = \frac{3956}{2.0} = 1978\ \mathrm{m/s} $$

Therefore the time of flight over $L=20\ \mathrm{m}$ is

$$ t = \frac{L}{v} = \frac{20\ \mathrm{m}}{1978\ \mathrm{m/s}} = 1.0111\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{s} = 10.11\ \mathrm{ms} $$

Collected into a conversion formula, this is $t[\mathrm{ms}] = 0.2528\,L[\mathrm{m}]\,\lambda[\mathrm{Å}]$, a relation used routinely at neutron facilities. A time of $10\ \mathrm{ms}$ is $1/4$ of the $40\ \mathrm{ms}$ period of a $25\ \mathrm{Hz}$ pulsed source (J-PARC), and fits comfortably within one frame.

(3) In the TOF method, the neutron wavelength is determined from the time of flight as $\lambda = 3956\,t/L$ ($t$ in s, $L$ in m, $\lambda$ in Å). If $L$ is fixed, then $\lambda\propto t$, so the relative error propagates directly:

$$ \frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{\Delta t}{t} $$

Inserting the pulse width $\Delta t = 70\ \mu\mathrm{s} = 7.0\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{s}$ (the uncertainty in “when the neutron departed”) gives

$$ \frac{\Delta\lambda}{\lambda} = \frac{7.0\times10^{-5}}{1.0111\times10^{-2}} = 6.92\times10^{-3} \simeq 0.69\% $$

Differentiating the Bragg equation $\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$ at fixed $\theta$ gives $\Delta d/d = \Delta\lambda/\lambda$, so the resolution in the lattice spacing is also $0.69\%$. For a crystal with a lattice constant of $4\ \mathrm{Å}$, a change as small as $4\times0.0069 = 0.028\ \mathrm{Å}$ can be distinguished. For a material with a thermal expansion coefficient of $10^{-5}\ \mathrm{K^{-1}}$, this corresponds to a temperature change of $700\ \mathrm{K}$, which is entirely insufficient for precise lattice-constant measurements. An actual diffractometer needs a much higher resolution.

Strictly speaking, the overall resolution is the sum of squares of several contributions:

$$ \left(\frac{\Delta d}{d}\right)^2 = \left(\frac{\Delta t}{t}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\Delta L}{L}\right)^2 + \left(\Delta\theta\cot\theta\right)^2 $$

The second term is the uncertainty in the flight distance due to the thicknesses of the sample and the moderator, and the third is the uncertainty in the scattering angle; the latter vanishes as $\theta\to90^\circ$ (backscattering) because $\cot\theta\to0$. This is why high-resolution powder diffractometers use a backscattering bank.

(4) We have $\Delta\lambda/\lambda = \Delta t/t = \Delta t\,v/L$, so if $\Delta t$ (the pulse width) and $v$ (the wavelength) are the same, the resolution is inversely proportional to $L$. Therefore, to improve it by a factor of $10$ we should take

$$ L' = 10\times20\ \mathrm{m} = 200\ \mathrm{m} $$

In that case $t = 101\ \mathrm{ms}$ and $\Delta\lambda/\lambda = 6.9\times10^{-4}$. In fact, SuperHRPD, the ultra-high-resolution powder diffractometer at J-PARC, has $L\simeq94\ \mathrm{m}$ and achieves $\Delta d/d\sim3\times10^{-4}$.

There are two prices to pay.

  • A drastic loss of intensity. The solid angle subtended by the detector (or the sample) as seen from the source is $\Omega\propto 1/L^2$. If $L$ is increased by a factor of $10$, $\Omega$ becomes $1/100$, and the number of neutrons obtained in the same measurement time drops by $2$ orders of magnitude. The statistical error worsens as $1/\sqrt{N}$, so obtaining the same statistical precision requires $100$ times the measurement time. A measurement of $1$ hour becomes $4$ days. This is why neutron scattering is said to be “a fight for intensity.”

  • Squeezing of the wavelength band (frame). A pulsed source emits neutrons every period $T_{\rm rep}$. If the fast neutrons of the next pulse catch up with the slow neutrons of the previous pulse, we can no longer tell which is which (frame overlap). From $t=L\lambda/3956$, the wavelength width that fits in one frame is

    $$ \Delta\lambda_{\rm frame} = \frac{3956\,T_{\rm rep}}{L} $$

    For $25\ \mathrm{Hz}$ ($T_{\rm rep}=40\ \mathrm{ms}$), this is $7.9\ \mathrm{Å}$ at $L=20\ \mathrm{m}$ but only $0.79\ \mathrm{Å}$ at $L=200\ \mathrm{m}$. The range of $d$ that can be measured at one time becomes $1/10$, making the setup unsuitable for phase identification or PDF analysis, where one wants to see a wide $Q$ region at once. There is the option of thinning out the pulses with a chopper to lengthen the effective period, but that means throwing away still more intensity.

In other words, resolution, intensity, and bandwidth stand in a three-way trade-off, and an instrument is designed by betting on one of them. This is why both high-resolution and high-intensity instruments stand side by side at the same source.

Verification. We check the conversion formulas themselves against known values. Inserting the standard thermal-neutron velocity $v=2200\ \mathrm{m/s}$ gives $\lambda = 3956/2200 = 1.798\ \mathrm{Å}$ and $E = 81.804/(1.798)^2 = 25.30\ \mathrm{meV}$, and converting to $k_BT$ gives $25.30/0.08617 = 294\ \mathrm{K}$ = room temperature ✓. This agrees with the triplet “$2200\ \mathrm{m/s}$, $25.3\ \mathrm{meV}$, $1.80\ \mathrm{Å}$” that appears in neutron-scattering textbooks. Checking dimensional consistency as well, since $E\propto\lambda^{-2}$ and $v\propto\lambda^{-1}$, we have $E \propto v^2$, consistent with the nonrelativistic $E=\frac12 m_nv^2$ ✓. Indeed, $\frac12\times1.675\times10^{-27}\times(1978)^2 = 3.277\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J} = 20.5\ \mathrm{meV}$, which agrees with $81.804/4 = 20.45\ \mathrm{meV}$ ✓.

Meaning. As stated in Section 16.6.2 of this book, the conversion formulas used in this problem come from the single fact that the neutron mass is $939.6\ \mathrm{MeV}$. The coincidence that a neutron with $\lambda=2\ \mathrm{Å}$ (the scale of interatomic distances) has $20\ \mathrm{meV}$ (the phonon scale) made it possible to measure $\bm{Q}$ and $\hbar\omega$ at the same time and with the same precision. And the TOF method treated in (2)–(4) translates this relation into an instrument in the form “measure the time and you know the energy.” Exactly the same principle by which the time-of-flight method is used for particle identification in particle-physics experiments becomes here a tool for following a $0.07\%$ change in the lattice constant. That the rationale for the design value of $94\ \mathrm{m}$ for the instrument length can be written down with only the neutron mass and the pulse width shows how transparent this field is.

Exercise 16.7: Quantifying defects with positrons

Problem (restated)

(1) The positron lifetime in aluminum is $\tau_b = 163\ \mathrm{ps}$ in the bulk and $\tau_v=244\ \mathrm{ps}$ at a monovacancy. A quenched sample gave a mean lifetime $\bar\tau=200\ \mathrm{ps}$. Find the trapping rate $\kappa$ from the two-state trapping model formula of Chapter 16 of this book.

(2) Taking the specific trapping rate of Al to be $\mu_v = 2.0\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$ (per atomic fraction), find the vacancy concentration.

(3) The sample was irradiated still more strongly and $\bar\tau=244\ \mathrm{ps}$ resulted. What is the vacancy concentration? State why it cannot be answered.

(4) An o-Ps lifetime $\tau_3 = 1.64\ \mathrm{ns}$ was measured in a polymer. Using the Tao–Eldrup formula ($\Delta R=0.166\ \mathrm{nm}$), find the radius $R$ of the free volume (trial and error is fine).

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1)–(3) are a direct application of the two-state trapping model $\kappa = \lambda_b(\bar\tau-\tau_b)/(\tau_v-\bar\tau)$ of Section 16.5.2 of this book, together with a check of the limits of its applicability. Part (4) is a problem of solving the Tao–Eldrup formula of Section 16.5.3 inversely for $R$; it cannot be solved analytically, so we close in on the answer numerically.

(1) First, find the bulk annihilation rate.

$$ \lambda_b = \frac{1}{\tau_b} = \frac{1}{163\times10^{-12}\ \mathrm{s}} = 6.135\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

Substitute $\bar\tau=200\ \mathrm{ps}$, $\tau_b=163\ \mathrm{ps}$, and $\tau_v=244\ \mathrm{ps}$ into the trapping-rate formula. It suffices to take the ratio of the lifetime differences with everything left in $\mathrm{ps}$ (the dimensions cancel):

$$ \kappa = \lambda_b\,\frac{\bar\tau-\tau_b}{\tau_v-\bar\tau} = 6.135\times10^{9}\times\frac{200-163}{244-200} = 6.135\times10^{9}\times\frac{37}{44} $$ $$ = 6.135\times10^{9}\times0.84091 = 5.159\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} $$

Let us confirm the meaning of this $\kappa$. A positron in the bulk state is exposed to a competition between annihilation (rate $\lambda_b$) and trapping (rate $\kappa$). The fraction trapped is

$$ \eta = \frac{\kappa}{\lambda_b+\kappa} = \frac{5.159}{6.135+5.159} = 0.457 $$

that is, $46\%$ of the positrons annihilate after falling into a vacancy. This is consistent with $\bar\tau$ lying slightly below the exact midpoint of $\tau_b$ and $\tau_v$ ($200$ is a little smaller than the midpoint $203.5$ of $163$ and $244$).

(2) The trapping rate is proportional to the vacancy concentration, and the constant of proportionality is the specific trapping rate $\mu_v$: $\kappa = \mu_v C_v$. Therefore

$$ C_v = \frac{\kappa}{\mu_v} = \frac{5.159\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}}{2.0\times10^{14}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}} = 2.58\times10^{-5} $$

This is $2.6\times10^{-5}$ in atomic fraction, that is, $26\ \mathrm{appm}$. It corresponds to $1$ vacancy per roughly $3.9$ × 10⁴ Al atoms.

Let us check the plausibility of this value against the thermal-equilibrium concentration. Taking the vacancy formation energy to be $E_v^f = 0.67\ \mathrm{eV}$ (the measured value for Al), the thermal-equilibrium concentration at $T = 900\ \mathrm{K}$, just below the melting point ($k_BT=0.0776\ \mathrm{eV}$), is

$$ C_v^{\rm eq} = \exp\!\left(-\frac{E_v^f}{k_BT}\right) = \exp(-8.63) = 1.8\times10^{-4} $$

Only a portion of this can be frozen in by quenching (some escapes to surfaces and dislocations during the rapid cooling), so a value of $26\ \mathrm{appm}$ is perfectly reasonable. Conversely, it also means that the quenching temperature can be estimated from the $37\ \mathrm{ps}$ increase in $\bar\tau$ measured by PALS.

(3) We have $\bar\tau = 244\ \mathrm{ps} = \tau_v$. Inserting this into the formula gives

$$ \kappa = \lambda_b\,\frac{244-163}{244-244} = \lambda_b\times\frac{81}{0} \to \infty $$

The denominator vanishes and the expression diverges. That is, the vacancy concentration cannot be determined from this measurement.

Physically, this is the state of saturation trapping. When there are enough vacancies, almost $100\%$ of the positrons are captured by vacancies before they can annihilate in the bulk state ($\eta\to1$ above). The lifetime spectrum then becomes a single component of $\tau_v$, and even if the vacancies increase further, $\bar\tau$ no longer moves. The measured quantity loses its sensitivity to the concentration.

All we can state is a lower limit. As noted in Section 16.5.2 of this book, saturation occurs at $C_v\gtrsim10^{-4}$, so we can conclude only that

$$ C_v \gtrsim 10^{-4} = 100\ \mathrm{appm} $$

The way out of this situation is to move to an observable other than the lifetime. For example, the Doppler broadening of the annihilation $\gamma$ rays (the S/W parameters) and coincidence Doppler broadening (CDB) remain sensitive to the chemical environment of the defect (which element surrounds it, and whether it is a vacancy cluster or a dislocation) even when trapping is saturated. Alternatively, one can vary the energy of the positron beam to measure the depth profile. “When a measured quantity saturates, move to a different observable” is a practice common to all spectroscopies.

(4) The Tao–Eldrup formula is

$$ \tau_{o\text{-}\mathrm{Ps}}\,[\mathrm{ns}] = \frac{1}{2}\left[1 - \frac{R}{R+\Delta R} + \frac{1}{2\pi}\sin\!\left(\frac{2\pi R}{R+\Delta R}\right)\right]^{-1} $$

Setting $x \equiv R/(R+\Delta R)$, the quantity in brackets is $f(x) = 1 - x + \sin(2\pi x)/(2\pi)$, and $\tau = 0.5/f(x)$. The value of $f$ corresponding to $\tau=1.64\ \mathrm{ns}$ is

$$ f = \frac{0.5}{1.64} = 0.30488 $$

We fix $\Delta R = 0.166\ \mathrm{nm}$, vary $R$, and close in on $f$.

Successive substitution in the Tao–Eldrup formula ($\Delta R=0.166\ \mathrm{nm}$)
$R\ [\mathrm{nm}]$$x=R/(R+\Delta R)$$2\pi x\ [\mathrm{rad}]$$\sin(2\pi x)$$f(x)$$\tau\ [\mathrm{ns}]$
0.240.591133.7142$-0.54182$0.322631.550
0.250.600963.7760$-0.59266$0.304711.641
0.260.610333.8348$-0.63901$0.287971.736
0.300.643784.0450$-0.78542$0.231222.162

At $R=0.25\ \mathrm{nm}$ we get $\tau=1.641\ \mathrm{ns}$, in perfect agreement with the measured value $1.64\ \mathrm{ns}$. Refining numerically gives $R = 0.2499\ \mathrm{nm}$.

The volume of a sphere with $R=0.25\ \mathrm{nm}$ is

$$ V = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \frac{4}{3}\pi\times(0.25)^3 = 0.0654\ \mathrm{nm^3} = 65.4\ \mathrm{Å^3} $$

This is a little smaller than the example taken in Section 16.5.3 of this book, $\tau_3=2.16\ \mathrm{ns}$, $R=0.30\ \mathrm{nm}$, $V=0.11\ \mathrm{nm^3}$. The lifetime has become only $1.64/2.16 = 0.76$ times as large, yet the volume is $0.0654/0.113 = 0.58$ times as large, so it responds more sensitively than $\tau$ does. This nonlinearity is precisely the reason PALS can distinguish small differences in free volume.

Verification. We check the result of (1) independently by a two-component decomposition. With $\lambda_v = 1/244\ \mathrm{ps} = 4.098\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}$, the intensity of the long-lived component is

$$ I_2 = \frac{\kappa}{\lambda_b-\lambda_v+\kappa} = \frac{5.159}{6.135-4.098+5.159} = 0.717 $$

The short-lived component has $\tau_1 = 1/(\lambda_b+\kappa) = 1/(1.1294\times10^{10}) = 88.5\ \mathrm{ps}$, so the mean lifetime is

$$ \bar\tau = I_1\tau_1 + I_2\tau_2 = 0.283\times88.5 + 0.717\times244 = 25.0 + 175.0 = 200.0\ \mathrm{ps}\ \checkmark $$

The given $\bar\tau$ is reproduced. The dimensions also work out: $\kappa$ is in $[\mathrm{s^{-1}}]$ and $\mu_v$ is in “$\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ per atomic fraction,” so the quotient is dimensionless = atomic fraction ✓. For (4), we check with limits. For $R\to0$, $x\to0$, $f\to1$, and $\tau\to0.5\ \mathrm{ns}$ (the positronium is fully immersed in the electron layer of the wall, which is just the pickoff rate $\lambda_{2\gamma}=2\ \mathrm{ns^{-1}}$) ✓. For $R\to\infty$, $x\to1$, $f\to0$, and $\tau\to\infty$ (in reality it saturates at the vacuum value of $142\ \mathrm{ns}$) ✓. Both limits are physically correct.

Meaning. This exercise shows numerically a scene in which the antiparticle has become an “everyday tool of the laboratory.” Note the sensitivity in (1)–(2). A mere $37\ \mathrm{ps}$ increase in the mean lifetime lets us read off a concentration of $26\ \mathrm{appm}$. $26\ \mathrm{appm}$ is hardly visible in transmission electron microscopy, and is hard to separate from other scattering sources in electrical-resistance measurements. What allows positrons to do this is the very property of the antiparticle predicted by the Dirac equation: because of its positive charge, it falls selectively into vacancies (regions that are negatively charged because positive ions are missing). On the other hand, the Tao–Eldrup formula in (4) rests on the vacuum o-Ps lifetime of $142\ \mathrm{ns}$ as its reference. And that $142\ \mathrm{ns}$ is a number that comes from the $C$-parity conservation law of Chapter 6 ($^3S_1$ has $C=-1$, so it can decay only into $3\gamma$ or more) and from the QED of Chapter 10 ($3\gamma$ is suppressed by one power of $\alpha$). The scale of the instrument that measures the free volume of a gas-separation membrane is graduated by $C$ parity and the fine-structure constant. And what (3) teaches is that every sharp tool has an operating range, and outside it we must honestly say “it cannot be answered.”

Exercise 16.8: Detector resolution and soft errors

Problem (restated)

(1) Find the statistical limit $\Delta E_{\rm FWHM}$ when Mn K$\alpha$ ($5.90\ \mathrm{keV}$) is measured with a Si drift detector ($\varepsilon=3.6\ \mathrm{eV}$, $F=0.11$).

(2) Find the value when the same line is measured with a TES (take $\varepsilon$ to be effectively equivalent to $10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $F=0.005$ equivalent), and state how many times better it is than (1).

(3) Find the resolution when the $662\ \mathrm{keV}$ line of $^{137}$Cs is measured with LaBr$_3$(Ce) (light yield $63000\ \mathrm{ph/MeV}$, light collection plus quantum efficiency $20\%$), and compare it with the measured value $2.7\%$ in Table 16.10.

(4) A cosmic-ray iron ion ($\mathrm{LET}=15\ \mathrm{MeV\,cm^2/mg}$) penetrates an SRAM cell with a depletion-layer thickness of $2\ \mu\mathrm{m}$. Using the LET conversion rule of Chapter 16 of this book, find the generated charge and compare it with the critical charge $Q_{\rm crit}=5\ \mathrm{fC}$.

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1)–(3) are all applications of the single formula $\Delta E_{\rm FWHM} = 2.355\sqrt{F\varepsilon E}$ of Section 16.8.1 of this book. By running three materials whose $\varepsilon$ differ by many orders of magnitude through the same formula, we can confirm numerically the claim that “the progress of detectors is a history of lowering $\varepsilon$.” Part (4) is a direct application of the rule $1\ \mathrm{MeV\,cm^2/mg}\leftrightarrow10.4\ \mathrm{fC/\mu m}$ of Section 16.7.3.

(1) Substitute $F=0.11$, $\varepsilon=3.6\ \mathrm{eV}$, and $E=5.90\ \mathrm{keV}=5900\ \mathrm{eV}$. First, the quantity under the square root is

$$ F\varepsilon E = 0.11\times3.6\ \mathrm{eV}\times5900\ \mathrm{eV} = 0.396\times5900 = 2336.4\ \mathrm{eV^2} $$ $$ \sqrt{F\varepsilon E} = 48.34\ \mathrm{eV} $$

Therefore

$$ \Delta E_{\rm FWHM} = 2.355\times48.34 = 113.8\ \mathrm{eV} \simeq 114\ \mathrm{eV} $$

In terms of relative resolution, $113.8/5900 = 1.93\%$. For reference, the number of electron-hole pairs produced is $N=E/\varepsilon = 5900/3.6 = 1639$. Without the Fano factor the fluctuation would be $\sqrt{1639}=40.5$, but it is suppressed by a factor of $\sqrt{F}=0.332$ to $13.4$. This agrees well with the catalog value of the SDD in Table 16.11, $125\ \mathrm{eV}$ @ $6\ \mathrm{keV}$ (the difference is the electronic noise of the preamplifier).

(2) In a superconducting TES, the energy $2\Delta\approx3.5k_BT_c$ needed to break a Cooper pair plays the role of the value for “one quantum.” Putting $\varepsilon=10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}$ and $F=0.005$ into the same formula, we obtain

$$ F\varepsilon E = 0.005\times1\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}\times5900\ \mathrm{eV} = 5\times10^{-6}\times5900 = 2.95\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{eV^2} $$ $$ \sqrt{F\varepsilon E} = 0.1718\ \mathrm{eV} $$ $$ \Delta E_{\rm FWHM} = 2.355\times0.1718 = 0.404\ \mathrm{eV} $$

Compared with (1),

$$ \frac{113.8}{0.404} = 281 $$

that is, the statistical limit is better by about a factor of $280$. Why this happens is clear from the formula: in $\Delta E\propto\sqrt{F\varepsilon}$, $\varepsilon$ drops from $3.6\ \mathrm{eV}\to10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}$, a factor of $3600$ smaller, and $F$ drops from $0.11\to0.005$, a factor of $22$ smaller. Together $F\varepsilon$ becomes $3600\times22 = 7.92\times10^{4}$ times smaller, and its square root, $\sqrt{7.92\times10^{4}}=281$, is directly the ratio of the resolutions. The number of quanta generated is as large as $N=5900/10^{-3}=5.9\times10^{6}$.

However, this is only the statistical limit. In an actual TES, thermal fluctuation (phonon noise) dominates; as calculated in Section 16.8.2 of this book, the theoretical limit is around $1\ \mathrm{eV}$ and the implemented value is $1.6\ \mathrm{eV}$. Even comparing with this implemented value,

$$ \frac{113.8}{1.6} = 71 $$

it is still better by a factor of $70$. A resolution of $E/\Delta E = 5900/1.6 = 3700$ is comparable to that of a crystal spectrometer.

(3) In a scintillator the “quantum” is the photoelectron. This is the point that is fundamentally different from semiconductors: not all of the emitted photons become signal, and only the fraction given by the product of the light-collection efficiency and the quantum efficiency of the photocathode becomes photoelectrons. The number of photoelectrons generated is

$$ N_{\rm pe} = 63000\ \mathrm{ph/MeV}\times0.662\ \mathrm{MeV}\times0.20 = 41706\times0.20 = 8341 $$

In a scintillator the emission process is complicated and the Fano factor is close to $1$, so we may use naive Poisson statistics:

$$ \frac{\Delta E}{E} = \frac{2.355}{\sqrt{N_{\rm pe}}} = \frac{2.355}{\sqrt{8341}} = \frac{2.355}{91.33} = 2.58\times10^{-2} = 2.6\% $$

This agrees well with the measured value $2.7\%$ in Table 16.10. Converted to energy, $0.026\times662 = 17\ \mathrm{keV}$.

This agreement is in fact not easy to obtain. When the same calculation is done for NaI(Tl) in Step 5 of Section 16.8.1 of this book, it gives $3.3\%$, yet the measured value is $6\text{–}7\%$, worse by a factor of $2$. The cause of the difference is the scintillation nonproportionality (the fact that the light yield is not strictly proportional to the energy; it originates from quenching at high exciton density, that is, from Birks’ law). LaBr$_3$(Ce) has a small nonproportionality, so the statistical limit is realized almost as it is. The very fact that “calculation and measurement agree” is proof of the excellence of this material. For the same reason, although the light yield of $63000\ \mathrm{ph/MeV}$ is only $17\%$ larger than the $54000$ of CsI(Tl), the resolutions differ by a factor of $2.4$, $6.5\%$ versus $2.7\%$. One must not choose a material by looking only at the light yield.

(4) The conversion rule derived in Section 16.7.3 of this book was

$$ 1\ \mathrm{MeV\,cm^2/mg} \;\longleftrightarrow\; 10.4\ \mathrm{fC/\mu m}\quad(\text{in Si}) $$

When an iron ion with $\mathrm{LET}=15\ \mathrm{MeV\,cm^2/mg}$ passes through a depletion layer of thickness $2\ \mu\mathrm{m}$, the generated charge is

$$ q = 15\ \mathrm{MeV\,cm^2/mg}\times10.4\ \mathrm{fC/\mu m}\times2\ \mu\mathrm{m} = 312\ \mathrm{fC} $$

Comparing with the critical charge $Q_{\rm crit}=5\ \mathrm{fC}$,

$$ \frac{q}{Q_{\rm crit}} = \frac{312}{5} = 62 $$

That is a full factor of $62$. If this ion hits, the bit is certain to flip.

Let us recount directly, without using the conversion rule. The density of Si is $\rho=2.33\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}$, so the mass thickness for a thickness of $1\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ is

$$ \rho\,\ell = 2.33\ \mathrm{g/cm^3}\times1\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{cm} = 2.33\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{g/cm^2} = 0.233\ \mathrm{mg/cm^2} $$

Therefore the energy deposited in $2\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ is

$$ \Delta E = 15\ \mathrm{MeV\,cm^2/mg}\times0.233\ \mathrm{mg/cm^2\,\mu m^{-1}}\times2\ \mu\mathrm{m} = 6.99\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The number of electron-hole pairs generated, using $\varepsilon=3.6\ \mathrm{eV}$, is $6.99\times10^{6}/3.6 = 1.94\times10^{6}$ pairs, and as a charge this is

$$ q = 1.94\times10^{6}\times1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{C} = 3.11\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{C} = 311\ \mathrm{fC}\quad\checkmark $$

This agrees with the $312\ \mathrm{fC}$ obtained from the conversion rule. We see that the number $10.4\ \mathrm{fC/\mu m}$ in the conversion rule is itself built from just the three quantities $\rho$, $\varepsilon$, and $e$ listed above ($0.233/3.6\times1.602\times10^{-19}\times10^{6} = 1.04\times10^{-14}\ \mathrm{C}$).

What the number “$62$ times” means is that it cannot in principle be prevented by countermeasures on the device side. To raise $Q_{\rm crit}$ by a factor of $62$ one would have to raise either the capacitance of the storage node or the supply voltage by a factor of $62$, which collides head-on with the trends toward miniaturization and low power consumption (and, as in Step 5 of Section 16.7.3 of this book, miniaturization acts in the direction of lowering $Q_{\rm crit}$). Making the depletion layer thinner (SOI) is effective: if the thickness is reduced from $2\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ to $0.1\ \mu\mathrm{m}$, the charge becomes $1/20$, or $16\ \mathrm{fC}$, but this is still $3$ times $Q_{\rm crit}$. In the end, the only remaining option is redundancy on the system side.

  • ECC (error-correcting code): detects and corrects a one-bit flip. It has become essential in server DRAM.
  • TMR (triple modular redundancy): holds three copies of the same circuit and takes a majority vote. The price paid is an area and power consumption that are $3$ times larger or more. It is used in spacecraft and nuclear reactor instrumentation.
  • Scrubbing: periodically rereads the memory and corrects errors, clearing them before a second bit flip overlaps.

Verification. We check (1) against another example in Section 16.8.1 of this book. There, for $6\ \mathrm{keV}$, one obtains $2.355\sqrt{0.11\times3.6\times6000} = 115\ \mathrm{eV}$. Since $\Delta E\propto\sqrt{E}$, at $5.90\ \mathrm{keV}$ we get $115\times\sqrt{5900/6000} = 114\ \mathrm{eV}$ ✓. It is also consistent with the result of $1.55\ \mathrm{keV}$ obtained for the high-purity Ge example ($\varepsilon=2.96\ \mathrm{eV}$, $F=0.11$, $E=1332\ \mathrm{keV}$). As for dimensions, $F$ is dimensionless and $\varepsilon$ and $E$ are energies, so $\sqrt{F\varepsilon E}$ has the dimension of energy ✓. The relative resolution in (3), $2.355/\sqrt{N}$, is dimensionless ✓. For (4), $[\mathrm{MeV\,cm^2/mg}]\times[\mathrm{fC/\mu m}]/[\mathrm{MeV\,cm^2/mg}]\times[\mu\mathrm{m}] = [\mathrm{fC}]$ ✓. Also, converting the charge to a number of electrons, $312\times10^{-15}/1.602\times10^{-19} = 1.95\times10^{6}$, which agrees with the number of electron-hole pairs counted above ✓.

Meaning. The three numbers in (1)–(3), $114\ \mathrm{eV}$, $0.40\ \mathrm{eV}$, and $2.6\%$, all come from the same single formula $\Delta E = 2.355\sqrt{F\varepsilon E}$. Only $\varepsilon$ differs, and it forms a staircase: $26\ \mathrm{eV}$ (scintillator, several times the band gap to emit one visible photon) $\to3.6\ \mathrm{eV}$ (semiconductor, about three times the band gap per electron-hole pair) $\to10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}$ (superconductor, $2\Delta\approx3.5k_BT_c$ to break a Cooper pair). And what supports the last step is the BCS relation $2\Delta = 3.5k_BT_c$, behind which lies the spontaneous breaking of the $\mathrm{U}(1)$ symmetry treated in Chapter 13. The resolution specification of next-generation X-ray spectrometers equipped with TESs (such as Athena/X-IFU) is, in the end, determined by a single condensed-matter quantity: that the superconducting gap is of order $\mathrm{meV}$. Incidentally, the Resolve detector of the XRISM satellite, which measures the turbulent velocities of galaxy-cluster plasma to an accuracy of $\mathrm{km/s}$, is not a superconducting TES but a semiconductor-type microcalorimeter that uses a Si ion-implanted thermistor as its thermometer, and its in-orbit resolution is about $5\ \mathrm{eV}$ at $6\ \mathrm{keV}$. Whereas the TES type has reached $1.6\ \mathrm{eV}$ in the laboratory, it is this one that has a flight record so far; we should keep in mind, including this point, that the staircase of $\varepsilon$ and the maturity of implementation are separate matters.

(4) is the flip side of this. In a detector a “small $\varepsilon$” is a weapon, but in a memory device the same property is a weakness. Precisely because the $\varepsilon=3.6\ \mathrm{eV}$ of Si is small, a track of $1\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ creates a charge of $10.4\ \mathrm{fC}$ that is “readable.” One reason why wide-gap semiconductors are regarded as favorable for radiation hardness in Table 16.9 is that “$\varepsilon$ is large,” and this is a disadvantage for a detector (the signal is smaller for the same energy). The same material property can be an advantage or a drawback depending on the application. Particle-physics detectors and radiation-hardened memories for spacecraft use exactly the same physics in opposite directions.

E.17 Solutions for Appendix A: Dirac Delta Function and Normalization

Exercise A.1: Basic properties of the delta function

Problem (restated)

(1) Show that $\delta(ax)=\delta(x)/\abs{a}$, for both $a>0$ and $a<0$, by integrating against a test function. Note that for $a<0$ the direction of the integration interval is reversed.

(2) Let $a>0$. Write $\delta(x^2-a^2)$ as a sum of simple delta functions.

(3) Using (2), evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\cos x\;\delta(x^2-\pi^2)\,\dd x$.

(4) Evaluate $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x^3\,\delta''(x-2)\,\dd x$.

(5) Write down $\delta(\sin x)$ and find $\displaystyle\int_{0}^{10}\ee^{-x}\,\delta(\sin x)\,\dd x$ (note that $10<4\pi=12.566$).

Solution

Strategy. We use only the three tools of Section A.1 of this book. They are the definition (“$\delta$ acquires meaning only when integrated against a test function”), the composite-function rule $\delta(f(x))=\sum_i\delta(x-x_i)/\abs{f'(x_i)}$ (Derivation 3 of this book), and the rule for derivatives $\int f\,\delta^{(n)}(x-a)\dd x=(-1)^n f^{(n)}(a)$ (Derivation 4 of this book). Part (1) follows from the very definition, parts (2)–(3) and (5) from the composite-function rule, and part (4) from the rule for derivatives.

(1) Take an arbitrary continuous function $f$ and evaluate $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,\delta(ax)\,\dd x$.

The case $a>0$. Substitute $y=ax$, so that $x=y/a$ and $\dd x=\dd y/a$. Since $a>0$, $y:-\infty\to\infty$ as $x:-\infty\to\infty$, and the direction of the integration interval does not change. Therefore

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,\delta(ax)\,\dd x = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f\!\left(\frac{y}{a}\right)\delta(y)\,\frac{\dd y}{a} = \frac{1}{a}\,f(0) $$

In the last equality we used the definition $\int g(y)\delta(y)\dd y=g(0)$ and $f(0/a)=f(0)$.

The case $a<0$. We make the same substitution $y=ax$, $\dd x=\dd y/a$, but now, since $a<0$, $x\to+\infty$ is mapped to $y\to-\infty$ and $x\to-\infty$ to $y\to+\infty$. That is, the direction of the integration interval is reversed.

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f(x)\,\delta(ax)\,\dd x = \int_{+\infty}^{-\infty}f\!\left(\frac{y}{a}\right)\delta(y)\,\frac{\dd y}{a} = -\frac{1}{a}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}f\!\left(\frac{y}{a}\right)\delta(y)\,\dd y = -\frac{1}{a}\,f(0) $$

Here the overall sign flipped when we interchanged the upper and lower limits. For $a<0$ we have $-1/a=1/\abs{a}$, so in this case too the result is $f(0)/\abs{a}$.

Summary. In both cases $\int f(x)\delta(ax)\dd x=f(0)/\abs{a}$, which agrees with $\int f(x)\left[\delta(x)/\abs{a}\right]\dd x$. Since the two are equal for arbitrary $f$, as distributions

$$ \delta(ax)=\frac{1}{\abs{a}}\,\delta(x)\qquad(a\neq0) $$

holds. Incidentally, the typical mistake is to skip the separation into $a>0$ and $a<0$, write only $\dd x=\dd y/a$, and give $1/a$ as the answer. The left-hand side $\delta(ax)$ does not change when the sign of $a$ is changed (because $\delta$ is an even function), whereas $1/a$ does change sign, so such an answer is inconsistent from the start.

(2) Let $f(x)=x^2-a^2$. The zeros, $f(x)=0$, are the two points $x=\pm a$, and since $a>0$ they are distinct simple zeros. The derivative is $f'(x)=2x$, so

$$ \abs{f'(+a)}=\abs{2a}=2a,\qquad \abs{f'(-a)}=\abs{-2a}=2a $$

(we used $a>0$). Substituting into the composite-function rule, we obtain

$$ \delta(x^2-a^2)=\frac{1}{2a}\Big[\delta(x-a)+\delta(x+a)\Big] $$

The two zeros carry equal weights because $\abs{f'}$ equals $2a$ at both, which reflects the fact that the graph of $x^2-a^2$ is symmetric about $x=0$.

There is a reason why the problem statement takes care to specify $a>0$. As $a\to0$ the two zeros merge at $x=0$, where $f'(0)=0$. The composite-function rule presupposes that the zeros are simple ($f'\neq0$), so the formula cannot be used in this limit. Indeed, the divergence of $1/2a$ is itself the signal of the breakdown. The symbol $\delta(x^2)$ has no meaning as a distribution as it stands.

(3) Setting $a=\pi$ in (2) gives

$$ \delta(x^2-\pi^2)=\frac{1}{2\pi}\Big[\delta(x-\pi)+\delta(x+\pi)\Big] $$

We insert this into the integral.

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\cos x\;\delta(x^2-\pi^2)\,\dd x = \frac{1}{2\pi}\left[\int\cos x\,\delta(x-\pi)\dd x+\int\cos x\,\delta(x+\pi)\dd x\right] = \frac{1}{2\pi}\Big[\cos\pi+\cos(-\pi)\Big] $$

Since $\cos\pi=\cos(-\pi)=-1$,

$$ = \frac{1}{2\pi}\left[(-1)+(-1)\right] = -\frac{1}{\pi} = -0.31831 $$

is the result.

(4) In the formula of Derivation 4 of this book, take $n=2$, $a=2$, and $f(x)=x^3$. Since $f'(x)=3x^2$ and $f''(x)=6x$,

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x^3\,\delta''(x-2)\,\dd x = (-1)^2 f''(2) = 6\times2 = 12 $$

The sign $(-1)^n$ is the product of the minus signs produced by each of the $n$ integrations by parts; for $n=2$ they cancel to give $+1$. To be safe, let us perform the integration by parts explicitly twice. The boundary terms all drop out because $\delta$ and its derivatives vanish at infinity, and

$$ \int x^3\delta''(x-2)\dd x=-\int 3x^2\,\delta'(x-2)\dd x=+\int 6x\,\delta(x-2)\dd x=12 $$

gives the same answer.

(5) The zeros of $f(x)=\sin x$ are $x=n\pi$ ($n\in\mathbb{Z}$), and from $f'(x)=\cos x$ we get $\abs{f'(n\pi)}=\abs{\cos n\pi}=\abs{(-1)^n}=1$. Since the weight is $1$ at every zero,

$$ \delta(\sin x)=\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}\delta(x-n\pi) $$

is a “comb of $\delta$’s.” Next we count the zeros lying in the integration interval $0\le x\le10$. Since $\pi=3.14159$, $2\pi=6.28319$, $3\pi=9.42478$, and $4\pi=12.56637$, we have $3\pi<10<4\pi$, so the zeros in the interval are the four points $x=0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi,\ 3\pi$. Of these, $x=0$ lies at the endpoint of the interval. There are different conventions for how to count a $\delta$ at an endpoint; following the hint of this book, we count only the three zeros in the interior of the open interval $0<x<10$, which gives

$$ \int_0^{10}\ee^{-x}\,\delta(\sin x)\,\dd x = \ee^{-\pi}+\ee^{-2\pi}+\ee^{-3\pi} $$

The numerical values are $\ee^{-\pi}=0.0432139$, $\ee^{-2\pi}=0.00186744$, and $\ee^{-3\pi}=0.0000806995$, so

$$ = 0.0432139+0.0018674+0.0000807 = 0.0451621 \simeq 0.0452 $$

Note that if we adopt the convention of counting the endpoint $x=0$ as “half,” we obtain $0.5+0.04516=0.5452$, and the answer changes drastically. Which is correct is determined by which interval the original physics refers to. The lesson of this subproblem is that, once you have written an expression in which the core of a $\delta$ sits on the end of the integration interval, you should stop there and check where the interval comes from.

Verification. We check in three ways. First, dimensions. As noted right after Derivation 2 of this book, the dimension of $\delta(x)$ is $[x]^{-1}$; the dimension of the right-hand side of (2), $\left[\delta(x-a)+\delta(x+a)\right]/2a$, is $[x]^{-1}\cdot[x]^{-1}=[x]^{-2}$, and that of the left-hand side $\delta(x^2-a^2)$ is $[x^2]^{-1}=[x]^{-2}$, so they indeed agree. Second, (3) can also be read directly, without going through the composite-function rule: $\delta(x^2-\pi^2)$ picks up the two points $x=\pm\pi$ with weight $1/2\pi$ each, and since $\cos x=-1$ at both points, we get $2\times(-1)\times1/(2\pi)=-1/\pi$, which agrees. Third, the series in (5) is a geometric series with common ratio $\ee^{-\pi}=0.0432$, whose first term accounts for $95.7\%$ of the total. The exact value extended to the infinite interval is $\ee^{-\pi}/(1-\ee^{-\pi})=0.045166$, which nearly coincides with the $0.045162$ we obtained. This comparison also confirms that the terms beyond $3\pi$ do not matter.

Meaning. The scaling law in (1) is a statement that $\delta$ “has the dimension of an inverse length.” This is not mere formalism but bears directly on practical work. For example, the density of states $D(E)=\sum_n\delta(E-\varepsilon_n)$ has units of $\mathrm{eV^{-1}}$, $\delta^3(\xx)$ has units of $\text{Å}^{-3}$, and the four-dimensional $\delta^4(p)$ has units of $\mathrm{GeV^{-4}}$. Checking that the dimensions of $(2\pi)^4\delta^4$ and $\dd^3p/[(2\pi)^32E]$ cancel in a scattering cross-section formula is the cheapest way to find errors in a calculation. The “comb” $\delta(\sin x)=\sum_n\delta(x-n\pi)$ of (5) has the same structure as the Poisson summation formula $\sum_{\bm R}\ee^{\ii\qq\cdot\bm R}=\frac{(2\pi)^3}{v_\text{cell}}\sum_{\bm G}\delta^3(\qq-\bm G)$ in Section A.2.2 of this book. The $\delta$ of a function with periodic zeros is a train of equally spaced $\delta$’s. That X-ray diffraction by a crystal produces sharp peaks only in the directions satisfying the Laue condition, and that Umklapp processes appear in electron-phonon scattering, are both consequences of this one line. It looks like a one-dimensional practice problem, but it is the very mathematics of the diffraction patterns that materials scientists look at every day.

Exercise A.2: The mass shell and invariant phase space

Problem (restated)

(1) Using the composite-function rule, show that $\delta(p^2-m^2)\theta(p^0)=\delta(p^0-E_\pp)/2E_\pp$.

(2) For a boost in the $z$ direction (velocity $\beta$), show that $\partial p'^3/\partial p^3=E'/E$, and verify directly that $\dd^3p/E$ is Lorentz invariant. Do not forget that $E$ depends on $p^3$.

(3) Find the value of the two-body phase space $\int\dd\Pi_2$ for $\pi^0\to\gamma\gamma$ ($m_{\pi^0}=134.977\ \mathrm{MeV}$, the photons are massless). Confirm that the answer does not depend on the mass of the $\pi^0$.

(4) For $\rho^0\to\pi^+\pi^-$ ($m_\rho=775.26\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $m_{\pi^\pm}=139.570\ \mathrm{MeV}$), find $\abs{\pp}$ in the center-of-mass frame and $\int\dd\Pi_2$, and compare with the value in (3).

Solution

Strategy. In the natural units $\hbar=c=1$ and with the metric $g^{\mu\nu}=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$ of this book, $p^2=(p^0)^2-\abs{\pp}^2$. Parts (1) and (2) are a reconstruction of Derivations 8 and 13 of this book, and parts (3) and (4) are numerical evaluations of the result $\int\dd\Pi_2=\abs{\pp}/(4\pi\sqrt s)$ of Derivation 14 of this book.

(1) Fix the spatial momentum $\pp$ and regard

$$ f(p^0)\equiv p^2-m^2=(p^0)^2-\abs{\pp}^2-m^2=(p^0)^2-E_\pp^2, \qquad E_\pp\equiv\sqrt{\abs{\pp}^2+m^2}\ (>0) $$

as a function of $p^0$. The zeros are the two points $(p^0)^2=E_\pp^2$, that is, $p^0=\pm E_\pp$. Whether $m>0$, or $m=0$ with $\pp\neq0$, we have $E_\pp>0$, so these two are distinct simple zeros. The derivative is $f'(p^0)=2p^0$, so

$$ \abs{f'(+E_\pp)}=2E_\pp,\qquad \abs{f'(-E_\pp)}=\abs{-2E_\pp}=2E_\pp $$

Substituting into the composite-function rule gives

$$ \delta(p^2-m^2)=\frac{1}{2E_\pp}\Big[\delta(p^0-E_\pp)+\delta(p^0+E_\pp)\Big] $$

We multiply this by the step function $\theta(p^0)$. The $\delta$ of the first term has its core at $p^0=+E_\pp>0$, which lies in the region where $\theta(p^0)=1$, so it survives. The $\delta$ of the second term has its core at $p^0=-E_\pp<0$, where $\theta(p^0)=0$, so it vanishes. Hence

$$ \delta(p^2-m^2)\,\theta(p^0)=\frac{1}{2E_\pp}\,\delta(p^0-E_\pp) $$

holds. Integrating this over $\dd^4p=\dd p^0\,\dd^3p$, the $p^0$ integral is disposed of by the $\delta$, and we obtain $\int\dd^4p\,\delta(p^2-m^2)\theta(p^0)\,g(p)=\int\frac{\dd^3p}{2E_\pp}g(E_\pp,\pp)$. On the left-hand side, $\dd^4p$ is invariant, $p^2-m^2$ is a scalar, and $\theta(p^0)$ is also invariant because the direction of time is preserved under proper orthochronous Lorentz transformations; hence $\dd^3p/2E_\pp$ on the right-hand side must also be Lorentz invariant.

(2) Boost with velocity $\beta$ in the $z$ direction. With $\gamma=1/\sqrt{1-\beta^2}$,

$$ p'^{\,3}=\gamma\left(p^3-\beta E\right),\qquad E'=\gamma\left(E-\beta p^3\right),\qquad p'^{\,1}=p^1,\quad p'^{\,2}=p^2 $$

The transformation of $\delta^3$ and $\dd^3p$ requires the Jacobian $\abs{\partial\pp'/\partial\pp}$, but since the transverse components $1,2$ transform by the identity, the determinant reduces to $\partial p'^{\,3}/\partial p^3$ alone.

Here is the key point. When we vary $p^3$ infinitesimally, $E$ is not an independent variable. Since the particle is on the mass shell, $E=\sqrt{(p^1)^2+(p^2)^2+(p^3)^2+m^2}$, which depends on $p^3$. Therefore

$$ \frac{\partial E}{\partial p^3}=\frac{p^3}{\sqrt{\abs{\pp}^2+m^2}}=\frac{p^3}{E} $$

Using this, we compute the Jacobian.

$$ \frac{\partial p'^{\,3}}{\partial p^3} =\gamma\left(1-\beta\frac{\partial E}{\partial p^3}\right) =\gamma\left(1-\beta\frac{p^3}{E}\right) =\frac{\gamma\left(E-\beta p^3\right)}{E} =\frac{E'}{E} $$

In the last equality we used the second boost equation, $E'=\gamma(E-\beta p^3)$. Therefore the volume element transforms as

$$ \dd^3p'=\frac{\partial p'^{\,3}}{\partial p^3}\,\dd^3p=\frac{E'}{E}\,\dd^3p \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \frac{\dd^3p'}{E'}=\frac{\dd^3p}{E} $$

and $\dd^3p/E$ is Lorentz invariant. At the same time, we have also learned that $\dd^3p$ by itself is not invariant but is off by the factor $E'/E$. This is the fundamental reason why the factor $2E$ is included in the relativistic normalization in Section A.5 of this book. That is, $\delta^3(\pp-\qq)$ transforms in the opposite way, $\delta^3(\pp'-\qq')=(E/E')\delta^3(\pp-\qq)$, so only the combination $E\,\delta^3(\pp-\qq)$ is invariant.

(3) The result of Derivation 14 of this book is, in the isotropic case, $\int\dd\Pi_2=\abs{\pp}/(4\pi\sqrt s)$. In $\pi^0\to\gamma\gamma$ the initial state is a $\pi^0$ at rest, so $\sqrt s=m_{\pi^0}$, and the final state consists of two massless photons, so $m_1=m_2=0$. From energy conservation in the center-of-mass frame, $\sqrt s=E_1+E_2=2\abs{\pp}$, we have

$$ \abs{\pp}=\frac{\sqrt s}{2} $$

Substituting this gives

$$ \int\dd\Pi_2=\frac{\sqrt s/2}{4\pi\sqrt s}=\frac{1}{8\pi}=0.0397887 $$

and $\sqrt s$ cancels completely between numerator and denominator, so the result does not depend on the mass. There is no need even to insert numbers: whether $m_{\pi^0}=134.977\ \mathrm{MeV}$ or $m_{\eta}=547.86\ \mathrm{MeV}$, the phase space of a massless two-body final state is the same $1/8\pi$. Note also that $\int\dd\Pi_2$ is dimensionless. Indeed, $\dd^3p/[(2\pi)^32E]$ has dimension $[\text{energy}]^2$, so two of them give $[\text{energy}]^4$, while $(2\pi)^4\delta^4$ has dimension $[\text{energy}]^{-4}$, and the product is dimensionless.

(4) In $\rho^0\to\pi^+\pi^-$ we have $\sqrt s=m_\rho=775.26\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and the final state consists of two bodies of equal mass $m_\pi=139.570\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Setting $m_1=m_2=m$ in the Källén function formula at the end of Derivation 14 of this book,

$$ \lambda(s,m^2,m^2)=s^2+m^4+m^4-2sm^2-2m^4-2sm^2=s^2-4sm^2=s\left(s-4m^2\right) $$

so that

$$ \abs{\pp}=\frac{\sqrt{\lambda(s,m^2,m^2)}}{2\sqrt s}=\frac{\sqrt{s(s-4m^2)}}{2\sqrt s}=\frac12\sqrt{s-4m^2}=\frac12\sqrt{m_\rho^2-4m_\pi^2} $$

We insert the numbers step by step.

$$ m_\rho^2=(775.26)^2=601028.07\ \mathrm{MeV^2}, \qquad 4m_\pi^2=4\times(139.570)^2=4\times19479.7849=77919.14\ \mathrm{MeV^2} $$ $$ m_\rho^2-4m_\pi^2=601028.07-77919.14=523108.93\ \mathrm{MeV^2}, \qquad \sqrt{523108.93}=723.263\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ $$ \abs{\pp}=\frac{723.263}{2}=361.63\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

Substituting this, the phase space is

$$ \int\dd\Pi_2=\frac{\abs{\pp}}{4\pi\sqrt s}=\frac{361.63}{4\pi\times775.26}=\frac{361.63}{9742.20}=0.0371200 $$

The ratio to $1/8\pi=0.0397887$ of (3) is

$$ \frac{0.0371200}{0.0397887}=0.93293 $$

In general this ratio equals $2\abs{\pp}/\sqrt s$. Indeed, $\int\dd\Pi_2/(1/8\pi)=\left[\abs{\pp}/(4\pi\sqrt s)\right]\times8\pi=2\abs{\pp}/\sqrt s$, and numerically too, $2\times361.63/775.26=0.93293$ agrees. Because the final-state pions are massive, the available momentum space is narrower, and the phase space has shrunk by just $6.7\%$.

Verification. We check in three ways. First, the limits. Setting $m_\pi\to0$ in the formula of (4) gives $\abs{\pp}\to m_\rho/2$, which connects continuously to the massless case of (3) and reproduces $1/8\pi$. Conversely, at the threshold $m_\rho\to2m_\pi=279.14\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $\abs{\pp}\to0$ and the phase space closes to zero. Both limits are physically correct. Second, the ratio $2\abs{\pp}/\sqrt s$ is precisely the speed of the final-state particles in the center-of-mass frame, $\beta^*=\abs{\pp}/E^*=\abs{\pp}/(\sqrt s/2)$, which must satisfy $0\le\beta^*<1$. The value $0.93293$ we obtained is indeed in this range. Third, dimensions. $\abs{\pp}/(4\pi\sqrt s)$ is $[\mathrm{MeV}]/[\mathrm{MeV}]$ and hence dimensionless, consistent with the dimensional accounting stated in (3).

Meaning. The two-body phase space $\int\dd\Pi_2=\abs{\pp}/(4\pi\sqrt s)$ merely counts “how many destinations the final state has.” The decay rate has the form $\Gamma\propto\abs{\mathcal M}^2\int\dd\Pi_2$, so no matter how large the matrix element $\mathcal M$ is, if there is nowhere to go, the decay does not occur. That near threshold $\abs{\pp}=\frac12\sqrt{s-4m^2}\propto\sqrt{s-s_\text{th}}$ rises as a square root is exactly the same mathematics as the three-dimensional free-electron density of states $D(E)\propto\sqrt E$ of Derivation 10 of this book rising as a square root from the band edge. In both cases the reason is that “we are counting the area of a spherical shell of radius $\abs{\pp}$ in three-dimensional momentum space.” On the materials science side, this has the same origin as the band-edge absorption spectrum of a semiconductor rising as $\sqrt{\hbar\omega-E_g}$, and as the phonon density of states being proportional to $\omega^2$ in the Debye region. When the dimension is lowered, the exponent changes too: in two dimensions the density of states is constant, and in one dimension it diverges (van Hove singularity). The operation of counting final states obeys the same rule, whether inside an accelerator or inside a crystal.

Exercise A.3: The Sokhotski–Plemelj formula and its applications

Problem (restated)

(1) Rationalize the denominator of $\dfrac{1}{x+\ii\epsilon}$, separate it into real and imaginary parts, and show that it becomes the Sokhotski–Plemelj formula in the limit $\epsilon\to0^+$.

(2) The local density of states is obtained from the imaginary part of $G^R(E)=\sum_n\dfrac{\abs{c_n}^2}{E-\varepsilon_n+\ii\eta}$. Compute $-\frac{1}{\pi}\mathrm{Im}\,G^R(E)$.

(3) Find $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\ee^{-x^2}}{x+\ii\epsilon}\,\dd x$.

(4) When the imaginary part of the quasiparticle self-energy in copper is $2\abs{\mathrm{Im}\Sigma}=0.10\ \mathrm{eV}$, find the quasiparticle lifetime $\tau=\hbar/2\abs{\mathrm{Im}\Sigma}$ in seconds. Also compare it with the lifetime of the $Z$ boson ($\Gamma_Z=2.495\ \mathrm{GeV}$). Use $\hbar=6.582\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}$.

Solution

Strategy. The Sokhotski–Plemelj formula $\displaystyle\lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}\frac{1}{x\pm\ii\epsilon}=\PV\frac{1}{x}\mp\ii\pi\,\delta(x)$ of Section A.4 of this book is the tool for every part. Part (1) is a reconstruction of its proof, parts (2) and (3) are applications, and part (4) is a numerical calculation that applies one and the same line, “the inverse of the Lorentzian width is the lifetime,” to two systems that differ by $10$ orders of magnitude.

(1) Keeping $\epsilon>0$ finite, we multiply the numerator and denominator by the complex conjugate of the denominator to make the denominator real.

$$ \frac{1}{x+\ii\epsilon} =\frac{x-\ii\epsilon}{(x+\ii\epsilon)(x-\ii\epsilon)} =\frac{x-\ii\epsilon}{x^2+\epsilon^2} =\underbrace{\frac{x}{x^2+\epsilon^2}}_{\text{real part}}\;-\;\ii\underbrace{\frac{\epsilon}{x^2+\epsilon^2}}_{\text{magnitude of the imaginary part}} $$

The real and imaginary parts are now completely separated. Below we examine the limit $\epsilon\to0^+$ of each.

Imaginary part. We can simply use the Lorentzian representation $\displaystyle\delta(x)=\lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{\epsilon}{x^2+\epsilon^2}$ of Section A.1.3 of this book. That is,

$$ \frac{\epsilon}{x^2+\epsilon^2}=\pi\cdot\frac{1}{\pi}\frac{\epsilon}{x^2+\epsilon^2}\;\xrightarrow[\epsilon\to0^+]{}\;\pi\,\delta(x) $$

The normalization is checked by $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\epsilon\,\dd x}{x^2+\epsilon^2}=\left[\arctan\frac{x}{\epsilon}\right]_{-\infty}^{\infty}=\pi$, which does not depend on $\epsilon$. Hence the contribution of the imaginary part is $-\ii\pi\delta(x)$.

Real part. What we must show is that, for any smooth test function $f$,

$$ \lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{x\,f(x)}{x^2+\epsilon^2}\,\dd x=\PV\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{f(x)}{x}\,\dd x $$

Fix a small $\eta>0$ and split the integral into the outer region $\abs{x}>\eta$ and the inner region $\abs{x}<\eta$. In the outer region the integrand converges uniformly to $f(x)/x$ as $\epsilon\to0$, so it coincides exactly with the outer part in the definition of the principal value. In the inner region we split $f(x)=f(0)+\left[f(x)-f(0)\right]$. The contribution of the first term is

$$ f(0)\int_{-\eta}^{\eta}\frac{x\,\dd x}{x^2+\epsilon^2}=0 $$

Since the integrand is an odd function of $x$ and the interval is symmetric, this is exactly zero regardless of the value of $\epsilon$. For the second term, the mean value theorem gives $\abs{f(x)-f(0)}\le M\abs{x}$ (with $M=\max\abs{f'}$), so

$$ \left|\int_{-\eta}^{\eta}\frac{x\left[f(x)-f(0)\right]}{x^2+\epsilon^2}\dd x\right| \le M\int_{-\eta}^{\eta}\frac{x^2}{x^2+\epsilon^2}\dd x \le M\int_{-\eta}^{\eta}\dd x=2M\eta $$

can be estimated, and this goes to zero as $\eta\to0$ independently of $\epsilon$. The same estimate holds on the principal-value side, so the inner contributions agree on both sides (both are zero). Therefore the real part equals the principal-value integral.

Combining. Adding the real and imaginary parts, we obtain

$$ \lim_{\epsilon\to0^+}\frac{1}{x+\ii\epsilon}=\PV\frac{1}{x}-\ii\pi\,\delta(x) $$

For the case $-\ii\epsilon$, only the sign of the imaginary part changes in the first step of making the denominator real, so we get $\PV\frac1x+\ii\pi\delta(x)$. Together, the two cases read $\displaystyle\frac{1}{x\pm\ii\epsilon}=\PV\frac1x\mp\ii\pi\delta(x)$.

(2) We apply the result of (1) to each term of the sum with $x=E-\varepsilon_n$ and $\epsilon=\eta$. Since $\abs{c_n}^2$ is real, it can be taken out of the imaginary part.

$$ G^R(E)=\sum_n\abs{c_n}^2\left[\PV\frac{1}{E-\varepsilon_n}-\ii\pi\,\delta(E-\varepsilon_n)\right] $$

Taking the imaginary part, the principal-value term (which is real) drops out, and

$$ \mathrm{Im}\,G^R(E)=-\pi\sum_n\abs{c_n}^2\,\delta(E-\varepsilon_n) $$

Therefore

$$ -\frac{1}{\pi}\,\mathrm{Im}\,G^R(E)=\sum_n\abs{c_n}^2\,\delta(E-\varepsilon_n) $$

This is the counting of the eigenstates $n$ weighted by $\abs{c_n}^2$, the weight of the projection onto the local orbital of interest; that is, it is the local density of states (LDOS). If we set $\abs{c_n}^2=1$, we return to the formula $-\frac1\pi\mathrm{Im}\,\Tr G^R(E)=D(E)$ for the total density of states in Section A.4 of this book. Moreover, if $\sum_n\abs{c_n}^2=1$ (completeness), then $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\left[-\frac1\pi\mathrm{Im}\,G^R(E)\right]\dd E=1$, so the LDOS is normalized.

(3) We use the Sokhotski–Plemelj formula with $f(x)=\ee^{-x^2}$.

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\ee^{-x^2}}{x+\ii\epsilon}\,\dd x =\PV\!\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\ee^{-x^2}}{x}\,\dd x-\ii\pi\,\ee^{-0^2} $$

The integrand $\ee^{-x^2}/x$ of the first term on the right-hand side is an odd function of $x$ (the numerator is even and the denominator is odd). The principal-value integral cuts out a symmetric neighborhood of $x=0$, so the contributions of the intervals $(-\infty,-\eta)$ and $(\eta,\infty)$ cancel exactly with opposite signs, and the principal value is zero. The second term is $-\ii\pi$ because $\ee^{0}=1$. Hence

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\ee^{-x^2}}{x+\ii\epsilon}\,\dd x=-\ii\pi $$

That the answer is purely imaginary is no accident. The principal-value part, which is the origin of the real part of the integrand, vanished thanks to the fact that $\ee^{-x^2}$ is an even function. If we insert, instead of $\ee^{-x^2}$, a test function that is not an even function of $x$, for example $\ee^{-(x-1)^2}$, the real part survives.

(4) For the copper quasiparticle, we simply insert the numbers into the given formula.

$$ \tau_\mathrm{Cu}=\frac{\hbar}{2\abs{\mathrm{Im}\Sigma}}=\frac{6.582\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}}{0.10\ \mathrm{eV}} =6.582\times10^{-15}\ \mathrm{s}=6.58\ \mathrm{fs} $$

For the $Z$ boson, we use the relation $\tau=\hbar/\Gamma$ between the Breit–Wigner width $\Gamma$ and the lifetime ($\tau=1/\Gamma$ in natural units). Since $\Gamma_Z=2.495\ \mathrm{GeV}=2.495\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{eV}$,

$$ \tau_Z=\frac{\hbar}{\Gamma_Z}=\frac{6.582\times10^{-16}\ \mathrm{eV\,s}}{2.495\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{eV}} =2.638\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{s} $$

Taking the ratio gives

$$ \frac{\tau_\mathrm{Cu}}{\tau_Z}=\frac{6.582\times10^{-15}}{2.638\times10^{-25}}=2.495\times10^{10} $$

so the two differ by a factor of about $2.5\times10^{10}$, or in orders of magnitude, a factor of $10^{10}$. That this ratio agrees with the ratio of the widths, $2.495\times10^9/0.10=2.495\times10^{10}$, is natural, since both use the same formula $\tau=\hbar/(\text{width})$.

Verification. We give three checks. First, dimensions: dividing the unit $\mathrm{eV\,s}$ of $\hbar$ by the energy unit $\mathrm{eV}$ leaves $\mathrm{s}$. A time came out, so this is correct. Second, we convert the obtained lifetimes into lengths to examine their physical plausibility. The $Z$ boson travels only $c\tau_Z=2.998\times10^8\times2.638\times10^{-25}=7.91\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{m}=0.0791\ \mathrm{fm}$. This is less than $1/10$ of the proton radius $0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$, which is consistent with the fact that the $Z$ is a “particle that cannot be seen as a track” and can be observed only as a peak in the invariant-mass distribution. On the other hand, for the copper quasiparticle, using the Fermi velocity $v_F=1.57\times10^6\ \mathrm{m/s}$, the mean free path is $v_F\tau_\mathrm{Cu}=1.57\times10^6\times6.582\times10^{-15}=1.03\times10^{-8}\ \mathrm{m}\simeq10\ \mathrm{nm}$. The mean free path obtained from the electrical conductivity of copper at room temperature is about $30\text{–}40\ \mathrm{nm}$, so the two are of the same order (the width $0.10\ \mathrm{eV}$ was chosen somewhat on the large side, so it is reasonable that the lifetime comes out shorter, that is, the mean free path comes out shorter). In any case, it is consistent with the picture of a “well-conducting metal,” in which the mean free path is several tens to a hundred times the lattice constant $3.6\ \text{Å}$. Third, the answer to (3) can also be confirmed by the alternative proof using the residue theorem in the Math Note of Section A.4 of this book. Going around the pole on the real axis by a half circle in the upper half-plane yields half of the residue, $-\ii\pi f(0)=-\ii\pi$, and the straight part (the principal value) vanishes because the integrand is odd. The answer is the same.

Meaning. The Sokhotski–Plemelj formula is a device that separates the real and imaginary parts in a single formula. The imaginary part picks up the $\delta$ function, that is, “processes that actually occur,” and the real part picks up the principal value, that is, “the phase shift due to virtual processes.” In particle physics this becomes Feynman’s $\ii\epsilon$ prescription, which selects the time-ordered product and gives rise to the optical theorem and the Cutkosky rules. In condensed matter physics it becomes $-\frac1\pi\mathrm{Im}\,G^R=D(E)$, giving the density of states, and together with causality it gives rise to the Kramers–Kronig relations. What the numbers in (4) show is this identity. An electron in copper is scattered in $6.6\ \mathrm{fs}$ with a width of $0.10\ \mathrm{eV}$, and a $Z$ boson decays in $2.6\times10^{-25}\ \mathrm{s}$ with a width of $2.495\ \mathrm{GeV}$. The two differ by a factor of $10^{10}$, yet both are the Lorentzian width of a spectrum, the same quantity entering at the same place in the same propagator. Reading the quasiparticle lifetime from the linewidth of the spectral function measured by ARPES, and reading the lifetime of the $Z$ from the linewidth of the invariant-mass distribution at an accelerator, differ only in the object measured; the analysis is literally identical.

Exercise A.4: The Yukawa potential and screening

Problem (restated)

(1) Take $m\to0$ in Derivation 15 and check that the result is consistent with $1/(4\pi r)$ being the Green function of $-\nabla^2$.

(2) Show by direct calculation the inverse transform $\displaystyle\int\dd^3r\;\frac{\ee^{-mr}}{4\pi r}\,\ee^{-\ii\qq\cdot\bm r} = \frac{1}{\abs{\qq}^2+m^2}$.

(3) Find the range, in fm, of the forces mediated by the $\pi^\pm$ ($139.570\ \mathrm{MeV}$) and the $W^\pm$ ($80.377\ \mathrm{GeV}$). Use $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$.

(4) Find the Thomas–Fermi screening length $\lambda_\mathrm{TF}$ of aluminum (three valence electrons, $n=18.1\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, $E_F=11.7\ \mathrm{eV}$) and compare it with the $0.55\ \text{Å}$ of copper. Use $e^2/4\pi\epsilon_0=14.400\ \mathrm{eV\,\text{Å}}$.

Solution

Strategy. The Yukawa-type Fourier transform $\displaystyle\int\frac{\dd^3q}{(2\pi)^3}\frac{\ee^{\ii\qq\cdot\bm r}}{\abs{\qq}^2+m^2}=\frac{\ee^{-mr}}{4\pi r}$ of Section A.6 of this book plays the leading role. Part (1) is a consistency check that compares its $m\to0$ limit with $-\nabla^2(1/4\pi r)=\delta^3(\xx)$ of Derivation 6 of this book; part (2) is a calculation running the same transform in the opposite direction; and parts (3) and (4) are numerical problems in which only “what to substitute for $m$” is changed.

(1) Taking $m\to0$ in the result $I(r)=\ee^{-mr}/(4\pi r)$ of Derivation 15 of this book, we have $\ee^{-mr}\to1$, so

$$ I(r)\;\xrightarrow[m\to0]{}\;\frac{1}{4\pi r} $$

We check from two directions whether this is consistent with its being the Green function of $-\nabla^2$.

From position space. Derivation 6 of this book showed that $\nabla^2(1/r)=-4\pi\delta^3(\xx)$, in other words

$$ -\nabla^2\left(\frac{1}{4\pi r}\right)=\delta^3(\xx) $$

That is, $1/(4\pi r)$ is the Green function of $-\nabla^2$ by the very definition.

From momentum space. Under the Fourier convention of this book, $f(\xx)=\int\frac{\dd^3k}{(2\pi)^3}\tilde f(\kk)\ee^{\ii\kk\cdot\xx}$, acting with $\nabla^2$ on a plane wave $\ee^{\ii\qq\cdot\bm r}$ gives $\nabla^2\ee^{\ii\qq\cdot\bm r}=-\abs{\qq}^2\ee^{\ii\qq\cdot\bm r}$, so the operator $-\nabla^2$ becomes multiplication by $+\abs{\qq}^2$ in momentum space. Also, the Fourier transform of $\delta^3(\xx)$ is $1$ (this is the completeness relation $\int\frac{\dd^3k}{(2\pi)^3}\ee^{\ii\kk\cdot\xx}=\delta^3(\xx)$ of Section A.3.1 of this book). Therefore, Fourier transforming $(-\nabla^2)G=\delta^3$ gives $\abs{\qq}^2\tilde G(\qq)=1$, that is, $\tilde G(\qq)=1/\abs{\qq}^2$, and the position-space Green function is

$$ G(r)=\int\frac{\dd^3q}{(2\pi)^3}\;\frac{\ee^{\ii\qq\cdot\bm r}}{\abs{\qq}^2} $$

This is none other than the integrand of Derivation 15 with $m=0$. Therefore the two viewpoints refer to the same quantity, and they must agree at $1/(4\pi r)$. In fact, recomputing the $m=0$ case from the beginning gives the same answer. Setting $m=0$ in the expression obtained up to Step 2 of Derivation 15, we get

$$ I(r)\big|_{m=0}=\frac{1}{2\pi^2 r}\int_0^\infty\dd q\;\frac{q\sin qr}{q^2} =\frac{1}{2\pi^2 r}\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin qr}{q}\,\dd q =\frac{1}{2\pi^2 r}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}=\frac{1}{4\pi r} $$

(we used $\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin u}{u}\dd u=\pi/2$, which is half of the normalization $\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\frac{\sin u}{u}\dd u=\pi$ of the sinc-form representation in Section A.1.3 of this book). From the side of the residue calculation, $m\to0$ is the limit in which the pole $q=+\ii m$ in the upper half-plane descends to the real axis; the residue $\ee^{-mr}/2$ merely approaches $1/2$, and nothing singular happens. As long as $r>0$ is fixed, the limit is smooth. In this way we have confirmed the consistency: the $m\to0$ limit of the Yukawa potential is the Coulomb potential $1/(4\pi r)$, which is the Green function of $-\nabla^2$.

(2) Let $J(\qq)$ denote the integral to be found.

$$ J(\qq)=\int\dd^3r\;\frac{\ee^{-mr}}{4\pi r}\,\ee^{-\ii\qq\cdot\bm r} $$

Step 1: Choose polar coordinates. Of the integrand, $\ee^{-mr}/4\pi r$ does not depend on the direction of $\bm r$. So we take the polar axis in $\bm r$ space along $\qq$, which lets us write $\qq\cdot\bm r=qr\cos\theta$ (with $q\equiv\abs{\qq}$), and $\dd^3r=r^2\dd r\,\dd\Omega$. Letting $u=\cos\theta$,

$$ J=\int_0^\infty r^2\dd r\;\frac{\ee^{-mr}}{4\pi r}\int_0^{2\pi}\dd\phi\int_{-1}^{1}\dd u\;\ee^{-\ii qru} $$

Step 2: Perform the angular integration. The $\phi$ integral gives $2\pi$. The $u$ integral is elementary:

$$ \int_{-1}^{1}\ee^{-\ii qru}\,\dd u=\left[\frac{\ee^{-\ii qru}}{-\ii qr}\right]_{-1}^{1} =\frac{\ee^{-\ii qr}-\ee^{+\ii qr}}{-\ii qr} =\frac{-2\ii\sin qr}{-\ii qr} =\frac{2\sin qr}{qr} $$

(even if the sign of $\qq\cdot\bm r$ were reversed, $\sin$ would appear in a combination that makes the result even, so it is the same as the result of Step 2 of Derivation 15 of this book). Collecting the angular part, $\int\dd\Omega\,\ee^{-\ii\qq\cdot\bm r}=4\pi\sin(qr)/(qr)$.

Step 3: Arrange it into the form of a radial integral.

$$ J=\int_0^\infty r^2\dd r\;\frac{\ee^{-mr}}{4\pi r}\cdot\frac{4\pi\sin qr}{qr} =\frac{1}{q}\int_0^\infty \ee^{-mr}\sin(qr)\,\dd r $$

The $r^2$, $1/r$, $1/r$, and $4\pi$ cancel neatly, leaving only a one-dimensional elementary integral.

Step 4: Perform the remaining integral. Using $\sin(qr)=\mathrm{Im}\,\ee^{\ii qr}$,

$$ \int_0^\infty \ee^{-mr}\sin(qr)\,\dd r =\mathrm{Im}\int_0^\infty \ee^{-(m-\ii q)r}\,\dd r =\mathrm{Im}\left[\frac{1}{m-\ii q}\right] =\mathrm{Im}\left[\frac{m+\ii q}{m^2+q^2}\right] =\frac{q}{m^2+q^2} $$

(since $m>0$, $\ee^{-(m-\ii q)r}$ converges to zero as $r\to\infty$, and the contribution of the upper limit vanishes).

Step 5: Put it together.

$$ J(\qq)=\frac{1}{q}\cdot\frac{q}{m^2+q^2}=\frac{1}{\abs{\qq}^2+m^2} $$

This is what was to be shown. The reason no factor of $(2\pi)^3$ appears in the prefactor is that the convention of Section A.3.1 of this book attaches “all the $2\pi$ to the side of the momentum integral.” The forward transform $\tilde f(\kk)=\int\dd^3x\,f(\xx)\ee^{-\ii\kk\cdot\xx}$ contains no $2\pi$ at all.

(3) First we confirm the definition of “range.” The exponential factor of the Yukawa-type potential $\ee^{-mr}/4\pi r$ drops to $\ee^{-1}=0.368$ at $r=1/m$. Therefore the range in natural units ($\hbar=c=1$) is $R=1/m$. To return to ordinary units, it is practical to write $m$ not as a mass but as the rest energy $mc^2$, giving
