$$ R=\frac{\hbar}{mc}=\frac{\hbar c}{mc^2} $$

If one remembers the numerator $\hbar c$ in $\mathrm{MeV\,fm}$, one only has to divide the rest energy in $\mathrm{MeV}$ to obtain $\mathrm{fm}$. This is why the number $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$ is memorized in particle physics (if one remembers $197.327\simeq200$, one can say even mentally that $1\ \mathrm{GeV}\leftrightarrow0.2\ \mathrm{fm}$).

The case of $\pi^\pm$. Since $mc^2=139.570\ \mathrm{MeV}$,

$$ R_\pi=\frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{139.570\ \mathrm{MeV}}=1.4138\ \mathrm{fm}\simeq1.41\ \mathrm{fm} $$

The case of $W^\pm$. Since $mc^2=80.377\ \mathrm{GeV}=80377\ \mathrm{MeV}$,

$$ R_W=\frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{80377\ \mathrm{MeV}}=2.4550\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm} $$

Taking the ratio, $R_\pi/R_W=1.4138/(2.4550\times10^{-3})=575.9$, which agrees with the mass ratio $80377/139.570=575.9$. This is natural, since the range is inversely proportional to the mass, but it serves as a check of the calculation.

(4) We use the Thomas–Fermi formula $k_\mathrm{TF}^2=e^2g(E_F)/\epsilon_0$ of Section A.6.2 of this book, the free-electron-approximation density of states $g(E_F)=3n/(2E_F)$, and the Gaussian-units form $k_\mathrm{TF}^2=4\pi\,\left(e^2/4\pi\epsilon_0\right)g(E_F)$.

Step 1: Find the density of states. For aluminum, $n=18.1\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$ and $E_F=11.7\ \mathrm{eV}$, so

$$ g(E_F)=\frac{3n}{2E_F}=\frac{3\times18.1\times10^{22}}{2\times11.7} =\frac{54.3\times10^{22}}{23.4}=2.3205\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}cm^{-3}} $$

Step 2: Convert the units to Å. Since $1\ \mathrm{cm}=10^{8}\ \text{Å}$, we have $1\ \mathrm{cm^3}=10^{24}\ \text{Å}^3$, so

$$ g(E_F)=\frac{2.3205\times10^{22}}{10^{24}}=0.023205\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}\text{Å}^{-3}} $$

Step 3: Find the screening wave number. Substitute $e^2/4\pi\epsilon_0=14.400\ \mathrm{eV\,\text{Å}}$.

$$ k_\mathrm{TF}^2=4\pi\times14.400\ \mathrm{eV\,\text{Å}}\times0.023205\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}\text{Å}^{-3}} =180.956\times0.023205=4.1991\ \text{Å}^{-2} $$ $$ k_\mathrm{TF}=\sqrt{4.1991}=2.0492\ \text{Å}^{-1} $$

Step 4: Find the screening length.

$$ \lambda_\mathrm{TF}=\frac{1}{k_\mathrm{TF}}=\frac{1}{2.0492}=0.4880\ \text{Å}\simeq0.49\ \text{Å} $$

Step 5: Compute copper by the same procedure and compare. If we kept the comparison value at the rounded $0.55\ \text{Å}$ of the problem statement, the ratio would be coarse, so we run the same three lines for copper as well ($n=8.47\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, $E_F=7.00\ \mathrm{eV}$, the values of Section A.6.2 of this book).

$$ g_\mathrm{Cu}(E_F)=\frac{3\times8.47\times10^{22}}{2\times7.00}=1.8150\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}cm^{-3}}=0.018150\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}\text{Å}^{-3}} $$ $$ k_\mathrm{TF}^2=180.956\times0.018150=3.2843\ \text{Å}^{-2}, \qquad k_\mathrm{TF}=1.8123\ \text{Å}^{-1}, \qquad \lambda_\mathrm{TF}^\mathrm{Cu}=0.5518\ \text{Å} $$

This reproduces, at the digits before rounding, the values $k_\mathrm{TF}=1.81\ \text{Å}^{-1}$ and $\lambda_\mathrm{TF}=0.55\ \text{Å}$ of Section A.6.2 of this book.

Compared with the $0.5518\ \text{Å}\simeq0.55\ \text{Å}$ of copper, the aluminum screening length is about $12\%$ shorter ($1-0.4880/0.5518=11.6\%$). That is, the screening is stronger. The reason is simple: aluminum has three valence electrons per atom, and its electron density is $2.1$ times that of copper. From the dependence $\lambda_\mathrm{TF}\propto1/\sqrt{g(E_F)}\propto\sqrt{E_F/n}$, one can read that the larger $n$ is, the shorter the screening length.

Verification. We check in three ways. First, scaling. Using $\lambda_\mathrm{TF}\propto\sqrt{E_F/n}$,

$$ \frac{\lambda_\mathrm{Al}}{\lambda_\mathrm{Cu}} =\sqrt{\frac{11.7/(18.1\times10^{22})}{7.00/(8.47\times10^{22})}} =\sqrt{\frac{6.464\times10^{-23}}{8.264\times10^{-23}}}=\sqrt{0.7822}=0.8844 $$

This agrees perfectly with the ratio of the directly obtained values, $0.4880/0.5518=0.8844$. Second, dimensions. The unit of $k_\mathrm{TF}^2$ is $\mathrm{eV\,\text{Å}}\times\mathrm{eV^{-1}\text{Å}^{-3}}=\text{Å}^{-2}$, which is correct for the square of a wave number. For (3) as well, $\mathrm{MeV\,fm}/\mathrm{MeV}=\mathrm{fm}$ is a length. Third, physical plausibility. Aluminum is face-centered cubic with lattice constant $a=4.05\ \text{Å}$, and the nearest-neighbor interatomic distance is $a/\sqrt2=2.864\ \text{Å}$. The screening factor is $\ee^{-2.864/0.4880}=\ee^{-5.87}=0.0028$, so by the time it reaches the neighboring atom the charge has dropped to $0.3\%$. Like the $\ee^{-2.56/0.5518}=0.0097$ for copper, this fits the standard picture of a metal, “almost gone by the neighboring atom.”

Meaning. (3) and (4) are two faces of the same Fourier transform. In (3), $m$ is the mass of the exchanged particle, and the nuclear force, which exchanges $\pi^\pm$, reaches only $1.41\ \mathrm{fm}$. Hideki Yukawa’s prediction in 1935 of the meson mass from the range of the nuclear force was none other than a back-calculation from this one line. The weak force, which exchanges $W^\pm$, reaches only $2.46\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}$, about $1/340$ of the proton radius. That “the weak force is weak” is not because the coupling constant is small, but because the range is this short. In (4), $k_\mathrm{TF}$ enters at the place of the same $m$ and becomes the screening length of an impurity potential in a metal. The formulas are identical word for word; only the reading $m\leftrightarrow k_\mathrm{TF}$ differs. If we read $k_\mathrm{TF}$ as an “effective photon mass,” a photon in aluminum has a mass of $\hbar c\,k_\mathrm{TF}=1973.27\ \mathrm{eV\,\text{Å}}\times2.0492\ \text{Å}^{-1}=4.04\ \mathrm{keV}$ (for copper, $3.6\ \mathrm{keV}$). A photon that is massless in vacuum and reaches infinitely far acquires an effective mass through its interaction with the medium—this is a perfect analog in matter of the Higgs mechanism. When you write the reciprocal-space term of an Ewald summation in a first-principles calculation, or when you estimate the depletion-layer width of a doped semiconductor, you are solving the same integral as Yukawa.

Exercise A.5: Practice with integral formulas

Problem (restated)

(1) Using the Gaussian moment formula, find $\displaystyle\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x^4\,\ee^{-ax^2}\dd x$.

(2) Verify the Feynman-parameter identity $\frac{1}{AB}=\int_0^1\dd x\left[xA+(1-x)B\right]^{-2}$ by carrying out the $x$ integral. Furthermore, set $n=3$ in the general Feynman-parameter formula and write down the expression for $1/ABC$.

(3) Find $\displaystyle\int_0^1 x^2(1-x)^3\,\dd x$ using the Beta function, and confirm that it agrees with the result of direct expansion. Also find $B(1/2,1/2)$.

(4) In the basic integral of dimensional regularization, set $n=2$ and $d=4-2\epsilon$, and write down the $1/\epsilon$ term and the finite term of the expansion as $\epsilon\to0$.

Solution

Strategy. We use the toolbox of Section A.7 of this book as it stands. For (1) it is the Gaussian moment $\int x^{2n}\ee^{-ax^2}\dd x=\frac{(2n-1)!!}{(2a)^n}\sqrt{\pi/a}$; for (2) it is Derivation 17 of this book; for (3) it is $B(\alpha,\beta)=\Gamma(\alpha)\Gamma(\beta)/\Gamma(\alpha+\beta)$; and for (4) it is the basic integral of dimensional regularization together with $\Gamma(\epsilon)=1/\epsilon-\gamma_E+O(\epsilon)$.

(1) Set $n=2$ in the Gaussian moment formula. Since $(2n-1)!!=3!!=1\cdot3=3$ and $(2a)^n=(2a)^2=4a^2$, we have

$$ \int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x^4\,\ee^{-ax^2}\,\dd x=\frac{3}{4a^2}\sqrt{\frac{\pi}{a}}=\frac{3}{4}\sqrt{\pi}\;a^{-5/2} $$

One can also derive the result without memorizing the formula. Differentiating the basic form $\int\ee^{-ax^2}\dd x=\sqrt{\pi/a}=\sqrt\pi\,a^{-1/2}$ with respect to $a$ brings down $-x^2$ on the left-hand side, so

$$ -\int x^2\ee^{-ax^2}\dd x=\sqrt\pi\cdot\left(-\tfrac12\right)a^{-3/2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \int x^2\ee^{-ax^2}\dd x=\tfrac12\sqrt\pi\,a^{-3/2} $$

Differentiating once more with respect to $a$ gives

$$ -\int x^4\ee^{-ax^2}\dd x=\tfrac12\sqrt\pi\cdot\left(-\tfrac32\right)a^{-5/2} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \int x^4\ee^{-ax^2}\dd x=\tfrac34\sqrt\pi\,a^{-5/2} $$

which is the same answer. For $a=1$ the numerical value is $\frac34\sqrt\pi=1.32934$.

(2) The case of two factors. Rewrite the denominator as $B+x(A-B)$ and integrate over $x$, assuming $A\neq B$. Since $\dd\left[B+x(A-B)\right]/\dd x=A-B$, the integral $\int\dd x\,(\cdots)^{-2}$ can be done elementarily:

$$ \int_0^1\frac{\dd x}{\left[B+x(A-B)\right]^2} =\left[\frac{-1}{(A-B)\left(B+x(A-B)\right)}\right]_{0}^{1} $$

At the upper limit $x=1$ the quantity in parentheses is $B+(A-B)=A$, and at the lower limit $x=0$ it is $B$, so

$$ =\frac{-1}{A-B}\left(\frac{1}{A}-\frac{1}{B}\right) =\frac{-1}{A-B}\cdot\frac{B-A}{AB} =\frac{A-B}{(A-B)AB} =\frac{1}{AB} $$

and the identity is verified. For $A=B$ the denominator no longer depends on $x$, and $\int_0^1\dd x/A^2=1/A^2=1/(AB)$, so the identity holds in that case as well.

The case of three factors. Take the general formula of Section A.7.2 of this book,

$$ \frac{1}{A_1A_2\cdots A_n} =(n-1)!\int_0^1\!\!\dd x_1\cdots\dd x_n\;\frac{\delta\!\left(1-\sum_{i=1}^n x_i\right)}{\left[\sum_{i=1}^n x_iA_i\right]^n} $$

set $n=3$, and write $A_1=A$, $A_2=B$, $A_3=C$, $x_1=x$, $x_2=y$, $x_3=z$. Since $(n-1)!=2!=2$,

$$ \frac{1}{ABC}=2\int_0^1\!\!\dd x\,\dd y\,\dd z\;\frac{\delta\left(1-x-y-z\right)}{\left[xA+yB+zC\right]^3} $$

The $\delta$ function picks out only the plane $x+y+z=1$ (the Feynman simplex). Disposing of the $z$ integral with the $\delta$ function and rewriting in terms of two variables, we obtain

$$ \frac{1}{ABC}=2\int_0^1\!\!\dd x\int_0^{1-x}\!\!\dd y\;\frac{1}{\left[xA+yB+(1-x-y)C\right]^3} $$

The integration region is a triangle because of the constraints $x,y\ge0$ and $z=1-x-y\ge0$.

(3) Using the Beta function. Matching the form $\int_0^1x^{\alpha-1}(1-x)^{\beta-1}\dd x=B(\alpha,\beta)$, we have $x^2=x^{3-1}$ and $(1-x)^3=(1-x)^{4-1}$, so $\alpha=3$ and $\beta=4$. Since these are positive integers, we can use $\Gamma(n)=(n-1)!$:

$$ \int_0^1x^2(1-x)^3\dd x=B(3,4)=\frac{\Gamma(3)\Gamma(4)}{\Gamma(7)}=\frac{2!\;3!}{6!}=\frac{2\times6}{720}=\frac{12}{720}=\frac{1}{60} $$

By direct expansion. Since $(1-x)^3=1-3x+3x^2-x^3$, the integrand is $x^2-3x^3+3x^4-x^5$. Integrating term by term,

$$ \int_0^1\left(x^2-3x^3+3x^4-x^5\right)\dd x =\frac13-\frac34+\frac35-\frac16 $$

We bring these to a common denominator. The least common multiple of the denominators is $60$, so

$$ =\frac{20}{60}-\frac{45}{60}+\frac{36}{60}-\frac{10}{60}=\frac{20-45+36-10}{60}=\frac{1}{60} $$

and the two results indeed agree. Numerically, $1/60=0.0166667$.

$B(1/2,1/2)$. From the formula,

$$ B\!\left(\tfrac12,\tfrac12\right)=\frac{\Gamma(1/2)^2}{\Gamma(1)}=\frac{\left(\sqrt\pi\right)^2}{1}=\pi $$

This too can be checked by direct calculation. In $B(1/2,1/2)=\int_0^1\frac{\dd x}{\sqrt{x(1-x)}}$ put $x=\sin^2\theta$ ($\theta:0\to\pi/2$). Then $\dd x=2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,\dd\theta$ and $\sqrt{x(1-x)}=\sin\theta\cos\theta$, so

$$ \int_0^1\frac{\dd x}{\sqrt{x(1-x)}}=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{2\sin\theta\cos\theta}{\sin\theta\cos\theta}\,\dd\theta=2\int_0^{\pi/2}\dd\theta=\pi $$

which agrees. As for $\Gamma(1/2)=\sqrt\pi$ itself, putting $t=u^2$ in $\Gamma(1/2)=\int_0^\infty t^{-1/2}\ee^{-t}\dd t$ gives $2\int_0^\infty\ee^{-u^2}\dd u=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}\ee^{-u^2}\dd u=\sqrt\pi$, which reduces to a Gaussian integral.

(4) Take the basic integral of Section A.7.4 of this book,

$$ \int\frac{\dd^d\ell}{(2\pi)^d}\;\frac{1}{\left(\ell^2-\Delta+\ii\epsilon\right)^n} =\frac{(-1)^n\,\ii}{(4\pi)^{d/2}}\;\frac{\Gamma\!\left(n-\frac d2\right)}{\Gamma(n)}\;\left(\frac{1}{\Delta}\right)^{n-d/2} $$

and set $n=2$, $d=4-2\epsilon$. We substitute step by step.

Step 1: Write down each factor. $(-1)^n=(-1)^2=+1$ and $\Gamma(n)=\Gamma(2)=1!=1$. Since $d/2=2-\epsilon$, we have $n-d/2=2-(2-\epsilon)=\epsilon$. Hence $\Gamma(n-d/2)=\Gamma(\epsilon)$, $(1/\Delta)^{n-d/2}=\Delta^{-\epsilon}$, and $(4\pi)^{d/2}=(4\pi)^{2-\epsilon}$.

$$ \int\frac{\dd^d\ell}{(2\pi)^d}\frac{1}{\left(\ell^2-\Delta+\ii\epsilon\right)^2} =\frac{\ii}{(4\pi)^{2-\epsilon}}\,\Gamma(\epsilon)\,\Delta^{-\epsilon} =\frac{\ii}{(4\pi)^2}\,(4\pi)^{\epsilon}\,\Gamma(\epsilon)\,\Delta^{-\epsilon} $$

Step 2: Expand in $\epsilon$. Rewrite in exponential form and expand to first order.

$$ (4\pi)^{\epsilon}=\ee^{\epsilon\ln4\pi}=1+\epsilon\ln4\pi+O(\epsilon^2), \qquad \Delta^{-\epsilon}=\ee^{-\epsilon\ln\Delta}=1-\epsilon\ln\Delta+O(\epsilon^2) $$

Also, the expansion of the Gamma function around its pole is $\Gamma(\epsilon)=\dfrac{1}{\epsilon}-\gamma_E+O(\epsilon)$.

Step 3: Multiply them together. Because of the $1/\epsilon$ term, the expansions must be kept through the $O(\epsilon)$ terms.

$$ \Gamma(\epsilon)\,(4\pi)^{\epsilon}\,\Delta^{-\epsilon} =\left(\frac{1}{\epsilon}-\gamma_E\right)\left(1+\epsilon\ln4\pi\right)\left(1-\epsilon\ln\Delta\right)+O(\epsilon) $$

When $1/\epsilon$ is multiplied by $\epsilon\ln4\pi$, what remains is $\ln4\pi$; when it is multiplied by $\epsilon(-\ln\Delta)$, what remains is $-\ln\Delta$. The product of $-\gamma_E$ with the $\epsilon$ terms is $O(\epsilon)$, so we drop it.

$$ =\frac{1}{\epsilon}-\gamma_E+\ln4\pi-\ln\Delta+O(\epsilon) $$

Step 4: Collect the terms.

$$ \int\frac{\dd^d\ell}{(2\pi)^d}\frac{1}{\left(\ell^2-\Delta+\ii\epsilon\right)^2} =\frac{\ii}{(4\pi)^2}\left[\frac{1}{\epsilon}-\gamma_E+\ln4\pi-\ln\Delta\right]+O(\epsilon) $$

The $1/\epsilon$ term is $\dfrac{\ii}{(4\pi)^2}\dfrac{1}{\epsilon}$, and the finite part is $\dfrac{\ii}{(4\pi)^2}\left[-\gamma_E+\ln4\pi-\ln\Delta\right]$. We also add the numerical values $(4\pi)^2=157.91$, $\gamma_E=0.5772157$, and $\ln4\pi=2.5310$. Note that in an actual renormalization calculation, it is customary to introduce a mass scale $\mu$ and multiply by $\mu^{2\epsilon}$ so as to keep the dimension of the coupling constant in $d$ dimensions; then $-\ln\Delta$ becomes $\ln(\mu^2/\Delta)$, and the argument of the logarithm becomes dimensionless. Discarding $\left[-\gamma_E+\ln4\pi\right]$ collectively in the $\overline{\mathrm{MS}}$ scheme comes later (Chapter 10).

Verification. We check four things. First, numerically integrating (1) at $a=1$ gives $1.3293404$, which agrees with $\frac34\sqrt\pi=1.3293404$. Second, the dimension of (1). For $\ee^{-ax^2}$ to be dimensionless we need $[a]=[x]^{-2}$. The answer $\frac34\sqrt\pi a^{-5/2}$ has dimension $[x]^{5}$, which agrees with the dimension $[x]^5$ of the left-hand side $\int x^4\dd x$. Third, the identity of (2) correctly reproduces $1/A^2$ in the special case $A=B$, and is symmetric under the exchange of $A$ and $B$ (they are interchanged by the substitution $x\to1-x$). Fourth, $B(1/2,1/2)=\pi$ in (3) is also consistent with $\Gamma(1/2)^2=\pi/\sin(\pi/2)=\pi$, obtained by setting $z=1/2$ in the reflection formula $\Gamma(z)\Gamma(1-z)=\pi/\sin\pi z$.

Meaning. This exercise is practice swings with the tools, but all four tools point toward a single goal, loop calculations. The Feynman parameters of (2) combine a denominator in which different quadratic expressions are lined up into a single one and make completing the square possible. What is used for this is $\delta(1-\sum x_i)$, so the $\delta$ function, the subject of this appendix, stands right at the entrance to renormalization calculations. The Gaussian integral of (1) appears after the square is completed, and the Beta function of (3) turns the radial integral in $d$ dimensions into a closed form. And the $1/\epsilon$ pole of (4) is the true nature of the ultraviolet divergence. Precisely because the divergence is organized in the form of a pole of the $\Gamma$ function, a “known mathematical object,” the prescription called renormalization can be carried out systematically. The same picture exists on the materials science side. In first-principles calculations with a plane-wave basis, the total energy behaves divergently as the cutoff energy is increased, and the only quantities meaningful as physical quantities are differences (formation energies, defect formation energies). Likewise, when $1/r$ is split into short-distance and long-distance parts in an Ewald summation, checking that the final result does not depend on the splitting parameter $\eta$ is the same task as checking that the dependence on the renormalization point $\mu$ disappears from the physical quantities. The discipline of separating “intermediate quantities containing divergences” from “finite physical quantities” is the same in both fields.

Exercise A.6: Density of states and box normalization (connection to materials science)

Problem (restated)

(1) Following Derivation 10, show that the density of states of two-dimensional free electrons is a constant $Am/\pi\hbar^2$, independent of $E$.

(2) For a three-dimensional free-electron gas, show that $D(E_F)=3N/2E_F$ ($N$ is the total number of electrons).

(3) For copper ($n=8.47\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, $E_F=7.00\ \mathrm{eV}$, one valence electron per atom), find the density of states per atom per eV.

(4) From the result of (3), find the electronic specific-heat coefficient $\gamma=\frac{\pi^2}{3}k_B^2\,D(E_F)$ in $\mathrm{mJ/(mol\,K^2)}$ and compare it with the measured value $0.695\ \mathrm{mJ/(mol\,K^2)}$. Use $k_B=8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/K}$, $N_A=6.022\times10^{23}$, and $1\ \mathrm{eV}=1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$.

Solution

Strategy. We use the two dictionaries of Section A.3 of this book: the correspondence between sums and integrals $\sum_\kk\to\frac{V}{(2\pi)^3}\int\dd^3k$ (in two dimensions, $\sum_\kk\to\frac{A}{(2\pi)^2}\int\dd^2k$), and the definition of the density of states $D(E)=\sum_n\delta(E-\varepsilon_n)$. To handle the $\delta$ function we use the composite-function rule. This problem is the low-dimensional version of Derivation 10 of this book, together with its numerical application.

(1) Step 1: Convert the sum into an integral. A two-dimensional free electron has $\varepsilon_\kk=\hbar^2\abs{\kk}^2/2m$. If we impose periodic boundary conditions on a square box of side $L$ and area $A=L^2$, the allowed $\kk$ points form a square lattice with spacing $2\pi/L$. Since each $\kk$ point occupies an area $(2\pi/L)^2=(2\pi)^2/A$ in wave-number space, including the spin degeneracy factor $2$ we have

$$ D_{2\mathrm{D}}(E)=2\sum_\kk\delta\!\left(E-\varepsilon_\kk\right) =\frac{2A}{(2\pi)^2}\int\dd^2k\;\delta\!\left(E-\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}\right) $$

Step 2: Carry out the angular integration. Since $\varepsilon_\kk$ depends only on $k\equiv\abs{\kk}$, in two-dimensional polar coordinates $\int\dd^2k=2\pi\int_0^\infty k\,\dd k$. Where the three-dimensional case has $k^2\dd k$, the two-dimensional case has $k\,\dd k$; this is the only difference.

$$ =\frac{2A}{4\pi^2}\cdot2\pi\int_0^\infty k\,\dd k\;\delta\!\left(E-\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}\right) =\frac{A}{\pi}\int_0^\infty k\,\dd k\;\delta\!\left(E-\frac{\hbar^2k^2}{2m}\right) $$

Step 3: Use the composite-function rule. Letting $f(k)=E-\hbar^2k^2/2m$, the zero with $k>0$ is

$$ k_0=\frac{\sqrt{2mE}}{\hbar},\qquad f'(k)=-\frac{\hbar^2k}{m},\qquad \abs{f'(k_0)}=\frac{\hbar^2k_0}{m} $$

(a zero exists only when $E>0$). Therefore

$$ D_{2\mathrm{D}}(E)=\frac{A}{\pi}\cdot\frac{k_0}{\abs{f'(k_0)}} =\frac{A}{\pi}\cdot k_0\cdot\frac{m}{\hbar^2k_0} =\frac{Am}{\pi\hbar^2} $$

Step 4: Read off the conclusion. The $k_0$ cancels completely between numerator and denominator, and the dependence on $E$ has disappeared. That is,

$$ D_{2\mathrm{D}}(E)=\frac{Am}{\pi\hbar^2}\qquad(E>0\ \text{: constant}) $$

The reason it is constant is clear. The one power of $k$ coming from the two-dimensional measure and the $1/\abs{f'}\propto1/k$ coming from the handling of the $\delta$ function cancel exactly. In three dimensions the measure is $k^2$, so $k^2/k=k\propto\sqrt E$ remains; in one dimension the measure is $k^0$, so $1/k\propto1/\sqrt E$ remains and diverges. The dimensionality determines the energy dependence of the density of states.

(2) The three-dimensional result of Derivation 10 of this book is

$$ D_{3\mathrm{D}}(E)=\frac{V}{2\pi^2}\left(\frac{2m}{\hbar^2}\right)^{3/2}\sqrt E\equiv C\sqrt E \qquad(E>0) $$

where $C$ is taken to be a constant independent of $E$. At absolute zero the electrons fill the states up to $E_F$, so the total number of electrons is

$$ N=\int_0^{E_F}D_{3\mathrm{D}}(E)\,\dd E=C\int_0^{E_F}E^{1/2}\dd E =C\cdot\frac{2}{3}E_F^{3/2}=\frac{2}{3}E_F\cdot C\,E_F^{1/2} $$

In the last step we split $E_F^{3/2}=E_F\cdot E_F^{1/2}$. But $C\,E_F^{1/2}$ is by definition $D(E_F)$ itself, so

$$ N=\frac{2}{3}E_F\,D(E_F) \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad D(E_F)=\frac{3N}{2E_F} $$

The only thing used in the derivation is the single fact that $D\propto\sqrt E$; the content of $C$ was not used at all. Even without knowing the specific values of $m$ or $V$, measuring just $N$ and $E_F$ fixes $D(E_F)$, a form that is convenient for experiment.

(3) Copper has one valence electron per atom, so counting per atom we have $N=1$. Inserting this directly into the formula of (2),

$$ \frac{D(E_F)}{N}=\frac{3}{2E_F}=\frac{3}{2\times7.00\ \mathrm{eV}}=\frac{3}{14.00}=0.21429\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}} $$

that is, $0.214$ states per atom per eV. Note that this counting includes spin (the $2\sum_\kk$ in Derivation 10 of this book is this spin degree of freedom). Incidentally, the value of the density $n$ need not be used in this calculation itself. One needs $n$ when determining $E_F$ oneself from the free-electron model. Since both are given here, let us check whether the given data are consistent with each other. Inserting $n=8.47\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}=8.47\times10^{28}\ \mathrm{m^{-3}}$ into $k_F=(3\pi^2n)^{1/3}$ and $E_F=\hbar^2k_F^2/2m$, we get

$$ k_F=\left(3\pi^2\times8.47\times10^{28}\right)^{1/3}=1.359\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{m^{-1}}, \qquad E_F=\frac{\hbar^2k_F^2}{2m}=1.127\times10^{-18}\ \mathrm{J}=7.03\ \mathrm{eV} $$

which reproduces the given $7.00\ \mathrm{eV}$ to within an error of $0.4\%$. Incidentally, the Fermi velocity also comes out as $v_F=\hbar k_F/m=1.57\times10^6\ \mathrm{m/s}$. This is exactly the value that was used to estimate the mean free path of copper in the verification of Exercise A.3.

(4) Step 1: Calculate in eV units. With $\pi^2/3=3.28987$ and $k_B=8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/K}$, we have $k_B^2=7.42527\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{eV^2/K^2}$. Multiplying by the per-atom $D(E_F)=0.21429\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}}$ gives

$$ \gamma_\text{atom}=\frac{\pi^2}{3}k_B^2D(E_F) =3.28987\times7.42527\times10^{-9}\times0.21429 =5.2346\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{eV/K^2}\ \text{(per atom)} $$

The dimension is $\mathrm{eV^2K^{-2}}\times\mathrm{eV^{-1}}=\mathrm{eV\,K^{-2}}$, which is correct for the specific heat divided by the temperature.

Step 2: Convert to SI units and per mole. Multiply by $1\ \mathrm{eV}=1.602\times10^{-19}\ \mathrm{J}$, and multiply by $N_A=6.022\times10^{23}$ atoms.

$$ \gamma=5.2346\times10^{-9}\times1.602\times10^{-19}\times6.022\times10^{23} $$

Calculating in order: $5.2346\times10^{-9}\times1.602\times10^{-19}=8.3858\times10^{-28}\ \mathrm{J/K^2}$ (per atom), and multiplying this by $6.022\times10^{23}$ gives

$$ \gamma=5.0500\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K^2)}=0.505\ \mathrm{mJ/(mol\,K^2)} $$

This is the result.

Step 3: Compare with the measured value. The measured value is $0.695\ \mathrm{mJ/(mol\,K^2)}$, so

$$ \frac{\gamma_\text{exp}}{\gamma_\text{calc}}=\frac{0.695}{0.505}=1.376\simeq1.38 $$

That is, the measured value is $1.38$ times the prediction of the free-electron model; conversely, the model value falls short at $0.505/0.695=72.7\%$ of the measured one (this is a “$27\%$ underestimate,” not a “$38\%$ underestimate”; the number changes depending on which is placed in the denominator, so when writing a ratio its direction must be stated explicitly). This ratio means that the “heaviness” of the electrons seen when the specific heat is measured is $1.38$ times the free-electron mass. That is, the thermal effective mass is $m^*_\text{th}/m=\gamma_\text{exp}/\gamma_\text{calc}=1.38$.

Verification. We check in three ways. First, using the result of (2), we construct a closed expression for $\gamma$ and obtain the number by another route. Substituting $D(E_F)=3N/(2E_F)$ gives

$$ \gamma=\frac{\pi^2}{3}k_B^2\cdot\frac{3N}{2E_F}=\frac{\pi^2}{2}\,\frac{N k_B^2}{E_F} $$

and for one mole, setting $N=N_A$ and using $N_Ak_B=R=8.3145\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}$, we can write $\gamma=\frac{\pi^2}{2}\frac{R\,k_B}{E_F}$. Inserting the numbers,

$$ \gamma=4.9348\times\frac{8.3145\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K)}\times8.617\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{eV/K}}{7.00\ \mathrm{eV}} =5.051\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{J/(mol\,K^2)} $$

which agrees with the $5.050\times10^{-4}$ of Step 2 to three digits. Second, the dimensions. The units of the final expression $\gamma=\frac{\pi^2}{2}Rk_B/E_F$ are $\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\times\mathrm{eV\,K^{-1}}/\mathrm{eV}=\mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-2}}$, which is correct. Third, for the result of (1): if we construct the relation between $N$ and $E_F$ by the same argument as in (2), we get $N=\int_0^{E_F}D_{2\mathrm{D}}\dd E=D_{2\mathrm{D}}\,E_F$, so that $D_{2\mathrm{D}}=N/E_F$, a simple two-dimensional version of the relation. The three-dimensional $3N/2E_F$, the two-dimensional $N/E_F$, and the one-dimensional $N/(2E_F)$ all follow from the same formula $(p+1)N/E_F$ for $D\propto E^{p}$ (with $p=1/2,0,-1/2$). That the differences between dimensions can be organized into one formula supports the correctness of the calculation.

Meaning. The heart of this problem is the number $1.38$ at the end. Measuring $\gamma$ amounts to measuring the density of states at the Fermi surface. And the reason the measurement is $1.38$ times the prediction of the free-electron model is that real electrons are not “bare electrons.” The band structure due to the periodic potential (in copper, hybridization with the d band) is the main cause, and on top of this come the electron–electron interaction and the electron–phonon interaction ($1+\lambda$, with $\lambda\simeq0.15$ for copper), which make the electrons near the Fermi surface heavy. What is picked up in the measurement is the renormalized mass, which is dressed in all of these effects. This is exactly the same picture as in particle physics, where one distinguishes the bare mass $m_0$ written in the Lagrangian from the physical mass $m$ measured in experiment, and relates the two through the self-energy $\Sigma$ (Chapter 10). Both are different manifestations of one fact: “the response of a particle immersed in an interacting field differs from the response of a free particle.” On the condensed-matter side, the ratio $m^*/m$ is tied to the electron–phonon coupling constant $\lambda$ of superconductivity by $m^*/m=1+\lambda$, and connects directly to the discussion of $T_c$. The breakdown of the value $1.38$ for copper is this: on top of the band-calculation value $\gamma_{\rm band}\simeq0.60\ \mathrm{mJ/(mol\,K^2)}$ (about $1.2$ times the free-electron $0.505$) comes a factor of $1+\lambda$ accounting for the remaining factor of about $1.15$. That is, copper has weak electron–phonon coupling ($\lambda\simeq0.15$), and for exactly that reason it is a metal that does not become superconducting—one must not read $1.38$ directly as $1+\lambda$ and conclude $\lambda=0.38$. Starting from the naive definition as a sum of $\delta$ functions, the measured quantity, the individuality of the material, and even the idea of renormalization are all connected in one thread; therein lies the power of the quantity called the density of states.

E.18 Solutions for Appendix B: Formulas for Decay Rates and Scattering Cross Sections

Exercise B.1: Kinematics of two-body decay

Problem (restated)

Use the two-body decay momentum formula of Appendix B of this book (the factorized form of the Källén function) to find the momentum $\abs{\pp}$ of the daughter particles emitted from a parent particle at rest. Use the values of the masses in this book ($m_{\pi^0}=134.977$, $m_{\pi^\pm}=139.570$, $m_{K^\pm}=493.677$, $m_\rho=775.26$, all in MeV).

(1) $\pi^0\to\gamma\gamma$. Both daughter particles are massless.

(2) $K^+\to\pi^+\pi^0$.

(3) $\rho^0\to\pi^+\pi^-$. Also, put the total width $\Gamma=149.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$ of the $\rho$ into the two-body decay rate formula and find $\abs{\mathcal{M}}$ ($S=1$).

(4) $\mu^-\to e^-\bar\nu_e\nu_\mu$ is a three-body decay. Find the maximum energy of the electron (Hint: the maximum occurs when the two neutrinos are emitted in the same direction and the electron in the opposite direction).

Solution

Strategy. We use only two tools. The first is the momentum formula of Section B.1.4 of Appendix B of this book

$$ \abs{\pp} = \frac{1}{2m_1}\sqrt{\Big[m_1^2-(m_2+m_3)^2\Big]\Big[m_1^2-(m_2-m_3)^2\Big]} $$

and the second is the two-body decay rate in the same section

$$ \Gamma_{1\to2+3} = \frac{S\,\abs{\pp}}{8\pi\hbar\,m_1^2}\,\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2 $$

. We compute in natural units with $\hbar=1$, and measure all masses in MeV. Only (4) is a three-body decay, but a single move, “regard the two neutrinos together as one virtual particle,” reduces it to a two-body problem. This reinterpretation is exactly the same idea as the recursive decomposition of the three-body phase space in Section B.1.5 of Appendix B of this book (a two-stage stacking of $1\to(23)+4$ and $(23)\to2+3$).

(1) Substituting $m_2=m_3=0$, both brackets become $m_1^2$.

$$ \abs{\pp} = \frac{1}{2m_{\pi^0}}\sqrt{m_{\pi^0}^2\cdot m_{\pi^0}^2} = \frac{m_{\pi^0}^2}{2m_{\pi^0}} = \frac{m_{\pi^0}}{2} = \frac{134.977}{2} = 67.4885\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

Since the photon is massless, $E_\gamma=\abs{\pp}=67.489\ \mathrm{MeV}$. The two photons are emitted back to back, each with exactly half of the parent mass as its energy. Energy conservation $E_2+E_3=2\times67.4885=134.977=m_{\pi^0}$ is of course satisfied as well.

(2) We compute the two brackets separately. First, $m_{K^\pm}^2=(493.677)^2=2.4371698\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{MeV^2}$. The sum and difference are, respectively,

$$ m_{\pi^\pm}+m_{\pi^0} = 139.570+134.977 = 274.547\ \mathrm{MeV}, \qquad m_{\pi^\pm}-m_{\pi^0} = 4.593\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

so that

$$ m_1^2-(m_2+m_3)^2 = 243716.98 - 75376.06 = 1.6834092\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{MeV^2} $$ $$ m_1^2-(m_2-m_3)^2 = 243716.98 - 21.096 = 2.4369588\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{MeV^2} $$

. The product is $4.102399\times10^{10}\ \mathrm{MeV^4}$, and its square root is $2.0254380\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{MeV^2}$. Dividing this by $2m_{K^\pm}=987.354\ \mathrm{MeV}$ gives

$$ \abs{\pp} = \frac{2.0254380\times10^{5}}{987.354} = 205.138\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

. This agrees with the hint value $205.14\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and with the values of the two brackets, $1.6834\times10^{5}$ and $2.4370\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{MeV^2}$. From the equation of Step 3 of Derivation 2 in Appendix B of this book, the energies are

$$ E_{\pi^+} = \frac{m_K^2+m_{\pi^\pm}^2-m_{\pi^0}^2}{2m_K} = 248.116\ \mathrm{MeV}, \qquad E_{\pi^0} = \frac{m_K^2+m_{\pi^0}^2-m_{\pi^\pm}^2}{2m_K} = 245.561\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

, and the kinetic energies are $108.55\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $110.58\ \mathrm{MeV}$, respectively.

(3) For $m_2=m_3=m_{\pi^\pm}$, the second bracket becomes $m_\rho^2-0=m_\rho^2$, so the formula simplifies.

$$ \abs{\pp} = \frac{1}{2m_\rho}\sqrt{\big(m_\rho^2-4m_{\pi^\pm}^2\big)\,m_\rho^2} = \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{m_\rho^2-4m_{\pi^\pm}^2} = \sqrt{\frac{m_\rho^2}{4}-m_{\pi^\pm}^2} $$

Numerically, from $m_\rho^2/4 = 601028.07/4 = 150257.02$ and $m_{\pi^\pm}^2 = 19479.78$,

$$ \abs{\pp} = \sqrt{150257.02-19479.78} = \sqrt{130777.23} = 361.631\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

. Next we solve the two-body decay rate formula for $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2$. With $S=1$ ($\pi^+$ and $\pi^-$ are distinguishable) and $\hbar=1$,

$$ \abs{\mathcal{M}}^2 = \frac{8\pi\,m_\rho^2\,\Gamma}{S\,\abs{\pp}} = \frac{8\pi\times601028.07\times149.1}{361.631}\ \mathrm{MeV^2} $$

Evaluating the numerator step by step, $8\pi\times601028.07 = 1.5105483\times10^{7}\ \mathrm{MeV^2}$, and multiplying this by $\Gamma=149.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$ gives $2.2522275\times10^{9}\ \mathrm{MeV^3}$. Dividing by $\abs{\pp}=361.631\ \mathrm{MeV}$ gives

$$ \abs{\mathcal{M}}^2 = 6.2280\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{MeV^2} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \abs{\mathcal{M}} = 2496\ \mathrm{MeV} = 2.50\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

. This agrees with the hint values $6.23\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{MeV^2}$ and $2.50\times10^{3}\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(4) Since this is a three-body decay, the electron energy has a continuous distribution. To find its upper limit, regard the sum of the four-momenta of the two neutrinos, $q=p_{\bar\nu_e}+p_{\nu_\mu}$, as the four-momentum of a single particle, and write its invariant mass as $m_{\nu\nu}\equiv\sqrt{q^2}$. The decay then becomes formally the two-body decay $\mu^-\to e^- + X$, and Step 3 of Derivation 2 can be used as it stands:

$$ E_e = \frac{m_\mu^2+m_e^2-m_{\nu\nu}^2}{2m_\mu} $$

The right-hand side is monotonically decreasing in $m_{\nu\nu}^2$, so $E_e$ is maximal when $m_{\nu\nu}=0$. If the neutrinos are taken to be massless,

$$ m_{\nu\nu}^2 = (p_{\bar\nu_e}+p_{\nu_\mu})^2 = 2\,p_{\bar\nu_e}\cdot p_{\nu_\mu} = 2\big(E_1E_2-\pp_1\cdot\pp_2\big) = 2E_1E_2\big(1-\cos\theta_{12}\big) $$

so $m_{\nu\nu}=0$ means $\theta_{12}=0$, that is, the two neutrinos are emitted in exactly the same direction (formally $E_1E_2=0$ also gives $m_{\nu\nu}=0$, but this is the boundary case in which one neutrino vanishes and the decay is effectively two-body; the value of $E_e$ is the same). In this case, by momentum conservation the electron is emitted in the opposite direction. This is precisely the situation of the hint in the problem statement. Therefore

$$ E_e^\text{max} = \frac{m_\mu^2+m_e^2}{2m_\mu} = \frac{(105.658)^2+(0.511)^2}{2\times105.658} = \frac{11163.613+0.261}{211.316} = \frac{11163.874}{211.316} = 52.8302\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

. The difference from $m_\mu/2 = 52.829\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is only $m_e^2/(2m_\mu)=1.24\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{MeV}$, so effectively $E_e^\text{max}\simeq m_\mu/2$.

The same formula also gives the lower end in one line. Since $E_e$ is a monotonically decreasing function of $m_{\nu\nu}^2$, $E_e$ is minimal when $m_{\nu\nu}$ is maximal, that is, when the electron is at rest and the two neutrinos carry away everything else, $m_{\nu\nu}=m_\mu-m_e$.

$$ E_e^\text{min} = \frac{m_\mu^2+m_e^2-(m_\mu-m_e)^2}{2m_\mu} = \frac{2m_\mu m_e}{2m_\mu} = m_e = 0.511\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The expected answer emerges (the total energy of an electron at rest is $m_e$). In other words, the total energy of the electron fills the range $m_e \le E_e \le 52.830\ \mathrm{MeV}$ continuously, or, in terms of kinetic energy, from $0$ to $52.319\ \mathrm{MeV}$. The power of this reinterpretation lies in the fact that both the upper and lower ends follow just by “inserting the extreme values of $m_{\nu\nu}$ into the two-body decay formula.”

Verification. We run three independent checks.

First, energy conservation in (2): $248.116+245.561 = 493.677 = m_{K^\pm}$, in perfect agreement. Also, $\sqrt{\abs{\pp}^2+m_{\pi^\pm}^2}=\sqrt{205.138^2+139.570^2}=\sqrt{42081.6+19479.8}=248.116\ \mathrm{MeV}$, which matches $E_{\pi^+}$.

Second, the symmetry in (3): since $\rho^0\to\pi^+\pi^-$ is a two-body decay into equal masses, we must have $E_{\pi^+}=E_{\pi^-}=m_\rho/2=387.63\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Indeed, $\sqrt{361.631^2+139.570^2}=\sqrt{130777.2+19479.8}=\sqrt{150257.0}=387.63\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

Third, a dimensional check: according to the dimension rule $[\mathcal{M}]=4-N$ of Section B.1.2 of Appendix B of this book ($N$ is the total number of external lines), a $1\to2$ decay has $N=3$, so $[\mathcal{M}]=1$; that is, $\abs{\mathcal{M}}$ has the dimension of mass. The value $\abs{\mathcal{M}}=2.50\ \mathrm{GeV}$ obtained in (3) indeed came out in units of MeV, and it is a value of “the same order” as $m_\rho=0.775\ \mathrm{GeV}$, being $3.2$ times as large. This reflects the dimensionless coupling constant being $O(1)$, a magnitude characteristic of the strong interaction. Moreover, if the $\rho\to\pi\pi$ amplitude is written as $\mathcal{M}=g_{\rho\pi\pi}\,\varepsilon\cdot(p_+-p_-)$ and averaged over the three polarizations of the $\rho$, then $\overline{\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}=\frac{4}{3}g_{\rho\pi\pi}^2\abs{\pp}^2$, so $g_{\rho\pi\pi}^2 = 3\times6.2280\times10^{6}/(4\times361.631^2)=35.72$ and $g_{\rho\pi\pi}=5.98$. This agrees well with the literature value $g_{\rho\pi\pi}\simeq6$.

The check of (4) is done with $E^2-\abs{\pp}^2=m^2$. Since $\abs{\pp_e}=(m_\mu^2-m_e^2)/(2m_\mu)=52.8278\ \mathrm{MeV}$, we have $(E_e+\abs{\pp_e})(E_e-\abs{\pp_e}) = m_\mu\times m_e^2/m_\mu = m_e^2$, which is identically satisfied.

Meaning. What (1), (2), and (3) show is that in a two-body decay the energies of the final state are completely determined by the masses alone. The $\gamma$ rays emitted in the rest frame of the $\pi^0$ always have $67.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$, and the $\pi^+$ emitted from a $K^+$ always has kinetic energy $108.5\ \mathrm{MeV}$; that is, they are monochromatic. This is extremely powerful experimentally. It is thanks to this monochromaticity that a materials-science experimental technique works: producing a fully polarized muon beam from the $4.12\ \mathrm{MeV}$ monochromatic muons emitted in $\pi^+\to\mu^+\nu_\mu$ (Section B.5.2 of Appendix B of this book) and using it as a local magnetic-field probe of matter by $\mu$SR (muon spin rotation). Precisely because the momentum is sharply fixed at $30\ \mathrm{MeV}$, one can make “surface muons” that stop at a constant depth from the sample surface.

In contrast, in the three-body decay of (4), as we have just seen, the electron energy is continuously distributed from $m_e$ to $52.83\ \mathrm{MeV}$ (from $0$ to $52.32\ \mathrm{MeV}$ in kinetic energy). This continuity is itself the evidence that “two invisible particles are being emitted,” and it is the same logic by which Pauli proposed the neutrino from the continuous spectrum of $\beta$ decay. The endpoint $52.83\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is still used today as an energy calibration point of detectors.

As for the connection to materials science, the “monochromatic vs. continuous” contrast of (1) through (3) appears just as it is in phonon decay processes. The anharmonic cubic term gives $\lambda\to\lambda'+\lambda''$, a two-body decay, whose final state is strongly restricted by the two conditions of momentum conservation $\qq=\qq'+\qq''+\bm{G}$ and energy conservation $\omega_\lambda=\omega_{\lambda'}+\omega_{\lambda''}$. The quartic term gives $\lambda\to\lambda'+\lambda''+\lambda'''$, a three-body decay, whose final-state distribution is continuous. The task of measuring the temperature dependence of the linewidth to separate the cubic and quartic contributions has exactly the same logic as the task in particle physics of determining the number of final-state particles by seeing whether the spectrum of the decay products is monochromatic or continuous.

Exercise B.2: The statistical factor $S$

Problem (restated)

Give the statistical factor $S$ for each of the following processes, and state the reason in one line.

(1) $\eta\to\pi^0\pi^0\pi^0$ (2) $\omega\to\pi^+\pi^-\pi^0$ (3) $e^+e^-\to\gamma\gamma$ (4) $e^-e^-\to e^-e^-$ (5) $pp\to pp\pi^+\pi^-$ (6) $H\to ZZ\to \mu^+\mu^-\mu^+\mu^-$

(7) When the decay rate of $\pi^0\to\gamma\gamma$ is written with the two-body decay formula, it is multiplied by $S=1/2$. If we forgot $S$, by how much would we get $\abs{\mathcal{M}}$ wrong?

Solution

Strategy. We simply apply the definition of Section B.1.3 of Appendix B of this book mechanically,

$$ S = \prod_{\text{pairs of identical particles}} \frac{1}{j!} $$

. All we do is count “how many particles in the final state have all quantum numbers the same and are indistinguishable,” and multiply by $1/j!$ for each group. There are three points to note. First, $S$ concerns only the final state; the particles of the initial state are irrelevant no matter how many of them are identical (no double counting occurs for the initial state). Second, a particle and an antiparticle can be distinguished, so they are not identical. Third, $S$ is a factor on the phase-space side, and it is a separate operation from adding exchange diagrams on the $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2$ side.

(1) $\eta\to\pi^0\pi^0\pi^0$. The final state consists of three identical $\pi^0$. There is a single group with $j=3$, so

$$ S = \frac{1}{3!} = \frac{1}{6} $$

If we integrate the three momenta independently, all $3!=6$ permutations of $(\bm{a},\bm{b},\bm{c})$ are counted as distinct final states. This factor divides that overcounting back out.

The meaning of this process becomes clear when seen on the Dalitz plot of Section B.1.5 of Appendix B of this book. Since the three $\pi^0$ are identical, the Dalitz plot becomes a figure with three symmetry axes and $6$-fold symmetry, and the physically independent information is contained only in a sector of $1/6$ of the whole. Multiplying by $S=1/6$ and integrating only over the independent $1/6$ region instead of the whole plot are two ways of describing the same operation. One should do either one, and must not do both.

(2) $\omega\to\pi^+\pi^-\pi^0$. Since $\pi^+$, $\pi^-$, and $\pi^0$ have different charges, they are distinguishable from one another. There is not a single pair of identical particles.

$$ S = 1 $$

All three are pions and siblings in an isospin triplet, but what $S$ asks is not “are they members of the same multiplet?” but “do they have all quantum numbers the same and are they physically indistinguishable?” If the charges differ, they are counted as different objects on the detector side as well, so no double counting from interchanging momenta occurs. This is the only difference from (1); even for the same “$3\pi$ final state,” $S$ differs by a factor of $6$, being $1/6$ and $1$.

(3) $e^+e^-\to\gamma\gamma$. The initial-state $e^+$ and $e^-$ are distinguishable, and in any case $S$ concerns the final state. The final state is two photons, and since the photon is its own antiparticle, they are completely identical.

$$ S = \frac{1}{2!} = \frac{1}{2} $$

In this process, on the amplitude side as well, two diagrams, a $t$-channel one and a $u$-channel one, arise according to which vertex emits which photon. Since they are bosons, the relative sign is $+$ when they are added. As in (4), adding the two diagrams and multiplying by $S=1/2$ are independent operations, and one must not omit one on the grounds of the other.

(4) $e^-e^-\to e^-e^-$ (Møller scattering). There are two $e^-$ in the final state.

$$ S = \frac{1}{2!} = \frac{1}{2} $$

There are also two $e^-$ in the initial state, but this does not affect $S$. Note that on the amplitude side, the direct $t$-channel diagram and the $u$-channel exchange diagram are added with a relative sign $(-1)$ because they are fermions, and then squared. An interference term appears. This operation on the amplitude side and $S=1/2$ are independent, and both are needed. Omitting one because the other has been done is a typical error against which Section B.1.3 of Appendix B of this book warns.

(5) $pp\to pp\pi^+\pi^-$. The final state has four particles, $p,p,\pi^+,\pi^-$. Of these, the two protons are identical, while $\pi^+$ and $\pi^-$ are different objects because their charges differ.

$$ S = \frac{1}{2!} = \frac{1}{2} $$

There are also two protons in the initial state, but, for the same reason as in (4), this does not affect $S$. Even when the number of final-state particles increases to four, what we count is only the “pairs of identical particles,” not the total number of particles. For comparison, if the final state were $pp\pi^0\pi^0$, the two $\pi^0$ would be identical, so $S=(1/2)\times(1/2)=1/4$, and even for the same “four bodies from $pp$,” $S$ changes by a factor of $2$ merely through the choice of charge states.

(6) $H\to ZZ\to\mu^+\mu^-\mu^+\mu^-$. The final state that is ultimately observed consists of two $\mu^+$ and two $\mu^-$. Since there are two groups of identical particles, we multiply by $1/2!$ for each.

$$ S = \frac{1}{2!}\times\frac{1}{2!} = \frac{1}{4} $$

What is important here is that $S$ is counted for the final state that is actually integrated over. If we stopped at the stage $H\to ZZ$ and took the two $Z$ as the final state, then $S=1/2!=1/2$. If we integrate the phase space of the four muons including the decays of the $Z$, then $S=1/4$. Decide where to cut first, then count. Note that this $S=1/4$ corresponds to what is called, in experiments, “two ways of pairing $\mu^+\mu^-$ in the four-lepton channel,” and it has the same root as the ambiguity, in the $H\to ZZ\to4\mu$ analysis, of which of the two pairings is to be taken as the $Z$ candidate.

(7) Solving the two-body decay rate formula

$$ \Gamma = \frac{S\,\abs{\pp}}{8\pi\hbar\,m_1^2}\,\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2 $$

for $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2$ gives

$$ \abs{\mathcal{M}}^2 = \frac{8\pi\hbar\,m_1^2\,\Gamma}{S\,\abs{\pp}} $$

. The measured quantity is $\Gamma$ (together with $m_1$ and $\abs{\pp}$), and these are fixed. If $S=1/2$ is correctly inserted,

$$ \abs{\mathcal{M}}^2_\text{correct} = \frac{16\pi\hbar\,m_1^2\,\Gamma}{\abs{\pp}} $$

but if one forgets $S$ and sets $S=1$, then

$$ \abs{\mathcal{M}}^2_\text{wrong} = \frac{8\pi\hbar\,m_1^2\,\Gamma}{\abs{\pp}} = \frac{1}{2}\,\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2_\text{correct} $$

. That is, one misjudges $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2$ to be half of the correct value, and $\abs{\mathcal{M}}$ is underestimated by a factor of $1/\sqrt2 = 0.707$. The size of the discrepancy is a factor of 2 in $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2$ (a factor of $\sqrt2=1.41$ in $\abs{\mathcal{M}}$).

In the opposite use, that is, when one computes $\abs{\mathcal{M}}$ from theory and predicts $\Gamma$, forgetting $S$ overestimates $\Gamma$ by a factor of 2. Instead of predicting the $\pi^0$ lifetime $8.43\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{s}$, one would get $4.2\times10^{-17}\ \mathrm{s}$, which is off from experiment by a factor of 2. In a world where the $O(\alpha)$ corrections are a few $\%$, a factor-of-2 discrepancy is fatal.

Verification. First we compare directly with Table B.1 of Appendix B of this book (examples of the statistical factor $S$). (1) $\eta\to\pi^0\pi^0\pi^0$ is $1/6$ in the table, (2) $\omega\to\pi^+\pi^-\pi^0$ is $1$ in the table, (3) $e^+e^-\to\gamma\gamma$ is $1/2$ in the table, and (4) Møller scattering $e^-e^-\to e^-e^-$ is $1/2$ in the table; all four agree with the values in the table. (5) is the process $pp\to pp\pi^0$ ($S=1/2$) in the table with the $\pi^0$ replaced by $\pi^+\pi^-$; since the two added particles are distinguishable from each other, $S$ does not change. (6) is a multistage decay not in the table, but it merely extends the way of reading the table, “$1/2$ for one pair of two identical particles,” to the case of two pairs. Even for a process not listed in the table, the answer follows automatically as long as the counting is the same.

One more way to confirm is another way of counting: the value of $S$ equals the reciprocal of “the number of ways of relabeling indistinguishable final-state particles.” In (1), the relabelings of the three $\pi^0$ number $3!=6$, so $S=1/6$; in (6), the product of 2 relabelings of $\mu^+$ and 2 relabelings of $\mu^-$ is $4$, so $S=1/4$; in (2), the only relabeling is the identity map, a single one, so $S=1$. All agree with the answers above.

Another check is the comparison with statistical mechanics. If $1/N!$ is not included in the partition function of an ideal gas of $N$ identical particles, Gibbs’s paradox occurs (the entropy of mixing does not vanish even for identical gases). The factor $1/j!$ that we are counting is exactly the same factor, and the two are manifestations of the general rule: “if indistinguishable things are integrated over independently, divide by the number of permutations at the end.” If one knows one of them, the other can be derived.

Meaning. The statistical factor is the most unglamorous and most error-prone component among the collected formulas. No matter how many hours one spends on the calculation of $\abs{\mathcal{M}}$, dropping a $1/2$ at the end shifts the conclusion by $\sqrt2$. Moreover, this error has the nasty property of being “hard to notice because the order of magnitude is right.” The reason Appendix B of this book deliberately sets up $S$ as an independent item is that the damage in practice is that great.

The same omission in counting occurs on the materials-science side too. When computing the decay rate in the three-phonon process of anharmonic phonons, $\lambda\to\lambda'+\lambda''$, a $1/2$ is needed if one sums over the pairs $(\lambda',\lambda'')$ running independently ($\lambda'$ and $\lambda''$ are particles of the same kind, “phonons”). Some papers adopt the convention of restricting the sum to a non-overlapping region, and in that case one must not multiply by $1/2$. It is a pitfall that actually occurs often that, when comparing the absolute value of the linewidth with other codes or experiments using a code such as ALAMODE, a factor-of-$2$ discrepancy arises from the difference in this coefficient convention. The caution of Appendix B of this book, “one must not do both,” applies just as it is to first-principles phonon calculations.

Exercise B.3: Conversions in natural units

Problem (restated)

Use $\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$, $\hbar=6.58212\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{MeV\,s}$, and $(\hbar c)^2=0.3894\ \mathrm{GeV^2\,mb}$.

(1) The total width of the $\rho(770)$ is $\Gamma=149.1\ \mathrm{MeV}$. Find its lifetime $\tau$ and flight distance $c\tau$, and compare with the proton radius $0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$.

(2) The lifetime of the $\tau$ lepton is $2.903\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{s}$. Find its total width in units of $\mathrm{meV}$.

(3) The cross section of a certain scattering process has been computed to be $\sigma=1.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$. Convert it to $\mathrm{nb}$.

(4) The range of the Yukawa potential is $1/m$. Find, in $\mathrm{fm}$, the range of the weak interaction mediated by the $W$ boson ($80.377\ \mathrm{GeV}$), and compare it with the proton radius.

Solution

Strategy. We use the three rules of Section B.3.2 of Appendix B of this book exactly as they stand. To get a length, multiply by $\hbar c$; to get a time, multiply by $\hbar$; to get an area, multiply by $(\hbar c)^2$. Which rule to use is fixed by dimensional analysis alone, so there are effectively only two numbers to remember ($\hbar c=197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}$ and $\hbar=6.58212\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{MeV\,s}$). $(\hbar c)^2=0.3894\ \mathrm{GeV^2\,mb}$ can be built from the first two, but it is used for cross sections every time, so in practice it is best to memorize it independently.

(1) From $\tau=\hbar/\Gamma$ in Section B.1.1 of Appendix B of this book, the lifetime is

$$ \tau = \frac{\hbar}{\Gamma} = \frac{6.58212\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{MeV\,s}}{149.1\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 4.4146\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{s} $$

The flight distance follows by multiplying by $c$:

$$ c\tau = 2.99792\times10^{23}\ \mathrm{fm/s}\times4.4146\times10^{-24}\ \mathrm{s} = 1.3235\ \mathrm{fm} $$

The same answer comes out even faster if we do not use $\hbar$ and $c$ separately but use $\hbar c$ in one step.

$$ c\tau = \frac{\hbar c}{\Gamma} = \frac{197.327\ \mathrm{MeV\,fm}}{149.1\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 1.3235\ \mathrm{fm} $$

Compared with the proton radius $0.84\ \mathrm{fm}$, this is only $1.3235/0.84=1.58$ times larger. That is, the $\rho$ meson decays after flying a distance of only about one hadron. This agrees with $c\tau=1.32\ \mathrm{fm}$ in Table B.5.

(2) This is the conversion in the opposite direction.

$$ \Gamma = \frac{\hbar}{\tau} = \frac{6.58212\times10^{-22}\ \mathrm{MeV\,s}}{2.903\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{s}} = 2.2674\times10^{-9}\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

Since $1\ \mathrm{MeV}=10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV}$,

$$ \Gamma = 2.2674\times10^{-9}\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{eV} = 2.2674\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV} = 2.267\ \mathrm{meV} $$

This agrees with the $2.27\ \mathrm{meV}$ of Table B.5. While we are at it, the flight distance is $c\tau = 2.99792\times10^{8}\ \mathrm{m/s}\times2.903\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{s}=8.703\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{m}=87.0\ \mu\mathrm{m}$, which also agrees with Table B.5. It is thanks to this length of $87\ \mu\mathrm{m}$ that the decay point of a $\tau$ lepton can be resolved as a “secondary vertex” in a silicon detector.

(3) A cross section has mass dimension $-2$, so we multiply by $(\hbar c)^2$.

$$ \sigma = 1.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}} \times 0.3894\ \mathrm{GeV^2\,mb} = 5.841\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mb} $$

Since $1\ \mathrm{mb}=10^{-3}\ \mathrm{b}$ and $1\ \mathrm{nb}=10^{-9}\ \mathrm{b}$, we have $1\ \mathrm{mb}=10^{6}\ \mathrm{nb}$. Therefore

$$ \sigma = 5.841\times10^{-4}\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{nb} = 584\ \mathrm{nb} $$

In practice one remembers $1\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}=3.894\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{nb}$ and finishes in one line: $1.5\times10^{-3}\times3.894\times10^{5}=584.1\ \mathrm{nb}$.

(4) The range of the Yukawa potential $V(r)\propto \ee^{-mr}/r$ is $1/m$. In natural units, $1/m_W = 1/80.377 = 1.2441\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-1}}$. Using Rule 1 (multiply by $\hbar c$ for a length), we get

$$ \frac{\hbar c}{m_Wc^2} = \frac{0.197327\ \mathrm{GeV\,fm}}{80.377\ \mathrm{GeV}} = 2.455\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm} $$

The ratio to the proton radius is

$$ \frac{0.84\ \mathrm{fm}}{2.455\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}} = 342 $$

That is, the range of the weak interaction is only about $1/340$ of the proton radius.

Verification. We verify all four independently by a different route.

(1): The route using $\hbar$ and $c$ separately gives $1.32345\ \mathrm{fm}$, and the route using $\hbar c$ in one step gives $1.32345\ \mathrm{fm}$. They agree. (Of course the two are the same calculation, but they differ in whether or not they cross the $10^{\pm22}$ orders of magnitude along the way, so this serves as a check against loss of significant digits.)

(2): Using the dictionary of Table B.4, “$1\ \mathrm{eV}$ corresponds to the time $\hbar/E$ of $0.65821\ \mathrm{fs}$,” for $\tau=2.903\times10^{-13}\ \mathrm{s}=2.903\times10^{2}\ \mathrm{fs}$ we get $\Gamma = 0.65821/290.3\ \mathrm{eV}=2.2674\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{eV}$. The value is the same.

(3): Using $1\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}=0.03894\ \mathrm{fm^2}$ (from $(\hbar c)^2=0.038938\ \mathrm{GeV^2\,fm^2}$), we get $\sigma=1.5\times10^{-3}\times0.03894=5.841\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{fm^2}$. Since $1\ \mathrm{fm^2}=10\ \mathrm{mb}$, this is $5.841\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{mb}$, in agreement with the above.

(4): Without using $\hbar c$, simply multiplying by the value $1\ \mathrm{GeV^{-1}}=0.197327\ \mathrm{fm}$ of Table B.3 gives $1.2441\times10^{-2}\times0.197327=2.455\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}$. The same.

Meaning. Both (1) and (4) are tasks of “laying a length ruler against the interaction to see what spatial scale its phenomena have.” The $c\tau=1.32\ \mathrm{fm}$ of the $\rho$ means that the $\rho$ decays practically without moving from the place where it was produced. Therefore the $\rho$ leaves no track and can only show up as a Breit–Wigner bump of width $149\ \mathrm{MeV}$ in the $\pi\pi$ invariant-mass distribution. Conversely, the $\tau$ lepton of (2) flies $87\ \mu\mathrm{m}$, so its decay point can be separated and measured spatially. The size of the width directly determines the experimental method.

The $2.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}$ of (4) is the basis for the fact that the weak interaction can be approximated as a “point contact.” On the scale of the size of a nucleon ($\sim1\ \mathrm{fm}$) or of an atomic nucleus (a few fm), $W$ exchange looks like a perfect point. Therefore at low energies the $W$ propagator may be replaced by the constant $1/(q^2-m_W^2)\to -1/m_W^2$, and from this the Fermi constant $G_F/\sqrt2 = g^2/(8m_W^2)$ follows. In fact, solving backward from $G_F=1.1664\times10^{-5}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}$ and $m_W^2=6460.5\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$, we obtain $g^2 = 4\sqrt2\,G_F m_W^2 = 0.4263$, $g=0.653$, and we see that the coupling constant of the weak interaction itself is $2.2$ times that of the electromagnetic interaction ($e=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}=0.303$), that is, if anything larger (independent check: $g^2=4\pi\hat\alpha(M_Z)/\sin^2\theta_W = 4\pi\times(1/128)/0.2312 = 0.425$, where $\hat\alpha(M_Z)\simeq1/128$ is a rough value in the $\overline{\rm MS}$ scheme, giving $g=0.652$. They agree). The weak interaction is “weak” not because its coupling is small but because $m_W$ is large and the range is short. The single line “$[G_F]=-2$” in Table B.2 states this situation in the language of dimensions.

The connection to materials science lies in the unit conversion of (3). Condensed-matter experimentalists express cross sections not in barns but through the absorption coefficient $\mu\ [\mathrm{cm^{-1}}]$ or the scattering length $b\ [\mathrm{fm}]$, but in substance it is always the same $\sigma$. For example, from the $b_\text{coh}(\mathrm{Ni})=10.3\ \mathrm{fm}$ used in neutron scattering we get $\sigma=4\pi b^2 = 4\pi\times106\ \mathrm{fm^2}=1333\ \mathrm{fm^2}=13.3\ \mathrm{barn}$. The particle physicist’s $(\hbar c)^2$ and the condensed-matter physicist’s $4\pi b^2$ are different pages of the same conversion table.

Exercise B.4: Mandelstam variables and the invariant cross section

Problem (restated)

Consider $1+2\to3+4$ with all masses negligible ($m_i=0$). Let $\theta$ be the scattering angle in the CM frame and $s$ the square of the center-of-mass energy.

(1) Use the CM-frame expression for $t$ in Section B.2.4 of Appendix B of this book to express $t$ and $u$ in terms of $s$ and $\theta$.

(2) Verify that $s+t+u=\sum_i m_i^2$ is satisfied.

(3) Show that the CM-frame formula for $\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega$ and the invariant formula for $\dd\sigma/\dd t$ are consistent, using $\abs{\pp_i}=\abs{\pp_f}=\sqrt{s}/2$.

(4) Find the allowed range of $t$. Also, when $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2\propto1/t^2$ (the case of exchange of a massless particle in the $t$-channel), show that the total cross section $\sigma=\int\dd\sigma$ diverges, and verify that the divergence comes from the forward direction ($\theta\to0$).

Solution

Strategy. Massless $2\to2$ scattering is the case in which the kinematics is simplest. In the CM frame all four particles have the same energy $\sqrt{s}/2$ and the same momentum magnitude $\sqrt{s}/2$, and the only independent variable is the scattering angle $\theta$. Thus the two variables $s$ and $\theta$ determine the kinematics completely, and $t$ and $u$ are dependent variables. The only tools we use are the CM-frame expression for $t$ in Section B.2.4 of Appendix B of this book and the two cross-section formulas of Sections B.2.3 and B.2.4.

(1) First we write down the CM-frame kinematics. Since the masses are zero, $E_1=E_2=E_3=E_4=\sqrt{s}/2$, and the momentum magnitudes are $\abs{\pp_i}=\abs{\pp_f}=\sqrt{s}/2$ as well ($\abs{\pp}=\sqrt{E^2-m^2}=E$). Putting $m_1=m_3=0$ into the formula of Section B.2.4 of Appendix B of this book,

$$ t = m_1^2+m_3^2-2E_1E_3+2\abs{\pp_i}\abs{\pp_f}\cos\theta $$

we obtain

$$ t = -2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2} + 2\cdot\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}\cdot\frac{\sqrt{s}}{2}\cos\theta = -\frac{s}{2}+\frac{s}{2}\cos\theta $$

that is,

$$ t = -\frac{s}{2}\big(1-\cos\theta\big) = -s\,\sin^2\frac{\theta}{2} $$

(the last step is the half-angle formula $1-\cos\theta = 2\sin^2(\theta/2)$).

We obtain $u$ by the same procedure. We have $u=(p_1-p_4)^2$, and since particle 4 emerges in the CM frame in the direction exactly opposite to particle 3, the angle between $\pp_1$ and $\pp_4$ is $\pi-\theta$. Therefore it suffices to replace $\cos\theta\to\cos(\pi-\theta)=-\cos\theta$ in the above expression:

$$ u = -\frac{s}{2}\big(1+\cos\theta\big) = -s\,\cos^2\frac{\theta}{2} $$

We can see at a glance that both $t$ and $u$ are always $\le0$.

(2) We add the three.

$$ s+t+u = s - \frac{s}{2}\big(1-\cos\theta\big) - \frac{s}{2}\big(1+\cos\theta\big) = s - \frac{s}{2} + \frac{s}{2}\cos\theta - \frac{s}{2} - \frac{s}{2}\cos\theta $$

The $\cos\theta$ terms cancel neatly, and

$$ s+t+u = s - \frac{s}{2} - \frac{s}{2} = 0 $$

On the other hand, the right-hand side is $\sum_i m_i^2 = 0+0+0+0 = 0$. The two sides agree. It is important that this holds in a form independent of $\theta$; this is the simplest check of the statement in Section B.2.4 of Appendix B of this book that “$s+t+u$ is an identity that does not depend on the details of the kinematics.”

Written in half-angle form, it is just the trigonometric identity $s\sin^2(\theta/2)+s\cos^2(\theta/2)=s$, and $-t-u=s$ is a restatement of the Pythagorean theorem.

(3) The two formulas are

$$ \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd\Omega}\bigg|_\text{CM} = \frac{S\,\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}{64\pi^2 s}\,\frac{\abs{\pp_f}}{\abs{\pp_i}}, \qquad \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd t} = \frac{S\,\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}{64\pi\,s\,\abs{\pp_i}^2} $$

Let us derive the latter from the former. First we construct the Jacobian of the change of variables. Differentiating the expression for $t$ in (1) with respect to $\cos\theta$, we get

$$ \frac{\dd t}{\dd\cos\theta} = 2\abs{\pp_i}\abs{\pp_f} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \dd t = 2\abs{\pp_i}\abs{\pp_f}\,\dd\cos\theta $$

If the distribution is symmetric in the azimuthal angle, $\dd\Omega = 2\pi\,\dd\cos\theta$, so

$$ \dd\Omega = 2\pi\cdot\frac{\dd t}{2\abs{\pp_i}\abs{\pp_f}} = \frac{\pi\,\dd t}{\abs{\pp_i}\abs{\pp_f}} $$

Now $\abs{\pp_i}=\abs{\pp_f}=\sqrt{s}/2$, so $\abs{\pp_i}\abs{\pp_f}=s/4$, and

$$ \dd\Omega = \frac{4\pi}{s}\,\dd t $$

Therefore

$$ \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd t} = \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd\Omega}\cdot\frac{\dd\Omega}{\dd t} = \frac{S\,\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}{64\pi^2 s}\cdot\underbrace{\frac{\abs{\pp_f}}{\abs{\pp_i}}}_{=1}\cdot\frac{4\pi}{s} = \frac{S\,\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}{16\pi\,s^2} $$

On the other hand, substituting $\abs{\pp_i}^2 = s/4$ directly into the invariant formula gives

$$ \frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd t} = \frac{S\,\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}{64\pi\,s\,(s/4)} = \frac{S\,\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}{16\pi\,s^2} $$

which is exactly the same expression. The two formulas are consistent.

It also agrees with the third way of writing it in Section B.2.4 of Appendix B of this book, $\dd\sigma/\dd t = S\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2/\big(16\pi\lambda(s,m_1^2,m_2^2)\big)$. For zero masses the Källén function is $\lambda(s,0,0)=s^2+0+0-0-0-0=s^2$, so the right-hand side is $S\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2/(16\pi s^2)$. All three expressions agree.

(4) $\cos\theta$ runs from $-1$ to $+1$. Substituting into the expression of (1),

$$ \theta=0\ (\text{forward}):\ t = -\frac{s}{2}(1-1) = 0, \qquad \theta=\pi\ (\text{backward}):\ t = -\frac{s}{2}(1+1) = -s $$

and since $t$ is a monotonically increasing function of $\cos\theta$,

$$ -s \le t \le 0 $$

is the allowed range of $t$. The allowed range of $u$ is likewise $-s\le u\le0$, with $u=-s$ when $t=0$ and $u=0$ when $t=-s$. At $\theta=\pi/2$, $t=u=-s/2$.

Next we form the total cross section with $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2 = C/t^2$ ($C$ a constant).

$$ \sigma = \int_{-s}^{0}\frac{\dd\sigma}{\dd t}\,\dd t = \frac{S\,C}{16\pi s^2}\int_{-s}^{0}\frac{\dd t}{t^2} $$

The integral is elementary. Since $\int \dd t/t^2 = -1/t$, taking the lower limit $-s$ and the upper limit $-\varepsilon$ (with $\varepsilon>0$ to be sent to zero afterward),

$$ \int_{-s}^{-\varepsilon}\frac{\dd t}{t^2} = \left[-\frac{1}{t}\right]_{-s}^{-\varepsilon} = \frac{1}{\varepsilon} - \frac{1}{s} \;\xrightarrow[\varepsilon\to0]{}\; \infty $$

That is, the total cross section diverges. The divergence comes from the upper limit $t\to0^-$, and $t=0$ is $\cos\theta=1$, that is, the forward direction $\theta\to0$. The contribution from the lower limit $t=-s$ (backward) is finite, $1/s$, so the divergence comes entirely from the forward direction.

Rewriting in terms of the angle gives the same conclusion. For small $\theta$, $t\simeq -s\theta^2/4$, so $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2\propto 1/t^2 \propto 16/(s^2\theta^4)$, while $\dd\Omega = 2\pi\sin\theta\,\dd\theta \simeq 2\pi\theta\,\dd\theta$. Therefore

$$ \sigma \sim \int \frac{1}{\theta^4}\,\theta\,\dd\theta = \int\frac{\dd\theta}{\theta^3} \;\propto\; \frac{1}{\theta_\text{min}^2} $$

so that when the forward cutoff angle $\theta_\text{min}$ is sent to zero, the cross section diverges quadratically. We have confirmed in the angular representation too that the divergence comes from the forward direction.

To stop the divergence, it suffices to give the exchanged particle a mass $m$, so that $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2 = C/(t-m^2)^2$. Then

$$ \int_{-s}^{0}\frac{\dd t}{(t-m^2)^2} = \left[-\frac{1}{t-m^2}\right]_{-s}^{0} = \frac{1}{m^2}-\frac{1}{s+m^2} = \frac{s}{m^2\,(s+m^2)} $$

which is finite. For $m^2\ll s$ it is $\simeq 1/m^2$, so the smaller the mass of the exchanged particle, the larger the cross section.

Verification. We carry out three checks.

First, we compare the result of (1) with the famous Rutherford angular dependence. Since $t=-s\sin^2(\theta/2)$,

$$ \frac{1}{t^2} = \frac{1}{s^2\sin^4(\theta/2)} $$

Putting $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2\propto1/t^2$ into the formula for $\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega$ gives $\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega \propto 1/\sin^4(\theta/2)$. This is exactly the angular dependence of the Rutherford cross section that appeared both in Section B.2.3 of Appendix B of this book and in the RBS discussion of Section B.2.5, so the origin, massless exchange in the $t$ channel, is indeed reproduced.

Second, we check the screened integral of (4) numerically. For $s=1$, $m^2=0.01$, we have $s/[m^2(s+m^2)] = 1/(0.01\times1.01) = 99.01$, which is close to the unscreened approximate value $1/m^2=100$ and is finite. As $m^2\to0$, $99.01\to\infty$, so we can also confirm that the divergence returns.

Third, a dimensional check. $[\mathcal{M}]=4-N=4-4=0$ (there are four external lines in $2\to2$), so $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2$ must be dimensionless. For $C/t^2$ to be dimensionless we need $[C]=4$, that is, $C$ has the dimension of mass to the fourth power. Indeed, in QED $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2 \sim e^4 s^2/t^2$, which is consistent because $e$ is dimensionless and $s^2$ has dimension mass to the fourth power. And $\dd\sigma/\dd t = S\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2/(16\pi s^2)$ has dimension $[\text{mass}]^{-4}$, and since $\dd t$ is $[\text{mass}]^{2}$, $\sigma$ is $[\text{mass}]^{-2}$, in agreement with the mass dimension $-2$ of the cross section in Table B.2.

Meaning. What (3) shows is that the “cardinal rule” of Section B.2.4 of Appendix B of this book—first calculate with the invariants $s,t$, and choose the frame last—is indeed safe. Since $\dd\sigma/\dd t$ takes the same value in whichever inertial frame it is computed, there is no danger of losing a sign or a factor buried in the Jacobian calculation. If one fixes the frame first, then, for example, in the angle transformation to the laboratory frame $\gamma_\text{CM}$ gets involved and the expression becomes troublesome.

The forward divergence of (4) is the cross-section-side expression of the fact that the range of the Coulomb interaction is infinite. However far away a particle passes, it is deflected a little, so the “area hit” becomes infinite. As we saw in Exercise B.3(4), if the exchanged particle is heavy like the $W$ boson, the range is finite ($2.5\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{fm}$) and the cross section is finite too. Whether it diverges or not is decided by whether the exchanged particle is massless.

In materials science, this divergence is in fact routinely dealt with as “screening.” The Coulomb potential felt by a charged particle in a solid turns, through the response of the conduction electrons, into the Yukawa type $V(r)\propto \ee^{-r/\lambda_\text{TF}}/r$ (Thomas–Fermi screening). The denominator of the propagator then becomes $1/(t-\lambda_\text{TF}^{-2})$, and, as we saw at the end of (4), the integral becomes finite. When one calculates the electrical resistance of a metal from impurity scattering, without screening the cross section would diverge and the resistance would become infinite. The Thomas–Fermi screening length, treated in “Introduction to Linear Response Theory,” Chapter 10, “Screening — Thomas–Fermi and the Lindhard Function,” exists precisely to stop this divergence.

Another practical manifestation is RBS. As we saw in Section B.2.5 of Appendix B of this book, RBS measures at backward angles, $\theta^\text{lab}\simeq170^\circ$. The cross section is large in the forward direction, but there it cannot be distinguished from the unscattered beam, and moreover, because of the $1/t^2$ divergence, small-angle scatterings pile up and the depth resolution is lost. If one restricts oneself to the backward direction, one uses only the finite, smooth region near $t\simeq-s$, and the mass separation by the kinematic factor $K$ is maximal. The design decision “avoid the divergent forward direction and measure backward, where the kinematics works well” follows directly from the properties of the integral in (4).

Exercise B.5: The $Z$ resonance and the number of neutrino generations

Problem (restated)

PDG 2022 values: $M_Z=91.1876\ \mathrm{GeV}$, $\Gamma_Z=2495.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $\Gamma_{ee}=83.92\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $\Gamma_{\mu\mu}=83.99\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $\Gamma_{\tau\tau}=84.08\ \mathrm{MeV}$, $\Gamma_\text{had}=1744.4\ \mathrm{MeV}$ (the partial widths of the charged leptons are the branching ratios multiplied by $\Gamma_Z$; the average over the three generations is $\Gamma_{\ell\ell}=83.984\ \mathrm{MeV}$).

(1) Use the relativistic Breit–Wigner formula of Section B.4.3 of Appendix B of this book to find the hadron production cross section at the $Z$ peak, $\sigma^\text{had}_\text{peak}$, in $\mathrm{nb}$.

(2) Similarly, find the peak cross section for $\mu^+\mu^-$ production, and compare it with the pure-QED value at the same $\sqrt{s}$ ($\sigma=86.8\ \mathrm{nb}/s[\mathrm{GeV^2}]$ in Section B.5.1 of Appendix B of this book).

(3) Subtract the contributions of the measured channels (hadrons plus the charged leptons of three generations) from the total width to find the “invisible width” $\Gamma_\text{inv}$.

(4) The Standard Model predicts $\Gamma(Z\to\nu\bar\nu)=167.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$ (per generation; this is the value from the PDG electroweak fit, and is $1/3$ of $\Gamma_\text{inv}^\text{SM}=501.7\ \mathrm{MeV}$). Find the number of neutrino generations $N_\nu$.

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1) and (2) simply insert numbers into the peak cross section of Section B.4.3 of Appendix B of this book,

$$ \sigma_\text{peak} = \frac{12\pi}{M^2}\,\frac{\Gamma_{ee}\Gamma_f}{\Gamma^2} $$

and convert with $(\hbar c)^2=0.3894\ \mathrm{GeV^2\,mb}$. Parts (3) and (4) use only the single line $\Gamma=\sum_i\Gamma_i$ of Section B.1.1 of Appendix B of this book, that is, “the total width is the sum of the partial widths.” Physically, (3) and (4) are the heart of the matter: we retrace one of the most beautiful experiments in particle physics, “measuring what cannot be seen by subtracting what can be seen from the whole.” We put all units in GeV: $\Gamma_Z=2.4952$, $\Gamma_{ee}=0.08392$, $\Gamma_{\mu\mu}=0.08399$, $\Gamma_{\tau\tau}=0.08408$, $\Gamma_\text{had}=1.7444\ \mathrm{GeV}$.

(1) We evaluate the prefactor first.

$$ \frac{12\pi}{M_Z^2} = \frac{37.6991}{(91.1876)^2} = \frac{37.6991}{8315.178} = 4.53377\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}} $$

The ratio of widths is

$$ \frac{\Gamma_{ee}\Gamma_\text{had}}{\Gamma_Z^2} = \frac{0.08392\times1.7444}{(2.4952)^2} = \frac{0.1463900}{6.226023} = 2.351261\times10^{-2} $$

(this quantity is just $B_{ee}B_\text{had}$, and is dimensionless). Multiplying the two gives

$$ \sigma_\text{peak}^\text{had} = 4.53377\times10^{-3}\times2.351261\times10^{-2} = 1.06601\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}} $$

A cross section has mass dimension $-2$, so we multiply by $(\hbar c)^2$ to convert it to an area. Using $1\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}}=3.894\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{nb}$,

$$ \sigma_\text{peak}^\text{had} = 1.06601\times10^{-4}\times3.894\times10^{5}\ \mathrm{nb} = 41.51\ \mathrm{nb} $$

This agrees with the $41.5\ \mathrm{nb}$ given in the Hint. It also agrees to within $0.1\ \%$ with the Born cross section measured at LEP, $\sigma^0_\text{had}=41.54\pm0.04\ \mathrm{nb}$ (the value after the luminosity was re-evaluated in 2020 with higher-order corrections to Bhabha scattering is $41.48\pm0.03\ \mathrm{nb}$).

(2) We simply replace $\Gamma_f$ by $\Gamma_{\mu\mu}$.

$$ \frac{\Gamma_{ee}\Gamma_{\mu\mu}}{\Gamma_Z^2} = \frac{0.08392\times0.08399}{6.226023} = \frac{7.048441\times10^{-3}}{6.226023} = 1.132094\times10^{-3} $$ $$ \sigma_\text{peak}^{\mu\mu} = 4.53377\times10^{-3}\times1.132094\times10^{-3} = 5.13265\times10^{-6}\ \mathrm{GeV^{-2}} = 1.999\ \mathrm{nb} $$

On the other hand, at the same $\sqrt{s}=M_Z$ the pure-QED value (only $\gamma^*$ exchange) follows from the one-line formula of Section B.5.1 of Appendix B of this book:

$$ \sigma_\text{QED} = \frac{86.8\ \mathrm{nb}}{s\,[\mathrm{GeV^2}]} = \frac{86.8}{8315.18} = 1.0439\times10^{-2}\ \mathrm{nb} = 10.44\ \mathrm{pb} $$

Taking the ratio,

$$ \frac{\sigma_\text{peak}^{\mu\mu}}{\sigma_\text{QED}} = \frac{1.999}{1.0439\times10^{-2}} = 191.5 $$

that is, the resonance enhances the cross section by a factor of about $190$. This agrees, within rounding, with the Hint’s “$2.00\ \mathrm{nb}$ versus $0.0104\ \mathrm{nb}$, a ratio of $192$.”

(3) The total width is the sum of the partial widths. The channels that could be measured are hadrons and the charged leptons of the three generations. Adding the charged-lepton contributions first,

$$ \Gamma_{ee}+\Gamma_{\mu\mu}+\Gamma_{\tau\tau} = 83.92+83.99+84.08 = 251.99\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

(that the three are nearly equal is a manifestation of lepton universality, which is itself an important test of the Standard Model). Therefore

$$ \Gamma_\text{inv} = \Gamma_Z - \Gamma_\text{had} - \big(\Gamma_{ee}+\Gamma_{\mu\mu}+\Gamma_{\tau\tau}\big) = 2495.2 - 1744.4 - 251.99 = 498.81\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

This agrees with the $498.8\ \mathrm{MeV}$ given in the Hint. Its share of the total width is $498.81/2495.2 = 20.0\%$, so one out of every five $Z$ decays is a decay in which “nothing is seen.”

(4) The invisible decay is the neutrino pair $\nu\bar\nu$ (within the Standard Model there is no other). Dividing by the predicted value per generation, $167.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$,

$$ N_\nu = \frac{\Gamma_\text{inv}}{\Gamma(Z\to\nu\bar\nu)} = \frac{498.81}{167.2} = 2.983 $$

This agrees with the $2.98$ given in the Hint. Rounding to an integer gives $N_\nu=3$; that is, there are only three generations of light neutrinos with $m_\nu<M_Z/2$.

The qualifier “light” is not decoration. For $Z\to\nu\bar\nu$ to be kinematically open we need $2m_\nu<M_Z$, that is, $m_\nu<45.6\ \mathrm{GeV}$. Therefore this measurement rules out only “a fourth neutrino that is lighter than $45.6\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and couples to the $Z$ just as in the Standard Model.” It places no constraint at all on heavier neutrinos, or on right-handed (sterile) neutrinos that do not couple to the $Z$. This is why the heavy right-handed neutrinos that appear in the seesaw mechanism of Chapter 14 do not contradict the LEP result.

Let us also look at the sensitivity. $N_\nu$ is proportional to $\Gamma_\text{inv}$, and $\Gamma_\text{inv}$ is obtained by subtraction from the total width, so

$$ \frac{\partial N_\nu}{\partial \Gamma_Z} = \frac{1}{167.2\ \mathrm{MeV}} = 0.0060\ \mathrm{MeV^{-1}} $$

An error of $1\ \mathrm{MeV}$ in $\Gamma_Z$ moves $N_\nu$ by $0.006$. To determine $N_\nu$ to a precision of $0.01$, the total width must be measured to $2\ \mathrm{MeV}$, that is, to a relative precision of $10^{-3}$. LEP accumulated $2\times10^{7}$ $Z$ bosons, and in calibrating the beam energy it even corrected for the stretching of the accelerator ring caused by the lunar tides and for stray currents from nearby trains, precisely to meet the demand of this one line.

Verification. We run three checks.

First, we check that the ratio of (1) and (2) is a ratio of widths. Since they share the same prefactor, the same $\Gamma_{ee}$, and the same $\Gamma_Z^2$, the ratio should be the ratio of the partial widths of the final states.

$$ \frac{\sigma_\text{peak}^\text{had}}{\sigma_\text{peak}^{\mu\mu}} = \frac{41.51}{1.999} = 20.77, \qquad \frac{\Gamma_\text{had}}{\Gamma_{\mu\mu}} = \frac{1744.4}{83.99} = 20.77 $$

They agree. This is a clean confirmation that the prefactor was not miscalculated.

Second, a check in the opposite direction. Assume $N_\nu=3$ and reconstruct the total width.

$$ \Gamma_\text{had}+\sum_\ell\Gamma_{\ell\ell}+3\Gamma_{\nu\bar\nu} = 1744.4+251.99+3\times167.2 = 2497.99\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The difference from the input $\Gamma_Z=2495.2\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is $2.79\ \mathrm{MeV}$, a relative error of $0.11\%$. The value $2.983$ of $N_\nu$ deviates slightly from $3$ because this $0.11\%$ is concentrated in $\Gamma_\text{inv}$ ($20\%$ of the total width), producing a shift of $2.79/167.2=0.017$; this lies within the experimental error (about $\pm3\ \mathrm{MeV}$, combining $\pm2.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for $\Gamma_Z$ and $\pm2.0\ \mathrm{MeV}$ for $\Gamma_\text{had}$). It is not a computational mistake.

Third, we check that the branching ratios sum to $1$. $B_\text{had}=1744.4/2495.2=69.91\%$, the total of the $B_{\ell\ell}$ $=251.99/2495.2=10.10\%$, and $B_\text{inv}=498.81/2495.2=19.99\%$. The total is $100.00\%$, which satisfies $\sum_i\mathrm{BR}_i=1$ of Section B.1.1 of Appendix B of this book. It also matches “$Z\to q\bar q\ (69.9\%)$” in Table B.5.

Meaning. This exercise is the place where all the tools of Appendix B of this book converge on a single experimental result. We measure the Breit–Wigner resonance curve and read off (i) $\Gamma_{ee}\Gamma_f/\Gamma^2$ from the height of the peak, (ii) $\Gamma_Z$ from its width, and (iii) $M_Z$ from its position. That alone reveals the number of generations of neutrinos, not one of which can be observed directly. LEP accomplished this with a precision of $N_\nu = 2.9840\pm0.0082$ (the value after the luminosity was re-evaluated in 2020 with higher-order corrections to Bhabha scattering is $2.9963\pm0.0074$). A fourth generation of light neutrinos is excluded at more than $5$ standard deviations.

All that is at work here is the seemingly obvious addition $\Gamma=\sum_i\Gamma_i$ of Section B.1.1 of Appendix B of this book. The logic is: “We know the sum of everything. We can measure what is visible. Therefore we can find what is invisible by subtraction.” This is a universal strategy in experimental physics, and it has the same form as Pauli’s argument (Chapter 2), in which the neutrino was inferred from the energy deficit in $\beta$ decay.

An example in which exactly the same logic is used in materials science is the fluorescence yield, also mentioned in Section B.3.2 of Appendix B of this book. The total width $\Gamma$ of a core hole can be measured from the peak width in XPS. The intensity of fluorescent X-rays gives $\Gamma_\text{X}$. The remainder, $\Gamma-\Gamma_\text{X}$, is the width of the Auger process; although this is not an “invisible width,” a quantity that is hard to measure directly is determined by subtraction. We actually carry out this calculation in Exercise B.6(2). The number of neutrino generations of the $Z$ boson and the Auger width of the $K$ shell of Cu are determined by the same subtraction.

One more point: the “resonance enhances by a factor of about $190$” of (2) is, on the materials side, the power of resonant excitation. In resonant inelastic X-ray scattering (RIXS) and resonant Raman scattering, the signal jumps by orders of magnitude when the incident energy is tuned to the absorption edge, precisely because the same Breit–Wigner denominator becomes small. Tuning $\sqrt{s}$ to $M_Z$ and tuning the X-ray energy to the Cu $L_3$ edge are the same operation.

Exercise B.6: Linewidths, lifetimes, and mean free paths in materials science

Problem (restated)
