The coefficient is $(\ii g_e)\times\ii\times(\ii g_e)=\ii^3g_e^2=-\ii g_e^2$. In Diagram 2 (emission first), reading from the right, “$u(p)$ → emission vertex → propagator → absorption vertex → $\bar u(p')$,” so

$$ -\ii g_e^2\,\bar u(p')\,\frac{\slashed\epsilon\left(\slashed p-\slashed k'+m\right)\slashed\epsilon'^{*}}{-2p\!\cdot\!k'}\,u(p) =+\ii g_e^2\,\bar u(p')\,\frac{\slashed\epsilon\left(\slashed p-\slashed k'+m\right)\slashed\epsilon'^{*}}{2p\!\cdot\!k'}\,u(p) $$

.

Step 8 (signs and symmetry factor). There is only a single fermion line and no closed loop. There are no external lines of identical fermions either (there is one electron incoming and one outgoing, and these are the two ends of the same single line). Nor are there any internal lines that could be interchanged with the external lines held fixed. Therefore the relative sign of the two diagrams is $+1$, and the symmetry factor is also $1$. The relative sign $(-1)$ of Section D.5.3 concerns only diagrams related by interchanging external lines of identical fermions, and does not apply here.

Step 9 (reading off the result). The sum of the two diagrams is $-\ii\mathcal{M}$:

$$ -\ii\mathcal{M}=-\ii g_e^2\,\bar u(p')\left[ \frac{\slashed\epsilon'^{*}\left(\slashed p+\slashed k+m\right)\slashed\epsilon}{2p\!\cdot\!k} -\frac{\slashed\epsilon\left(\slashed p-\slashed k'+m\right)\slashed\epsilon'^{*}}{2p\!\cdot\!k'}\right]u(p) $$

Dividing both sides by $-\ii$, we obtain

$$ \mathcal{M}=g_e^2\,\bar u(p')\left[ \frac{\slashed\epsilon'^{*}\left(\slashed p+\slashed k+m\right)\slashed\epsilon}{2p\!\cdot\!k} -\frac{\slashed\epsilon\left(\slashed p-\slashed k'+m\right)\slashed\epsilon'^{*}}{2p\!\cdot\!k'}\right]u(p) $$

This agrees with the formula in the hint of this book. We want to stress that the minus sign inside the bracket does not come from Fermi statistics; it comes only from the fact that the second denominator was $-2p\!\cdot\!k'$.

On the order of the factors. That $\slashed\epsilon'^{*}$ is on the left and $\slashed\epsilon$ on the right is because in Diagram 1 the absorption comes first (right) and the emission afterward (left). In Diagram 2 the order is reversed. Since the $\gamma$ matrices do not commute with one another, this order must not be interchanged.

(2) We apply the same procedure to $e^+e^-\to\gamma\gamma$. From Table D.1, the external-line factors are $u(p_1)$ for the incoming $e^-(p_1)$, $\bar v(p_2)$ for the incoming $e^+(p_2)$, and $\epsilon^{*}_3,\epsilon^{*}_4$ for the two outgoing photons. As in Example (4) of Section D.2.4 of this book, the fermion line is the single line $\bar v(p_2)\cdots u(p_1)$, onto which the two photons attach. Again there are two orderings of attachment, so there are two diagrams.

We follow the line against the arrow starting from $u(p_1)$ at the right end. In Diagram A, photon 3 is emitted first (internal line $p_1-p_3$), and then photon 4 is emitted:

$$ \bar v(p_2)\left(\ii g_e\slashed\epsilon_4^{*}\right) \frac{\ii\left(\slashed p_1-\slashed p_3+m\right)}{(p_1-p_3)^2-m^2} \left(\ii g_e\slashed\epsilon_3^{*}\right)u(p_1) =-\ii g_e^2\,\bar v(p_2)\frac{\slashed\epsilon_4^{*}\left(\slashed p_1-\slashed p_3+m\right)\slashed\epsilon_3^{*}}{(p_1-p_3)^2-m^2}u(p_1) $$

Diagram B is obtained by interchanging $3\leftrightarrow4$, and its internal line is $p_1-p_4$. Since the two particles in the final state are bosons, the relative sign $(-1)$ of Section D.5.3 does not appear, and the two diagrams are added with the same sign. Hence

$$ \mathcal{M}=g_e^2\,\bar v(p_2)\left[ \frac{\slashed\epsilon_4^{*}\left(\slashed p_1-\slashed p_3+m\right)\slashed\epsilon_3^{*}}{(p_1-p_3)^2-m^2} +\frac{\slashed\epsilon_3^{*}\left(\slashed p_1-\slashed p_4+m\right)\slashed\epsilon_4^{*}}{(p_1-p_4)^2-m^2}\right]u(p_1) $$

The denominators can be written, in the same way as in (1), as $(p_1-p_3)^2-m^2=-2p_1\!\cdot\!p_3$ and $(p_1-p_4)^2-m^2=-2p_1\!\cdot\!p_4$, so factoring out the minus sign, we can also write

$$ \mathcal{M}=-g_e^2\,\bar v(p_2)\left[ \frac{\slashed\epsilon_4^{*}\left(\slashed p_1-\slashed p_3+m\right)\slashed\epsilon_3^{*}}{2p_1\!\cdot\!p_3} +\frac{\slashed\epsilon_3^{*}\left(\slashed p_1-\slashed p_4+m\right)\slashed\epsilon_4^{*}}{2p_1\!\cdot\!p_4}\right]u(p_1) $$

.

Checking the symmetry. The exchange $3\leftrightarrow4$ means relabeling the indices as $p_3\leftrightarrow p_4$ and $\epsilon_3\leftrightarrow\epsilon_4$. Under this operation the first term goes into the second and the second into the first. Since a sum does not depend on the order of its terms, the whole of $\mathcal{M}$ is invariant, that is, symmetric under $3\leftrightarrow4$. This is the Bose symmetry required of a final state of two identical bosons, and it is none other than check item 7 of Table D.8 in Section D.6.5 of this book.

The Compton scattering of (1) and the pair annihilation of (2) are in fact the same amplitude connected by crossing (Section D.6.3 of this book). One only has to pass the incoming photon $k$ to the outgoing photon $p_3$ and the outgoing electron $p'$ to the incoming positron $p_2$. Indeed, in the answer to (2), both the structure of the numerators containing $m$ and the form of the denominators are of the same type as in (1).

(3) The external lines of Compton scattering are two photons and two electrons, so $n=4$. Therefore, by the theorem of Section D.6.1 of this book, $[\mathcal{M}]=4-4=0$, that is, it must be dimensionless. Let us actually count. From Table D.7:

  • $[g_e^2]=0$ (a renormalizable coupling is dimensionless)
  • $[\bar u]=[u]=\tfrac12$, together $\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1$
  • $[\epsilon_\mu]=[\epsilon^{*}_\mu]=0$ (from the normalization $\epsilon^{*}\!\cdot\!\epsilon=-1$)
  • The numerator of the propagator, $[\slashed p+\slashed k+m]=1$ (momentum and mass both have dimension $1$)
  • The denominator of the propagator, $[2p\!\cdot\!k]=2$, so its contribution is $-2$

Adding up, $0+1+0+1-2=0$. This agrees with $[\mathcal{M}]=0$, and the check is passed.

Verification. Besides dimensions, we can check using the Ward identity of Section D.6.2 of this book. Replacing the polarization of the incoming photon by $\epsilon_\mu\to k_\mu$, we decompose $\slashed k=(\slashed p+\slashed k-m)-(\slashed p-m)$, and use the following: on the right, $(\slashed p-m)u(p)=0$ (the Dirac equation), and on the left, $(\slashed p+\slashed k-m)$ pairs with the numerator $(\slashed p+\slashed k+m)$ of the first term to cancel the denominator $2p\!\cdot\!k$. In the second term, $\slashed k$ comes at the left end adjacent to $\bar u(p')$, so from momentum conservation $k=p'+k'-p$ and $\bar u(p')(\slashed p'-m)=0$ we rewrite $\bar u(p')\slashed k=-\bar u(p')(\slashed p-\slashed k'-m)$, and this pairs with the numerator $(\slashed p-\slashed k'+m)$ to cancel the denominator $-2p\!\cdot\!k'$. In this way the contributions of the two diagrams cancel exactly, giving $k_\mu\mathcal{M}^\mu=0$. If even one diagram were dropped this would be violated, so this is a check that “no diagram has been left out.” In addition, that the power of the coupling constant $g_e^2$ is consistent with two vertices (item 2 of Table D.8), and that the amplitude of (2) is symmetric under $3\leftrightarrow4$ (item 7), are each independent checks.

Meaning. The Compton amplitude assembled here becomes the Klein–Nishina formula itself when the spin sums are taken and $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2$ is formed. In the low-energy limit $\omega\ll m$ it reduces to the Thomson scattering cross section $\sigma_T=8\pi\alpha^2/3m^2=0.665\ \mathrm{barn}$, which is an instance of the check in Section D.6.4 of this book that “the nonrelativistic limit reduces to the known result.” From the materials-science side, Compton scattering is not merely a particle-physics process but a means of measuring the electron momentum distribution. When high-energy X-rays are directed at a sample and the energy width of the scattered photons is measured, one obtains the momentum distribution of the recoil electrons, $J(p_z)=\iint n(\bm p)\,\dd p_x\dd p_y$ (the Compton profile), from which the Fermi surface and the anisotropy of bonding can be read off. That the electron momentum $p$ enters the denominator $2p\!\cdot\!k$ of (1) is precisely the origin of this sensitivity. It is a fine example of an amplitude written with the Feynman rules serving directly as the analysis formula of a synchrotron-radiation experiment.

Exercise D.2: Checking the Higgs decay width by dimensional analysis

Problem (restated)

Consider the decay of the Higgs into a fermion pair, $H\to f\bar f$.

(1) From $[\mathcal{M}]=4-n$, find the mass dimension of the amplitude of this process. Also count the dimension directly from the Yukawa vertex $-\ii m_f/v$ and the spinor bilinear $\bar u v$, and confirm that the two agree.

(2) Check the mass dimensions of both sides of the decay-width formula

$$ \Gamma\left(H\to f\bar f\right)=\frac{N_c\,m_H\,m_f^2}{8\pi v^2}\,\beta_f^3, \qquad \beta_f=\sqrt{1-\frac{4m_f^2}{m_H^2}} $$

($N_c$ is $3$ for quarks and $1$ for leptons).

(3) With $m_H=125.25\ \mathrm{GeV}$, $v=246.2\ \mathrm{GeV}$, $m_b=4.18\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and $N_c=3$, find $\Gamma(H\to b\bar b)$ in MeV. Also, with $m_\tau=1.77686\ \mathrm{GeV}$ and $N_c=1$, find $\Gamma(H\to\tau^+\tau^-)$, and confirm that the ratio $\Gamma_{bb}/\Gamma_{\tau\tau}$ equals $N_c(m_b/m_\tau)^2$.

Solution

Strategy. Parts (1) and (2) need only Table D.7 in Section D.6.1 of this book and the theorem $[\mathcal{M}]=4-n$. Part (3) is a job for a calculator, but it helps to see in formulas, before putting in numbers, that the final ratio is exactly $N_c(m_b/m_\tau)^2$ up to the difference in $\beta^3$.

(1) There is one external line for $H$, one for $f$, and one for $\bar f$, so $n=3$. Therefore

$$ [\mathcal{M}]=4-n=4-3=1 $$

that is, $\mathcal{M}$ has the dimension of mass. This is in contrast to $2\to2$ scattering ($n=4$), where it was dimensionless.

Next, we count from the side assembled with the Feynman rules. There is only one diagram. The external-line factors are $1$ for the scalar $H$ (Section D.2.1 of this book), $\bar u(p_1)$ for the outgoing fermion, and $v(p_2)$ for the outgoing antifermion. The vertex is the Yukawa vertex $-\ii m_f/v$ of Section D.4.5 of this book (no $\gamma$ matrix is attached). There are no internal lines, hence no propagators. Therefore

$$ -\ii\mathcal{M}=\left(-\ii\frac{m_f}{v}\right)\bar u(p_1)v(p_2) \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad \mathcal{M}=\frac{m_f}{v}\,\bar u(p_1)\,v(p_2) $$

As for dimensions, $[m_f/v]=1-1=0$ (a ratio of masses, hence dimensionless) and $[\bar u\,v]=\tfrac12+\tfrac12=1$ (in Table D.7 the dimension of a spinor is $1/2$). The total is $0+1=1$, which agrees with $[\mathcal{M}]=1$.

Note that it is no accident that the Yukawa coupling is dimensionless here. As stated in the second-to-last row of Table D.7, all coupling constants of a renormalizable theory are dimensionless. Counting the dimensions of $\Lag\supset-(m_f/v)H\bar\psi\psi$ gives $1\times1+\tfrac32+\tfrac32=4$, which indeed satisfies $[\Lag]=4$.

(2) The left-hand side is a decay rate, and since $\Gamma=1/\tau$ ($\tau$ is the lifetime, $[\tau]=-1$), we have $[\Gamma]=1$. Now we count the right-hand side.

$$ \left[\frac{N_c\,m_H\,m_f^2}{8\pi v^2}\beta_f^3\right] =\underbrace{0}_{N_c}+\underbrace{1}_{m_H}+\underbrace{2}_{m_f^2}-\underbrace{2}_{v^2}+\underbrace{0}_{\beta^3} =1 $$

The factor $8\pi$ is dimensionless, and $\beta_f$ is the square root of a mass ratio and hence dimensionless. Both sides equal $1$, so they agree.

In the same way as in example (3) of Section D.6.1 of this book, we also check from the side of the decay-rate formula of Appendix B. For a $1\to2$ decay,

$$ \Gamma=\frac{S\abs{\bm p}}{8\pi m^2}\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2 \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad [\Gamma]=1-2+2\times1=1 $$

(with $[\abs{\bm p}]=1$, $[m^2]=2$, $[\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2]=2[\mathcal{M}]=2$). This also gives $1$, consistent with $[\mathcal{M}]=1$ found in (1).

(3) We put in numbers. First we prepare the common ingredients.

$$ m_H^2=125.25^2=15687.5625\ \mathrm{GeV^2}, \qquad v^2=246.2^2=60614.44\ \mathrm{GeV^2} $$ $$ 8\pi v^2=25.13274\times60614.44=1.5234070\times10^{6}\ \mathrm{GeV^2} $$

The $b$ quark case. We have $m_b^2=4.18^2=17.4724\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$.

$$ \beta_b^2=1-\frac{4m_b^2}{m_H^2}=1-\frac{4\times17.4724}{15687.5625} =1-\frac{69.8896}{15687.5625}=1-0.0044551=0.9955449 $$ $$ \beta_b=\sqrt{0.9955449}=0.997770, \qquad \beta_b^3=0.9933248 $$

The prefactor without $\beta^3$ is

$$ \frac{N_c\,m_H\,m_b^2}{8\pi v^2} =\frac{3\times125.25\times17.4724}{1.5234070\times10^{6}} =\frac{6565.254}{1.5234070\times10^{6}} =4.30959\times10^{-3}\ \mathrm{GeV} =4.3096\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

Multiplying by $\beta_b^3$ gives

$$ \Gamma\left(H\to b\bar b\right)=4.3096\times0.9933248=4.2808\ \mathrm{MeV}\simeq4.28\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The $\tau$ lepton case. We have $m_\tau^2=1.77686^2=3.157231\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$.

$$ \beta_\tau^2=1-\frac{4\times3.157231}{15687.5625}=1-\frac{12.628926}{15687.5625} =1-8.05028\times10^{-4}=0.99919497 $$ $$ \beta_\tau=0.99959740,\qquad \beta_\tau^3=0.9987927 $$ $$ \frac{N_c\,m_H\,m_\tau^2}{8\pi v^2} =\frac{1\times125.25\times3.157231}{1.5234070\times10^{6}} =\frac{395.44318}{1.5234070\times10^{6}} =2.59578\times10^{-4}\ \mathrm{GeV}=0.259578\ \mathrm{MeV} $$ $$ \Gamma\left(H\to\tau^+\tau^-\right)=0.259578\times0.9987927=0.259265\ \mathrm{MeV}\simeq0.2593\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

Taking the ratio. Numerically,

$$ \frac{\Gamma_{bb}}{\Gamma_{\tau\tau}}=\frac{4.28082}{0.259265}=16.511 $$

On the other hand, the quantity asked about is

$$ N_c\left(\frac{m_b}{m_\tau}\right)^2=3\times\left(\frac{4.18}{1.77686}\right)^2 =3\times\left(2.3524645\right)^2=3\times5.534089=16.602 $$

If we form the ratio from the formula, the common factor $m_H/(8\pi v^2)$ cancels completely, giving

$$ \frac{\Gamma_{bb}}{\Gamma_{\tau\tau}} =\frac{N_c^{(b)}m_b^2\,\beta_b^3}{N_c^{(\tau)}m_\tau^2\,\beta_\tau^3} =N_c\left(\frac{m_b}{m_\tau}\right)^2\times\left(\frac{\beta_b}{\beta_\tau}\right)^3 $$

That is, the two differ only by the factor $(\beta_b/\beta_\tau)^3$. Indeed,

$$ \left(\frac{\beta_b}{\beta_\tau}\right)^3=\frac{0.9933248}{0.9987927}=0.994525, \qquad \frac{16.511}{16.602}=0.994525 $$

and the two agree to six decimal places. Therefore the statement “the ratio equals $N_c(m_b/m_\tau)^2$” holds exactly in the limit $\beta\to1$, and for the actual values the ratio is smaller by $0.55\ \%$. This is because the heavier $b$ quark feels the phase-space suppression $\beta^3$ more strongly.

Verification. We verify the given decay-width formula itself by deriving it from the amplitude written in (1). We sum $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2$ over the final-state spins (since $H$ has spin 0, no averaging over the initial state is needed). Using the same Casimir’s trick as in Section D.7.3 of this book, we obtain

$$ \sum_{\rm spins}\abs{\bar u(p_1)v(p_2)}^2 =\Tr\left[\left(\slashed p_1+m_f\right)\left(\slashed p_2-m_f\right)\right] =4\left(p_1\!\cdot\!p_2-m_f^2\right) $$

(terms with an odd number of $\gamma$ matrices drop out). From $m_H^2=(p_1+p_2)^2=2m_f^2+2p_1\!\cdot\!p_2$ we have $p_1\!\cdot\!p_2=(m_H^2-2m_f^2)/2$, so

$$ 4\left(p_1\!\cdot\!p_2-m_f^2\right)=2m_H^2-8m_f^2=2m_H^2\left(1-\frac{4m_f^2}{m_H^2}\right)=2m_H^2\beta_f^2 $$

Multiplying by the color sum $N_c$ gives $\sum\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2=N_c(m_f^2/v^2)\,2m_H^2\beta_f^2$. The final-state momentum is $\abs{\bm p}=(m_H/2)\beta_f$, and since the particles are not identical, the statistical factor is $S=1$. Inserting these into the formula of Appendix B gives

$$ \Gamma=\frac{\abs{\bm p}}{8\pi m_H^2}\sum\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2 =\frac{m_H\beta_f/2}{8\pi m_H^2}\cdot N_c\frac{m_f^2}{v^2}2m_H^2\beta_f^2 =\frac{N_c\,m_H\,m_f^2}{8\pi v^2}\,\beta_f^3 $$

and the formula in the problem statement is reproduced. The breakdown of the cube in $\beta^3$ also becomes visible: one power comes from the final-state momentum $\abs{\bm p}\propto\beta$, and the remaining two come from the $\beta^2$ in the squared amplitude. The latter reflects the fact that the scalar coupling $\bar u v$ behaves like a $P$ wave (to form a final state with $J^{PC}=0^{++}$, one unit of orbital angular momentum is needed). Recomputing the numbers along this route also gives $\Gamma_{bb}=4.2808\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

Meaning. The single fact that the Yukawa coupling is proportional to mass fixes the ranking of the Higgs decay channels. At $m_H=125\ \mathrm{GeV}$ the $t\bar t$ channel is not open, so the $b$ quark, the heaviest of the open fermions, takes the leading role, and indeed $\mathrm{BR}(H\to b\bar b)\simeq58\ \%$. The $4.28\ \mathrm{MeV}$ obtained here is a tree-level value that uses the $\overline{\rm MS}$ mass $\overline m_b(\overline m_b)=4.18\ \mathrm{GeV}$ for $m_b$ (the pole mass is $4.78\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and $4.18$ is not the pole mass), and to compare with measurement one must replace $m_b$ by the running mass at the $m_H$ scale, $\overline{m}_b(m_H)\simeq2.79\ \mathrm{GeV}$. Then $\Gamma_{bb}\simeq1.9\ \mathrm{MeV}$, which, with QCD corrections added, approaches $\simeq2.4\ \mathrm{MeV}$. The lesson of Section D.7.6 of this book, “tree level gives the order of magnitude and the ratios,” applies here as well. As for the ratio $\Gamma_{bb}/\Gamma_{\tau\tau}$, the $3$ of $N_c$ remains even when the running mass is substituted. The color degrees of freedom survive in the ratio, and this is the same argument as for the $R$ ratio in Exercise D.6. As a connection to materials science, the Higgs boson plays the same role as the amplitude mode (Higgs mode) of the superconducting order parameter, and the fact that $H\to f\bar f$ is $\propto m_f^2$ corresponds to the fact that the strength with which the amplitude mode decays into quasiparticle pairs is proportional to the square of the gap $\Delta$. The amplitude mode observed in Raman scattering in NbSe$_2$ and charge-density-wave systems is precisely the condensed-matter version of this structure.

Exercise D.3: From the closed fermion loop to Thomas–Fermi screening

Problem (restated)

(1) Using the loop-number formula $L=I-V+1$, find the number of loops of the following diagrams: (a) the tree diagram of $e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-$, (b) the electron self-energy (one loop), (c) the photon self-energy (one loop), (d) the two-loop electron self-energy ($V=4$, $I=5$).

(2) Using the rules of Section D.5.2, write down the photon self-energy $\ii\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q)$. Do not forget the leading $(-1)$ and the trace.

(3) Show that the static, long-wavelength limit of the Lindhard function is $\chi_0(\bm q\to0,0)=-N(\varepsilon_F)$ ($N$ is the density of states per unit volume, including both spins).

(4) For the free electron gas, use $N(\varepsilon_F)=3n/2\varepsilon_F$ to calculate the Thomas–Fermi screening wavenumber $k_{\rm TF}^2=4\pi e^2N(\varepsilon_F)$ (Gaussian units) for copper. You may use $k_F=1.36\ \mathrm{\AA^{-1}}$ and $a_0=0.529\ \mathrm{\AA}$ (it can be rewritten as $k_{\rm TF}^2=4k_F/\pi a_0$). Find the screening length $1/k_{\rm TF}$ in $\mathrm{\AA}$ and compare it with the interatomic distance $2.56\ \mathrm{\AA}$.

Solution

Strategy. Part (1) is a counting exercise that simply applies the derivation of the loop-number formula in Section D.5.1 of this book. Part (2) is an application of the rules of Section D.5.2 of this book. Part (3) is a limiting procedure on the Lindhard function placed in the “Connection to Materials Science” of Section D.5 of this book, using the fact that the numerator and denominator both vanish at first order in $\bm q$. Part (4) merely turns the elementary formulas for a free electron gas into numbers, but at the end we check it against the measured values for copper.

(1) The formula is $L=I-V+1$, and the external lines $E$ do not enter. When counting internal lines $I$, note that fermion internal lines and boson internal lines are counted equally as one line each.

(a) The tree diagram of $e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-$ (Figure D.8 of this book): the only internal line is one virtual photon, so $I=1$, and there are two vertices, left and right, so $V=2$. Therefore

$$ L=1-2+1=0 $$

There is no loop; that is, it is a tree. As we saw in Section D.7.2 of this book, the $q$ integral was eaten by the first $\delta^4$ and did not remain. The formula restates that fact in terms of counting.

(b) The electron self-energy (one loop): this is the diagram in which an electron emits a photon and reabsorbs it. The internal lines are one electron and one photon, so $I=2$, and the vertices are emission and absorption, so $V=2$. Therefore

$$ L=2-2+1=1 $$

(c) The photon self-energy (vacuum polarization, one loop): this is the diagram in which a photon creates an $e^+e^-$ pair and disappears. There are two fermion internal lines forming the loop, so $I=2$, and $V=2$. Therefore

$$ L=2-2+1=1 $$

(d) The two-loop electron self-energy ($V=4$, $I=5$):

$$ L=5-4+1=2 $$

In every case the result agrees with “the number of rings counted by looking at the picture.”

Check by counting. In QED, exactly three line ends meet at every vertex (two fermion lines and one photon line). An internal line has both ends at vertices and so supplies two ends, and an external line supplies one end. Therefore

$$ 3V=2I+E $$

holds identically. We use this to examine the four cases above. (a) $3\times2=6$, $2\times1+4=6$. (b) $3\times2=6$, $2\times2+2=6$. (c) $3\times2=6$, $2\times2+2=6$. (d) $3\times4=12$, $2\times5+2=12$. All of them match. If one miscounts $I$ and $V$ independently, this relation is the first thing to fail, so it serves as a practical check. Incidentally, substituting $I=(3V-E)/2$ into $L=I-V+1$ gives $L=(V-E+2)/2$, which shows that, for a fixed number $E$ of external lines, each increase of the number of vertices by two adds one loop. This is a convenient feature of QED: the order of perturbation theory is directly the order of the loop expansion.

(2) Following the rules of Section D.5.2 of this book, we attach the factors to the diagram (c). Let the momentum of one internal fermion line be $k$ and that of the other $k+q$ (momentum conservation at the vertices). The rules are: (i) a factor $(-1)$ for each closed fermion loop, (ii) the trace of the product of $4\times4$ matrices arranged along the loop, (iii) $\int\dd^4k/(2\pi)^4$ over the remaining free momentum (there are $L=1$ of them). The vertices are $\ii g_e\gamma^\mu$ and $\ii g_e\gamma^\nu$, and the propagators are $\ii(\slashed k+m)/(k^2-m^2)$ and $\ii(\slashed k+\slashed q+m)/((k+q)^2-m^2)$. Therefore

$$ \ii\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q)=(-1)\int\frac{\dd^4k}{(2\pi)^4} \Tr\!\left[\left(\ii g_e\gamma^\mu\right)\frac{\ii\left(\slashed k+m\right)}{k^2-m^2} \left(\ii g_e\gamma^\nu\right)\frac{\ii\left(\slashed k+\slashed q+m\right)}{(k+q)^2-m^2}\right] $$

Counting the imaginary units, $\ii\times\ii\times\ii\times\ii=\ii^4=+1$, so pulling the coefficient out front we can write

$$ \ii\Pi^{\mu\nu}(q)=-g_e^2\int\frac{\dd^4k}{(2\pi)^4} \frac{\Tr\!\left[\gamma^\mu\left(\slashed k+m\right)\gamma^\nu\left(\slashed k+\slashed q+m\right)\right]} {\left(k^2-m^2\right)\left[(k+q)^2-m^2\right]} $$

The trace appears because the two ends of the loop are connected and the spinor indices close up ($\sum_a M_{aa}=\Tr M$), and the $(-1)$ is the sign of an odd permutation arising when the fermion operators are rearranged into a ring in Wick contraction.

This integral is ultraviolet divergent, but the Ward identity $q_\mu\Pi^{\mu\nu}=0$ of Section D.6.2 of this book requires the transverse form $\Pi^{\mu\nu}=(q^2g^{\mu\nu}-q^\mu q^\nu)\Pi(q^2)$, and the divergence is pushed into the constant part of $\Pi(q^2)$ and absorbed in the renormalization of the charge. The remaining $q^2$-dependent part gives the running coupling constant $\alpha_{\rm eff}(q^2)=\alpha/[1-\Pi(q^2)]$ in the example of Section D.5.2 of this book.

(3) The Lindhard function obtained in the “Connection to Materials Science” of Section D.5 of this book is

$$ \chi_0(\bm q,\omega)=2\sum_{\bm k} \frac{f(\varepsilon_{\bm k})-f(\varepsilon_{\bm k+\bm q})}{\omega-\left(\varepsilon_{\bm k+\bm q}-\varepsilon_{\bm k}\right)+\ii\eta} $$

(where $\sum_{\bm k}$ is per unit volume, that is, it means $\int\dd^3k/(2\pi)^3$; the leading $2$ comes from the spin trace).

Step 1: The static limit. Set $\omega=0$.

$$ \chi_0(\bm q,0)=2\sum_{\bm k}\frac{f(\varepsilon_{\bm k})-f(\varepsilon_{\bm k+\bm q})}{-\left(\varepsilon_{\bm k+\bm q}-\varepsilon_{\bm k}\right)+\ii\eta} $$

Step 2: Expand the numerator and denominator simultaneously in the long-wavelength limit. As $\bm q\to0$, both the denominator and the numerator vanish at first order in $\bm q$. So we expand both to first order. The energy is

$$ \varepsilon_{\bm k+\bm q}-\varepsilon_{\bm k}\simeq \bm q\cdot\nabla_{\bm k}\varepsilon_{\bm k}\equiv\bm q\cdot\bm v_{\bm k} $$

($\bm v_{\bm k}$ is the group velocity), and the difference of the distribution functions, by the chain rule, is

$$ f(\varepsilon_{\bm k})-f(\varepsilon_{\bm k+\bm q}) \simeq-\bm q\cdot\nabla_{\bm k}f(\varepsilon_{\bm k}) =-\left(\bm q\cdot\bm v_{\bm k}\right)\frac{\partial f}{\partial\varepsilon} $$

Step 3: Cancel. Substituting both, $\bm q\cdot\bm v_{\bm k}$ cancels completely between numerator and denominator ($\ii\eta$ does not matter in this limit, because numerator and denominator are both real and have the same factor):

$$ \frac{-\left(\bm q\cdot\bm v_{\bm k}\right)\partial f/\partial\varepsilon}{-\left(\bm q\cdot\bm v_{\bm k}\right)} =\frac{\partial f}{\partial\varepsilon} $$

Therefore

$$ \chi_0(\bm q\to0,0)=2\sum_{\bm k}\frac{\partial f}{\partial\varepsilon}\bigg|_{\varepsilon=\varepsilon_{\bm k}} $$

Step 4: Take $T\to0$. The Fermi distribution $f(\varepsilon)=[\ee^{(\varepsilon-\mu)/k_BT}+1]^{-1}$ becomes a step function as $T\to0$, and its derivative is

$$ \frac{\partial f}{\partial\varepsilon}\;\longrightarrow\;-\delta\left(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_F\right) $$

(the minus sign appears because the step goes downward). Thus

$$ \chi_0(\bm q\to0,0)=-2\sum_{\bm k}\delta\left(\varepsilon_{\bm k}-\varepsilon_F\right)=-N(\varepsilon_F) $$

The last equality is exactly the definition of the density of states per unit volume including both spins, $N(\varepsilon)\equiv2\sum_{\bm k}\delta(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_{\bm k})$. This is what was to be shown.

The negative sign is meaningful. When a positive charge is placed, electrons gather there; that is, the response is in the direction that cancels the external field. This becomes screening in (4) below.

(4) First we verify the given rewriting. For a free electron gas,

$$ n=\frac{k_F^3}{3\pi^2},\qquad \varepsilon_F=\frac{\hbar^2k_F^2}{2m} $$

so the density of states is

$$ N(\varepsilon_F)=\frac{3n}{2\varepsilon_F} =\frac{3}{2}\cdot\frac{k_F^3}{3\pi^2}\cdot\frac{2m}{\hbar^2k_F^2} =\frac{m\,k_F}{\pi^2\hbar^2} $$

Substituting this gives

$$ k_{\rm TF}^2=4\pi e^2N(\varepsilon_F)=\frac{4\pi e^2\,m\,k_F}{\pi^2\hbar^2} =\frac{4e^2m\,k_F}{\pi\hbar^2} =\frac{4k_F}{\pi a_0} $$

In the last step we used the Bohr radius $a_0=\hbar^2/me^2$. The rewriting in the problem statement is obtained.

Numerical values. Insert $k_F=1.36\ \mathrm{\AA^{-1}}$ and $a_0=0.529\ \mathrm{\AA}$.

$$ k_{\rm TF}^2=\frac{4\times1.36}{\pi\times0.529}=\frac{5.44}{1.66190}=3.2734\ \mathrm{\AA^{-2}} $$ $$ k_{\rm TF}=\sqrt{3.2734}=1.8092\ \mathrm{\AA^{-1}} $$ $$ \frac{1}{k_{\rm TF}}=0.5527\ \mathrm{\AA} $$

Comparing with the interatomic distance,

$$ \frac{2.56\ \mathrm{\AA}}{0.5527\ \mathrm{\AA}}=4.63 $$

that is, the screening length is only about $1/4.6$ of the nearest-neighbor interatomic distance. In a metal, the Coulomb interaction is screened so strongly that it does not reach even the neighboring atom.

Verification. We check in three ways. First, the dimensions. In Gaussian units $[e^2]=$ energy $\times$ length and $[N(\varepsilon_F)]=1/($energy $\times$ volume$)$, so $[e^2N]=1/$length$^2$, which is indeed the dimension of $k_{\rm TF}^2$. Second, we check whether the actual values for copper are reproduced from $k_F$. We have $n=k_F^3/3\pi^2=1.36^3/(3\pi^2)=0.08496\ \mathrm{\AA^{-3}}=8.50\times10^{22}\ \mathrm{cm^{-3}}$, which agrees to within $0.3\ \%$ with $4/a^3=0.0847\ \mathrm{\AA^{-3}}$ for face-centered cubic copper (lattice constant $a=3.615\ \mathrm{\AA}$, four atoms per unit cell, one valence electron per atom). Also the nearest-neighbor distance is $a/\sqrt2=2.556\ \mathrm{\AA}$, which agrees with the $2.56\ \mathrm{\AA}$ in the problem statement. The Fermi energy is $\varepsilon_F=\hbar^2k_F^2/2m=3.810\times1.36^2=7.05\ \mathrm{eV}$, which agrees with the textbook value $7.00\ \mathrm{eV}$ for copper. Third, evaluating $4\pi e^2N(\varepsilon_F)$ directly with numbers gives the same result: with $e^2=14.400\ \mathrm{eV\,\AA}$ and $N(\varepsilon_F)=3n/2\varepsilon_F=3\times0.08496/(2\times7.047)=0.018084\ \mathrm{eV^{-1}\AA^{-3}}$, we get $4\pi\times14.400\times0.018084=3.272\ \mathrm{\AA^{-2}}$, which agrees with the $3.2734$ above to three digits.

Meaning. The closed fermion loop of (2) is the Lindhard function of (3), and the RPA dielectric function $\epsilon(\bm q,0)=1+k_{\rm TF}^2/q^2$, obtained by summing it up with Dyson’s equation, gives the screened interaction $v_{\rm eff}(\bm q)=4\pi e^2/(q^2+k_{\rm TF}^2)$. This has the same form as the propagator of a massive vector particle in Section D.3 of this book, and in position space it becomes the Yukawa potential $\left(e^2/r\right)\ee^{-k_{\rm TF}r}$. That is, inside a metal the photon effectively acquires a mass $k_{\rm TF}=1.81\ \mathrm{\AA^{-1}}$ (about $3.6\ \mathrm{keV}$ when converted to natural units). On the particle-physics side, meanwhile, the weak interaction looked like a contact interaction because the $W$ boson has a mass of $80\ \mathrm{GeV}$ (Section D.3.4 of this book). The origins differ (one is the polarization of the Fermi sea, the other the vacuum expectation value of the Higgs field), but the formulas are exactly the same.

And what is decisive for the practice of materials science is the shortness of $1/k_{\rm TF}=0.55\ \mathrm{\AA}$. That the screening length is much shorter than the interatomic distance means that the influence of other electrons felt by a given electron is almost entirely contained within its own atom, and this is nothing other than the main reason why the one-body approximation (band calculations, the Kohn–Sham equations) works well. Conversely, in systems where the carrier density is low and $k_{\rm TF}$ is small (lightly doped semiconductors, dilute two-dimensional electron systems, the vicinity of Mott insulators), screening is ineffective, and many-body effects such as excitons, magnetic order, and charge order come to the fore. A single number, the screening length, draws the boundary of whether the one-body approximation can be used.

Exercise D.4: Using crossing symmetry

Problem (restated)

Consider the limit in which all masses are neglected. The Mandelstam variables are $s=(p_1+p_2)^2$, $t=(p_1-p_3)^2$, $u=(p_1-p_4)^2$, with $s+t+u=0$.

(1) In the invariant expression obtained in Section D.7.3 of this book, set $m_\mu\to0$ and rewrite the inner products in terms of the Mandelstam variables, and show that

$$ \braket{\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}_{e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-}=2g_e^4\,\frac{t^2+u^2}{s^2} $$

holds.

(2) Using crossing ($s\leftrightarrow t$), state that the spin-averaged squared amplitude of $e^-\mu^-\to e^-\mu^-$ is $2g_e^4(s^2+u^2)/t^2$, and explain that it diverges as $t\to0$ (forward scattering) and what the physical reason for this is.

(3) In the center-of-mass frame, use $t=-\tfrac{s}{2}(1-\cos\theta)$ and $u=-\tfrac{s}{2}(1+\cos\theta)$ to confirm that the result of (1) equals $g_e^4(1+\cos^2\theta)$. Find its value at $\theta=90^\circ$ in units of $g_e^4$.

Solution

Strategy. The starting point is the invariant expression obtained in Section D.7.3 of this book:

$$ \braket{\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}=\frac{8g_e^4}{s^2} \left[(p_1\!\cdot\!p_3)(p_2\!\cdot\!p_4)+(p_1\!\cdot\!p_4)(p_2\!\cdot\!p_3)+m_\mu^2\,(p_1\!\cdot\!p_2)\right] $$

Part (1) translates this into Mandelstam variables, part (2) applies the crossing theorem of Section D.6.3 of this book, and part (3) converts back to the angle. The metric is $g^{\mu\nu}=\mathrm{diag}(1,-1,-1,-1)$, and we use natural units.

(1) Step 1: Express the dot products in terms of Mandelstam variables. Setting all masses to zero gives $p_i^2=0$, so

$$ s=(p_1+p_2)^2=p_1^2+2p_1\!\cdot\!p_2+p_2^2=2\,p_1\!\cdot\!p_2 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_1\!\cdot\!p_2=\frac{s}{2} $$ $$ t=(p_1-p_3)^2=-2\,p_1\!\cdot\!p_3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_1\!\cdot\!p_3=-\frac{t}{2} $$ $$ u=(p_1-p_4)^2=-2\,p_1\!\cdot\!p_4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_1\!\cdot\!p_4=-\frac{u}{2} $$

Step 2: Express the remaining dot products in the same variables. Using the total momentum conservation $p_1+p_2=p_3+p_4$, we have $p_1-p_3=p_4-p_2$, so

$$ t=(p_1-p_3)^2=(p_4-p_2)^2=-2\,p_2\!\cdot\!p_4 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_2\!\cdot\!p_4=-\frac{t}{2}=p_1\!\cdot\!p_3 $$

Similarly, from $p_1-p_4=p_3-p_2$,

$$ u=(p_3-p_2)^2=-2\,p_2\!\cdot\!p_3 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p_2\!\cdot\!p_3=-\frac{u}{2}=p_1\!\cdot\!p_4 $$

These two equalities, that is, “diagonally opposite dot products are equal,” are the reason the bracket below becomes a neat sum of squares.

Step 3: Substitute. Since $m_\mu\to0$, the third term drops out. The remainder is

$$ \left[\;\right]=(p_1\!\cdot\!p_3)(p_2\!\cdot\!p_4)+(p_1\!\cdot\!p_4)(p_2\!\cdot\!p_3) =\left(-\frac{t}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{t}{2}\right)+\left(-\frac{u}{2}\right)\left(-\frac{u}{2}\right) =\frac{t^2+u^2}{4} $$

Step 4: Assemble the result.

$$ \braket{\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}_{e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-} =\frac{8g_e^4}{s^2}\cdot\frac{t^2+u^2}{4} =2g_e^4\,\frac{t^2+u^2}{s^2} $$

This is what we wanted to show. The $s^2$ in the denominator is the square of the propagator $1/s$, and it marks this as an $s$-channel process.

(2) Crossing. The theorem of Section D.6.3 of this book says: when an external-line particle is moved to the other side, replace the particle by its antiparticle and the momentum by $p\to-p$ at the same time. In $e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-$, move the incoming $e^+(p_2)$ to the final state and the outgoing $\mu^-(p_3)$ to the initial state; the diagram that was $s$-channel then becomes, as it stands, the $t$-channel diagram of the elastic scattering $e^-\mu^+\to e^-\mu^+$ (Figure D.7 of this book). If instead we want to build $e^-\mu^-\to e^-\mu^-$, we move $e^+(p_2)$ and $\mu^+(p_4)$, and the replacement is then $s\to u$, $t\to s$, $u\to t$; but, as we shall see below, the numerator is symmetric under $s\leftrightarrow u$, so the final expression is the same, $2g_e^4(s^2+u^2)/t^2$. In terms of momenta, this amounts to reading $p_2\to-p_3$, $p_3\to-p_2$, so the Mandelstam variables become

$$ s=(p_1+p_2)^2\;\longrightarrow\;(p_1-p_3)^2=t, \qquad t=(p_1-p_3)^2\;\longrightarrow\;(p_1+p_2)^2=s $$

That is, they are interchanged as $s\leftrightarrow t$, while $u=(p_1-p_4)^2$ stays invariant ($s+t+u=0$ is also preserved by this interchange). Therefore, applying $s\leftrightarrow t$ to the result of (1), we immediately obtain

$$ \braket{\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}_{e^-\mu^-\to e^-\mu^-}=2g_e^4\,\frac{s^2+u^2}{t^2} $$

There is no need to redo the trace computation. This is exactly check item 5 of Table D.8 in Section D.6.5 of this book.

Note that the numerator $s^2+u^2$ of the expression obtained here is symmetric under $s\leftrightarrow u$. Depending on which way the external lines are moved (whether we build $e^-\mu^-\to e^-\mu^-$ or $e^-\mu^+\to e^-\mu^+$), the roles of $s$ and $u$ may be interchanged, but thanks to this symmetry the final expression is the same. This is why Section D.6.3 of this book can omit the details and simply write “$s\leftrightarrow t$.”

Divergence. The denominator is now $t^2$. In the center-of-mass frame we can write $t=-\tfrac{s}{2}(1-\cos\theta)=-2E^2(1-\cos\theta)=-4E^2\sin^2(\theta/2)$, so for $\theta\to0$ (forward scattering) $t\to0$ and $\braket{\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}\to\infty$. More concretely, from $s+t+u=0$ we get $u\to-s$ as $t\to0$, and the numerator bracket approaches $s^2+u^2\to2s^2$, so

$$ \braket{\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}\simeq\frac{4g_e^4s^2}{t^2}\propto\frac{1}{\sin^4(\theta/2)} $$

that is, exactly the same $1/\sin^4(\theta/2)$ divergence as in the Rutherford cross section (Section D.6.4 of this book).

Physical reason. $-t=Q^2$ is the square of the momentum transfer, and $t\to0$ means “scattering in which almost nothing happens,” in other words a very large impact parameter (scattering in which the particle grazes past from far away). Because the exchanged particle is a massless photon, the range of the force is infinite (Coulomb potential $\propto1/r$), and no matter how far away the particle passes, it is always deflected slightly. Hence there are arbitrarily many events that count as “scattered,” and the total cross section $\int\dd\Omega\,\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega$ diverges. The type of divergence is a power law (quadratic): since $\dd\sigma/\dd t\propto1/t^2$, we have $\int\dd t/t^2\propto1/\abs{t}_{\min}$; written in terms of the angle, $\int\theta\,\dd\theta/\theta^4\sim1/(2\theta_{\min}^2)$, which diverges like $1/\theta_{\min}^2$ as $\theta_{\min}\to0$ (a logarithmic divergence arises for the $1/\theta^2$ type, for example in the infrared divergence of soft photons). This is not a failure of the calculation; it is the correct consequence of a force of infinite range.

When the divergence is cut off. If the exchanged boson has a mass $m$, the denominator of the propagator becomes $t-m^2$ and stays finite even for $t\to0$. This corresponds to the range of the Yukawa potential $\ee^{-mr}/r$ being cut off at $1/m$. In matter, screening plays this role. As found in Exercise D.3, in a metal the factor becomes $1/(q^2+k_{\rm TF}^2)$, and $k_{\rm TF}=1.81\ \mathrm{\AA^{-1}}$ acts as an effective photon mass, so that the forward divergence levels off at $\abs{t}\lesssim k_{\rm TF}^2$. This is why the cross sections of electron diffraction and low-energy electron energy-loss spectroscopy are finite.

(3) Substitute the given expressions.

$$ t^2+u^2=\frac{s^2}{4}\left[(1-\cos\theta)^2+(1+\cos\theta)^2\right] $$

Expanding the bracket, the first-order terms in $\cos\theta$ cancel, giving

$$ (1-\cos\theta)^2+(1+\cos\theta)^2 =1-2\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta+1+2\cos\theta+\cos^2\theta =2\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right) $$

Therefore

$$ t^2+u^2=\frac{s^2}{4}\times2\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right)=\frac{s^2}{2}\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right) $$

Putting this into the result of (1),

$$ \braket{\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}=2g_e^4\cdot\frac{1}{s^2}\cdot\frac{s^2}{2}\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right) =g_e^4\left(1+\cos^2\theta\right) $$

This agrees with the result of converting the trace computation of Section D.7.3 of this book to the center-of-mass angle in Section D.7.4 (the case $\beta\to1$).

Value at $\theta=90^\circ$. Since $\cos90^\circ=0$, $1+\cos^2\theta=1$, that is,

$$ \braket{\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}\Big|_{\theta=90^\circ}=g_e^4 $$

Numerically, from $g_e=\sqrt{4\pi\alpha}=0.30282$ in Section D.4.1 of this book,

$$ g_e^2=0.091701,\qquad g_e^4=\left(0.091701\right)^2=8.409\times10^{-3} $$

that is, $\braket{\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}=8.41\times10^{-3}$ (dimensionless). Writing $g_e^4=(4\pi\alpha)^2=16\pi^2\alpha^2$ gives the same value: $16\times9.8696\times(1/137.036)^2=8.409\times10^{-3}$.

Verification. The result passes three independent checks. First, dimensions: $\braket{\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2}$ for a $2\to2$ process must be dimensionless. $t^2+u^2$ and $s^2$ both have mass dimension $4$, so their ratio is dimensionless, and $g_e^4$ is dimensionless too. Passed. Second, comparison at special angles: at $\theta=0$ we have $t=0$ and $u=-s$, so the expression in (1) gives $2g_e^4(0+s^2)/s^2=2g_e^4$, and the expression in (3) gives $g_e^4(1+1)=2g_e^4$. They agree. At $\theta=180^\circ$ as well, $t=-s$ and $u=0$ give $2g_e^4$ again. Third, non-negativity (item 8 of Table D.8): $2g_e^4(t^2+u^2)/s^2$ is manifestly non-negative, and $g_e^4(1+\cos^2\theta)$ lies between $g_e^4$ and $2g_e^4$. It satisfies the property that is only natural for the square of a probability. Furthermore, integrating the cross section $\dd\sigma/\dd\Omega=(\alpha^2/4s)(1+\cos^2\theta)$ of Section D.7.5 of this book over the solid angle gives $4\pi\alpha^2/3s$, and we can also confirm that the value at $\theta=90^\circ$ is exactly $3/4$ of the mean value ($1/(4/3)=0.75$).

Meaning. The point of this exercise is that one and the same function $2g_e^4(t^2+u^2)/s^2$ describes a completely different experiment merely by exchanging the roles of the variables. Seen in the $s$ channel, it is pair production at an $e^+e^-$ collider; seen in the $t$ channel, it is fixed-target elastic scattering. The amplitude of a field theory is connected as a single analytic function of $s,t,u$, and the physically accessible region is simply divided into three parts. This is a tool for reducing the amount of computation, and at the same time a strong test of the internal consistency of the theory.

The angular distribution $1+\cos^2\theta$ is a direct fingerprint of the fact that the exchanged particle is a spin-1 vector particle and that the coupling is vector-like (parity-conserving, $\gamma^\mu$ only). If the exchanged particle were a scalar, the distribution would be isotropic, and if a $V-A$ coupling were mixed in, a forward–backward asymmetry would arise (the $Z$ interference in Section D.7.6 of this book). Measuring the angular distribution is measuring the structure of the $\gamma$ matrices in the vertex factor. The same logic exists on the materials-science side. Reading off the symmetry of the interaction responsible for the scattering (nuclear or magnetic scattering, dipole or quadrupole) from the angular and polarization dependence of neutron scattering or X-ray scattering is exactly the same kind of inference, “guessing the form of the vertex from the shape of the distribution.” And the conclusion of (2), that the $t\to0$ divergence is cut off by screening, is nothing other than the same phenomenon as the Thomas–Fermi screening of Exercise D.3, viewed from the scattering side.

Exercise D.5: Obtaining the $Z$ boson decay width from the vertex factors

Problem (restated)

The partial decay width of the $Z$ can be written, using $c_V,c_A$ of Table D.4, as

$$ \Gamma\left(Z\to f\bar f\right)=\frac{g_z^2\,m_Z}{48\pi}\left(c_V^2+c_A^2\right)N_c $$

(Chapter 12). Let $g_z=0.7446$ and $m_Z=91.188\ \mathrm{GeV}$.

(1) Find the common factor $g_z^2m_Z/48\pi$ in GeV.

(2) Find $\Gamma(Z\to e^+e^-)$ and $\Gamma(Z\to\nu\bar\nu)$ (per generation) in MeV, and compare them with the measured values $83.98\ \mathrm{MeV}$ and $\Gamma_{\rm inv}/3=166.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$.

(3) Add up all the channels (three charged leptons, three neutrinos, two up-type quarks ($u,c$; the $t$ is too heavy to be produced), and three down-type quarks ($d,s,b$)) to find $\Gamma_Z$, and compare it with the measured value $2.4952\ \mathrm{GeV}$. What is the main cause of the discrepancy?

Solution

Strategy. We use as they are the neutral-current vertex $-\ii(g_z/2)\gamma^\mu(c_V^f-c_A^f\gamma^5)$ of Section D.4.4 of this book and the resulting $c_V^2+c_A^2$ of Table D.4. In the calculation, we find the common factor just once, and then simply multiply by $(c_V^2+c_A^2)N_c$ for each channel and add. The final-state fermion masses are small compared with $m_Z$ and are neglected (even for the $b$, $m_b/m_Z=0.046$).

(1) We compute in order.

$$ g_z^2=0.7446^2=0.55442916 $$ $$ g_z^2\,m_Z=0.55442916\times91.188=50.5573\ \mathrm{GeV} $$ $$ 48\pi=48\times3.1415927=150.7964 $$ $$ \frac{g_z^2m_Z}{48\pi}=\frac{50.5573}{150.7964}=0.335268\ \mathrm{GeV}=335.27\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

That is, the common factor is $0.33527\ \mathrm{GeV}$. Below we denote it by $\Gamma_0$. We have $[\Gamma_0]=1$ (dimension of mass), which matches $[\Gamma]=1$ ($c_V,c_A,N_c$ are all dimensionless).

(The hint in this book gives $0.33528\ \mathrm{GeV}$. This is the value obtained by rounding the numerator to $50.558$, giving $50.558/150.796=0.335274$, and then rounding up at the last digit. Carried through without rounding, the value is $0.335268\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and the difference is only $0.004\ \%$, so it does not affect the conclusions below. From here on we use $0.335268$.)

(2) We use the rightmost column of Table D.4.

Electron. With $c_V^e=-1/2+2\times0.2312=-0.0376$ and $c_A^e=-1/2$,

$$ \left(c_V^e\right)^2+\left(c_A^e\right)^2=0.0376^2+0.5^2=0.001414+0.25=0.251414\simeq0.2514 $$

Since $N_c=1$ (leptons have no color),

$$ \Gamma\left(Z\to e^+e^-\right)=0.335268\times0.2514=0.084286\ \mathrm{GeV}=84.29\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The difference from the measured value $83.98\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is

$$ \frac{84.29-83.98}{83.98}=+0.37\ \% $$

Neutrino. Since $c_V^\nu=+1/2-2\times0\times0.2312=+0.5$ and $c_A^\nu=+1/2$, we have $c_V^2+c_A^2=0.25+0.25=0.5$ and $N_c=1$.

$$ \Gamma\left(Z\to\nu\bar\nu\right)=0.335268\times0.5=0.167634\ \mathrm{GeV}=167.63\ \mathrm{MeV} $$

The difference from the measured value (per generation) $166.3\ \mathrm{MeV}$ is

$$ \frac{167.63-166.3}{166.3}=+0.80\ \% $$

Both are within $1\ \%$. With only the tree-level vertex factors and the numbers in Table D.4, the partial widths of the $Z$ come out right to $1\ \%$ accuracy.

The neutrino width is about twice the electron width because $c_V^e$ is almost zero (the example in Section D.4.4 of this book). Taking the ratio gives $0.5/0.2514=1.989$, so $\Gamma_\nu\simeq2\Gamma_e$ holds.

(3) For each channel, multiply by $(c_V^2+c_A^2)N_c$ and add.

Charged leptons (three kinds, $e,\mu,\tau$, with $N_c=1$).

$$ 3\times0.335268\times0.2514=3\times0.084286=0.252859\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Neutrinos (three kinds, $N_c=1$).

$$ 3\times0.335268\times0.5=3\times0.167634=0.502902\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Up-type quarks (two kinds, $u,c$, with $N_c=3$ and $c_V^2+c_A^2=0.2868$).

$$ 2\times3\times0.335268\times0.2868=6\times0.096155=0.576930\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Down-type quarks (three kinds, $d,s,b$, with $N_c=3$ and $c_V^2+c_A^2=0.3696$).

$$ 3\times3\times0.335268\times0.3696=9\times0.1239152=1.115237\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Total.

$$ \Gamma_Z^{\rm tree}=0.252859+0.502902+0.576930+1.115237=2.44793\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

Compared with the measured value $2.4952\ \mathrm{GeV}$,

$$ \frac{2.44793-2.4952}{2.4952}=-1.89\ \% $$

that is, it is about $1.9\ \%$ too small.

Main cause of the discrepancy. It is the QCD correction to the hadronic final state (quark pairs). $Z\to q\bar q$ is accompanied by $Z\to q\bar q g$ (gluon emission) and so on, and at lowest order a factor $1+\alpha_s/\pi$ multiplies the width. Since $\alpha_s(m_Z)=0.118$,

$$ 1+\frac{\alpha_s}{\pi}=1+\frac{0.118}{3.14159}=1.03756 $$

The hadronic part is the sum of the up-type and down-type contributions,

$$ \Gamma_{\rm had}^{\rm tree}=0.576930+1.115237=1.692167\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

so after the correction it is $1.692167\times1.03756=1.755725\ \mathrm{GeV}$, and the total width becomes

$$ \Gamma_Z=0.252859+0.502902+1.755725=2.51149\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

The difference from the measured value is

$$ \frac{2.51149-2.4952}{2.4952}=+0.65\ \% $$

That is, the $1.9\ \%$ deviation shrinks to $0.7\ \%$. The remainder comes from higher-order electroweak corrections (vertex corrections, the top-quark-loop contribution to the $\rho$ parameter, and so on) and from the effect of the $b$-quark mass.

Verification. We perform three independent checks.

(i) Branching ratio. The hadronic branching ratio including the QCD correction is

$$ \frac{\Gamma_{\rm had}}{\Gamma_Z}=\frac{1.755725}{2.51149}=0.6991 $$

This agrees with the measured value $69.91\ \%$ to four digits. Even though the total width itself is off by $0.65\ \%$, the ratio agrees with high accuracy because the correction cancels between numerator and denominator; this is an example of the ratio being theoretically more robust.

(ii) Number of neutrino generations. We follow numerically the same argument as the example in Section D.4.4 of this book. Dividing the measured value $5.943$ of $\Gamma_{\rm inv}/\Gamma_{\ell\ell}$ by the theoretical per-generation ratio $\Gamma_\nu/\Gamma_e=0.5/0.2514=1.9889$ gives

$$ N_\nu=\frac{5.943}{1.9889}=2.988\simeq3 $$

Thus the fact that there are three generations of light neutrinos follows from $c_V,c_A$ of Table D.4 alone.

(iii) Rederivation from an independent normalization. Combining $g_z^2=g_w^2/\cos^2\theta_W$, $m_W=m_Z\cos\theta_W$, and $G_F/\sqrt2=g_w^2/8m_W^2$ (Table D.7) gives $g_z^2=4\sqrt2\,G_Fm_Z^2$, and the common factor can be rewritten as

$$ \frac{g_z^2m_Z}{48\pi}=\frac{G_F\,m_Z^3}{6\sqrt2\,\pi} =\frac{1.16638\times10^{-5}\times758251}{6\times1.41421\times3.14159}=0.33177\ \mathrm{GeV} $$

This agrees with the $0.33527\ \mathrm{GeV}$ obtained in (1) to $1.1\ \%$ (the difference arises because the three input values $g_w=0.6529$, $\sin^2\theta_W=0.2312$, and $G_F$ are not perfectly consistent with one another). Since the same order of magnitude comes out of completely different inputs, we have confirmed that the factor $48\pi$ is placed correctly.

Meaning. What this exercise shows is the fact that a single table of vertex factors yields experimental values to $1\ \%$. All that was needed were the three numbers $g_z$, $m_Z$, and $\sin^2\theta_W$; the rest was the algebra $c_V=T^3-2Q\sin^2\theta_W$, $c_A=T^3$ of Table D.4 and the color factor $N_c=3$. Group-theoretic labels, weak isospin and electric charge, are translated directly into the numerical values of the decay widths.

Moreover, the fact that the $1.9\ \%$ deviation is nearly explained by the QCD correction is itself quantitative evidence for the existence of the strong interaction. LEP used this argument in reverse, determining $\alpha_s(m_Z)$ from the precise measurement of $\Gamma_Z$. In addition, from the invisible width $\Gamma_{\rm inv}$ the number of neutrino generations $N_\nu=2.984\pm0.008$ was obtained (LEP 2006; the value after the Bhabha luminosity was reevaluated in 2020 is $2.9963\pm0.0074$), which fixed the backbone of the Standard Model: “there are only three kinds of light neutrinos.” Particles that cannot be seen directly in the detector were counted by subtraction from the total width that is seen. This method of counting the invisible from what is missing is used routinely in materials science as well. For example, deriving the density of states at the Fermi surface from the Sommerfeld coefficient of the specific heat, $\gamma=\pi^2k_B^2N(\varepsilon_F)/3$, comparing it with the value from a band calculation, and reading off the enhancement factor due to electron correlation (mass renormalization) from the difference is an inference with exactly the same structure.

Exercise D.6: The $R$ ratio—counting quark colors from cross sections

Problem (restated)

The process by which hadrons are produced in $e^+e^-$ collisions is, at lowest order, $e^+e^-\to q\bar q$. The diagram is identical to that of $e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-$, with the final-state muons simply replaced by quarks, so the ratio of the cross sections is determined solely by the ratio of the squares of the vertex factors.

(1) For a quark of charge $Q_q$, use the fact that the vertex factor is $-\ii g_eQ_q\gamma^\mu$ to derive

$$ R\equiv\frac{\sigma\left(e^+e^-\to\text{hadrons}\right)}{\sigma\left(e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-\right)}=N_c\sum_{q}Q_q^2 $$

(the sum is taken over the quarks that can be produced at that energy).

(2) With $N_c=3$, find the value of $R$ in the three regions (a) $\sqrt s<2m_c$ ($u,d,s$), (b) $2m_c<\sqrt s<2m_b$ ($u,d,s,c$), and (c) $\sqrt s>2m_b$ ($u,d,s,c,b$). What would happen if $N_c=1$?

(3) Find the hadron production cross section at $\sqrt s=10\ \mathrm{GeV}$ in nb (use $\sigma=86.9\ \mathrm{nb}/s[\mathrm{GeV^2}]$ from Section D.7.6 of this book).

Solution

Strategy. We reuse the calculation of $e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-$ carried through in Section D.7 of this book, replacing only the final state. Only two things change: (i) the charge factor $Q_q$ of the right-hand vertex, and (ii) the counting of the color degrees of freedom. The propagator, the external-line factors, and the phase space stay as they are. Therefore there is no need at all to redo the trace calculation.

(1) Step 1: Rewrite the amplitude. The amplitude obtained in Section D.7.2 of this book was

$$ \mathcal{M}_{\mu}=-\frac{g_e^2}{s}\left[\bar v(p_2)\gamma^\mu u(p_1)\right]\left[\bar u(p_3)\gamma_\mu v(p_4)\right] $$

Here the right-hand vertex is $\ii g_e\gamma^\nu$, that is, the form that has absorbed $Q_\mu=-1$. When the final state is replaced by quarks, the QED vertex $-\ii g_eQ_f\gamma^\mu$ of Section D.4.1 of this book turns only the right-hand vertex into $-\ii g_eQ_q\gamma^\nu\delta_{ij}$ (the $\delta_{ij}$ expresses that the photon carries no color and therefore does not change the color). The electron vertex on the left does not change, since $Q_e^2=1$. Therefore the amplitude for producing a quark and an antiquark of color $i$ is

$$ \mathcal{M}_{q,i}=\frac{Q_q}{Q_\mu}\,\mathcal{M}_{\mu}\big|_{m_\mu\to m_q} =-Q_q\,\mathcal{M}_{\mu}\big|_{m_\mu\to m_q} $$

(we used $Q_\mu=-1$). That is, the magnitude of the amplitude is merely multiplied by $\abs{Q_q}$, and the overall sign $-1$ disappears upon squaring in the next step.

Step 2: Square and count the colors. If the amplitude is multiplied by $Q_q$, then $\abs{\mathcal{M}}^2$ is multiplied by $Q_q^2$. Next we count the colors. The initial-state $e^+e^-$ carries no color, so there is no need to average over color (only the spins are averaged; the $1/4$ in Section D.7.3 of this book is exactly that). The final-state quark pair, on the other hand, consists of $N_c$ mutually distinguishable states $q_i\bar q_i$ ($i=1,\dots,N_c$), all of which have amplitudes of the same magnitude. Since we sum over the final state,

$$ \sum_{\rm colors}\abs{\mathcal{M}_{q}}^2=N_c\,Q_q^2\,\abs{\mathcal{M}_{\mu}}^2 $$

The crucial point is that, thanks to $\delta_{ij}$, only the $N_c$ combinations in which the quark and antiquark colors match survive, and the factor is not $N_c^2$.

Step 3: Convert to the cross section. In the region $\sqrt s\gg2m_q$ we have $\beta_q\to1$, and the phase-space factor is exactly the same as for $\mu^+\mu^-$. Therefore the total-cross-section formula of Section D.7.5 of this book can be used as it stands, giving

$$ \sigma\left(e^+e^-\to q_i\bar q_i\;\text{all colors}\right)=N_c\,Q_q^2\;\sigma\left(e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-\right) $$

Step 4: On to hadrons. Because of color confinement, the produced $q\bar q$ pair turns into hadrons with probability 1. Hadronization is a long-distance, slow process, occurring at $\Lambda_{\rm QCD}^{-1}\sim1\ \mathrm{fm}$, whereas pair production is a short-distance, fast process, occurring at $1/\sqrt s$; the two can therefore be separated, and hadronization does not change the total cross section (it only changes what is produced). Summing over all flavors that can be produced, we obtain

$$ \sigma\left(e^+e^-\to\text{hadrons}\right)=\sum_q N_cQ_q^2\;\sigma\left(e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-\right) $$

Dividing both sides by $\sigma(e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-)$, we obtain

$$ R=N_c\sum_q Q_q^2 $$

This is what was to be derived. Both $\alpha$ and $s$ have dropped out completely, and only the counting of charges and colors is left in $R$.

(2) From Section D.4.1 of this book, the quark charges are $Q_u=Q_c=Q_t=+2/3$ and $Q_d=Q_s=Q_b=-1/3$. Squaring gives $4/9$ and $1/9$.

(a) $\sqrt s<2m_c$ (three flavors, $u,d,s$):

$$ \sum Q_q^2=\frac49+\frac19+\frac19=\frac69=\frac23, \qquad R=3\times\frac23=2 $$

(b) $2m_c<\sqrt s<2m_b$ (four flavors, $u,d,s,c$): Since $c$ adds $4/9$,

$$ \sum Q_q^2=\frac69+\frac49=\frac{10}{9}, \qquad R=3\times\frac{10}{9}=\frac{10}{3}=3.33 $$

(c) $\sqrt s>2m_b$ (five flavors, $u,d,s,c,b$): Since $b$ adds $1/9$,

$$ \sum Q_q^2=\frac{10}{9}+\frac19=\frac{11}{9}, \qquad R=3\times\frac{11}{9}=\frac{11}{3}=3.67 $$

If $N_c=1$. The values are simply those above divided by $3$.

$$ R=\frac23=0.67,\qquad \frac{10}{9}=1.11,\qquad \frac{11}{9}=1.22 $$

The measured $R$ is higher than the tree-level value by a few $\%$, because of the QCD correction $1+\alpha_s/\pi+\cdots$, and is $\simeq2.2$, $\simeq3.5$, and $\simeq3.9$, respectively (consistent with the tree-level values $2$, $3.33$, and $3.67$). In contrast, $N_c=1$ is off by a factor of three and does not agree at all. Even $N_c=2$ gives $1.33,\,2.22,\,2.44$, which do not agree. The measured $R$ uniquely fixes $N_c$, a discrete integer, to be $3$.

(3) Since $\sqrt s=10\ \mathrm{GeV}$, we have $s=100\ \mathrm{GeV^2}$. From the result of Section D.7.6 of this book,

$$ \sigma\left(e^+e^-\to\mu^+\mu^-\right)=\frac{86.9\ \mathrm{nb}}{100}=0.869\ \mathrm{nb} $$

Multiplying by $R=11/3=3.667$ from (2)(c), we obtain

$$ \sigma_{\rm had}=3.667\times0.869=3.19\ \mathrm{nb} $$

.

A note on thresholds. We used $R=11/3$ here because the problem statement follows the division of (2)(c) ($\sqrt s>2m_b=8.36\ \mathrm{GeV}$, using the $\overline{\rm MS}$ mass $m_b=4.18\ \mathrm{GeV}$). In experiment, however, the true threshold for $b$ quarks to emerge continuously as hadrons is the threshold of the pair $B\bar B$ of the lightest open-bottom mesons, $2m_B=2\times5.279=10.56\ \mathrm{GeV}$. Since $\sqrt s=10\ \mathrm{GeV}$ lies below this, in reality $b\bar b$ appears only as the narrow resonances $\Upsilon$ (bottomonium), and the continuum $R$ stays at $10/3=3.33$ from $u,d,s,c$. Using this value, $\sigma_{\rm had}=3.33\times0.869=2.90\ \mathrm{nb}$. Multiplying further by the QCD correction $1+\alpha_s/\pi$ (which is $1.054$ for $\alpha_s(10\ \mathrm{GeV})\simeq0.17$), we get $R\simeq3.33\times1.054=3.51$ and $\sigma_{\rm had}\simeq3.51\times0.869=3.05\ \mathrm{nb}$, which corresponds to the value measured just below the $\Upsilon(4S)$ ($R\simeq3.5$). As a tree-level counting, $3.19\ \mathrm{nb}$ is the answer, but when comparing with experimental values we must remember that the “quark-mass threshold” and the “hadron threshold” are different things.

Verification. First, dimensions and orders of magnitude. $R$ is a ratio of cross sections and so must be dimensionless; the result of (1) consists only of a sum of squared charges and the integer $N_c$, and is indeed dimensionless. $\sigma_{\rm had}=3.19\ \mathrm{nb}$ is $3.7$ times $\sigma_{\mu\mu}=0.869\ \mathrm{nb}$, which is reasonable as an order of magnitude (item 10 of Table D.8).

Next we compare the values of $R$ with the staircase structure of experiment. As $\sqrt s$ is raised, the experimental $R$ goes from $\simeq2$ (below $3\ \mathrm{GeV}$) to $\simeq3.3$ ($5\sim9\ \mathrm{GeV}$) to $\simeq3.6$ (above the $B$ threshold), jumping in steps each time a new quark opens up. Looking at the size of the steps, it is $3\times4/9=1.33$ for $c$ and $3\times1/9=0.33$ for $b$, and the ratio is $4:1$, that is, exactly the ratio of squared charges $(2/3)^2:(1/3)^2$. The measured steps also have this ratio. $N_c$ sets the overall scale and $Q_q^2$ sets the size of the steps, so two independent pieces of information are verified at the same time.

One more thing to check is what we stated in Step 2 of (1), namely that “there are $N_c$ color possibilities, not $N_c^2$.” If the colors of $q$ and $\bar q$ could be chosen independently, $N_c$ ways each, the prefactor would be $N_c^2=9$ rather than $N_c=3$. That is, it would be three times the correct value, giving $R=9\times\tfrac23=6$, $9\times\tfrac{10}9=10$, and $9\times\tfrac{11}9=11$ in the three regions, which is off by a factor of three from the measured $2,\,3.3,\,3.6$. The fact that the photon vertex is color-diagonal ($\delta_{ij}$) correctly gives the factor $N_c$.

Meaning. The $R$ ratio is the clearest example in particle physics of counting becoming an observable directly. Although we measure a continuous quantity, a cross section, the answer that emerges is only discrete, group-theoretical information: “there are three colors” and “the charges are $2/3$ and $-1/3$.” Both $\alpha$ and $s$ cancel in the ratio, so the result is not contaminated by the details of the dynamics. The establishment of $R\simeq2$ ($N_c=3$) in the 1970s, together with the spin statistics of the $\Delta^{++}$ and the decay width of $\pi^0\to\gamma\gamma$, settled the existence of color charge.

This line of argument recurs in materials science as well, as a measurement that “counts the degeneracy.” For example, the coefficient of the linear term in the specific heat of a metal, $\gamma=\pi^2k_B^2N(\varepsilon_F)/3$, contains the spin degeneracy $2$ in the density of states as it is, and if one splits it by Zeeman splitting in a magnetic field and sees $\gamma$ divide into halves, one has counted the spin degrees of freedom. The same structure underlies the ratio of the Pauli paramagnetic susceptibility to the specific heat (the Wilson ratio $R_W=\pi^2k_B^2\chi/(3\mu_B^2\gamma)$), in which the mass renormalization $m^*/m$ cancels between numerator and denominator, leaving only information on the degeneracy and on spin correlations (such as the Landau parameter $F_0^a$) (in a Fermi liquid $R_W=1/(1+F_0^a)$, and in Kondo systems and heavy-electron systems it takes values around $2$. It is not that the result is “independent of the details of the interaction”; what cancels is the mass-renormalization part). By taking a ratio, we eliminate the dynamics and leave only the number of degrees of freedom—this one sentence sums up the lesson of the $R$ ratio.

References

  1. D. Griffiths, Introduction to Elementary Particles, 2nd rev. ed., Wiley-VCH (2008).—Many of the exercises in this book are adaptations of problems in that book, recast for materials science.
  2. Particle Data Group (R. L. Workman et al.), “Review of Particle Physics”, Prog. Theor. Exp. Phys. 2022, 083C01 (2022).—All numerical values are taken from here.
  3. F. Halzen, A. D. Martin, Quarks and Leptons, Wiley (1984).—For when you want to check the details of the calculation.
  4. M. E. Peskin, D. V. Schroeder, An Introduction to Quantum Field Theory, Westview (1995).
